Title: Improving Affordability and Accessibility of Modern Energy: Tax‐Cut or Direct Subsidy?
Authors: Jing Wang, Yanfei Lan, Hongyang Zou, Kuishuang Feng, Ying‐Ju Chen, Huibin Du
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management Beijing Jiaotong University Beijing China; College of Management and Economics Tianjin University Tianjin China; Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS) Tianjin University Tianjin China; Department of Geographical Sciences University of Maryland College Park Maryland USA; School of Business and Management (ISOM) The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Hong Kong China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Promoting off‐grid solar (OGS) products is a cost‐effective way to expand access to modern energy. However, limited purchasing power in energy‐deficit regions creates an affordability gap, leaving the households most in need unable to afford it. This paper investigates the effectiveness of two key policies for promoting OGS adoption: direct subsidies providing financial support to consumers and tax cuts reducing firms' tax burden. We employ a three‐echelon game model comprising a government, an OGS firm, and consumers with heterogeneous affordability to delineate the applicability conditions of the two policies and identify their underlying mechanisms. Our analysis reveals that both policies can expand OGS coverage and generate a win‐win‐win outcome for the government, the firm, and consumers. The optimal policy choice is jointly determined by both consumer affordability and the tax environment. Under high‐tax environments, the optimal policy shifts from subsidies to tax cuts as consumers' affordability improves; under low‐tax environments, subsidies can unlock latent demand even when intervention would otherwise be unnecessary. The core difference stems from their price pass‐through efficiency. Contrary to the intuition that subsidies act directly on consumers and therefore achieve full pass‐through, we show that tax cuts deliver complete pass‐through, while subsidies are partially captured by the firm through strategic price adjustments.

Title: Capacity investment with inventory: a path-dependent real options model under multi-factor demand process
Authors: Anna Maria Gambaro, Ioannis Kyriakou, Gianluca Fusai
Abstract: In this paper, we develop a stochastic optimization framework for production capacity planning that integrates inventory management and demand backlogging in a discrete-time, dynamic newsvendor-type setting. Our model explicitly accounts for both inventory storage and demand shortage, incorporates revenues and costs within the plant’s cash flow structure, and treats profit as a function of stochastic factors, including commodity prices and demand, with the latter evolving according to a Markov multi-factor process. We contribute to the literature in two key ways. First, we develop a joint capacity and inventory optimization problem to capture the dependence of inventory levels on both the system state and the time-weighted sum of values along the demand path. Second, to efficiently address the resulting path-dependence, we introduce a tree-based method. Subsequently, using empirically calibrated models, we evaluate profitability under different scenarios, with and without inventory management, for varying holding and backlog cost parameters. By recasting the joint problem as a real options model that depends on cumulative demand, we provide a unified and tractable framework that captures both the operational complexity and the financial flexibility involved in capacity investment decisions under uncertainty.

Title: The individual‐team discontinuity effect on institutional choices: Experimental evidence in voluntary public goods provision
Authors: Kenju Kamei, Katy Tabero
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics Keio University Minato‐ku Tokyo Japan; Department of Politics and International Relations University of Southampton Southampton UK
Abstract: Abstract A laboratory experiment finds that teams acting as a decision‐making unit through communication behave more efficiently than individuals. Decision‐making units vote on formal and informal sanctions in a repeated public goods dilemma. When a formal scheme is selected, teams vote for deterrent sanction rates more frequently than individuals. When an informal scheme is selected, teams inflict costly punishment more frequently toward low contributors. As such, teams sustain cooperation more efficaciously than individuals. The results underscore the effectiveness of utilizing teams as a decision‐making unit in organizations in combating moral hazard, such as free riding.

Title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
Authors: Kfir Eliaz, Ran Spiegler
Affiliations: Tel Aviv University and King's College London (email: ); Tel Aviv University and University College London (email: )
Abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

Title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
Authors: Suman Banerjee, Ravi Jagannathan, Kai Wang
Affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology (email: ); Northwestern University and NBER (email: ); Northwestern University (email: )
Abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

Title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
Authors: Yair Antler, Daniel Bird, Daniel Fershtman
Affiliations: Coller School of Management, Tel Aviv University, and CEPR (email: ); The Eitan Berglas School of Economics, Tel Aviv University (email: ); Tel Aviv University, Emory University, and CEPR (email: )
Abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

Title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
Authors: Arthur Campbell, C. Matthew Leister, Philip Ushchev, Yves Zenou
Affiliations: Monash University, Australia (email: ); ECARES, ULB, Belgium (email: ); Monash University, Australia, and CEPR (email: )
Abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

Title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
Authors: Daniel Quint, Fuhito Kojima
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Wisconsin-Madison (email: ); University of Tokyo (email: )
Abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

Title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
Authors: Joyee Deb, Jack Fanning
Affiliations: Department of Economics, New York University (email: ); Department of Economics, Brown University (email: )
Abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

Title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
Authors: Kun Zhang
Affiliations: Auburn University and University of Queensland (email: ).
Abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

Title: The Perils of Overreaction
Authors: Konstantin von Beringe, Mark Whitmeyer
Affiliations: Arizona State University (email: )
Abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

Title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
Authors: Roberto Brunetti, Carl Gaigné, Fabien Moizeau
Affiliations: LEMMA, Université Paris-Panthéon-Assas (email: ); INRAE, SMART, Rennes, France; Laval University, CREATE, Quebec, Canada; and CNRS-TEPP, France (email: ); Univ Rennes, CNRS, CREM-UMR6211, F-35000 Rennes, France (email: )
Abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

Title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
Authors: Marcos Y. Nakaguma, Danilo Souza
Affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics, FGV (email: ); University of Sao Paulo (email: )
Abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

Title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
Authors: Piotr Evdokimov, Umberto Garfagnini
Affiliations: University of Surrey (email: ).
Abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

Title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
Authors: Chen Cheng, Xiao Han, Xin Tong, Yusheng Wu, Yiqing Xing
Affiliations: School of Economics, Renmin University of China (email: ); School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China (email: ); Faculty of Business and Economics, the University of Hong Kong (email: ); Department of Mathematics, University of Southern California (email: ); China Center for Economic Research, NSD, Peking University (email: )
Abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

Title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
Authors: Maria Titova
Affiliations: Department of Economics, Vanderbilt University (email: )
Abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

Title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
Authors: Steven Callander, Nicolas S. Lambert, Niko Matouschek
Affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University (email: ); Department of Economics, University of Southern California (email: ); Kellogg School of Management, Northwestern University (email: )
Abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

Title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
Authors: Shanglyu Deng, Qiyao Zhou
Affiliations: Department of Economics, University of Macau (email: ); Department of Economics, Wilfrid Laurier University (email: )
Abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

Title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
Authors: Tat-How Teh, Julian Wright
Affiliations: Division of Economics, Nanyang Technological University (email: ); Department of Economics, National University of Singapore (email: )
Abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

Title: The Effect of a Miscarriage Compared to a Completed Pregnancy on Mental Health Care Use, Labour Market and Family Outcomes
Authors: Pieter Bakx, Pilar García‐Gómez, Sara Rellstab
Affiliations: Erasmus School of Health Policy and Management Erasmus University Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Erasmus Center for Health Economics Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Erasmus School of Economics Erasmus University Rotterdam Rotterdam the Netherlands; Tinbergen Institute Rotterdam the Netherlands; Università Della Svizzera italiana Lugano Switzerland
Abstract: ABSTRACT Miscarriages occur in about 15% of recognised pregnancies and often cause grief and stress. We investigate the effect of a miscarriage on mental health care use, labour market and family outcomes of women and their partners using an event study framework applied to Dutch linked administrative data. After a miscarriage, women's use of mental health care temporarily increase compared to before the miscarriage, while their partner's use is unaffected. Furthermore, miscarriages affect labour market trajectories and reduce the probability of living together. Results are similar when comparing the effects of a miscarriage with the effects of having a child using a matched sample of women with a completed pregnancy.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Prophet Secretary Against the Online Optimal
Authors: Paul Dütting, Evangelia Gergatsouli, Rojin Rezvan, Yifeng Teng, Alexandros Tsigonias-Dimitriadis
Affiliations: Google Switzerland GmbH, 8004 Zürich, Switzerland; University of Wisconsin–Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706; University of Texas at Austin, Austin, Texas 78712; Google Research, USA, New York, New York 10011; Universidad de Chile, Santiago 8330111, Chile
Abstract: We study the prophet secretary problem, a well-studied variant of the classic prophet inequality, where values are drawn from independent known distributions but arrive in uniformly random order. Upon seeing a value at each step, the decision maker has to either select it and stop or irrevocably discard it. Traditionally, the chosen benchmark is the expected reward of the prophet, who knows all the values in advance and can always select the maximum one. In this work, we study the prophet secretary problem against a less pessimistic but equally well-motivated benchmark: the online optimal. Here, the main goal is to find polynomial-time algorithms that guarantee near-optimal expected reward. Our main result is a polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem. The approximation scheme builds on careful discretization and bundling arguments, in combination with a novel “front-loading” technique that helps reduce the number of decisions the algorithm has to make.

Title: Public Signals in Affine Network Congestion Games with Uncertain Free-Flow Times
Authors: Svenja M. Griesbach, Martin Hoefer, Max Klimm, Tim Koglin
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, RWTH Aachen University, 52074 Aachen, Germany; Institute of Mathematics, Technische Universität Berlin, 10587 Berlin, Germany; and Department of Economics, Sciences Po, 75007 Paris, France
Abstract: Travel times in road networks are subject to stochastic uncertainty resulting from various parameters. A benevolent mobility service provider observing the actual travel times from data may use its informational advantage to steer the traffic equilibrium in a favorable direction through a processs known as signaling or Bayesian persuasion. Previous work has shown that the underlying signaling problem can be NP-hard to approximate better than [Formula: see text], even for static Wardrop flows with affine cost functions with stochastic offsets. In contrast, we show that in this case, the signaling problem is easy for many networks. First, we tightly characterize the class of single-commodity networks in which full information revelation is always an optimal signaling strategy. Second, we construct a reduction from optimal signaling to computing an optimal collection of active edges for the Wardrop equilibrium. For two states, this allows us to efficiently compute an optimal signaling scheme whenever the number of different active edge sets is bounded by a polynomial in the input size. Using a cell decomposition technique, we extend the approach to a polynomial-time algorithm for multicommodity parallel-edge networks provided that both the number of commodities and states are constant. Title: Failures of contingent reasoning in screening decisions
Authors: Gonzalo Arrieta, Maxim Bakhtin
Affiliations: University of Zurich; Analysis Group Inc
Abstract: Abstract Screening decisions—choosing a costly action that reveals information about an unknown quality—can be crucial in various situations, such as hiring workers or designing policies. Choosing whether to screen can be difficult because it requires recognizing and trading off the benefits of information with the costs of getting it. We investigate whether people recognize when the benefits of screening dominate its costs and what causes them to choose otherwise. Our online experiment simulates a hiring scenario with an initial trial task. Participants can first reveal candidates’ quality at a small cost and then choose which candidate to hire. Most participants choose the dominated task that does not reveal the candidates’ quality, and this mistake persists even with experience and feedback. We show that this insufficient screening is driven by failures to anticipate inference and plan the full strategy.

Title: Brave new cities? Governance configurations for sustainable city logistics
Authors: Hugo de Tarragon, Christina Theodoraki
Affiliations: University of Limoges Department of CREOP, , Limoges; Aix-Marseille University IAE Aix-Marseille Graduate School of Management, CERGAM, , Aix-en-Provence, , and Department of Management, School of Business, University of Nicosia, UNIC Athens, Athens, Greece
Abstract: Purpose Despite extensive research and policy efforts, there is still no consensus over the aspects that must be influenced to mitigate the environmental and social impact of city logistics. Existing approaches have primarily focused on optimizing urban freight operations but have struggled to generate lasting and systemic improvements. Building on recent supply chain management (SCM) calls to conceptualize supply chains as socially embedded systems, this study aims to investigate why cities implementing broadly similar collaborative governance initiatives produce different sustainable city logistics outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative configurational analysis was conducted across twenty French city logistics initiatives. Drawing on Furnari et al.’s (2021) configurational theorizing toolkit, governance conditions were iteratively identified and combined to explain variation in sustainable city logistics outcomes. Findings The analysis identifies five governance configurations. Rather than depending on collaborative governance alone, high-impact outcomes emerge from the interaction among governance structure, stakeholder representation, structural commitment and intervention scale. Research limitations/implications The governance configurations identified are grounded in French city logistics initiatives and should be further strengthened through fieldwork, and then examined in other institutional contexts. Future research should investigate how governance configurations evolve over time and across different socially embedded supply chains. Practical implications Managers and public authorities should focus less on replicating individual governance practices and more on assembling governance configurations that combine broad stakeholder representation, collaborative decision-making, structural commitment and coordinated ecosystem-level interventions. Originality/value The study advances SCM research by reconceptualizing sustainable city logistics as a governance and coordination challenge embedded within socially embedded supply chains. By doing so, it further demonstrates how configurational theorizing explains wicked sustainability problems in SCM by shifting attention from isolated governance mechanisms toward governance configurations as the appropriate unit of analysis.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Manufacturer's Agency Selling and Reselling Choices and Online Intermediary's Information Sharing: The Role of Product Quality Decisions
Authors: Xiaojie Wu, Xin Liu, Xiaogang Lin, Ying‐Ju Chen
Affiliations: School of Management Guangdong University of Technology Guangzhou China; School of Business and Management (ISOM) Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Clear Water Bay Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT Meeting consumers' product‐quality demands is essential. Online intermediaries typically possess more accurate demand information than manufacturers and may share it to support quality adjustments. Manufacturers can adopt two selling formats: agency selling, in which they sell directly to consumers through intermediaries and pay commissions, and reselling, in which intermediaries purchase products from manufacturers at wholesale prices and then resell them to consumers. Manufacturers may also sell to downstream resellers who distribute through intermediaries. We develop a game‐theoretic e‐commerce supply chain model in which a manufacturer adjusts product quality in response to realized demand and chooses between agency selling and reselling, while the intermediary decides whether to disclose demand information to the manufacturer, the reseller, or both. Our results yield several insights. First, sharing demand information only with the manufacturer may reduce product quality under both selling formats. Second, under agency selling, the intermediary may disclose information either only to the manufacturer or to both parties; endogenous quality decisions increase full disclosure while reducing manufacturer‐only sharing. Under reselling, with exogenous quality, the intermediary either shares information only with the reseller or withholds it. However, when quality improvement is sufficiently efficient, it may disclose information to both parties despite higher wholesale‐price uncertainty. Furthermore, anticipating the intermediary's disclosure strategy, the manufacturer may still choose higher product quality under agency selling even when this results in a lower expected wholesale price than under reselling. Thus, the manufacturer's preferred selling format depends on which format better induces the intermediary to restrict information disclosure to the intended party. Finally, we show that agency selling can improve consumer surplus and social welfare and may also benefit all supply chain members with endogenous quality decisions.

Title: Optimizing Multi‐Fuel Operations for Green Container Shipping: Models, Analysis, and Solution Approach
Authors: Xuecheng Tian, Yidan Shangguan, Shining Wu, Shuaian Wang
Affiliations: Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Hung Hom Hong Kong
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the optimization of multi‐fuel operations for container shipping in the context of evolving environmental regulations. Faced with increasing pressure to reduce emissions, particularly of sulfur oxides and carbon dioxide, the maritime industry must navigate a complex regulatory landscape in terms of energy use. Key policies include Sulfur Emission Control Areas, the European Union's (EU) Maritime Emissions Trading System, and the FuelEU Maritime Regulation. We propose a novel mathematical programming model to minimize total operational costs, including fuel and carbon emission costs, while maintaining regulatory compliance. Our model integrates three fuel types (very low‐sulfur fuel oil, marine gas oil, and renewable energy) to determine optimal fuel selection and sailing speed in different regulatory zones. To reduce computational complexity, we transform the model from a shipping leg‐wise formulation to a segment type‐wise formulation by categorizing all shipping legs of a route into six segment types, leading to a more efficient representation. Through a comparative analysis of the cost competitiveness and environmental effectiveness of the three fuel types, we derive four possible fuel selection strategies that determine the candidate or optimal fuel types for each segment type. We then develop an exact condition‐based sequential optimization algorithm to evaluate the feasibility of each strategy and identify a globally optimal multi‐fuel operations solution for a given container shipping service. Extensive computational experiments validate the efficacy of our approach, offering practical insights for shipping companies to strategically manage multi‐fuel operations and achieve cost‐efficiency while complying with environmental mandates.

Title: Even flow in dynamic networks for wastewater treatment
Authors: Antton Kasslin, Jeremias Berg
Abstract: Abstract Network flow allocation is a central problem within operations research. Arguably, the most classic setting of flow allocation problems is a static one in which the arcs of a directed graph need to be assigned flow values in a way that respects the capacities of each edge and, for example, maximizes the amount of flow that arrives at a sink node. The numerous applications of flow problems have resulted in several variants being proposed and studied. In this paper, we study a variant of dynamic network flow. Dynamic network flow generalizes the static setting by introducing a notion of time and allowing the flow to move over time in the network. In our setting, the sink of the network also has a maximum capacity of flow it can receive at each timestep, and we are interested in computing flow allocations that distribute an even amount of flow to the sink of the network over all timesteps. Additionally, we assume that new flow can be generated at each non-sink node in each timestep, and that the nodes can temporarily store a limited amount of the flow. In a central instantiation of the problem, the non-sink nodes of the network are pumping stations that need to transfer wastewater to a treatment plant, which is the sink of the network. To evaluate our solving approaches in practice, we worked with the Helsinki Region Environmental Services Authority to collect and create a new open-source benchmark set based on wastewater quantities in the Helsinki region. More precisely, we study the applicability of linear programming for solving real-world benchmarks of this dynamic network flow optimization problem. As our main contributions, we: (i) extend and modify a previously proposed constraint model for computing feasible allocations to the dynamic setting and allow more flexible allocations, (ii) introduce several different approaches to even the workload arriving at the sink at each timestep, (iii) collect a new open-source dataset based on real-world wastewater flow quantities, and (iv) report on an extensive experimental evaluation of our model on three differently-sized time spans of the new dataset using state-of-the-art solvers. Our evaluation demonstrates that, among our evenness approaches, minimizing the difference between the maximum and minimum hourly incoming water to the treatment plant consistently yields the highest evenness in the flow arriving at the treatment plant. Additionally, we demonstrate the flexibility of our model by incorporating additional constraints aimed at reducing the energy consumption of the pumps.

Title: Assessing comprehensive impact of autonomous electric taxis via an integrated modeling framework

Title: Implementation via political parties
Authors: Luis C. Corchón, Guadalupe Correa-Lopera
Abstract: We address the implementation of public policies (alternatives) when the feasible set is unknown to the planner. The implementing agents are the political parties, who know the feasible set. They care about the implemented alternative, which reflects their ideology, and their share in parliament and office. They face a mechanism that, given the alternatives proposed by all parties, asks the voters to rank them and determines the chosen alternative and the shares in parliament and office. We identify conditions on parties’ preferences that guarantee the socially optimal policy is the outcome of the unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium of the electoral game played by the parties. The existence of the equilibrium does not require any assumptions about the parties’ ideology. To ensure uniqueness, shares must prevail over ideology: office or parliamentary shares in two-party systems, and strictly office shares in systems with more than two parties.

Bi-level stochastic optimisation of integrated bed allocation and inpatient scheduling in dedicated inpatient systems with overflow capability
Authors: Xuran Gong, Jianjun Zhou, Jiajun Dai, Na Geng
Affiliations: Sino-US Global Logistics Institute, Antai College of Economics & Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Inpatient beds serve as the cornerstone of efficient care delivery and timely access to medical services. Managers typically allocate beds to individual departments. When a department’s dedicated beds reach full capacity, inpatients are often transferred to non-primary departments. This practice is termed ‘patient overflow'. Furthermore, uncertainties in inpatient arrival rates and length of stay hinder bed management optimisation, undermining efficiency and increasing care delays. This paper proposes a collaborative solution for bed allocation and inpatient scheduling. A two-stage stochastic programming (TSP) model is developed to optimise bed allocation while integrating daily patient scheduling to minimise patient waiting, diversion, and overflow costs. The first-stage determines bed allocations, whereas the second-stage then optimises scheduling decisions under sampled demand scenarios. To support the evaluation and implementation of these allocation decisions, two inpatient scheduling policies are proposed. The first is a rolling horizon scheduling policy, that updates a TSP model on a daily basis using real-time data on current hospitalisations/waitlists. The second is a threshold-based policy, that regulates patient queue lengths and bed reservation quantities through simulation-based optimisation. Computational experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed bed allocation and scheduling approaches over conventional benchmarks, and yield practical, actionable managerial insights for healthcare operations management.

Title: Nonlinear trade-offs in GenAI application pricing: a game-theoretic analysis of API and psychological costs
Authors: Liaoliao Li, Yali Zhang, Jun Sun, Zhaojun Yang
Affiliations: Northwestern Polytechnical University; University of Texas Rio Grande Valley; Xidian University
Abstract: In the rapidly evolving generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) ecosystem, downstream application providers face persistent challenges in designing optimal pricing strategies. These challenges arise from dual cost pressures: application programming interface (API) costs imposed by upstream model platforms and psychological frictions experienced by end consumers. This study develops a game-theoretic model to analyze application providers’ strategic choice between subscription-based and usage-based pricing under both monopolistic and duopolistic market structures. The analysis reveals that the optimal strategies are shaped by a nonlinear interplay among psychological costs, model API costs, and consumer valuation. Under low psychological-cost conditions, API costs exert an inverted U-shaped effect on competing providers’ profits. By contrast, under high API-cost regimes, subscription-based and usage-based models exhibit asymmetric sensitivities to psychological costs: profits under usage-based pricing decline with rising psychological costs, whereas subscription-based profits stabilise. Fthermore, elevated API and psychological costs attenuate competitive intensity, driving duopolistic equilibria toward monopoly-like outcomes. These findings remain robust after incorporating a broad set of realistic market frictions. The results provide actionable insights for GenAI application providers balancing cost pass-through, user engagement, and competitive positioning in pricing decisions.

Title: Improvement of steel strip quality based on reinforcement learning with offline data constraints
Authors: Yue Huang, Zhen Chen, Di Zhou, Ershun Pan
Affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Donghua University
Abstract: In hot-rolling finishing stands, control parameters are numerous and diverse, and quality metrics are tightly coupled. Optimising parameters to improve product quality requires high precision, safety, and fast response. Offline reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach for parameter optimisation, but out-of-distribution (OOD) issues undermine its effectiveness. To address this, we propose a new offline RL framework for control-parameter optimisation. First, we construct an offline dataset for four key quality metrics, comprising 1,048,576 state transition processes. Second, we introduce an offline RL algorithm. The policy update adapts to constraints derived from the state and action distributions of the original dataset, thereby reducing incorrect generalisation to OOD samples. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method can mitigate OOD risk. Moreover, we develop an offline policy-evaluation technique that combines the neural predictive model with the system state-space equations to simulate the rolling environment with reduced approximation error. Extensive experiments show that the proposed approach, evaluated within the simulation framework and supported by temporal-split validation, improves quality metrics by more than 10% on an independent test set compared to existing control methods. Moreover, it reduces convergence time steps by over 50%, yielding more conservative policies and enhanced decision support for production.

Title: Orchestration of Organisational Technologies: Synergies, Challenges, and Contingencies
Authors: Mohamad Ali Mezher, Indra Gunawan, Sajad Fayezi
Affiliations: Adelaide University; Flinders University
Abstract: Rapid technological advances create a pressing challenge for firms: coordinating diverse organisational technologies. Companies must balance and integrate emerging and established technologies, notably Industry 4.0 technologies (I4T) and Lean technologies (LT). Yet guidance on how to integrate these systems remains limited. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review (SLR) of I4T (as emerging technologies) and LT (as established technologies). We synthesise evidence on synergies, challenges, and contingencies, and translate these insights into guidance for operational excellence. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) and Contingency Theory (CT), we argue that combining I4T and LT yields synergistic resource bundles that can potentially deliver sustained competitive advantage. Unlike past research that treats these technologies separately, we introduce an ‘Orchestrated VRIO' perspective that conceptualises value, rarity, inimitability, and organisation as emergent properties of sociotechnical bundles formed through managed orchestration, rather than as static attributes of discrete resources. Building on this framing, we extend CT via a Contingency Bundling Framework that specifies internal and external factors shaping whether bundles deliver value. The review culminates in an integrative framework linking bundle configurations to expected benefits and trade-offs, and highlights implementation risks that can erode advantage.

Title: Single-machine batch scheduling with split jobs and a maintenance activity
Authors: Junyi Zhang, Juan Zou, Ran Ma
Affiliations: Qufu Normal University; Qingdao University of Technology
Abstract: Motivated by batch-dependent processing constraints in semiconductor testing and other time-critical industrial applications, we consider a single-machine batch scheduling problem with a fixed maintenance activity, where jobs have equal processing time but different sizes. Each job can be split and processed in two consecutive batches if necessary. For the objective of minimising the makespan, we prove the NP-hardness of the problem and provide an approximation algorithm with a worst-case ratio of 32, which is the best possible polynomial-time approximation algorithm under the assumption that P≠NP. For the objective of minimising the total completion time, we prove that the problem is NP-hard, and then present a pseudo-polynomial time dynamic programming algorithm and a 32-approximation algorithm. Moreover, through computational experiments, we demonstrate that the approximation algorithm performs very well in practice, achieving an average relative error of only 0.36%.

Title: Machine learning in feature recognition for manufacturing: taxonomy, analytical review, comparisons, trends, challenges, and outlook
Authors: Peizhi Shi, Yuchu Qin, Fanlin Meng, Paul J. Scott, Xiangqian Jiang
Affiliations: University of Leeds; University of Huddersfield; University of Exeter
Abstract: Feature recognition is an important topic in the area of intelligent manufacturing and production research. This technique is utilised to extract and recognise functional components and geometric shapes, such as slots, holes, and pockets, from solid models. The term ‘learning-based feature recognition’ refers to the feature recognition methods implemented based on machine learning. This topic was examined three decades ago but has been growing quickly in the recent five years. In this paper, a taxonomy and review of learning-based feature recognition methods are presented. This paper categorises the literature, examines basic components of a learning-based feature recognition method, identifies the technical evolution of these components, examines their impact on the overall feature recognition process, provides a broader overview of existing methods, identifies the milestone learning paradigms, makes comparisons among different approaches, assesses their practical capabilities, and identifies the gaps between research and real-world applications. By reading this paper, researchers and industry professionals can understand different learning-based feature recognition methods and their underlying principles, gain insights into design decisions made in a learning-based system, and understand their applied situations.

Title: Generative models for energy modelling and management: a structured framework for technology adoption in energy systems
Authors: Leonardo Fontoura, Daniel Luiz de Mattos Nascimento, Julio Neto, Guilherme Luz Tortorella
Affiliations: Fluminense Federal University; University of Barcelona Business School; The University of Melbourne; Universidad Austral; Fundacao Dom Cabral
Abstract: The growing complexity of modern energy systems demands intelligent, adaptable, and theoretically grounded approaches to modelling and management. Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen-AI) and Deep Learning Models (DLMs) configured for generative tasks offer significant potential for scenario simulation and rare-event modelling; however, their adoption remains constrained by conceptual ambiguity and the absence of structured, theory-informed frameworks. To address this gap, this study proposes the Generative Models for Energy Modelling and Management (GM-EMM) framework. By establishing a functional taxonomy of generative approaches, the research addresses critical analytical challenges, including counterfactual reasoning and data scarcity in decentralised energy systems. A multi-method research design was employed, integrating a scoping review, expert elicitation via the Fuzzy Delphi method, and non-parametric statistical prioritisation using Friedman and Nemenyi tests to evaluate six core technologies (RNNs, GANs, GNNs, TNNs, VAEs, and CNNs). Based on expert consensus and statistical differentiation, technologies were positioned across four analytically defined phases: Deployment, Validation, Exploration, and Monitoring. To enhance practical relevance, an interpretive validation stage with industry experts confirmed the roadmap’s coherence and decision-support value.

Title: Farming contract design with random yield and private farmer information
Authors: Xinyan Cao, Xiang Fang, Yuanjie He, Wei Hu, Xiao Xiao
Affiliations: Northern Illinois University; University of Colorado Denver; California State Polytechnic University, Pomona; Nankai University; California State University Stanislaus
Abstract: We study an agricultural supply chain in which a distributor purchases products from a farmer who holds private information regarding their own random yield and costs. We develop an efficiency index to streamline the farmer's three pieces of private information and categorise the farmer as either efficient or inefficient. Following the principal-agent model, we design the optimal forward contract menu for the distributor. Our findings indicate that when the probability of an efficient farmer is low, the distributor will engage both types of farmers. Conversely, when this probability is high, a contract is exclusively offered to the efficient farmer. Interestingly, while improvements in the farmer's efficiency consistently benefit the distributor, they may either increase or decrease the farmer's expected profit. Additionally, the farmer's production cost has a more substantial impact on both parties' profits and values of information than the backup cost. Finally, we analyse the contract design problem with risk-averse farmers to highlight the impact of the farmers' risk aversion on the agriculture supply chain.

Title: Construction and application of a multimodal knowledge graph for machining deformation uncertainty analysis
Authors: Zhaoze Sun, Xiaoyue Li, Guangyuan Si, Erpeng Wang, Hui Xu, Deguo Yao, Yuanqing Sun
Affiliations: Qingdao University; College of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Ltd.; .; Shandong North Binhai Machinery Co., Ltd.
Abstract: Uncertainty analysis of machining deformation is crucial for improving product quality, reliability, and manufacturing efficiency. Current machining deformation uncertainty problems still face many challenges, such as complex mechanism, scattered information, and high dependence on expert experience. In order to solve the aforementioned problems, the paper constructs a multi-modal knowledge graph for machining deformation uncertainty analysis, and designs a large model-augmented intelligent system driven by a multimodal knowledge graph. The constructed multi-modal knowledge graph realises the multi-integration of text information, chart information and finite element simulation information, and covers key links such as ontology construction, knowledge extraction, knowledge fusion, knowledge inference, and knowledge storage. Aiming at the knowledge inference link, the principal component analysis (PCA) and multi-head self-attention mechanism (MHSA) are innovatively introduced to enhance feature extraction, proposing a new knowledge inference method. Additionally, through multi-stage large model enhancement strategies and expert large model training approaches, the generalisation ability and multimodal interaction capability of the intelligent system have been effectively improved. Finally, a multimodal knowledge graph of machining deformation uncertainty is constructed, and an intelligent system is developed to provide multimodal decision support for machining deformation uncertainty analysis from a full life-cycle perspective, with its performance validated.

Title: Reconfiguring a mixed-model robotic assembly line considering lifespan, obsolescence, and retrofit in a manufacturing 4.0/5.0 environment
Authors: Daniel Schibelbain, Milton Luiz Polli, Luiz Carlos De Abreu Rodrigues, Leandro Magatão
Affiliations: Federal University of Technology – Paraná (UTFPR)
Abstract: This paper addresses the challenges of reconfiguring mixed-model robotic assembly lines to face volatile market demand, new products, and technological innovations from the Manufacturing 4.0 and 5.0 Industries. The literature extensively studies designing new manufacturing systems or balancing reconfigurable ones. However, to adapt existing lines to these issues, considering lifespan and obsolescence remains an underexplored domain, along with the emerging trend of retrofitting in-house resources. A multi-step MILP-based method is proposed to bridge this gap. An exhaustive set of scenarios is compared with exact and heuristic benchmarks. The method’s effectiveness is evaluated in a large-scale industrial case study, assessing the influence of flexibility on the system. This real-world industrial case is optimised, achieving an average improvement of 4.69% over the conventional approach and better results in more than 82% of instances. Furthermore, a statistical analysis is conducted and reveals the correlation between robots’ task accessibility and their assignments. In a complementary way, a financial assessment and bottom-up analysis from Process Engineering have also been explored. Therefore, this research provides a method to reconfigure manufacturing lines considering variable operational conditions and practical issues. This leads to several managerial insights and contributes to more sustainable and profitable assembly systems.

Title: A multi-level modelling approach for magnesium-carbon brick die-casting digital twin workshop oriented to production anomaly detection
Authors: Dengli Yi, Xinfeng Wang, Chuanqi Li, Lu Bai
Affiliations: Institution of Mechanical and Power Engineering; Beijing Gangyan Hydrogen Metallurgy Technology Research Institute Co., Ltd; Automation Research and Design Institute of Metallurgical Industry
Abstract: The manufacturing process of magnesia-carbon bricks involves complex equipment and dense workflows, leading to frequent production anomalies that are hard to diagnose. Traditional modelling methods struggle with multi-level anomaly detection and process awareness. This paper proposes a digital twin-based multi-layer modelling framework for anomaly detection in magnesia-carbon brick production. The framework unifies equipment behaviour and workshop logic through three layers: equipment twin, workshop twin, and system decision-making. It addresses modelling gaps by dividing equipment into five component types, creating a three-level twin structure (unit, chain, and equipment) to map structure-action-state relationships. For workshop logic, a complex event processing method models process events using behaviour correlation matrices and directed graph adjacency matrices, capturing time evolution and path dependencies. A prototype system was developed, integrating data collection, state mapping, anomaly detection, and visualisation. Initial tests in a pilot workshop confirmed its feasibility and scalability. This research offers a structured, multi-level modelling approach for anomaly detection in complex manufacturing, enhancing digital twin expressiveness and workshop intelligence.

Title: Risk propagation modelling and resilience assessment of supply chain networks based on an improved SIS model
Authors: Yu Wang, Yufeng Sun, Zhining Zhang, Fulin Zhang, Zihan Wang
Affiliations: School of Reliability and Systems Engineering, Beihang University; School of Information Resource Management, Renmin University of China
Abstract: Traditional assessment methods fail to capture the dynamic interplay between risk propagation and managerial interventions, and cannot precisely quantify the evolutionary mechanisms underlying Supply Chain Network Resilience (SCNR). This study proposes a decision-embedded SIS dynamics model that explicitly integrates performance-state-triggered intervention detection, dynamic resource mobilisation, and topology-aware resource allocation into the modelling framework, enabling intervention behaviours to be endogenously activated by real-time system performance dynamics. Grounded in the complete life-cycle trajectory of disruption–intervention–recovery–adaptation, this study constructs a comprehensive four-dimensional resilience assessment framework encompassing absorptive, recovery, adaptive, and structural dimensions. The findings demonstrate that, while physical topology integrity governs SCNR under low-intensity shocks, the contribution of dynamic performance resilience metrics significantly surpasses that of structural factors under extreme shocks inducing large-scale structural fragmentation, thereby emerging as the decisive determinant of system viability. By breaking the autonomy constraint inherent in classical risk propagation models, this study provides a quantitative decision-making benchmark for differentiated resilience governance of SCNs under resource constraints.

Title: Resilience analysis of supply chain networks under cascading failure model considering tolerance state and competitive recovery
Authors: Bin Hou, Xinyu Wang, Jiafu Tang
Affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: Stability and resilience of supply chains are crucial for enterprise operations. Supply chains are vulnerable to disruption risks, potentially resulting in cascading failures (i.e. the ripple effect). This study aims to delve into the dynamic characteristics of cascading failures and explore effective approaches to enhancing supply chain resilience (SCR). We propose a cascading failure model named CFM-TSCR, which incorporates tolerance state and competitive recovery. The tolerance state represents the manifestation of an enterprise's willingness to tolerate risk, thereby influencing the timing of its execution of recovery measures. Competitive recovery acknowledges that recovery is a process of bilateral selection among enterprises within a competitive environment rather than unilateral efforts. Essentially, the tolerance state and competitive recovery reflect when enterprises initiate the recovery process and how enterprises respond to the recovery process, respectively. Additionally, we investigate the effects of modelling parameters and diverse disruption scenarios on SCR. These findings play a significant role and hold substantial value in identifying critical nodes within supply chain networks, refining enterprises' recovery strategies and enhancing SCR.

Title: Jointly optimising assembly line feeding and supermarket layouts
Authors: Ebenezer Olatunde Adenipekun, Veronique Limère, Nico André Schmid
Affiliations: GhentUniversity, Ghent, Belgium; Flanders Make@UGent–core lab CVAMO; Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 -- LEM -- Lille Economie Management
Abstract: Customised products increase the complexity of managing assembly systems efficiently, particularly when multiple part variants are required for assembly, necessitating adept handling of limited space within assembly lines. Leveraging diverse feeding policies efficiently optimises space utilisation and minimises logistical complexity in part feeding. Moreover, strategic decisions regarding the placement and sizing of preparation areas are crucial for smooth intra-logistics flows. Precise cell placement facilitates efficient transportation between preparation areas and assembly lines, reducing transportation costs, while optimal sizing minimises spatial costs. In response to these challenges, we propose a mixed-integer optimisation model that determines a feeding policy for each part and assigns parts requiring preprocessing to either regular or line-integrated cells. The collection of these cells forms the supermarket. Exploiting a callback procedure, the model ensures that navigating regular cells sharing the same delivery frequency and assembly station sequence is done by the dedicated automated guided vehicle. We enhance model efficiency using valid inequalities and symmetry-breaking constraints and validate the approach through extensive experiments on artificial instances. The results demonstrate that our cell-design optimisation approach is more cost-effective than both a simplified supermarket-based planning strategy that omits detailed cell structures and an operational simplification case restricted to line-integrated cells.

Title: Tri-objective based scalable balancing of reconfigurable manufacturing systems subject to resource constraints and task processing time uncertainty
Authors: Siwar Arbi, Audrey Cerqueus, Evgeny Gurevsky, Alexandre Dolgui, Ali Siadat
Affiliations: IMT Atlantique; CNRS; University of Nantes; LCFC, Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology; Arts et Métiers Institute of Technology
Abstract: This article studies reconfigurable manufacturing systems and their ability to efficiently evolve (or scale) through the use of a limited number of additional resources to improve two analysed system characteristics: productivity and robustness against task processing time uncertainty. The goal is to find an initial system configuration (or balancing) representing the best potential for scalability. To this end, we propose a multi-step based multi-objective approach, where productivity and robustness are considered as two objectives to be maximised and the number of used additional resources as the third objective to be minimised. Thus, for a given balancing, we first explore the set of its non-dominated (in the sense of Pareto) configurations, reflecting relevant possibilities for additional use of resources. Then, we calculate its corresponding tri-objective hyper-volume and suggest to consider it as a scalability metric. Finally, to find the most scalable balancing, we develop an efficient simulated annealing algorithm, where the proposed metric is used as a fitness function. The algorithm is tested and analysed on small- and medium-sized instances, extracted and adapted from the well-known benchmark dataset. The numerical results obtained demonstrate the stability and efficiency of the developed algorithm and confirm the relevance of the proposed scalability metric.

Title: Process intervention decisions in biomanufacturing under lead time constraints
Authors: Yasemin Limon, Tugce Martagan, Ananth Krishnamurthy
Affiliations: Bilkent University; Northeastern University; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Title: Labour assignment with convergent product structures: an assessment by simulation
Authors: Matthias Thürer, Nuno O. Fernandes
Affiliations: Chemnitz University of Technology; Instituto Politécnico de Castelo Branco; Universidade do Minho
Abstract: Most labour in practice is somehow flexible, and most shops in practice use some form of labour flexibility to cope with varying demand. A large literature on labour assignment rules that decide when and where to shift or reassign workers has consequently emerged. But this literature typically neglects convergent assembly structures. There is the implicit assumption that results from other shop structures are directly transferable. Results from discrete event simulations show that this is not the case. Although previous literature indicates that shifting workers to the station with the longest queue and considering critical parts improve performance, these results are not confirmed in our study. In assembly systems, the flow of jobs is constrained by synchronisation requirements and capacity availability, determining both waiting times overall performance. Labour assignment has a direct impact on both if workers are shared among assembly stations, which has direct implications for the rule to adopt. In terms of research, we confirm the literature on inventory diagnosis and highlight its importance for labour assignment. In terms of practice, we contribute by supporting managers in finding the appropriate labour assignment rule for their shop.

Title: Healthcare network resilience analysis under equipment failure and patients’ preferences
Authors: Claudia Piffari, Alexandra Lagorio, Roberto Pinto
Affiliations: University of Bergamo
Abstract: We propose a resilience analysis framework to assess the resilience of an elective healthcare network subject to low-impact-high-frequency (LIHF) disruptions, thereby identifying the most critical facility, considering both the impact of disturbances and the probability of their occurrence. The proposed framework combines agent-based simulation with design of experiment (DOE) and patient behaviour modelling. The framework has been tested with data from a real case, demonstrating its usefulness for conducting resilience analyses and prioritising resilience-enhancing actions to improve network performance. Two resilience-enhancing actions with different characteristics have been tested. The distinctive feature of the framework is the consideration of patient preferences in the simulation, allowing patients to be considered as active actors who can influence the behaviour of the system during a disturbance.

Title: Robust real-time optimisation for train rescheduling and platforming in high-speed railways under a route-locking sectional-release mechanism
Authors: Huimin Zhang, Wenhui Qi, Zebin Chen, Shukai Li
Affiliations: Qingdao University; Beijing Jiaotong University; Shantou University
Abstract: The route-locking sectional-release (RLSR) interlocking mechanism has been shown to significantly improve operational efficiency and station throughput in large stations. However, most existing studies rely on simplified interlocking rules, particularly in real-time rescheduling problems. To address this gap and enhance operational efficiency and resilience under dynamic perturbations, including dwell disturbances, running disturbances, and disruptions, this paper proposes a robust real-time optimisation framework for the train rescheduling and platforming problem (TRPP) in high-speed railways, with RLSR explicitly incorporated into the model formulation. Dwell and running disturbances are characterised by uncertainty sets, and the resulting model is reformulated into a tractable robust counterpart, while disruption-related uncertainty is handled through a rolling horizon framework with real-time feedback. To reduce computational complexity and meet real-time requirements, a Lagrangian relaxation-based decomposition algorithm is embedded within the rolling horizon framework. At each rolling horizon stage, the problem is decomposed into two parallelizable subproblems: the train timetable rescheduling problem (TTRP) and the train platforming problem (TPP). Numerical experiments using real-world data validate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed approach. Furthermore, several managerial insights are derived for practitioners.

Title: Estimation of process capability indices for high-dimensional data
Authors: Shuai Wang, Mengying You, Yi Li, Jyun-You Chiang
Affiliations: Hainan University; Shanghai University of International Business and Economics; Chengdu Technological University; Southwestern University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: In high-dimensional manufacturing environments, quality assessment must account for multiple correlated characteristics, posing significant challenges for multivariate process capability indices (MPCIs). This study focuses on identifying and improving MPCIs suitable for such settings. Among several candidates, volume-ratio-based indices are found to retain interpretability and sensitivity under high dimensionality. However, their practical applicability is hindered by instability in covariance matrix estimation. To address this issue, a modified adaptive thresholding approach is developed, incorporating a positive-definiteness constraint to ensure reliable and bounded MPCI estimation. Theoretical analysis establishes the consistency of the proposed estimator. We further develop interval estimation procedures for high-dimensional MPCIs and evaluate their coverage and length properties via bootstrap-based and asymptotic approaches. In addition, we propose a diagnostic variable-ranking strategy to identify and prioritise the characteristics most responsible for capability degradation, providing actionable guidance for process improvement. Simulation studies across various sample sizes, sparsity levels, and dimensions confirm the superior accuracy of the proposed framework over existing methods. A semiconductor manufacturing case study further demonstrates its practical relevance for high-dimensional process capability analysis.

Title: Nonparametric change-point detection for unstructured 3D point cloud data with an application in additive manufacturing
Authors: Zhiqiong Wang, Pingping He, Yangyang Zang, Shuguang He, Zhen He
Affiliations: Tianjin University of Technology; AVIC China Aero-Polytechnology Establishment; Tianjin University
Abstract: In contrast to key product characteristics, unstructured 3D point cloud data with coordinates at random measurement locations can be collected from 3D scanning systems to reflect product geometry entirely. However, challenges such as high dimensionality, registration complexity, and sensitivity to small process changes hinder effective modelling and monitoring of such data. Furthermore, there is very limited research on Phase I analysis of unstructured point cloud data in the literature. To this end, this paper proposes two novel nonparametric change-point detection methods for unstructured 3D point cloud data to identify the presence and location of a change point in a historical dataset. Specifically, we first introduce the Laplace-Beltrami (LB) operator spectrum as an intrinsic geometrical property of unstructured 3D point clouds by leveraging tools from differential geometry. Then, we develop two nonparametric control charts for detecting a change point among the LB spectra. Finally, we provide an effective procedure to determine critical values for the control charts. Extensive numerical simulations demonstrate the superiority of the proposed methods in detecting and estimating the change point while maintaining in-control performance. In addition, an application in additive manufacturing illustrates the implementation of the proposed methods and validates their effectiveness to pinpoint the change point.

Title: Uncovering economic policy uncertainty during conflict
Authors: Sophie Brochet, Hannes Mueller, Christopher Rauh
Abstract: The correct measurement of economic policy uncertainty (EPU) plays a critical role in many policy settings - in particular where economic policy decisions need to be taken in response to large shocks. One such large shock is armed conflict. But, counterintuitively, the standard text-based EPU index systematically declines during armed conflict periods. Using a global news corpus covering 192 countries and over 5 million articles, we show that this decline is driven not by reduced uncertainty, but by a crowding out of reporting on economics and policy. We show that a combination of topic modeling and two-way fixed effects can be used to adjust the measurement of EPU, providing a new view on political risk during armed conflict. After adjustment, the EPU aligns more closely with firm perceptions, political risk insurance and investment during armed conflict.

Title: The geometric adjudication of water rights in international rivers
Authors: Ricardo Martínez, Juan D. Moreno-Ternero
Abstract: We study the adjudication of water rights in international rivers. We characterize allocation rules that formalize focal principles to deal with water disputes in a basic model. Central to our analysis is a family of geometric rules that implement concatenated transfers downstream. They can be seen as formalizing Limited Territorial Sovereignty, as suggested in the Rio Declaration on Environment and Development. We apply our rules to the case of the Nile River, with a long history of disputes between downstream and upstream nations

Title: Interviewers as instruments: estimating the wage penalty of drug use
Authors: Sergey Alexeev, Mark Wooden
Abstract: Abstract We exploit quasi-random interviewer assignment in the Australian HILDA Survey to instrument for self-reported drug use and estimate its effect on wages. Applying the optimal formula IV framework to six substance categories, we find that IV estimates largely mirror WLS for cannabis, ecstasy, and hallucinogens but diverge sharply for methamphetamine and inhalants — notably, the meth estimate reverses sign, indicating a wage penalty of 10% for frequent users, equivalent to the earnings loss from forgoing a high school diploma. Point estimates under IV suggest a larger premium for high cocaine use, but remain statistically similar to WLS. Romano-Wolf multiple-inference adjustment confirms substance-level significance for five of six drugs; the methamphetamine result, while just outside conventional thresholds after adjustment, is substantively large and clinically plausible. These findings demonstrate the empirical value of interviewer-driven variation for studying the labour-market effects of sensitive behaviours.

Title: How can firms implement smart manufacturing through supply chain collaboration? A multiple-case study from China
Authors: Weihua Liu, Jiahe Hou, Yang Cheng
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; Center for Industrial Production, Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; School of Business Administration, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: The complex system characteristics of Smart manufacturing (SM) require firms collaborating with supply chain members to implement SM transformation. However, the motives, methods, and influencing factors of such collaboration remain unclear. Addressing this gap, we conduct a multi-case study of four manufacturing firms and obtain three findings based on complex adaptive system theory. First, the motives of supply chain collaboration include the adaptation to the environment of high customisation, technical complexity, policy, and horizontal competition. Second, firms collaborate with supply chain members in terms of equipment customisation and information interconnection, to establish the data and equipment foundation of SM. This process is affected by the scale and volume of invested resources. Based on these, firms further build collaborative platforms to realise the integrated management of all supply chain links and improve the SM capability through the iteration of solutions, which are affected by the degree of security in data sharing. Third, supply chain collaboration improves the quality and satisfaction, reduces the cost, and shortens the cycle of SM implementation. This study not only addresses whether and how supply chain collaboration influences SM implementation, but also provides guidance to help companies implement SM through a gradual multi-stage collaboration in supply chain.

Title: The impact of LLM-based recommendations on decisions under uncertainty
Authors: Marty Haoyuan Chen, Emel Filiz-Ozbay, Erkut Y. Ozbay
Affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park
Abstract: Abstract We study how large language model (LLM) based recommendations affect evaluations of uncertainty. We elicit certainty equivalents for (i) lotteries that share the same reduced-form winning probability but vary in cognitive demands because they are compound, and (ii) an Ellsberg-style ambiguous lottery. Across all lottery types, valuations from participants who receive LLM-based recommendations before each valuation exhibit second-order stochastic dominance relative to valuations from participants who do not. Hence, LLM-based recommendations leave mean valuations unchanged but compress the distribution, reducing the incidence of extreme valuations. Consistent with this pattern, LLM-based recommendations reduce the intensity of risk, complexity, and ambiguity aversion, while leaving the fraction of participants classified as averse unchanged.

Title: Borrowed plumes: the gender gap in claiming credit for teamwork
Authors: Klara Kinnl, Jakob Moeller, Anna Walter-Dockx
Affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business: Wirtschaftsuniversitat Wien; Institute for Advanced Studies Vienna
Abstract: Abstract Teamwork is prevalent in many forms of production, but individual contributions to team output are often ambiguous. We use a large-scale online experiment with an interactive team task to investigate gender differences in claiming credit for contributions to teamwork with misaligned incentives: Team members have an incentive to exaggerate their contribution, but this harms the other team member. In this setting, we observe that men claim to have contributed more than equally contributing women. Using two further between-subject treatments, we find no evidence that gender differences in altruism or in overconfidence explain the observed gender claim-gap. Further, the gender gap is present only among high contributors, and we show that the gap is particularly pronounced for large claims, which has potentially important consequences for gender equity in labour market outcomes.
