Title: Sustainable development goals and waste management in the wheat supply chain under uncertain conditions: implications from an emerging economy
Authors: Mahsa Rezaee Shirsavar, Misagh Rahbari, Mohammad Mohammadi
Abstract: Wheat, as one of the most fundamental crops, plays a strategic role in the food security of societies. The importance of wheat supply has been a critical issue in every society from the past to the present. Therefore, the aim of this research was to present a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to optimize the wheat supply chain under uncertainty, which simultaneously incorporated the three main dimensions of sustainable development (economic, social, and environmental). In addition, various other features, such as wheat quality and supplier selection, were considered in this research. Furthermore, the chance-constrained programming (CCP) approach was employed to deal with the problem's uncertainty. To validate the problem practically, a real case study for the wheat supply chain in Iran was considered. Concerns about the generation of large volumes of waste throughout the wheat supply chain and the significant waste of production output led to the selection of the recycling (animal feed) method. This method not only combats waste disposal but also utilizes it as a potential source of profitability. Subsequently, an analysis of the employed waste management method was conducted by comparing it with the disposal (landfilling) method. Indeed, both waste management methods were applied in the model, and the results of each method were compared dimensionally. Finally, a sensitivity analysis was performed to validate the model and examine the impact of changes in key parameters on the problem's performance. Analysis of the results revealed that in the economic dimension, the highest profit earned was observed in the sale of processed products (40%), and also the highest cost incurred was related to wheat procurement costs (20%). In the social dimension, the largest share of job opportunities created was related to products transportation from silo to factory (29%). In the environmental dimension, the most significant negative impact was associated with the amount of electricity consumption for products production in factory (30%).

Title: Learning Dominant States in Elementary Resource Constrained Shortest Path Problems
Authors: Saverio Basso, Alessandro Minoli, Matteo Salani
Abstract: Abstract In this work, we investigate whether machine learning can be leveraged to identify promising states in dynamic programming algorithms, focusing on Elementary Resource Constrained Shortest Path Problems (ERCSPP). More in detail, we solved 41 single resource instances from SPPRCLIB using iterative relaxation techniques through the PathWyse library, systematically collecting all generated states (i.e. labels). We designed ad-hoc features computable in constant time and constructed two datasets: one containing all generated labels (G) and another with only those inserted into data pools (I), totaling several hundred million labels. Machine learning tools are then employed to explore these datasets, revealing significant patterns between successive relaxations. Leveraging these insights, we propose a normalization approach and apply supervised learning techniques to distinguish dominating states, both within subsequent relaxations of the same problem and in previously unseen instances. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on Dataset G, while for Dataset I, performance varies, showing strong results within the same instance but declining for unseen ones. We therefore propose a data-driven policy that leverages trained models to prioritize the extension of promising labels during dynamic programming. Preliminary evaluation shows consistent reductions in the number of extended states across almost all instances, with speedups emerging on larger ones, supporting the viability of data-driven dynamic programming algorithms.

Title: High-Probability Polynomial-Time Complexity of Restarted Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient Method for Linear Programming
Authors: Zikai Xiong
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences, Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois 60208
Abstract: The restarted primal-dual hybrid gradient method (rPDHG) is a first-order method recently known for its computational effectiveness in solving linear programming (LP) problems. Despite its impressive practical performance, the theoretical iteration bounds for rPDHG can be exponentially poor. To investigate this gap from a probabilistic perspective, we show that rPDHG achieves polynomial-time complexity in a high-probability sense, under assumptions on the probability distribution from which the data instance is generated. We consider both Gaussian and more general sub-Gaussian distribution models. For standard-form LP instances with m constraints and n variables, our bounds take a particularly simple form when m is not too close to n: rPDHG iterates settle on the optimal basis in [Formula: see text] iterations, followed by [Formula: see text] iterations to compute an [Formula: see text]-optimal solution, with probability at least [Formula: see text] for [Formula: see text] that is not exponentially small. The Stage I bound further improves to [Formula: see text] in the Gaussian distribution model. Experimental results confirm the tail behavior and the polynomial-time dependence on problem dimensions of the iteration counts. As an application of our probabilistic analysis, we explore how the disparity among the components of the optimal solution bears on the performance of rPDHG, and we provide guidelines for generating challenging LP instances. Title: Cut the chit-chat: a new framework for the application of generative language models for portfolio construction
Authors: Francesco A. Fabozzi, Ionut Florescu
Abstract: Current applications of generative language models (GLMs) for portfolio construction utilize the chat functionality of such models to forecast expected returns. The current literature classify outputs of these models using discrete labels that ignore the magnitude of sentiment. We show that this procedure is not optimal for cross-sectional portfolio construction. In this paper, we introduce Logit Extraction , a methodology for extracting the model’s assigned probabilities to sentiment labels, allowing for the formulation of a continuous-valued ranking variable for portfolio construction. We demonstrate that Logit Extraction significantly enhances risk-adjusted returns over previous discrete label approaches. We make available an open source implementation of Logit Extraction in the python package “TokenProbs”.

Title: Compulsory schooling mitigates health inequality: Anthropometric evidence from two centuries of height data
Authors: Caroline Namubiru, Joerg Baten, Alberto Batinti, Joan Costa-Font
Abstract: Although compulsory education (CE) laws have widened access to schooling and shaped economic, social, and health outcomes, it remains unclear whether they reduce long-run health inequalities. We study the effect of CE policies on health inequality using height Gini indices for 66 countries between 1810 and 2000, estimating intent-to-treat effects through a staggered difference-in-differences design. Our results indicate that CE exposure reduces the height Gini. The inequality-reducing effect appears to operate mainly through increased years of schooling and reduced fertility. The effect is not uniform across regions, being largest in Europe, and it is driven largely by later extensions of CE duration rather than initial adoption alone. Overall, the findings indicate that education policy can meaningfully narrow health disparities over time, but its effectiveness depends on the scale of the mandate and the timing of adoption.

Title: Error Bound Analysis for the Regularized Loss of Deep Linear Neural Networks
Authors: Po Chen, Rujun Jiang, Peng Wang
Affiliations: School of Data Science, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China; Department of Artificial Intelligence, University of Macau, Taipa, Macau SAR, China
Abstract: The optimization foundations of deep linear networks have recently received significant attention. However, because of their inherent nonconvexity and hierarchical structure, analyzing the loss functions of deep linear networks remains a challenging task. In this work, we study the local geometry of the regularized squared loss of deep linear networks around each critical point. Specifically, we obtain a closed-form characterization of the critical point set building on existing results and establish an error bound for the regularized loss under mild conditions on network width and regularization parameters. Notably, this error bound quantifies the distance from a point to the critical point set in terms of the current gradient norm, which can be used to derive linear convergence of first-order methods. To support our theoretical findings, we conduct numerical experiments and demonstrate that gradient descent converges linearly to a critical point when optimizing the regularized loss of deep linear networks. Title: Disasters bite less deeply, but they do not stop biting: four decades of structural transformation and disaster sensitivity in Vietnam
Authors: Duc Huu Nguyen, Huan Huu Nguyen, Tam Ha Minh Nguyen
Abstract: Comparable levels of realised disaster impact were associated with substantially smaller macroeconomic losses after Vietnam's late-1990s development transition—not because the available meteorological indicators became systematically weaker, but as the economic transmission of realised impacts changed. This paper examines how the relationship between natural disaster impacts and macroeconomic losses evolves as economies develop. Using annual data for Vietnam from 1986 to 2025, we construct a multidimensional Natural Disaster Impact Index (NDII), positioned within the hazard–exposure–vulnerability framework, that captures realised physical and social damage across four dimensions. Hansen's threshold regression identifies a statistically significant transition around 1999, coinciding with agriculture's share of GDP declining to approximately one-quarter and a broader period of industrialisation and international integration. Beyond this threshold, the estimated marginal association between disaster impacts and economic losses is roughly half its earlier magnitude. The attenuation is considerably larger for economic damage than for social damage, while agricultural share independently reproduces the transition and significantly conditions disaster sensitivity. These patterns provide stronger support for structural transformation than for institutional adaptation or financial buffering alone. Purely meteorological indicators produce no comparable threshold, making a hazard-only explanation less consistent with the evidence. The findings show how structural transformation can reorganise the transmission of disaster impacts without eliminating the exposure accompanying continued development.

Title: Land-based climate policy, land prices, and the green transition trilemma: Evidence from Bolivia
Authors: Guilherme Magacho, Isabella Rodrigues de Brito, Danilo Spinola
Abstract: Land-based climate policies in forest-rich developing economies are often assessed separately, overlooking how land scarcity, land prices, and macroeconomic constraints shape feasibility. This paper examines the macro-financial challenges of sustainable agriculture and forest conservation in Bolivia, where deforestation is high and fiscal and external constraints bind. We develop a dynamic version of the Exposure to Structural Transformation in an Ecologic-Economic Model (D-ESTEEM) to jointly analyse Bolivia's Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) policies for forest conservation and agricultural productivity. The locally calibrated, environmentally extended input-output model combines continuous-time monetary system dynamics, endogenous land prices, and demand-led adjustments in a small open economy. Forest conservation reduces environmental pressures but raises land prices, weakening the competitiveness of land-intensive activities and worsening fiscal and balance-of-payments pressures. Agricultural productivity measures ease land pressures and support output but rely on imported inputs, reinforcing external dependence. Overall, the NDCs improve economic activity and environmental outcomes while worsening fiscal and trade imbalances. Fiscal consolidation and exchange-rate adjustment mitigate some imbalances but entail inflationary pressures or lower output and employment. Environmental gains may therefore come at the cost of macroeconomic fragility. The paper shows how conservation-induced land scarcity and land price dynamics interact with fiscal and balance-of-payments constraints to determine the feasibility of land-based transitions in resource-dependent economies.

Title: Evaluating mobility-as-a-service solutions for long-distance commuting

Title: Exploring inequalities in 15-minute walkable neighborhoods: A typology of perceived accessibility-preference mismatch
Authors: Kunbo Shi, Lingkun Meng, Yang Hu, Liang Ma, Tianren Yang
Abstract: One of the goals of 15-minute walkable neighborhoods is to provide equitable opportunities for all individuals within a 15-minute walk. This has motivated numerous studies to identify vulnerable groups living outside such neighborhoods using objective spatial data. However, very little research examines inequalities from a subjective perspective. More importantly, it remains unknown whether people outside such neighborhoods actually prefer them. Using data from a nationwide survey of 7,155 respondents across 81 Chinese cities, we employ multilevel linear regression models to assess inequalities in perceived accessibility, and multinomial logistic regression models to examine which population groups fall into a four‑group typology, i.e., HA‑HP (high accessibility & high preference), LA‑HP (low accessibility & high preference), LA‑LP (low accessibility & low preference), and HA‑LP (high accessibility & low preference), based on the match or mismatch between perceived accessibility and accessibility preference. The results indicate that socioeconomically disadvantaged groups (e.g., low‑education, low‑income, low‑car‑ownership, renters) tend to report poorer perceived accessibility to daily or recreational facilities. However, the typology analysis further shows that only some of them have unmet needs (LA‑HP), while others hold low accessibility preferences (LA‑LP). Moreover, different facility types exhibit distinct patterns. For daily facilities (e.g., shopping facilities, restaurants, bus stops), typical LA‑HP groups include low‑income, low‑education, and non‑full‑time employed residents. For recreational facilities (e.g., cultural facilities, sport facilities, leisure facilities), LA‑HP groups include men, low‑income groups, non‑local Hukou holders, and residents in low‑street‑density areas. These findings demonstrate that combining perceived accessibility with preference provides a more accurate and policy‑relevant identification of vulnerable groups than conventional approaches. Particular policy attention should be devoted to LA‑HP residents, i.e., those who desire better walkable access but perceive it as poor.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Impact of traffic management center functionality on speed harmonization in urban networks under mixed traffic environments
Authors: Seung-Hyeon Lee, Hyunsoo Yun, Seung Woo Ham, Dong-Kyu Kim
Abstract: The effectiveness of speed harmonization using connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) in urban mixed traffic depends on both traffic management center (TMC) functionality and the data available for control. Using multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), this study examines whether performance differences among TMC functionality configurations vary with data availability. Three TMC functionality configurations are considered, represented by distinct training and execution paradigms: centralized training and execution (CTE), centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), and decentralized training and execution (DTE). Each configuration is evaluated under standalone autonomous vehicle (SAV), infrastructure-assisted (IA), and fully connected (FC) conditions, representing progressively broader access to onboard sensing, infrastructure data, and planned route information. Experiments are conducted with 20 and 40 simultaneously controlled CAVs in a calibrated microsimulation and supplemented by an FC experiment in the TAVF-Hamburg network, where the existing sensing and communication infrastructure corresponds to the FC condition. CTE achieves the most consistent performance across SAV, IA, and FC, with the strongest overall results under FC. Under SAV and IA conditions with 20 CAVs, CTDE shows pronounced performance degradation, whereas its performance improves substantially with 40 CAVs. The independent-learner DTE configuration exhibits considerable variability in performance across data availability and fleet-size conditions. The results reveal an asymmetric and configuration-dependent relationship between TMC coordination authority and data availability. These findings indicate that institutional constraints on TMC functionality and regulatory restrictions on data access and sharing should be considered jointly when selecting configurations for early CAV deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Despite the odds: assessing Africa’s new social welfare landscape
Authors: Yonatan L. Morse
Abstract: Over the past decades more attention has been given to the growth of social welfare related programs in sub-Saharan Africa. However, to date there are still insufficient empirical observations, which makes it difficult to assess these changes or the factors behind them. This article introduces the Structure of Social Welfare (SSWA) dataset. Rather than rely on spending data, which is sporadically reported, the SSWA gathers data on the design elements of diverse social welfare programs for 44 African countries between 1960 and 2022. These data are used to create indexes of social welfare that take into consideration intended coverage as well as institutional and fiscal sustainability. The SSWA data demonstrates that despite difficult material conditions there is considerably more social welfare in Africa today, but that there is also important variation across countries in terms of the level of commitment. The utility of the SSWA data is then demonstrated by reevaluating the contested impact of democratization on welfare expansion in Africa. The results indicate a positive yet underexplored relationship.

Title: The impact of regional growth on internal migration: a district-level analysis for Malawi
Authors: Mauro Lanati, Rainer Thiele
Abstract: Research on the nexus between development and migration has mainly focused on cross-border flows. How income changes affect migration within developing countries is much less well researched even though addressing this topic might provide essential information about the process of structural transformation needed for economic development. In this paper, we provide new evidence on the link between income growth and internal migration for Malawi, a developing country where migration is predominantly internal. Employing a gravity approach and performing an instrumental variable regression based on a shift-share instrument, we robustly find that, on average, rising incomes – proxied by changes in nightlight intensity – are associated with higher emigration rates. This effect is mainly driven by people emigrating from comparably richer urban areas. In the poorer rural districts, by contrast, migration tends to fall with increasing economic activity, which is in accordance with the notion that poverty may force people to leave their home in response to negative shocks. Our results also suggest a specific sorting pattern: While in urban areas rising incomes mainly facilitate the emigration of lower-skilled people to non-urban destinations, in rural areas it is higher-skilled people who most likely leave their home in response to falling incomes, often moving to urban destinations. This empirical finding is consistent with a standard theoretical model where populations sort themselves geographically on the basis of skills, for which there is relatively higher demand and a higher return in urban areas.

Title: Voluntary sustainability standards and economic and ecological outcomes: panel evidence from Rwanda’s coffee sector
Authors: Marlene Yu Lilin Wätzold, Amanda Cooke, Carolina Ocampo-Ariza, Bruno Paz, Françoise Umarishavu, Meike Wollni

Title: Is it abundance or scarcity? Reassessing freshwater resources and civil war onset (1960–2023)
Authors: Sanggyu Suh

Title: Electric vehicles and driving behavior: evidence from Swedish register and GPS data
Authors: Elisabeth Lång, Emeli Adell, Lena Winslott Hiselius
Abstract: We examine whether electric vehicle (EV) users differ from internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) users in real-world driving behavior, and whether observed patterns arise from trip frequency, trip length, or car and user characteristics. Using evidence from Sweden—a mature EV market—we use register data on annual vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) alongside multi-month GPS travel diaries capturing daily mobility patterns. Register-based estimates indicate that battery electric vehicles (BEVs) have 13–17 % higher annual VKT than comparable ICEVs. Plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) also exhibit higher annual VKT, although the differences are smaller and more sensitive to controls for car characteristics. GPS data show similar patterns: BEV users drive longer daily distances but do not make more trips, whereas the corresponding estimates for PHEVs are generally statistically insignificant. Overall, the higher VKT among EVs may reflect selection into EV adoption or behavioral responses consistent with lower perceived marginal driving costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Pair rationality and top trading cycles on single-peaked and single-dipped domains
Authors: Özgün Ekici, M. Bumin Yenmez
Abstract: In a recent study, Ekici and Bumin Yenmez (2026) characterize top trading cycles (TTC) on the unrestricted domain by strategy-proofness, individual rationality, and pair rationality, uncovering a correspondence between the axiomatic foundations of TTC and deferred acceptance, matching theory’s two canonical rules. We show that their characterization fails on the single-peaked domain, but it holds on the single-dipped domain even without strategy-proofness. They also show that pair rationality can be replaced in their characterization by two weaker conditions concerning agents’ first and second choices. In contrast, this replacement fails on the single-dipped domain, even when strategy-proofness is imposed.

Title: Nonlinear panel data models with robust correlated random effects
Authors: Daniel J. Henderson, Emma Kate Henry, Andros Kourtellos

Title: Pricing over a bundle network
Authors: Trivikram Dokka, Sonali SenGupta

Title: Negative electricity prices and strategic energy storage resources with high renewable penetration
Authors: Zhenhua Zhang, Michael R. Davidson
Abstract: Negative electricity prices are becoming increasingly frequent in electricity markets due to incentive-driven bidding behaviors associated with renewable support schemes. This paper investigates the impact of price-making energy storage resources on market outcomes in the presence of renewable production incentives. We develop a bi-level model to examine three dimensions of strategic storage behavior: system costs and storage profits, electricity prices, and supplier surplus across generators. The upper level represents a storage profit maximization model, and the lower level represents the market operator’s economic dispatch problem. Using the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) system in the U.S. as a case study, we find that strategic storage behaviors increase storage arbitrage profits by 22%–126%, while raising system generation cost by less than 1% relative to a centrally controlled storage benchmark, when storage power capacity equals 14% of peak demand. In addition, negative electricity prices become more frequent due to storage’s capacity withholding mechanisms. Fossil-fueled generators experience surplus gains of up to 3% under strategic storage at high renewable penetration levels with negative price conditions. Future wholesale market designs should explicitly incorporate renewable policy incentive design and strategic storage behaviors, particularly given their joint effects on negative price formation and welfare distribution.

Title: Asymmetric impacts of clean energy investment and Fintech on land degradation: Kernel quantile evidence from Pakistan
Authors: Sami Ullah, Zuopeng Justin Zhang, Runqing Zhu

Title: Responsible AI-driven decision-making for fair and efficient continuity of care among older adults
Authors: Somayeh Ghazalbash, Manaf Zargoush, Vedat Verter, Anand Nair

Title: Efficient auction mechanism for allocation and pricing of cloud manufacturing services
Authors: Jian Chen, Mingyue Sun, Yingqian Zhang, Bentao Su, Naiming Xie
Affiliations: College of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Department of Industrial Engineering & Innovation Sciences, Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven
Abstract: Cloud manufacturing (CMfg) is an emerging service-oriented paradigm that collects dispersed manufacturing resources and provides on-demand services on the cloud platform. From an operational perspective, the major issue in implementing CMfg is how to schedule services to satisfy requests of clients and at what prices. The article designs an efficient one-side Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (O-VCG) auction mechanism to maximize social welfare with truthful bidding from clients. The O-VCG auction mechanism is proved to be incentive compatible, individually rational, approximate allocative efficient, and budget balanced. We consider a centralized operating mode and propose a service allocation model. This service allocation model can achieve an efficient allocation of geographically dispersed services to clients. The computational results show that the proposed O-VCG achieves better social welfare, a higher utility of cloud platform and clients, and a better order completion rate as the number of service windows, the number of clients, and service region increase. We also find that a non-profit-oriented cloud platform can achieve optimal social welfare, while a profit-oriented cloud platform can still yield near optimal social welfare when making profits for itself. A joint cloud platform will yield higher social welfare than several independent cloud platforms, even for the same area size.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Stable matching for long-term carpooling: an approach based on knowledge rules and Benders decomposition
Authors: Tingwen Zheng, Yanping Jiang, Zhan Gao
Affiliations: School of Business Administration, Northeastern University
Abstract: Carpooling can help in fully utilising empty seats by matching drivers and riders, thereby effectively improving transportation utilisation efficiency. This study proposes a stable matching method for long-term carpooling. First, it describes the stable matching problem of long-term carpooling (SMLC) and outlines the relevant definitions of fair stable matching. Second, fair and nearly fair stable matching models are constructed to maximise the matching number of carpooling travellers. Subsequently, a heuristic algorithm based on knowledge rules and Benders decomposition is proposed. Finally, the propose method’s feasibility and effectiveness are verified through numerical experiments.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Enhanced grey relational analysis for structural relationship: an application to economic structure classification
Authors: Hui Li, Naiming Xie, M. Zied Babai
Affiliations: College of Economics and Management, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; Operations Management and Information Systems, Kedge Business School
Abstract: Grey relational analysis (GRA) evaluates the relationship between system variables. However, it is challenging to assess the structure relationship between systems represented by compositional data sequences with fixed sum constraints. To address this issue, the structural correlation degree is studied using the construction concept of Deng’s grey relational degree. First, the point correlation difference in Deng’s correlation is replaced by Aitchison distance to measure the difference between compositional data structures, thereby constructing a novel grey structural relational analysis model based on compositional data with consistent structure. Second, an arithmetic example of the novel model is designed to demonstrate its detailed calculation process. Finally, based on the economic structure data of three major industries from 1998 to 2022, an example analysis of the economic structure correlation between provinces and cities in East China is conducted to show the practicability of the proposed method. This model enriches the analysis of inter-system correlation and broadens the application scope of the GRA model.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Machine learning & fairness: an integrated multicriteria approach for the evaluation of supervised classifiers
Authors: Jean-David Fermanian, Panos Xidonas, Salvatore Corrente
Affiliations: Institut Polytechnique de Paris; ESSCA École de Management; University of Catania
Abstract: Does Multiple Criteria Decision Aiding (MCDA) improve the process of evaluating Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, when critical criteria of fairness are concurrently considered, beyond predictive power? To address this question, we employ several notions of fairness, such as Demographic Parity, Equalized Odds, and Lack of Disparate Mistreatment, and we appraise a set of supervised ML classifiers, under one of the most popular MCDA outranking methods, that is, the Preference Ranking Organization Method for Enrichment Evaluation (PROMETHEE) II. Moreover, to avoid any arbitrary choice in the importance attached to the criteria we apply the Stochastic Multicriteria Acceptability Analysis (SMAA), providing information in statistical terms through simulations. The empirical testing is processed over well-known databases, with several representative sub-datasets, securing variation in terms of observations’ volume. Overall, a series of ranking patterns that persists in the evaluation of the ML classifiers, across the utilized MCDA methodology and datasets, offers valuable relevant insights and documents specific useful interpretations. The obtained findings provide robust support that MCDA can be effectively exploited for the appraisal of ML classifiers, when aiming at the simultaneous consideration of critical fairness metrics, apart from the typical dimensions related to predictive power.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Hybrid Hungarian Algorithm and GVNS metaheuristic for the patient admission scheduling problem
Authors: Rahma Borchani, Malek Masmoudi, Bassem Jarboui
Affiliations: Higher Institute of Business Administration of Gafsa (ISAEG), University of Gafsa; Laboratory of Modeling and Optimization for Decisional, Industrial, and Logistic Systems (MODILS), University of Sfax; College of Engineering, University of Sharjah; University of Jean-Monnet; Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University; Université Polytechnique Hauts-de-France, LAMIH, CNRS, UMR-8201
Abstract: Patient Admission Scheduling involves assigning elective inpatients to hospital beds while considering various constraints such as bed availability, patient medical requirements, departmental and room specifications, patient preferences, and resource utilization. To tackle this complex combinatorial optimization problem, we propose a novel approach combining the Hungarian Algorithm (HA) with the General Variable Neighbourhood Search (GVNS), called HA-GVNS. This method benefits from the strengths of the HA and the iterative improvement capabilities of the GVNS. Extensive experimentation on 12 benchmark instances demonstrates that, in most cases, HA-GVNS outperforms or matches the best solutions of the 24 best state-of-the-art solving techniques. Notably, HA-GVNS effectively balances solution quality with computational efficiency, making it a promising approach for addressing the PAS problem.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Are acquirer stock price reactions to M&A announcements in any way predictable? A machine-learning analysis
Authors: João Quariguasi Frota Neto, Konstantinos Bozos, Marie Dutordoir, Konstantinos Nikolopoulos
Affiliations: Manchester Business School, University of Manchester; Leeds University Business School, University of Leeds; University of Durham
Abstract: We examine whether acquirer stock price reactions to M&A deal announcements can be forecasted based on ex ante acquirer, target, deal, and macroeconomic characteristics. We employ machine learning methodologies with out-of-sample testing and standard cross-validation procedures to assess the forecasting accuracy of various parametric and nonparametric models. While overall predictability is low, nonparametric models exhibit some ability to forecast acquirer stock price reactions to M&A announcements, whereas parametric models do not. Feature importance analyses reveal that a handful of predictors, including acquirer size and (relative) deal size, contribute most to the predictions. Our findings have practical implications for corporate managers and various corporate stakeholders.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: From individual intention to network diffusion: investigating the spread of green travel behavior intention within a scale-free network based on TPB
Authors: Ranran Yang, Jing Wang, Si Zhou, Aoqi Wang
Affiliations: School of Management, Hefei University of Technology; Philosophy and Social Sciences Laboratory of Data Science and Smart Society Governance, Ministry of Education
Abstract: Green travel, as a sustainable mode of transportation, plays a crucial role in promoting low-carbon urban lifestyles. This study investigates the factors influencing urban residents’ green travel intentions and the diffusion of such intentions within social networks. Based on an extended Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and using survey data from 817 respondents in the Yangtze River Delta region, we construct a behavioral interaction model to examine how individual-level psychological factors affect green travel intentions. Furthermore, we incorporate these findings into a scale-free network simulation to explore how individual intentions evolve into collective behavioral patterns. The results show that subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and perceived behavioral results significantly influence interpersonal promotion of green travel. Simulation results reveal that reducing the threshold for social information interaction and enhancing perceived behavioral results coefficient can effectively accelerate the spread of green travel behavior within urban communities. These findings provide theoretical and practical insights for policymakers aiming to design targeted interventions and foster large-scale adoption of sustainable travel practices through social influence mechanisms.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A novel hybrid optimization framework for short-term mine production scheduling: synergizing linear programming relaxation and genetic algorithms
Authors: Pranjal Pathak, Biswajit Samanta
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur
Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid optimization methodology by embedding Linear Programming Techniques within Genetic Algorithms to efficiently solve real-scale instances of short-term mine production scheduling problem. The methodology involves the linear programming relaxation of the mixed-integer programming model of the short-term mine production scheduling problem and deploying a priority mechanism developed in this work to construct feasible schedules. This process of schedule generation is then embedded within the customized genetic algorithms to efficiently solve the industrial scale instances of short-term mine production scheduling problem. Computational experiments demonstrate that proposed hybrid optimization framework is an efficient framework to obtain near-optimal solutions to large-scale instances of short-term mine production scheduling problem within a reasonable computation time.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Sensitivity of model parameter estimates in stress testing the probability of default: evidence over the financial crisis
Authors: Zheqi Wang, Jonathan Crook, Galina Andreeva
Affiliations: Hunan University; University of Edinburgh Business School
Abstract: We extend a Bayesian method for predicting Value at Risk (VaR) for credit risk by incorporating not only macroeconomic uncertainty, but also parameter uncertainty (including parameter instability over time and parameter estimation uncertainty). We apply this method to estimate the capital required by banks to cover credit risk. By simulating default rate distributions based on models built on crisis and tranquil periods, we explore how shifts in model parameters across economic conditions influence stress testing results. We use parameter posterior distributions from the Bayesian framework in VaR computation to mitigate estimation risk arising from reliance on point estimates. In an illustration for mortgages our results show that accounting for parameter instability and estimation uncertainty increases the required capital by over 170%.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Enhanced fuel consumption prediction using dimensionality reduction and ensemble learning
Authors: Sajan Shaikh, Shuyan Chen, Rajasekhar Balasubramanian, Yongfeng Ma, Aamir Hussain, Qianqian Pang
Affiliations: Southeast University; National University of Singapore
Abstract: Accurate fuel consumption prediction is crucial for focusing on pressing environmental concerns, optimising fuel efficiency, and reducing operational costs in the transportation sector. Despite its importance, existing prediction models often struggle with high dimensionality, complexity, and low computational speed, simultaneously achieving high prediction accuracy. To address these gaps, this study explores an approach using Vehicle Energy Data to predict the fuel consumption of Internal Combustion Engine vehicles with enhanced performance. Firstly, the Autoencoder was used on a large real-world vehicle energy dataset to convert into a low-dimensional spaces. Secondly, low-dimensional data was fed to the Extreme Gradient Boosting model to predict fuel consumption accurately. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model, its performance was compared with state-of-the-art approaches. The results revealed that the proposed model performs better than other state-of-the-art models with 98% accuracy. Further sensitivity analysis disclosed that the proposed model simultaneously reduces the computational complexity and increases the predictive performance of the downstream model. The study demonstrates an effective and innovative method for analysing fuel consumption during real vehicle operating conditions in terms of accuracy and real-time capability. This study can be applied to other high-dimensional data to extract various insights regarding fuel consumption.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Robust de novo programming models for supporting site selection decisions in renewable energy
Authors: Noureddine Kouaissah, Hanane Ait Lahoussine Ouali, Tarik Aouam
Affiliations: Africa Business School, Mohammed VI Polytechnic University; African Sustainable Agriculture Research Institute (ASARI), Mohammed VI Polytechnic University; Faculty of Economics and Business Administration, Ghent University
Abstract: This paper develops novel robust de novo programming models to accurately select optimal locations for concentrated solar power (CSP) plants under high levels of uncertainty. The CSP selection problem is a typical uncertain multi-objective decision-making (MODM) optimal design challenge that involves conflicting environmental, societal, and economic criteria. This paper makes the following contributions: (i) it develops robust counterparts to the conventional de novo programming (DNP) model and its meta-goal programming solution procedure to address a wide range of decision-making problems under conditions of uncertainty, (ii) it proposes a robust revised multi-choice DNP model, and (iii) it contributes to ongoing debates on sustainable development and clean energy transitions by identifying optimal locations for CSP plants in Morocco. The proposed robust methodologies provide decision-makers with increased flexibility for addressing uncertainty in MODM problems, allowing them to express their level of conservatism and preferences by setting priority weights, defining aspiration levels, and merging original explicit goals into meta-goals. Finally, the hypothetical application illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed formulations and demonstrates that they can assist decision-makers in identifying the optimal locations for CSP plants in Morocco under high levels of uncertainty.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Data-Driven Dynamic Pricing: Sticky Fairness Concerns and the Exploitation-Exploration Trade-Off
Authors: Himanshu Rathore, Sunil Tiwari
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Lucknow; University of Bristol Business School, University of Bristol
Abstract: In online retail, pricing policies are often implemented when the demand for a product is unknown. This stream of work is known as dynamic pricing with demand learning. Such dynamic pricing policies are usually based on resolving exploitation-exploration trade-offs prevalent in sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Should a price be revised based on the realised revenues in prior history, or should it be revised based on the promise of a better performance in the future? We examine whether prices should be selected solely based on apparent revenue consideration or should they also account for the behavioural underpinnings of the purchase intention. This paper proposes a data-driven dynamic pricing policy based on reinforcement learning that maximises revenues while incorporating the cumulative (un)fairness concerns based on customers’ prior experience with previous price revisions. Cumulative (un)fairness accumulates (un)fairness for all prior price revisions and is termed as ‘sticky’ fairness concerns. We find that the proposed policy favours implementing smaller prices compared to higher prices in realising higher revenues. We test this counterintuitive finding by conducting numerical and lab experiments in various demand settings. The proposed dynamic pricing policy demonstrates logarithmic regret in time.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Project portfolio selection and scheduling considering net present value and delayed delivery
Authors: Hongbo Li, Zhijie Yuan, Manman Yang, Zhaoying Yuan, Xianchao Zhang
Affiliations: School of Management, Shanghai University; Key Laboratory of Medical Electronics and Digital Health of Zhejiang Province, Jiaxing University; Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Human Health Situation Awareness of Zhejiang Province, Jiaxing University
Abstract: In project management, the rational selection of project portfolios and the effective scheduling of scarce resources directly affect the project’s revenue and delivery time, constituting a critical factor in ensuring project success. Therefore, we propose and investigate the bi-objective project portfolio selection and scheduling problem (BOPPSSP) with the objective of maximising the net present value and minimising the total delay cost of the portfolio. In the BOPPSSP, we also consider project revenue reinvestment as well as the exclusive and complementary relationships among projects and their impacts on the portfolio’s cash flow. We formulate a bi-objective integer programming model for the BOPPSSP. To efficiently solve the NP-Hard BOPPSSP, we design an improved non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm III (iNSGA-III) by incorporating problem-specific components such as schedule encoding and decoding mechanisms, chromosome selection, and neighbourhood search. Based on large-scale computational experiments, the performance of our iNSGA-III algorithm is analysed and compared with the exact solver CPLEX and three baseline meta-heuristic algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms both CPLEX and the baseline meta-heuristics in most scenarios.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Assessment of renewable energy systems through the integrated SWARA-LOPCOW-EDAS decision-making method with a novel Fermatean fuzzy scoring function
Authors: Madhumita Behera, Amaresh Chandra Panda
Affiliations: C.V. Raman Global University
Abstract: This study proposes a novel Fermatean fuzzy (FF) multi-criteria decision-making framework to evaluate renewable energy systems under uncertainty, focusing on sustainable development and efficient energy utilisation. The novelty lies in developing a new scoring function for FF sets that enhances the differentiation of closely ranked alternatives and in extending step-wise weight assessment ratio analysis and logarithmic percentage change-driven objective weighting methods into the FF domain for computing subjective and objective weights, respectively. The integrated framework employs the distance-based evaluation from average solution method to rank five renewable sources, solar, wind, hydro, biomass, and geothermal across four sustainability main criteria and eighteen sub-criteria. Data are collected through structured expert surveys involving professionals from the renewable energy sector. The analysis identifies policy alignment (weight: 0.09985) and emission reduction potential (weight: 0.07838) as the most influential criteria. Solar energy ranks highest with a performance score of 0.83208, followed by wind (0.65355), while biomass scores lowest (0.24781). Sensitivity and comparative analyses validate the robustness and consistency of the proposed model. The results suggest prioritising solar and wind energy and offer actionable insights for policymakers to develop resilient and uncertainty-aware renewable energy strategies.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Sequential three-way decision on Euclidean distance-based EDAS (Evaluation Based on Distance from Average Solution) method for last-mile logistics applications
Authors: Bea Ubod, Dylan Jones, Ashraf Labib, Lanndon Ocampo
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering, Cebu Technological University; Center for Applied Mathematics and Operations Research, Cebu Technological University; Centre for Operational Research and Logistics, University of Portsmouth; School of Mathematics and Physics, Faculty of Technology, University of Portsmouth; Faculty of Business and Law, University of Portsmouth
Abstract: As a popular approach to last-mile delivery, third-party logistics (3PL) has drawn much attention in managing supply chains. Due to the presence of multiple factors, 3PL service provider evaluation is a multi-criteria decision-making problem. This study introduces methodological enhancements to the EDAS (Evaluation based on Distance from the Average Solution) method to generate more intuitive insights into decision-making. First, instead of the L1-metric, we introduced Euclidean-based EDAS (EDAS-E) to capture the underlying geometry of the space generated by a relatively high number of decision criteria in more comprehensive 3PL provider evaluations. Second, adopting the notion of “thinking in threes,” we developed an algorithm to implement a sequential three-way decision (3WD) that addresses ambiguity and provides more explainability in the evaluation process. An actual case study evaluating five 3PL service providers under 17 criteria demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed sequential 3WD-EDAS-E, aiding decision-makers to systematically distinguish between acceptable and unacceptable alternatives and those requiring further evaluation. The comparative analysis yields a high agreement between the results generated by the proposed approach and those of other multi-criteria methods. Finally, implications for the field of decision making and avenues for future research are detailed.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Optimal trade credit strategies for capital-constrained suppliers
Authors: Qiangqiang Wang
Affiliations: Dongbei University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: This paper examines how trade credit adoption influences the profitability of capital-constrained suppliers. We develop a game-theoretic model with two suppliers and one retailer, incorporating liquidity risk, accounting periods, and competition. The analysis shows that offering trade credit does not always reduce supplier profits relative to cash transactions; it can be beneficial when liquidity risk is low or accounting periods are extended. Although trade credit may create free-riding effects, competition helps mitigate them. Uniform adoption lowers supplier profits, while heterogeneous adoption has mixed outcomes depending on liquidity risk and competition intensity. When competition is low, trade-credit adoption by a low-risk supplier reduces profits for all suppliers, whereas adoption by a high-risk supplier benefits the offering supplier but harms its rival. Under intense competition, all suppliers’ profits decline. For the retailer, trade credit may also be disadvantageous, particularly under monopoly or low competition with high-risk suppliers. This study provides valuable insights for suppliers by highlighting the complex effects of trade credit in competitive markets. Suppliers should carefully assess liquidity risk and accounting periods, while factoring in competitive dynamics when deciding whether to offer trade credit.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: FOMC Supply-Side Communication and Long-Term Inflation Expectations
Authors: Abhinay Mishra, Kshitij Bhalchandra Shingwekar

Title: On the Strategic Benefits of Diversity in Teamwork and other Aggregative Games
Authors: Martin Kaae Jensen

Title: Channel competition in airline distribution: A game-theoretic analysis of Global Distribution System and New Distribution Capability
Authors: Yutao Guo, Changmin Jiang, Ruotian Chen, Hongwei Wang
Abstract: This paper examines how New Distribution Capability (NDC) reshapes the airline distribution value chain long dominated by Global Distribution Systems (GDS). We build a three-tier game-theoretic model of airline, technology provider, and travel agency across four structures—GDS monopoly, NDC monopoly, dual-channel competition, and incumbent-led integration—to identify the mechanisms of channel competition and incumbent transformation. Results show that GDS incentives are neutral in the benchmark model: fee adjustments and pass-through leave final prices and demand unchanged, helping explain the persistence of legacy models. Under an NDC monopoly, airlines have stronger incentives to invest in service quality, while agencies shift from rebate recipients to paying users. With GDS–NDC competition, platform fees fall and allocative efficiency improves; NDC’s technological edge is non-linear, as aggregators may employ penetration pricing once quality crosses a threshold. Incumbent-led integration—where a GDS operates both the legacy GDS and an NDC channel—internalizes inter-channel rivalry and restores monopoly pricing power. Welfare results reveal a trade-off: competition raises efficiency via lower fees, whereas incumbent-led integration can deliver higher dynamic welfare when technology-upgrade costs are low, despite stronger pricing power. Further extensions examine endogenous quality choice, fee rigidity, and NDC-exclusive ancillary bundling. They show how market structure shapes long-run airline quality investment, demonstrate that constrained GDS fees can turn agency incentives into a competitive instrument, and indicate that differentiated bundles strengthen NDC demand while making content access central to the welfare assessment of integration. Guided by these results, we propose a staged regulatory path: foster interoperability and entry when adoption costs are high; protect contestability during consolidation; and, at maturity, shift from price control to performance-based oversight.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: An energy-efficient coordinated procurement, production, and batch delivery scheduling system for sustainable operations with Net-Zero emissions
Authors: Sayem Ahmed, Ripon Kumar Chakrabortty, Alireza Abbasi, Tsan-Ming Choi
Abstract: Over the last decade, rising energy prices, global warming, the harmful effects of energy use, and carbon emissions have highlighted the importance of energy and carbon efficiency. In response to local energy regulations and carbon-sensitive markets, manufacturers and logistics organizations are actively seeking effective methods to improve energy and carbon efficiency. This research enhances supply chain planning and scheduling by combining procurement, production, and delivery decisions to support sustainable operations through simultaneously optimizing costs, energy consumption, and carbon emissions. An E nergy- E fficient C oordinated P roduction- D istribution S ystem ( EE-CPDS ) is designed, accounting for a flexible job-shop scheduling environment with inter-machine transport times and sequence-dependent setup times to reflect real production configurations. To address the computational challenge, we propose a novel multi-objective adaptive search memetic algorithm (MOASMA) that outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of solution quality, i.e., generating global solutions closer to true Pareto front with average hypervolume (HV) value of 0.7131 and Inverted Generational Distance Plus (IGD + ) value of 0.0249 across nine test instances, which is further endorsed by nonparametric statistical analysis. Among the instances solved by all competing algorithms, MOASMA provides better solutions for 77% of them. The correctness and effectiveness of the developed algorithm are verified by comparing the results with an exact solver (Gurobi), which is effective for small and medium-sized instances, while MOASMA proves efficient for larger-scale problems. The proposed system and algorithm will assist enterprises in solving practical-sized instances while rationalizing coordinated procurement, production, and distribution decisions that support sustainable operations and drive progress toward net-zero emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Defensive decoupling and resilience redistribution in the global power battery supply chain: A cascading failure framework with a context-dependent supplier rupture mechanism
Authors: Chao Wang, Sining Ma, Ming K. Lim
Abstract: Compliance and geopolitical pressures can destabilize supply relationships even when production capacity remains intact. Yet downstream continuity may reveal little about losses elsewhere in the supply chain. When interfirm transaction flows are unobserved, it is difficult to assess how defensive sourcing decisions and constrained reallocation shape these uneven outcomes. This study develops a cascading-failure framework integrating gravity-style flow reconstruction, context-dependent supplier rupture with nonlinear interference effects, constrained order reallocation, and overload and throughput-depletion exits. Flow reconstruction combines product–tier-normalized firm-scale proxies, technical coefficients, political alignment, and geographical distance. The framework is applied to a disclosed-core power-battery supply network of 295 firms and 615 directed relationships. Matched-edge Pearson and full-matrix QAP comparisons assess the reconstructed flows, while benchmarks, ablations, and sensitivity analyses examine cascade dynamics. In the focal reconstruction-origin stress test, eight of nine EU-facing terminal firms survive despite 75 firm exits, 70 caused by throughput depletion. Defensive rupture drives structural deterioration, while reallocation supports terminal-firm survival and network-wide survival. These asymmetric outcomes primarily reflect endogenous adjustment: the six initial compliance disconnections add approximately 0.07 percentage points to weighted flow loss. Separate interventions on model-stationary networks show that screening can induce additional exits, depending on behavioral settings, the pre-intervention network, and ESG-update rules. Sobol analysis identifies distinct parameter influences on modeled activity loss, fragmentation, and survival. The findings explain how relationship decisions and constrained adaptation produce uneven resilience across tiers, supporting whole-chain assessment that distinguishes ongoing network adjustment from the additional effects of compliance intervention.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Hot–cold reciprocation gaps
Authors: Riccardo Ghidoni, Sigrid Suetens, Jierui Yang
Affiliations: University of Bologna; Tilburg University; Xiangtan University
Abstract: Abstract We study whether and why the mode of decision-making affects reciprocation in a binary trust game, using three preregistered online experiments. Trustees – some of whom were exogenously induced to be surprised by trust – either decided whether to reciprocate after observing their partner’s choice ( hot mode) or committed in advance to a contingent response plan ( cold mode). In our Baseline experiment, once participants gained experience, reciprocation became more likely under hot than under cold decision-making, especially when trust was unlikely – consistent with a model in which positive surprise at being trusted increases the utility of reciprocating. Results from the other two experiments show that surprise promotes reciprocation only when trust reflects an intentional choice by the trustor and when cognitive load in the decision environment is not too high.

Title: Testing capacity-constrained learning
Authors: Andrew Caplin, Daniel Martin, Philip Marx, Anastasiia Morozova, Leshan Xu
Affiliations: New York University; University of California, Santa Barbara; Louisiana State University
Abstract: Abstract We introduce a general test of capacity-constrained learning models. Learning has capacity constraints when the set of possible ways to learn is exogenously fixed, as in the widely used fixed-capacity versions of rational inattention (Sims, 2003) and efficient coding (Woodford, 2012). With such models, changes in incentives do not alter the extent of attention, only how individuals decide to allocate their scarce attention. We show that choice data are consistent with capacity-constrained learning if and only if they satisfy a No Improving (Action or Attention) Switches (NIS) condition. Based on existing experiments in which the incentives for being correct are varied, we find strong evidence that participants fail NIS for a wide range of standard perceptual tasks: identifying the proportion of ball colors, recognizing shapes, and counting the number of balls. We further show that violations of NIS occur systematically in response to higher incentives, suggesting that incentives often expand attention beyond what capacity-constrained models allow. However, we find that this is not true for all existing perceptual tasks in the literature, which offers insights into settings where we do or do not expect incentives to impact the extent of attention.

Title: Platform financing and government subsidies for heterogeneous smallholder farmers under yield uncertainty
Authors: Shuchen Ni, Chun Feng
Affiliations: School of Transportation and Logistics, Southwest Jiaotong University; National United Engineering Laboratory of Integrated and Intelligent Transportation
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Exploring the distribution and evolution of decision-making autonomy for plants in international manufacturing networks: embedded case studies from the machinery industry
Authors: Yang Cheng, Tao Huang, John Johansen, Jan Olhager
Affiliations: Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; School of Business Administration, Jiangxi University of Finance and Economics; Department of Industrial and Mechanical Sciences, Lund University

Title: Generative artificial intelligence and international green supply chain performance: dynamic capabilities as strategic enablers
Authors: Shaofeng Wang, Hao Zhang
Affiliations: Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade International Business School, , Fuzhou, , and School of Management, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China; Zhejiang Shuren University School of Economics and Management, , Hangzhou
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption is associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage in cross-border e-commerce enterprises. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and the Technology–Organization–Environment–Human framework, the authors examine absorptive capacity and transformative capacity as intermediate capability mechanisms and artificial intelligence turbulence as a contingency. Design/methodology/approach The authors use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative strand combines survey data from 334 Chinese cross-border e-commerce enterprises with partial least squares structural equation modeling, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and importance-performance map analysis. The subsequent qualitative strand draws on semi-structured interviews with ten managers and executives directly involved in GAI implementation, which are integrated with the quantitative evidence at the interpretation stage. Findings GAI adoption is positively associated with absorptive and transformative capacities, which are in turn positively associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage. International green supply chain performance shows the largest estimated association with international competitive advantage. Artificial intelligence turbulence positively moderates the relationships between GAI adoption and both capacities, and the configurational analysis identifies five equifinal configurations sufficient for high international competitive advantage. Practical implications Managers should develop absorptive and transformative capacities alongside GAI implementation, integrate sustainability requirements into artificial intelligence-enabled supply chain decisions and pursue internally coherent implementation routes rather than a single ideal template. Originality/value This study integrates variance-based, configurational and qualitative evidence to explain the capability pathways through which GAI adoption is associated with environmental and competitive outcomes in cross-border supply chain settings rather than in dyadic buyer–supplier relationships.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Geometric portfolio equilibria: constraint curvature and asset pricing
Authors: Massimiliano Ferrara
Abstract: Institutional investors optimise over feasible sets whose shape is dictated by regulation and mandate. This paper asks whether the intrinsic geometry of those sets, as distinct from the shadow cost of the constraints that define them, carries independent information for equilibrium prices. We answer the question in two steps. First, we show that the position limits and linear matching requirements most commonly invoked in this literature generate polyhedral feasible sets whose smooth strata are affine and therefore intrinsically flat, so that no curvature mechanism can be attributed to them; the correct analytical tools there are tangent and normal cones and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker multipliers. Second, we isolate a class of genuinely nonlinear constraints, of which the active boundary of a quadratic rebalancing budget is the leading case, whose transversal intersection with the wealth constraint is a smooth submanifold of dimension $$N-2$$ N - 2 with non-vanishing sectional curvature. On that class we formulate a competitive equilibrium with price impact, prove existence and uniqueness under an explicit curvature domination condition, and derive a three-term decomposition of expected excess returns into a zero-beta rate, a classical covariance premium, and a curvature term that is written explicitly as a second fundamental form contracted with the multiplier vector. A fully specified four-asset example computes every object in the decomposition in closed form and shows that the curvature term vanishes when the constraint is replaced by its tangent hyperplane, which separates it from the shadow cost of a binding constraint. An empirical exercise on S&P 500 index funds documents a priced constraint-proximity factor that is not spanned by the Fama–French–Carhart factors; we interpret this factor as a measure of crowding near regulatory limits rather than as an estimate of Riemannian curvature, and we state the conditions under which the two coincide.

Title: Kalman Filter Learning, Bounded Rationality and Informational Consistency
Authors: Szabolcs Deák, Paul Levine, Joseph Pearlman, Bo Yang
Affiliations: Department of Economics University of Exeter Exeter UK; School of Social Sciences, Economics University of Surrey Guildford UK; Department of Economics City St George's, University of London London UK; Department of Economics Swansea University Swansea UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a behavioural New Keynesian model with rational (RE) and boundedly rational (BR) agents. The latter are anticipated utility learners and use simple heuristic rules to forecast aggregate variables exogenous to their micro‐environment. For the RE agents, we study two information assumptions: standard perfect information and imperfect information (II‐involving Kalman‐filter learning). We show that a consistent set of II for the modeller and the private sector generates endogenous persistence of decisions in response to unobserved exogenous shocks and thus RE under II dominates the BR specifications in empirical comparisons. We reveal substantial evidence of composite RE(II)‐BR structure with estimated proportions of RE and BR agents. Our results highlight the importance of informational consistency for the analysis of behavioural heterogeneity.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Childbirth Effects of the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami
Authors: Elizabeth Kayoon Hur, Seung‐hun Lee
Affiliations: Department of Economics Michigan State University East Lansing Michigan USA; Taipei School of Economics National Tsing Hua University Hsinchu Taiwan
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper evaluates the effect of in utero exposure to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami on birth outcomes in Indonesia. Exploiting variation in the timing of exposure, we find that the probability of a successful pregnancy drops by 5.4 percentage points (pp), while miscarriages increase by 5.0 pp for those exposed in the first trimester of pregnancy. Gestation length shortens by 0.28 months, and the likelihood of preterm birth rises by 5.4 pp. We find suggestive evidence that post‐disaster health investments by households may have shielded later cohorts from harmful effects, while measures of maternal health and socioeconomic status have limited explanatory power. Our results suggest the importance of considering fetal loss as a first‐order cost in natural disasters and highlight that facilitating household investment in health through various policies may mitigate negative birth effects in the aftermath.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Scaffolding the void: Digital platforms as intermediaries in supply chain traceability
Authors: Quynh Do, Claudia Colicchia, Alessandro Creazza, Mark Stevenson, Stella Viscardi
Abstract: In response to the escalating regulatory and normative demands for supply chain traceability and transparency, digital platforms offer a novel solution that overcomes the limitations of the conventional, siloed approach to managing opaque, multi-tiered supply networks. However, little is known about how these third-party intermediaries help firms address supplier resistance and relational deficits inherent in multi-tier supply chains. This research addresses this gap by developing an empirically grounded framework that explains the scaffolding roles of digital platform organizations. Employing an abductive, multiple-case study approach, we analyze four use cases of traceability-oriented platforms within the garment and footwear sectors. Our findings first reveal that traceability challenges constitute an institutional void, a space where rapid legislative advancement outpaces existing norms and shared understandings in the industry. This in turn creates architectural, cognitive, and relational deficits that hinder traceability efforts. We then uncover three scaffolding mechanisms in which platforms enable firms to bridge these gaps: constructing interoperability layers, interpreting legislative demands to bridge cognitive gaps, and mediating relational trust. This study contributes to institutional theory and supply chain literature by showing how platforms scaffold socio-technical change to embed traceability practices in multi-tier settings. We also provide a strategic guide for managers to leverage platform networks to trace their supply chains.

Title: Material use and its relationship with per capita income. A panel data analysis at the global level
Authors: Tommaso Luzzati, Emilio Padilla Rosa, Bhavesh Gulati, Vicente Rios, Angela Parenti, Stefan Giljum
Abstract: Global use of materials has significantly increased over recent decades, causing a wide range of environmental and social concerns. In this study, we use the latest available data from the UN database on global material flows to investigate the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis for two widely used material flow indicators, Domestic Material Consumption and Material Footprint, for a dataset of 147 countries. Using both semiparametric and parametric methods over a longer period than any previous study (1970–2019), we find no evidence in support of the EKC hypothesis. A concerning result is that material-income elasticities are higher after 1989, implying that the situation has not improved. We conclude that major changes have not yet occurred in the income-material use relationship and that strong policy measures remain necessary to reduce material consumption.

Title: Street-scale heat exposure mapping for urban cyclists: Integrating vision transformer-GAN with aggregated Strava cycling activity data
Authors: Jin Rui, Zhaowen Xu
Abstract: Street-scale variation in the thermal environment is difficult to represent using spatially coarse meteorological data, limiting the assessment of cycling environments during extreme heat. This study develops a street-scale heat-exposure mapping framework and applies it alongside aggregated cycling activity records in Melbourne. The framework combines street-view imagery and environmental metadata using a Vision Transformer and a conditional generative adversarial network to predict calibrated operative-temperature-equivalent fields. These fields serve as environmental heat-exposure proxies. Direct assessment of thermal comfort and physiological heat stress requires additional subjective and physiological observations. The model achieved a mean absolute error of 3.42°C against calibrated reference label fields on the independent test set. Analysis of 35,416 street-view images identified six landscape types, with higher predicted exposure in dense built-up environments and lower exposure in green-dominated environments. Multi-kernel support vector regression was used to examine the predictive importance of streetscape indicators, while aggregated Strava records from 4 to 13 March 2024 were used to compare cycling activity during the heatwave and adjacent comparison days. The principal contribution is a framework for characterising fine-scale environmental heat-exposure patterns and supporting their investigation alongside cycling activity. Its application informs the screening of potentially heat-vulnerable cycling environments, while the short observation window and aggregate data limit inference about individual adaptation and causal effects.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: “Made in heaven, matched by parents”: Can arranged marriage restrict labour market autonomy and participation of women?
Authors: Sugata Bag, Anirban Kar
Abstract: Female labour force participation in India has stagnated despite gains in other aspects. Do Indian women prefer to stay out of labour market voluntarily or do social norms prevent their participation? We identify parental involvement in partner choice during marriage as an important bottleneck. We first find that women who had some degree of involvement in partner choice enjoy significantly more autonomy in post-marriage labour market choices than those whose marriages were arranged solely by parents. We use a marriage tradition instrument to estimate causal effects. Since autonomy and participation affect each other, next, we estimate simultaneous equations for autonomy and participation for only rural women. We use parental involvement in marriage and district-level share of drought-affected villages as two exogenous variables the former for autonomy and the latter for participation. We find that autonomy significantly increases participation. We further explain the mechanism through a theoretical model. To distinguish between autonomy and participation; we introduce a new household delegation game. The main message of the theoretical model is that parental involvement in partner choice reduces women’s ability to screen partners leading to relatively more mismatches, i.e., women who are inclined to work mismatched with men who prefer

Title: Invisible bridge: Digital infrastructure, energy transition, and energy poverty
Authors: Shunlin Jin, Shuai Shao, Weidong Wang, Yuanren Zhou
Abstract: We study the effect of digital infrastructure on household energy poverty. We develop a theoretical framework in which digital infrastructure reduces labor-market and information frictions, raising household income and improving access to modern energy technologies. Using the rollout of China's largest national digital infrastructure program, the Broadband China Pilot (BCP) policy, and multiple micro-household tracking datasets, we find that the policy alleviates household energy poverty by approximately 2.7 percentage points in treated cities. The effect operates mainly through higher off-farm income and improved access to modern energy equipment, and is stronger in poorer and more remote markets. A distinctive rural survey dataset shows that digital connectivity also benefits older households with limited off-farm employment opportunities through neighbor-assisted transfer arrangements involving adult children and nearby connected households, while generating village-level information spillovers in modern energy equipment adoption. The findings highlight the role of digital infrastructure in promoting household energy transition and reducing energy poverty.

Title: When mortality jumps: Optimal portfolio design for defined contribution pension schemes
Authors: Davide Feleppa, Immacolata Oliva
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Identification of priority areas for inclusive automated vehicle infrastructure investment
Authors: Arkar Than Win, John D. Nelson, Chinh Ho
Abstract: Highly automated vehicles (AVs) have the potential to improve mobility for older adults and people with disabilities. Planning for AVs requires substantial infrastructure investments, but limited resources make simultaneous upgrades impractical. Understanding how potential mobility gains differ by locations is useful for targeting investments, yet little is known about these differences. To address this gap, this study uses propensity score matching with moderation analysis to examine how built environment characteristics moderate the potential impacts of AVs on trip frequencies of older adults and people with disabilities using two Australian datasets. Findings suggest that potential mobility gains vary by location. Potential mobility gains for people with disabilities are larger in areas with low density, public transport accessibility, diversity, and high cumulative accessibility; whereas those for older adults are greater in areas with high cumulative accessibility and road connectivity. These findings provide guidance for prioritising AV-related infrastructure investments to promote social inclusion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Where is the Swiss safe haven? Geopolitical risk, bank deposits and custody portfolios
Authors: Dimitris Anastasiou, Athanasios Michairinas, Steven Ongena, Athanasios Sakkas
Abstract: Switzerland is the archetypal financial safe haven, yet its bank deposits do not behave like one. Using Swiss National Bank data, we find no robust positive deposit response to geopolitical risk. The clearer response appears in custody portfolios. After a one-standard-deviation rise in European geopolitical risk, the non-resident equity share falls by 1.16 p.p. relative to the resident share after two years, while the bond and money-market share rises by 0.78 p.p. after one year and 0.68 p.p. after two years. Global geopolitical threats and acts generate opposite relative-share responses, a pattern consistent with precautionary de-risking.

Title: A regional multi-criteria assessment of European education and training systems
Authors: Fernando J. Osório, Luís C. Dias
Abstract: This paper proposes a multi-criteria sorting and ranking approach based on ELECTRE TRI to assess educational performance across 200 European regions, across the 2020-2024 period. The analysis relies on criteria from early childhood education to adult learning within the European Union’s Education and Training 2030 (ET2030) framework. To address uncertainty in preference-related parameters, the worst and best categories each region can attain over an admissible parameter space are identified using linear programming. Rankings are obtained under pessimistic and optimistic perspectives, both derived to be consistent with the sorting results.
