The results are complemented with a SMAA-TRI analysis producing category acceptability indices, which are further aggregated to yield alternative compatible rankings. Through four modelling scenarios, the study examines the effects of imposing veto thresholds and a partial order on criteria weights favouring earlier education stages. The results reveal a persistent geographical divide, with lagging regions concentrated in Romania and southern Italy, and top performers mainly in Northern and Western Europe. The greatest improvements were observed across Ireland, Poland, Sweden, Hungary, and Croatia, while Romania remains stagnant and most German regions declined.

Title: Assessing the resilience of international multimodal container transport networks from a perspective of temporal accessibility
Authors: Yifan Zhu, Mengqiao Xu, Ran Yan, Adolf K.Y. Ng
Abstract: Multimodal container transport has become the predominant mode for international freight movement, but its supporting transport infrastructure is under threat from various risks. Therefore, accurately assessing the resilience of the international multimodal container transport network is critical to countries’ trade and economic development. This paper proposes a framework for assessing the resilience of international multimodal container transport networks (IMCTNs) that integrate road, inland rail, and international maritime shipping. First, an algorithm is developed to identify time-respecting international multimodal transport paths while considering transfer and schedule constraints. Based on these paths, the framework defines temporal accessibility metrics for international multimodal transport under two common multimodal modes (i.e., road-rail-sea and road-sea) at both the 10-km grid level and the city level. Second, the proposed accessibility metrics serve as performance indicators for evaluating the resilience of countries’ international multimodal transport networks against disruption risks. Finally, the effectiveness of this framework is illustrated through an application to a real IMCTN in Mainland China. The accessibility analysis reveals clear regional disparities, with a general decline from east to west and south to north under the two multimodal modes, and with clear daily variations in low-accessibility areas under the road-rail-sea mode. Analysis of this network’s resilience under a typical disaster scenario reveals that local disasters could have a nationwide impact, and areas with better infrastructure access, higher GDP, and greater distance from the disruption sources would exhibit higher resilience. These findings have important implications for enhancing the accessibility and improving the risk management of international multimodal container transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A model-based systems engineering framework for integrated asset information modelling and simulation
Authors: Shouxuan Wu, Chao Yang, Yufan Liu, Haoxuan Zhang, Zhen Zhang, David B. Cameron, Foivos Psarommatis, Arild Waaler, Dimitris Kiritsis, Yuanwei Qu, Guoxin Wang, Jinzhi Lu
Affiliations: Beijing Institute of Technology; University of Oslo; Aalto University; École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne; Beihang University

Title: Economics of ad-blocking: An analysis of customer incentivization and whitelisting content provider models
Authors: Ayesha Arora, Tarun Jain
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Calcutta; Indian Institute of Management Bangalore
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Revisiting the ordinal priority approach in multi-attribute decision-making: A centralized DEA-based preference voting interpretation
Authors: Renlong Wang
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Rice University; School of Emergency Management Science and Engineering, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The impact of AI investment on shipping outsourcing strategies for easing congestion under coastal piggybacking regulation
Authors: Naimeng Liu, Cheng Zhang, Bin Liu
Abstract: This paper examines the strategic interactions among AI adoption, shipping outsourcing mode selection, and coastal piggybacking (CPB) regulation in a multi-level shipping supply chain consisting of a cargo agent (CA), a liner shipping company (LS), a flag-of-convenience carrier (FOC), and a transshipment port (FOT). We develop a game-theoretic model in which AI serves dual roles: it enhances demand forecasting accuracy (information-precision effect) and reduces service time (service-time reduction effect). The cargo agent chooses between consignment and turnkey contracting under different information structures. We find that AI generates opposing effects on the CA’s outsourcing preference: the information-precision effect favors turnkey, while the service-time reduction effect favors consignment, leading to a counterintuitive outcome in which advanced AI makes consignment more attractive. The LS’s AI investment is profitable only under certain conditions and depends critically on the learning efficiency of the technology, revealing an asymmetry in how AI affects the LS versus the CA. Furthermore, AI improves social welfare only when congestion is sufficiently severe; otherwise, its demand-expansion effect may worsen congestion. CPB unambiguously reduces congestion and improves welfare, but its interaction with AI is conditional: complements when AI is immature, substitutes when mature. These findings challenge conventional wisdom and provide implications for the sequencing of regulatory and technology policies.

Title: Dynamic Programming-Compatible Uncertainty Sets in Robust Markov Decision Processes
Authors: Julien Grand-Clément, Nian Si, Shengbo Wang
Affiliations: Information Systems and Operations Management Department, Ecole des Hautes Etudes Commerciales de Paris, 78350 Jouy-en-Josas, France; Department of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Hong Kong; Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90007
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the compatibility of robust Markov decision processes (RMDPs) with dynamic programming under various assumptions on the uncertainty set (i.e., we investigate when one can solve an RMDP by solving a fixed-point equation. We show that in all generality, s-rectangular and sa-rectangular uncertainty sets are the only models of uncertainty that are compatible with dynamic programming. Our analysis shows that existing nonrectangular models, including r-rectangularity, are only weakly compatible with dynamic programming as they require the assumption that rewards do not depend on the next state. In this case, our results imply that one can always construct a rectangular uncertainty set that is equivalent for both policy evaluation and optimization to the dynamic programming-compatible nonrectangular model. This highlights a key limitation; dynamic-programming-compatible nonrectangular uncertainty sets, although practically relevant for uncertainty quantification, do not provide a genuinely distinct assessment of policy performance. Interestingly, our proof techniques rely on identifying a novel simultaneous solvability property, which we show is central to several important properties of RMDPs, including the existence of stationary optimal policies and dynamic programming-based formulations. The simultaneous solvability property enables a unified approach to studying all existing models of uncertainty, rectangular and nonrectangular alike. Funding: The work described in this paper was partially supported by the Research Grants Council, University Grants Committee [Grant HKUST603/25] and the Agence Nationale de la Recherche [Grant HKUST603/25]. J. Grand-Clément was also supported by the Labex Ecodec [Grant ANR-11-LABEX-0047].

Title: Policy strategies for improving multimodal freight transport: A two-stage framework for Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) project
Authors: Sarawut Jansuwan, Zhuowei Wang, Anthony Chen
Abstract: The multimodal transportation network is critical to a country's economic development, acting as a lifeline for containerized cargo flows from domestic to international destinations and vice versa. Reliable infrastructure, such as railways, roadways, and seaports, allows for better cargo processing and speedier transit, all of which contribute significantly to the system's seamlessness and cost-effectiveness. Thailand's Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) has been designated to promote the country's investment in advancing innovation and technology for future generations. However, as with many other freight routes, the EEC is currently experiencing congestion, accidents, and poor roadway service because of the widespread use of large container load vehicles, which limits capacity and leads to delays and subpar delivery performance. To address these issues, this paper develops a two-stage planning framework for assessing policy strategies for enhancing multimodal freight transport in EEC. The first stage uses a bi-level programming model to estimate the network's reserve capacity, while the second stage assesses travel time reliability (TTR) to determine the cost-effectiveness of infrastructure upgrades. The data reveal that the EEC network can only accommodate 78% of freight demand, with rail freight accounting for only 1.33% of total volume. Critical bottlenecks have been identified on Motorway 7, Highway 3, and Highway 36. The findings indicate that expanding these roadways and improving rail infrastructure, through initiatives such as the single rail transfer operator (SRTO), can dramatically reduce congestion and enhance dependability. It also suggests policy measures such as short-term operational optimizations, mid-term bottleneck reduction, and long-term integrated planning to improve network efficiency, support sustainable growth, and has the potential to position Thailand as a regional logistics hub in Southeast Asia. The two-stage planning framework and policy strategies can be used to broaden examples of multimodal freight transportation network expansion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Institutions and social attitudes: The origin and impact of state ownership preferences in China
Authors: Pengfei Li, Ming Lu

Title: Time-varying impacts of government spending on CO2 emissions
Authors: Stefano Di Bucchianico, Mario Di Serio, Matteo Fragetta, Giovanni Melina
Abstract: A Bayesian factor-augmented interacted vector autoregression framework purified of expectations is employed to analyze how government spending shocks have impacted CO 2 emissions in the United States from the 1980s to the pre-pandemic period. Consumption-generated emissions are found to have generally risen following fiscal expansions, although their elasticity to government spending has declined substantially over time—with the five-year elasticity dropping from about 0.6 in the early 1980s to around zero by 2019. In contrast, positive government spending shocks increased production-generated emissions in the early 1980s — with a five-year elasticity near 0.5 — but reversed course by the end of the 1980s, eventually reaching an elasticity of −0.7 by the end of the sample. Examination of time-varying interaction variables suggests that environmental regulation, tertiarization, and a larger share of spending on public goods are associated with a mitigation — or even a reversal — of the emissions growth related to economic expansions driven by government spending. The income channel plays a more limited role, mostly confined to the earlier part of the sample. Furthermore, government consumption and investment are both associated with these shifts in emissions elasticities.

Title: Aggregation models with optimal weights for distributed Gaussian processes
Authors: Haoyuan Chen, Rui Tuo
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Texas A&M University
Abstract: GP models have received increasing attention in recent years due to their superb prediction accuracy and modeling flexibility. To address the computational burdens of GP models for large-scale datasets, distributed learning for GPs are often adopted. Current aggregation models for distributed GPs is not time-efficient when incorporating correlations between GP experts. In this work, we propose a novel approach for aggregated prediction in distributed GPs. The technique is suitable for both the exact and sparse variational GPs. The proposed method incorporates correlations among experts, leading to better prediction accuracy with manageable computational requirements. As demonstrated by empirical studies, the proposed approach results in more stable predictions in less time than state-of-the-art consistent aggregation models.

Title: Privacy attack against federated tensor decomposition-based models
Authors: Yichen Ma, Michael Biehler, Jianjun Shi
Affiliations: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Wisconsin–Madison
Abstract: Federated adaptations of popular dimensionality reduction methods, such as tensor decomposition, have been widely implemented to address data transmission constraints and enable privacy-sensitive sharing across distributed systems. Federated learning (FL) typically involves training models collaboratively across multiple sites with a global server or aggregator while keeping raw data decentralized. While these methods often claim to preserve privacy through various mechanisms, we show that the shared information essential for FL can be exploited to reconstruct local sites’ private data. Furthermore, models that achieve better approximations to the true data and more effective FL approaches are increasingly vulnerable to attacks. We propose a novel attention-based privacy attack framework, along with theoretical analysis that quantifies privacy leakage using mutual information and entropy, to assess the vulnerability of federated tensor decomposition-based models, specifically Tucker decomposition. Simulations on synthetic three-dimensional point clouds and two case studies on healthcare correlation tensors and facial images demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, underscoring the need for stronger privacy measures in federated analytics.

Title: Modeling two-scale degradation with heterogeneity: A unified random-effects inverse Gaussian framework
Authors: Liangliang Zhuang, Yizhong Ma, Guanqi Fang, Ancha Xu
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Department of Management Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology; School of Statistics and Data Science, Zhejiang Gongshang University; Collaborative Innovation Center of Statistical Data Engineering, Technology & Application, Zhejiang Gongshang University; Laboratory for Statistical Monitoring and Intelligent Governance of Common Prosperity, Hangzhou, China
Abstract: Accurate modeling of product degradation is essential for reliable life prediction and maintenance planning. In many applications, degradation is jointly driven by age (calendar time) and usage (cumulative operation), and further complicated by unit-to-unit heterogeneity due to manufacturing or environmental variations. While existing models often focus on single-scale processes or assume homogeneous systems, few frameworks can flexibly accommodate both two scales and population-level variability. This paper proposes a unified two-scale degradation model based on additive reparameterized inverse Gaussian processes with random effects. The model captures monotonic degradation under the joint influence of age and usage, and introduces two forms of random effects to flexibly capture varying degrees of heterogeneity across units. It provides closed-form expressions for failure time distributions, enabling efficient reliability analysis. Two inference methods are developed: (i) a maximum likelihood estimator via an expectation-maximization algorithm with bootstrap intervals, and (ii) a Bayesian approach using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. Simulation studies confirm the accuracy and robustness of the proposed estimators and highlight the risks of model misspecification in reliability assessment. A real-world case study on outdoor coating degradation further demonstrates the model’s practical applicability. An open-source R package is provided to support implementation, with additional materials available online.

Title: A Bayesian jump model-based pathwise sampling approach for online anomaly detection
Authors: Dongmin Li, Miao Bai, Di Wang, Xiaochen Xian
Affiliations: H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology; Department of Operations and Information Management, University of Connecticut; Department of Industrial Engineering and Management, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: Moving vehicle-based sensors (MVSs) have received growing attention for real-time anomaly detection in various applications such as wildfire and oil spill detection. To tackle challenges due to the spatial covariance structure among observations, uncertainties under partial observations, as well as the physical MVS movements, we propose a Bayesian jump model-based pathwise sampling approach to detect abrupt changes in an area of interest in real time using MVSs. Specifically, a jump-model based Bayesian scheme is proposed to exploit spatial correlation and real-time partial observations for status update, and to quantify uncertainties arising from noisy observations, limited observability, and anomaly occurrences. Based on the updated status, a Bayesian upper confidence bound is constructed as the sampling statistic to balance exploration and exploitation under noisy and partial observations. Guided by the sampling statistic, a route optimization model is then formulated to adaptively coordinate the routes of multiple MVSs for quick anomaly detection. We perform theoretical investigations and conduct simulations to confirm the exceptional effectiveness of the proposed method. A case study for early wildfire detection demonstrates that our proposed method outperforms benchmark methods, which contributes to the reduction of the area of affected land and wildfire-related costs.

Title: A stochastic defender-attacker-defender model for smart system resilience enhancement against hybrid cyber-physical risks
Authors: Zhaoyuan Yin, Chao Fang, Yiping Fang, Min Xie
Affiliations: Department of Systems Engineering, City University of Hong Kong; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Hong Kong Polytechnic University; School of Management, Xi’an Jiaotong University; Laboratoire Génie Industriel, CentraleSupélec, Université Paris-Saclay
Abstract: With the advancement of digital and communication technology, modern critical infrastructure systems, e.g., power grids, tend to be controlled automatically and remotely through cyber systems. Such cyber-physical systems (CPS) promote more efficient operations but induce synergetic physical and cyber vulnerabilities in coupling network structures. These hybrid threats necessitate risk analysis and resilience enhancement of CPS from the cyber-physical perspective. We propose a stochastic defender-attacker-defender model with the consideration of both uncertain physical disruptions and malicious cyberattacks to secure CPS against hybrid risks. The developed model provides decision makers with resilient allocating and operating strategies for distributed energy resources and intelligent firewalls in CPS. The most threatening cyberattack scenario, which targets the availability and integrity of information systems simultaneously, is formulated with the consideration of incomplete knowledge to realistically simulate cyber risks. A column-constraints-generation based adaptive algorithm is developed to address the challenges that come from multilevel stochastic optimization and asymmetric information. Detailed case studies are conducted in the Hong Kong distribution system and Florida power grid with their communication systems to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The analytical results reveal the interactions and characteristics of concurrent cyber-physical threats and offer valuable managerial insights for decision makers to deploy defense strategies.

Title: Condition-based maintenance for production systems: Inferring degradation states from quality characteristics
Authors: Ziyu Wang, Shuguang He, Xiujie Zhao, Mengzi Zhen
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; School of Mechanical Engineering, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: With the growing complexity of production systems, direct monitoring of system degradation has become increasingly challenging, posing difficulties for decision makers to plan appropriate maintenance actions. This paper presents a systematic framework that utilizes the quality characteristics of products to develop the optimal maintenance strategy for production systems. The degradation process of the system is modeled by a Wiener process. Product quality characteristics and underlying system states are mapped by a random function. The variability in the mapping mechanism is characterized by a normal distribution. Leveraging the partially observable Markov decision process, the optimal dynamic maintenance strategy is determined, and its structural properties are explored via in-depth stochastic analyses. Analytical results indicate that the optimal maintenance strategy is a control limit policy, with a threshold that divides the decision space into two mutually exclusive subspaces. Furthermore, numerical examples motivated by maintenance of vacuum molding machines are elaborated to illustrate the proposed model. Comparisons with common methods demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, whose performance outperforms that of the benchmarks under both finite and infinite horizons. It is also found that the increased uncertainty in the mapping mechanism between product quality and underlying states leads to a noticeable change in the optimal strategy and a higher maintenance cost.

Title: Robust condition-based fleet operations and maintenance: Integrating multi-asset degradation rate interactions and operations-induced degradation
Authors: Deniz Altinpulluk, Farnaz Fallahi, Murat Yildirim, Mohammad Javad Feizollahi
Affiliations: Industrial and Systems Engineering, Wayne State University; JP Morgan Chase
Abstract: Effective operations and maintenance (O&M) in modern production and service systems hinges on a careful orchestration of economic and degradation dependencies across a fleet of assets. While the economic dependencies are well studied, incorporating degradation dependencies and their impact on system operations remain an open challenge. In this article, we consider a general operations & maintenance problem, where a fleet of assets are utilized to satisfy the demand. Assets undergoing maintenance are temporarily unavailable for production. The degradation rate is influenced by two primary decision-dependent factors. First, higher production rates lead to faster degradation of assets. Second, a degrading asset can accelerate the degradation of related assets in the system. To address these dependencies, we model condition-based production and maintenance decisions for multi-asset systems with degradation interactions. We provide the first O&M model to optimize O&M in multi-asset systems with embedded decision-dependent degradation interactions. We formulate robust optimization models that inherently capture degradation and failure risks by embedding degradation signals via a set of constraints, and building condition-based uncertainty sets to model probable degradation scenarios. Our approach offers a seamless integration of data-driven degradation modeling and mathematical programming to bridge the gap across predictive and prescriptive models. Performance of the proposed O&M model is evaluated through extensive experiments, where the degradation is represented using vibration-based readings from a rotating machinery system. The proposed model provides significant improvements in terms of operation, maintenance, and reliability metrics.

Title: A communication-efficient distributed algorithm for online monitoring in big data systems
Authors: Miaomiao Yu, Wei Zhao, Fugee Tsung
Affiliations: Key Laboratory of Advanced Theory and Application in Statistics and Data Science-MOE, and School of Statistics and Academy of Statistics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, East China Normal University; Department of Statistics, Shanghai Polytechnic University; Department of Industrial Engineering and Decision Analytics, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; The Information Hub, Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)
Abstract: In the era of big data, the vast amounts of available information pose significant challenges to traditional monitoring algorithms. The sheer volume of data often results in its distribution across multiple machines, making full communication between these data points impractical due to prohibitive costs or privacy concerns. To address these challenges in constructing online monitoring statistics, we propose a communication-efficient distributed algorithm. Specifically, this algorithm transfers only summarized statistics between machines, rather than individual-level data. This approach not only mitigates the issue of large data volumes that cannot be centralized on a single machine but also overcomes the privacy concerns associated with direct data sharing. Furthermore, we introduce a divide-and-conquer scheme that enhances communication efficiency by focusing on the integration of gradient information for shift estimation. To further reduce communication costs, only vector-type information is exchanged, rather than matrix or more complex data. The proposed algorithm leads to an enhanced exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) control chart, thereby improving its monitoring capabilities. The reliability of the method is rigorously validated. Finally, simulation results and a practical example illustrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed scheme.

Title: Regional favoritism and educational attainment in Africa
Authors: Zareh Asatryan, Thushyanthan Baskaran, Patrick Hufschmidt, Alexander Stöcker
Abstract: Abstract We investigate the impact of regional favoritism on educational attainment in Africa. Using geocoded, individual-level survey data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), we show that men who grew up in areas geographically linked to a national leader attain higher levels of education later in life. In contrast, we observe no beneficial effects of geographical leader connections for women on average; only a subset of women who have additional ethnic ties and are possibly from wealthier families experience such effects. We interpret these results using a discrete choice framework that models decisions regarding whether children continue schooling based on perceived returns to education versus the costs of that education. This framework suggests that preferential educational policies are unlikely to be the primary cause of the higher attainment observed for men and the subset of women mentioned previously. Instead, educational choices appear to respond to expectations of local economic booms in geographically connected regions. Additional evidence, such as regarding the likelihood of skilled employment later in life, supports this interpretation.

Title: Optimizing product return timing in integrated viable circular manufacturing systems: a two-stage stochastic approach
Authors: Sobhan Mostafayi Darmian, Fabio Sgarbossa
Abstract: This study examines how product return timing links configuration selection and recovery planning in circular manufacturing systems under disruption. We develop a two-stage stochastic mixed-integer linear programming model that selects a product configuration before uncertainty is revealed and adapts return timing, production, and recovery allocation to each scenario. Return timing changes prescribed inspection-grade shares and thus the quantities available to eligible recovery routes. The model incorporates a configuration sustainability requirement, production and recovery capacities, market absorption limits, and conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of recovery-duration-weighted disruption impacts. In an illustrative LED luminaire case, adaptive timing reduces the penalized objective under a feasible projected-plan rule. Most of this difference comes from avoiding shortage penalties. Adaptive timing matches the earliest-feasible rule at the base early-return cost; a separate benefit from optimizing timing appears at higher early-return costs. The results identify when controllable withdrawal timing can preserve service and support recovery, while distinguishing shortage avoidance from operating-cost savings.

Title: Territorial capture by illicit economies along Brazil’s Amazon BR-319 highway
Authors: Lucas Ferrante, Igor Deodoro Souza Lisboa, Bruno Campos de Souza, Rodrigo Machado Vilani, Raoni Rajão, Andrea Garcia, Thais Menezes, Leonor Patrícia Cerdeira Morellato, Kei Otsuki, Cassiano Gustavo Messias, Rafael Pinto Costa
Abstract: The BR-319 highway in the Brazilian Amazon connects Porto Velho, in the deforestation arc, to Manaus in Central Amazonia, crossing one of the world’s largest tropical forest blocks. Opened in 1976, the highway was abandoned in 1988 following economic unviability and loss of trafficability, and maintenance resumed in 2015 under a new license. More recently, Brazil’s General Environmental Licensing Law (Law No. 15,190/2025) introduced simplified licensing provisions for maintenance, improvement, and paving of pre-existing infrastructure, creating a new regulatory context for BR-319 consolidation without prior establishment of adequate territorial-governance and enforcement safeguards. We combined satellite land-use monitoring, cattle supply-chain records, field validation, documentary evidence, and directed network analysis to examine associations among road accessibility, illicit land occupation, commodity chains, and political–institutional factors. Within the 40-km road-influence buffer, deforestation shifted from a declining pre-2015 trend of − 565 ha yr⁻ 1 to a post-2015 increase of + 2,965 ha yr⁻ 1 , significantly diverging from the non-road-connected Trans-Purus controls of Pauini ( p = 0.029) and Tefé ( p = 0.039). Post-2015 pasture formation exceeded 70% in Humaitá and approached 90% in Tapauá, while illegal side-road access points in Vila Realidade occurred every 10–15 km. Network analysis identified a structured relational system linking deforestation, illegal roads, land grabbing, mining, drug trafficking, cattle laundering, slaughterhouses, export markets, and political–institutional feedbacks ( R 2 = 0.67, p = 0.001). Convergent network, documentary, field, and land-use evidence indicates that increased road accessibility is associated with the territorial expansion of illicit economies. Actors embedded in or connected to these networks also occupy relational positions associated with political and institutional processes supporting licensing, regulatory changes, and paving agendas. This configuration is consistent with institutional and territorial capture, in which illicit economic interests intersect with infrastructure governance and may reinforce organized criminal networks. Given limited command-and-control, environmental-enforcement, land-tenure, and public-security capacity, the findings support reassessing and revoking licenses and legal or regulatory measures that enable further road consolidation without adequate safeguards. Governance, territorial control, environmental enforcement, public security, and protection of Indigenous and traditional territories should precede further increases in road accessibility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Summer heatwave travel behaviour adaptations vary across purposes, modes, space, and time
Authors: Shiv G. Yücel, Tim Schwanen
Abstract: During summer heatwaves, travel modes and trip timings provide insights into heat exposure and adaptive responses; however, the moderating roles of trip purposes, space, and time remain underexplored. This analysis links England’s National Travel Survey with ERA5 climate reanalysis data, defining heatwaves using a heat index (‘feels like’ temperature). Probit discrete choice models of travel modes and Cox proportional hazards models of departure times assess differences across trip purposes and spatio-temporal factors. The models estimate population-level associations for trips longer than one mile and provide limited evidence of uniform differences during heatwaves; both travel behaviours vary widely across space and time. The relationships suggest that typically cooler locations exhibit travel behaviours consistent with heat-avoidance during extreme heatwaves, urbanization is associated with greater public transit usage and heat-avoidant departure timing, and over 15 years, there are tendencies towards typically more sheltered modes for commuting and heat-avoidant departure timing during extreme heatwaves.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Identifying gross particle emitters: Insights from periodic technical inspections of diesel vehicles
Authors: Anastasios Melas, Jacopo Franzetti, Pascal Buekenhoudt, Andreas Gavros, Alejandro Checa, Ricardo Suarez-Bertoa, Barouch Giechaskiel
Abstract: Periodic technical inspections (PTI) are used globally to ensure in-use vehicle fleet roadworthiness. Since 2022, five European countries have added a particle number test (PN-PTI) to PTI for diesel vehicles with particulate filters to identify high ultrafine particle emitters and mandate repairs. This study examines PN-PTI results from nearly two million Euro 5 and Euro 6 diesel vehicles inspected between 2022 and 2024 in the Flemish region of Belgium and the Netherlands and evaluates different PN limits. The analysis reveals lower failure rates in newer vehicles meeting more recent Euro standards and significant differences between brands. High mileage increases failure rates in older vehicles but has little effect on newer ones. Using three machine learning models, the study identifies first registration year as generally the most important feature associated with PN-PTI failure, followed by brand and mileage. Overall, PN-PTI emerges as an effective policy tool for mitigating gross particle emitters.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Rice farming, social norms, and industrial specialization
Authors: Chang Li, Chang Xue

Title: Tax design and household risk-taking over the life cycle
Authors: Valentinas Rudys
Abstract: The growing interest in wealth taxation has renewed debate over how taxes on accumulated wealth affect household financial decisions. This paper studies how recurring wealth and capital gains taxation affect life-cycle saving, portfolio allocation, and tax payments. In simulations, a 1% annual wealth tax and a revenue-equivalent capital gains tax with a full loss offset reduce financial wealth near retirement by approximately 5% and 7%, respectively. These taxes also increase optimal investment in risky assets. A wealth tax raises the risky portfolio share by up to 6 percentage points over the second part of the life cycle, while a capital gains tax with a full loss offset increases the risky share by 1 to 20 percentage points over the life cycle. These effects arise through two channels. First, lower financial wealth increases the relative importance of human capital, leading investors to allocate a larger share of financial wealth to risky assets. Second, capital gains taxes with a full loss offset partially reduce downside investment risk, increasing the attractiveness of risky assets for risk-averse investors.

Title: Monetary and macroprudential policy with imperfectly competitive banks
Authors: Athanasios Andrikopoulos
Abstract: We study the interaction between monetary and macroprudential policy when banks have market power and funding costs are subject to a lower bound. In a Cournot loan market, banks lend more than a macroprudential authority’s target, and the authority can implement its target with a state-contingent capital requirement. Above the funding floor, a monetary tightening raises the target-implementing capital ratio. Below the floor, the target-implementing capital ratio becomes unresponsive to monetary policy.

Title: Characterizing maximum Nash welfare: Envy-freeness and proportionality
Authors: Karen Frilya Celine, Warut Suksompong, Nicholas Teh
Abstract: When allocating indivisible goods, the maximum Nash welfare rule is known to be the unique welfarist rule satisfying envy-freeness up to one good. We strengthen this characterization by showing that envy-freeness up to one good can be replaced by substantially weaker fairness requirements: envy-freeness up to 𝑘 goods or proportionality up to 𝑘 goods, for any fixed 𝑘 . Our characterization holds even for profiles with identical goods.

Title: The hold-up problem and communication: Experimental evidence
Authors: Felix C. Meickmann, Patrick W. Schmitz
Abstract: The hold-up problem plays a central role in organizational and institutional economics. According to standard theory, an investor may have insufficient incentives to invest in a relationship with a trading partner when the investor anticipates that in future negotiations the trading partner might behave opportunistically, so the investor’s costs might not be recouped. In a prominent paper-and-pencil experiment, Ellingsen and Johannesson (2004a) have shown that communication can mitigate the hold-up problem. They allow either the investor or the trading partner to send a single text message to the other player. In order to study the robustness of their findings, we replicate their setup in an online experiment, allowing for a larger number of observations and a different subject pool. Moreover, we extend the original setup by adding a treatment with bilateral communication in order to find out whether or not the possibility of arguing back and forth can further alleviate the hold-up problem.

Title: Finding capacity in the NSW statewide PICU System—collaborative MVP simulation development in a complex stakeholder environment
Authors: William Jones, Hassan Assareh, Danielle Ritz Shala, Corrine Balit, Marino Festa, Hari Ravindranathan, Andrea Christoff, Linda Williams, Rosemarie Sadsad

Title: Natural disasters and political beliefs
Authors: Costanza Naguib-Stettler, Beatrice Palmieri
Abstract: This paper examines whether local exposure to extreme weather affects support for national climate and energy policies in Switzerland. We construct a municipality-referendum panel linking high-resolution MeteoSwiss data on extreme heat and intense precipitation to municipal voting outcomes in federal referenda. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design and Callaway–Sant’Anna event-study estimators, we compare municipalities first exposed to extreme weather shocks with not-yet-treated municipalities. The results provide little evidence that extreme weather increases support for environmental policy. If anything, the estimates point in the opposite direction: in selected rainfall specifications, environmental yes-shares decline by around 2.7–2.8 percentage points after extreme shocks. These estimates are based on small, geographically concentrated treated cohorts and should therefore be interpreted as cohort-specific. The findings are consistent with the view that salient local shocks may reduce willingness to support costly environmental policies, rather than producing experience-based updating in favor of climate action.

Title: Port coordination dilemmas in green shipping corridors under unilateral carbon policies
Authors: Xinyang Xu, Yang Yang, Tunan Yang, Jijiao Yin, Peiling Jiang
Abstract: Under unilateral carbon regulation, including the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), green shipping corridors (GSCs) face asymmetric coordination challenges among ports and shipping companies (SCs). We develop a tripartite evolutionary game incorporating reduced-form SC heterogeneity, carbon-price feedback, an attractiveness-based green-capacity allocation rule, and stochastic disturbances. A real-world-informed synthetic Europe–Southern Africa container-shipping scenario supports the analysis. Results show that the EU ETS strengthens SC cooperation incentives, but full cooperation requires sustainable port payoffs. The developing-country port lies near its cooperation threshold and is sensitive to incremental green-business revenue, subsidies, and green operational capability. Under the specified rule, improvements in this port’s attractiveness increase its modeled share of configurable green-service demand and can support cooperation without undermining the developed-country port’s cooperation incentive. Stochastic disturbances amplify differences across evolutionary paths for the weaker port. Green-capacity allocation thus links port heterogeneity, competition, and cooperation.

Title: Maskin’s two-person impossibility without rationality
Authors: Nuh Aygün Dalkıran, Oral Ersoy Dokumacı, Ömer Uçkaç
Abstract: With two individuals and unrestricted rational preferences, Nash implementation of Pareto efficiency forces dictatorship (Hurwicz and Schmeidler, 1978; Maskin, 1999). We show that this conclusion needs very little rationality. On any domain containing two families of states — blocking and polarization — a behaviorally efficient social choice rule is Nash implementable if and only if it equals, at every state, one fixed individual’s choice from the grand menu. The rational domain recovers the classical theorem, while all WARP-violating choice profiles qualify with at least four alternatives. Two-person implementation of efficiency is dictatorial with this much rationality, and it needs no more.

Title: Design of hybrid multi-energy systems under uncertainty: An adjustable robust optimization approach

Title: Two-Echelon Electric Vehicle Routing with Mobile Parcel Lockers: A Three-Stage Adaptive Matheuristic with Exact Replenishment
Authors: Nima Moradi, Fereshteh Mafakheri, Chun Wang
Abstract: Two-echelon delivery systems and Mobile Parcel Lockers (MPLs) are emerging urban last-mile solutions that reduce failed home deliveries, ease curbside pressure, and support cleaner electric operations. This study introduces the Two-Echelon Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Mobile Parcel Lockers (2E-EVRP-MPL), which jointly optimizes first-echelon e-truck replenishment, second-echelon MPL routing, satellite activation, stopping-point selection, customer assignment, and charging decisions in a self-collection system. We formulate a mixed-integer linear program that captures battery and payload limits in both echelons, customer-to-stopping-point coverage, parking capacity, locker-compartment capacity, the stationary energy drawn by a parked locker, satellite activation, and stopping-point costs. We then develop a three-stage matheuristic combining an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search with Variable Neighborhood Descent (ALNS-VND) for the second echelon, an exact dynamic-programming replenishment solver for the first echelon whose optimality we establish analytically and verify against an independent exact formulation, and an integrated post-local search for cross-echelon improvement. On newly generated benchmark instances, the method attains the proven optimum on every small instance closed by Gurobi, matches or improves its incumbent on all medium instances, and returns feasible solutions on all large instances, including those where Gurobi finds none within one hour, at a fraction of the exact solver’s runtime. When adapted to related benchmark instances, it matches or improves the published best-known values for 87 of 96 tested instances. A scenario analysis quantifies how total cost changes with the walking radius, stopping-point price, and MPL and satellite design under the tested operating conditions.

Title: Does advertising expand the market for hospital services? Evidence from Medicare
Authors: Abby Alpert, Atul Gupta, Michael Richards, Sarah Schutz, Christopher Whaley
Abstract: Direct-to-consumer advertising is pervasive in US healthcare markets, but little evidence exists on the effects of advertising by hospitals, second only to drug manufacturers in medical marketing. Advertising may help facilities increase market share by stealing existing patients, expanding the market for hospital care, or both. Regardless, it has important public finance implications due to the large sums of taxpayer funds spent by federal and state governments to subsidize hospital operations and finance care through public insurance programs. This paper provides the first causal evidence on the market expansion effects of hospital advertising. To obtain causal estimates, we leverage the fact that spikes in political advertising significantly crowd out hospital advertising in the same market, motivating an instrumental variables design. Using claims data on the universe of Traditional Medicare beneficiaries, we find that advertising expands aggregate patient volume and spending on inpatient care – though to a modest degree (implied elasticities are 0.06 and 0.05, respectively). Although the overall effect of advertising on hospital outpatient care is small and imprecise, for-profit hospitals obtain higher outpatient Medicare volume and revenue.

Title: Evaluation of Collaboration Policy in a Warehousing System With Heterogeneous Robots
Authors: Wanying (Amanda) Chen, Wenqi Zhao, Kai Liu, Bipan Zou
Affiliations: School of Management and E‐business Zhejiang Gongshang University Hangzhou China; School of Business Administration Zhongnan University of Economics and Law Wuhan China; Leeds School of Business University of Colorado Boulder Colorado USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates a novel collaborative warehousing system that employs transportation robots and retrieving robots for order fulfillment. The system features a central platform with peripheral racks and workstations located at the ends. Retrieving robots transfer items from racks to transportation robots, which then deliver them to workstations for processing orders. We develop a fork–join queuing network with two semi‐open queuing networks as its branches to capture the collaboration between the two types of robots and the synchronization of robots and orders, thereby enabling an accurate representation of the overall system performance. An approximation algorithm is designed to solve the queuing network model, and its accuracy is validated through simulation. We analyze several key collaboration policies, including dwell point policies, the optimal transportation‐to‐retrieving robot ratio, and the location of battery charging zones. The study yields several managerial insights: (1) The effectiveness of dwell point policies depends on warehouse size: The point of service competition policy outperforms in small layouts, whereas the point of designated position policy excels in large systems. (2) The optimal location of the battery charging zone varies with warehouse dimensions and order arrival rates. (3) Sequentially operating homogeneous robotic systems show advantages in high‐demand scenarios and with small fleets, whereas parallel operating heterogeneous robotic systems perform better under moderate demand with large robot populations. Beyond a critical fleet‐size threshold, heterogeneous robotic systems consistently dominate across all demand levels. (4) Furthermore, based on our model, we determine the optimal ratio of transportation robots to retrieving robots under different demand scenarios and operational policies.

Title: The Impact of Supply and Demand Heterogeneity on Queue Configurations at Passenger–Taxi Stations: Pooled, Dedicated, and Hybrid
Authors: Zhiheng Zhong, Meng Zhang, Xiaole Chen
Affiliations: Department of Electronic Business South China University of Technology Guangzhou China; School of Business Sun Yat‐sen University Guangzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the impact of supply and demand heterogeneity on queue configurations in service systems such as passenger‐taxi stations at transportation hubs. There exist two types of passengers (short‐haul and long‐haul) and two types of drivers (short‐haul and long‐haul). Long‐haul passengers offer a larger reward for drivers, and long‐haul drivers incur a larger opportunity cost for traveling to the station. Using a queueing‐game theoretical framework, we analyze the equilibrium joining behaviors of long‐haul and short‐haul drivers and compare system performance across three queue configurations: pooled, dedicated, and hybrid systems. Our results reveal that when the rewards for serving a long‐haul passenger and a short‐haul one are both at relatively intermediate values, the dedicated system can outperform the pooled one in terms of overall boarding rate. However, the improved overall boarding rate in the dedicated system sometimes comes at the expense of a lower boarding rate for either short‐haul or long‐haul passengers. We find that the hybrid system can serve as an economically viable remedy to the dedicated system by achieving a Pareto improvement, that is, improving the overall and short‐haul boarding rates without compromising the long‐haul boarding rate while also generating additional revenue sufficient to offset the subsidy cost. Furthermore, we propose a novel modified hybrid system that can potentially improve the overall, long‐haul, and short‐haul boarding rates simultaneously.

Title: Balanced assignments of periodic tasks
Authors: Héloïse Gachet, Frédéric Meunier
Abstract: This work addresses the problem of assigning periodic tasks to workers in a balanced way, i.e., so that each worker performs every task with the same frequency over the long term. The input consists of a list of tasks to be repeated weekly at fixed times and a number of indistinguishable workers. In the basic version, the sole constraint is that no worker performs two tasks simultaneously. In the extended version, additional constraints can be introduced, such as limits on the total number of working hours per week. Regarding the basic version, a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a balanced assignment is established. This condition can be verified in polynomial time. For the extended version, it is demonstrated that whenever a balanced assignment exists, a periodic balanced assignment exists as well, with a tighter bound on the period for the basic version.

Title: Managing supply disruption risks under trade conflict: the value of NLP technology in a global supply chain
Authors: Wenhui Zhou, Chao Wu, Hongmei Yang
Abstract: With the increasingly complex international situation, global supply chain disruptions caused by trade conflicts are becoming more severe. To mitigate the losses caused by supply disruptions, global brands have started purchasing from local companies, even from the local competitors. This emergency procurement may lead to higher production costs and delivery delays. Therefore, global brands are now adopting natural language processing (NLP) technology to predict disruptions and procure products from local competitors in advance. However, under supply disruption, the value of NLP technology on firms’ performance and their co-opetition relationships remains unclear. Therefore, based on the NLP technology decision and the presence or absence of disruptions, we consider four scenarios to explore the effects of NLP technology on firms’ performance and their co-opetition relationships. We find that the adoption of NLP technology is conducive to predicting disruptions in advance and reducing emergency production costs, promoting a co-opetition relationship between the global brand (GB) and the local brand (LB). We also find that adopting NLP technology has two primary effects: the first is the risk response effect, which enables the GB to avoid the second-mover disadvantage; the second is the cost-saving effect, which allows the LB to produce components in advance, avoiding the increase of the emergency production cost. Only if the emergency production cost is high and the NLP technology investment cost is low, the combined advantages of these effects outweigh the investment cost, making the GB adopt NLP technology. Further, the LB can also benefit from the NLP technology when the emergency production cost is sufficiently high. Therefore, there exists a win-win outcome where adopting NLP technology benefits both the GB and the LB.

Title: D-MAPPO-ABC: distributed multi-agent proximal policy optimization enhanced with artificial bee colony for edge computing task scheduling
Authors: Muhammed Sara, Koray Özdemir, Süleyman Eken, Adem Tuncer
Abstract: Edge computing task scheduling faces critical challenges in dynamic, resource-constrained environments, where multiple edge devices must coordinate to process time-sensitive tasks. Traditional scheduling methods struggle with the exploration-exploitation trade-offs and scalability issues. This paper presents D-MAPPO-ABC, a novel hybrid approach that integrates Distributed Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) with the ABC algorithm for efficient edge task scheduling. Unlike centralized approaches, our method models ABC’s three bee roles (employed, onlooker, and scout) of the ABC algorithm as distinct MAPPO policies, enabling distributed decision-making while maintaining the benefits of swarm intelligence. Through extensive experiments on a 10-agent edge computing simulation, evaluated across ten independent random seeds with Welch t -tests, D-MAPPO-ABC achieves a 95% reduction in mean task latency relative to classical heuristics (21 versus 456 ms), a mean policy inference time of only 0.02 ms, zero observed deadline violations, and positive reward performance compared with twelve baseline methods spanning classical heuristics, Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) approaches, recent hybrid swarm–RL methods, and pure MAPPO. Systematic ablation experiments validate the independent contribution of each bee role and the bidirectional D-MAPPO-ABC integration mechanism. New fault-tolerance and network-sensitivity experiments show that the framework continues operating when 30% of the agents fail mid-episode and degrades gracefully under packet loss rates of up to 10%. D-MAPPO-ABC outperforms the best MARL baseline by 27.8% in terms of reward and exhibits a zero percent deadline miss rate across 360,000 simulated decisions. The source code is available at GitHub .

Title: Combining value-at-risk and expected-shortfall forecasts via the model confidence set
Authors: A. Amendola, V. Candila, A. Naimoli, G. Storti
Abstract: To comply with increasingly stringent international standards in risk management and regulation, several approaches have been developed in the literature for forecasting tail-risk measures such as Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES). However, the accuracy of these measures can be significantly affected by multiple sources of uncertainty, including model misspecification, data limitations and estimation procedures. To address these challenges and enhance the predictive performance of individual models, this study introduces novel forecast combination strategies based on the Model Confidence Set (MCS) methodology. Specifically, a strictly consistent joint VaR-ES loss function is employed to identify the best-performing models, which constitute the Set of Superior Models (SSM). Subsequently, the VaR and ES forecasts of the models included in the SSM are combined using various weighting schemes. An empirical analysis based on nine stock market indices at the 2.5\% and 1\% risk levels provides evidence that the proposed combined predictors are a robust alternative for forecasting tail-risk measures, successfully passing standard backtests and consistently entering the SSM of the MCS.

Title: Undiscounted Equilibrium in Positive Recursive Absorbing Games with Nonrectangular Absorption Structure
Authors: Eilon Solan, Nicolas Vieille
Affiliations: School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv 69978, Israel; Department of Economics and Decision Sciences, HEC Paris, Jouy-en-Josas 78 351, France
Abstract: An absorbing game is a stochastic game with a single nonabsorbing state. Such a game is called recursive if all players receive a payoff of zero in the nonabsorbing state and positive if all payoffs in absorbing states are positive. An action profile is nonabsorbing if, when it is played, the game remains in the nonabsorbing state with probability one. The set of nonabsorbing action profiles can be partitioned into the connected components of an undirected graph whose vertices are these profiles, with two vertices joined by an edge whenever the corresponding profiles differ in the action of a single player. A connected component is said to be rectangular if it is the Cartesian product of subsets of the players’ action sets. We prove that every positive recursive absorbing game whose nonabsorbing components are all nonrectangular admits an undiscounted equilibrium payoff. Funding: E. Solan acknowledges the support of the Israel Science Foundation [Grant 211/22].

Title: Carbon taxes crowd out low-carbon choices: Evidence from a consumer experiment
Authors: Alice Pizzo, Christina Gravert, Jan M. Bauer, Lucia A. Reisch
Abstract: We examine the impact of a carbon tax on consumer choices via a large-scale online randomized controlled trial. Higher taxes generally reduce the demand for high-carbon goods. Compared to an import tax, a carbon tax reduces demand when the tax is zero (i.e., announced but not levied) but leads to relatively higher demand for high-carbon goods when a positive tax is introduced. This difference in demand responses, despite identical prices, is concentrated among climate-concerned consumers. Our findings suggest that carbon taxes can crowd out the effect of climate concerns on consumer choices, with important implications for policy.

Title: The role of immigrant caregivers in improving the welfare of elders and reducing public health costs
Authors: Lisa Capretti, Joanna Aleksandra Kopinska, Rama Dasi Mariani, Furio Camillo Rosati
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines the impact of paid migrant home care on elderly health outcomes in Italy. The results show that an increase in migrants’ presence reduces both the frequency and duration of hospitalisations. Specifically, a 1 percentage-point increase in the migrant-to-elderly ratio leads to a decline in long-term and rehabilitation inpatient (LRI) admissions of 118 cases per 100,000 elders, with no measurable effect on acute inpatient stays. There is also a reduction in the average length of stay of 0.141 days, rising to 0.956 days for LRI cases. These effects are driven by diagnoses related to traumatic injuries, musculoskeletal, and genitourinary conditions — areas closely linked to home mobility and care management. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest that the average annual increase of 1.3 percentage points in the migrant-to-elderly ratio observed during the study period corresponds to an 8% reduction in elderly LRI hospitalisation costs, equivalent to 252.3 million euros.

Title: Mitigating School Closures: Parental Responses and Tutoring Vouchers
Authors: Hyunjae Kang, TaeYoung Kang, Sunham Kim
Affiliations: Kyoto University Kyoto Japan; KAIST Seoul Republic of Korea; Korea Development Institute Sejong Republic of Korea
Abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate how school closures affect educational outcomes through parental responses. Using quasi‐experimental variation in school‐level closure days and linked administrative‐survey data, we find that 10 additional closure days raise private tutoring expenditure by 4.1% and within‐school test‐score dispersion by 25%; over the average 53‐day closure, low‐income students lose 0.09 SD. To quantify substitution between schooling and parental investment and evaluate compensatory policy, we estimate a tournament model in which schooling and tutoring jointly produce test scores. Tutoring substitutes for in‐person days, burdening low‐income households disproportionately. Counterfactuals show a means‐tested voucher fully offsets the resulting rise in inequality.

Title: Uncertainty-aware stock selection and portfolio optimization with deep learning-based return prediction
Authors: Mustafa Etcil, Burak Kolukısa, Burcu Bakır Güngör
Abstract: Portfolio optimization allocates capital to balance return and risk. Mean–variance optimization (MVO), its foundational framework, is highly sensitive to expected-return estimation errors. Recent studies increasingly apply machine and deep learning to improve return estimation for portfolio construction. However, despite the inherent uncertainty of financial return prediction, most prediction-driven approaches treat forecasts as equally reliable point estimates, overlooking the model’s confidence in individual predictions. To address this gap, we propose an uncertainty-aware portfolio-construction framework in which a long short-term memory (LSTM) network with Monte Carlo dropout generates return forecasts and forecast-specific epistemic uncertainty estimates. These estimates guide stock selection through ranking and screening and adjust the expected-return inputs to an uncertainty-aware MVO (UA-MVO). The framework is evaluated through a rolling out-of-sample analysis using 100 large-cap, highly liquid S&P 500 stocks over 2018–2023. Empirical results show that epistemic uncertainty provides a forward-looking signal of forecast reliability, as higher uncertainty is associated with larger subsequent forecast errors across months and volatility levels, while lower-uncertainty forecasts exhibit smaller average errors. Incorporating this information into portfolio construction, UA-MVO generally achieves higher returns, better risk-adjusted performance, and lower downside risk than benchmark allocations. Comparisons with uniform shrinkage, volatility-based adjustment, and robust optimization suggest that the gains arise from forecast-specific reliability rather than common shrinkage, historical volatility, or robust penalties. These findings remain robust across portfolio sizes and parameter settings. Overall, the findings suggest that incorporating forecast-specific model confidence into prediction-driven portfolio decisions can improve portfolio performance relative to approaches that rely solely on point forecasts.

Title: Interior-Point Methods for Optimal Power Flow with Scheduled Topological Changes under Uncertain Demand
Authors: Silvia Maria Simões Carvalho, Demacio Costa de Oliveira, Aurelio Ribeiro Leite Oliveira, Magda da Silva Peixoto
Abstract: Abstract Effective operation of modern power systems relies on optimization models that can account for both demand uncertainty and scheduled network reconfigurations. This paper presents a two-stage stochastic formulation of the pre-dispatch problem with scheduled line and bus switching, formulated within the linearized DC power flow framework. In the first stage, generation setpoints are scheduled before demand is realized; in the second stage, these decisions are adapted to multiple demand scenarios and the resulting topologies after switching. Network maneuvers are represented through a unified binary configuration matrix, which compactly represents simultaneous line and bus events while preserving the sparsity of the model. The resulting block-structured problem is solved efficiently with a specialized primal-dual interior-point method. The proposed approach integrates stochastic modeling, explicit representation of switching actions, and advanced solution techniques into a unified and scalable framework. By contrasting the method with chance-constrained DC-OPF, the paper highlights the advantages of scenario-based redispatch in capturing both uncertainty and topological flexibility. This work advances the state of the art in stochastic optimization for power system operation, providing a rigorous yet practical foundation for secure and economical decision making in increasingly uncertain and dynamic environments.

Title: Multiagent Assortment Optimization in Sequential Matching Markets
Authors: Alfredo Torrico, Margarida Carvalho, Andrea Lodi
Affiliations: Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California 90089; Centre Interuniversitaire de Recherche sur les Reseaux D’entreprise, la Logistique et le Transport (CIRRELT), Université de Montréal, Montreal, Quebec H3T 1J4, Canada; and Département D’informatique et de Recherche Opérationnelle, Université de Montréal, Montreal, Quebec H3T 1N8, Canada; Joan and Irwin Jacobs Technion-Cornell Institute, Cornell Tech, New York, New York 10044
Abstract: Motivated by the challenges faced by choice-based matching platforms, in this work, we study a generalization of the two-sided assortment optimization model. Specifically, this model consists of two sides (e.g., customers and suppliers) who have preferences over the opposite side in the form of discrete choice models. A matching is realized through a two-step process where the platform’s decision is to initially present to each agent on one side an assortment of users of the opposite side. The ultimate goal of the platform is to maximize the total expected revenue collected from the matching. Because of the computational complexity of this problem, we focus on the design of approximation algorithms with constant-factor guarantees for the constrained version of the problem under general choice preferences. First, to the best of our knowledge, we are the first to draw connections with the literature of submodular optimization and show that one-sided choice-oblivious approaches perform arbitrarily badly. Second, we show that, for the general setting, there exists a two-sided choice-aware randomized algorithm that achieves a [Formula: see text]-approximation factor, which is the best possible. Third, we design an algorithm that is asymptotically optimal when one side follows the well-known multinomial logit (MNL) choice model under the small probability regime. Fourth, we provide a simple and effective algorithm with a [Formula: see text]-approximation guarantee for the unconstrained setting, with both sides following MNL models. Finally, we assess the performance of our proposed methods with a detailed computational study and discuss several extensions. Funding: M. Carvalho thanks the support of the Institut de valorisation des données (IVADO) and Fonds de recherche du Québec (FRQ) through the FRQ-IVADO Research Chair and of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) [Grant 2019-04557]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/moor.2024.0740 .

Title: Full Convergence of Regularized Methods for Unconstrained Optimization
Authors: Andrea Cristofari
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering and Computer Science Engineering, University of Rome “Tor Vergata,” 00133 Rome, Italy
Abstract: Typically, the sequence of points generated by an optimization algorithm may have multiple limit points. Under convexity assumptions, however, (sub)gradient methods are known to generate a convergent sequence of points. In this paper, we extend the latter property to a broader class of algorithms. Specifically, we study unconstrained optimization methods that use local quadratic models regularized by a power [Formula: see text] of the norm of the step. In particular, we focus on the case in which only the objective function and its gradient are evaluated. Our analysis shows that, by a careful choice of the regularized model at every iteration, the whole sequence of points generated by this class of algorithms converges if the objective function is pseudo-convex. The result is achieved by employing appropriate matrices to ensure that the sequence of points is variable metric quasi-Fejér monotone.

Title: Simulation-based policy evaluation for bicycle safety under cooperative perception: Linking occlusion modeling to detection performance
Authors: Mario Ilic, Tanja Niels, Klaus Bogenberger
Abstract: Urban intersections remain critical for vulnerable road user (VRU) safety, particularly under occlusion-rich conditions that limit the perception performance of connected and automated vehicles (CAVs). While cooperative perception extends the field of view of CAVs by sharing perception information among them, systematic methodologies linking occlusion modeling with VRU-focused safety assessment remain limited. This study presents an occlusion-aware framework for evaluating VRU safety under cooperative perception. Building on the open-source simulation framework FTO-Sim, geometric ray tracing models static and dynamic occlusions at an urban intersection. Traditional binary visibility metrics are extended toward a Level of Perception Potential, incorporating detection redundancy and sensor performance assumptions. In addition, VRU-specific spatio-temporal detection rates are complemented by a perception-aware VRU perception rate as well as redundancy distributions and occlusion level analysis. A case study evaluates regulatory intersection re-design measures, varying observer penetration rates and heterogeneous observer fleets. The results show that improvements in geometric visibility do not automatically translate into higher VRU detection rates, as dynamic occlusion remains a dominant constraint in dense intersection environments. Increasing homogeneous observer penetration yields marginal improvements in occlusion-critical settings, whereas heterogeneous observer perspectives substantially enhance VRU detection performance. Spatial mapping of full occlusion hotspots reveals persistent blind spots that overlap with historical accident locations, indicating locations for targeted infrastructure-based sensor deployment. The proposed framework provides a reproducible methodology for integrating occlusion modeling into VRU-focused safety assessment and supports evidence-based infrastructure and cooperative perception system design. Source code, simulation outputs and results are publicly available to support transfer to other use cases.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Cross-regional coordination of comprehensive transportation emergency networks: A multi-disaster perspective
Authors: Cuiping Ren, Shijing Zhou, Fengjie Xie, Xueyan Zhou
Abstract: With the challenges of cross-regional transportation emergency coordination, this study innovatively integrates the efficiency of comprehensive transportation modes with the risk of multi-disaster. A two-layer network of comprehensive transportation emergency is constructed, which contains a transportation efficiency sub-network and a disaster risk sub-network. To quantitively evaluate the emergency capacity of cross-regional coordination, the study proposes three indices, namely node strength, node imbalance index, and edge coordination index. An empirical study is conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method by comparing comprehensive and single disasters. Result shows that seven node types and critical imbalanced nodes are identified in study areas. Cities with low-efficiency low-risk occupied most (31.4%) can provide potential backup nodes, while cities with high-efficiency high-risk (14.3%) should enhance the emergency network resilience. Meanwhile, four types of coordination path are classified. The number of risky path (34.1%) is more than golden path (12.5%), which highlights an obvious structural imbalance in the cross-regional coordination network. Then, cross-regional emergency coordination planning is generated by jointly considering the functional roles of nodes and paths. This study may offer valuable theoretical insights for supporting cross-regional transportation emergency coordination under multi-disaster scenarios at a strategic planning level.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Reflective–evaporative semi-flexible pavements for urban thermal regulation
Authors: Qun Lu, Aimin Sha, Yujing Chen, Xinghua Liu, Yangsen Cao, Wei Jiang, Wenxiu Jiao
Abstract: Urban pavements influence heat exchange between transport infrastructure and the surrounding atmosphere, yet how surface evolution alters their cooling performance remains unclear. This study investigates the reflective–evaporative cooling of water-retentive semi-flexible pavements with progressively exposed aggregates. Controlled polishing, optical–thermal characterization, outdoor monitoring, mechanical evaluation, and ENVI-met simulation were integrated to link surface evolution with pavement and street-canyon thermal response. Aggregate exposure increased albedo to 57.8% for limestone and 47.4% for granite, whereas diabase and basalt remained optically constrained. Relative to SMA, the proposed pavements reduced peak surface temperature by up to 11.01 °C; each 10 percentage-point albedo gain corresponded to a 0.67 °C reduction. Street-canyon simulation predicted a near-ground air temperature decrease of up to 1.07 °C. Granite provided a favorable thermal–mechanical balance, suggesting aggregate selection as a practical pathway for heat-mitigating urban pavement design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Participation and revelation in the KitaMatch clearinghouse
Authors: Gian Caspari, Manshu Khanna
Abstract: Private childcare providers in Germany generally cannot be compelled to join municipal clearinghouses, so participation is a binding design constraint. Germany’s first childcare clearinghouse, KitaMatch, runs provider-proposing deferred acceptance (KDA). This paper provides a rationale for that choice based on providers’ participation incentives. Providers hold incomplete priorities, which a public ranking completes subject to provider autonomy: the ranking may resolve comparisons a provider leaves open but may not reverse its strict priorities or alter its acceptable set. Under this refinement, KDA gives each provider its best stable assignment, and its transcript of proposals and rejections certifies which top-priority families are stably enrollable. Participation is robust to any aftermarket that settles on a stable outcome, and the guarantee does not rest on the public tie-breaking.

Title: Whose behavior matters? Gender and responses to social information on honesty and generosity
Authors: Haimanti Bhattacharya, Subhasish Dugar
Abstract: We experimentally examine how social information about a reference group’s honesty and generosity affects prosocial behavior, by recipients’ and reference groups’ genders. We vary reference-group gender (men, women, or unspecified) and majority behavior (80% or 20% prosocial). Women exhibit opportunistic conformity: non-prosocial majorities reduce their prosociality, whereas prosocial majorities have negligible effects, regardless of reference-group gender. Men increase prosociality for female reference groups irrespective of majority behavior, suggesting a desire to outcompete women. For male or unspecified groups, men adjust insignificantly toward the majority, though prosocial and non-prosocial treatments differ significantly. Thus, whose behavior matters depends on who receives it.

Title: Hierarchical graph reinforcement learning for energy-efficient dual-resource distributed flexible job shop scheduling
Authors: Nianmin Zhang, Xiao Li, Jintao Xue, Yinyi Wei
Abstract: Dual-resource-constrained distributed flexible job shop scheduling problems (DCDFJSSPs), which involve coupled decisions on cross-factory job allocation and within-factory machine–worker scheduling, have attracted increasing research attention. However, most existing studies remain time- and workload-driven and rarely incorporate explicit energy-control policies, leaving the joint effects of cross-factory allocation, machine–worker matching, and energy control underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce an energy-efficient DCDFJSSP (EDCDFJSSP) and formulate a bi-objective model that integrates machine speed scaling to jointly optimize makespan and energy consumption. We further propose a hierarchical graph reinforcement learning (HGRL) method, where a high-level agent balances workloads across factories, and low-level agents jointly decide machine selection, worker assignment, and speed level using multi-level graph representations and a factored action space. Experiments on instances of varying sizes demonstrate that HGRL consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves superior makespan–energy trade-offs.

Title: Balancing the Burden: Shared Responsibility in Intergenerational Financial Support in Rural Ghana
Authors: Frederick Amon-Armah, Kristina Czura, Hanna Fromell, Robert Lensink
Abstract: Old-age poverty is a growing concern in Sub-Saharan Africa, where pension coverage remains low, particularly in rural areas. Traditionally, older adults have relied on financial support from their children, but demographic and social changes are weakening this intergenerational contract. This study examines parents’ savings decisions within the framework of the intergenerational contract, focusing on the interaction between parental savings and child transfers in financing old-age security. Using a lab-in-the-field experiment with cocoa-farming households in rural Ghana, we analyze parental savings decisions, expectations of child support, and children’s transfer behavior. Our findings show that parents save substantial amounts regardless of expected or actual child transfers, and children do not adjust their contributions based on parental savings. We find no evidence of strategic under-saving or crowding out of private savings by expected future child transfers. The experimental results are consistent with elicited social norms that prescribe both parental savings and children’s financial support, pointing to an intergenerational contract based on shared responsibility rather than strategic substitution in rural Ghana. These findings suggest that in contexts with weak formal pensions, informal intergenerational contracts and private savings can coexist as complementary pillars of old-age security.

Title: Environmental regulation, markup, and price: Evidence from China’s paper industry
