Title: Bus lane design problem with Steiner tree constraints to account for road congestion
Authors: Satoshi Sugiura, Fumitaka Kurauchi, Kam-Fung Cheung, Michael G.H. Bell, Glenn Geers
Abstract: This paper addresses the design of a bus lane network that connects key bus stops (or bus interchanges) while minimizing overall traffic impact. We seek a Steiner tree configuration of bus lanes that maximizes benefits for transit passengers (minimizing total passenger-hours) while simultaneously minimizing the adverse impact on private vehicles (minimizing additional vehicle-hours). This problem is formulated as a bi-level program that incorporates a user equilibrium (UE) condition for private vehicles as a constraint. To navigate the vast solution space efficiently, we introduce an innovative sensitivity analysis method based on bush-based UE assignment. This method is embedded within a link-swapping Tabu search heuristic, enabling the proposed optimization framework to scale to large, realistic urban networks. Numerical experiments conducted on the 215-node Gifu City network demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our approach.

Title: Integrated time-variant quay crane assignment and yard crane capacity allocation with uncertainty under multi-ship blocks-sharing strategy
Authors: Runzhi Tan, Yaoming Zhou, Wei Qin, Heng Huang
Abstract: Traditional yard management strategies that require segregated storage for simultaneously berthed vessels may lead to increased equipment empty moves and gate congestion in automated container terminals (ACTs). The newly proposed multi-ship blocks-sharing strategy (MSBSS) attempts to mitigate this issue by enabling shared yard blocks among vessels. However, MSBSS introduces coordination challenges for yard crane capacity allocation at the short-term planning level, particularly when synchronizing with quay crane assignments under operational uncertainties. A deterministic mixed-integer programming model is first formulated to coordinate quay-side handling capacity and yard-side workload allocation while accounting for capacity mismatch, QC switching costs, and unfinished-workload penalties. Building on this formulation, a two-stage robust optimization model is developed to address two operational uncertainty sources: disruptions in the arrivals of external trucks and yard-health-induced task redistribution within the yard template, thereby enabling more resilient decision-making in volatile operational environments. To solve the robust model, an exact Benders-C&CG algorithm is developed by dynamically combining dual-cut and scenario-block refinements. A dual-informed adaptive heuristic is further proposed to improve computational scalability on large-scale instances. Comprehensive numerical experiments validate the proposed framework and provide managerial insights for short-term planning in ACTs. The results show that bimodal truck arrival patterns can reduce system costs by up to 15.24% compared with uniform arrival patterns, while longer planning horizons can offset up to 16.98% of the cost increase caused by yard-health deterioration. These findings indicate that adopting flexible arrival scheduling and implementing preventive maintenance protocols with extended planning cycles could enhance operational resilience in ACTs facing uncertainty.

Title: Note on Stochastic Vehicle Routing With Delivery Choice Under Recourse Options
Authors: Prahalad Venkateshan, Kamlesh Mathur
Affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Ahmedabad India; Weatherhead School of Management Case Western Reserve University Cleveland Ohio USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we consider the stochastic vehicle routing problem with delivery choice, where, upon reaching a particular customer, the driver has the choice of how much to deliver once the customer demand is revealed. In our earlier work, a basic version of the problem was considered, in which the driver cannot return to the depot midway in a route to replenish the cargo on board (see Venkateshan and Mathur 2025). In the present work, we expand on the choices that the driver has by allowing the driver to return to the depot to replenish before returning to the same customer or to proceed to the next customer. We prove the optimality of different threshold‐based fulfillment policies. Tests show that these policies significantly reduce the computational effort needed to determine the optimal fulfillment policy along a route, as well as its associated expected profit. We also show that a single‐vehicle tour that visits all customers is optimal even if multiple vehicles are allowed.

Title: Traumatic brain injury metaheuristic optimization: harnessing memory and learning for enhanced problem solving
Authors: Kassem Danach, Abbas Tarhini, Hussin José Hejase, Abbas Rammal
Abstract: In recent years, metaheuristic optimization algorithms have gained increasing popularity due to their effectiveness in addressing complex problems. This study introduces a novel approach, Traumatic Brain Injury Metaheuristic Optimization (TBI-MO), which draws inspiration from the memory and learning processes involved in traumatic brain injury (TBI). TBI-MO represents a groundbreaking methodology that fundamentally changes how solution spaces are explored. Unlike traditional algorithms that prioritize common solutions, TBI-MO emphasizes solutions with unique characteristics, adapting based on the frequency of attributes encountered along the search path. This adaptive mechanism allows the algorithm to bypass conventional pitfalls and discover innovative, non-traditional solutions. By integrating this dynamic process, TBI-MO enhances the versatility and adaptability of optimization techniques. A comprehensive analysis of this approach is expected to revolutionize problem-solving strategies across various fields.

Title: Does digital transformation improve the supply chain resilience?
Authors: Jianlan Zhong, Limeng Qian, Linhan Ouyang, Fu Jia
Abstract: To enhance operational efficiency and market competitiveness, enterprises are accelerating their digital transformation. While digital transformation can improve the responsiveness and resilience of supply chains, it also gives rise to a digital paradox, where excessive reliance on complex digital systems may lead to decreased system stability. Based on this notion, this study utilizes data from Chinese A-share listed companies and their suppliers from 2010 to 2024 to explore the impact of digital transformation on supply chain resilience. The findings indicate that although digital transformation can enhance supply chain resistance capability, it may simultaneously weaken recovery capability due to dependence on highly integrated digital systems. Furthermore, mechanism analysis reveals that digital transformation improves supply chain resilience by alleviating financing constraints and strengthening internal controls. Supply chain concentration further moderates the main relationship, amplifying its beneficial effects. Heterogeneity analysis shows that non-state-owned enterprises, high-tech firms, and companies in regions with strong government-market relationships benefit more from digital transformation. This study highlights the dual-edged effect of digital transformation on supply chain resilience from the perspective of the digital paradox, providing valuable strategic insights for enhancing supply chain resilience across different types of enterprises.

Title: Correction: MOARO: An improved artificial rabbits optimization using shift-based density estimation for solving multi-objective optimization problems
Authors: Djaafar Zouache, Fouad Ben Abdelaziz, Farid Boumaza, Meriem Hemici

Title: The effect of new housing supply in structural models: A forecasting performance evaluation
Authors: Stefan Girstmair
Abstract: This paper investigates the importance of including data on new housing supply in dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models for forecasting the Great Financial Crisis (GFC) in the United States. Existing models have added a financial and a real estate sector but have largely overlooked housing supply. I develop an extended DSGE model that combines a sophisticated financial sector with an endogenous housing supply sector and show that forecasting accuracy improves substantially once housing supply data are added to the estimation. A robustness check that turns the supply sector on but withholds the data confirms that the model extension and observable housing data are jointly necessary, with neither sufficient on its own. A historical shock decomposition attributes the contraction primarily to negative housing-demand shocks, transmitted through hand-to-mouth construction workers and impatient-household collateral, and this finding holds across alternative prior specifications. The paper additionally addresses the zero lower bound in modelling forward guidance through a regime change approach.

Title: Long-lead forecasting of El Niño–Southern Oscillation using score-driven models with many predictors
Authors: Janneke van Brummelen, Sebastian Jensen, Siem Jan Koopman, Desislava Petrova
Abstract: We consider long-lead forecasting of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) climate phenomenon. This is widely seen as a challenging task from a methodological perspective. At the same time, ENSO events are of substantial societal importance. We adopt a class of score-driven models to capture the key dynamic features of the Niño 3.4 index and include a large set of previously designed predictors. We provide details of our forecasting methodology and assess the forecast accuracy for a range of different model specifications and estimation strategies. We conclude that a model with a good description of the dynamic features in the data is also able to provide accurate forecasts for almost all lead times, up to 18 months ahead. The large set of predictors is shown to support the provision of accurate long-range forecasts for specific lead times.

Title: Stable Set Polytopes with Rank |V(G)|/3 for the Lovász–Schrijver SDP Operator
Authors: Yu Hin (Gary) Au, Levent Tunçel
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of Saskatchewan, Saskatoon, Saskatchewan S7N 5E6, Canada; Department of Combinatorics and Optimization, Faculty of Mathematics, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 3G1, Canada
Abstract: We study the lift-and-project rank of the stable set polytope of graphs with respect to the Lovász-Schrijver SDP operator [Formula: see text] applied to the fractional stable set polytope. In particular, we show that for every positive integer [Formula: see text], the smallest possible graph with [Formula: see text]-rank [Formula: see text] contains [Formula: see text] vertices. This result is sharp and settles a conjecture posed by Lipták and Tunçel [27] in 2003 as well as answers a generalization of a problem posed by Knuth [21] in 1994. We also show that for every positive integer [Formula: see text] there exists a vertex-transitive graph on at most [Formula: see text] vertices with [Formula: see text]-rank of at least [Formula: see text]. Title: Navigating public and private funding options for conservation measures: A cross-country comparison of western European farmers' preferences
Authors: Moritz Peter Fritschle, Laure Kuhfuss, Tobias Vorlaufer
Abstract: Evidence in economics highlights the importance of the design of agri-environmental contracts for farmers' participation. However, there is little evidence on Western European farmers' preferences between alternative public and private contracts and labels, and on their synergies with participation in farmer clusters. In addition, cultural or institutional differences may lead to variation in contract design preferences across countries. Thus, we apply a discrete choice experiment using an online survey to estimate farmers' preferences for the contract organiser ( government, retailer, NGO ), the payment method ( fixed per hectare payment, price premium associated with a label ), and participation in a farmer cluster including technical assistance by a facilitator as part of the contractual arrangement ( no farmer cluster, optional participation, mandatory participation ) in the United Kingdom, France and the Netherlands. Based on a sample of 767 farmers, respondents prefer, on average, government-organised contracts to contracts from retailers or NGOs. Farmers prefer fixed per hectare payments over price premiums associated with a label and contracts granting the option to join a farmer cluster. The results vary between farm types and countries.

Title: Corrigendum to “Work “as if people mattered”: Reassessing the contribution of E. F. Schumacher” [Ecol. Econ. (251) 109229, (2027)]
Authors: Franck Bailly, Benjamin Dubrion
Abstract: The authors regret that the reference list contains several formal errors. The affected references should read as follows: Leonard, R., in press. In Maynard's Shadow: E. F. Schumacher's Hidden Contribution to Keynes's Wartime Currency Plan. Forthcoming in: Modern Intellectual History.

Title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
Authors: Corinna Dengler, Pooja Patki, Clara Porak
Abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life.

Title: Modeling acceptance of shared and private autonomous vehicles with social-media-informed psychological variables
Authors: Dongdong Feng, Sylvia Y. He
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) are emerging rapidly in the AI era, and many countries are actively advancing AV pilot tests and regulations in metropolitan cities. Despite numerous studies exploring factors influencing public acceptance of AVs, few have proposed a comprehensive framework that integrates social media insights into survey design. This study develops a modeling framework to examine the joint effects of psychological and observed factors on AV acceptance using social-media-informed psychological variables. Comments on Douyin videos are collected to capture public perceptions of AVs, and a survey is subsequently designed and deployed in Shenzhen, China. Structural equation modeling is used to identify five latent factors (e.g., task–technology fit, attitudes, technology adoption propensity), followed by a discrete choice model to examine acceptance of private and shared AVs. Results show that technology adoption propensity, trust in AV performance, and attitudes directly affect acceptance, while trust in AV institution and technology adoption propensity indirectly influence acceptance through attitudes and trust in AV performance. AV exposure emerges as a significant antecedent of both perceptions and acceptance. We further distinguish potential users of private and shared AVs based on their socio-demographic characteristics and travel behaviors. The findings offer theoretical contributions and practical implications for urban planners, policymakers, and AV operators, particularly in tech-forward urban environments with rapid AV deployment.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Mind the mismatch: mapping stakeholder-interest divergence in urban e-mobility across major western anglophone arenas using large language models
Authors: Zixuan Xiao, Jun Ma, Yuping Jin
Abstract: Urban e-mobility has emerged as a cornerstone of sustainability transitions, yet electric vehicle (EV) adoption has slowed in key markets despite robust policy support, exposing societal tensions in transition governance, and more fundamentally, a persistent gap in understanding how stakeholder-interest misalignments may erode the legitimacy of climate action itself. This research examines stakeholder-interest divergence as an indicator of potential coordination friction in e-mobility transitions, focusing on how government, academia, news media and the public within major Anglophone discursive arenas articulate differing priorities, framings, and concerns. Drawing on a corpus of Western-centric policy documents, scholarly articles, news stories and social-media posts from 2020 to 2024, we deploy a large language model (LLM) pipeline to analyse topic salience and sentiment across discursive arenas. Results show that government and academic arenas devote less than 3% of their coverage to user experience and maintenance, concerns that dominate public discussion, while concentrating on incentives, regulation and technological advance. News media appear to follow the same institutional pattern, reported as an exploratory signal given the lower cross-model consistency of that corpus. In negative narratives, news outlets attribute opposition to subsidy shortfalls, likewise an exploratory signal, while citizens emphasize persistent cost gaps under current tax regimes, helping contextualize why generous incentives coexist with purchase hesitancy. By pinpointing where conversations stray and whose concerns remain unheard, the study provides a transferable diagnostic for informing the realignment of stakeholder agendas and supporting more credible, publicly trusted low-carbon transitions in cities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How does China’s unilateral visa-free policy affect its international aviation market? empirical evidence on passenger volume, flight frequency, and airfare
Authors: Jianxiu Xiao, Hangjun Yang, Xiangru Wu, Kun Wang, Changmin Jiang, Meng Hou
Abstract: China introduced a unilateral visa-free policy in late 2023 as part of its broader effort to restore international mobility and support post-pandemic economic reopening. The policy grants ordinary passport holders from selected countries visa-free entry to China for short stays, thereby reducing travel frictions and potentially stimulating inbound tourism and business travel. Against this background, this study examines how China’s unilateral visa-free policy has shaped the recovery and structural evolution of its international aviation market. Using route-level data from January 2023 to March 2025, we apply a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) framework to identify policy-induced changes in passenger volume, flight frequency, and airfare. The empirical results show that the policy substantially increases international passenger volume and flight frequencies. Airfares rise in the short term following the policy change, but this increase fades over time. Heterogeneity analyses further uncover substantial variation across regional markets and routes departing from Chinese airports with different levels of slot constraints. Specifically, on European routes, capacity expansion is driven primarily by the deployment of larger aircraft, whereas on Asian routes it is achieved mainly through increased flight frequency. Moreover, estimated airfare effects are positive on routes serving more slot-constrained airports and negative on routes serving less constrained airports, consistent with differences in the flexibility of capacity adjustment. These findings offer nuanced insights into the joint responses of passenger traffic, airline capacity, and airfares to visa facilitation, providing actionable guidance for airline capacity optimization and strategic aviation policy design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Why identity matters for development
Authors: Ashwini Deshpande
Abstract: This paper argues that while development economics has moved beyond income-based metrics toward a broader capabilities framework, it remains insufficiently attentive to the role of social identity in shaping life chances. Identities such as caste, race, gender, and ethnicity structure access to resources, opportunities, and power in ways that conventional and multidimensional indices fail to capture. Drawing on evidence from global gender disparities and caste-based inequalities in India, the paper demonstrates how identity-blind policies risk reinforcing structural hierarchies. It concludes by advocating an identity-conscious development framework that centres historical injustice, targeted interventions, and inclusive governance to advance equitable development.

Title: Gas flaring, agricultural productivity and labor reallocation: Evidence from Nigeria
Authors: Arinze Nwokolo
Abstract: of the Paper This paper investigates the impact of natural gas flaring—a byproduct of oil production—on agricultural productivity in Nigeria. Using a panel dataset of Nigerian households from the Living Standards Measurement Study (LSMS) spanning 2012–2018, combined with geocoded data on monthly gas flaring volumes from oil fields, the study employs variation in the timing of interview surveys to assess effects of gas flaring during harvest and planting seasons. The analysis focuses on southern Nigeria, where oil production is concentrated, and leverages a 2010 policy reform (Local Content Act) that increased local onshore oil activities and thus gas flaring. The empirical strategy includes fixed effects (household, and region-by-month-by-year) to control for unobserved heterogeneity, weather variables (precipitation and temperature), and an instrumental variable approach using global oil price changes interacted with pre-sample flaring intensity to address endogeneity. Key outcomes measured are real crop yield per hectare and labor productivity (real agricultural output divided by worker-days). The findings reveal significant negative effects during the harvest season, particularly in rainy periods, but minimal impacts during planting. Mechanisms are explored through satellite data on air pollutants, showing elevated levels of black carbon, sulfur dioxide, and nitrogen dioxide in flaring areas. Robustness checks confirm the results against various confounders like conflicts, oil spills, and placebo tests. The paper contributes to literature on the impact of air pollution on worker productivity and crop yields and climate change impacts on agriculture, highlighting policy needs to mitigate environmental costs from extractive industries in developing countries.

Title: Empirical analysis of perceived inaccessibility in the Netherlands
Authors: Roberto Nacxit Ramirez Juarez, Jeroen Bastiaanssen, Anna Grigolon, Karst Geurs
Abstract: A growing body of research examines how people perceive accessibility, typically drawing from small-scale surveys in either urban or rural areas. The novelty of this study lies in analysing the heterogeneity in the perceived inability to reach different destinations, accounting for differences across population segments, regions, and transport modes at a nationwide scale. We apply destination-specific ordered logistic regression models and negative-exponential impedance functions, with data from the Dutch National Travel Survey (n = 81,182) alongside a dataset of nationwide cumulative opportunity accessibility measures. Results show that household income, employment, car or E-bike availability, and frequency of biking and driving are associated with lower perceived inaccessibility. Conversely, migration background and use of public transport are associated with higher perceived inaccessibility. The study findings highlight the importance of incorporating people’s capabilities in transport policy to improve accessibility and overall wellbeing.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Constrained interactions and the evolution of conventions: An experimental analysis
Authors: Ennio Bilancini, Leonardo Boncinelli, Gergely Horváth, Lian Xue

Title: The invisible architect: Fiscal incentives and floor area ratio growth in China
Authors: Zhihao Su, Yugang Tang, Quanfei Zhang
Abstract: This study examines how local fiscal incentives shape the regulation of residential floor area ratio (FAR). We exploit China's intergovernmental land transfer revenue sharing reform as a quasi-natural experiment and implement a continuous-treatment DID using spatially matched land parcel data. We find that when local governments face declines in their share of land transfer revenues, they reallocate land supply toward commercial uses to broaden business tax bases, with stronger responses in cities where business tax potential is higher. This reallocation is accompanied by higher residential FAR, especially in cities with stronger business-tax potential. The floor-space results suggest that higher FAR partially offsets the contraction in residential land area. These findings provide evidence from China that fiscal institutions can shape building-intensity regulation.

Title: Causal mediation analysis with nonignorable missingness in covariates, mediator, and outcome
Authors: Zihan Zhang, Dehui Wang, Lianyan Fu
Abstract: Causal mediation analysis typically assumes that all variables are fully observed, yet missingness is common and often nonignorable. We develop a framework for mediation analysis when pretreatment covariates, the mediator, and the outcome are all subject to missing not at random (MNAR). We propose three interpretable MNAR mechanisms, namely response continuation, self selection, and missingness driven by covariates and the mediator. Under each, we establish nonparametric identification of mediation effects using a shadow variable and completeness conditions. Empirical results show that subjective well-being partially mediates the association between job satisfaction and depressive symptoms.

Title: Consumer support for minority entrepreneur farmers
Authors: Michelle S. Segovia, Shuoli Zhao, Marco A. Palma, Rodolfo M. Nayga, Ron L. Rainey
Abstract: This study examines whether beginning farmers’ race and gender influence consumer support, measured through monetary contributions, voluntary effort, and willingness to pay for agricultural products. Using an incentivized online experiment with 1459 U.S. consumers, we exogenously manipulate the farmer’s race (White, Hispanic, and Black) and gender (male and female) on product labels. We do not detect statistically significant effects of race or gender across the three support outcomes. Overall, our findings indicate broadly similar levels of consumer support across the racial and gender groups studied, while not ruling out smaller or context-dependent forms of discrimination. These findings have implications for the economic viability of beginning farmers.

Title: A cultural transmission explanation for the Little Divergence: The shock of the Black Death
Authors: Li Wang, Nobuaki Hori, Yufei Zhang, Qing Wang
Abstract: Before the Industrial Revolution, Northwestern Europe was characterized by late marriage under the European Marriage Pattern (EMP) and persistently high wages, two central features of the Little Divergence. Yet individuals following the EMP had fewer children, raising the question of how this norm could persist. We develop a cultural-transmission model to address this puzzle. Holding cultural composition fixed, higher wages raise fertility for both cultural types. Over time, however, sustained high wages increase the prevalence of the lower-fertility EMP type. This cultural-composition effect reduces average fertility and population pressure, thereby helping sustain high wages. The resulting feedback generates a weak-EMP/low-wage equilibrium and a strong-EMP/high-wage equilibrium. We further argue that regional differences in the severity of the Black Death shifted European societies between these equilibria. Regions with larger population losses experienced more persistent labor scarcity and high wages, allowing the EMP to spread and persist. The model therefore explains the joint persistence of late marriage and high wages in Northwestern Europe.

Title: Disease and development: productivity, exchange, and social segregation
Authors: Javier A. Birchenall
Abstract: This is an analytical and historical study of the social effects of disease and their impact on economic development. I analyze model economies where health spillovers influence aggregate efficiency through worker sorting and (endogenous) social barriers that limit sociality and the extent of the market. I also catalogue historical examples of distance-based rules likely aimed at social segregation by disease via interpersonal, temporal, and spatial separation. Under the maintained assumptions of the model, a development accounting exercise suggests that the aggregate efficiency gains from eliminating disease spillovers or health disparities within developing countries may be of a similar order of magnitude as the proximate income gains from improvements in health.

Title: Boundary Equilibria in Conflict and Natural-Resource Exploitation: A Comment on Rohner (2006)
Authors: Pavlo Buryi
Abstract: This note revisits the two-player, two-period model of conflict and natural-resource use in Rohner (2006). The interior reaction functions reported in that model are based on a stationary point that is not a payoff maximum: under the economically relevant parameter restrictions, the second derivative of payoff with respect to own extraction is positive. Because extraction is bounded, best responses are instead determined by boundary payoff comparisons. I derive the resulting best-response correspondence and characterize the symmetric pure-strategy equilibria of the original model. Under Rohner’s numerical calibration, zero current extraction is a strict best response in both resource cases, yielding a unique Nash equilibrium at zero extraction. The renewable-resource case therefore implies underexploitation, whereas the negative-externality case implies efficient conservation rather than overexploitation.

Title: Pricing, ownership, and licensing in pharmaceutical alliances: a proportional-contract model
Authors: Amirhossein Mostofi, Vipul Jain, Sameer Kumar, Charu Chandra, Yi Mei
Abstract: This study develops a deterministic proportional-contract model for pricing, ownership allocation, and licensing payments in a two-partner pharmaceutical alliance. The model derives the capacity-consistent profit-maximizing price, feasible ownership candidates, and royalty–lump-sum combinations that equalize the partners’ cooperative gains under the stated tax and investment assumptions. Operating factors entering both partners’ ideal gains through the same joint-venture operating profit, including symmetrically incurred transportation and handling costs, affect price, quantity, profit, cooperative surplus, licensing value, and feasibility, but cancel out in the marginal free-tax operational gain ( MG s ). MG s is therefore a useful tax-adjusted diagnostic, but when the foreign firm’s license-income and JV-income tax rates differ, it does not by itself determine the global ownership optimum; the feasible endpoints must be compared. When capacity binds, the optimal price is the greater of the unconstrained profit-maximizing price and the market-clearing price at capacity. An illustrative vitamin-A calibration demonstrates the calculation procedure and sensitivity to partner returns, demand parameters, aggregate unit operating cost, capacity, and fixed investment. The framework is a transparent normative benchmark rather than an empirical validation of observed alliance arrangements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Strategic adoption of live streaming in a duopoly under consumer-perceived quality belief updates
Authors: Pingping Chen, Huiru Zhang, Xinyu Feng, Zhuzhu Song, Qingchun Meng
Affiliations: Shandong University; Tongji University; China Agricultural University

Title: MTA model for finished goods inventory management aimed at minimising inventory costs and maximising product availability
Authors: Anna Kosieradzka, Cezary Szwed, Olga Ciechańska-Kopeć
Affiliations: Warsaw University of Technology

Title: On the benefits of temporal aggregation on forecasting and stock control: empirical evidence from statistical and machine learning methods
Authors: Evangelos Theodorou, Vasileios Bougioukos, Konstantinos Nikolopoulos
Affiliations: National Technical University of Athens; Richmond American University London; Durham University

Title: Context-specific lean Industry 4.0 maturity model from the organisational learning perspective
Authors: Renan Silva Santos, Rodrigo Goyannes Gusmão Caiado, Peter Hines, Carlos Alejandro Diaz Schery
Affiliations: Industrial Engineering Department, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro; South East Technological University

Title: A structured framework for improving digital transformation maturity in food supply chains
Authors: Shiyi Wang, Abhijeet Ghadge, Emel Aktas
Affiliations: Cranfield University Centre for Logistics and Supply Chain Management, Cranfield School of Management, , Cranfield
Abstract: Purpose Digital transformation is the transition from traditional to digital supply chains, enabled by emerging technologies. A digital transformation maturity assessment is necessary to manage this transition effectively. However, existing maturity frameworks for digital transformation in supply chains lack a structured process with detailed actions guiding maturity improvement. This research, therefore, aims to develop a digital transformation maturity improvement framework with evidence from food supply chains (FSCs). Design/methodology/approach In-depth case studies conducted in two food companies were used to gain insights into the digital transformation journey. Adopting diffusion of innovation (DOI) theory, a seven-step maturity improvement process was established, taking into account context-specific influences. Insights obtained from 32 FSC practitioners through a workshop were used to confirm the framework and identify additional improvement actions. Findings The developed prescriptive digital transformation maturity improvement framework presents a circular improvement process, beginning with an evaluation of the current digital transformation status and progressing through the seven steps (initiation planning, alignment, preparation, configuration, pilot testing, scaling and sustaining), followed by re-evaluation to support continuous improvement. The identified internal and external contextual influences highlight their relevance to FSCs. Step-specific actions are provided for advancing digital transformation maturity. Originality/value This study extends the application of DOI theory to develop a maturity improvement process for digital transformation in FSCs. It enriches the understanding of DOI by emphasising the “sustaining” step, which aims to maintain achieved maturity levels and accommodate the evolving nature of digital supply chains.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Machine Learning‐Assisted Optimization for Dynamic Supply Network Design in the Additive Manufacturing Platform
Authors: Behrang Bootaki, Guoqing Zhang
Affiliations: Supply Chain Management and Logistics Optimization Research Lab, Department of Mechanical, Automotive and Materials Engineering University of Windsor Windsor Ontario Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT Distributed manufacturing enabled by additive manufacturing (AM) allows supply chains to rapidly adapt to changing market conditions through flexible facility relocation and capacity adjustment. However, existing studies largely overlook the logistical aspects of AM‐based supply chains and typically treat facility location and logistics decisions separately. This study addresses this gap by developing a novel AM supply network design model that simultaneously considers the dynamic relocation of AM facilities, the adjustment of production capacities, and delivery routing decisions over multiple periods. We formulate the problem as a mixed‐integer linear programming model (MILP). Given the computational challenges associated with the delivery routing component, we propose a machine learning genetic algorithm (MLGA) approach to solve the problem efficiently. MLGA incorporates a machine learning surrogate to estimate the cost of the capacitated vehicle routing subproblem (CVRP), thereby significantly accelerating the convergence of the genetic algorithm (GA). We train two different machine learning surrogates: One based on a neural network model and the other on an XGBoost model. The MLGA solution methodology, under both surrogate models, performs satisfactorily in terms of solution quality and computation time across a set of randomly generated instances. Extensive sensitivity analyses are also conducted on a realistic use case to evaluate the model's applicability under varying service area, demand, and cost scenarios, offering valuable managerial insights and practical implications.

Title: Implications of drone delivery: Strategic interaction and competitive equilibrium
Authors: Zhuzhu Song, Zhongfeng Qin, Tian-Liang Liu
Abstract: Logistics capability has emerged as a critical strategic asset that shapes business models and competitive landscapes. Within this context, drone delivery represents a disruptive technology that is redefining the nature of interfirm competition and cooperation. This study explores the strategic interactions between a smart retailer that uses drones for delivery and a traditional retailer that relies on conventional methods only, utilizing both Stackelberg and Nash games to analyze drone adoption and pricing decisions. The effective delivery capability of drones and consumer preferences for delivery efficiency are critical factors in this study. The findings suggest that drones enable retailers to increase prices while expanding their market share, thereby creating a competitive advantage for smart retailers when drones are used exclusively. Traditional retailers are more inclined to adopt drones when effective delivery capabilities are high, whereas smart retailers may focus on using drones to optimize efficiency under varying delivery conditions, depending on consumer preferences. Finally, drone-enabled delivery can generate multi-win outcomes under certain conditions, where retailer profits, consumer surplus, and social welfare are simultaneously improved compared with the truck-only benchmark. Moreover, higher operational availability strengthens the economic viability of drone deployment.

Title: Electric vehicles versus drones for mountainous last-mile delivery
Authors: Ruoxi Tan, Guangmin Wang, Zhijia Tan
Abstract: Mountainous rural areas face significant challenges for last-mile parcel delivery due to low demand density, poor road conditions, and high transportation costs. This study develops a cost-benefit analysis framework to compare electric vehicle (EV) and drone delivery modes in mountainous terrain. The framework includes a slope-dependent energy consumption model for EVs, a three-dimensional grid-based path planning algorithm for drones accounting for vertical takeoff and landing costs, and optimization models for charging station placement and signal relay tower deployment. Using empirical data from a postal delivery network in mountainous ZhaoDian Township, China, we find that EV delivery is more cost-effective for high-demand, clustered areas, while drone delivery is economically viable for remote, low-demand destinations with limited road access. Demand uncertainty and weather-related flight cancellations reduce the economic viability of drone-only systems. Based on these findings, we derive policy recommendations for establishing a comprehensive cost-benefit analysis framework to evaluate EV and UAV delivery in mountainous regions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Reconstructing flood-induced human mobility using LLM agent with disaster context adaptation
Authors: Zijing Zhang, Fengjue Huang, Junqing Tang, Pengjun Zhao
Abstract: Understanding human mobility during extreme flood events is critical for emergency evacuation and resilient transport planning, yet flood-induced behavioral heterogeneity remains difficult to characterize. Progress has been constrained by data scarcity and the inherent complexity of emergency decision-making, which often induces abnormal travel behaviors and anomalous mobility fluxes. We propose the Disaster-aware Trajectory Generator (DTG), integrating Large Language Model (LLM) agents into an agent-based framework to generate individual-level mobility trajectories under evolving urban flood conditions. Validated against 1.32 billion mobility records from the 2021 “7.20” Zhengzhou flood in China, DTG outperforms all traditional and LLM-enabled baselines, achieving a flood-induced inflow-shift prediction accuracy of 0.713 with outflow and OD distribution JSD of 0.069 and 0.047 during the disaster period. By combining accessibility-constrained disaster context reasoning with the representation of heterogeneous socio-demographic responses, DTG reveals critical infrastructure vulnerabilities and abnormal behavioral patterns, offering actionable insights for flood-resilient transport planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: On utility functions for money
Authors: Pavlo Blavatskyy
Abstract: In choice under risk, the curvature of Bernoulli utility function for money captures attitudes towards risk (under expected utility theory). Two popular functional forms for Bernoulli utility are an exponential function, which exhibits constant absolute risk aversion, and a power function, which exhibits constant relative risk aversion. Both struggle to capture a relatively high risk aversion over large stakes coexisting with a relatively low risk aversion over small stakes. This note presents a new utility function for money expressed via the modified Bessel function of the second kind that overcomes this problem. This utility function exhibits a constant coefficient xu(x)’’/u(x).

Title: The Effects of Hype and Social Preferences on Crypto Investing
Authors: Hans Degryse, Alberta Di Giuli, Naciye Sekerci, Francesco Stradi
Abstract: Using a survey and a pre-registered experiment, we provide evidence on the role of hype and social preferences on crypto investing. Our survey shows that crypto investors are more likely to be influenced by hype and exhibit lower social preferences. Our experiment helps us establish causal relationships: the hype treatment (i.e., information on the number of investors becoming millionaires daily through Bitcoin investing) increases the amount invested in crypto, with evidence consistent with higher expected returns playing a role, whereas the social treatments (i.e., information on crypto’s environmental impact and association with illegal activities) reduce the investment amount without altering financial expectations. Overall, our study helps to understand what encourages and hampers crypto investing.

Title: A Decision‐Support System for Prioritizing the Transformational Dynamics of Autonomous Trucks Deployment
Authors: Emmanuel Anu Thompson, Pan Lu, Xinyi Yang, Ryan Jones, Denver Tolliver
Affiliations: Department of Transportation, Logistics, and Finance Upper Great Plains Transportation Institute, North Dakota State University Fargo North Dakota USA; Department of Transportation, Logistics, and Finance, College of Business North Dakota State University Fargo North Dakota USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT The implementation of autonomous technologies in commercial freight transportation has advanced significantly, with pilot programs demonstrating technical viability on major interstate highways. However, existing studies on freight innovation predominantly focus on technology adoption and efficiency metrics, often neglecting the broader organizational consequences of automation in logistics. Thus, the integration of autonomous trucks represents more than labor substitution or marginal productivity improvement. It initiates reconfigurations of freight flow control, service contracting, and the distribution of operational authority. Accordingly, this study analyzes the transformational dynamics of autonomous trucking deployment within North Dakota State's freight systems using integrated fuzzy consensus building (FCB) and fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) techniques. Through the analysis of 25 experts, this study identifies 16 critical transformation factors and models their causal interdependencies and structural importance. Results demonstrate that tech firm logistics control, industry structure transformation, and tech firm market entry exhibit the highest centrality values. In contrast, the traditional trucking market share declines systematically in dynamic simulations. A scenario‐based sigmoid sensitivity analysis is performed to assess the robustness of the results. The findings suggest stakeholders should urgently implement strategic adjustments before market dynamics solidify around platform‐dominant structures.

Title: Patent agglomeration and environmental efficiency: effects and mechanisms in Africa
Authors: Rockson Sai, Hongping Yuan, Ebenezer Kwabena Takyi, Hermas Abudu, Stephen Duah Agyeman

Title: Learning from common knowledge: A multi-agent cooperative ramp merging framework for decentralized autonomous vehicles
Authors: Ang Ji, Zhennan Ma, Hongtai Yang, Asad J. Khattak, David Levinson
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Non-stop train systems to alleviate the accessibility and commercial speed trade-off: An analytical framework and optimal planning
Authors: Yichan An, Sua Keum, Hoon Sohn, Jinwoo Lee
Abstract: Balancing accessibility and commercial speed is a fundamental challenge in passenger rail systems: more frequent stops improve first- and last-mile access but reduce commercial speed through stop-induced in-vehicle time losses. This study analyzes a non-stop modular train system with the potential to alleviate this structural trade-off. In this system, the main train body maintains cruising speed, while modular vehicles dynamically decouple and recouple at intermediate stations to enable passenger boarding and alighting. We develop an analytical framework to evaluate total passenger travel time, including access, waiting, and in-vehicle components, under both conventional and non-stop operations, and apply it to the KTX Gyeongbu Line, a major high-speed rail corridor in Korea. Under the same average station spacing and fleet size, non-stop operations reduce waiting time by 38 % and in-vehicle travel time by 36 %, lowering total passenger travel time from 2.66 to 2.07 h, a 22 % reduction, by eliminating intermediate dwell time and repeated acceleration and braking of the main train body. Extending the analysis to optimal planning, we determine the station spacing and fleet size that minimize total daily cost, defined as the sum of passenger time, operating, and infrastructure costs, for both conventional and non-stop cases. Under peak-demand constraints, the optimized non-stop system achieves a 43 % smaller optimal station spacing and a 22 % lower total daily cost than the optimized conventional system. The results indicate that even optimized conventional designs remain constrained by the inherent accessibility–speed trade-off, whereas optimized non-stop operations can improve both spatio-temporal accessibility and commercial speed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Container terminal cooperation with cold ironing: Optimization, market mechanisms, and the value of infrastructure heterogeneity
Authors: Vasileios Sitokonstantinou, Ioannis-Paraskevas Ioannou, George Ioannou, Evangelos I. Kaisar, Mihalis Golias
Abstract: Stakeholder cooperation has been identified as a critical but understudied dimension of shore power research. This paper addresses this gap by developing a vessel-based cooperative optimization model for container terminals with heterogeneous Cold Ironing (CI) capabilities, incorporating endogenous concession fees, environmental subsidies as market-based mechanisms (MBMs), and valid inequalities that enable tractable solutions for 3–4 terminal systems. Through 21,768 optimization runs across four operational profiles and varying infrastructure configurations, we establish four main findings. First, the efficiency-equity trade-off is remarkably narrow: maximizing minimum terminal profit (equity) sacrifices only 0.94% of total system surplus compared to profit maximization (efficiency) when concession-fee transfers are frictionless. Second, cooperation is most valuable under capacity stress: it generates 4.1 × greater value in overbooking scenarios than under normal operations. Third, partial CI deployment (1–2 terminals) yields 6–10% higher cooperation gains than universal deployment, revealing a “Differentiation Principle” where, under CI subsidies, infrastructure scarcity creates valuable subsidy-capture opportunities. This is a conditional, transition-period property of terminal-side cooperation value under the cost, subsidy, and demand structure studied here; it is not an argument against universal CI deployment, which remains the first-best environmental objective. Fourth, lower subsidies are more cost-effective: traditional return on investment (ROI), which attributes the entire cooperation gain to the subsidy, exceeds 5 × at $5/TEU but falls to roughly 1.4 × at $20/TEU, while the incremental ROI of raising the subsidy is only 0.12–0.13. These findings provide operational guidance for terminal operators forming cooperative agreements and inform the design of MBMs that leverage—rather than eliminate—infrastructure heterogeneity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Automakers or traditional insurers? a strategic analysis of insurance for autonomous vehicles
Authors: Amin Abbasi-Pooya, Nagarajan Sethuraman, Suman Mallik
Abstract: As vehicles increasingly become equipped with autonomous driving capabilities, the auto insurance market is undergoing significant changes. Alongside the emergence of autonomous vehicles (AVs), a notable trend is automakers offering insurance for their AVs. In this context, we propose game-theoretic models to study the operational dynamics and competition between a traditional insurer and an AV manufacturer. Our models explicitly consider varying automation levels, dissimilar operational costs of the two insurers, accident risks from technology failures as well as human errors, and information advantage of the manufacturer resulting from in to vehicle telematics. We establish the unique equilibrium of the game and show that as the level of automation increases, the potential for multiple competitors offering insurance for AVs shrinks. We also find that as the level of automation increases, it is possible that the profits of both insurers decrease simultaneously. Safer technology benefits only the insurer with higher operational cost. We show that higher automation does not necessarily improve consumer surplus. We extend our base model to show that availability of better information about human risk to the traditional insurer does not necessarily improve its profit. Rather, it might reduce the profit of the manufacturer. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first paper to study competition between an AV manufacturer and a traditional insurer for insuring AVs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Adaptive Bayesian very short-term wind power forecasting based on the generalised logit transformation
Authors: Tao Shen, Jethro Browell, Daniela Castro-Camilo
Abstract: Wind power plays an increasingly significant role in achieving the 2050 Net Zero Strategy. Despite its rapid growth, its inherent variability presents challenges in forecasting. Accurately forecasting wind power generation is one key demand for the stable and controllable integration of renewable energy into existing grid operations. This paper proposes an adaptive method for very short-term forecasting that combines the generalised logit transformation with a Bayesian approach. The generalised logit transformation processes double-bounded wind power data to an unbounded domain, facilitating the application of Bayesian methods. A novel adaptive mechanism for updating the transformation shape parameter is introduced to leverage Bayesian updates by recovering a small sample of representative data. Four adaptive forecasting methods are investigated, evaluating their advantages and limitations through an extensive case study of over 100 wind farms ranging four years in the UK. The methods are evaluated using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score and we propose the use of functional reliability diagrams to assess calibration. Results indicate that the proposed Bayesian method with adaptive shape parameter updating outperforms benchmarks, yielding consistent improvements in CRPS and forecast reliability. The method effectively addresses uncertainty, ensuring robust and accurate probabilistic forecasting which is essential for grid integration and decision-making.

Title: Shared value vs plural values. Contesting renewable energy projects of the Enel Group
Authors: Daniela Del Bene, Roberto Cantoni, Antonio Bontempi, Louisa Jane Di Felice, Giuseppina Siciliano
Abstract: The energy transition triggers urgent questions about what values are important, who controls transitional processes, and who has the power to define the answers to the climate crisis. Energy companies claim their central role in the development of renewable energy as the ultimate solution. However, communities affected by large-scale renewable energy projects have extensively raised environmental and social justice concerns and denounced the industry's poor practices and abuses. In this article, we analyse 15 socio-environmental conflicts around renewable energy projects owned by the Enel Group, one of the world's largest energy utilities, through the values and valuation languages of the affected communities. We map them onto five dimensions: environmental, health-related, socio-economic, ontological, and political. We build on environmental justice and ecological economics literature on valuation languages and employ counter-accounting to gather bottom-up evidence of grievances. We argue that, while the company claims that RE is the ultimate solution and the ‘Creating Shared Value’ approach is beneficial to all parties, those impacted by Enel's projects question the corporate model of energy transition and defend a plurality of values embedded in relational worldviews that are systematically misrecognised. We eventually criticise the corporate self-attributed moral and value-centred mandate in the energy transition and call for inclusive research about desirable energy futures rooted in plural and relational value systems.

Title: Evaluating the influence of climate finance on reducing water, energy, and food vulnerabilities driven by climate change in African countries
Authors: Mikémina Pilo, Bawoupati Bitassa, Komlan Ametowoyo Adeve
Abstract: Climate finance flows disproportionately toward Africa's most climate-exposed economies, yet this targeting rarely yields commensurate reductions in vulnerability, a “targeting-impact paradox” that raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of global adaptation and mitigation funding. Using an original panel dataset covering 23 African countries from 2000 to 2019, this paper models the joint determination of water, energy, and food (WEF) vulnerabilities and climate finance through a simultaneous-equations framework, estimated via three-stage least squares and two-step efficient IV-GMM. The results show that both global and mitigation-specific climate finance significantly reduce vulnerability, with the strongest effects in food and water systems, yet these gains are neither uniform nor unconditional: they are powerfully mediated by income level, institutional quality, and the tight interdependencies binding the WEF nexus together. Food vulnerability emerges as a critical amplifier of energy and water risk, while energy vulnerability feeds back through food and water systems, revealing a self-reinforcing architecture of risk that undermines siloed policy responses. For African economies confronting escalating climate stress, these findings carry a clear imperative: climate finance can fulfil its transformative promise only where it is deployed through integrated, cross-sectoral strategies explicitly aligned with national development plans and international finance flows, making the coherence of its design as decisive as its volume for building lasting, systemic resilience.

Title: Impacts of ending consumer purchase incentives on electric vehicle adoption: Evidence from interrupted time series analysis
Authors: Aosen Cheer, Yi Qian
Abstract: As electric vehicle (EV) markets mature and governments worldwide consider ending costly financial incentives, there is a lack of empirical evidence on the sustained effectiveness of these incentives once they are reduced or eliminated. Exploiting the sudden pause of the Canada iZEV purchase subsidy program as a natural experiment and using the quasi-experimental controlled interrupted time series approach, this nationwide study estimates the causal impacts of the purchase subsidy on the uptake of zero-emission electric vehicles (ZEVs) over the 7-year period from 2019 to 2025. The results show that after accounting for the pre-pause quadratic growth trend in ZEV adoption, ending the purchase subsidy in the first quarter of 2025 immediately reduced the new ZEV adoption rate by 10.2 percentage points, representing more than half (55%) of the adoption rate that would have been observed in the absence of the subsidy exit. Furthermore, the new ZEV adoption rate grew only linearly over time in the post-subsidy period, losing the quadratic growth enjoyed in the pre-pause period. Our analysis also reveals substantial heterogeneity in the impacts of ending the purchase subsidy across ZEV types (battery EVs vs. plugged-in EVs) and across regions with different population sizes and EV market maturity. These findings help inform the boundaries of subsidy effectiveness, the design of subsidy exit schemes, and the forecasts of policy impacts, thus supporting more efficient allocation of public resources.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Extreme weather and human capital formation: evidence from Qing China
Authors: Weilong Li, Hua Liao, Meixuan Teng
Abstract: Weather shocks can constrain educational investment and human capital formation. In Qing China, education spending rose and fell with weather-sensitive farm income. Using a two-century panel (1646–1904) covering 234 prefectures, we find that a drought occurring one year before the examinations and additional droughts within the past five years reduce jinshi (the highest degree in the imperial examination system) density by approximately 6 % and 2.6 % per period, respectively. Adaptive measures such as the introduction of sweet potatoes, savings from surplus years, and flexible pricing mechanisms prove effective in mitigating drought effects. For robustness, we proxy regional recording capacity with the word count of meteorological entries and augment the baseline with controls for social unrest and epidemic shocks, with results remaining stable. By bringing long-run historical evidence to bear, this study enriches the literature on how extreme weather affects human capital formation.

Title: Transformer-based approach for roadside air pollutant prediction using multi-site smart lamppost data
Authors: Lubing Li, Kejun Du, Faizan A. Kashmiri, Yinghui Wu, Hong K. Lo
Abstract: Roadside air quality significantly impacts public health and the urban ecosystem. This study develops a Transformer-based deep learning model to predict short-term roadside NO 2 and PM 2.5 concentrations using data from multi-sensor smart lampposts at three tested sites in Hong Kong. The model integrates traffic volume, speed, and meteorological factors through a self-attention mechanism that captures complex temporal dependencies. The smart lamppost data, collected directly at the roadside, provide high-fidelity measurements without the need for emission estimation algorithms. A year-long dataset spanning hourly, weekly, and seasonal variations is used for training and validation, with single-site, cross-site, and mixed-site testing strategies. The Transformer is compared against statistical, neural network, and tree-based machine learning baselines, achieving promising prediction accuracy. SHAP and sensitivity analyses reveal that NO 2 is more sensitive to traffic factors while PM 2.5 is more influenced by meteorological conditions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Adaptive dispatch for integrated land-air mobility under uncertain traveler demand
Authors: Weiyao Kong, Enqi Wu, Jianjun Wu, Tiantian Chen, Hongliang Ding
Abstract: Electric vertical take-off and landing vehicles (eVTOLs) can provide fast, potentially lower-carbon trunk services for long-distance urban commuting, but they require coordination with ground feeder modes because they cannot provide door-to-door service. Under fluctuating passenger arrivals, fixed timetables are easy to operate but inflexible, whereas load-based departure rules improve utilization but create unpredictable waiting. This study proposes an adaptive soft-target dispatch strategy that schedules eVTOL departures based on passenger accumulation, stranded demand, and vehicle availability. The integrated land-air dispatch problem is formulated as an event-driven, multi-line decision process and solved using multi-agent reinforcement learning. Numerical experiments show that the proposed strategy reduces average system cost by 22.57% relative to fixed timetables and 0.51% relative to full-match rules, with the largest gains under low-to-medium demand and medium-to-high values of time. A Chengdu airport case study further confirms its cost-saving potential.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Panamax container ship decarbonization: Lifecycle emissions, ownership costs, and break-even carbon pricing
Authors: Yeon-Chan Seong, Ran Yan
Abstract: Carbon pricing may shift fuel choice without selecting the lowest-emission pathway. We evaluate heavy fuel oil (HFO), liquefied natural gas (LNG), hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), green hydrogen, and green ammonia for a 4,253 TEU Panamax ship on the Singapore–Tokyo route, 2026–2050. The framework combines total cost of ownership (TCO), well-to-wake (WtW) emissions, cargo-capacity loss, transition timing, and two-tier fuel-intensity pricing. Without pricing, HFO minimizes TCO and emits 5,206.3 kt CO 2 e. At Tier 1 and Tier 2 prices of US$100/t CO 2 e and US$380/t CO 2 e, LNG Newbuild 2026 minimizes TCO. For a 10-year-old vessel, it reduces emissions by 11.8% but raises TCO by 89.5% over no-policy HFO. HVO switching in 2026 reduces emissions by 78.2%. Raising Tier 1 lowers LNG’s Tier 2 threshold but raises parity TCO. Appraisal should consider thresholds, ownership costs, and lifecycle emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Sustainable data-driven energy management with physics-informed neural networks for optimizing delivery routes
Authors: Yuan Liu, Haoqing Wang, Shuaian Wang
Abstract: Energy consumption during unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flight is an important factor for operational range, mission feasibility, and economic efficiency in aerial logistics. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PI-NN) for instantaneous-power prediction. By embedding established aerodynamic and kinematic principles directly into the neural network architecture, the PI-NN represents power as the exact sum of non-negative lift, drag, and propulsion components. On UAV flight data, PI-NN achieves R 2 = 0.9383 , MAE = 30.03 W, and MAPE = 9.31 % . Recording-level tests show a significantly lower MAE than the strongest black-box benchmark. SHAP identifies the contribution of non-electrical flight variables to individual predictions. Predicted power is converted into arc-level energy and incorporated into an energy-aware mixed-integer linear programming model. In the four-UAV, 22-task base instance, the proposed optimization model yields a feasible 209.10-Wh routing plan and satisfies the prescribed 1% optimality-gap tolerance. Benchmark comparisons, calibrated energy quantiles, and sensitivity analyses further evaluate routing performance, prediction uncertainty, and computational scalability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: A city-level assessment framework for intercity mobility resilience in China
Authors: Yi Long, Haoran Jiang, Shaozhi Hong, Beifei Yuan, Xinyi Chen, Xinhui Xing
Abstract: Aggregate mobility recovery provides incomplete information about changes in intercity connections. We examine this distinction using 230.8 million Amap migration-index records spanning the Wuhan lockdown, Zhengzhou flood, Shanghai lockdown and New Ten policy transition. Daily response curves describe trough retention, cumulative loss, rebound and later levels; monthly origin–destination (OD) comparisons describe network change. Results show that: (1) Wuhan experienced the deepest trough, Shanghai the largest cumulative loss and Zhengzhou the mildest decline; (2) later city-level index levels and monthly OD changes were not consistently associated, while network-loss rankings depended on reference months; and (3) regional background, socioeconomic conditions, built-environment features and network position showed nonlinear, event-specific predictive associations with cumulative loss. New Ten followed a separate release-and-overshoot trajectory. The study identifies the limits of aggregate recovery as evidence of restored intercity relations and supports interpreting daily responses alongside monthly network observations within China’s intercity mobility system.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Financial risk and technology shifting: Firm-level evidence from the rise of AI
Authors: Andrea Bacchiocchi, Germana Giombini, Ludovica Segneri, Francesco Venturini
Abstract: Does financial risk affect firms’ decisions to develop new technologies? We address this question in the context of the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Using data on 28,020 Italian firms observed between 2012 and 2019 and matched with patent records, we find that firms more exposed to financial risk, proxied by cash-flow volatility, are more likely to innovate in AI. The result is robust to financial, economic, market-uncertainty and technological controls. By contrast, financial risk has significantly weaker effects on innovation in more mature technologies. Our findings suggest that financially risk-exposed firms are more willing to invest in high-uncertainty/high-reward innovation domains, possibly to reduce future financial distress.

Title: What does sovereign borrowing signal?
Authors: Yang K. Lu, Bowen Qu
Abstract: We assess the relative importance of three common sources of government private information in asymmetric-information models of sovereign debt: time preference, default costs, and future economic fundamentals. We develop a parsimonious signaling model that nests all three information structures and show that only private information about future fundamentals can generate a state-dependent signaling effect of sovereign borrowing on default risk. More borrowing signals stronger fundamentals when public repayment conditions are favorable, but weaker fundamentals when they are unfavorable.

Title: Identifying heterogeneous decision rules from choices when menus are unobserved
Authors: Larry G. Epstein, Kaushil Patel
Abstract: Consider aggregate choice data from a population with heterogeneity in both preferences (or more general decision rules) and in menus, and where the analyst has limited information about how menus are distributed across the population. We determine what can be inferred from aggregate data about the distribution of preferences by identifying the set of all distributions that are consistent with the preceding. Our main theorem strengthens and generalizes existing results on such identification and provides an alternative analytical approach (using convex capacities) to study the problem.

Title: Optimizing environmental taxes for synergistic governance: From tax-rate to tax-system optimization
Authors: Yiting Yang, Guobao Song, Wei Pu, Yi Zhang, Xin Wang, He Xu
Abstract: Environmental taxes are key market-based instruments for promoting the synergistic governance of pollution reduction and carbon mitigation. However, existing research has focused primarily on policy effectiveness, paying limited attention to how environmental tax systems can be systematically optimized to sustain long-term synergistic governance. This study develops a dynamic computable general equilibrium model to evaluate two sequential policy pathways in China: tax-rate optimization within the existing environmental tax system and tax-system optimization through carbon tax integration. Using a unified analytical framework, we examine their long-term impacts on economic growth, industrial restructuring, energy consumption, environmental performance, and synergistic governance. The results show that optimizing environmental tax rates enhances synergistic governance at relatively low economic cost by promoting industrial restructuring and improving the energy consumption mix. Dynamic tax rate scenarios outperform fixed-rate policies in balancing economic development and environmental objectives. However, the marginal gains from tax-rate optimization diminish as tax rates increase, revealing a policy boundary within the existing environmental tax system. Beyond this boundary, integrating a carbon tax generates substantially greater synergistic benefits while maintaining overall macroeconomic stability, demonstrating that tax-system optimization is more effective than further tax-rate increases. These findings suggest that environmental tax optimization follows a progressive evolution from tax-rate optimization to tax-system optimization, providing a new analytical framework for optimizing green tax systems and strengthening long-term synergistic governance.

Title: A geospatial decomposition method for huge-scale maximum covering facility location problems
Authors: Valentijn Stienen, Britt W.J.R. van Veggel, Dick den Hertog, Marije Jochemsen, Joris C. Wagenaar
Abstract: Large-scale maximum covering (facility) location problems (MCLPs) are central to many humanitarian applications, including finding locations for schools, hospitals, or water wells. These problems usually involve a very large number of demand points and candidate facility locations. Therefore, direct solution approaches are computationally intractable due to, for instance, large memory requirements. This paper proposes a decomposition approach to efficiently solve huge-scale MCLPs. The approach consists of three steps: (i) decomposing the original problem into smaller subproblems with a reduced number of demand and potential facility locations, (ii) combining the solutions of all subproblems into a solution for the original problem, and (iii) deriving an upper bound on the optimality gap induced by the decomposition. We show that using the clustering method DBSCAN in Step (i) results in an exact optimal solution for the original problem after Step (ii). For Step (ii), we develop a dynamic programming method that efficiently constructs the overall solution from the subproblem solutions. For arbitrary decomposition methods, we propose a general framework to efficiently compute upper bounds on the resulting optimality error in Step (iii). We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through a real-world case study conducted in collaboration with 510 (an initiative of The Netherlands Red Cross), focusing on the placement of water wells in West Darfur (Sudan). Computational results demonstrate that both capacitated and uncapacitated problems can be solved within reasonable computation times while providing optimality guarantees where appropriate, in settings where existing methods are not able to even provide feasible solutions.

Title: Distributionally robust elective surgery scheduling for day-ahead capacity assessment of the post-anesthesia care unit
Authors: Jianfeng Ren, Haodong Wu, Jiguang Chen, Qingguo Bai
Abstract: Elective surgery scheduling shapes operating room (OR) completion patterns and post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) demand. We study whether a proposed limit on staffed PACU beds can be met through day-ahead assignment and sequencing, and how more restrictive limits affect completion-time punctuality. Our framework evaluates each candidate schedule through separate surgery-side punctuality and recovery-side capacity assessments linked by patient-level planned completion targets. The surgery side optimizes these targets by minimizing a two-sided punctuality risk index that accounts for the frequency and magnitude of early and late deviations. The recovery side uses the resulting targets to specify planned PACU admission times. A scenario-wise distributionally robust model describes surgery and recovery durations through separate ambiguity sets. Both assessments admit exact finite reformulations, allowing planned PACU peak occupancy to be evaluated in continuous time without a time grid. We develop an exact logic-based Benders decomposition that coordinates the two assessments, and provides global optimality or infeasibility certificates. Experiments on a public multi-OR benchmark show that sequencing can meet lower PACU bed limits for some case sets, while no sequence under existing bookings can do so for others. Among feasible cases, the punctuality cost of a tighter bed limit varies across case sets, while out-of-sample results show that capacity-aware schedules generally reduce the frequency of realized PACU overload.

Title: Manufacturer sales mode selection and green technology investment, and platform-recycler integration in a closed-loop supply chain
Authors: Kunhua Shang, Ruozhen Qiu, Minghe Sun, Zhi-ping Fan
Abstract: Driven by the low-carbon and platform economies, green technology and trade-in programs have become crucial for carbon emission reduction. This study examines a closed-loop supply chain comprising a manufacturer, an online platform, and a recycler, developing Stackelberg-Nash game models to investigate the manufacturer’s sales mode selection and green technology investment, and platform-recycler integration under a cap-and-trade mechanism. Some important findings are obtained. The product greenness decreases with higher initial carbon emissions but increases with higher residual values of used products under both the agency and reselling modes. When the manufacturer invests in green technology and the platform and recycler are not integrated, the trade-in value decreases with a higher residual value of used products for a low incremental coefficient of consumer valuation under both the agency and reselling modes. Furthermore, when initial carbon emissions are low, platform-recycler integration under the agency mode increases the manufacturer’s profit while reducing the combined profit of the platform and recycler, whereas platform-recycler integration under the reselling mode benefits all supply chain members, regardless of green technology investment. Green technology investment benefits the manufacturer and enhances overall supply chain profit only when the incremental coefficient of consumer valuation and initial carbon emissions satisfy specific conditions. Finally, extensions considering positive production costs of new products and heterogeneous residual values of used products confirm the robustness of the main findings while yielding additional managerial insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Temporal bin packing of last-in-first-out: A Lagrangian relaxation integrated decomposition-based approach
Authors: Chenhao Zhou, Xiaorong Ren, Li Xue, Qiang Meng
Abstract: Motivated by applications in logistics, this paper introduces a temporal bin packing problem (TBPP) subject to last-in-first-out (LIFO) constraints. We consider a scenario where items are loaded into and unloaded from a group of bins (e.g., a fleet of train carriages) at various stops, with the objective of minimizing the total number of bins utilized. To ensure operational efficiency at intermediate stops, a strict LIFO handling sequence is enforced. To solve this problem, we develop a novel logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) approach. By embedding Lagrangian relaxation into the master problem, the objective function is reformulated from a single-component to a dual-component structure. This reformulation enables the generation of a new class of optimality cuts, significantly accelerating convergence. Furthermore, we propose two enhancement methods to provide valid lower bounds and improve the performance of both exact and heuristic methods. Computational experiments demonstrate that our proposed approach outperforms benchmark methods in terms of solution quality and optimality gaps. The results show that even as the number of items and stops increases, the approach maintains reasonable computation times and produces practical solutions, highlighting its viability for real-world logistics operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Proactive hybrid fleet allocation for ride-hailing platforms during rush hour
Authors: Guowei Zhang, Manni Cong, Zhu Meng, Luqiu Zhao, Jianjun Wu
Abstract: While the advent of ride-hailing platforms has dramatically reshaped urban transportation, enhancing travel convenience and accessibility, a critical challenge remains: maintaining an optimal spatial balance between supply and demand during rush hour, especially with the involvement of crowd-sourced drivers.
