In this study, we propose a hybrid supply-side management strategy that integrates the physical repositioning of company-owned vehicles with the utilization of crowd-sourced vehicles through spatial surge pricing. We formulate the problem as a bilevel program, where the upper level jointly optimizes company-owned vehicle allocation and spatial surge pricing to minimize operational costs under demand uncertainty, and the lower level characterizes crowd-sourced drivers’ repositioning choices through a multinomial logit model based on relocation utilities. To address the resulting bilevel optimization structure, we reformulate the MNL model as a convex lower-level program. Given uncertainty in spatial demand, we adopt a Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) approach, employing a Wasserstein ambiguity set, which hedges against worst-case distributions near the empirical data. Crucially, we show that the Linear Decision Rule (LDR) approximation preserves optimality and yields a tractable convex optimization problem. Using a real-world dataset from RideAustin, we show that the proposed DRO approach yields more reliable out-of-sample performance than benchmark models, reducing the average out-of-sample objective value by 37.4% relative to SAA in the best case. We further find that hybrid fleets outperform both pure company-owned and pure crowd-sourced fleets, with the average-cost-minimizing crowd-sourced vehicle ratio attained at 0.7, and that stronger driver responsiveness to surge pricing improves operational efficiency by reducing reliance on company-owned vehicles.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Inspecting supplier process quality under demand information asymmetry
Authors: Yingdan Zhang, Ruina Yang, Zelong Yi, Yelin Fu
Abstract: This paper studies a retailer’s choice between a traditional audit mechanism and a blockchain-based mechanism for inspecting supplier process quality under asymmetric demand information. In our model, a supplier sells products to a retailer who has private demand information. Under the audit mechanism, the retailer determines whether to share demand information, while the supplier decides whether to engage in noncompliant production (causing process quality defects) and whether to hide defects to evade audits. Our analysis reveals that sharing demand information can mitigate the supplier’s defect-hiding behavior, when the unit production cost is great and the cost of hiding defects is intermediate. Consequently, a retailer can be encouraged to share demand information. Under a blockchain-based inspection mechanism, demand information is transparent, and the supplier is forced to be compliant as defects can no longer be concealed. Our comparative analysis shows that even when process quality defects offer significant cost savings and minimal brand damage, the retailer may still prefer the blockchain-based mechanism to the traditional audit mechanism. This is especially true for the case with high unit production costs and moderate hiding costs. Finally, we check the robustness of our results with a few model extensions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Joint scheduling of customized bus and urban rail transit for spectator assembly in mega-events
Authors: Xiaojie An, Ziyan Feng, Xiang Li
Abstract: In the pre-event assembly stage of mega-events, customized buses (CBs) and urban rail transit (URT) are typically jointly responsible for transporting spectators from remote assembly points to the event venue. Without properly coordinated scheduling, transfer operations may suffer severe congestion, prolong the assembly process, and increase the risk of delays. This paper studies the coordinated scheduling of CBs and URT services for pre-event spectator assembly in mega-events under predefined planning settings, including assembly locations, service areas, connecting URT stations, and the URT network. A mixed-integer nonlinear programming model is formulated to capture key factors such as multi-batch spectator organization, cyclic CB scheduling, and train safety operations. The objective is to minimize the latest arrival time across all spectator batches to enhance overall assembly efficiency. To address the resulting computational complexity, the model is first linearized into a mixed-integer linear programming model. An accelerated Benders decomposition algorithm equipped with three acceleration strategies, time-window preprocessing, model restructuring with conflict-driven cut generation, and valid inequalities, is then developed to improve exact solution efficiency. Numerical experiments and a real-world case study based on the Beijing URT network demonstrate that the proposed model and algorithm can generate high-quality coordinated schedules within reasonable computing times, confirming their effectiveness and applicability to practical mega-event planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Securing the flow: Strategic storage and corridor design for maritime energy security under chokepoint disruptions
Authors: Monit Sharma, Hoong Chuin Lau
Abstract: Maritime disruption planning requires joint strategic storage and transport capacity decisions under uncertainty. We develop a two-stage stochastic multi-commodity network-design model for national energy security that integrates corridor commitments, port--commodity inventories, storage expansion, and scenario-dependent routing for crude oil, LNG, LPG, and fertilizer. The formulation incorporates decision-dependent probabilities, corridor concentration limits, and mean--CVaR risk, admitting an exact MILP reformulation. In a data-anchored India-inspired case study, stochastic modeling outperforms the expected-value policy by 1.35%, with decision-dependent probabilities worth 0.67%. Service levels are heterogeneous: crude and fertilizer maintain full coverage, while LNG and LPG drop to 34.6% and 33.3% under worst-case scenarios. Storage expansion adds 1,775 capacity units across seven port--commodity pairs and reduces active corridor commitments. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that dependence alters economic exposure while preserving policy optimality, though cost stresses modify first-stage decisions with a maximum regret of 1.1673%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Incentive deadlocks and collaborative breakthroughs in digital transformation: an agent‑based evolutionary game of platform strategies for traditional logistics enterprises
Authors: Yutong Wu, Weimin Ma
Abstract: Platform-based digital transformation in traditional logistics enterprises often stalls even when its long-run value is recognised, because cross-side scale benefits are tied to fulfilment-constrained operations and delayed data learning rather than instant digital gains. This study examines how incentive deadlocks arise and under what conditions collaborative breakthrough becomes possible in this setting. We develop a multi-agent evolutionary game in which traditional logistics enterprises choose self-build, collaborative development, or platform joining, while digital logistics service providers choose customised integration or platform-oriented ecosystem building. Agents use Roth–Erev reinforcement learning with Softmax choice; the model embeds capacity-constrained network effects and delayed data network effects and is evaluated through baseline and case-calibrated simulations, one-at-a-time and Morris–Sobol sensitivity analysis, and robustness tests. The system typically escapes early stagnation but converges to incomplete ecosystem conversion: enterprise-side joining grows faster than platform-side productisation because the two sides face distinct commitment thresholds. Breakthrough occurs only when these thresholds are crossed jointly. Delayed data network effects mainly amplify value after participation has scaled, whereas stronger network attraction can accelerate take-off while also worsening congestion, service erosion, and fragmentation. The study reframes logistics platformisation as a bilateral coordination problem and supports staged coordination of incentives, capability building, and monetisation under fulfilment constraints.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Cooperation mode selection of manufacturer and online freight platform under heterogeneous services and platform matching capabilities
Authors: Weihua Liu, Zhe Li, Yongzheng Gao, Jiahe Hou, Ou Tang
Abstract: Amid the integration of the digital economy and intelligent technologies, and rising heterogeneity in drivers’ service quality, online freight platforms are reshaping manufacturers’ transportation through service level matching. However, because platform collaboration involves commission costs and reduced pricing autonomy, it is not always superior to traditional delegation. Manufacturers thus face a key strategic decision regarding platform collaboration and mode selection. To address this, this study develops game-theoretic models for three modes: traditional delegation, platform-managed transportation, and information-matching, analyzing manufacturer profitability under various conditions and evaluating the effects of platform collaboration on freight system profits and social welfare. The findings indicate that, first, cooperation with the platform generally enhances the manufacturer’s sales and profits. The information-matching mode consistently yields sales volumes no lower than those of the other two modes; however, this advantage does not necessarily translate into higher profits. When the market size is relatively large and service levels converge to the mean, demand homogenization renders the commission costs unrecoverable, resulting in a “high sales, low profit” phenomenon. Second, the platform-managed transportation mode exhibits greater profit competitiveness when high-service-level drivers are scarce. Under high service heterogeneity, its advantage extends to larger market size intervals. Conversely, the information-matching mode attains a profit advantage only when the commission rate is controllable and market size is moderate. Lastly, under the benchmark in which drivers are price takers, while platform-based cooperation generally improves freight system performance, traditional delegation may retain a competitive advantage in large markets with low service-price elasticity. Moreover, when high-service-level drivers capture information rents, the social welfare advantage of platform-based cooperation is further reinforced. This study offers theoretical insights for manufacturers’ mode selection and platform operational optimization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrated scheduling and charging optimization for a heterogeneous electric bus fleet
Authors: Jiaqian Lin, Yinghui Wu, Lubing Li
Abstract: We study an integrated scheduling and charging problem for a heterogeneous electric bus fleet in which vehicles differ in configuration cost, battery capacity, and energy consumption under both service and deadheading operations. The problem jointly determines vehicle type deployment, trip assignment, and charging decisions while accounting for the partial charging strategy, restricted charging-station availability, and time-of-use (TOU) electricity pricing. We formulate the problem as a mixed-integer programming model that minimizes total operating costs. While small-scale instances can be solved to optimality using a commercial solver, realistically sized instances are computationally intractable. To address this challenge, we develop an adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) heuristic that incorporates two problem-specific destroy operators—worst-cost removal and sequential removal—designed to exploit the cost structure and temporal clustering inherent in electric bus operations. Computational experiments based on an urban bus network show that the proposed ALNS outperforms a commercial solver and two widely used metaheuristics in both solution quality and computational efficiency, and that the problem-specific operators consistently outperform benchmark operators. The results demonstrate that fleet heterogeneity enables demand-responsive deployment across peak and off-peak periods, TOU pricing shifts charging toward low-price periods, and charging infrastructure investments substantially reduce long-run operating costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Impacts of high-speed rail speed-up on China’s aviation industry during 2026–2030: based on weighted similarity algorithms and machine learning
Authors: Chunan Wang, Yuqing Hu, Xiaoqian Wang, Tianyi Bi, Yingying Yin, Weijun Liao, Qing Ji
Abstract: We examine the potential effects of high-speed rail (HSR) speed-up on China’s domestic aviation system during 2026–2030 under alternative speed scenarios. While existing research has focused on demand diversion from air to rail, less is known about how faster HSR affects airline network formation, flight frequency adjustment, and the resulting carbon emission path at the system level. To address this gap, we combine a long panel of city pair data from 1996 to 2024 with information on rail speeds, airline operations, and regional economic conditions, and develop an integrated framework to predict potential route formation, flight frequency, and per-flight emissions. The results indicate that faster HSR produces a pronounced structural shock to domestic aviation, especially in short haul markets. Relative to the baseline scenario, the cumulative number of newly added routes declines by about 38% over 2026–2030, and total flights in 2030 are around 11% lower under the 400 km/h scenario. Although aviation demand continues to grow with economic expansion, the network becomes sparser and more spatially balanced as short haul routes are reduced and capacity is reallocated. These adjustments generate persistent emission savings. Cumulative carbon dioxide reductions exceed 25 million tons during the Fifteenth Five Year Plan period, driven jointly by short haul substitution, network contraction, flight frequency changes, and improvements in per flight emission efficiency. The findings show that HSR speed-up can serve as a structural decarbonization pathway for aviation by reshaping network structure and capacity allocation, thereby complementing technology-based measures and providing a basis for more integrated air–rail policy design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Urban air mobility shuttle service optimisation in multi-airport systems
Authors: Yunxiang Shu, Kam K.H. Ng, Cheng-Lung Wu, Hong Kam Lo
Abstract: A Multi-Airport System (MAS) is a network of airports located near each other that provide essential aviation connectivity for a region. These systems often suffer from imbalanced resource utilisation among airports: primary hubs operate near or over capacity, causing congestion and delays, while secondary airports remain underutilised. Inspired by existing collaborative frameworks within MAS and recognising the airport shuttle as a promising early application for Urban Air Mobility (UAM), we propose a UAM-based inter-airport shuttle service designed to enhance connectivity and promote operational efficiency. We develop a decomposition framework consistent with the current transportation-as-a-service business model, comprising a demand pooling stage and an electric Vertical Take-off and Landing (eVTOL) aircraft recharging and scheduling stage. Both stages are formulated as mixed-integer linear programming models, with the latter reformulated using a set partitioning approach. To solve the eVTOL aircraft recharging and scheduling problem, we design a tailored branch-and-price algorithm. In order to accelerate the pricing subproblem, we introduce a customised label-setting algorithm with a bi-directional search strategy. Extensive computational experiments using synthetic demand instances constructed from real-world commercial flight schedules in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) of southern China validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. Our numerical test results reveal that increasing passenger willingness to share rides can reduce total demand pooling costs by up to 44.6%. Across the tested demand compositions, increasing the proportion of demands involving UAM connections between commercial flights at different airports from 20% to 80% also concentrates more demands along corridors connecting primary and secondary airports. Together, these changes provide additional opportunities for demand pooling and eVTOL aircraft scheduling and reduce the average operational cost per demand by 18.3%.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: On-demand spatial services: Operational taxonomy, layered decision architectures, and evidence synthesis
Authors: Yiming Yan, Xi Lin, David Z.W. Wang
Abstract: On-demand spatial service systems coordinate time-sensitive requests with mobile resources under uncertainty and binding decision deadlines. Yet the literature remains fragmented by application labels and method names, obscuring which methodological components fit which operating conditions. This structured scoping and integrative review synthesizes 14 service families and 50 primary studies within a generic rolling decision framework. An operational taxonomy characterizes service systems by mobility pattern, task structure, and decision focus, while a layered methodological architecture distinguishes problem representations, temporal architectures, computational or policy engines, uncertainty treatments, and execution-support modules. A requirement–capability crosswalk and a quality-weighted outcome-evidence map show that no method dominates across settings. Constraint-rich problems increase the relevance of certifying optimization, decomposition, and constraint-aware heuristics; rapid state change supports rolling or event-driven control; material future-state dependence creates value for sequential and anticipatory methods; and decision-sensitive uncertainty supports stochastic, risk-aware, or robust treatment. These relationships remain conditional on feasibility, scale, data, and decision latency. A deadline-constrained formulation further shows that performance depends on the feasible action released by the deadline, including incumbent or fallback execution; greater lookahead, model detail, or uncertainty protection may therefore worsen realized outcomes despite improving the preferred solution. Similarities across service families support structural comparison and component-level reuse, but do not establish portability of complete configurations across markets or operating regimes. Method selection is therefore best understood as configuring a complete observation-to-execution architecture around the binding operating requirement and evaluating it under common feasibility, timing, and execution boundaries.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A decoupled large language model reprogramming framework with validation-selected operating thresholding for sparse railway freight forecasting
Authors: Hesong Zhao, Li Wang, Xianghao Wang, Mengchen Wang, Xiaoli Nie
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) reprogramming adapts frozen pretrained models to time-series forecasting when training data are limited. However, applying this approach to sparse railway freight forecasting requires addressing two problems: 1) Continuous forecasters do not separate the occurrence of a positive record from its magnitude. 2) Standard objectives do not specify how event scores should be converted into decisions using validation data. To overcome the aforementioned limitations, a decoupled LLM reprogramming framework with validation-selected operating thresholding (DLR–VOT) is proposed for sparse railway freight forecasting. First, DLR is developed to use prototype reprogramming to map numerical freight patches into frozen LLM representations in separate magnitude and event streams. Candidate magnitudes are produced by the magnitude stream, while ranking scores are produced by the event stream and refined using past recorded states and teacher guidance confined to training. Second, VOT is designed to select and lock a threshold on validation data under a declared false positive rate (FPR) budget, which may be increased when higher recall is preferred. A candidate magnitude is retained when its event score exceeds the threshold; otherwise, the forecast is set to zero. Among forecasters, DLR–VOT achieves the lowest FPR and highest pooled F 1 scores with native outputs, retaining the highest F 1,active under validation-selected rules. These results show that DLR–VOT provides competitive magnitude forecasting while preserving recorded zeros and recovering positive records in zero-heavy freight data. The code is available at https://github.com/sototheng12138/DLR-VOT.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Structural loss exposure in freight operations: cost–revenue imbalance and dispatch-time predictability
Authors: Ednan Ayvaz, Aydan Savıcı Polat, Bayan Mohammad Mustafa Freihat, Yavuz Kılınç
Abstract: Freight trips generate losses when realized revenue is insufficient to cover the operating costs associated with serving them. Using 85,410 completed truckload trips, we reconstruct trip-level margins and examine how realized losses vary across routes, customers, and information available at dispatch. Negative realized profit occurs in 13.7% of trips and is disproportionately concentrated among shorter movements with lower revenues relative to operating costs. Profitability varies substantially more across routes than across customers, while severe route–customer loss pockets occur mainly on routes that are already economically weak. Losses are also concentrated within a small part of the freight network: the five routes with the largest numbers of loss-making trips account for 45.9% of all loss-making trips and the top ten account for 68.4%. Idle and detention times differ little between profitable and loss-making trips, whereas route average profit and profit margin remain statistically significant in the multivariable analysis after shipment and customer characteristics are considered. Loss exposure is also identifiable before execution. A logistic model using information available at dispatch achieves an out-of-sample ROC–AUC of 0.928, and the highest-risk 10% of dispatches contain 52.5% of realized loss-making trips. ROC–AUC declines to 0.795 when test routes are completely excluded from model estimation, indicating that part of the predictive signal is route-specific. Lane-level loss concentration can inform pricing and commercial review, while dispatch-time risk estimates can identify individual movements for additional screening before execution.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Disrupting risk cascades in traffic networks: V2X-enabled occlusion management and proactive intervention
Authors: Jiayu Yang, Yilan Zhao, Jaeyoung Jay Lee, Constantinos Antoniou
Abstract: Urban intersections face compounding hazards because occlusions hide critical interactions and conflicts can propagate into network-level risk cascades. Existing studies typically address perception gaps or vehicle-level conflicts in isolation, leaving occlusion-induced propagation and its mitigation insufficiently characterized. This study proposes a propagation-aware framework integrating V2X cooperative perception, dynamic conflict networks, compartmental risk propagation, and multi-agent reinforcement learning. The perception, network and propagation analyses use TUMTraf-V2X recordings, while control is evaluated in a simulator calibrated to the same intersection. Infrastructure-assisted sensing makes 77.1% of conflicts jointly observable, against 48.8% for the ego vehicle alone, and recovers 72.2% of those the ego vehicle misses; observer-specific line-of-sight blockage, rather than object-level occlusion labels, governs these failures. In the recorded sequences, each initial conflict is followed by 1.03 later conflict onsets. Observable conflicts have a higher estimated clearance hazard than hidden ones, and applying these observability-conditioned hazards on a common physical interaction network reduces the next-generation reproduction number by 1.8% in nine of ten sequences, against 32.2% when moving from fully hidden to fully observable conditions. In simulation, the cooperative-and-risk observation raises success mainly under high-risk and dense interaction, by up to 5.1 percentage points, whereas supplying the propagation indicators directly to the policy yields no measurable gain; their value lies in constructing a risk-progressive curriculum and stratifying episode difficulty. The framework thus links restored observability to conflict clearance, network-level propagation and risk-aware intervention.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Multi-centre cutting service composition in cloud manufacturing: a hierarchical decision model with guillotine cutting evaluation
Authors: Peng Qi, Yunqing Rao, Xiaofei Xu, Qianhang Lyu
Affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

Title: The influence mechanism of firm green technology cooperation: a supply chain perspective with evidence from chinese cases
Authors: Weihua Liu, Qi Wang, Yuenan Cao, Yang Cheng, Yu Gong, Jianqiang Zhang
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics, Tianjin University; Department of Materials and Production, Aalborg University; Southampton Business School, University of Southampton

Title: Optimizing sequential competitive facility location and attractiveness design
Authors: Chenyu Liu, Yiling Zhang, Hai Wang, Xin Wang, Mingyao Qi
Affiliations: Research Center for Modern Logistics, Tsinghua University Shenzhen International Graduate School; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, University of Minnesota; School of Computing and Information Systems, Singapore Management University; Department of Industrial Engineering, Tsinghua University; COSCO SHIPPING Advanced Technology Institute

Title: Building antifragile humanitarian supply chains: the role of transactive memory systems and big data analytics culture
Authors: Murilo Zamboni Alvarenga, Susana Carla Farias Pereira, Maciel M. Queiroz, Rodolfo Modrigais Strauss Nunes
Affiliations: IFES – Campus Barra de São Francisco Postdoctoral Researcher at FGV EAESP and Department of Business Administration, , Barra de São Francisco; FGV EAESP Department of Operations Management, , São Paulo; CEMADEN Department of Administration, , São José dos Campos
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how big data analytics culture (BDAC) contributes to the development of antifragile humanitarian supply chains. Specifically, this study examines the mediating role of transactive memory systems (TMSs) and the moderating role of the frequency of natural disasters in the relationship between TMS and antifragility. Design/methodology/approach The authors collected 290 survey responses from key humanitarian professionals involved in disaster response operations. To test the proposed relationships among BDAC, TMS, antifragility and disaster frequency, the authors used Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results of this study reveal that BDAC enhances antifragility only when fact-based decision-making improves information credibility, member specialization and coordination, core manifestations of TMS. TMS fully mediates the relationship between BDAC and antifragility, while the positive effect of TMS on antifragility is stronger in contexts with frequent natural disasters. Originality/value This paper advances the literature by empirically demonstrating TMS as the underlying mechanism linking BDAC to antifragility in humanitarian supply chains, showing how TMS operate as microfoundations of dynamic capabilities that enable collective sensing, coordinated decision-making and the reconfiguration of practices.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Exploring multi-horizon cryptocurrency forecasting: can machine learning drive profitable trading strategies?
Authors: Filippo Dal Lago, Rocco Andrea D’Alterio, Faizal Hafiz, Davide La Torre, Jianyi Lin
Abstract: This paper explores the integration of machine learning and automated machine learning (AutoML) in the field of cryptocurrency price forecasting, using Solana as the focal case study before extending the analysis to a balanced panel that adds Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP and Dogecoin. Support vector machines (SVM), random forest (RF) and multilayer perceptrons (MLP) are compared with their MLJAR AutoML counterparts on identical data and splits, each classifying the direction of the next movement at 1, 7, 14 and 30 days. The SVM emerges as the most effective model, reaching over 64% accuracy and balanced accuracy on Solana at the 14-day horizon, whereas RF and MLP overfit the validation split and fail to generalise, mirroring the limitations observed in the AutoML outputs. Across the panel the best model and the best horizon prove asset-conditional. A conceptual trading strategy built on these predictions, net of transaction costs, outperforms both buy-and-hold and a random benchmark on six of the seven asset–horizon–model combinations that are statistically significant and practically accurate. Shapley additive explanations attribute the forecasts principally to momentum and price-level indicators, which take 66% of the attribution, while volume and volatility contribute little; the balance shifts from momentum towards price level as the horizon lengthens, and the leading indicators vary across the panel.

Title: Monopoly Versus Dual‐Channel Distribution With Multiple Retailers
Authors: Cong Pan
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics Kyoto Sangyo University Kyoto Japan
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how downstream competition shapes a manufacturer's decision to adopt a dual‐channel structure—supplying independent retailers via secret two‐part tariff contracts while also operating a direct channel. We show that the shape of the inverse demand function plays a key role in this decision. Under strictly concave demand, expanding total output raises price sensitivity, while the manufacturer responds less aggressively through its direct channel. These effects lead to a sharp price drop, discouraging aggressive retailer behavior and favoring a dual‐channel structure. In contrast, under strictly convex demand, output expansion reduces price sensitivity, and the manufacturer retreats aggressively. The resulting mild price decline leads each retailer to believe that its own output increase has little market impact, encouraging aggressive competition. As a result, with multiple retailers, the manufacturer may avoid supplying the indirect channel even when only two retailers are present. We further show that under the dual‐channel structure, a higher direct‐channel cost can increase consumer surplus by overly shifting output toward the more efficient indirect channel.

Title: Natural capital: the boom and bust of a metaphor? Insights from Scotland
Authors: Alys Daniels-Creasey, Janet A. Fisher, Marc J. Metzger, Hanna Wheatley
Abstract: Despite a fifty-year academic history, the concept of ‘natural capital’ has only been translated into national policy and practice more recently. Since the early 2000s, global initiatives like The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity and the UN System for Environmental Economic Accounts have spurred country-level adoption of natural capital approaches around the world. To examine the implications of this uptake, we traced the concept’s evolution in Scotland through a discourse analysis of 14 interviews, supplemented by key documents and events. Natural capital entered the Scottish context in the early 2010s, intended to make nature visible to decision-makers through economically valuing the environment. By the 2020s, concerns over insufficient public funding for ecological restoration, conceptualised as a nature finance gap, shifted focus to making nature financeable by the private sector. Subsequently, natural capital became emblematic of emergent nature markets, particularly carbon-based mechanisms, precipitating a boom in private sector interest. As the risks of operationalising these markets became apparent to investors, confidence in natural capital faltered by 2023. This prompted the public sector to assume responsibility for de-risking market development. We argue natural capital has facilitated a discursive slide from advocacy for valuation towards commodification practices, framing environmental crises as apolitical market opportunities. This trajectory tends towards privatisation of potential returns while socialising risk through public mechanisms. While natural capital may enhance aspects of nature’s legibility within existing political and economic systems, we caution that its discursive dominance constrains more transformative ambitions to reconfigure the structures that harm nature and its restoration.

Title: Transit lines structures when users’ costs are dismissed: Lessons from stylized networks
Authors: Sergio Jara-Díaz, Diego de Amesti, Antonio Gschwender
Abstract: The primary trade-off faced in public transport planning and design is between the level of service experienced by users and the costs borne by the operators. It has been shown that these latter weigh more when imposing self-financing policies at the expense of the relevance of users’ costs (their time), inducing smaller than optimal fleets of larger than optimal vehicles. This study analyzes the effects of ignoring user costs (UC) in the strategic design of public transport systems from a structural perspective, with a particular focus on spatial design. The problem is addressed using three simplified networks (cross-shaped, triangular, and Y-shaped), over which traditional line structures are compared: Feeder-Trunk, Hub-and-Spoke, Direct (avoiding transfers), and Exclusive (avoiding transfers and intermediate stops). For each network and line structure, operational variables —frequencies and bus sizes— are optimized under two objectives: minimizing operator cost (OC) and minimizing OC + UC. Four elements stand out in the analysis: transfers, idle capacity, excess distance traveled, and stopped utilization. The main result is that the optimal structure varies with the level and distribution of demand when OC + UC are minimized, but when UC is omitted, the structure that generally dominates is the Exclusive one, always operating with an undersized fleet of oversized buses running at lower frequencies than those of the OC + UC optimum. Differences with what is reported in the literature are discussed, motivating further analysis in more complex networks.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The emission-inequality nexus across stages of development
Authors: Francesco Lamperti, Elisa Palagi, Tommaso Perniola
Abstract: Does a more unequal society emit more CO 2 ? The nexus between carbon emissions and income inequality has been at the core of a vast literature yielding conflicting results. Here, we provide robust evidence of a non-linear relationship that depends on the structural composition of the economy. Specifically, we document a positive association between income inequality—measured using five different indicators, for both pre-tax and post-tax income—and per capita carbon emissions in highly tertiarized countries. By contrast, this relationship turns negative in non-service-intensive economies. We provide evidence for plausible mechanisms mediating this non-linear association. In particular, the investment carbon footprint of the top 1% and the size of the manufacturing sector emerge as key dimensions underlying the observed patterns. Our results point to the structural composition of the economy as a crucial factor shaping the emission-inequality nexus. As such, economic structure helps identify phases of development in which reducing inequality comes with climate-related benefits.

Title: Carbon avoidance hubs under unilateral emissions trading: Far East–Europe analysis
Authors: Xinyang Xu, Yang Yang, Tunan Yang, Jijiao Yin
Abstract: The inclusion of maritime shipping in the European Union Emissions Trading System may encourage carriers to add non-European Union transshipment calls to reduce compliance costs, creating potential carbon-avoidance hubs and reshaping liner networks. This study identifies such hubs on the Far East–Northwest Europe route using 2024 automatic identification system data. A structure–service framework first evaluates port comprehensive importance by combining improved topological indicators with turnaround efficiency, berth capacity and operational stability. An avoidance-attractiveness model then incorporates carbon price, fuel pathway, detour and port costs, feeder connection, secondary emissions, physical accommodation and risk exposure. Results show a stable Far East-centered network and clear differences between structural and service-based port rankings. Avoidance expansion is threshold-based: Tanger Med and Suez-adjacent ports are robust avoidance-sensitive nodes, whereas West African ports are marginal only at high carbon prices. Green ammonia removes the carbon-saving basis, and risk constraints narrow feasible options.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Are urban residents trapped by high temperatures? A travel-based heat segregation analysis
Authors: Dingzhong Fang, Mei-Po Kwan
Abstract: Rapid urbanization has profoundly reshaped urban thermal environments and mobility patterns. While socioeconomic segregation has been widely studied, it remains unclear whether daily mobility connects places with similar or dissimilar thermal conditions. This study proposes a travel-based heat segregation index and applies it to dockless bike-sharing trips and diurnal land surface temperature data in Shenzhen, China. Spatial analysis and explainable machine learning reveal widespread heat segregation, with high-temperature and high-segregation clusters concentrated mainly in peripheral districts. Inflow-based segregation varies more between daytime and nighttime, whereas outflow-based segregation differs more between weekdays and weekends. Mobility features are the strongest predictors: greater mobility diversity, more variable flows, and greater spatial extent of OD flows are generally associated with lower heat segregation. Urban environmental factors also show nonlinear, context-dependent effects. These findings support spatially targeted and temporally adaptive heat-mitigation strategies, particularly where high LST coincides with strong OD-based heat segregation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The indirect city: transport, environment, and perceived livability as pathways to subjective well-being
Authors: Luis A. Guzman, Daniel Gonzalez, Victor A. Cantillo-Garcia, Carlos Moncada, Olga L. Sarmiento
Abstract: Transport shapes daily life in dense cities by exposing residents to noise, pollution, and insecurity as they travel. Drawing on a 2023–2024 household survey of 2,448 adults around a high-demand corridor in Bogotá, we examine how the perceived livability of this travel-and-residential environment relates to subjective well-being (SWB). We model livability as a second-order construct reflected in five domains (transport, environment, neighborhood, local services, and security) and estimate an SEM-MIMIC linking it to SWB through perceived health and social capital. Livability shows no direct association with SWB and instead operates through better health and stronger social capital, with health the strongest predictor. Conditions of the travel environment, such as harassment, crime, noise, and pollution along the corridor, are among its strongest manifestations. Livability is most strongly reflected in security and environmental quality. Transport and environmental policies may raise SWB most when they reduce chronic stressors such as insecurity, noise, and pollution, and strengthen social resources, with implications for equity-oriented planning in Global South cities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How does monetary policy affect corporate innovation along the supply chain? The role of suppliers’ financial multiplier
Authors: Li Li, Xinyi Li, Xiaoyun Cheng, Wenjing Zang
Abstract: This study presents granular evidence that highly leveraged suppliers magnify the propagation of contractionary monetary policy shocks through supply chains. Drawing on Chinese supply-chain data covering 2015Q1–2024Q1, we find that monetary tightening triggers sharper declines in innovation among downstream customers tied to high-leverage suppliers than among those linked to low-leverage suppliers. Mechanism analysis suggests that this amplification operates through disruptions to supplier–customer relationships and weakened knowledge spillovers along the supply chain. Moreover, this amplification is especially pronounced when suppliers provide more differentiated inputs and when supplier–customer relationships have longer durations.

Title: Who benefits from corporate entrepreneurship disclosure? Evidence from credit ratings
Authors: Debasish Kar, Sharad Nath Bhattacharya, Mousumi Bhattacharya
Abstract: The study introduces a scalable textual measure of corporate entrepreneurship disclosure (CED) and establishes its relevance to external credit ratings. CED increases over the sample period and firms with higher semantic CED receive more favorable external credit ratings, although financial constraints weaken this association. Rating agencies discount entrepreneurial activity in financially constrained firms, which reflects their perceived uncertainty about whether these firms can finance ongoing operations while sustaining entrepreneurial activities.

Title: Risk preference, investment decision, and household welfare: Evidence from a microcredit experiment in Bangladesh
Authors: Md Amzad Hossain, Sherry Xin Li, Mohammad Abdul Malek
Abstract: Recent microcredit field experiments document low microcredit uptake and heterogeneous treatment effects. We posit the risk preference of households as a possible explanation. In a randomized field experiment in Bangladesh, we find that, in response to a microcredit intervention, household risk preference is significantly associated with microcredit uptake and its outcomes. Households with a more risk-seeking attitude are more likely to take microcredit, rent more land under fixed-rental contracts than share-cropping, adopt more technology, and expand businesses; these responses are accompanied by higher total income. In contrast, risk-averse households did not show such gains. Our results suggest that risk preference is an important dimension of heterogeneity in microcredit uptake and responses to the intervention.

Title: Capacity imbalance and default risk in new energy firms
Authors: Boqiang Lin, Jiangnan Li
Abstract: Against the background of the global energy transition, China's new energy (NE) industry has experienced a large-scale expansion. The concentrated release of firms' production capacity in the short term has led to structural or temporary supply-demand imbalances within the industry, resulting in mounting debt pressure and intensified default risk. In the face of weakening domestic market demand and escalating international trade frictions, examining the relationship between capacity imbalance and default risk among NE firms is of great significance for deepening the understanding of energy supply chain security. Based on firm-level panel data of NE enterprises from 2009 to 2023, this paper employs a high-dimensional fixed effects model to investigate the impact of capacity imbalance on distance to default. The results show that: (1) capacity imbalance reduces firms' distance to default, thereby increasing default risk; (2) the moderating effect analysis indicates that the traditional current ratio exacerbates default risk under capacity imbalance, while an improvement in fixed asset turnover can alleviate default pressure by optimizing asset allocation efficiency; and (3) capacity imbalance has a stronger effect on increasing default risk among firms with higher fixed asset ratios and state-owned enterprises. This study suggests establishing a dynamic capacity monitoring and risk warning mechanism to promote the healthy and sustainable development of the NE industry.

Title: Mind the gap: Emissions adjustment dynamics and firm performance
Authors: Shilpa Garg, Anil Kumar Sharma
Abstract: This study extends the Partial Adjustment Model from corporate finance to corporate emissions, modeling climate transition risk as a gradual process of emissions adjustment. Using firm-level panel data, it estimates emissions persistence, derives speed of adjustment (SOA), and examines how SOA and deviations from target emissions are associated with firm performance. The findings suggest that firms have implicit target emissions levels, reflecting firm-specific attributes and the prevailing transition environment, toward which they converge slowly. The preferred System-GMM estimate indicates an annual SOA of 9.8% and a half-life of 6.69 years. The modified PAM shows that this adjustment speed is not uniform across firms, with energy intensity capturing an important source of this variation. Although energy-intensive firms have higher emissions exposure, they converge more quickly, suggesting that transition pressure may sometimes outweigh adjustment-cost frictions. The performance analysis shows that the association between adjustment speed and profitability is conditional on firms' emissions-gap position, becoming more positive when firms are substantially above their target emissions. Overall, the study develops a dynamic view of transition risk, emphasizing the process of emissions adjustment rather than static emissions levels. This perspective underscores the importance of considering both emissions exposure and adjustment toward target emissions in understanding firms' transition dynamics and financial performance.

Title: Looking Back, Moving Forward: A Guiding Framework for Future Research in Supply Chain Management
Authors: Domenico Mecca, Andrea S. Patrucco, Andreas Wieland, Christian F. Durach, Robert B. Handfield, Ethan Nikookar
Affiliations: Department of Marketing, Operations and Supply EADA Business School Barcelona Spain; Department of Operations Management Copenhagen Business School Frederiksberg Denmark; ESCP Business School Berlin Germany; Department of IT, Analytics and Operations North Carolina State University Raleigh North Carolina USA; Centre for Supply Chain Research, School of Business University of Wollongong Wollongong New South Wales Australia
Abstract: ABSTRACT In 2016, Wieland, Handfield, and Durach mapped future research themes in supply chain management (SCM). This research revisits their work to examine how the field has continued to evolve, the themes scholars believe should and will matter in the coming years, and new research intersections that offer promising opportunities for future research. We begin with a “looking back” analysis of 2413 articles published between 2014 and 2023 in the Journal of Business Logistics , Journal of Operations Management , Journal of Supply Chain Management , and Production and Operations Management . When we classified these articles against the 35 themes identified by Wieland et al., we found that the original framework captured 84.1% of the articles' thematic focus, suggesting it remained useful despite the turbulent and unforeseen events of the last decade. We then employed a three‐phase design to explore future themes, i.e., “moving forward”. First, 185 SCM scholars proposed themes they considered important for the next 5 years. These responses were consolidated into 48 themes, which 186 scholars evaluated in terms of what should become important and what they expect will become important. Finally, eight scholars reflected on intersections among these themes and broader developments shaping the field. Bringing the three analyses together, we develop a guiding framework for future SCM research under overlapping global crises. It connects three areas: the human implications of AI in supply chains; environmental sustainability and social equity; and public policy, geopolitical change, and supply network reconfiguration. Human, social, and humanitarian concerns cut across the three areas.

Title: How will robotaxis reshape the ride-hailing market? Impacts of robotaxi deployment scale, subsidy level and social responsibility
Authors: Weijun Liao, Qing Ji, Hua Wang, Jiancheng Long
Abstract: Using a random coefficients discrete choice model and the large-scale ride-hailing service data (over 7.5 million ride-hailing trip records), we in this paper investigate multi-faceted impacts of Robotaxi deployment on urban ride-hailing market. A couple of insights have been drawn from the perspectives of Robotaxi’s substitution effect and social-economic efficiency. For the substitution effect, it is revealed that Robotaxi’s lower prices and high-tech services drive substantial market-share shifts in consumer behavior, especially among price-sensitive users and during peak-demand period. Robotaxi can simultaneously substitute conventional ride-hailing services and expand the total ride-hailing mobility demand. Meanwhile, service price sensitivity far outweighs transport time factor in reshaping customer choices. For the social-economic efficiency, scenario analyses indicate that, while implementing subsidies and optimizing fleet sizes can boost the ride-hailing orders and market share, excessive subsidies lead to diminishing profitability, namely a “scale trap”. Moreover, the interplay between profitability, employment, and emissions catches our attention. Overall, profit maximization alone rarely achieves net job growth or environmental benefits. Only under a narrow “win–win” regime (a regime with high service efficiency, moderate subsidy, strategic scaling), profit and net employment of Robotaxi-involved ride-hailing business rises simultaneously. More interestingly, total urban transport emissions may paradoxically increase with the expansion of Robotaxi fleet, unless environmental constraints are integrated into Robotaxi policy-making in prior. These managerial insights could help to design effective policies and management strategies for forming a new, sustainable, and intelligent urban mobility system under the autonomous driving era.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: When heat hits: Short-run saving and withdrawal behavior among microfinance clients in Benin
Authors: Anna Mader, Oliver Mußhoff
Abstract: Increased access to finance is widely viewed as a key driver to increase adaptive capacity in response to climate change. However, apart from limited studies on borrowing behavior, little is known about how exposure to extreme heat impacts microfinance clients’ financial behavior. This study addresses this gap by investigating the short-run effects of unusual heat on microfinance clients’ saving and withdrawal behavior. In a case study, it combines geo-located temperature data with a unique dataset of around 50,000 clients of a leading Microfinance Institution (MFI) in Benin. Applying two-way fixed effects, seemingly unrelated regression, and ordinary least square models, the study finds that exposure to extreme heat is heterogeneously associated with microfinance clients’ financial behavior. Specifically, non-agricultural clients show suggestive evidence for the accumulation of precautionary savings after extreme heat days in the precedent quarter, while agricultural clients statistically significantly reduce their savings following exposure to extreme heat in the precedent quarter. Microfinance clients increase their withdrawals when exposed to extreme heat within the precedent quarter, but the association is not robust to agricultural clients’ withdrawals in response to an increase in annual extreme heat days. Addressing the heterogeneous financial responses across different clients to extreme heat consequently requires explicit policy attention. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the impact of extreme weather events on individual economic outcomes, how financial behavior relates to weather risk, and how microfinance clients respond to shocks.

Title: Does increasing inequality threaten social stability? Evidence from the lab
Authors: Fabrizio Adriani, Abigail Barr, Anna Hochleitner, Silvia Sonderegger
Abstract: We investigate the impact of rising inequality on social instability through a novel multi-period laboratory experiment. In each period, members of two groups are randomly matched to play a battle of the sexes game, in which payoffs are either zero for both or positive but unequal. At the beginning of the game, the implied payoff inequality is low but, under some treatments, it increases over time. While under low initial inequality, unequal conventions – where one group is systematically better off – tend to emerge, increasing inequality causes destabilization. This is initiated by the group disadvantaged by the unequal convention and is particularly pronounced when not only the relative, but also the absolute position of the disadvantaged group is worsening. These findings are consistent with a simple model incorporating disadvantageous inequality aversion. Finally, we show that history matters; responses to current inequality depend on past experiences of inequality and stability.

Title: Sibling sex composition, race, and marriage in the United States
Authors: Raymond Kim, Jose Rosa
Abstract: Using the universe of Texas births from 1976–1997, matched to marriage records through 2019, we provide the first U.S. evidence on how sibling sex composition affects marriage outcomes. First-born individuals with a same-sex younger sibling are more likely to marry, and to marry earlier, consistent with evidence from other settings. The scale and diversity of our setting further let us examine how these effects differ across race and ethnicity. We find they are concentrated among White individuals and in wealthier counties, with Hispanic women also responding in higher-income areas.

Title: Behavioral tokenomics: Myopic voting and token-weighted governance
Authors: Nicole Tsz Yeung Liu, Samuel N. Kirshner, Eric T.K. Lim
Abstract: Crowdsourcing-based decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) often aggregate members’ information and beliefs through token-weighted voting. Existing research shows that token-weighted voting erodes information aggregation when members vote myopically, whereas strategic members adjust the weight on their private signals inversely to their token holdings to unravel the weighting mechanism. We test voters’ behavior in a controlled experiment, finding that participants vote myopically, conservatively weighting their private signals, and that the voting mechanism does not influence their propensity to act strategically. Our results provide an important first step in developing a behavioral understanding of DAOs.

Title: Consumer sophistication and firm strategy when social feedback is untrustworthy
Authors: Bikram Ghosh, Michael R. Galbreth
Abstract: This paper analyzes the effect of consumer sophistication on consumer assessment of social feedback (such as user reviews), and ultimately on a firm’s strategic decisions. Consumer sophistication is defined on a continuum of cognitive sophistication, with high levels corresponding to careful deliberation of available information and low levels corresponding to naive information processing. Consumers are aware that social feedback may be untrustworthy, and they tend to trust (distrust) positive (negative) feedback about a product for which they have a higher valuation. Optimal price, profit, and sales decrease (increase) with sophistication at low (high) levels of sophistication. Optimal sales, however, falls for a larger range of sophistication than price. At low levels of sophistication, the firm chooses to serve most consumers, and an increase in sophistication lowers the valuation of the marginal consumer, forcing the firm to cut prices. Marginal revenue also falls, lowering optimal sales. The dynamic reverses when sophistication is high, because an increase in sophistication increases the dispersion of consumer valuations. In an extension, we consider how the results change when consumers know that a firm aggressively suppresses negative feedback. Our results suggest that suppressing negative feedback harms the firm by nullifying the dispersion-enhancing effect of sophistication.

Title: Generalized fractional order momentum for deep reinforcement learning in dynamic flexible job shop scheduling
Authors: Meixin Huang, Jianguo Zheng
Abstract: Dynamic flexible job shop scheduling (DFJSS) couples routing and sequencing decisions under stochastic arrivals, heterogeneous machine capabilities, and due date constraints. This study develops a decomposed deep reinforcement learning framework with independently trained routing and sequencing policies optimized by generalized fractional derivative stochastic classical momentum (GFD–SCM). The update modulates momentum attenuation and gradient scale as functions of the iteration without storing historical gradients or changing the computational order at each iteration. Under uniformly bounded stochastic gradients, the analysis establishes boundedness and asymptotic forgetting of the internal momentum state. The policies use compact state descriptors, slack sensitive rewards, and asynchronous transitions. In the primary routing experiments, the routing policy improves normalized performance by approximately 1.2 to 4.5 percentage points relative to CT and records win rates of 65 to 70%. In a separate benchmark, the GFD–SCM policy pair yields lower cumulative tardiness than Transformer–RL, Hierarchical–RL, and MLP after Holm correction.

Title: No bunching, yet response: Household electricity demand under increasing block pricing with intermittent billing
Authors: Jinmahn Jo
Abstract: This paper studies residential electricity demand under Increasing Block Pricing (IBP) with intermittent billing, where cycle-level information on realized usage and billed charges becomes available only after a billing cycle ends. Using monthly billing records for 199,090 households served by the Sacramento Municipal Utility District between 2005 and 2008, I apply a sharp regression discontinuity (RD) design around the lower-tier Baseline Usage Quantity, where the marginal price rises discontinuously. The estimate indicates a reduction of 0.058 kWh/day in average daily consumption during the subsequent billing cycle, equivalent to about 0.26% of the local control-group mean. Under the RD assumptions, this estimate represents a local, cycle-averaged threshold-crossing effect near the cutoff. This ex post response coexists with the absence of sharp ex ante bunching in observed consumption, showing that the absence of sharp bunching need not imply the absence of price responsiveness under intermittent billing. The design does not distinguish among competing behavioral mechanisms, but the next-cycle timing pattern makes feedback timing a relevant consideration for nonlinear tariff design.

Title: Editorial Board
The impacts of externality and government subsidies on the adoption of new-generation products
Authors: Jing Wang, Siyu Shi, Ya Liu, Yufei Huang
Abstract: New-generation products provide consumers with new value and give enterprises competitive edges in the market, but they often come with high production costs. Meanwhile, consumers’ willingness to adopt these products is influenced by how many others have already adopted them. This phenomenon, known as externality, occurs because consumers may hesitate to purchase unfamiliar products. To promote the adoption of new-generation products, the government can choose to alleviate the enterprise's cost burden by implementing subsidy schemes that differ in timing, i.e., in the early period, the late period, or both periods. This study employs a two-period game-theoretic model with dynamic pricing to examine how the externality and government subsidies affect equilibrium outcomes and the efficiency of subsidy schemes. First, our analysis shows how the government determines the optimal subsidy level under each subsidy scheme. Specifically, under the scheme that subsidizes only the late period, the government does not need to provide subsidies when the externality level is below a certain threshold. Second, our results indicate that the effect of externality on prices and market demands varies depending on subsidy schemes. Counterintuitively, total demand does not always increase with the externality level in certain situations. Finally, the results demonstrate that subsidizing only the late period is not optimal in our analysis. If consumers are less patient, the government should subsidize the enterprise only in the early period. However, when consumers are more patient, it may occur that subsidizing the enterprise in both periods is optimal.

Title: Green absorptive capacity and environmental sustainability: unveiling the interplay and moderating roles of blockchain and supply chain finance
Authors: Mahmoud Barakat
Affiliations: Arab Academy for Science, Technology and Maritime Transport College of International Transport and Logistics, , Alexandria
Abstract: Purpose Drawing on dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view, this study aims to examine how green absorptive capacity (GAC) enhances environmental sustainability performance (ESP) through financial performance (FP) and operational performance (OP) and how blockchain technology (BCT) and supply chain finance (SCF) strengthen these indirect relationships. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 522 organisations in Egypt and 508 in Jordan. Covariance-based structural equation modelling was used to test the moderated mediation model. Findings The results show that in both Egypt and Jordan, GAC improves ESP indirectly through FP and OP. In Jordan, blockchain technology strengthens the indirect relationship through both financial and operational performance, whereas in Egypt these blockchain effects are not supported. Supply chain finance strengthens the indirect relationship through operational performance in both countries, but not through financial performance. The nested model comparison indicates that whilst the overall model applies to both contexts, BCT and SCF exert varying degrees of influence in Egypt and Jordan. Research limitations/implications The results can support policymakers and organisational stakeholders by showing how digital technologies and green financing mechanisms can be used to strengthen the impact of green knowledge on performance and accelerate progress towards environmental sustainability. Originality/value This study develops and tests an integrated moderated mediation framework explaining how green absorptive capacity enhances environmental sustainability performance through financial and operational performance and how blockchain technology and supply chain finance strengthen these indirect relationships. By comparing Egypt and Jordan, the study extends dynamic capability theory and the natural resource-based view through context-specific evidence from two Arab emerging economies and reveals country-specific differences in the effectiveness of digital and financial enablers.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Integration of joint energy commodity price forecasts with hydrogen energy system planning under uncertain climate policies
Authors: Hongtao Ren, Caiyu Chen, Li Su, Hui Gao, Hui Qiao, Wenji Zhou
Abstract: Deep decarbonization via green hydrogen requires rigorous assessment of fossil fuel prices and evolving climate policy risks. To quantify these impacts, we propose an integrated framework that links multivariate density forecasting with long-term energy system optimization. A vector error correction model with dynamic conditional correlation GARCH is employed to generate joint coal and gas price densities that capture cross-market co-movements. These probabilistic inputs are systematically incorporated into a hydrogen planning model featuring coverage-adjusted emissions trading scheme allowance price paths. Results from the scenario matrix indicate that while high and volatile fossil fuel prices accelerate green hydrogen cost competitiveness, climate policy uncertainty significantly delays investment decisions. By bridging econometric forecasting and system optimization, this hybrid framework improves probabilistic calibration relative to benchmarks and reduces planning uncertainty for investors and policymakers.

Title: Trauma in humanitarian operations: A replication and extension of Brooks et al. (2023)
Authors: Iana Jackson, Llord Brooks, David D. Dobrzykowski
Affiliations: J.B. Hunt Transport Department of Supply Chain Management, Walton College of Business University of Arkansas Fayetteville Arkansas USA; School of Marketing and Innovation, MUMA College of Business University of South Florida Tampa Florida USA; Harbert College of Business, Department of Supply Chain Management Auburn University Auburn Alabama USA
Abstract: Abstract We develop a two‐part study that first performs a methods‐only replication of Brooks, Shaheen, and Dobrzykowski's study of trauma in humanitarian operations and then extends the model to investigate secondary trauma. Using data from 442 volunteer humanitarian workers collected through a scenario‐based vignette experiment, we replicate the original experimental design with a new, substantively important population. Additionally, the methods‐only replication reconsiders the relationship between trauma exposure and volunteer behaviors. Yet, the replication results reaffirm several key relationships observed among professional relief workers, including the negative effects of trauma exposure on cooperative disposition and internal integration and the moderating role of supervisor support. However, we find that trauma significantly reduces organizational commitment among volunteers; a relationship not observed in the original professional sample, highlighting important contextual differences in how trauma affects workers with less formal organizational attachment. In the second part of the study, we extend the model by introducing secondary trauma, a critical factor for a new volunteer sample. Our results show that secondary trauma operates differently from primary trauma and provides additional explanatory power in understanding behavioral responses in volunteer humanitarian settings. Together, these findings strengthen the robustness of prior theory while expanding it to account for volunteer contexts and indirect trauma exposure. The study contributes to replication research in operations and humanitarian management by demonstrating how trauma mechanisms generalize and where they diverge across organizational roles, offering implications for the management and support of volunteer workforces in disaster response.

Title: An agenda for plastics crisis research in the synthetic age
Authors: Borja Nogué-Algueró, Richard York, Stefano B. Longo, Ekaterina Chertkovskaya, Patrick Trent Greiner
Abstract: This survey synthesizes insights from environmental social sciences to recast the plastics crisis as a structural feature of growth-dependent economies instead of a problem solvable by consumer choice or incremental technologies. Rather than a within-field review of ecological economics, it maps adjacent literatures to specify what this field could study and how, clarifying researchable questions, suitable methods, and tractable indicators. The synthesis foregrounds connections between expansionary political-economic dynamics, globally uneven socio-ecological burdens across the plastics life cycle, and the power and knowledge relations that shape what is produced, measured, and governed. It calls for comparative, mixed-methods, multi-scalar work and for open, standardized data on plastics flows to strengthen causal inference and comparability. Shifting attention upstream—from end-of-pipe fixes to the transformation of provisioning systems—the paper charts lines of inquiry capable of aligning social metabolism with biophysical limits and human needs, providing a roadmap for ecological economics to organize and accelerate research beyond consumer or techno-managerial framings.

Title: Understanding conflict in protected areas: integrating justice considerations with economic perspectives
Authors: Ester Rita Lucia Sanna, Marta Meleddu
Abstract: Despite broad agreement on the urgency of sustainability transitions that protect biodiversity, conservation conflicts continue to rise. This paper examines environmental conflicts in protected areas (PAs), highlighting the overlooked link between conflict and justice. Existing frameworks often fail to distinguish between conflict manifestations and determinants, or to integrate justice theories with economic perspectives. This study provides a comprehensive review of the literature to support the analysis of PA conflicts and develops a robust framework that integrates justice considerations with the economic perspective. Conflicts are viewed as inherent to complex social–ecological systems, shaped by social relations and rights over ecosystem services. The framework is structured around three analytical axes: substance (what the conflict is about), process (how it unfolds), and relation (who is involved with-whom). It differentiates between how conflicts appear (i.e., manifestation) and what causes them (i.e., determinants), framed through distributive, procedural, and recognition justice. This perspective challenges linear assumptions that conflicts always stem from injustices, emphasizing their potential to drive institutional change. The framework offers a novel approach to assessing justice-conflict dynamics in PAs governance, providing comprehensive toolkit for promoting equitable conservation strategies.

Title: Modelling behavioural responses to infrastructure development in megacity regions
Authors: Bowen Zhang, Chen Zhong, Zahratu Shabrina
Abstract: Understanding how large-scale transport infrastructure shapes mobility patterns and the spatial structure is essential for assessing the impacts of urban development and policy. However, it is a challenging task given the dynamic nature of urban processes, and it is even more so in a megacity context. This study proposes a simulation-based framework that combines travel behaviour modelling with functional zone delineation to assess the impacts of infrastructure development. The framework builds on a two-step spatial interaction model in which localised distance-decay parameters are estimated for socioeconomically differentiated area clusters. Predicted flows from the spatial interaction model, incorporating projected population and updated travel time, are fed into a regionalisation algorithm that delineates urban functional zones. We illustrated the framework through a case study of the Shenzhen–Dongguan–Huizhou–Zhongshan region, simulating the opening of the Shenzhen–Zhongshan Bridge in the China Bay Area. Results demonstrated substantial reductions in cross-estuary travel impedance and a reconfiguration of functional boundaries, with parts of Zhongshan becoming functionally integrated into Shenzhen. However, average travel distances increase as greater accessibility enables longer-distance commuting, which is a counterintuitive yet insightful observation. Overall, the proposed framework has been shown to be a scalable instrument for linking behavioural heterogeneity, infrastructure modifications, and the emergent urban spatial structure within rapidly integrating mega-city regions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The future of game-based logistics: a systematic review of applications, functions, and evidence
Authors: Seyed Sina Mohri, Russell G. Thompson, Lele Zhang, Michael Kirley
Abstract: Game-based approaches are increasingly employed to address complex challenges in logistics and freight transport. While traditionally employed for education and workforce training, they have broader applications and untapped potential. In particular, advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are creating new opportunities to design, personalise, and scale these interventions. Despite this growing interest, a comprehensive understanding of how game-based approaches have evolved, who they target, what functions they serve, and where future opportunities lie remains limited. This study presents a systematic review of 87 studies on game-based interventions in freight transport and logistics, synthesising evidence across five application domains: warehouse operations management, terminal operations management, transport planning and optimisation, reverse logistics, and risk management and resilience. The findings reveal that games are evolving beyond training applications towards behavioural research, decision support, stakeholder engagement, and consumer behaviour change. Target audiences have similarly expanded from students and operational personnel to include managers, planners, consumers, and participants in behavioural research settings. Nevertheless, evidence regarding the long-term effectiveness of these interventions remains scarce, and several logistics challenges remain largely unexplored. Building on evidence-based gaps identified in the literature, this review proposes future research directions and highlights the potential of AI to enable adaptive, personalised, and scalable game-based interventions. By consolidating fragmented knowledge and outlining emerging opportunities, this study provides a foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to harness game-based approaches to understand and improve logistics and freight transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Equity trade‑offs in global aviation education: evidence from a micro‑credential transition across 141 countries
Authors: Suzanne Kearns, Ammar Abulibdeh, Amr ElAlfy, Gülnaz Bülbül, Ju Eun Lee, Laura Camastra
Abstract: Online professional aviation education holds significant potential to address the global aviation workforce shortage and advance equity for underrepresented learners, yet large-scale empirical evidence on participation, completion, and equity outcomes remains scarce. This study evaluates the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO)–the University of Waterloo Aviation Fundamentals Education programme (AVIFUN), a longitudinal online professional education initiative spanning 3,026 learners across 141 countries from 2020 to 2025, with a focus on the equity implications of a structural transition from a long-format 20-hour model to a modular micro-credential architecture in July 2025. Using multivariable binary logistic regression, pre/post comparative analysis with Wilson score confidence intervals, and interaction modeling, the study examines how programme format, gender, Least Developed Country (LDC) status, and ICAO region independently and jointly predict certificate attainment. The micro-credential transition was associated with a near-fivefold increase in LDC participation (from 2.8% to 14.7%) and a rise in female enrolment from 26.1% in 2020 to 46.8% in 2025. These access gains were, however, accompanied by a significant decline in certificate attainment, with micro-credential learner-level certification (76.5% certifying any module) not significantly different from long-format certificate attainment (73.8%; learner-level OR = 1.105, p = 0.619). A 22.6 percentage-point gender completion gap within micro-credentials and significant regional heterogeneity further characterize the equity landscape. Module-level analysis confirms that gender and region did not systematically influence content selection, a positive equity outcome. The findings reveal a fundamental access-completion trade-off in micro-credential delivery and offer actionable design recommendations for second-generation programme architectures to sustain both access equity and completion equity in global aviation professional education.

Title: Political elites and access to economic opportunities in China’s rural market transition
Authors: Lin Xie, Mengting Liang, Qingxiao Li, Shaozhuang Wang, Xiao Lei
Abstract: Understanding whether political elites maintain advantages in accessing economic opportunities during market transitions is crucial for assessing the distributional consequences of market-oriented reforms. This study examines whether political status provides rural households with advantages in accessing production resources and income opportunities during China’s recent wave of marketization, and how these advantages vary with the degree of market development. Using three waves of the China Family Database spanning 2015–2019 and employing an instrumental variable approach, we find that political elites maintain persistent advantages in accessing economic opportunities. Relative to non-elites, cadre households exhibit 20.1 percentage points higher rates of receiving agricultural subsidies, 38.8 percentage points higher rates of owning agricultural machinery, and 9.7 percentage points greater likelihood of operating nonfarm businesses. As marketization advances, the sources of elite advantage shift from agriculture to commercial activities. While advantages in agricultural production weaken, reflecting reduced state-controlled resource allocation channels, advantages in business operations strengthen consistent with elites converting political capital into entrepreneurial opportunities. Our findings suggest that rural marketization in China reallocates rather than reduces opportunity gaps. This pattern indicates that even as market reforms diminish traditional avenues for political privilege, they simultaneously open new market-based opportunities that preserve elite advantage. These findings have broader implications for understanding how political power influences access to opportunities during market transitions in developing economies.

Title: Optimal electricity consumption and storage under short-term renewable supply variability
