Title: Balancing emission reduction and regulatory burden under inspection limits for diesel fleets
Authors: Junchao Zhao, Jiaxin Lu, Tingting Zhang, Yunjing Wang, Zhenyu Luo, Xingrui Cai, Xinping Yang, Leqi Zhang, Yanjun Wang, Hongli Wang, Weicheng Chen, Hang Yin, Huan Liu, Yan Ding
Abstract: Effectively regulating in-use vehicle emissions requires methods that can identify high-impact emitters within heterogeneous vehicle fleets. This study develops a vehicle-level NOx accounting method based on inspection data, converting measured NOx concentrations into estimated emissions and aggregating these estimates to the fleet level. This approach enables fleet-scale emission accounting that explicitly reflects heterogeneity in both vehicle emission intensity and activity levels. In the study region, using a full-sample 2024 dataset, we assess fleet-level emission heterogeneity and reduction potential under alternative Inspection and Maintenance limits. We find that China V diesel trucks dominate fleet emissions due to their large population size and substantial vehicle activity. Furthermore, tightening the inspection limit reveals a trade-off between emission reduction benefits and compliance costs. The proposed NOx Reduction Effectiveness Index (NREI) identifies an optimal threshold range where emission reduction efficiency peaks, providing a scientific basis for balancing environmental benefits with maintenance burdens in policy optimization.

Title: Flowing innovation: Bureaucratic transfers and collaborative innovation

Title: Parallel axiomatizations of the concave and convex integrals
Authors: Yangyi Deng, Chiu Yu Ko
Abstract: We provide parallel axiomatic foundations for the concave and convex integrals, which represent optimistic and pessimistic rules for aggregating interacting attributes. For the concave integral, we show that the existing characterizations hold once accordance for additive capacities is required for every finite attribute set rather than only when the attribute set is a singleton. Without this strengthening, the original axioms admit a family of distinct functionals. For the convex integral, we derive a representation as the maximum of ordinary integrals over additive measures dominated by the capacity and establish parallel axiomatic characterizations, with the relevant inequalities reversed relative to their concave counterparts.

Title: The economics of free bets
Authors: Karl Whelan
Abstract: Sportsbooks offer promotional “free bets” that return profits if the bets win, but not the stake provided. These bets can be hedged to produce guaranteed profits. This paper shows how to value the guaranteed profit from these stake-not-returned free bets under a simple constant-margin pricing rule in which sportsbooks, on average, keep a fraction m of the money staked. The guaranteed hedged value is a nonlinear function of the free bet’s probability of winning, reaching a maximum when this probability is m(1−m)[jls-end-space/]. Empirical evidence from odds on tennis bets confirms this prediction.

Title: Reassessing the evidence on Spain's energy poverty amid the green transition: A replication and augmentation
Authors: Purushottam Yadav, Sajal Ghosh, Kakali Kanjilal
Abstract: This paper replicates and augments the study of Ramzan et al. (2025), which investigates the drivers of energy poverty in Spain using a multivariate quantile-on-quantile regression framework. While the original study reports that renewable energy consumption (REN), green innovation (GIN), natural resource rents (RNT), and information globalization (IGL) reduce energy poverty, our replication identifies fundamental conceptual and empirical flaws that undermine these outcomes. A key issue concerns the use of access to electricity (AEP) as a proxy for energy poverty, despite Spain maintaining near-universal electricity access throughout the study period. Our replication shows that higher renewable energy consumption is often associated with lower AEP values, contrary to the positive relationship reported in the original study. Green innovation effects also vary across quantiles, with both positive and negative impacts, contrary to uniformly beneficial effects. Robustness tests confirm the replication findings. We further strengthen the analysis by employing “population unable to keep home adequately warm” (AEPN) as an alternative measure of energy poverty and by incorporating additional control variables. In contrast to Ramzan et al. (2025), the AEPN-based estimates suggest that renewable energy expansion does not uniformly reduce energy poverty and is associated with higher energy deprivation across several quantiles. The additional controls show that energy prices, energy intensity, urbanisation, and inequality also play an important role in shaping the distributional dynamics of energy poverty. The results imply that renewable energy policies alone may be insufficient to alleviate energy poverty unless accompanied by measures addressing affordability, energy prices, and household vulnerability.

Title: An engine of (pay) growth? Productivity and wages in the UK auto industry
Authors: Agnes Norris Keiller, Tim Obermeier, Andreas Teichgraeber, John Van Reenen
Abstract: To what extent do identical workers in an industry benefit from productivity growth in the same industry? We study this question in the context of the UK auto industry which experienced a thirteen-fold increase in output per worker between 1980 and 2018. Over the same period, auto workers saw substantially stronger hourly wage growth than workers in other manufacturing industries. Controlling for unobserved worker heterogeneity, the auto wage premium over other manufacturing workers doubled from 8% in the 1980s to 17% in the 2010s, while the manufacturing premium over the rest of the economy remained roughly stable at 5%. Interpreted through the lens of a rent sharing model, we estimate that 63% of the increase in the raw firm-level auto wage premium can be accounted for by strong productivity growth. In contrast, differential bargaining power between auto workers cannot account for these changes.

Title: The unseen pain of the Vietnam War: long-term effects of Agent Orange on labor market outcomes
Authors: Luu Duc Toan Huynh, Po Yin Wong
Abstract: Abstract We examine the long-term labor market consequences of exposure to Agent Orange during the Vietnam War, focusing on cohorts whose childhoods overlapped the spraying period. Exploiting district-level variation in herbicide exposure intensity, we find exposed individuals attain lower levels of schooling and reduce their labor supply by 7% relative to the mean. Among individuals who remain in their birth provinces, labor income is reduced by 26.7%. We show that cognitive and physical health impairments do not fully explain the effects. Exposure also reduced household income and pushed individuals toward primary industries, away from wage employment. We further document intergenerational effects, as children of exposed parents exhibit lower educational attainment and reduced labor supply. These findings highlight the lasting and multigenerational economic costs of wartime chemical exposure.

Title: Managing failure risks in unmanned aerial vehicles: a human factor-integrated three-way group classification framework using online reviews
Authors: Dun Liu, Yiqiang Mu, Chengnan Gao
Abstract: The constant advancement and innovation of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have offered new growth prospects. However, frequent UAV accidents have highlighted significant safety risks posed by product failures. Given the critical role of UAV manipulators, this paper proposes a human factor-integrated three-way group classification (HF-TGC) framework driven by online reviews to identify UAV failure modes and support their risk classification and management. Firstly, to construct domain-specific dictionaries for UAV components, failures, and human factors, we integrate TF-IDF and Word2Vec with multi-platform online reviews to extract UAV failure mode triplets. Secondly, considering the inconsistency in group risk assessments and the behavioral characteristics of decision makers, we integrate the minimum consensus cost model (MCCM) and the TODIM method to calculate risk priority, while determining the degree of human-factor involvement based on two types of human factor words. Then, to enable effective classification and management of UAV failure modes, we introduce the generalized three-way decision (TWD) theory to develop a UAV risk management framework that incorporates both risk priority and human factors. Finally, the effectiveness of the HF-TGC framework is validated through a case study of consumer-grade DJI UAVs. Comparative analysis and sensitivity analysis demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework and the critical role of human factors. A total of 44 primary UAV failure modes and 884 sub-failure modes were identified. These elements, together with their classification results, were integrated into a human factors knowledge graph to facilitate efficient management of UAV failure modes.

Title: A patent-driven SCOR-IFCM framework to prioritize generative AI adoption for supply chain resilience
Authors: Chunhua Ju, Ke Li, Chonghuan Xu, Hongli Liu
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) has considerable potential to enhance supply chain resilience (SCR), but its effective adoption remains subject to technological uncertainty. This study integrates BERTopic, the Supply Chain Operations Reference (SCOR) model, intuitionistic fuzzy sets (IFS), and clamped intuitionistic fuzzy cognitive map (IFCM) simulation to develop a patent-driven framework for screening and prioritizing potential Gen AI applications. Based on 139,661 Gen AI patent abstracts associated with Chinese listed firms, the framework identifies 870 fine-grained technology topics, maps them onto 29 SCOR-oriented nodes, and uses patent-text evidence to construct a technology propagation structure and a 29×5 technology-performance allocation matrix. Four main findings emerge. First, patent portfolio analysis focuses on enabling, data-processing, and infrastructure capabilities, with semantic evidence linking these capabilities to SCR dimensions such as reliability, responsiveness, agility, cost, and asset management. Second, counter- and unresolved evidence reveal constraining pathways, with negative propagation concentrated in limited cross-node relationships. Third, sustained support for selected driver nodes creates selective spillovers rather than uniform gains; under the soft-clamped scenario, engineering quality and progress management, order lifecycle management, and intelligent logistics path planning achieve the highest non-driver activation. Fourth, SCOR contributions depend jointly on steady-state activation and patent-semantic associations, so strong semantic support alone does not guarantee high modeled contribution. Overall, the framework provides patent-evidence-based decision support for screening candidate technologies, prioritizing staged evaluation, and comparing conditional SCOR performance profiles.

Title: Regret aversion and anchoring effects in advanced parking information system adoption: The behavioral economics of parking choices
Authors: Meng Guo, Doosun Hong, Eunhyang Lee, Sunghoon Jang
Abstract: Advanced parking information systems (APISs) aim to alleviate urban parking challenges by providing real-time information and reservations. Their effectiveness, however, depends on how drivers respond to these services when they coexist with uncertain current parking options. This decision process is shaped by psychological mechanisms which standard utility-maximizing models often fail to capture. This study addresses this gap by examining drivers’ APIS choices through an anchored generalized random regret minimization (AG-RRM) model, extended within a latent class framework. By introducing the Self-Report Parking Habit Index (SRPHI), we further quantify the strength of ingrained parking routine and its impact on APIS choices. Results from a stated preference survey reveal parking behavior spans a spectrum from asymmetric regret aversion to linear attribute trade-offs. Familiar current parking serves as a reference anchor associated with stronger regret responses when APIS options underperform. We identify two distinct driver segments based on SRPHI scores. Efficiency-oriented drivers (38.8%) respond rationally to quantifiable APIS benefits. Conversely, habitual or anchor-bound drivers (61.2%) represent the majority, exhibiting stronger regret aversion and anchoring-related responses involving current parking. For the anchor-bound majority, the estimated responses suggest that marginal price signals alone may be insufficient to nudge adoption. These insights provide a behavioral foundation for personalized measures and de-anchoring interventions promoting APIS usage. We suggest APIS operators leverage psychological nudges, such visualizing invisible cruising costs, to weaken the perceived surcharge-free advantage of current parking options. By reframing the mental anchor, such non-monetary interventions have the potential to address behavioral inertia and improve parking efficiencies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The Olympic effect revisited: 1950–2019
Authors: Renjing Chen, Meng Gao, Wenzheng Gao, Wei Jin, Yuqian Sun
Abstract: Rose and Spiegel (2011) identified a positive trade-promoting effect of hosting the Olympic Games, yet they did not account for multilateral resistance terms in their analysis, which are emphasized in the structural gravity model by Anderson and van Wincoop (2003). This paper revisits the trade effects of the Olympics using a nonparametric matching method developed by Chang and Lee (2011), analyzing a comprehensive gravity dataset encompassing 187 economies from 1950 to 2019. Our findings suggest that hosting the Olympics is positively associated with bilateral trade. For pairs in which both countries have hosted, the matching estimate corresponds to a long-run trade difference with an implied increase of approximately 15 times relative to matched nonhost pairs. Under an assumed trade elasticity of 4, this estimate corresponds to an illustrative trade-cost equivalent of approximately 50%.

Title: Drought, women’s time poverty, and the development costs of water collection in Sub-Saharan Africa
Authors: Xueyang Wang, Wenling Liu
Abstract: Drought can impose development costs that are not fully captured by income, production, or formal water access indicators. This paper examines one such hidden cost in Sub-Saharan Africa by focusing on women’s time poverty arising from household water collection. Combining harmonized Demographic and Health Surveys with geocoded drought exposure measured at the survey cluster level, we estimate how local drought conditions are associated with women’s annual water collection burden and broader household adjustments. We find that drought exposure is associated with higher water-collection time for women, with larger estimated increases among women living in poor households, women with no formal education, and women living in households without piped-water access. Intermediate-outcome evidence shows that drought is associated with lower local water availability and a higher likelihood of very long collection trips, particularly journeys exceeding 60 minutes. These water-time burdens are also associated with greater engagement in flexible, household-based, family-based, and self-employed forms of work among women rather than with a simple expansion of protected paid employment. In addition, higher community water burdens are associated with poorer schooling outcomes among girls, including a greater likelihood of being out of school and larger grade-for-age gaps. Household-linked evidence further shows that poorer girls’ schooling outcomes are associated with larger household shares of adult women in unpaid or in-kind work, self-employment, and family work. The findings suggest that drought-related water insecurity can redistribute adaptation costs within households, making women’s unpaid time a key margin through which climate stress produces hidden development costs.

Title: Editorial Board
Decarbonizing oxy-fuel glass furnaces through multi-objective batch and energy planning
Authors: Hossein Arshad, Chiara Caccamo, Thiago Lima Silva, Ernesto Cattaneo
Abstract: Decarbonizing high-temperature glass production requires coordinated decisions on batch composition, energy sourcing, and furnace operation. However, existing research has not sufficiently integrated virgin raw materials, internal and external cullet, multiple hydrogen pathways, electric boosting, inventories, lead times, and operational constraints within a unified short-term production planning and control framework for oxy-fuel glass furnaces. This study develops a multi-period, multi-objective linear programming model to address this gap. The model jointly optimizes batch composition and energy allocation across natural gas, green, blue, and grey hydrogen, and renewable and grid electricity. It links material choices to melting-energy requirements, process emissions, and direct and indirect energy-related emissions, while incorporating storage, electricity availability, ordering decisions, ramping limits, hydrogen-blending limits, and energy-mix constraints. Two conflicting objectives are considered: minimizing operating cost and emissions. Lexicographic optimization generates cost- and emission-priority solutions, while a normalized weighted-sum approach identifies intermediate trade-offs. The model is evaluated using three European industrial cases in container-glass and fiberglass production over a 24-hour planning horizon. Results show that higher cullet utilization can reduce emissions by up to 25.6%, energy use by up to 19.3%, and cost by up to 18.9%. Under emission-priority operation, green-hydrogen scale-up reduces emissions by up to 10.7% at a cost increase of approximately 4%. Cost-priority solutions remain dominated by natural gas, whereas lower-emission operation requires greater use of green hydrogen and renewable electricity. Although the model is deterministic and does not capture detailed furnace physics, it provides structured decision support for plant-specific decarbonization planning.

Title: Optimal unemployment insurance under statistical profiling
Authors: Sergio Cappellini, Sofía Ruiz-Palazuelos
Abstract: How should unemployment insurance (UI) be designed? We characterize the optimal contract when employability is statistically assessed at the beginning of a claim and progressively revised based on elapsed job search duration. In our setting, workers can manipulate future assessments through current search behavior, generating endogenous learning rents that must be compensated to sustain search effort. We show that these rents increase with unemployment duration and UI generosity, raising the relative attractiveness of search monitoring and assistance. Ignoring learning rents may therefore lead to insufficient search incentives, lower job-finding rates, and biased estimates of the returns to search-incentivizing programs.

Title: Reconsidering “Why do people dislike inflation?”
Authors: William J. Luther, Monica Escaleras
Abstract: In a widely cited article, Shiller (1997) found that the public dislikes inflation to a greater extent than economists—and dislikes inflation for different reasons. We fielded a contemporary version of Shiller’s survey to consider how economists’ and the public’s views on inflation have changed over time. We find that, in some respects, economists’ views on inflation more closely resemble those of the public in our survey than was originally reported by Shiller (1997). But important differences remain.

Title: On the number of high-frequency surprise factors in U.S. monetary policy
Authors: Roland von Campe
Abstract: I revisit the factor decomposition methodology developed by Gürkaynak et al. (2005) and Swanson (2021) using the new U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database (USMPD) provided by Acosta et al. (2025). I present evidence supporting a four-factor rather than three-factor decomposition and propose a procedure that structurally interprets the additional factor as an information factor. In particular, I demonstrate that the monetary policy surprises employed by Swanson (2021) yield three factors in pre-ZLB samples, with a fourth factor emerging following the Fed’s adoption of large-scale asset purchases. The suggested procedure has the merit that it preserves the well-established three-factor decomposition of Swanson (2021) while accommodating an additional information factor. The new evidence underlines that central bank announcements constitute high-dimensional communication events.

Title: When women take all: Direct election and female leadership
Authors: Davide Cipullo
Abstract: This paper investigates how direct election regimes (à la presidential democracy) affect the selection of women into political offices compared to indirect appointment (à la parliamentary). Exploiting the staggered phase-in across Italian municipalities of a reform to the local institutional regime, I find that the introduction of direct elections increased the fraction of female mayors substantially. The results are stronger in cities with a high pre-reform share of female politicians and driven by high-quality female officials replacing undereducated incumbents. Taken together, the results of this paper inform that direct election regimes ease the selection of competent politicians into office.

Title: Finite foresight in Chomp
Authors: Zachary Breig, Hai Anh Pham
Abstract: We experimentally study sequential rationality in the Game of Chomp, a two-player win-lose game whose rules are simple but whose subgame-perfect Nash equilibria vary in complexity across initial states. Subjects frequently deviate from SPNE: the probability of making an SPNE-consistent move falls with the distance to the end of the game, and most can correctly implement SPNE only three to five moves ahead. Experience mainly improves play at intermediate distances. We also document a common opening heuristic that, although often theoretically suboptimal, is still associated with higher chances of winning.

Title: Revealing tax evasion: Experimental evidence from a representative survey of Indonesian firms
Authors: Christopher Hoy, Filip Jolevski, Anthony Obeyesekere
Abstract: Measuring tax evasion by firms is notoriously difficult: direct questions yield biased responses while administrative data captures only detected violations. This paper examines the prevalence of reported tax non-compliance in Indonesia through a randomized, double-list experiment embedded in a nationally representative survey of 2,955 registered firms that preserves anonymity. The results indicate that around one-quarter of firms indirectly report not paying all taxes they are required to pay. An indicative back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that the associated revenue losses could be economically meaningful, in the order of two percent of GDP. Heterogeneity analyses suggest higher reported non-compliance among firms that do not export, face informal-sector competition, and view tax administration as a major obstacle. These findings help inform tax authorities, which face substantial challenges in estimating levels of tax evasion and identifying non-compliant taxpayers, by providing the first representative estimates of firm tax evasion in a major middle-income country.

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Adaptive scheduling for FJSPT: a two-stage deep reinforcement learning approach with scale-invariant action space
Authors: Yuxin Mo, Chunyan Duan, Zehao Zhang, Anhu Li
Abstract: The Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem with Transportation involves complex spatio-temporal coupling that challenges traditional scheduling methods. While deep reinforcement learning offers promise, existing approaches often suffer from the curse of dimensionality and fail to generalize across varying problem scales. To address these limitations, this study proposes a transfer-learning-enabled deep reinforcement learning system designed for rapid adaptation to large-scale instances. We first construct a dimension-independent composite action space that coordinates machine and automated guided vehicle dispatching rules, ensuring the action dimension remains invariant to resource quantity. Subsequently, a dual-agent framework is established to bridge the generalization gap. A generalist agent captures invariant scheduling priors using NoisyLinear-enhanced exploration, while a specialist agent rapidly adapts to specific instances via a transferred backbone and an LSTM-based temporal projection interface. Furthermore, an annealed probability sampling mechanism is integrated into the policy network to dynamically balance exploration and exploitation, thereby preventing premature convergence. This generalization-to-adaptation mechanism alleviates the cold-start training burden of deep reinforcement learning by providing a transferable initialization for rapid fine-tuning on target instances. Experimental results on benchmarks and large-scale synthetic datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms classical heuristics and state-of-the-art meta-heuristics, exhibiting superior stability and solution quality in complex manufacturing scenarios.

Title: A structure-guided reinforcement learning framework for joint scheduling and acceptance in R&D projects under technical risk
Authors: Xinyue Wang, Chaoming Hu, Haojun Fang, Zhiming Liu, Hao Cheng, Xinbao Liu
Abstract: R&D projects are inevitably exposed to technical risk, as continued development expenditures may fail to improve technical performance or ensure project profitability. This creates a fundamental challenge for project management as technical performance unfolds: when to accept the current outcome and how to schedule further development. We study joint task scheduling and acceptance decisions for an R&D project under stochastic technical performance evolution and limited capacity, formulating the problem as a Markov decision process to maximize expected net present value. The problem features the curse of dimensionality with a state-dependent, combinatorial action space. We propose a Structure-Guided Conservative Approximate Policy Iteration framework that integrates a tailored branch-and-Benders-cut optimizer for structure-exploiting action selection, a graph neural network-based actor-critic architecture for policy learning, and a conservative policy improvement scheme to stabilize policy updates. Extensive computational experiments across diverse problem settings show that the proposed approach significantly outperforms benchmark methods, including well-established deep reinforcement learning algorithms and approximate dynamic programming methods, demonstrating its superiority and practical applicability.

Title: Income redistribution, preventive care, and longevity
Authors: Pablo Garcia-Sanchez, Olivier Pierrard
Abstract: Would government intervention aimed at reducing socioeconomic inequalities lead to a healthier population and longer lives? We address this question using a structural life-cycle model with heterogeneous agents. The model is calibrated to U.S. survey and actuarial data, reproducing the age-at-death distribution, income inequality, medical expenditure patterns, the value of a statistical life, and the education–longevity gradient. We find that a universal basic income flattens the longevity gap across education levels but reduces overall longevity by weakening incentives for preventive care, a result that contrasts with recent statistical studies suggesting redistribution would increase population longevity. Instead, subsidies for preventive care raise average longevity but steepen the education–longevity gradient. In both cases, welfare effects remain uneven across education groups.

Title: Cross-border risk co-movement and multidimensional network resilience in global clean energy markets: Evidence from a higher-order downside co-movement network
Authors: Yaoxun Deng, Yongzeng Lai, Tianlei Zhu, Zisheng Ouyang
Abstract: The globalization of clean energy investment has intensified cross-market risk dependence, making the resilience of clean energy financial networks increasingly important. This study constructs a higher-order downside co-movement network for nine global clean energy equity markets using firm-level data for 829 companies from January 2013 to March 2025. Free-float-market-capitalization-weighted indices and the 5% asymmetric-slope CAViaR model are used to measure market-level downside tail risk, while ERA5 meteorological observations and a TVP-VAR framework are used to evaluate the resistance and recovery of system-level network topology and market-specific network roles to climate physical risk shocks. The results show that higher-order relations account for 75.0% of the retained baseline network, although their numerical prevalence and weighted contribution evolve differently. Major shocks are associated with distinct network reconfigurations: the COVID-19 episode sharply strengthens downside co-movement and shifts dominant relations toward higher-order configurations, whereas the U.S. Paris Agreement withdrawal announcement broadens relation coverage while the dominant relations remain largely pairwise. Climate-shock resilience is also multidimensional: network breadth exhibits stronger resistance and faster recovery than average relation strength, while Europe shows the strongest market-level network-role resilience and Brazil the weakest. More generally, network importance does not mechanically imply greater climate vulnerability. These findings provide a higher-order network perspective for monitoring systemic downside risk and assessing climate resilience in global clean energy markets.

Title: A novel two-phase preventive maintenance and inventory policy considering random lead times for spare parts
Authors: Yongchao Liu, Xiujie Zhao, Shuguang He, Guanjun Wang
Abstract: Existing studies on joint spare parts inventory and preventive maintenance mainly rely on fixed inspection intervals and replacement thresholds, which fail to capture the dynamic interaction between system degradation and inventory availability. To address this limitation, this paper develops an integrated adaptive maintenance and spare parts ordering policy with non-periodic inspections under a semi-Markov decision process framework. The operating process is divided into two phases: the spare parts consumption phase after delivery and the spare parts replenishment phase during the random lead time. In the consumption phase, we establish structural properties of the optimal policy, showing that it admits an inventory-dependent control-limit structure and that both the optimal replacement threshold and the optimal inspection interval are non-increasing with respect to the inventory level, while the inspection interval is also non-increasing with respect to the degradation level. In contrast, the optimal decision in the replenishment phase does not exhibit a simple threshold structure and is significantly influenced by the elapsed ordering time. Numerical experiments further validate the theoretical results. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis and comparisons with benchmark policies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed policy in reducing the long-run average cost.

Title: Patient sorting and downstream spending: evidence from an information disclosure program
Authors: Nicole Holz

Title: Place-based variation in health care: evidence from mandatory movers in the U.S. military health system
Authors: Roxana Leal, William P. Luan, Jonathan Skinner, John Zhou
Abstract: There is increasing evidence on regional variations in US Medicare health care utilization based on older patients who move. Yet moving for the elderly population is typically endogenous, and evidence is limited for younger populations. In this paper, we harness the mandatory migration of military personnel to estimate supply and demand factors in a system of care for younger enrollees in which military physicians are salaried and copayments and deductibles are negligible. Our preferred estimates imply that supply effects explain between one-half and two-thirds of overall regional variation. These variations cannot be explained by differences in quality of care, but appear consistent with location-specific differences in physician beliefs. Title: Supply disruptions, economic slack, and the state‐dependent Phillips curve
Authors: Ufuk Devrim Demirel, Matthew Wilson
Affiliations: Congressional Budget Office Washington District of Columbia USA
Abstract: Abstract This paper investigates how supply disruptions and economic slack affect the responsiveness of inflation to changes in aggregate demand. We propose and estimate a nonlinear Phillips curve, whereby the sensitivity of inflation to changes in demand varies with supply conditions and the amount of slack in the economy. We find evidence that supply disruptions and low unemployment both steepen the Phillips curve, thereby amplifying the inflationary effects of increased demand. Our results suggest that the effects of fiscal policy on inflation depend on the prevailing supply conditions and the level of unemployment in the economy.

Title: Helicopter drops in an open economy when markets are incomplete
Authors: Sara Eugeni
Affiliations: Department of Economics Durham University Business School Durham University Durham UK
Abstract: Abstract We characterize the spillover effects of helicopter drops and optimal monetary policy in a tractable two‐country overlapping generations model with incomplete markets. As helicopter drops can affect the distribution of income across countries, they create room for redistribution policies which are particularly relevant when agents are heterogeneous and markets are incomplete. Under cooperation, central banks can implement the conditionally Pareto optimal allocation using helicopter drops (and suctions) to “lean against the wind.” In a non‐cooperative setting, helicopter drops exacerbate the incomplete markets' friction by making income more volatile. This paves the way for gains from cooperation.

Title: Intellectual property rights and innovation in vertically related industries
Authors: Michael A. Klein
Affiliations: Department of Economics Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute Troy New York USA
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines the economic impact of intellectual property rights in the context of complementary vertical innovation by firms in upstream and downstream industries. Empirical patterns suggest that industry downstreamness is associated with a greater relative importance of patents versus trade secrecy in firm appropriation strategies. Using a novel model of endogenous growth, I show that strengthening patent protection generates downstream‐biased technical change in most cases. The corresponding reallocation of resources creates distributional effects from patent policy that existing analysis do not account for. I examine the impact of these effects on economic growth, welfare, and optimal patent policy.

Title: Can zoning reform reduce housing costs? Evidence from rents in Auckland
Authors: Ryan Greenaway‐McGrevy, Yun So
Affiliations: University of Auckland Auckland New Zealand; Economic Policy Centre University of Auckland Auckland New Zealand
Abstract: Abstract Zoning reform is increasingly advocated to redress unaffordable housing, but few real‐world examples demonstrate its efficacy. However, Auckland recently upzoned approximately three‐quarters of its residential land, precipitating a housing construction boom. We investigate whether the reform reduced housing costs, adopting a synthetic control method to estimate rental prices in Auckland under the counterfactual of no zoning change. Eight years after the reform, the synthetic control under our preferred empirical specification implies that rents decreased by 23% due to the reform. These findings are robust across a range of specifications and support the proposition that widespread upzoning can enhance housing affordability.

Title: Issue Information
Management control practices and circular economy capabilities: a configurations’ combinations fuzzy-set approach proposal
Authors: Issam Laguir, Rebecca Stekelorum, Shivam Gupta, Sameer Kumar, Ana Beatriz Lopes De Sousa Jabbour
Affiliations: MBS School of Business; Department of Strategy and Entrepreneurship, ICN Business School, CEREFIGE; Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain & Decision Making, NEOMA Business School; Opus College of Business, University of St. Thomas; EM Normandie Business School, Metis Lab
Abstract: The role of management controls in steering firms’ circular economy capabilities (CEC) has yet to be studied in a detailed manner. This study aims to investigate the use of management control (MC) practices combinations to promote CEC. A fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis conducted with input from 211 surveyed manufacturing firms provide multiple combinations of MC practices in achieving circular economy capabilities. The study reveals that MC practices found to be effective on their own should not be necessarily all employed at the same time to reach high levels of circular economy capabilities. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view, three configurations’ combinations (C1, C2, C3) of MC practices are proposed to guide the evolving CEC development process at firm level. It is identified which MC practices suit firms depending on firms’ aims to become more sustainable. C1 is about intensive use of boundary and diagnostic controls for firms aim to create routinely procedures to consolidate CEC. C2 concerns the use of diagnostic and interactive controls combined with no use of belief controls to lead high CEC in a situation in which already exists a CE mindset and the aim is to flourish CEC. And C3 suggests a high use of belief controls combined with no utilisation of diagnostic, boundary and interactive systems to lead a high level of CEC, enabling firms to really embed them into firms’ strategy and operations. A practical roadmap is suggested to managers to apply the configurations’ combinations.

Title: Organizational capabilities driving the circular economy: proposal and validation of a conceptual framework
Authors: Maria Clara da Cunha Bezerra, Cláudia Fabiana Gohr
Affiliations: Universidade Federal da Paraíba – UFPB
Abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) is a complex process enhanced by leveraging organizational capabilities (OC). This study aims to: (1) present, based on a systematic literature review (SLR), an overview of the of the state of research in OC in the CE context; (2) develop and validate, through the Delphi method, a framework that comprehensively categorizes the organizational capabilities that drive the transition to a circular economy (OCCE); and (3) propose a research agenda to guide future investigations in the field. The SLR analyzed 200 articles, resulting in a conceptual framework that systematizes existing findings and introduces 15 OCCE categories. These OCCE categories were hierarchized into three degrees, demonstrating that the capabilities at one degree can influence the development of capabilities at a higher degree. This hierarchy was validated by experts through the Delphi method. The study contributes to bringing organizations closer to the effective implementation of CE by identifying key organizational capabilities. Additionally, it offers a consolidated view of the literature, highlighting relevant trends, approaches and connections, thereby deepening the understanding of OC in the context of CE. Finally, a research agenda comprising 15 priority questions is proposed to direct future investigations into the organizational capabilities required for the circular transition.

Title: Postponement strategies for supply chain environmental and economic sustainability: a systematic review, conceptual framework, and future research agenda
Authors: Trung-Hieu Le, Lorenzo Prataviera, Heather Skipworth, Abhijeet Ghadge
Affiliations: Centre for Logistics, Procurement and Supply Chain Management, Cranfield School of Management, Cranfield University; Department of Management, University of Verona
Abstract: Supply chains (SCs) are increasingly challenged to deliver greater value with fewer resources while minimising environmental impact. Postponement strategies have emerged as a potential solution to strike this balance, yet their impact on environmental sustainability beyond economic considerations remains under-examined. A systematic literature review provides a design-oriented approach combined with the Contexts, Interventions, Mechanisms, and Outcomes (CIMO) logic to deepen the understanding of the effects of postponement strategies on environmental and economic sustainability. The study reconceptualises postponement and traces its recent evolution, expanding it beyond delaying uncertainty-increasing value-adding activities to include their geographical location and the involvement of different supply chain partners. This further enabled the precise characterisation of contemporary postponement applications, leading to the development of propositions that suggest under which conditions postponement strategies may enhance or harm both the environmental and economic performances of SCs. Finally, a future research agenda is proposed to advance postponement and further support sustainable SCs.

Title: Profiling cold chain risks through text analytics: bridging theory and real-world insights
Authors: Yuhong Li, Long Xia, Wanting Lu, Kedong Chen, Dmitry Ivanov
Affiliations: Department of Information Technology and Decision Sciences, Strome College of Business, Old Dominion University; Department of Management and Entrepreneurship, Love School of Business, Elon University; D’Amore-McKim School of Business, Northeastern University; Lally School of Management, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; Department of Supply Chain and Operations Management, Berlin School of Economics and Law (HWR Berlin)
Abstract: A thorough understanding of cold chain risks (CCR) is essential for effective mitigation, yet maintaining an up-to-date understanding remains challenging. This study addresses this issue by identifying root causes, categories, and practical significance of CCR through an integrated approach combining theoretical frameworks and text analytics.A risk assessment framework is derived from a systematic literature review, followed by analysis of news articles to capture emerging and underreported CCRs. Results are summarised in the risk register table, which provides comprehensive overview of CCRs. Findings highlight the need for greater research attention to risks in the make and warehouse phases, particularly those related to organisational and management, product-related, and technology. Network community detection further reveals relationships among these risks. Overall, this study advances our understanding of CCR,strengthening the foundation for more effective risk management strategies.

Title: The synergetic role of Lean and Industry 4.0 in the Industry 5.0 transition: a literature-informed framework
Authors: Maria Pia Ciano, Mirco Peron, Guido Orzes, Patrick Dallasega, Nicolò Saporiti
Affiliations: Operations Management and Information Systems Department, University of Nottingham, Nottingham University Business School; Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain Management & Decision Support, NEOMA Business School; Faculty of Engineering, Free University of Bozen-Bolzano; Scuola di Ingegneria Industriale, Carlo Cattaneo – LIUC University
Abstract: Lean and Industry 4.0 (I4.0) mutually reinforce operational excellence. Recently, however, companies have been urged to move beyond efficiency towards Industry 5.0 (I5.0), centred on sustainability, resilience, and human-centricity. Since I5.0 builds on I4.0 technologies, and Lean-I4.0 synergies are well established, scholars have suggested that their integration could support the transition to I5.0. Yet research remains limited and fragmented, often addressing the three pillars separately and discussing Lean and I4.0 at a high level, without identifying concrete practice-technology pairings for implementation. This study addresses this gap through a systematic literature review and proposes a framework showing how Lean practices and I4.0 technologies contribute to the three I5.0 pillars. The findings reveal multiple pairings, while also showing that several Lean practices remain underexplored, some relevant I4.0 technologies lack Lean integration, and current links focus mainly on manufacturing and shop-floor management. A future research agenda is proposed.

Title: An information-centric framework for sales and operations planning in engineer-to-order manufacturing: evidence from four industrial cases
Authors: Hafez Shurrab, Patrik Jonsson
Affiliations: College of Business Administration, Ajman University; Division of Supply and Operations Management, Department of Technology Management and Economics, Chalmers University of Technology
Abstract: Traditional sales and operations planning (S&OP) frameworks, designed for stable products and predictable demand, are not well-suited to engineer-to-order (ETO) manufacturing with its extreme customisation, project-based work, and complex interdependencies. ETO environments face two challenges: epistemic uncertainty (unknown final requirements) and equivocality (conflicting interpretations of available information). Using organisational information processing theory (OIPT) and planning quality, we explore how these challenges create unique information processing requirements (IPRs) that demand an adaptive S&OP process. In a multiple-case study of four ETO manufacturers, our analysis reveals sources of these challenges (9 uncertainty and 16 equivocality drivers) and persistent mismatches between IPRs and existing information processing capacity (IPC), especially related to order-size impact analysis, specification management, and resource allocation. These findings inform an IPC-building framework comprising 52 strategies that shift the focus from process standardisation to the development of adaptive S&OP capabilities. The framework emphasises organisational prerequisites (e.g. learning culture) and digital technologies.

Title: Embedding environmental sustainability in manufacturing operations: evidence from the fashion and textile industry in an emerging economy
Authors: Mazed Islam, Amy V. Benstead, Simeon Gill
Affiliations: Department of Fashion and Textiles, University of Southampton; Department of Materials, The University of Manchester
Abstract: The fashion and textile industry comprises complex supply chain operations with significant environmental impacts, highlighting the importance of integrating sustainable manufacturing practices. This exploratory case study investigates the implementation of environmental sustainability practices in upstream fashion manufacturing, focusing on how operations adopt, manage, and operationalise these practices. An inductive approach was adopted, drawing on semi-structured interviews with 43 manufacturing practitioners, followed by within-case and cross-case analysis. The findings provide comprehensive insight into the diversity and complexity of environmental issues, identifying 25 indicators of sustainable practices, 23 indicators of unsustainable practices and the multifaceted nature of their implementation. The study categorises a wide range of sustainable practices, identifies critical areas requiring improvement, and outlines practical strategies supported by a process map to guide operational adoption. A conceptual model is developed to advance theoretical insights and practical implementation of environmental sustainability in fashion manufacturing. Although based in the fashion industry, the findings provide transferable insights applicable to multi-tier supply chains across manufacturing sectors, benefiting wider stakeholders and sustainability transitions.

Title: Openness and control in digitally-enabled construction platforms: a comparative case study of supply-chain strategies
Authors: Shanjing (Alexander) Zhou, Daniel Hall, Jennifer Whyte
Affiliations: Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, University College London; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Management in the Built Environment, Faculty of Architecture and the Built Environment, TU Delft; School of Project Management, University of Sydney
Abstract: While product platforms in vertically-integrated firms are well studied, prior explanations become limited where platforming firms face tensions between openness and control in managing supply-chains. This paper explores how construction firms govern supply-chain interactions through digitally-enabled product platforms with varying interface openness. Drawing on a comparative case study of four firms, the research establishes that process embedding and process generativity serve as common foundational mechanisms required to bridge physical production constraints and digital workflows. Furthermore, the study provides new insight on process streamlining and process improvement as the distinctive control mechanisms used to dynamically adjust supply-chain governance. Depending on interface openness, firms configure proprietary or democratised process streamlining to control data flows and stakeholder workflows. Simultaneously, they deploy highly centralised or self-initiating process improvement loops to maintain authority over platform evolution. The paper extends platform governance theory from a physical-digital setting, by providing strategies to resolve the openness paradox and retain control over value creation.

Title: Humanitarian supply chain operations and COVID-19: the roles of data-driven innovations
Authors: Nnamdi Ogbuke, Yahaya Y. Yusuf, Angappa Gunasekaran, Xiaojun Wang
Affiliations: Hertfordshire Business School, University of Hertfordshire; Lancashire School of Business and Enterprise, University of Central Lancashire; School of Business and Public Administration, California State University; School of Management, University of Bristol
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic revealed a poor level of preparedness by the manufacturing sector in building resilient operations and logistics framework to respond to severe global supply chain disruptions. This research focuses on the effectiveness of data-driven innovation strategies in mitigating the impacts on humanitarian operations of Covid-19 related supply chain interruptions. The review is supported by the outcome of a major conceptual issues and uncovered two main topics of debate notably (i) the significant role of big data analytics and Artificial Intelligence in boosting firm performance by untangling supply chain disruptions and (ii) the paucity of research in this emerging area of literature. Consequently, this paper proposes a conceptual model for humanitarian supply chain operations to highlight how big data analytics and AI technologies could be deployed by firms to gain a competitive advantage by responding promptly and effectively to severe disruptions akin to those experienced during recent COVID-19 pandemic.

Title: From factory to consumer: how net-zero manufacturing signals shape trust, value, and adoption
Authors: Santanu Mandal, Payel Das, Angappa Gunasekaran, Raghu Raman
Affiliations: Amrita School of Business, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore, India; Penn State Harrisburg; Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham
Abstract: This study examines how consumers’ perceptions of manufacturing sustainability signals are associated with behavioural responses in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Drawing on Signalling Theory and selected behavioural logic from the Theory of Planned Behaviour, it compares perceived low-carbon factory practices, circular packaging features, and environmental certification credibility. Survey data from 338 Indian consumers were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). All three signals were positively associated with green trust and perceived green value. Low-carbon factory practices and certification credibility were negatively associated with perceived greenwashing risk, whereas circular packaging showed no significant association. Green trust and perceived green value were positively associated with purchase intention, while perceived greenwashing risk was negatively associated with it. Purchase intention was positively associated with willingness to pay a premium. Environmental concern strengthened the perceived green value–purchase intention relationship, whereas perceived regulatory support strengthened the certification credibility–green trust relationship. Because the study examines consumer perceptions rather than objectively verified factory performance, the findings explain how manufacturing sustainability investments are interpreted in the marketplace. The study further proposes a consumer-informed Signal Investment Prioritisation Matrix that integrates estimated total effects and boundary conditions into a practical decision-support framework for sequencing manufacturing sustainability investments.

Title: Generative AI in supply chains: a qualitative study on decision-making and human-AI collaboration
Authors: Zeena Qarqash, Anna Putintseva, Tim Gruchmann, Dmitry Ivanov
Affiliations: Wirtschaftswissenschaften, Berlin School of Economics and Law; Faculty of Business Studies, Dortmund University of Applied Sciences and Arts
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has recently gained attention as a technology that supports supply chain decision-making due to its unique natural language capabilities. In this context, it is seen as a top-layer augmentation to traditional analytical and optimisation-based technologies, accelerating decision support needed to keep businesses competitive. While extant literature largely discusses the conceptual potentials of GenAI, empirical evidence on its implications for human-AI collaboration and its boundaries with other AI technologies remains limited. Therefore, the present study adopts an abductive qualitative approach to explore GenAI-based decision-making through semi-structured interviews with experts. The empirical data were analysed using thematic analysis and subsequently interpreted through the lens of a recent AI decision-making framework. By theorising the empirical insights, this study clarifies GenAI’s current role as a cognitive decision-support layer rather than an autonomous decision-maker, along with its limitations. The findings contribute to the literature by providing empirical validation of GenAI as an augmentative technology and by offering evidence-based guidance on how organisations can responsibly leverage GenAI to enhance decision quality, operational efficiency, and operational resilience.

Title: The conditional value relevance of ESG and innovation disclosures: a multi-method analysis of European firms combining panel econometrics and machine learning
Authors: Andreas Errikos Delegkos, Evangelia Arsenou, Dionisis Cavouras, Emmanouil Pyrgiotakis, Petros Kalantonis
Abstract: Abstract This study examines the value relevance of accounting fundamentals, social and governance performance, and innovation-related disclosures for non-financial European firms. Building on the Ohlson (1995) framework, the analysis combines panel-data econometrics with Random Forest machine learning to evaluate both inferential and predictive dimensions of value relevance. We find that non-financial disclosures are not uniformly value relevant. Social-governance performance and environmental innovation exhibit no direct linear association with firm value, while SDG 9 innovation orientation is negatively priced. Environmental innovation, however, emerges as the strongest non-financial predictor in the Random Forest models, revealing predictive content that fixed-effects specifications miss. Value relevance is further conditional on signal interaction: environmental innovation attenuates the valuation effect of social-governance performance, while stronger social-governance performance reduces the negative pricing of SDG 9 disclosure. Overall, our results indicate that disclosure type, signal interaction, and nonlinear predictive structure jointly determine whether sustainability and innovation information is priced by markets.

Title: High-dimensional portfolio optimization with weight constraints: Forecasting models utilizing GARCH-EVT, R-vine copula, and SCAD penalty
Authors: Jian Lv, Chenxu Wang, Wenyong Yuan
Abstract: This study presents a forecasting methodology for high-dimensional portfolios by integrating the ARMA-GARCH model with extreme value theory to model asset return marginals and tail behavior. To handle the challenges from high dimensionality—such as complex dependence structures and intricate trading rules—our approach employs an R-vine copula to capture inter-asset dependence and incorporates the SCAD penalty to enhance sparsity and robustness. To address numerical issues, we solve the constrained portfolio optimization problem using penalized quantile regression. In the empirical analysis, we first use 10 sector indices to validate the effectiveness of the R-vine copula dependence structure. We then apply the full framework to high-dimensional portfolios constructed from constituents of the CSI 300 Index. Investment performance is evaluated along five dimensions: portfolio sparsity and stability, tail risk (VaR and CVaR), cumulative returns, risk-adjusted performance (RAROC and Sharpe ratio), and computational efficiency. Statistical differences in cumulative returns, RAROCs, and Sharpe ratios across portfolios are examined using the Scheffé test. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively captures large-scale asset dependence, improves portfolio sparsity and stability, reduces tail risk, and enhances risk-adjusted returns.

Title: Assessing the conditional calibration of interval forecasts using decompositions of the interval score
Authors: Sam Allen, Julia Burnello, Johanna Ziegel
Abstract: Forecasts for uncertain future events should be probabilistic. Probabilistic forecasts are commonly issued as prediction intervals, which provide a measure of uncertainty in the unknown outcome whilst being easier to understand and communicate than full predictive distributions. The calibration of a $(1 - \alpha)$-level prediction interval can be assessed by checking whether the probability that the outcome falls within the interval is equal to $1 - \alpha$. However, such coverage checks are typically unconditional and therefore relatively weak. Although this is well known, there is a lack of methods to assess the conditional calibration of interval forecasts. In this work, we demonstrate how this can be achieved via decompositions of the well-known interval (or Winkler) score. We study notions of calibration for interval forecasts and then introduce a decomposition of the interval score based on isotonic distributional regression. This decomposition exhibits many desirable properties, both in theory and in practice, which allows users to accurately assess the conditional calibration of interval forecasts. This is illustrated on simulated data and in three applications to benchmark regression datasets.

Title: Tax distortion on capital and resource misallocation: evidence from China’s VAT reform
Authors: Chang Liu, Guangrong Ma, Stephen Teng Sun
Abstract: While tax distortion on capital can significantly impact resource allocation in developing economies, credible causal evidence remains scarce. This study provides novel evidence by examining China’s 2009 value-added tax (VAT) reform, which allowed specific firms to deduct taxes on capital inputs, thereby mitigating distortions in the taxation of capital. Using firm-level tax return data from 2006 to 2015, we demonstrate that the reform enhanced the allocative efficiency of capital by reducing the dispersion in marginal revenue product of capital (MRPK) within industries. Our empirical results show that firms with high ex-ante MRPK experienced a 10.5% increase in physical capital and a 6.0% decrease in MRPK post-reform, relative to low-MRPK firms within the same industry. The effects were particularly pronounced among smaller firms and those with restricted access to debt, consistent with the reform alleviating binding financial constraints. At the supply-side margin, the reform’s misallocation-reducing effect was amplified in localities with greater access to banking services, consistent with local credit availability facilitating the translation of latent capital demand into actual investment. Moreover, the reform improved labor allocation through input complementarity and the alleviation of financial constraints. Our calibration exercise suggests that the reform increased the aggregate productivity of treated firms by 3.1–4.0%, with nonlinear approximations that account for cumulative dynamics yielding estimates of up to 7.8%. These findings highlight the importance of addressing tax distortions for efficient resource allocation in developing economies.

Title: Crime on the move? The effect of ridesharing services on crime
Authors: Emtiaz Hossain Hritan
Affiliations: Department of Health, Society, & Behavior University of California, Irvine Irvine California USA
Abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of ridesharing services like Uber and Lyft has transformed urban transportation, yet their effects on crime remain underexplored. Leveraging a natural experiment from their staggered rollout across U.S. cities, this study examines how ridesharing influences crime rates. Using a two‐way fixed effects model, I find that ridesharing services reduce violent crimes by 4.6%, property crimes by 5.6%, and burglaries by 10.5%, while the baseline estimates show no significant effects on larceny, motor vehicle theft, or arson. Exploring potential mechanisms, I show that improved employment opportunities generated by ridesharing platforms play a key role in these crime reductions.

Title: Institution or major? Understanding student preferences in college admissions
Authors: Kuan‐Ming Chen, Yu‐Chang Chen, Chi‐Chao Hung, Hau‐Hung Yang
Affiliations: Department of Economics National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan; Institute of Statistical Science Academia Sinica Taipei Taiwan
Abstract: Abstract In many countries outside the United States, students must choose an institution–major pair simultaneously, creating a trade‐off between institutional prestige and field of study. Using data from Taiwan's centralized admissions system, we study how applicants navigate this choice. We find that students strongly prioritize institutional ranking, with little heterogeneity across demographic groups and only a weak link between program choice and expected earnings. Counterfactual analysis shows that students forgo about 15% of their annual income by favoring institutions over earnings‐maximizing alternatives, suggesting that nonpecuniary factors—especially institutional reputation—play a central role in shaping college decisions.

Title: Information and communication technology innovations and labor hours: A business cycle analysis
Authors: Sangheon Ahn, Soojin Jo, Myungkyu Shim
Affiliations: School of Economics Yonsei University Seoul South Korea; Department of Economics the University of Texas at Austin Austin Texas USA
Abstract: Abstract This paper examines the impact of changes in information and communication technologies (ICTs) on skilled and unskilled labor at the business cycle frequency. To achieve this, we construct aggregate hours series for both labor groups using the monthly outgoing rotation group of the Current Population Survey from 1994 to 2023. Our empirical analysis, conducted with a structural vector autoregressive model, shows that the working hours of both groups respond positively to ICT innovations with similar magnitudes. We demonstrate that our findings are consistent with a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model in which ICT capital complements both skilled and unskilled labor, and suggest a plausible range of elasticity of substitution between capital and labor.

Title: Data Sharing in Hybrid Marketplaces With Endogenous Fee Setting
Authors: Federico Navarra, Flavio Pino, Luca Sandrini
Affiliations: Charles River Associates Brussels Belgium; Polytechnic of Turin Turin Italy; Department of Economics and Management (dSEA) University of Padova and ZEW ‐ Mannheim Padua Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study a hybrid marketplace where a vertically integrated platform competes with a seller, who pays the platform a transaction fee, in a horizontally differentiated downstream market. The platform has a data advantage that allows it to price discriminate against consumers and can choose to share such data with the seller. First, in a setting where the transaction fee is exogenous, we show that the platform may opt to share data with the seller. However, although data sharing increases total welfare, such practice is never Pareto‐improving: in particular, whenever data sharing increases the platform's profits, it also hurts consumers. Second, we show that, if the platform can endogenously choose the transaction fee, it always shares data, as it sets the fee to avoid competition with the seller, leading to higher profits and lower consumer surplus. This result is robust to a large family of consumer distributions. From a policy perspective, we show how a consumer‐oriented policymaker would prefer to ban the practice of price discrimination altogether, as this policy would also level the playing field while simultaneously avoiding the surplus extraction stemming from price discrimination. Finally, we also discuss the welfare consequences of banning the hybrid business model, and we argue that the incentives of the platform to soften downstream competition to increase surplus extraction would remain qualitatively unchanged.

Title: Adaptive Importance Sampling Estimation of an Open Economy Model With Fiscal Policy
Authors: Stefano Grassi, Marco Lorusso, Francesco Ravazzolo
Affiliations: University of Rome Tor Vergata Rome Italy; Department of Political Science University of Perugia Perugia Italy; Newcastle University Business School Newcastle UK; BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway; Free University of Bozen‐Bolzano Bozen‐Bolzano Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose and estimate an open economy general equilibrium model that includes international trade between Canada and the United States. We estimate our model using a new adaptive methodology based on the mixture of student's by Importance Sampling weighted Expectation–Maximisation (MitISEM). Our findings for the Canadian economy indicate that an increase in productive spending initially worsens the trade balance, whereas unproductive spending leads to a more persistent improvement through the contraction in private demand. We also show that the domestic real exchange rate appreciates on impact after both productive and unproductive government spending shocks, although the response is sharper and less persistent following a productive expenditure shock. Our structural framework uncovers highly asymmetric spillovers from the United States to Canada, successfully resolving the international transmission puzzle highlighted by Justiniano and Preston [12]. Finally, we conduct counterfactual exercises that consider alternative trade‐elasticity assumptions and a policy experiment involving a sizeable increase in US trade barriers.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Simple and Effective: A Deterministic Auction with Support Information
Authors: Rishikesh Parma, Çağıl Koçyiğit, Benny Mantin
Affiliations: TBS Business School, 31000 Toulouse, France; Department of Engineering, Department of Economics and Management, University of Luxembourg, 4365 Esch-sur-Alzette, Luxembourg
Abstract: We study an auction design problem where a seller aims to sell a single item to multiple bidders with independent private values. The seller knows only an upper bound on these values and does not know their distribution. The objective is to devise a deterministic auction mechanism effective across a broad set of distributions. We propose a second price auction with a reserve price set at half of the upper bound. Even though no deterministic mechanism can achieve a positive fraction of the maximum achievable expected revenue across all distributions, we show that our mechanism achieves at least [Formula: see text] ([Formula: see text] under independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) values) of the maximum expected revenue for a broad range of distributions of practical importance, where [Formula: see text] depends on the number of bidders and takes values in [Formula: see text]. Numerical experiments under randomly generated distributions demonstrate the superior performance of our mechanism in the vast majority of the generated instances compared to benchmark mechanisms from the literature. We also account for errors in the upper bound estimate. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design.

Title: Overlapping Schwarz Scheme for Linear-Quadratic Programs in Continuous Time
Authors: Hongli Zhao, Mihai Anitescu, Sen Na
Affiliations: Department of Statistics, The University of Chicago, Chicago, Illinois 60637; and Mathematics and Computer Science Division, Argonne National Laboratory, Lemont, Illinois 60439; School of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332
Abstract: We present an optimize-then-discretize framework for solving linear-quadratic optimal control problems (OCPs) governed by time-inhomogeneous ordinary differential equations. Our method employs a modified overlapping Schwarz decomposition based on the Pontryagin Minimum Principle, partitioning the temporal domain into overlapping intervals and independently solving Hamiltonian systems in continuous time. We demonstrate that the convergence is ensured by appropriately updating the boundary conditions of the individual Hamiltonian dynamics. The cornerstone of our analysis is to prove that the exponential decay of sensitivity exhibited in discrete-time OCPs carries over to the continuous-time setting. Unlike the discretize-then-optimize approach, our method can flexibly incorporate different numerical integration methods for solving the resulting Hamiltonian two-point boundary-value subproblems, including adaptive-time integrators. A numerical experiment on a linear-quadratic OCP illustrates the practicality of our approach in broad scientific applications. Title: Gradient Descent Avoids Strict Saddles with a Simple Line-Search Method Too
Authors: Andreea-Alexandra Musat, Nicolas Boumal
Affiliations: Institute of Mathematics, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, EPFL SB MATH, CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland
Abstract: It is known that gradient descent (GD) on a [Formula: see text] cost function generically avoids strict saddle points when using a small, constant step size. However, no such guarantee existed for GD with a line-search method. We provide one for a modified version of the standard Armijo backtracking method with generic, arbitrarily large initial step size. The proof underlines the role of the Luzin [Formula: see text] property for the iteration maps and allows us to forgo the habitual Lipschitz gradient assumption. We extend this to the Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) setting, assuming the retraction is real analytic (though the cost function still only needs to be [Formula: see text]). In closing, we also improve guarantees for RGD with a constant step size in some scenarios. Title: Blockchain technology and agricultural insurance interaction in the agricultural supply chain
Authors: Hongping Li, Haixin Ni, Xiaobei Shen, Hao Shu
Abstract: With the expanding applications of both blockchain technology and agricultural insurance in the agricultural sector, examining their interaction mechanisms has become crucial. Accordingly, this study investigates and contrasts four representative scenarios: (i) neither blockchain nor insurance, (ii) insurance without blockchain, (iii) blockchain without insurance, and (iv) the joint applications of blockchain and insurance. Our findings indicate that blockchain adoption incentivizes the utilization of agricultural insurance. However, insurance adoption exerts a facilitative or inhibitory influence on blockchain application, which depends on the raw material procurement cost and the blockchain R&D cost coefficient. Moreover, insurance application incentivizes the farmer to upload comprehensive agricultural product information to the blockchain. Notably, in the scenario with blockchain and insurance adoption, if the blockchain service provider acts as the leader, the cost associated with the blockchain application can be allocated flexibly between the farmer and the insurer. However, if the insurer acts as the leader, it is optimal for the insurer to bear the blockchain application cost when the farmer’s labor input cost coefficient is low, whereas it becomes preferable for the farmer to assume the cost otherwise. We further extend our model to the multi-period scenario and the government subsidy for the blockchain fee scenario to verify the robustness of our conclusions. This analysis can serve the applications of blockchain and insurance in agriculture, thereby facilitating the advancement of modern agricultural practices.

Title: Data-driven distributionally robust machine learning for inventory and pricing control
Authors: Xinyu Bi, Jianjun Xu, Feng Liu, Raymond Chiong

Title: The impact of firm-specific climate change exposure on vertical integration
Authors: Miaomiao Zhang, Hugo K.S. Lam, Yangchun Xiong, Peter K.C. Lee, Andy C.L. Yeung, T.C.E. Cheng
Abstract: Firm-specific climate change exposure, which captures market perceptions of climate change-related risks and opportunities faced by a firm, has important implications for firm decisions. However, it remains unclear how such exposure may affect firms’ buy-versus-make decisions in supply chains. Our study addresses this research gap by drawing on the theoretical lens of Transaction Cost Economics (TCE) to examine vertical integration as a strategic response to firm-specific climate change exposure. Following the TCE logic, we further investigate the moderating roles of geographic diversity and financial stability. Using panel data from 1,395 publicly listed U.S. manufacturing firms from 2007 to 2020, our analysis shows that firms with higher climate change exposure are more likely to pursue vertical integration. Moreover, this effect is stronger for firms with more geographically dispersed operations and greater financial stability. Overall, our findings highlight the importance of perception-based climate change exposure in shaping firms’ boundary decisions, providing important implications for both research and managerial practices.

Title: Is Europe a laggard? Comparing the EU and the US using an interdisciplinary well-being framework
Authors: Annegeke Jansen, Ranran Wang, Jan-Emmanuel De Neve, Paul Behrens, Rutger Hoekstra
Abstract: Well-being is increasingly recognized as a more meaningful measure of societal progress than economic output, yet most international comparisons continue to emphasize economic indicators. This focus has reinforced the perception that Europe is lagging behind the United States, with the productivity gap shaping the European Commission’s recent competitiveness agenda. Here, we compare European and American development from 1990–2023 using an interdisciplinary well-being framework that integrates five scientific schools of thought. We find that while the US increasingly outperformed the EU on productivity and income, the EU caught up in terms of various well-being indicators, including life satisfaction and education, while increasingly outperforming the US in life expectancy and safety. Europe also exhibits more equitable well-being outcomes and achieves them at lower environmental cost. However, in both regions, the conditions underpinning future well-being are under increasing pressure. These results challenge the dominance of economic metrics in evaluating progress and emphasize the need for inclusive development strategies that place sustainable well-being at their core.

Title: Ethics, economics, and environmental stewardship: Religious moral frameworks as constraints for rational policy choice
Authors: Nir Becker, Frank A. Ward
Abstract: Environmental policy often embeds ethical judgments implicitly in discount rates, welfare weights, prices, or informal constraints. This paper develops a constraint-based framework that makes major ethical commitments explicit before economic optimization begins. Drawing on convergent principles in Jewish, Islamic, Christian, Indigenous, Buddhist, and secular traditions, it identifies stewardship, restraint of waste, intergenerational responsibility, ecological limits, and institutional responsibility as candidate non-compensatory constraints. Economic analysis then compares costs, trade-offs, and institutional feasibility only among policies that satisfy the adopted constraints. Applied water-policy illustrations show how this approach can clarify minimum access, pricing, desalination, and wastewater-reuse choices without claiming that these policies were historically caused by the ethical framework. The contribution to ecological economics is methodological: moral commitments define the admissible policy space, while economics identifies efficient pathways within it. This division of labor improves transparency under moral pluralism and environmental scarcity.

Title: Assessing the impact of public–private partnerships and enabling factors on port efficiency: evidence from Latin America and the Caribbean
Authors: Ancor Suárez Alemán, Oscar Ponce de León
Abstract: In response to the challenges posed by outdated infrastructure and fiscal constraints, Latin American and Caribbean (LAC) countries initiated comprehensive port sector reforms during the 1990 s and 2000 s. At present, LAC is a global leader in the domain of private port operations, with 96% of container throughput—mostly through Public-Private Partnership (PPP) operators under the landlord model. While there have been over 150 PPP port projects implemented since 1990, there is a lack of empirical evidence regarding their impact on port performance. This study presents a longitudinal analysis of container-handling ports in 22 LAC countries, based on selected years between 2001 and 2024, depending on data availability. The findings indicate that PPP-operated ports demonstrate 4641% higher technical efficiency compared to state-run ports. A comparative analysis reveals that ports managed by global terminal operators demonstrate a 3129% higher performance than those managed by local operators. The efficiency gains observed are primarily concentrated among medium-sized terminals.
