Competitive selection processes have been demonstrated to enhance efficiency, with the impact intensifying as the number of bidders rises. The findings of this study underscore the critical role of regulatory and policy instruments in the design of PPP contracts and procurement processes to drive port performance and optimize investment outcomes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: What are safer streets worth? Bridging resident preferences and policy design in traffic calming
Authors: Katsuya Tanaka, Jennifer Dill, Nathan McNeil, Roger Geller, Noriaki Kondo
Abstract: Traffic calming is widely adopted, yet implementation is often contested, and little is known about which treatments residents prefer or whether they would support a funded traffic-calming program. We surveyed 1717 residents living within 650 feet of 19 corridors in Portland, Oregon. A best–worst scaling (BWS) task elicited relative preferences among eight treatments; a single-bounded contingent valuation (CVM) question elicited support for a funded traffic calming program at a randomly assigned monthly household contribution, from which willingness to pay (WTP) was derived. Median refuge islands were most preferred, followed by mini roundabouts, shared streets, and gateway treatments; diverters, speed humps, and pinchpoints ranked lowest, with diverters and speed humps the most polarizing. Support for the funded program was higher among residents who perceived nearby streets as busy, preferred walking or wished to bike more, or had young children, and lower among older residents and those concerned about crime. Derived WTP averaged US $34 per household per month (median $30). Relative design preference and support for funding did not always align: preference for median refuge islands was associated with lower support, whereas preference for shared streets and diverters was associated with higher support. The combined design is best understood as a low-burden instrument for prioritization and public engagement rather than for formal economic appraisal.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Transport capital and regional economic performance in Korea: Implications for balanced regional development under the public investment appraisal system
Authors: Changhoon Lee, John Preston, Shahram Heydari
Abstract: In 1999, Korea introduced the Preliminary Feasibility Study (PFS), a mandatory appraisal framework for large-scale public investment projects that designates balanced regional development as a core policy objective. As the primary gateway for major public construction projects, the PFS plays a pivotal role in shaping the scale and spatial allocation of transport investment, yet empirical evidence on whether it is associated with reduced regional economic disparities remains limited. Using panel data for 15 Korean regions from 2000 to 2023, this study estimates output elasticities of transport capital with a multilevel Cobb-Douglas framework that allows road and railway elasticities to vary by region and accounts for temporal dependence in the residuals. The results reveal substantial regional and modal heterogeneity: road elasticities average about 0.12 and are highest along the Seoul-Busan corridor, while railway elasticities average about 0.15 and are highest in the Seoul metropolitan area and the adjacent Chungcheong corridor. By contrast, several less developed regions, including areas prioritised by the PFS balanced development component, exhibit generally positive but low elasticities for both modes. These uneven productivity returns suggest that transport investment alone, as shaped by the PFS, is unlikely to resolve Korea’s interregional economic disparities, underscoring the need for complementary, place-based policies tailored to regional industrial structure and absorptive capacity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: From decentralized to collaborative ATFM: A simulation-based assessment of FF-ICE/R1 in Southeast Asia
Authors: Darryl Teo, Rakesh Nandi, Gengling Dai, Peter Jackson, Nuno Antunes Ribeiro
Abstract: Addressing air traffic congestion requires both infrastructure expansion and improved management of existing capacity. This paper quantifies the system-level benefits of tactical Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM) when implemented collaboratively across national boundaries. This analysis is particularly relevant in regions that currently operate in a decentralized manner, such as Southeast Asia, the case study of this work. Aligned with ICAO's Flight and Flow Information for a Collaborative Environment (FF-ICE/R1) concept, this work evaluates the operational impacts of cross-border information sharing and Calculated Take-Off Time (CTOT) assignment. This work develops a rolling horizon discrete event simulation of the Southeast Asia region and compares a decentralized baseline against a collaborative regime (R1). Across all scenarios, R1 reduces airborne time and fuel consumption relative to the baseline. Average airborne delay decreases by 18% under nominal capacity conditions and by 16% under reduced-capacity conditions, even though ground and arrival delays increase as flights are deliberately held at the gate. While proactive gate-holding inherently increases ground delays, this strategic trade-off optimizes predictability and environmental performance, translating to estimated weekly network benefits of $0.09M to $1.13M USD. Crucially, the analysis reveals a powerful concentration effect: participation by just five core Air Navigation Service Providers (ANSPs) captures approximately 65% of total regional savings, with early adopters securing substantial per-flight benefits regardless of peripheral participation. These findings offer actionable policy insights for regional aviation authorities, establishing clear investment thresholds for phased implementation and demonstrating that full institutional consensus is not a prerequisite for achieving viable economic returns.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Governing Indigenous territories: trust, moral economy, and the legitimation of Indigenous territorial authority in the Honduran Moskitia
Authors: Fernando Galeana
Abstract: Formalizing Indigenous land rights is critical for environmental justice and sustainable development. Yet legal recognition often creates new territorial governing bodies tasked with managing collective lands, whose legitimacy cannot be assumed. This study examines how trust in Indigenous territorial authorities is built, contested, and withdrawn following the formalization of collective land rights in the Honduran Moskitia. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork and household interviews in three villages across diverse socio-ecological settings, the study analyzes how residents assess their territorial authorities. The analysis treats trust as multidimensional and relational. The study examines different forms of trust—dispositional, rational, affinitive, and procedural—to identify the rationales that drive assessments of authority in each village. These rationales are interpreted through the lens of a Miskitu moral economy, framing trust assessments in terms of what residents expect of a territorial authority to be considered legitimate. A moral economy lens contributes analytically to a multidimensional trust framework by explaining why certain forms of trust feel more salient when evaluating authority performance and how they interact with one another. The central finding is that the socio-spatial configuration of land conflicts shapes which evaluative dimensions of trust become most salient. A multidimensional and relational trust analysis contributes a more granular understanding of this process: it shows how different forms of trust interact and shift through everyday encounters with authority, identifying the specific points at which legitimacy is strengthened, strained, or quietly lost.

Title: Dependent development at the energy transition: placing lithium imaginaries in Neoliberal and Contentious Peru
Authors: José Carlos Orihuela, Arturo Mendieta, Sergio Serrano
Abstract: We examine lithium and development imaginaries in mining-dependent Peru, asking: What are these imaginaries? What narratives underpin them? Who articulates and shares them, and from where? What forms of state (in)action are envisioned in relation to them? The case study elucidates how alternative “imagined futures” coexist within a natural resource–dependent economy. The ruling national elites in Lima have a neoliberal imagination, treating lithium like any other mineral resource in the country. In contrast, professional elites in the mineral-rich but peripheral region of Puno adopt a resource nationalist view, advocating for direct state involvement in lithium industrialization and the transformation of the domestic energy system, shaped by beliefs on Bolivia’s developmental pathway. Among rural community leaders as well as political and social leaders in the districts near lithium and uranium deposits, however, the prevailing idea is that of a social license. In this view, each community has the capacity to negotiate development terms with mining companies independently. In the broader imagination at the resource periphery of a peripheral national economy, the state is perceived primarily as a minimalist governmental actor, necessary only to oversee and ensure the enforcement of mine-community agreements and to provide basic infrastructure. Thus, elites at the political center and communities near expected resource developments converge in their immediate pursuit of rents promised by resource commodification. In the dominant discourses, environmental concerns are often subordinated to economic development goals.

Title: Terrorism and altruistic giving: Evidence from child sponsorship
Authors: Alberto Posso, Simon Feeny
Abstract: We study how terrorist attacks targeting educational institutions affect private development aid through child sponsorship. Conceptually, terrorist events may increase sponsorship by signaling greater need or reduce it if affected communities are seen as less effective destinations to support. We combine global administrative data from Plan International on child sponsorship across 50 countries over the 2008-2018 period, aggregated at the Primary Sampling Unit (PSU) level, with geocoded terrorism events from the Global Terrorism Database. Our core specification focuses on attacks against educational institutions within 20 km of each PSU. We estimate the causal effect using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences approach suited to staggered, non-absorbing treatments. We find that attacks on educational institutions reduce the share of sponsored children by about 3 percentage points, a 4 percent decline relative to the mean. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest this corresponds to funding losses of approximately US$615,000 across affected communities over the study period. Since sponsorship is geographically targeted, these losses fall on the specific communities, underscoring the need to buffer local development funding against security shocks.

Title: Multiphase emissions from rubber modified asphalt: phase-partitioning and secondary pollutant formation potential
Authors: Lingwen Li, Tao Zhou, Liping Cao, Hu Yang, Ajit K Sarmah, Zejiao Dong, Runtao La
Abstract: Rubber modified asphalt (RMA) fumes constitute a critical precursor reservoir for atmospheric pollution, posing significant risks to ecosystems. However, current knowledge remains limited regarding the multiphase emissions in RMA fumes and its environmental impacts of phase-shifting dynamics. The results demonstrate that RMA emissions undergo temperature- and CR content-dependent phase shifting, which in turn drive distinct secondary pollutant formation and inhalation exposure potential. Specifically, we introduced a quantitative phase-shifting index to characterize multiphase partitioning behavior. By integrating emission intensity and phase shifting with ozone formation potential, secondary organic aerosol formation potential (SOAFP), and respiratory deposition potential, we identified a critical transition temperature, which dominant mechanism of SOAFP transitions from gas-phase dominance toward coupled gas–liquid contributions. Correspondingly, the liquid-phase contribution to SOAFP increases to 44–49%. These findings provide new insights into how reshape fume emission, establishing a mechanistic framework to support the sustainable formulation of RMA and development of high-temperature emission control strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Consumer preferences for vehicle types informed by direct and indirect emission estimates
Authors: Yujin Seo, Baruch Fischhoff, Thuy Nguyen, Nicholas Z. Muller
Abstract: As financial incentives for EVs wane and price parity approaches, engaging mainstream adopters is critical to sustaining market growth. While early adopters are driven by environmentalism and proactive information-seeking, the broader market remains hesitant due to knowledge gaps regarding EV benefits. We evaluate how communication of state-specific emission estimates for five vehicle types (ICE, HEV, PHEV, BEV, and FCEV) influences vehicle perceptions, rankings, and fleet composition. Surveying 908 participants across four states (CA, FL, PA, TX), we find that, while emissions information shifts vehicle rankings, political identity and charging feasibility remain the primary determinants of top preferences. Furthermore, participants favor fleets with a diverse composition over a single technology. Our findings suggest that providing state-level emission estimates effectively reshapes consumer preferences and reduces the desired share of high-emission vehicles. This research provides a strategic framework for policymakers and manufacturers to sustain market momentum through transparency and targeted communication.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Electrification reshapes BRICS vehicle urban mining: Material flows and circularity by 2050
Authors: Chenghui Zeng, Ziyan He, Guochang Xu, Yemei Li, Shuhan Hu, Xijin Zhao, Zhengjun Gong, Zhengyang Zhang, Kenichi Nakajima
Abstract: Vehicle electrification is increasing demand for critical battery materials and shifting end-of-life management from whole vehicle scrap toward component-level streams, especially retired vehicle batteries. The five BRICS founding countries—Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa—represent a critical and diverse testing ground for this transition because they combine large and growing vehicle markets, divergent electrification pathways, and uneven recycling capacities. Here, we develop a stock-driven dynamic material flow model to project vehicle electrification, end-of-life vehicle generation, and retired battery generation from 2025 to 2050. By combining material intensity data with country-specific end-of-life parameters, we estimate secondary material re-supply and vehicle-to-vehicle circularity for major vehicle and battery materials. By 2050, circularity for recoverable battery materials under current systems ranges from approximately 3 % to 24 % across countries and materials, indicating continued dependence on primary supply. Improved collection and refining can raise circularity for these materials to 24 %–56 %, with NiSO 4 reaching approximately 49 %–56 % in China, South Africa, Russia, and Brazil; however, FeSO 4 , graphite, and carbon black remain unrecovered under the modeled conditions. Our analysis shows the need to synchronize electrification with formal collection, component-level dismantling, quality-preserving refining, and targeted policy support.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Optimal investment-based crowdfunding: Crowdblessing versus scale
Authors: Matthew Ellman, Sjaak Hurkens
Abstract: This paper examines crowdfunding of a risky, constant-returns project. The crowdfunder chooses a threshold and interest rate. These jointly determine profit and welfare outcomes by influencing investors’ decisions to acquire information and to bid and by aggregating the information their bids reveal into a project funding decision. A higher threshold funds fewer projects but, fixing investor strategies, raises the ratio of good to bad quality among those that get funded by a factor we call the “crowdblessing.” At the same time, raising the threshold, or the interest rate, reduces incentives to acquire and use private information. Optimal design trades off crowdblessing against investment scale. Surprisingly, profit-maximizers sometimes induce excessive information acquisition to limit investor rent. In our comparative statics, information acquisition falls with the cost of information and with prior optimism but precision has an ambiguous impact. Costly information reduces welfare but may raise profits by facilitating rent-extraction.

Title: Next job: Matera. How tourism and spotlight shape the local labour market
Authors: Luca Favero, Ilaria Malisan
Abstract: Tourism is an important source of income and employment, and is regularly promoted by governments and international initiatives as a tool for development. We study the causal effects of hosting a mega cultural event on tourism and local economic development. We exploit the shortlisting and subsequent selection of Matera, a culturally rich but poorly connected and previously overlooked city in southern Italy, as the 2019 European Capital of Culture. Using synthetic difference-in-differences to compare Matera with unaffected Italian cities, we find substantial growth in tourism, number of establishments and employment in hospitality and construction, alongside lower unemployment, higher income, greater nighttime light intensity, and rising property prices. These effects emerge during the selection phase, before the event year, suggesting a spotlight effect through which media exposure raised Matera’s profile, promoted investment and stimulated local economic activity. Our findings indicate that cultural mega events like the European Capital of Culture can provide a credible pathway to development for overlooked destinations, particularly where labour-market slack allows increased tourism demand to translate into employment.

Title: Optimizing the vaccine distribution network design problem under uncertainty
Authors: Paulina Kus Ariningsih, Chandra Ade Irawan, Antony Paulraj, Jing Dai
Abstract: This paper investigates the vaccine distribution network that is applicable in emerging countries. We propose a two-stage stochastic programming model for the multi-period vaccine network design problem, taking into account uncertain demand, product perishability, flow of products between hubs, and capacity expansion. The model is expressed using a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model. The primary goal is to minimize the total cost by optimizing the locations of the distribution centers, the optimal period to install storage devices, and the flow of vaccines in the network. The dynamic transmission compartment model (DCM) is used to generate more accurate stochastic demand scenarios in the face of epidemic disruptions. The data preparation algorithm to transform the DCM data into demand scenarios is developed using the k -means clustering method. The proposed two-stage stochastic programming model is solved using the Sample Average Approximation method. The proposed framework for the solution method is assessed using datasets inspired by Indonesia’s COVID-19 vaccination project. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework obtains good solutions that can be implemented by the relevant stakeholders.

Title: Joint optimization of omni-channel distribution framing (replenishment, allocation, and fulfilment) under demand uncertainty
Authors: Shuangpeng Yang, Qiang Guo, Chao Liang
Abstract: This study focuses on the distribution operations problem encountered in the context of multiproduct, multiperiod sales under demand uncertainty in a capacitated retail network for omnichannel retailers (o-tailers). By implementing the ship-from-store strategy, all the stores within the network can fulfil orders across channels within inventory constraints with the aim of maximizing the o-tailer’s profit. At the beginning of each period, the o-tailer determines the replenishment quantity for each product at the DC and the allocation quantity from the DC to each store. At the end of each period, the o-tailer decides whether to fulfil realized online orders from the DC, specific stores, or both simultaneously. To address this problem, we developed a multiperiod stochastic model and employed a linear decision rule (LDR) approach, informed by strong duality theory, to adaptively determine the replenishment , allocation , and fulfilment quantities. The experimental results demonstrate that the LDR consistently generates high-quality solutions, including efficiency gaps less than 8.46% in comparison with the benchmark expected value given perfect information (EVPI) across various cases. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis confirms that omnichannel fulfilment remains beneficial for retailers across different parameter settings.

Title: Product deletion decision based on multitype feature fusion: A deep learning predictive approach with temporal modeling
Authors: Decui Liang, Haoxin Tang
Abstract: Product deletion, as an important part of product management, can timely release productivity and reduce the impact of suboptimal products on consumer satisfaction. An informed product deletion decision is based on the observation of the temporal changes in multitype features. However, with increasing market volatility, traditional product deletion decision-making methods are becoming less effective and more inefficient for highly dynamic market environments. Thus, this paper proposes a novel AI-based deep neural network architecture to address the increasingly complex product deletion decision-making problem. First, we have developed three sub-models to capture local and global patterns from heterogeneous information: namely consumer, market, and consumer-market sub-model. Each sub-model incorporates a convolutional neural network (CNN), a recurrent-skip neural network (RSNN), and a gated recurrent unit (GRU), which respectively extract non-linear, long-term, and short-term temporal dependencies. To address the challenge of deep learning in capturing fixed-scale changes between multivariate time series (MTS) and the decision target, we additionally design an automatic logistic regression component running in parallel with the three sub-models. Through a series of experiments, the effectiveness and robustness of our proposed approach have been validated in product deletion decision-making. It demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional machine learning and time series classification algorithms. In general, this paper not only offers potential business value for product deletion decision-making, but also provides a reference framework for similar complex prediction problems in interdisciplinary fields.

Title: Sustainable operations strategy for low-carbon resource platforms: Sharing efforts and membership size
Authors: Yunxiang Lv, Yu Yang, Yilong Han, Lu Liu
Abstract: As facilitators of widespread low-carbon resource exchange among firms, low-carbon resource platforms (LRPs) have garnered increasing attention. Yet, despite their recognized potential to reduce carbon emissions, they face operational challenges, e.g., declining resource sharing and decreasing user participation, that leave the question of how these platforms sustain operations insufficiently understood. To address this gap, this study employs a differential game model to capture the dynamic interactions between LRPs and their member firms and, based on the model’s equilibrium outcomes, explores operational strategies that support long-term platform sustainability. The findings indicate that although LRPs commonly operate on a free-access basis, platforms with a moderate number of members may need to introduce usage fees when their operational efficiency is higher than that of member firms, whereas less efficient platforms should incentivize greater participation. We further show that both the platform and its members can benefit from the entry of a new firm, even if the entrant is a competitor, and that a decline in platform efficiency or an increase in low-carbon resource deterioration necessitates a larger membership base to maintain viability. We then conduct a numerical analysis to assess the robustness of our model. In addition, we extend the base model to examine several scenarios. Our findings yield actionable managerial implications for sustaining the long-term operations of LRPs.

Title: Spillover effects of punishments: customers' environmental penalty exposure and suppliers’ green innovation
Authors: Honghui Zou, Qian Wang, Liming Zhao, Yan Jiang
Abstract: Environmental penalty (EP) exposure has been recognized as a significant factor influencing the green innovation (GI) of penalized firms. However, the spillover effects of these penalties, particularly within the context of supply chain relationships, have been inadequately explored. Our study seeks to fill this gap by exploring the spillover effects of customers' EP exposure on the GI of their suppliers based on stakeholder theory. Leveraging firm-level EP data manually gathered from publicly listed Chinese firms between 2007 and 2022, our findings indicate that customers' EP exposure significantly promotes suppliers' GI, demonstrating a spillover effect within the supply chain. Additionally, we examine the moderating factors that influence this effect, focusing on the heterogeneous characteristics of customer-supplier relationships. Specifically, we find that customer concentration and stability strengthen the positive spillover effect of customers' EP exposure on suppliers' GI. In contrast, this effect is weakened when customers and suppliers are geographically dispersed. This study not only elucidates the spillover effects of customers' EP exposure on suppliers’ GI from the supply chain perspective but also provides important practical implications for enhancing GI.

Title: The efficiency-driven sales mode: Blockchain-enabled carbon reduction in competitive supply chain
Authors: Zichen Zou, Mingwu Liu, Yu Gong, Xinwei Dong
Abstract: The global drive for low-carbon transformation has drastically intensified competitive complexity for manufacturers across e-commerce platforms. Low-carbon manufacturers are increasingly adopting blockchain technology to strengthen the credibility of carbon information disclosure. Nevertheless, they confront a pivotal challenge in selecting optimal sales modes to reconcile economic benefits with environmental constraints. We introduce the concept of Blockchain-Enabled Carbon Emission Reduction Efficiency (BCER), which measures the carbon emission reduction capability achieved per unit of blockchain service cost. BCER reflects the efficiency with which blockchain-related investment supports carbon reduction outcomes. Based on this construct, we examine how different low-carbon value realization capabilities enabled by blockchain reshape the sales model choices of low-carbon manufacturers. Our results show that, from the profit-maximization perspective, multi-stakeholder alignment on the reselling mode is only achievable when BCER is at an intermediate level, representing a critical cost-efficiency balance point. At high BCER levels, the Low-carbon manufacturer aggressively favors the agency selling mode to capture pricing power, destroying channel coordination. Second, blockchain adoption does not necessarily boost the demand for low-carbon products. Under the reselling mode, its positive effect is offset via adjustments in wholesale prices. Finally, from the perspective of profit increment, low-carbon manufacturers consistently favor the reselling mode, which contradicts the conventional wisdom that such manufacturers opt for the agency selling mode. These findings yield nuanced guidance for manufacturers’ investment decisions amid efficiency-driven low-carbon competition.

Title: How accurate is the Taylor approximation of bond returns?
Authors: Jean-Michel Maeso, Vincent Milhau
Abstract: By using a comprehensive dataset on US Treasury securities, we study the accuracy of first- and second-order approximations for bond returns. Using the duration alone leads to a systematic underestimation of returns, especially for long-term instruments, but a daily duration-convexity approximation is accurate at all maturities. For both approximations, including the “passage of time”, which is the contribution of discounting to the bond return, is essential, else returns are severely underestimated, especially if interest rates are high. A monthly approximation still gives acceptable results, but an annual one is less accurate, even if all terms are included.

Title: Disruptions to foreign trade and US banks’ returns
Authors: Michele Modugno, Berardino Palazzo, Carlos A. Ramírez, Thiago Ferreira
Abstract: We study whether bank loan portfolios help explain differences in their stock returns during major disruptions to foreign trade. Using stock market reactions during the 2018 U.S.-China trade war and the April 2025 tariff announcements, we identify industries that are systematically vulnerable and resilient to trade disruptions. We then combine these classifications with confidential supervisory lending data to construct a measure of trade exposure for large U.S. banks. We find that banks with greater exposure experienced significantly larger stock price declines following the April 2025 tariff announcements.

Title: Research choices of agentic artificial intelligence
Authors: Brett A. McCully
Abstract: Researchers increasingly rely on agentic artificial intelligence to assist with research. I examine the sampling and specification choices AI agents make and compare them to those of human experts. Fixing the research question and raw data across 156 agent runs, AIs tend to cluster on certain options. Compared to 145 human expert analyses of the same question and data, estimation outcomes are broadly similar. AI achieves this, however, via systematically different choices. Agentic AI thus remains an imperfect substitute for human researchers for the models tested.

Title: Confidence at the long end: Central-bank satisfaction and household inflation expectations
Authors: Martin Meier
Abstract: Using 252,993 responses from the Bank of England Inflation Attitudes Survey, this paper examines the relationship between central-bank confidence, the term structure of inflation expectations, and forecast accuracy. Dissatisfied households show stronger pass-through from perceived inflation to medium- and long-term expectations. Among respondents in the same wave and current-inflation and one-year-expectation categories, their five-year expectations remain 0.37 percentage points higher. A Shapley decomposition leaves 40% of the five-year gap unexplained by those beliefs. Dissatisfied households make larger five-year forecast errors under midpoint and interval-consistent coding. The evidence is consistent with weaker long-term anchoring rather than more accurate pessimism.

Title: Corporate bond factor momentum
Authors: Davide Sandretto
Abstract: Recent studies show that momentum in factor premia, rather than in individual asset returns, drives the momentum anomaly in equity markets. We examine whether factor momentum extends to corporate bonds, using a novel manually cleaned dataset of 155 corporate bond factors spanning 1985 to 2023. We document a factor momentum effect although it is economically modest and sample dependent, with monthly alphas ranging from 10 to 28 basis points. Cross-sectional strategies built on bond-level and within-firm factors are the most robust, remaining significant even after accounting for conservative transaction costs. Time series strategies, by contrast, do not survive trading frictions. Bond-level and within-firm factor momentum are not subsumed by bond or equity price momentum, whereas the reverse holds only for its equity variant. The results of this study (i) extend the factor momentum literature to a market that has so far received little attention, (ii) provide evidence that return continuation is not pervasive across risk factors, and (iii) document that price and factor momentum, although related, originate from different sources of return variation.

Title: Nighttime ethics: Do moral choices differ by time-of-day/night?
Authors: David L. Dickinson
Abstract: ABSTRACT We examine time-of-day (TOD) effects on moral choice by comparing afternoon ( DAY : 3pm-5pm) and nighttime ( NIGHT : 3am-5am) decisions across three incentivized tasks. While the NIGHT treatment successfully induced sleepiness, we report no evidence that circadian suboptimality shifts decisions towards one’s default ethical tendencies. Rather, the NIGHT treatment increased dishonesty in a victimless Die-Roll task but not when dishonesty harms another participant (modified Coin-Flip task) or in consequential moral dilemmas affecting only others’ outcomes (Payoff-Trolley task). Exploratory response-times evidence is consistent with immoral choices resulting from deliberative processes. Overall, these results indicate that moral choice exhibits task-dependent stability during circadian fatigue.

Title: Younger households’ inflation is more responsive to monetary policy
Authors: Aeimit Lakdawala, Timothy Moreland
Abstract: When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, prices faced by younger households fall more than prices faced by older households. Using age-specific distributional consumer price indices together with high-frequency monetary policy shocks, we document a monotone age gradient in inflation responses, from households under 25 through households 75 and older. A simple decomposition combining BLS major-group CPI responses with age-specific CEX expenditure shares accounts for most of the gap between the youngest and oldest households. Transportation and medical care drive the result: younger households spend disproportionately on transportation (including motor fuel, vehicles, and auto insurance), whose prices respond strongly to monetary policy, while older households spend disproportionately on medical care, whose prices respond less.

Title: Sustainability for a greener economy
Authors: Xinyuan Zhong, Yingxian Tan, Xiang Gao
Abstract: We introduce a sustainability constraint into a two-sector production economy with green and brown capital, requiring the welfare measure to be non-decreasing over time. The constraint binds only when the brown capital share is high. When it binds, the planner reduces current consumption and reallocates resources toward investment, especially green investment. The constraint also lowers the risk-free rate and raises the risk premium and Tobin’s q[jls-end-space/].

Title: Data-use limits and information complementarities
Authors: Hailin Zhu
Abstract: This paper studies how privacy-induced data-use limits affect production-side aggregate productivity when firms endogenously choose whether to produce high-precision information. Firms can pay a fixed cost to obtain a more precise productivity signal. Data-use limits reduce the effective precision of this signal, lowering the return to information production and raising the cutoff type for becoming informed. Aggregate productivity falls not only because informed firms receive less precise signals, but also because fewer firms choose to produce information. When information choices are locally strategic complements, the extensive-margin response is amplified in general equilibrium, so productivity losses can exceed partial-equilibrium effects.

Title: When does the mean welfare change exist? Compensating variation and the price–quality divide in random-coefficient logit
Authors: Yu-Chin Chen
Abstract: In random-coefficient logit, compensating variation (CV) is a log-sum difference divided by the marginal utility of income. A log-sum-exp bound shows that pure price-change CV is bounded and has finite moments under every admissible coefficient distribution. For quality changes, finite moments of policy-relevant willingness-to-pay (WTP) coefficients are sufficient. Under independence, finite taste moments, and a nondegenerate policy effect, finite inverse moments of income sensitivity are also necessary. Mean welfare existence therefore depends on the policy and the induced coefficient distribution, not on preference- versus WTP-space parameterization itself. Simulations illustrate this distinction and show why finite sample means cannot establish the existence of a population mean.

Title: Perceptions of own social class and local affluence: Effects on preferences for redistribution
Authors: Javier Olivera, Paola Villa-Paro
Abstract: This paper studies how perceptions of own social class and local affluence shape preferences for redistribution. We conduct a survey experiment with 1293 respondents in Lima Metropolitana, randomly correcting beliefs either about respondents’ own socio-economic status (SES) under Peru’s official five-class classification, or about the share of affluent households in their district. Misperceptions are strongly asymmetric: about 70% of respondents overestimate their own SES and about 50% overestimate the local share of affluent households. The effects of information, however, are not uniform. The clearest evidence comes from respondents who substantially overestimate local affluence: correcting this belief increases support for redistribution. For own SES, effects are concentrated among respondents who overestimate their position by at least two classes (34% of the relevant sample); among respondents whose misperceptions are smaller, the evidence is weaker. Neither treatment shifts support for a wealth tax, and perceived fairness of the income distribution is largely unaffected. Using geocoded data, we further show that local SES and local affluence are positively associated with respondents’ perceptions, while local inequality itself is only weakly related to redistributive preferences in the control group. The results suggest that corrective information can affect redistributive attitudes when perceived-actual gaps are large, but that these effects depend on the type and magnitude of misperceptions.

Title: Dynamic last-mile delivery with fatigue under travel time uncertainty
Authors: Liqin Yang, Yu Zhang, Roberto Baldacci, Sihan Wang, Siyue Lei
Abstract: Last-mile delivery is increasingly challenged by the dual pressures of ensuring driver safety and maintaining service reliability. Driver fatigue significantly elevates accident risks, while the stochastic nature of urban travel times disrupts schedules and accelerates physical exhaustion. To address these heavily coupled issues, this paper introduces a Dynamic Pickup and Delivery Problem with Fatigue under Uncertain Travel Times (DPDPF-Robust). We employ a rolling-horizon approach that seamlessly integrates a budgeted robust optimization framework with a biomathematical fatigue model. To satisfy strict real-time dispatching requirements, we develop a tailored Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) algorithm. Small static subproblems are benchmarked against the corresponding Piecewise-Linear MILP, while multi-epoch comparisons with a Tabu Search and factorial operator ablations evaluate the proposed ALNS under a common computational budget. The results support the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm under the tested settings. Across the tested settings, the results indicate a favorable cost–safety trade-off: the integrated model mitigates extreme fatigue violations while incurring a slight safety premium of under 2.5%. By quantifying the low “shadow price” of fatigue prevention against real-world crash liabilities, this research provides an empirically evaluated decision-support approach for logistics platforms to harmonize economic efficiency, driver workload equity, and service resilience.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Towards open innovation with shared risk and output in EV: Multi-attribute procurement auction design
Authors: Dong Cai, Lian Bai, Chunxiang Guo, Kee-hung Lai
Abstract: When purchasing open innovation project in the electric vehicle (EV) field, there is often a relatively high risk of innovation output, and the innovation output will bring considerable value to the supplier. Therefore, we studied the multi-attribute procurement auction of open innovation project in the EV field, considering risk sharing and output sharing, aiming to promote open innovation in the EV field. We found that: 1) Before submitting the bid price, the supplier must jointly optimize the promised innovation output and the innovation effort. Specifically, the supplier also should consider the expected utility of the achievement level of innovation output with output risk, as well as the innovation output value to the supplier. 2) When the buyer adopts the first or second score multi-attribute procurement auction, the supplier’s bid price is influenced by the risk-sharing mechanism’s reward and penalty, as well as the innovation output value. The reward will decrease the bid price, the penalty will increase it, and the innovation output value will decrease it. 3) When the buyer adopts an efficient or optimal mechanism, the buyer will transfer all the moral hazard of the supplier’s insufficient effort, and the innovation output risk caused by random factors that affect the actual innovation output, to the supplier through the design of the risk-sharing mechanism. By rewarding and punishing the achievement level of innovation output, the buyer can stimulate the supplier’s innovation effort. At the same time, the risk-sharing mechanism increases expected social welfare and the buyer’s expected utility, indicating its effectiveness. 4) When the buyer adopts the efficiency mechanism, the buyer should truthfully disclose its preference for the promised innovation output. However, when the buyer adopts the optimal mechanism, the buyer’s disclosure of its preference for the promised innovation output should be downwardly distorted. 5) For open innovation procurement of consumer demand-oriented technologies, the government should mainly provide support to the supplier. For open innovation procurement of social benefit-oriented technologies, the government should provide support to both the buyer and the supplier simultaneously.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Statistics and dynamics of air transport delays in Balkan airports
Authors: Stefanija Lazareva, Marija Beleska, Ilinka Ivanoska, Massimiliano Zanin
Abstract: Delays, a common and challenging problem in air transport, have long attracted the attention of the scientific community, in the attempt of characterising them and designing ways to mitigate their propagation. Most works have focused on large markets, e.g. Europe, US, and China, while peripheral regions have seldom been considered. We here fill this gap by considering airports in the Balkan region, and compare them with larger airports in the neighbouring Europe. We specifically tackle two aspects: the statistical characterisation of delays, and the description of their propagation through functional networks. Results depict a rich dynamics: delays in Balkan airports have markedly less extreme events, suggesting that they are caused by more random and independent events; but are also strongly influenced by the status of the system in Europe. These results are put in context of extant literature, and further used to draw operational insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Dynamic effects of population aging on natural interest rates
Authors: Hongyi Chen, Jingyi Zhang
Abstract: Declining fertility and rising longevity are accelerating population aging worldwide. We study their effects on interest rates using a quantitative life-cycle model that explicitly accounts for the long lag between birth and labor-market entry, and features Barro-Becker parental preference, endogenous human capital accumulation, and a public pension system. Reducing fertility raises the interest rate during a sustained transition, as agents increase consumption in anticipation of future labor shortages and wage growth, before converging to a lower steady state. Increasing longevity instead monotonically reduces the interest rate by raising precautionary savings. These divergent dynamics are robust to variations in the pension system, human capital inputs, and child-related allocations. A historical decomposition further shows that fertility shocks have been the dominant demographic driver of U.S. interest rate fluctuations since 1960. These findings challenge the view that aging uniformly lowers interest rates and highlight the distinct implications of fertility- and longevity-driven aging.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: On the empirical relevance of the exchange rate as a shock absorber at the zero lower bound
Authors: David Finck, Mathias Hoffmann, Patrick Hürtgen
Abstract: The New Keynesian argument is that flexible exchange rate regimes cannot stabilize cyclical developments at the ZLB, as the real exchange rate appreciates in response to adverse demand shocks. We estimate the effects of a negative domestic demand shock on the real exchange rate for the euro area vis-à-vis the United States, Canada, and Japan by state-dependent sign-restricted local projection methods. We find a real depreciation when interest rates are not at the ZLB, but also when they are. The exchange rate can accommodate considerable variations in output, confirming its shock-absorbing capacity away and during ZLB episodes. The stabilizing role of the exchange rate is accompanied by a significant expansion of the ECB’s balance sheet at the ZLB, while it remained unaffected in the non-ZLB period.

Title: Along and beyond the curve: Disentangling the volatility effects of renewable energy
Authors: Ziyi Lan, Feng Song, Tielong Wu
Abstract: How does the expansion of renewable energy affect electricity price volatility? Despite a growing body of empirical work, the evidence remains mixed, with divergent effects reported across markets and technologies. We develop a theoretical framework that helps reconcile this mixed evidence by decomposing the volatility effect into two channels: the curvature effect, through which renewables shift the equilibrium along the merit-order curve, and the dispersion effect, through which renewables alter the variability of residual demand. We empirically assess this framework using hourly real-time data from the Shandong and Shanxi electricity spot markets in China. We document divergent intraday effects between wind and solar, opposing wind effects across the two provinces, and a sign reversal in the solar effect at the daily scale. These seemingly contradictory patterns can be coherently interpreted as the interplay of the curvature and dispersion channels, demonstrating that the framework provides a unified account for understanding the divergent volatility effects of renewables across technologies, markets, and frequencies.

Title: Being collaborative or collusive? The role of common institutional investors in corporate carbon emissions
Authors: Jing Zhou, Kaiwen Wu, Xiang Zhang, Yanmei Fan
Abstract: Amid rising concerns over the emissions of greenhouse gases and climate change, the imperative to reduce corporate carbon emissions has become increasingly critical. This study constructs a novel theoretical model for exploring the collaborative governance and anti-competitive views on the role of common institutional investors (CIIs) in corporate carbon emissions. Using a sample of Chinese A-share-listed manufacturing firms from 2009 to 2021, our results show strong evidence of the anti-competitive view, suggesting that CIIs play a collusive role in affecting corporate carbon emissions positively. Greater market power of CIIs and intensified industry competition are found to be the underlying mechanisms. Notably, the anti-competitive effect of CIIs is more pronounced in firms with market-driven short-term CIIs, low financing constraints, and those in low-carbon industries. Additionally, our further evidence shows that industry competition amplifies the anti-competitive effect of CIIs by strengthening their incentives to reduce costly environmental competition among portfolio firms. By shedding light on the relationship between CIIs and corporate carbon emissions, the study provides valuable insights into whether there should be incentives or restrictions on CIIs in achieving carbon reduction and addressing global challenges in sustainable development.

Title: An extended energy system model for renewable energy expansion planning: The net energy perspective
Authors: Yong Yang, Hui Wang, Yang Bai
Abstract: Renewable energy expansion is fundamental to climate change mitigation. Representing the available energy for activities outside energy sectors, net energy is a key concern in renewable energy development. Ignoring the net energy issue in renewable energy planning will likely undermine energy sufficiency. To address this, this study proposes an extended energy system model by integrating the energy return on investment (EROI) feedback into the cost-minimization of energy systems. Reflecting an endogenous adjustment of final energy consumption to EROI variations, this feedback can preserve net energy availability throughout the optimization process. Varying energetic learning rates are applied to investigate the impacts of technology-level uncertainties in technological improvements. Applying the proposed model to China reveals that renewable energy expansion reduces systemwide EROI to below the 2020 level, with a maximum reduction of 30.4% in extreme situations. Integrating the EROI feedback into energy planning can mitigate EROI declines and reduce renewable energy curtailment. Moreover, the proposed method for determining overcapacity and storage can improve the net energy performance compared to existing approaches. Uncertainty analysis reveals that technological improvements of PV have stronger impacts on renewable energy expansion pathways, and accelerating PV improvements from slow to fast can increase the minimum EROI by 7.8%.

Title: The impact of comprehensive student support on crime: Evidence from the pathways to education program
Authors: Adam Lavecchia, Philip Oreopoulos, Noah Spencer
Abstract: This paper presents estimates of the causal effect of a multifaceted support program for low-income high school students on crime. The program, called Pathways to Education, bundles a number of supports including regular coaching, tutoring, group activities, free public transportation tickets and bursaries for postsecondary education. Our empirical strategy uses administrative data on high school enrollment linked to administrative court records and a difference-in-differences methodology that compares the evolution of crime outcomes of students living in the public housing communities where Pathways operates to similar public housing students who are ineligible for the program. We find that eligibility for Pathways reduces the likelihood of being charged with a crime at its Regent Park location by 6 percentage points (33 percent of the pre-treatment mean) and has no statistically significant effect at its Rexdale and Lawrence Heights locations. Our results suggest that the reductions in criminal activity are driven by the reduction of property crimes.

Title: Order of entry and market performance in the global smartphone industry
Authors: Wenzhuo Lu, Chuanhao Lu, Xiaochen Xie
Abstract: The global cell phone market has transitioned significantly from feature phones to smartphones since 2007. This particular period of smartphone industry expansion, and a detailed product-level dataset of all the cell phones sold in 40 major economies between 2007 and 2016, give us an unprecedented chance to study how the order of entry affects the performance of the same firm in different markets. We begin with a theoretical framework wherein the order of a firm’s entry affects both consumers’ preferences and suppliers’ delivery costs. We then document a market sales advantage for early entrants, especially those originating from developed countries, offering higher-priced products, or having diversified product lines. Finally, we show that adopting product-specific innovations, such as the Android operating system and high-performance hardware components, can help late followers leapfrog over formerly leading firms.

Title: Artificial intelligence technologies, skills demand and employment: Evidence from linked job ads
Authors: Lennert Peede, Michael Stops
Abstract: We study how artificial intelligence (AI) is related to labour demand at the establishment level. We use the share of AI related vacancy postings at the establishment level to identify activities in developing, implementing or using AI technologies. Low overall AI vacancy shares between 2015 and 2023 suggest that we study a phase of early AI adoption where establishment AI activities are rather associated with discernable changes in skill demand. We find a small reduction in the demand for those hard skills, denoting skills required for the tasks specific to a certain occupational activity, that are not related to AI technologies and that are mainly required to complete analytical non-routine tasks like, e.g., “analysis”, “development”, “software implementation”. We found no overall association with employment growth, nor did we identify any correlation between AI-related activities or different skill groups.

Title: Reviewing lean manufacturing and Industry 4.0 technologies in the supply chain
Authors: John Reyes, Josefa Mula, Manuel Diaz-Madroñero
Affiliations: Universidad Técnica de Ambato; Universitat Politècnica de València
Abstract: This paper aims to provide a literature review of how lean manufacturing (LM) and Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies are integrated in a supply chain (SC) context. The PRISMA methodology is followed for data collection in the Web of Science and Scopus databases, where 92 papers were selected and reviewed. The analytic categories were based on the following: (1) SC structure; (2) decision levels; (3) research methodology and modelling approach; (4) lean waste types; (5) development tools, LM tools and I4.0 technologies; (6) practical application; (7) benefits and SC performance; (8) limitations. The main results provide a compilation of the literature on real-world waste and I4.0 planning challenges that are specific to certain sectors. The research focused mainly on conceptual, descriptive and exploratory methodologies. The case study was the main empirical modelling approach, followed by mathematical programming and simulation models. The lean tools that are most integrated with I4.0 technologies are kanban, just in time (JIT) and total productive maintenance. The Internet of Things (IoT), big data and cloud computing stand out for having more interactions with LM tools.

Title: Blockchain integration for cost-effective EV battery remanufacturing in closed-loop supply chains
Authors: Keru Duan, Gu Pang, Kannan Govindan, Hannan Amoozad Mahdiraji
Affiliations: University of Birmingham; Centre for Sustainable Operations and Resilient Supply Chains (CSORSC), School of Management, College of Business and Law, Adelaide University, Adelaide, Australia
Abstract: This study examines strategies to enhance the economic viability and environmental sustainability of lithium-ion battery (LiB) remanufacturing in electric vehicles (EVs). It evaluates centralised and decentralised closed-loop supply chain (CLSC) models, integrating blockchain technology and dynamic optimisation to improve transparency, coordination, and cost efficiency. Using Tesla’s battery collection and remanufacturing operations in China as a case study, the research employs expert interviews, legal framework analysis, and industry reports. Optimisation techniques, including Python’s PuLP and Monte Carlo simulations, identify cost-effective network configurations. Findings reveal that economies of scale and blockchain integration significantly reduce costs by over 86% for moderate volumes and 81% for large volumes. The study challenges the perception of LiB remanufacturing as unprofitable, demonstrating its commercial feasibility at scale. Strategic measures, including regional remanufacturing centres and optimised logistics, are recommended to support the circular economy and long-term sustainability in the EV industry.

Title: Impact of digital twin adoption on food supply chain performance: a system dynamics approach
Authors: Ying Huang, Abhijeet Ghadge, Nicky Yates
Affiliations: Cranfield University
Abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology provides a promising solution to challenges within the food supply chain (FSC) due to its unique characteristics. While existing literature highlights the potential of DTs to enhance real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and operational efficiency, a quantitative assessment of the overall impact of DT implementation on FSC performance is missing. This study bridges this research gap by integrating experimental and analytical approaches. Empirical data were collected through questionnaires from food industry practitioners, combined with literature to develop a mental model for capturing the interrelationships among DT-relevant technologies, FSC operations, and supply chain performance. Later, by deploying systems thinking and system dynamics (SD) modelling approaches, the impact of DT adoption on FSC operational metrics is evaluated. The findings indicate that the DT positively impacts inventory levels, actual delay (lead time), and unfulfilled orders in the short term, while contributing to cost reduction and food waste in the long term. The SD models not only highlight the impact of integrative technology adoption on the operations of FSCs but also provide a comprehensive framework for modelling and assessing SC systems under the influence of technology. This study contributes by providing quantitative evidence of DT's impact on the FSC.

Title: Metadesign survey and vision for Industry 5.0 production systems
Authors: Xifan Yao, Guangjun Ran, Kun Hu
Affiliations: Fuyao University of Science and Technology; South China University of Technology; Tongji University
Abstract: The industrial landscape has evolved through multiple revolutions, each shaping design engineering (DE) practices. DE 1.0 focused on cost reduction, DE 2.0 aimed at scaling production, DE 3.0 emphasised integrating design with manufacturing, and DE 4.0 pursued enhanced production efficiency in alignment with Industry 4.0. Industry 5.0, however, marks a shift towards a human-centric approach that balances human and societal needs with environmental sustainability and industrial resilience. This transition introduces DE 5.0, closely linked to the emerging concept of metadesign – whose conceptual roots trace back to the late Industry 3.0 era and developed further during Industry 4.0. Metadesign redefines traditional systems design by enabling collaborative processes in which users become active designers, expressing creativity through meaningful engagement. Within the context of Industry 5.0, metadesign is poised to fully flourish, particularly as it integrates into the industrial metaverse. This paper surveys the evolution of DE across industrial revolutions leading to Industry 5.0, proposes a metadesign framework for product design and production systems, outlines key enabling technologies along with a case study, and discusses limitations, biases, and challenges for metadesign in Industry 5.0, as well as the contributions, implications, and future research directions of this study.

Title: Neural network-assisted optimisation of production rescheduling under incomplete data
Authors: Maria E. Samouilidou, Nikolaos Passalis, Georgios P. Georgiadis, Michael C. Georgiadis
Affiliations: Aristotle University of Thessaloniki
Abstract: This work presents a novel decision-support system integrating Neural Networks (NNs) and a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model to enhance production scheduling and rescheduling in single-stage, multi-line, multi-product dynamic manufacturing facilities. Production engineers frequently face unexpected challenges requiring immediate schedule adjustments and regular product changeover operations which increase downtime and waste. To tackle these challenges, a novel framework is developed for quick generation of flexible production schedules. A NN is trained to embed products into a space where distances reflect changeover durations, facilitating their clustering by production line while minimising internal changeover times. In the case of absent data, another NN predicts unknown changeover times based on products’ characteristics. The predictions and allocations produced are incorporated into an MILP scheduling model, tightening the formulation and improving computational performance. The predictive accuracy of the NN is evaluated against standard methods, whereas the proposed scheduling framework against a conventional monolithic MILP approach. Several cases concerning two real industrial plants show that the proposed system achieves better production schedules in significantly faster solution times. A weekly production horizon with daily disruptions is studied, further highlighting the flexibility and robustness of the approach, making it a promising tool for real-time decision-making in production environments.

Title: Multi-objective planning model for sustainable agri-food supply chains: balancing profitability and fairness
Authors: Yameng Huang, Takashi Hasuike
Affiliations: Waseda University
Abstract: Smallholder agriculture constitutes an integral component of the global agri-food system; however, smallholders remain susceptible to systemic risks arising from socio-economic inequities and uncertainty in production and markets. This study proposes a multi-objective planning model for sustainable agri-food supply chains that integrates profitability with multi-dimensional fairness. Fairness is represented through three dimensions: distributional fairness, financial-risk resilience, and service fairness. The problem is formulated as a mixed-integer non-linear programming model, incorporating multi-period and multi-product decisions across planting, harvesting, packing, storage, sorting, and transport stages. To capture uncertainty in crop yield and market price, a scenario-based stochastic programming approach was developed and compared with a deterministic benchmark. The model was solved using Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm (NSGA-II), Multi-Objective Particle Swarm Optimisation (MOPSO), and Multi-Objective Whale Optimisation Algorithm (MOWOA), and the ϵ-constraint method. Computational experiments demonstrate that the stochastic model achieves more robust fairness outcomes under uncertainty while maintaining comparable expected profit. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses reveal how fairness-weight preferences and structural constraints shape the trade-offs between profitability and the three fairness dimensions. These findings provide actionable insights for contract design, resource allocation and fairness-oriented decision-making in sustainable agri-food supply chains.

Title: ChatEMT: large language model framework for energy-efficient machine tools – review, paradigm, and perspectives
Authors: Miao Yang, Wei Wu, Congbo Li, George Q. Huang
Affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Chongqing University
Abstract: The increasing demand for sustainable manufacturing has intensified the need for energy-efficient machining solutions that support economic, environmental, and societal sustainability. While emerging large language models (LLMs) have been successfully applied to other manufacturing problems, their application to energy-efficient machine tool management remains limited, leaving significant gaps in integrating LLM intelligence with energy-oriented machining services. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel LLM-enabled framework for energy-efficient machine tools, termed ChatEMT. This framework provides explainable, user-friendly, and semantically grounded energy services (e.g. analysis, monitoring, and optimisation) for sustainable machining. First, recent studies on the energy consumption of machine tools are systematically reviewed. Then, the paradigm and architecture of ChatEMT are presented, in which LLMs serve as the core layer that bridges energy data, domain knowledge, and diverse models. Specifically, LLMs incorporate domain knowledge of machine tool energy, retrieve production information, perform semantic reasoning over machining processes, and orchestrate tool invocations to support a wide range of energy services. Finally, open challenges and future research directions are discussed to guide subsequent studies. This work highlights the critical role of LLMs in enabling explainable, flexible, and context-aware energy intelligence for machining systems.

Title: Investigating the productivity in different assembly system configurations for a better accommodation of disabled workers
Authors: Serena Finco, W. Patrick Neumann, Azin Setayesh
Affiliations: University of Padova; Toronto Metropolitan University (formerly Ryerson University)
Abstract: In the context of Industry 5.0, socially sustainable manufacturing demands assembly systems that support diverse worker capabilities, including those of individuals with disabilities. This study investigates the impact of disability severity on system throughput and identifies which assembly configurations best promote inclusion while maintaining productivity. Using discrete event simulation, serial and parallel system flows were analysed under varying levels of product variability, buffer capacity, and worker impairment. Disability was modelled through two parameters: the increment of assembly time, representing the percentage increase in task duration for the disabled worker, and the percentage of station time executed by the disabled worker, capturing different levels of task involvement. Findings reveal that throughputs in serial systems decline sharply with higher disability severity, especially under conditions of high variability and limited buffering. In contrast, parallel flow systems exhibited greater resilience, sustaining higher performance despite severe impairments. Decision-tree analysis identified task time variability, the number of workstations, and extended task durations as critical factors in determining optimal system configurations. These effects were context-dependent and influenced by system layout. The results demonstrate that inclusive system design can be achieved without sacrificing efficiency, provided structural flexibility is embedded, especially via parallel processing strategies. This research underscores the importance of integrating flow strategy and task allocation approaches when including workers with diverse abilities, contributing to the broader vision of human-centred and inclusive manufacturing in Industry 5.0.

Title: A hybrid decision-support framework for cost-efficient manufacturing system design and operations under demand uncertainty
Authors: Roohollah Younessinaki, Azadeh Sadeghi, Hadi Mosadegh, Gürsel A Süer
Affiliations: Northern Illinois University; University of Michigan-Flint; Amirkabir University of Technology; Ohio University
Abstract: Uncertainty in supply chains amplifies the challenges of manufacturing system design, where strategic and operational decisions must be aligned to avoid inefficiencies such as underutilised capacity and excess Work-In-Process (WIP), which compromise cost efficiency. Although prior studies have examined cost, utilisation, and WIP, these factors are typically addressed separately, with limited attention to their combined trade-offs in system design. This study develops a five-step hybrid decision-making framework for designing and evaluating a cost-efficient layered Cellular Manufacturing System (CMS). At its core, a Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) model is proposed to minimize total cost while accounting for resource utilisation and queueing-based WIP estimation under uncertainty. Discrete Event Simulation (DES) evaluates the design, with flow time and WIP linked through Little’s Law to throughput as indicators of steady-state system. Regression analysis examines how KPI variation influences total cost, demonstrating robustness. A desirability-based method is then used to synthesize cost and KPIs to select the optimal configuration. Results show that the proposed design outperforms classical and layered CMS benchmarks by lowering total cost and stabilising utilisation and WIP. Moreover, sensitivity analysis on demand variation shows that the optimal cell configuration is preserved across all scenarios, indicating structural robustness with only modest cost variation.

Title: Product change-driven stress tests for supply chains: towards resilience and viability
Authors: Yi Yang, En-Zhi Cao, Chen Peng
Affiliations: Yancheng Institute of Technology; China Jiliang University; Shanghai University
Abstract: Large-scale supply chain (SC) disruptions have exposed the limitations of conventional SC-oriented resilience strategies in addressing long-term component shortages. This study proposes a product change strategy with stress testing to enhance SC viability. First, a three-layer supplier-component-supplier network model is constructed to quantify change propagation effects caused by component changes and identify components requiring synchronous changes. Second, a simulation-embedded mixed integer programming stress test model is developed. Third, a two-stage solution approach is proposed, whereby the identification of changed components is prioritised, followed by the optimisation of supply portfolios and production plans. Simulation results illustrate managerial implications. The product change strategy improves customer order fulfillment rates by up to 60.28 percentage points and reduces profit losses by up to 4.88 percentage points under severe disruptions. Increasing the component design margin from 0–0.006 to 0.03–0.05 reduces the number of components requiring synchronous changes from 18 to only 2, thereby lowering the implementation costs by approximately 4.86 percentage points and improving profit levels by 8.89 percentage points. The findings demonstrate that the proposed strategy extends the SC viability theory from concept to SC recovery practices from an integrated product-SC perspective. The methods provide quantifiable decision-making tools and actionable managerial guidance for enterprises.

Title: Enhancing inspection efficiency in high-quality environments using a process capability-based skip-lot sampling strategy
Authors: Chein-Wei Wu, Shih-Wen Liu
Affiliations: National Tsing Hua University; National Chin-Yi University of Technology
Abstract: This study extends the conventional skip-lot sampling (SkSP) framework by proposing a two-level skip-lot sampling plan (SkSP-2L) based on variables inspection using the process capability index Cpk. While the traditional SkSP-2L, rooted in attributes inspection, has demonstrated efficiency in reducing the average sample number (ASN), it becomes increasingly impractical in modern high-quality manufacturing environments where defect rates are extremely low. In such contexts, attributes-based methods often require prohibitively large sample sizes to ensure statistical validity. To overcome this limitation, the proposed variables-based SkSP-2L integrates the widely adopted Cpk index to facilitate more efficient and informative lot evaluation, aligned with contemporary process performance assessment practices. The study outlines the plan’s operating procedure, mathematical formulation, and sensitivity analysis. Comparative evaluations demonstrate the proposed method’s superiority over traditional SkSP-2 and single sampling plans in reducing ASN. A real-world case study further validates its practical applicability in precision-focused manufacturing settings with stringent quality requirements.

Title: Digital-model-driven distributed control for production and planning in smart manufacturing systems
Authors: Bianca Caiazzo, Teresa Murino, Alberto Petrillo, Stefania Santini, Andrea Somma
Affiliations: Universitas Mercatorum; University of Naples Federico II
Abstract: With the aim of improving Smart Manufacturing System performance, novel Production Planning and Control (PPC) tools, combining the new Industry 4.0 technologies with traditional scheduling methods, are necessary. Among the different PPC challenges, herein, we focus on Multi-Job-Shop Scheduling Problems (MJSSP), which, due to their high complexity, are critical for ensuring an optimal production management. Planning, organising and assigning a set of multiple jobs on different groups of machines, especially in the presence of limited resources and with predetermined processing time, is an NP-hard problem. The problem becomes challenging when also considering unexpected events altering the system production flow. To address this issue, this work proposes a Distributed Production Control Approach which, by leveraging digital tools, properly manages the MJSSP, both in a literature case study and in a real-world scenario, while ensuring resilience in Smart Manufacturing Systems against unforeseen events. Simulation results confirm the effectiveness, robustness, and scalability in terms of makespan, total flowtime and computational time of the proposed approach, showing advantages compared to the centralised solutions obtained via benchmarking Genetic Algorithm. Most notably, the obtained results highlight the potential of this control to optimise production in complex manufacturing systems, paving the way for a full integration in real-world manufacturing companies.

Title: The role of the Industry 4.0 technologies for Industry 5.0 development in small and medium enterprises
Authors: André de Mendonça Santos, Carlos Jefferson De Melo Santos, Ava Santana Barbosa, Ângelo Márcio Oliveira Sant’Anna
Affiliations: Federal University of Bahia; Federal University of Recôncavo of Bahia
Abstract: This paper aims to identify how Industry 4.0 technologies adopted by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) contribute to the development of Industry 5.0. It also identifies which technologies are most suitable and should be prioritised for implementation. Correspondence Analysis was used to map the alignment between specific technologies and the Industry 5.0 pillars. The Fuzzy-DEMATEL method was also applied to identify and prioritise the most prominent and influential technologies. The results show a strong alignment of IoT, Big Data analytics, and AI with the Sustainability pillar, while augmented reality, automation, and mobile technologies align more with Human-centricity. The Fuzzy-DEMATEL analysis identifies AI and IoT as the primary ‘cause’ technologies, holding the highest influence and prominence. This research offers novel insights to guide strategic technology adoption in resource-constrained environments, making theoretical and practical contributions. Theoretically, the study provides valuable insights into which technologies managers should align with their strategic objectives. For practical application, the findings offer significant support to managers, enabling them to create a clear roadmap for implementation and to prioritise technologies most aligned with their specific goals for the Industry 5.0 pillars. This insight helps managers avoid wasting valuable financial and time resources on non-priority technologies.

Title: Leveraging CNN and LSTM-based perception towards reconfigurable human-robot collaborative operations
Authors: Apostolis Papavasileiou, Stelios Nikoladakis, Dimitris Boulbasakos, Sotiris Aivaliotis, Sotiris Makris
Affiliations: University of Patras
Abstract: Efficient human-robot collaboration requires the ability of industrial workstations to be easily reconfigured. However, conventional systems rely on predefined task execution and limited perception capabilities, restricting their ability to adapt to product variability. This paper presents the implementation of a human-robot collaborative paradigm for reconfigurable industrial operations utilising dynamic perception capabilities. The proposed approach follows an experimental evaluation methodology based on a production time cost model at workstation level. Process and human perception techniques are deployed to dynamically adapt to changes in product variations and environmental scene updates. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based pipeline is introduced for automatically retraining and accurately detecting diverse industrial parts. A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based module is also deployed to identify the operator’s state and adapt robot behaviour. The synchronisation of execution flow is achieved through a service-based orchestration architecture acting as a state holder for monitoring the overall system while incorporating results provided by the perception modules. The system is validated through a case study derived from the white goods industry, using key operational metrics including production time, system utilisation, and assembly reliability. Experimental results demonstrated improved workstation adaptability and reduced operational delays when new components are introduced while maintaining high assembly reliability.

Title: Drivers and constraints of agentic AI in supply chain management: an exploratory study
Authors: Nicolò Trifone, Fabrizio Dallari, Alexandra Brintrup
Affiliations: LIUC University; Institute for Manufacturing, University of Cambridge; British Library
Abstract: Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have led to the emergence of AI Agents, autonomous systems performing complex tasks and pursuing defined objectives with minimal human interaction. Early research in AI Agents in supply chain (SC) management is pointing to their potential for enhancing visibility, resilience, and operational efficiency. However, as AI Agents are an emerging technology, several aspects of their application remain unclear. The literature lacks understanding of the SC processes they can support, the main drivers and constraints influencing their adoption, and practitioners’ perspectives on these aspects. Moreover, as their implementation inevitably reshapes human actors’ roles, scholars have called for further investigation into the nature of agent interaction with humans. This exploratory qualitative study addresses these gaps through semi-structured interviews with experienced practitioners in AI and SC.
