Title: Balancing and scheduling of transfer lines for cycle time and peak power minimisation: a learning-enhanced multi-objective variable neighbourhood search
Authors: Pedram Beldar, Ehsan Mahmoodi, Mostafa Kermani, Gary Linnéusson, Olga Battaia
Affiliations: University of Skövde; KEDGE Business School

Title: Decarbonisation under cap-and-trade: an integrated network Data Envelopment Analysis model with a second-scoring auction mechanism
Authors: Elnaz Azadi, Ali Emrouznejad, Xun Zhou
Affiliations: Surrey Business School, University of Surrey
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Economies of Scale to Consumption in Collective Households
Authors: Hsin‐Yuan Hsieh, Arthur Lewbel, Krishna Pendakur
Affiliations: Department of Economics National Tsing Hua University Hsinchu Taiwan; Department of Economics Boston College Chestnut Hill Massachusetts USA; Department of Economics Simon Fraser University Burnaby British Columbia Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT Browning et al. (2013) model collective‐household economies of scale in goods consumption by having each good be partly shared, instead of each good being public or private. We modify their model to achieve simple point identification and estimation of the economies of scale of consumption of each good, and we provide a new index of household level economies of scale. Our model has a linear form, permits households of varying composition, including children, and accommodates unobserved heterogeneity in both preferences and in the economies of scale of each good. We provide estimates using Canadian Surveys of Household Spending data.

Title: Fairness‐Aware Pricing for Platform‐Operated Restaurants With Social Interactions
Authors: Yuanguang Zhong, Mingyu Tian, Qiyang Li, Jiazi Yang
Affiliations: School of Business Administration South China University of Technology Guangzhou China; School of Economics and Management Fuzhou University Fuzhou China; School of Management Guangdong University of Technology Guangzhou China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Many restaurants have transformed themselves into platform‐operated outlets by introducing online delivery channels through platforms, in addition to their traditional dine‐in channels. Restaurants typically use differential pricing or uniform pricing for price management. While conventional wisdom suggests that uniform pricing inherently ensures fairness compared to differential pricing, we challenge this notion by demonstrating how platform‐driven social promotion subsidies (e.g., shareable coupons) can create de facto price disparities even under uniform pricing regimes. Such subsidies not only dilute the perceived fairness advantage of uniform pricing but also amplify social interactions among consumers, generating a value‐enhancement effect that paradoxically boosts consumer utility while complicating pricing coordination. This study examines the impact of social interactions and consumers' fairness‐awareness on restaurants' pricing strategies. The most interesting finding we reveal is that when the channel competition is not fierce and the consumers' unfairness aversion is low, the restaurant's preference over pricing strategies switches twice from differential pricing to uniform pricing and then back to differential pricing, as the value‐enhancement effect increases. For platforms, uniform pricing can be more profitable if the value‐enhancement effect is weak, despite the impacts of consumers' fairness awareness and channel competition. In addition, we uncover that uniform pricing leads to a higher consumer surplus when the value‐enhancement effect is moderate, and the region where uniform pricing achieves a higher consumer surplus forms a “scissor‐shaped” pattern as the consumers' fairness awareness increases.

Title: Optimization modeling in business and government: in honor of Professor John M. Mulvey on his 80th birthday
Authors: David Saunders, Stavros A. Zenios

Title: N-LAS-IAM: Climate change in a balance-of-payments framework
Authors: Wellington Santos de Amorim, Leonardo Flauzino de Souza, Marcelo C. Pereira
Abstract: Climate change is becoming a macro-financial development problem for peripheral economies, yet integrated assessment models remain poorly equipped to analyse climate vulnerability in externally constrained developing countries. Existing heterodox models are mostly closed or global, while balance-of-payments-constrained growth models treat climate in reduced form and incompletely formalise the financial channel. This paper introduces the N-LAS-IAM, a recursive framework coupling a Thirlwall–Hussain growth core with endogenous green structural change, capital flows under financial fragility, sovereign risk, and a climate module mapping global emissions into damages that feed back into profitability and sovereign fragility. Green structural change is endogenised through logistic diffusion equations governing trade income elasticities as functions of green R&D and the real exchange rate. The model is explored via Monte Carlo experiments in which damage intensity and climate-to-risk transmission vary while emissions, policy, and structural-change parameters remain fixed. Three results emerge. First, higher damage produces a more fragile debt regime with elevated spreads, tighter financing, and prolonged deleveraging. Second, damages widen the elasticity gap between exports and imports, slowing green upgrading and locking the economy into lower-sophistication trade patterns. Third, the damage-to-fragility relationship is nonlinear: below a threshold the economy absorbs shocks, but above it a self-reinforcing regime emerges where lower productivity, higher spreads, weaker inflows, and structural regression feed on one another. These findings suggest that physical damages erode policy capabilities by raising external finance costs when green investment is most needed, and that early mitigation may yield convex macroeconomic returns for peripheral economies under balance-of-payments constraints.

Title: Know its worth? Factors affecting the social acceptability of water reuse: A mixed methods planned behavior model
Authors: Pierre Rebesco, Mikaël Akimowicz
Abstract: Due to strong demographic pressure, rapid urban development, and climate change, water demand is increasing while usable freshwater supplies are being depleted. The reuse of treated wastewater (RTWW) is one of the avenues currently being explored to ensure the quantitative and qualitative security of the water supply. The interests for social acceptability emerged with risk management approaches and the subsequent debates on the role of technical progress, the implementation of major development projects, and their consequences for the environment between the late 1970s and early 1980s. The purpose of this article is to identify the factors that influence the building of RTWW acceptability. This study was carried out in southern France. It combines a quantitative survey on behavior related to engaging in RTWW, based on Ajzen's theory of planned behavior, with a qualitative socioeconomic study aimed at understanding representations and beliefs regarding RTWW. The findings show that a lack of knowledge about RTWW and the implementation of only a few RTWW projects result in a normative gap and a perceived lack of control. In addition, trust in managers and public authorities, the quality of treatments, as well as risks perceptions – particularly those relating to health – significantly influence intentions to engage in RTWW. Lastly, several factors such as emotions, types of uses, and environmental awareness play an underlying role by helping build perceptions of water reuse, trust in relevant stakeholders, and more accurate perceptions of risks.

Title: Deforestation in the Colombian amazon biome: socioeconomic and socio-environmental conflict drivers
Authors: Jorge Higinio Maldonado, Rocío Moreno-Sánchez, Jorge Montero-Mestre
Abstract: Colombia is one of the world’s most biodiverse countries, home to over 10% of the planet’s biodiversity. Much of this richness is found in the Amazon biome, which spans over 43% of the country’s land surface. Despite its ecological importance, the region is subject to growing threats from deforestation, leading to loss of biodiversity and degradation of ecosystem services. Key drivers of this deforestation include socio-environmental conflicts, such as land conversion, coca cultivation, and illegal mining, all of which are compounded by Colombia’s longstanding internal armed conflict. Socioeconomic conditions in local communities further reinforce these drivers, yet limited access to reliable data constrains understanding and has led to a gap in literature. This study examines the links between socioeconomic factors, socio-environmental conflicts, and deforestation across the Amazon biome in Colombia. Using different sources of information, we construct a broad set of indicators and use econometric methods and machine learning (ML) techniques to identify the main drivers of forest loss. The results show that while the contribution of coca cultivation to deforestation has declined, land grabbing has emerged as a leading driver. Mining causes significant disturbances to the Amazon biome, but its link to deforestation is marginal. Other consistent predictors include poverty and the presence of basic trails and roads. The analysis also confirms that the northwestern zone remains the most threatened subregion, and that forest conservation is positively associated with the presence of Indigenous communities.

Title: Do workers value formal jobs? Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Katharina Fietz
Abstract: Informal employment, and the resulting lack of social insurance coverage, remains widespread in low- and middle-income countries. This paper contributes to the debate on the determinants of informality by estimating workers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for a formal job using a sample of 4997 Brazilian dependent workers. On average, workers are willing to forgo 15.1% of their wages for a signed work card, with higher WTP among formal and highly educated workers. Predicted eligibility for non-contributory social assistance lowers WTP, while predicted eligibility for contributory social insurance increases it. A simple calculation suggests that workers’ WTP may not fully offset employer contributions if passed on through lower wages. Providing additional information on formality raises WTP, but mainly among those already having a higher valuation of formality.

Title: Who is inclined to embrace green options in on-demand mobility?
Authors: Andrea Pellegrini, Andres Fielbaum
Abstract: Shared on-demand mobility can be made more environmentally friendly, but this involves trade-offs in comfort and cost: electric vehicles may require higher fares due to charging time, while walking segments can reduce vehicle-kilometres-travelled at the expense of door-to-door convenience. This study examines travellers’ willingness to choose green shared mobility options using an integrated choice and latent variable model estimated from a discrete choice experiment conducted in Sydney, Australia. Respondents chose among three shared mobility options differing in walking requirements, travel times, emissions, and price, and answered attitudinal questions capturing car safety, pro-walk orientation, time sensitivity, and variety-seeking behaviour. Willingness-to-pay values are computed for five distinct user profiles. Results indicate that (i) users are generally willing to pay to reduce emissions; (ii) personalised options yield greater emission reductions than uniform policies; and (iii) regular public transport users show higher willingness to walk, highlighting potential synergies between on-demand mobility and transit.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: How metro networks respond to extreme rainfall: a coupled To–Through resilience perspective
Authors: Yao Shen, Pingyan Hu, Yunjie Feng, Wanyin Han
Abstract: Underground metro systems are widely regarded as reliable components of urban mobility during adverse weather, yet their performance under extreme climate stress remains insufficiently understood. Existing studies largely rely on static network metrics or scenario-based simulations, providing limited insight into the dynamic evolution of resilience during real disruptions. This study conceptualises metro network resilience as two interrelated dimensions: To-resilience, capturing various functional robustness of stations against external demand, and Through-resilience, characterising the transmission efficiency of segments under propagated network pressure. Critically, degradation at stations can trigger flow redistribution and pressure amplification along segments, which in turn propagate back to stations, precipitating coupled failure risk and systemic breakdown. Leveraging sophisticated mobility data, both dimensions are quantified and local resilience zones are delineated to support differentiated planning interventions. The framework is empirically applied to the Zhengzhou underground metro system under extreme rainfall conditions. Results show that normal-day flow-weighted functional centrality substantially outperforms topology-only structural centrality in explaining station resilience loss, while weighted betweenness centrality exhibits early sensitivity to segment degradation. Scenario simulations further demonstrate that passive containment strategies yield limited local benefits, whereas topology-oriented interventions that enhance corridor-level redundancy significantly improve system-wide resilience. This study provides a data-driven basis for spatially targeted resilience planning of underground systems under intensifying climate extremes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: When simulator experiences shape later choices: Measuring behavioural spillover on travel preferences
Authors: Gloria Amaris, Stephane Hess, Stepan Vesely
Abstract: Behavioural spillover, where one behaviour affects others, is widely studied in psychology but underexamined in transport, despite its potential to improve sustainability. We offer a novel contribution by combining immersive driving simulator data with stated choices to test spillover effects on preferences for travel time and carbon emissions. Our design captures how real-time, experience-based feedback, augmented by personalised driving advice, influences behaviour. We find evidence of behavioural shifts, and a link between those shifts in preferences and behaviour in the simulator. Crucially, we reveal substantial heterogeneity in responses, underscoring the need to move beyond homogeneous assumptions. The willingness to accept longer journeys in return for reduced CO2 emissions increases from 22.6 mins per kg to 39.87 mins per kg after seeing the driving advice information. The findings have implications for designing policies that harness spillover mechanisms to reduce transport-related emissions, making a valuable contribution to environmental research and transport policy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Devour the future: Locust plagues and educational disruption in Ethiopia
Authors: Jiale Yan
Abstract: I study the impact of locust swarms on secondary education in Ethiopia. Combining high-resolution spatial data on locust swarm activity with administrative records from secondary schools, I use a difference-in-differences event-study design to identify the causal effects of locust shocks. I find that locust shocks reduce secondary school enrollment and completion by approximately 9.1% and 9.5%, respectively, while increasing the secondary school dropout rate by about 2.9 percentage points. These effects are particularly pronounced in remote and highly agriculture-dependent woredas. Further analysis provides suggestive evidence that these educational disruptions are associated with agricultural income losses, increases in local food prices, and declines in junior secondary school enrollment and completion. These findings highlight how biological disasters can disrupt educational progress in developing countries.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: How confirmation bias makes persuaders more honest
Authors: Minseo Choi, Daeyoung Jeong
Abstract: We study a Bayesian persuasion game in which a decision maker (DM) incurs psychological costs from belief-disconfirming information and chooses whether to engage with the sender’s experiment. We model preference-based confirmation bias as psychological discomfort from exposure to signals that conflict with the DM’s prior beliefs. Whenever persuasion is feasible, the sender must commit to a strictly more informative experiment than in the Kamenica–Gentzkow (2011) benchmark. This increases the DM’s “actual” welfare, defined as material welfare excluding the psychological cost term, when confirmation bias is moderate, while persuasion fails when the bias exceeds a threshold and the DM disengages. We then introduce processing-based confirmation bias, modeled as systematic misperception of signals. In isolation, it does not change equilibrium behavior or the DM’s “actual” welfare, but when combined with preference-based bias it strengthens the disciplining effect for the DM. A dynamic extension shows that future engagement concerns further increase the sender’s incentive to provide informative signals.

Title: The carbon reduction effects of new infrastructure construction: Evidence from local government special bonds in China
Authors: Hongyu Ding, Peng Tian, Yuyue Kong
Abstract: This paper takes the new infrastructure special bonds (NISB) issued by Chinese local governments as the research object and explores the carbon reduction effects of new infrastructure construction (NIC) from the perspective of public investment. Using a newly constructed city-level dataset, this paper finds that NISB issuance significantly reduces carbon emissions, with this impact being more pronounced in cities with strong fiscal capacity, high industrial value-added, and effective policy coordination. On the one hand, NISB promote the penetration rate of digital technology and intelligent equipment in production, thus contributing to carbon reduction through improved production efficiency. On the other hand, NISB channel fiscal funds and social capital toward low-carbon industries, which helps to lock in lower carbon emissions over a longer period. Further evidence indicates that following the COVID-19 outbreak, local governments reoriented NISB policy priorities from a balanced focus on carbon reduction and economic growth goals toward greater emphasis on boosting economic recovery, a shift that also weakened the carbon reduction effects of NISB to some extent. This paper offers new evidence that targeted public investment can contribute to climate change mitigation, while emphasizing the short-run trade-off between long-term emission reduction and stable growth during economic downturns.

Title: Breaking it down: How does multiline messaging affect service quality in text‐based customer support?
Authors: Noyan Ilk, Guanyi Lu, Guangzhi Shang
Affiliations: Department of Business Analytics, Information Systems & Supply Chain, Herbert Wertheim College of Business Florida State University Tallahassee Florida USA; Department of Supply Chain Management, W. P. Carey School of Business Arizona State University Tempe Arizona USA
Abstract: Abstract Computer‐mediated communication channels, such as text‐based chat, can improve response speed and scalability while lowering operational costs for customer support. Yet, there has been a growing concern regarding the remote nature of digital communication leading to customer dissatisfaction. This study investigates how communication style—specifically, multiline messaging—can alleviate this concern and affect quality in digital service interactions. Leveraging a unique data set of text‐based conversations from a service center, we show that breaking down lengthy statements into multiple lines (i.e., multiline messaging) can improve problem resolution. However, this impact exhibits an inverted U‐shaped relationship; although moderate segmentation aids task‐oriented problem resolution, excessive multiline messaging backfires by inducing cognitive overload. In contrast, we find that customer satisfaction increases monotonically with multiline messaging intensity. Finally, we demonstrate that multiline messaging interacts positively with agent sentiment to further enhance both problem resolution and customer satisfaction. Our work contributes to the digital service literature by identifying a low cost, communication‐based mechanism that can improve service performance, thereby addressing the cost–benefit trade‐off often debated in the field. It also enriches the emerging people‐centric operations literature by introducing a novel, effective communication construct to the set of human‐related drivers of work performance.

Title: Decision science in the agentic era: Research frontiers on agentic AI and human–agent collaboration
Authors: Yingjie Zhang, Tianshu Sun
Affiliations: Guanghua School of Management Peking University Beijing China; Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business Beijing China
Abstract: Abstract Decision science is entering a new era in which decisions are no longer made solely by humans, but increasingly by autonomous AI (Artificial Intelligence) agents and human–agent collectives. Prior research often treated AI as a tool for prediction or support. Agentic systems now decide, act, learn, and coordinate over time, changing the unit of analysis for decision science. In this perspective, we argue that this shift requires new conceptual foundations and a sharper research agenda. We outline a design‐oriented framework that decomposes human–agent systems into atomic structures, decision architectures, and field‐to‐model mappings, enabling comparison, experimentation, and cumulative knowledge building. Building on this framework, we introduce the mission of the new “Agentic AI and Human–Agent Collaboration in Business” department. The department emphasizes two central topics: agents as decision‐makers in single‐ and multi‐agent systems, and human–agent collaboration. We also highlight preferred methods, including lab, field, and simulated experiments, as well as agent‐driven research that uses AI agents for exploration, hypothesis generation, and knowledge discovery. The goal is to guide rigorous research on how agentic systems reshape decision‐making in business and society.

Title: Issue Information
The fast and the studious? Ramadan observance and student performance
Authors: Kyra Hanemaaijer, Olivier Marie, Marco Musumeci
Abstract: Abstract We examine how religious observance affects educational performance by studying the years in which Ramadan overlapped with the national end-of-secondary-school exams in the Netherlands. Using administrative microdata and a difference-in-differences design, we find that students who are most likely to fast obtain lower exam scores and are more likely to fail to graduate. As expected given the structure of the Dutch exam system, the increase in failure risk is concentrated among students near the pass threshold. Effects are larger in more religiously segregated schools. For longer-term outcomes, we document a substantially higher likelihood of dropping out among students aged 18 and older, who are legally permitted to leave school and therefore at risk of doing so. Finally, analyses of exam timing suggest that modest adjustments—such as avoiding scheduling two exams on the same day during Ramadan—may help reduce the disadvantages experienced by observant students.

Title: The job-shop and robot scheduling problem with multi-shelf robots and human intervention
Authors: Yu Wang, Hu Qin, Nan Huang, Hongjian Hu, Gangfeng Liu
Affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Hamad Bin Khalifa University; Xuzhou Xugong Automobile Manufacturing Co., Ltd.

Title: A mathematical programming model in path planning of a human-cobot order picking system
Authors: Xiaoya Chen, Donglei Du, Xi Zhu
Affiliations: School of Management, Tianjin University of Technology, Tianjin, People's Republic of China; Faculty of Management, University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, New Brunswick, Canada

Title: A face-level machining operation strategy prediction method for prismatic parts based on transformer and B-Rep learning
Authors: Shuai Niu, Fangwei Ning, Maolin Cai, Feirui Zhang, Xiaomeng Tong
Affiliations: Beihang University

Title: A decision-support model for productivity upgrading in global value chains
Authors: Charilaos Mertzanis, Marios Tsioufis, Apostolos Vetsikas, Athanasios Pavlopoulos, Mohamed Shaker Ahmed
Affiliations: Abu Dhabi University; University of the Peloponese; University of Thessaly; Al Ain University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Supply chain risk identification using AI-powered topic modelling: implications for demand forecasting in oil and gas companies
Authors: Arda Gezdur, Jyotirmoyee Bhattacharjya, Anastasios Panagiotelis, Hriddhi Doley
Affiliations: The University of Sydney Business School. Merewether Building; Monash University. Caulfield Campus
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing: the mediating role of supply chain complexity in technology-driven operations
Authors: Aamir Rashid, Rizwana Rasheed
Affiliations: York College, City University of New York Department of Business and Economics, School of Business and Information Systems, , Jamaica; IQRA University Department of Business Administration, , Karachi
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between digital ecosystems and supply chain resilience in manufacturing firms, with particular attention to the statistical mediating role of supply chain complexity. It addresses the limited understanding of how digital technologies, including AI, IoT, and cybersecurity, operate collectively rather than in isolation. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the resource-based view (RBV) and dynamic capability view (DCV), the study employs a quantitative research design using survey data from 732 managerial and supervisory respondents working in manufacturing firms in Mississippi, West Virginia, and Arkansas. Structural equation modeling (SEM) using AMOS is applied to test the proposed relationships. Findings The results indicate that digital ecosystems are positively associated with supply chain resilience, with cybersecurity exhibiting the strongest association with the Digital Ecosystem construct. Supply chain complexity shows a positive but comparatively smaller association with resilience and the statistically significant indirect relationship is consistent with partial mediation. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to manufacturing firms in selected U.S. states, which may affect generalizability. Future research could explore cross-industry and cross-country contexts and examine additional mediating or moderating mechanisms. Practical implications The findings suggest that managers should consider investing in integrated digital infrastructure, prioritizing cybersecurity capabilities and using data-driven technologies while proactively managing the complexity of digital transformation. Originality/value This study advances a systems-level understanding of digital ecosystems in supply chains by showing that integrated digital capabilities, rather than isolated technologies, are positively associated with resilience in complex operational environments.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: School Starting Age and the Gender Pay Gap Over the Life Cycle
Authors: Kamila Cygan‐Rehm, Matthias Westphal
Affiliations: Faculty of Business and Economics Dresden University of Technology Dresden Germany; Faculty of Business Administration and Economics FernUniversität in Hagen Hagen Germany; RWI ‐ Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Essen Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper replicates and extends the evidence on the lifetime effects of school starting age on earnings by Fredriksson and Öckert (2014) for Sweden. Using German data for individuals born between 1945 and 1965, we examine a more rigid system of ability tracking in secondary education, a potential driver of long‐term effects. We confirm negligible effects of later school entry for men and positive effects for women. These gender differences arise despite similar effects on educational attainment. By unfolding the gender gaps over the lifecycle, assessing fertility decisions, and maternal employment around the first birth, we show that childbirth postponement and increased labor market attachment after the first birth seem to be plausible mechanisms.

Title: Interruptible cross-docking scheduling for perishable food supply chains
Authors: Fei Pan, Enmin Fu, Tijun Fan
Abstract: The significant spoilage losses in perishable food supply chains necessitate highly efficient logistics operations. Cross-docking, which eliminates storage time, is a promising solution. However, traditional cross-docking typically employs a non-interruptible (NI) pattern, where trucks’ unloading/loading processes cannot be interrupted once started. This rigid pattern restricts operational flexibility and leads to mismatches between unloading and loading operations, prolonging food accelerating deterioration. To overcome these limitations, we propose a flexible Interruptible (I) scheduling pattern, which allows trucks to enter and exit docks multiple times, dynamically improving the matching between inbound unloading and outbound loading operations. To precisely evaluate the benefits and costs of this flexible pattern, we formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear programming model with linear constraints and nonlinear objective to jointly minimize deterioration cost and interruption cost. Given the NP-hard nature of the problem, we develop a tailored Two-Phase Hybrid Metaheuristic algorithm. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed model and algorithm. Compared to the NI pattern, the I pattern achieves average total cost savings of 3.8%–5.4% (driven by deterioration cost savings of 9.7%–23.0%), with only 1.5 to 2.3 additional dock entries/exits on average. Managerial insights from sensitivity analyses highlight truck changeover time exerts a more significant impact on cost performance than transit time. And the I pattern is most valuable when there is significant heterogeneity in deterioration rates among products.

Title: The knowledge system of human symbiotic system management in the age of digitization
Authors: Zhan Zheng, Xusong Xu, Guo Li, Xin Lu, Wei Zhao, Xiaolong Tao, Yanrong Huang
Abstract: This study explores the complexity of systems in which human behavior operates within a social context, termed the “human symbiotic system”. Through theoretical analysis, it investigates the functional structure, levels of management research, and mechanisms that underlie this complexity. The primary management objectives of the human symbiotic system are innovation and harmony. We identify three dimensions of harmony: the relationship between humans and nature, interactions among individuals, and considerations for present and future generations. Furthermore, the study introduces a comprehensive knowledge framework, called the Complex Scientific Management 18151 System, which provides theories and tools for managing human symbiotic systems. Our study provides managers and policymakers with a systemic framework for improving innovation efficiency, reducing coordination failures, and enhancing the long-term economic sustainability of complex social systems under digital transformation. This research marks a significant departure from traditional management approaches and offers a new perspective for advancing management studies by addressing the challenges of managing complex social systems.

Title: Building resilient animal husbandry and meat production supply chains
Authors: Aman Goswami, Benjamin Melamed, Alok Baveja, Fred Roberts, Victoria Kiernan, Dennis Egan, Peter March
Abstract: The advent of the COVID-19 pandemic brought a growing recognition of the need to enhance national security by building resilient supply chains. While governments and firms have increasingly focused on supply chains of strategic significance, not all such supply chains have received sufficient scholarly attention. A case in point is the broad class of Animal Husbandry and Meat Production (AHMP) supply chains. This paper focuses on Veterinary Medical Product (VMP) supply chains and Meat Production (MP) supply chains, which are representative examples of upstream and downstream components of the class of AHMP supply chains. Although VMP supply chains interact with MP supply chains, they are rarely analyzed in an integrated manner. Leveraging scholarly research and field experience of subject matter experts (SMEs), this paper utilizes a case study approach, called Focal-firm Supply-chain Integrated Methodology (FSIM), to analyze VMP and MP supply chains subject to disruptions. The paper introduces a comprehensive resiliency framework, dubbed the Multi-Dimensional Resiliency (MDR) framework, which augments FSIM by providing resiliency strategies for VMP and MP supply chains. The paper shows that FSIM and MDR are efficacious in analyzing complex supply chains, identifies robust and sustainable resiliency strategies for VMP and MP supply chains and explains why the general methodology is applicable to a wide variety of supply chains. This work is grounded in the US AHMP supply chains with broader methodological implications.

Title: Spatial perspective on perceived fairness of climate-related fuel tax increases
Authors: Tikli Loivaranta, Piia Lundberg, Jukka Käyhkö
Abstract: We explore the perceived fairness of fuel tax increases from a spatial perspective. Actions in transport sector are needed to meet climate change mitigation targets, but such policies may disproportionately impact rural and urban residents, leading to spatially varying experiences of injustice. Perceived fairness is the most important determinant of public opinion towards mitigation policies, but perceived fairness of these policies itself has been understudied. We combine our inquiry of perceived fairness regarding fuel tax increases with considerations of spatial justice. We explore, whether residential area type, region, and variables such as climate concern, trust in climate policies, political orientation and use of fossil-fuelled car, are associated with perceived fairness of increasing fuel tax, and whether there are regional differences in these variables. Data were collected via a survey in June 2022 in three regions with different characteristics in Finland: Helsinki, Finland Proper, and Northern Ostrobothnia. Our results reveal that residents in rural areas and sparsely populated regions perceive fuel tax increases as less fair. Climate concern, trust and political orientation were found to influence fairness perceptions. Moreover, climate concern and trust were lower in sparsely populated regions. Considerations of fairness perceptions are important for successful climate mitigation policy.

Title: Mobile internet connectivity and climate change literacy in Africa
Authors: Yacouba Kassouri
Abstract: Addressing climate change requires individual behavioral shifts and a deep understanding of its impacts, yet the role of information and communication technologies (ICT), a powerful driver of social movements and cultural shifts, in shaping climate change literacy remains underexplored. This study addresses a critical gap by exploring how ICT, particularly mobile Internet connectivity, influences climate change literacy in Africa. I provide the first systematic evidence on the impact of mobile Internet connectivity on climate change literacy by exploiting variations in peer-based Internet connectivity in an instrumental variable strategy. Using newly georeferenced individual-level data on climate change literacy from over 42,000 respondents across 31 African countries, I show that mobile Internet connectivity has a modest yet robust effect on climate literacy, raising it by approximately 0.57 points for a typical adopter. Heterogeneity analysis shows that mobile Internet access primarily enhances the knowledge-based dimensions of climate literacy, particularly climate awareness and understanding, while also improving risk perceptions to a lesser extent. This suggests that mobile Internet contributes to climate literacy mainly by expanding access to factual information and knowledge about climate change. Suggestive evidence reveals that Internet connectivity can help close climate-related information gaps, among socio-economically disadvantaged groups, such as women, farmers, and those without formal education. Although Internet connectivity increases the frequency of using Internet and social media for news, there is no strong evidence that these platforms serve as channels linking Internet connectivity to climate literacy.

Title: Early-life adversity and long-term outcomes: evidence from the cocoa swollen shoot virus outbreak in the Gold Coast
Authors: Mohammed Iddrisu Kambala
Abstract: How do early-life economic shocks that do not directly affect human biology shape long-term development outcomes? While a large body of work documents persistent effects of early-life exposure to health crises, famines, and natural disasters, much less is known about shocks that operate through economic disruption. This study addresses this gap by examining the long-term effects of the Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus Disease (CSSVD), an agricultural epidemic that devastated cocoa production in the Gold Coast (now Ghana) during the 1940s. Combining historical data on climatically suitable cocoa-growing areas with georeferenced household survey data, I exploit variation in exposure across birth timing and space to estimate the epidemic’s long-term effects. The results show that exposure during early childhood and school-going years led to substantial and persistent human capital deficits. Individuals exposed during early childhood lost about one year of schooling and were 8.5 percentage points (pp) less likely to obtain formal education, while those exposed during school-going years lost about 0.8 years of schooling and were 7.0 pp less likely to obtain formal education. Exposure is also associated with worse health outcomes, increasing morbidity by 6.2–8.5 pp and disability by 5–7.5 pp. In contrast, there is no systematic evidence of long-term effects on employment type or labor supply. Evidence on potential mechanisms points to both educational and occupational channels. Conditional on ever attending school, exposed individuals completed fewer years of schooling and were more likely to have incomplete primary education, indicating disruptions to both school progression and initial access to schooling. In addition, exposed individuals are more likely to work in the agricultural sector in adulthood, consistent with reduced educational attainment having narrowed their occupational options. These findings demonstrate that industry-specific economic shocks can generate long-term human capital deficits, even in the absence of direct biological exposure.

Title: Manufacturer encroachment under probabilistic selling of deceptive counterfeits in the presence or absence of non-deceptive counterfeits
Authors: Hao Yang, Jianbin Li, Ziyi Wang
Abstract: Brand manufacturers typically rely on retailers to sell authentic products. However, in many emerging markets, retailers seeking higher margins may procure deceptive counterfeits at low wholesale prices and probabilistically mix them with authentic products, even at the risk of incurring penalties. In practice, some branded product categories are exposed only to deceptive counterfeits, whereas others also face competition from non-deceptive counterfeits. We develop a model with a brand manufacturer and a retailer selling authentic products and deceptive counterfeits probabilistically, while a non-deceptive counterfeiter may be either present or absent from the market. We examine whether the brand manufacturer should encroach when the retailer probabilistically sells deceptive counterfeits. Our results show that, although manufacturer encroachment may increase the sales of deceptive counterfeits, it can still serve as an effective strategy to combat probabilistic selling when the encroachment cost is relatively low. Interestingly, manufacturer encroachment strengthens the disciplinary effect of penalties on the selling of deceptive counterfeits. A higher detection rate also strengthens the brand manufacturer's incentive to encroach but may reduce social welfare by lowering consumer surplus and increasing inspection costs. Furthermore, we find that non-deceptive counterfeits attract price-sensitive consumers and intensify market competition, thereby reducing the price and demand of the retail channel. More importantly, their presence reduces the incremental profit generated by encroachment and weakens the brand manufacturer's incentive to establish a direct sales channel. Finally, manufacturer encroachment reduces both the price and sales of non-deceptive counterfeits.

Title: Information, goal setting and performance: Experimental evidence
Authors: Haoran He, Marcus Roel, Ronghai Su, Qian Weng
Abstract: We investigate how information about relative performance shapes goal setting and subsequent performance. Combining a field experiment in a university course with a complementary laboratory experiment, we exogenously vary whether individuals receive baseline relative-performance feedback before or after setting non-binding goals. We document that uninformed individuals anchor goals primarily on subjective, often inaccurate beliefs. Providing information systematically corrects these distortions: individuals who underestimate their relative ability revise their goals upward, whereas overestimators adjust their targets downward. However, the effect of information on performance is limited – it only improves performance for underestimators in the field experiment. To explore the underlying mechanism, we leverage laboratory evidence to examine voluntary goal resetting. We find that delayed feedback affects final goals only when individuals reset them. Accordingly, treatment differences in final goals are substantially attenuated for underestimators but remain sizable for overestimators. Once this goal-adjustment process is accounted for, upward revisions among underestimators improve performance, whereas downward revisions among overestimators reduce challenge and impair ultimate performance.

Title: Models for the Discrete Ordered Median Problem based on DC decomposition
Authors: Stefan Nickel, Justo Puerto, Simon Ramoser, Alberto Torrejon
Abstract: The Discrete Ordered Median Problem is a flexible model for a large variety of location problems. It relies on sorting allocation costs non-decreasingly before applying a weight vector. Being a non-linear operation, the cost-sorting is particularly challenging from a modeling point of view. Promising approaches use radius variables or reformulations of the ordered median objective function leading to efficient mixed-integer linear programming models. This study introduces an alternative modeling paradigm that exploits a known DC decomposition of ordered median functions. The proposed framework offers a systematic way to combine existing formulations and to derive new ones. To illustrate its potential, we develop several new models for the Discrete Ordered Median Problem based on this concept. An extensive computational study is conducted to evaluate their performance against current state-of-the-art formulations. The results show that the proposed approach can lead to highly competitive and previously undiscovered models.

Title: Spatio-temporal graph reinforcement learning for multi-period supply chain synchronization: Joint procurement, warehousing, and multimodal routing with multiple 3PL providers
Authors: Jinjin Cai, Rui Song, Shiwei He, Jushang Chi, Kai Yan
Abstract: The multi-period supply chain synchronization problem (MP-SCSP) jointly coordinates procurement, inter-period warehousing, and multimodal transport across multiple third-party logistics providers under period-dependent constraints. To address the rapidly growing combinatorial complexity of the MP-SCSP, a mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a corresponding Markov decision process are established, together with STAGRL-PPO, a spatio-temporal-aware graph reinforcement learning framework based on proximal policy optimization. STAGRL-PPO combines an edge-attention graph neural network for multimodal topology encoding, temporal embeddings for period-dependent dynamics, and topology-aware action masking to ensure operational feasibility without heuristic post-processing. Experiments on Chicago-regional networks demonstrate strong computational performance. On small instances, STAGRL-PPO matches exact solutions while reducing computation time by 99.45%, with an average optimality gap of 1.33%. On large-scale instances where exact solvers fail within two hours, it obtains high-quality solutions in 10.24 s, with gaps of 8.4% to feasible upper bounds and 4.94% to theoretical lower bounds. On extreme-scale instances, the mean bound gap is 14.65% with a mean inference time of 24.79 s. Without additional training, the policy transfers to the unseen Manhattan-LION and Rhine–Alpine-40 networks with a mean objective difference of 2.50% relative to QMEA and a mean solution-time reduction of 94.92%. Ablation studies show that edge attention is critical to feasibility, whereas temporal embeddings accelerate convergence. Managerially, the framework adapts provider selection to price fluctuations, exploits intermodal routing to bypass capacity bottlenecks, and selects faster modes to satisfy strict delivery deadlines.

Title: Time–dependent manned–unmanned collaborative delivery routing with partial charging and locker configuration of unmanned ground vehicles
Authors: Wenheng Liu, Ge Feng, Weicun Zhang, Wenyan Zhao
Abstract: This paper focuses on the routing problem with collaborative delivery of manned delivery vehicles (MDVs) and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) for urban last-mile logistics, subject to time windows, UGV’s locker and energy constraints, and traffic congestion. The objective is to minimize the total delivery cost. In the proposed collaborative delivery system, MDVs and UGVs operate in parallel, while UGVs perform multiple trips for small- to medium-sized parcels due to limited locker capacity, and partially recharge according to subsequent energy requirements. A mixed-integer nonlinear programming model is formulated for the problem. Given its NP–hard nature, an improved adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm incorporating arc–based path relinking (IALNS-APR) is developed. The algorithm features dedicated removal and insertion operators, and search strategies (e.g., multiplier–triggered operator selection, charging station number optimization, and elite set update). Extensive experiments on benchmark and tailored instances show that IALNS-APR outperforms Gurobi and other leading algorithms. Sensitivity analyses reveal that traffic congestion has a pronounced effect on the total cost, and partial charging reduces the total cost compared with full charging. Furthermore, optimizing locker configuration is critical for reducing travel cost and proves robust to collaborative delivery capacity.

Title: Optimal size and composition of government spending in small open economies
Authors: Qingyuan Du, Pedro Gomis-Porqueras, Solmaz Moslehi, Chung Tran
Abstract: We study optimal ﬁscal policy over the business cycle in a small open economy within a currency union that faces downward nominal wage rigidity. Government spending consists of public consumption and productive public investment, with investment accumulating into public capital subject to a time-to-build requirement. In this environment, we characterize the Ramsey allocation when the policymaker jointly chooses consumption taxes, public consumption, and public investment. Fiscal instruments operate through distinct but complementary margins. The consumption tax mitigates unemployment distortions when wage rigidity binds, while spending composition provides an additional intertemporal stabilization margin. Because public capital is subject to time-to-build and has limited short-run elasticity, counter-cyclical public investment smooths private consumption and stabilizes relative prices with modest contemporaneous distortions. Calibrating the model to France, we ﬁnd that coordinated ﬁscal policy substantially reduces unemployment risk and generates measurable welfare gains relative to regimes that rely solely on taxes or keep government spending composition ﬁxed. These results are robust to alternative calibrations and to an extension with government production of non-tradable public goods.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Early Social Security claiming and slow asset decumulation: experimental evidence
Authors: John Duffy, Yue Li
Abstract: Retirement behavior in the U.S. exhibits two well-documented patterns: most individuals claim Social Security benefits early, before reaching their full retirement age, and retirees decumulate their assets more slowly than predicted by standard life-cycle models. This paper provides experimental evidence that these patterns emerge even in a controlled individual decision-making environment where early claiming and slow decumulation are not optimal. In a baseline treatment calibrated to current U.S. Social Security rules, participants display both early claiming and slower-than-optimal asset decumulation. Replacing larger annuities with lump-sum incentives in two alternative treatments, as has been proposed by the U.S. Congress, accelerates asset decumulation but does not lead to delayed claiming. These findings generalize from a convenience student sample to an older sample aged 45–55 and broadly resemble the observed behavior of similarly situated respondents in the Health and Retirement Study. We show that a wealth-preservation motive can jointly generate early claiming and slow asset decumulation, consistent with the experimental evidence.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Carbon mitigation potential of metro-based underground urban logistics under operational constraints
Authors: Bing Yan, Xiang Liu, Zhigang Liu, Chengcheng Yu
Abstract: Rising urban freight and decarbonization pressures raise an increasingly pressing question: can metros provide green freight mobility without harming passengers? We develop a policy-evaluation framework for metro-based underground logistics (MUL) that integrates multi-task demand forecasting, capacity-constrained freight realization, and emissions accounting under passenger-priority operations. Shanghai's empirical results have showed that freight demand peaks tend to occur outside passenger peaks, while high-volume freight OD flows are less concentrated along major passenger commuting corridors. Under our baseline setting, MUL realizes 66.69% of metro-replaceable demand on weekdays and 92.28% on weekends, with estimated net CO 2 reductions of 14.86% and 24.32%, respectively, after accounting for feeder travel, detours, and unrealized demand. The weekend estimate is more sensitive to freight-demand prediction uncertainty. Scenario comparisons identify station-proximate eligibility, direct routing, off-peak operation, and freight capacity allocation as the main operational levers shaping mitigation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Is full disclosure always optimal? Strategic information design for vaccine campaigns via Bayesian persuasion
Authors: Letian Zhang, Tengfei Nie, Yizhen Li, Jianghua Zhang
Abstract: Timely disclosure of information on vaccine effectiveness is crucial in shaping public perceptions of its benefits, ultimately influencing vaccination decisions. This study employs a Bayesian persuasion framework to examine how a health organization can strategically design information campaigns on vaccine effectiveness to influence public vaccination choices. We derive the optimal strategies for both the health organization and the public and explore how factors such as vaccine externality affect the effectiveness of information design. Although it is commonly believed that full disclosure is the optimal strategy for maximizing social welfare, our findings challenge this view. In a scenario with a sufficient vaccine supply, moderate vaccination costs, and a relatively low public prior belief in high vaccine effectiveness, a partial disclosure strategy is more effective in improving vaccine coverage and enhancing social welfare. In a scenario with limited vaccine supply, the optimal information disclosure strategy for the health organization depends on the supply level. When the vaccination cost is low and the public's prior belief in high effectiveness is high, the health organization can strategically limit the frequency of signals indicating high vaccine effectiveness through partial disclosure to ensure efficient vaccine allocation and maximize social welfare. Additionally, we show that the value of information design is maximized when the public's prior belief is moderate. Our research offers practical insights for health organizations by providing guidance on how to effectively manage information disclosure, especially in the context of vaccine hesitancy.

Title: Beyond targeting women: Intrahousehold contexts and the effectiveness of food vouchers
Authors: Seollee Park, Yaeeun Han, Hyuncheol Bryant Kim
Abstract: Many transfer programs target women based on evidence that mothers are more likely than fathers to allocate resources toward child welfare. However, findings on gendered impacts remain mixed-likely because parental knowledge, preferences, and household decision-making roles differ across contexts. In this study, we experimentally vary the intrahousehold informational context itself through a randomized controlled trial in rural Ethiopia. Specifically, employing a factorial design, we cross-randomize two key dimensions: (1) which parent receives nutrition behavior change communication (BCC) - neither, mother only, or both; and (2) which parent receives a household food voucher - mother or father. We find that, pooled across settings in which fathers do not receive BCC, vouchers assigned to mothers generate larger improvements in child-feeding practices than vouchers assigned to fathers. The largest effects occur when mothers receive both BCC and the voucher. This maternal advantage attenuates and is no longer detectable when fathers also receive BCC. We provide suggestive evidence that when mothers have both a knowledge advantage and control over resources, they are better able to mobilize greater intrahousehold support. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for intrahousehold contexts, not just recipient gender, when designing nutrition interventions.

Title: Cognitive decline, education, and dynamic selection
Authors: Michael E. Darden
Abstract: I estimate a model of health investment, health, and sample participation, and I find substantially wider gaps in cognitive health by education relative to reduced-form estimators, even after accounting for the endogeneity of education. Selective exits (mortality or attrition) among less-educated respondents generate cross-sectional comparisons between highly educated individuals and the subset of healthier, less-educated individuals who survive. Furthermore, I find that education gaps widen at relatively early stages of cognitive decline—contrary to a large literature arguing that education affects levels but not slopes. Finally, I show that differential rates of cigarette smoking by education do not explain these gaps in cognitive health.

Title: A simulation-based framework for chronic disease management to improve health equity
Authors: Usame Yakutcan, Eren Demir, John R. Hurst
Affiliations: University of Hertfordshire; University College London
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management considering consumer behavior toward sustainability
Authors: Ikhyun Jo, Soongeol Kwon
Abstract: As consumer attention to sustainability grows in response to climate change concerns, firms face increasing pressure to align their supply chain strategies with evolving market responses. This study aims to support managerial decision-making by examining how firms should strategically design and manage their supply chains when consumer demand is shaped by cumulative, multidimensional, and uncertain responses to sustainability performance. To this end, we develop a consumer-responsive sustainable supply chain management framework, embedding a feedback loop between sustainability-driven operations and market demand. We formulate a multi-period mixed-integer linear programming model that links demand to consumers’ sustainability perception, which is formed cumulatively based on firms’ past sustainability performance. Sustainability performance is evaluated using carbon emissions, differentiated across emission scopes, and translated into an overall sustainability evaluation from the consumer perspective. To capture uncertainty in consumer behavior, the framework is extended to a two-stage stochastic programming model that reflects the evolution of sustainability-conscious consumers over time. Numerical experiments validate the proposed model and its internal feedback mechanism, illustrating how sustainability investments dynamically reshape consumer perception, demand realization, and subsequent supply chain decisions. The results show that incorporating consumer responsiveness can simultaneously increase profit and reduce total emissions, while sensitivity analyses reveal systematic shifts in optimal strategies with respect to consumer evaluation characteristics. Under uncertainty, the model favors precautionary sustainable capacity expansion and diversified parallel contracting as effective strategic hedges against evolving market conditions. These findings yield meaningful managerial implications and provide insights into how consumer-driven market mechanisms can support firms’ progress toward net-zero emission targets.

Title: Redistribution meets decarbonisation: Exploring universal basic income through an ecological macroeconomic integrated assessment model
Authors: Iñaki Arto, María Victoria Román, Simone D'Alessandro, Kurt Kratena, Guilherme Spinato Morlin, Manuel Tomás, Paola López-Muñoz, Ignacio Cazcarro, Ole van Allen
Abstract: The dual challenge of climate change and rising inequality calls for policies capable of delivering both ecological sustainability and social equity. Within the field of Ecological Macroeconomics (EM), integrated assessment models (IAM) with biophysical and socio-economic linkages provide a promising approach to explore policy trade-offs ex ante. This paper contributes to this literature by employing the Within Limits Integrated Assessment Model (WILIAM), an EM-IAM that combines a macroeconomic multi-regional input–output structure with explicit representations of energy and material flows, biophysical constraints, and climate damages. We assess a policy mix designed to support a just low-carbon transition in 21 European countries over the period 2025–2050, including a universal basic income (UBI) financed through a wealth tax, alongside a carbon tax aimed at internalising the external costs of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. We examine the interactions between redistribution and emissions within a unified modelling framework that accounts for household heterogeneity, economic rigidities and ecological limits. Our results show that the policy mix substantially reduces income inequality and improves social outcomes. However, the introduction of UBI generates rebound effects through increased consumption, which can be partially mitigated in the presence of carbon pricing. These findings highlight a potential trade-off between equity and environmental objectives. We discuss the mechanisms driving these dynamics and explore policy design implications, including the role of complementary measures to decouple well-being from material throughput. The paper illustrates the value of EM-IAMs for analysing complex policy interactions and advancing the integration of social and ecological dimensions in macroeconomic modelling.

Title: Obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition
Authors: R. Pablo Arribillaga, Jordi Massó, Alejandro Neme
Abstract: We define and study obvious strategy-proofness with respect to a partition of the set of agents. It encompasses strategy-proofness as a special case when the partition is the coarsest one and obvious strategy-proofness when the partition is the finest. For any partition, it falls between these two extremes. We establish two general properties of this new notion and apply it to the simple anonymous voting problem with two alternatives and strict preferences.

Title: Experience-based pairwise comparison dynamics
Authors: Jiabin Wu
Abstract: This paper introduces the experience-based pairwise comparison dynamics—a deterministic evolutionary process in which each agent, upon having the opportunity to revise her strategy, compares her realized payoff with that of another agent. The key departure from standard dynamics is that agents compare realized payoffs from actual matches rather than expected payoffs of strategies. Thus, agents need not know the population distribution of strategies and compute expected payoffs. In a uniformly random pairwise matching environment, this dynamic process is markedly more sensitive to the cardinality of the underlying game’s payoff structure than standard dynamics based on comparing the expected payoffs of different strategies. This heightened sensitivity yields equilibrium selection results in coordination games without the long waiting times typical of stochastic stability models. We further show that the strictly dominated strategy in the prisoner’s dilemma can survive.

Title: From pollution prevention to circular economy capabilities: The mediating role of absorptive capacity and moderating role of innovation orientation
Authors: Stephanie Graham, Trevor Cadden, Guangming Cao
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the need for firms to develop advanced capabilities to tackle the complex challenges of climate change. The purpose of this study is to examine a range of factors that support the development of circular economy capabilities (CEC). A theoretical framework grounded in the natural resource-based view (NRBV) and absorptive capacity theory (ACT) is developed to empirically test the antecedent role of preliminary capabilities (pollution prevention) in supporting the development of CEC. The role of other supporting mechanisms, such as absorptive capacity and cultural orientation, in the development of CEC is also considered. To test our hypotheses, data was collected via survey from 521 UK-based firms across a range of industries and analysed using structural equation modelling. The results provide support for the antecedent role or preliminary capabilities, such as pollution prevention, in supporting the development of CEC. This antecedent role is strengthened when mediated by absorptive capacity mechanisms. We also find support for the moderating role of sustainable innovation culture on the link between some, but not all, pollution prevention capabilities and CEC. Our study contributes to existing research in this area by highlighting a range of factors that can support the development of advanced environmental capabilities such as CEC. These insights are also useful for managers, who can draw on them to understand how to leverage their experience and cultural environment to support the development of advanced environmental capabilities.

Title: The timing fingerprint: A rank-based test of market timing
Authors: André A.P. Santos, Lorenzo Pascual Caneiro
Abstract: Traditional market-timing tests such as the Treynor–Mazuy and Henriksson–Merton tests are known to over-detect timing ability when fat tails and state-dependent volatility are present, and are based on rigid parametric assumptions about the timing payoff. We propose a test of market timing built on the concept of timing fingerprint, a rank-based test that presumes no functional form for the timing payoff and is calibrated to nominal size by a null-imposing wild bootstrap. We show that, while the same bootstrap restores the size of the classical tests, the fingerprint method identifies the direction and location of timing-like behavior across the entire benchmark distribution and is substantially more powerful against timing payoffs the classical tests do not span. We assess the finite-sample performance of the fingerprint test using Monte Carlo simulations and employ it to evaluate a large panel of U.S. equity mutual funds.

Title: Constant resource shares and Samuelson’s Shibboleth
Authors: Arthur Lewbel, Krishna Pendakur
Abstract: Suppose each individual in a community is given some fixed constant fraction of total available expenditures to spend. Samuelson (1948, 1954, 1956) argued that this would be a shibboleth (i.e., a procedure that doesn’t have meaning) because such a procedure cannot generally be rationalized by any social welfare function defined over the utilities of individuals. For modern collective household models, Samuelson’s shibboleth has been taken to imply that household resource shares (the fraction of a household’s budget allocated to each household member) cannot be constants. We show Samuelson’s claim depends on an assumption that is inappropriate for collective household models, and when that assumption is dropped, there is no shibboleth: resource shares can be any regular functions, including fixed constant fractions.

Title: Power outages, multi-product firms, and firm productivity: Theory and evidence from China
Authors: Jian Yu, Chen Zhao, Ying Li, Nan Wu
Abstract: This study develops a model of multi-product firms (MPFs) to examine their responses to power outages and the consequent effects on firm productivity. In the model, MPFs mitigate the adverse effects of power outages by discontinuing their less-productive products and focusing more on their core varieties. This buffering mechanism, however, comes at the cost of reduced product variety and a more concentrated product mix. We test this theory using firm–product-level export data from the Chinese metals and articles thereof industry from 2005 to 2015, combined with a text-based power outage index. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we find that a 1% increase in power outages reduces the productivity of single-product firms (SPFs) by 0.43%. MPFs experience a 0.31% smaller decline in productivity; however, this comes at the expense of a 0.20% reduction in product variety within these firms. We further calibrate the model and show that a 1% reduction in the observed 2005 outage level raises aggregate welfare by 0.017%, of which more than one-third is driven by MPF-specific within-firm reallocation and variety recovery. Our theory reconciles the findings on the impacts of power outages across countries, underscoring the critical role of the intra-firm extensive margin in economic loss assessments.

Title: Advanced tabu search for the multi-depot heterogeneous vehicle routing problem with backhauls
Authors: Wenjie Hu, Yang Wang, Rafael Martí, Anna Martínez-Gavara
Abstract: This work investigates the Multi-Depot Heterogeneous Vehicle Routing Problem with Backhauls (MD-VRPB), an important extension of the classical routing problem models that explicitly accounts for multiple depots and a heterogeneous fleet. The problem is motivated by large-scale distribution systems with multiple distribution centers and diverse vehicle types, where delivery and pickup operations must be jointly coordinated in a cost-effective manner. To address this problem, we propose a learning enhanced tabu search algorithm with long-term memory (LE-TS-LM). The proposed method embeds learning and long-term memory mechanisms into a tabu search framework and is built upon four complementary components: a greedy randomized construction procedure for generating diverse initial solutions throughout the iterative search process, a tabu search procedure with long-term memory for effective intensification and diversification, dedicated post-optimization techniques to refine route and vehicle-type decisions, and a probability updating and refinement mechanism that exploits historical high-quality solutions to guide future search. Extensive computational experiments are conducted on a total of 144 benchmark instances. The results demonstrate that LE-TS-LM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods for this problem in terms of solution quality while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. In particular, the proposed algorithm identifies 120 new best known solutions, significantly advancing the current benchmarks for the MD-VRPB. Additional analyses further highlight the contribution of each algorithmic component to both performance improvement and solution robustness, extending in this way the scope of the paper since these successful elements and strategies proposed here can be adapted to solve other hard optimization problems.

Title: Adapting continuous metaheuristics to discrete problems: A taxonomy-oriented review
Authors: Ru Yang, Qiyuan Jiang, Ling Ding, Bo Zhang
Abstract: Continuous metaheuristics are difficult to apply directly to discrete optimization because their real-valued operations are incompatible with structured discrete solution spaces. Existing studies also lack a unified framework for classifying and comparing discretization strategies. Following a systematic multi-database search and mechanism-focused screening, this review constructs a purposively curated corpus of 299 studies published between 2008 and 2025. It develops a two-dimensional taxonomy of discretization logic and discrete problem structure, formally defines three mechanisms—Operator Replacement, Mapping, and Encoding Reconstruction—and clarifies their boundaries and strictly defined hybrid combinations. The review also identifies five non-exclusive solution structures and an additional Mixed-type label, and descriptively examines recurring method–problem associations within the curated corpus. The framework standardizes terminology and offers practice-informed, non-prescriptive considerations for selecting and designing discretization strategies for continuous metaheuristics.

Title: Heterogeneous manpower group scheduling in automotive RO–RO operations: Optimization models and algorithms
Authors: Ziqiao Mei, Zhou Xu, Feng Chen
Abstract: This paper investigates a loading and unloading routing problem in automotive Roll-On/Roll-Off (RO–RO) terminals, where drivers transport batches of cars between vessels and yard sections. Each batch is modeled as an arc-based task, and a manpower group can transport at most as many cars as it has drivers. Unlike previous studies, this work adopts a more flexible and practical problem setting by incorporating heterogeneous manpower groups and a non-exclusive transport mode, allowing multiple groups to jointly serve a single arc-based task. While this setting improves resource utilization and operational efficiency, it also increases the complexity of jointly deciding group assignment and visit frequency for each task. Consequently, different combinations of heterogeneous manpower groups for a task affect the number of required visits, thereby altering the path for these manpower groups. We prove that the problem is NP-hard and formulate it as both arc-based and path-based mixed integer linear programming models. To tackle this problem, we develop a hybrid bilevel memetic algorithm that combines a decomposition-based math-heuristic for generating initial solutions effectively and employs a bilevel variable neighborhood descent to improve solutions through local search. We conducted extensive experiments on instances generated based on real operational data. The results show that the path-based model excels on small-scale instances, while the hybrid bilevel memetic algorithm outperforms alternatives on medium- and large-scale instances. On average, the total group traveling cost of a rule-based heuristic derived from planner experience is 46.74% higher than that of our algorithm. Sensitivity analyses show that heterogeneous group sizes enable more efficient transport combinations, reducing idle drivers and extra visits.

Title: Hybrid mechanism and data driven active scheduling method for dynamic flexible job shop
Authors: Yang Yue, Guodong Sa, Mingjie Hou, Zhenyu Liu, Chan Qiu, Jianrong Tan
Abstract: Under the trend of personalized customization and intelligent manufacturing, the prevalence of uncertain disturbances and the flexibility of manufacturing systems significantly affect scheduling performance. Existing technologies heavily rely on heuristic rules or data driven deep learning methods in problem modeling and solving for dynamic flexible job shop (FJS), failing to fully exploit the structural knowledge embedded in scheduling mechanism. This leads to difficulties in model management and suboptimal scheduling performance. To this end, this paper proposes a hybrid mechanism and data driven active scheduling method for FJS under job insertion scenarios. A dual attention network model for FJS considering job insertions and a mechanism-based model are constructed to enable real-time and reliable representation of the workshop state. A self-attention-based phased policy network is proposed to capture the relationships among pending operations, thereby enabling active scheduling and extending the decision-making paradigm of completely reactive scheduling. Furthermore, a dual-layer phasic policy gradient optimization algorithm is introduced, which integrates dual state representation into the training process, thus ensuring efficient learning of both representation and decision-making models for FJS. Experiments on FJS instances with job insertions show that the proposed method achieves an enhanced performance over the state-of-the-art deep learning models and outperforms benchmark models across instances of different scales and properties, demonstrating strong research and practical value.

Title: Understanding heterogeneous green transitions: An evolutionary approach to policy, innovation, and technological change
Authors: Fausto Cavalli, Alessandra Mainini, Enrico Moretto, Ahmad Naimzada
Abstract: Economies facing similar environmental challenges and broadly comparable policy interventions can nevertheless follow very different green-transition paths: some quickly adopt clean technologies, while others remain locked into carbon-intensive production. To account for this puzzle, we develop an evolutionary model in which market selection between clean and dirty technologies coevolves with environmental policy. A welfare-maximizing regulator taxes emissions and allocates the revenues between current pollution abatement and investments that progressively improve the environmental performance of clean production. This links short-run environmental policy with long-run technological change. We characterize the possible long-run technological regimes and study their evolutionary stability. We find that the same policy stance can support multiple stable long-run outcomes: economies facing identical policies may converge to different regimes depending on their initial technological composition, providing a theoretical basis for understanding the observed heterogeneity across countries. We show that policy can promote innovation even when only dirty producers are active, thereby paving the way for a green transition. We also show that even a predominantly green economy may remain vulnerable to the re-entry of dirty technologies. Finally, we analyze the ability of a regulator to dynamically adapt the policy mix, in order to redirect the transition path toward a predetermined long-run environmental target. Although adaptive policies can mitigate lock-in and path dependence, they cannot completely eliminate them. Finally, simulations show that more stringent environmental targets may even lead to outcomes opposite to those intended because of scale effects.

Title: Time-of-use pricing and peak shifting in residential EV charging: a quasi-experimental study from China
Authors: Jingjing Li, Erik T. Verhoef, Shuai Chen, Yacan Wang
Abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) has intensified peak load pressures on electricity systems. Time-of-use (TOU) pricing aims to alleviate this pressure by incentivizing intertemporal load shifting, yet causal evidence on its effectiveness, drawn from real-world, high-frequency charging data, remains scarce. This study employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to evaluate the impact of TOU pricing on residential EV charging behavior, utilizing high-frequency hourly data from over 20,000 users in Shandong Province, China. Findings reveal that TOU pricing significantly reduces peak-period charging while increasing off-peak consumption, indicating a pronounced intertemporal substitution effect. Despite reduced peak demand, total charging volume marginally increases due to lower charging costs. CES model estimates detect weak own-price elasticity between peak and off-peak periods but significant cross-price elasticity. Welfare analysis indicates that TOU pricing enhances consumer surplus. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that users with higher peak-hour dependence and greater consumption volatility exhibit stronger adjustments. Overall, the findings demonstrate that TOU pricing not only mitigates peak load stress but also promotes EV usage and supports the electrification of transport. These results underscore the institutional value of TOU mechanisms in facilitating vehicle-grid integration and advancing coordinated development between the energy and transport sectors.

Title: Beyond traditional emissions modelling in high value manufacturing: a hybrid approach for net zero supply chains
Authors: Victoria Omeire, Okechukwu Okorie, Paul Mativenga, Maria Sharmina, Peter Hopkinson

Title: Mitigating supply chain transparency barriers with blockchain: a dynamic capabilities perspective
Authors: Eric Ragan, Mohammad H. Eslami

Title: Energy-efficient scheduling of unrelated parallel machines under time-of-use electricity pricing with release dates
Authors: Peng Wu, Jing Lu, Nan Li, Jintao Lu
