Title: Premarital migration and marriage payments: Evidence from Indonesian men
Authors: Hugues Champeaux, Elsa Gautrain, Karine Marazyan
Abstract: While bride price customs are widespread in many developing countries, little is known about their consequences on men’s decisions. In this paper, we exploit a quasi-natural experiment of a school-building program in Indonesia (INPRES) to investigate the relationship between marriage norms and the internal migrations of young men. Combining anthropological, administrative, and individual-based datasets, we implement a triple-difference approach. We show that the less advantaged young men, who have fewer resources to cope with rising marriage costs, are more likely to migrate out of their district of origin when the women they are expected to marry benefit from the program. These findings suggest that the interaction between marital norms and policies can result in unintended consequences, shaping major economic decisions such as premarital migration.

Title: Foreign aid and power play: Political cycles in world bank’s procurement allocation
Authors: Antoine Boucher, Lisa Chauvet, Marin Ferry
Abstract: This paper examines the existence of political cycles in the awarding of World Bank procurement contracts around elections. We analyze elections in the home country of firms winning these contracts, distinguishing between firms based in the aid recipient country (i.e., domestic firms) and those from other supplier countries (i.e., foreign firms). Our findings indicate that domestic firms are more likely to secure larger contracts around elections in their home country, especially when corporate donations to candidates are allowed. Additionally, our results reveal an increase in contract sizes awarded to foreign firms before elections in their home country. This cross-border political cycle appears to be driven by strong aid partnerships and historical colonial ties between the supplier and recipient countries. These findings reveal a political dimension in procurement dynamics with potential implications for development resource allocation. Understanding these patterns can help enhance the transparency and effectiveness of aid-funded contracting.

Title: Educational legacies of christian missions: Evidence from the Democratic Republic of the Congo
Authors: Pierre Donat-Bouillud, Coralie Hirschi, Etienne Le Rossignol
Abstract: This paper investigates the educational legacies of Christian missions established before independence, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, focusing on contemporary disparities in educational content, quality, access, and outcomes. Using georeferenced data from over 20,000 schools and two million students participating in the Examen National d’État (Exetat) between 2016 and 2019, as well as primary data from a phone survey of 624 school directors, we explore how proximity to Catholic and Protestant missions during the colonial period influences educational opportunities today. We find that schools near historical Christian missions offer a broader and higher-quality curriculum, with increased access to study tracks outside the basic Pedagogy section. Students attending these schools are more likely to pass the Exetat and achieve grades qualifying for university admission, although the magnitude of the effect is modest. Observable school-environment and quality characteristics attenuate the Catholic missionary-proximity coefficient by about half, while demand-side patterns point to additional differences in student composition. Our findings reveal that the strong partnership between missions and the colonial state entrenched spatial inequalities in educational access and quality, inequalities that persist to this day.

Title: Communication failure: The hidden face of the tragedy of the commons
Authors: Philippe Colo, Guillaume Pommey
Abstract: This paper studies communication failure regarding risks in the commons. It argues that strategic issues might explain why years of scientific reporting regarding future risks have failed to trigger sufficient climate awareness. We consider a game of contribution to a public bad, where there is uncertainty regarding the damage generated by externalities. Prior to the game, agents receive non-certifiable information regarding the damage from an informed utilitarian expert. We show that in large-scale public good problems information transmission usually fails. We compare this result with the cases of Rawlsian and anti-Rawlsian experts and discuss the implication for climate expert panels. We also investigate the influence of the value of information in our result, which provides us with some insight on the part played by deontology on scientific communication.

Title: Targeted bidders in government tenders
Authors: Matilde Cappelletti, Leonardo M. Giuffrida
Abstract: A set-aside promotes a more equitable procurement process by restricting participation in government tenders to small or disadvantaged businesses. Yet its micro-effects on tender outcomes (competition and contract efficiency) and targeted firm performance entail trade-offs, which we evaluate empirically using a decade of US federal procurement data. At the tender level, we employ a two-stage approach. First, we use random forest techniques to compute the propensity score for a tender being set aside based on rules implementation. Second, we employ the scores in an inverse probability weighting framework. We find that set-asides prompt more competition — implying that the rise in participation of targeted firms more than offsets the exclusion of untargeted ones — and contract inefficiency, measured by cost overruns and delays. We argue that adverse selection and moral hazard are mechanisms behind contract inefficiency. We then study the targeted firm behavior to uncover whether long-run benefits mitigate short-run drawbacks. We compare businesses differentially exposed to a set-aside spending shock through an event study framework. We find mixed evidence on firm growth.

Title: Biometric responses to unjustified and justified-envy in school choice allocations
Authors: Valon Vitaku, Alexander L. Brown, Marco A. Palma
Abstract: The two most prominent strategy-proof school choice mechanisms, Deferred Acceptance and Top Trading Cycles, offer a trade-off between eliminating justified-envy and Pareto efficiency, respectively. We introduce a novel, biometric approach to investigate how much individuals care about and physiologically react to each property. Using an experimental design that randomly varies whether subjects learn about others’ assignments in a school choice game, we measure arousal through galvanic skin response and valence through facial expressions when subjects experience envy with and without justification. We find increased arousal associated with receiving successively lower-ranked allocations, i.e., the (unjustified) envy of the allocation(s) of others. We note additional arousal when that envy is justified, but that result requires an explicit message to accentuate the justification. Eye-tracking data confirm that subjects do not notice markers of justified-envy until receiving this message. Facial-expression valence yields less conclusive results, but this may be due to the limitations of that method for anger detection.

Title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Rolling Horizon Optimization algorithm for dynamic scheduling in AGV-Supported rice production
Authors: Yaping Zhao, Weilei Feng, Xinyue Zhang, Lianmin Zhang, Jingyi Zhao
Abstract: The integration of machine learning and rolling horizon optimization provides a promising pathway for improving operational efficiency and sustainability in modern agriculture. This study investigates a dynamic scheduling problem in AGV-supported rice production, addressing two key challenges: (i) coordinating hybrid solar–main-grid energy usage under uncertainties in rice yield and solar irradiance, and (ii) dynamically synchronizing automated drying schedules with transportation logistics. To tackle these challenges, we develop a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based predictor to forecast uncertain variables, and integrate it into a Machine Learning-Enhanced Rolling Horizon Optimization (ML-RHO) framework. The framework continuously updates scheduling and routing decisions through rolling time windows, thereby combining AI-based forecasting with stochastic simulation and optimization. Using parameters calibrated from a large-scale rice farm in China together with controlled Monte Carlo scenarios, we benchmark ML-RHO against conventional methods and a perfect-foresight theoretical optimum. The results show that ML-RHO achieves near-optimal solutions (average deviation of 2.85%) while reducing computation time by more than 90%. This work demonstrates how AI and stochastic simulation can be jointly leveraged to develop scalable, energy-resilient scheduling frameworks for agriculture and related operations management domains.

Title: Robust qualification management in semiconductor manufacturing
Authors: Antoine Perraudat, Abdelkrim Yelles-Chaouche, Stéphane Dauzère-Pérès
Abstract: This paper studies a tactical/strategic (machine, operation) qualification management problem in semiconductor manufacturing systems, where demand uncertainty is a significant factor. To be eligible to process an operation on wafers, a machine must be qualified to ensure yield and quality requirements. Qualifying a machine for a specific operation is usually a time-consuming and costly process. Given a set of parallel non-identical machines in the work center of a semiconductor manufacturing facility, the problem solved in this paper consists in minimizing the combined cost of qualification and lost sales while considering demand uncertainty. New robust models and solution approaches are proposed. First, a deterministic mixed-integer linear program is introduced. Then, the demand uncertainty is modeled using a polyhedral uncertainty set. This modeling is used to define a static and affinely adjustable robust reformulations of the deterministic model. Subsequently, a two-stage solution approach, based on a column-and-constraint generation approach, is proposed. The different models and approaches are discussed and compared, notably through computational experiments on industrial data from a semiconductor manufacturer. The limits of the different solution approaches are also discussed, and recommendations are provided. The numerical results show that coping with demand uncertainty in semiconductor manufacturing does not require a large number of qualifications, but that it is critical to determine the relevant ones.

Title: Exact approach to joint order acceptance and non-permutation flow shop scheduling via logic-based benders decomposition
Authors: Gongjie Xu, Naiqi Wu, Yan Qiao, Siwei Zhang
Affiliations: Institute of Systems Engineering and Collaborative Laboratory for Intelligent Science and Systems, Macau University of Science and Technology

Title: Control or co-creation: exploring ecosystem configurations based on power dynamics and sustainability focus
Authors: Taylan Kilinc, Wiebke Reim
Affiliations: Luleå University of Technology

Title: Correction
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The Value of an Attorney: Collateral Source Rule Changes as an Invalid Instrument
Authors: Eric Helland, Jungmo Yoon
Affiliations: Robert Day School of Economics and Finance Claremont McKenna College Claremont California USA; College of Economics and Finance Hanyang University Seoul Korea
Abstract: ABSTRACT The value of lawyers to their clients is notoriously difficult to estimate because of endogeneity. We utilize modifications to the collateral source (CS) rule that require reducing trial awards by the amount of payments from first‐party insurance as an instrument for hiring a lawyer. The problem with our instrument is that modifications to the CS rule have a direct effect on recovery and, hence, violate the exclusion restriction required for a valid instrument. We develop a new identification and estimation method that uses CS rule changes as an invalid instrument and bounds the impact of lawyers. We find that our estimated impact's upper and lower bounds are lower than estimates that do not correct for endogeneity. Our estimates of the impact of lawyers on total payment are consistently negative, although not precise enough to claim statistical significance. The upper bound of the effect of hiring a lawyer on total payment received is negative after fees in our preferred specification. This suggests that even in the most optimistic scenario, lawyers appear to reduce total recovery.

Title: A privacy-preserving distributed credit evaluation model based on blockchain
Authors: Xianhua Kuang, Chaoqun Ma, Konstantinos N. Baltas, Shiyu Jia, Yi-Shuai Ren
Abstract: Multi-source data fusion is crucial for improving the predictive performance of credit evaluation models. However, cross-organizational collaborative modeling faces challenges such as data privacy breaches, difficulty in verifying computational results, and a lack of transparency and auditability in the collaboration process. To address collaborative logistic regression modeling with vertically distributed data, this paper proposes a privacy-preserving method based on matrix transformation and further designs a trusted collaborative modeling mechanism integrating blockchain and trusted execution environment technologies. The results indicate that the proposed privacy-preserving method achieves lossless model accuracy while safeguarding data privacy and resisting collusion attacks. This method is more efficient for training and requires less communication than most federated learning schemes. The designed decentralized collaborative modeling mechanism provides a trust foundation for multiple parties without relying on a centralized trusted third party, ensuring the reliability of model results and enabling traceability and auditability throughout the entire collaborative modeling process.

Title: Benchmarking adaptive pricing policies for Mississippi River container-on-barge service
Authors: Alex Carroll
Abstract: Ports increasingly compete on the performance of their hinterland connections, where inland waterway transport (IWT) can provide high-capacity, lower-emission container flows but faces commercial uncertainty driven by volatile demand and shared asset constraints. This paper studies weekly pricing for an anonymized industry-proposed “fast barge” service serving five inland corridors on the Mississippi River system. We formulate a finite-horizon Markov decision process with stochastic, price-sensitive demand, corridor limits, and a shared fleet-hours allocation problem. Shipment manifests calibrate seasonality but contain no transaction prices, so reference tariffs and elasticities are explicit modeling assumptions. We compare transparent tariff, myopic, one-period, and shadow-price policies with proximal policy optimization (PPO), advantage actor–critic (A2C), and soft actor–critic (SAC), using common continuous actions, ten training seeds, and 200 paired evaluation seeds. A loose reference case remains price-boundary driven. A prespecified 300-hour benchmark has an interior unconstrained price and a positive deterministic capacity dual in 48.1% of weeks. In final evaluation, PPO and SAC improve on the validation-selected transparent benchmark by 0.089% (USD 51,800/year) and 0.362% (USD 211,100/year), respectively, with positive hierarchical intervals. Neither meets the prespecified 0.5% primary adoption screen, and the transparent benchmark retains 99.6% of SAC’s mean profit. The economic case for RL is therefore conditional on whether its annualized implementation and governance costs fall below the measured incremental value, rather than supporting an unconditional replacement recommendation.

Title: Randomized Subspace Gradient Method for Constrained Optimization
Authors: Ryota Nozawa, Pierre-Louis Poirion, Akiko Takeda
Affiliations: Graduate School of Information Science and Technology, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan; Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo 103-0027, Japan; and Center for Advanced Intelligence Project, RIKEN, Tokyo 103-0027, Japan
Abstract: We propose randomized subspace gradient methods for high-dimensional constrained optimization. Whereas there are related studies on unconstrained optimization problems, there are relatively few for constrained optimization problems because of the difficulty of handling constraints. Our algorithms project gradient vectors onto a subspace that is a random projection of the subspace spanned by the gradients of active constraints. We determine the worst case iteration complexity under linear and nonlinear settings and theoretically confirm that our algorithms can take a larger step size than their deterministic counterpart. From the advantages of taking longer steps and randomized subspace gradients, we show that our algorithms can be especially time-efficient when gradients are expensive to obtain. Furthermore, they perform well in cases in which gradients could not be obtained directly, and instead, gradients are obtained using directional derivatives. Funding: This work was partially supported by JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research(B) [JP23H03351] and JST CREST [Grant JPMJCR24Q2].

Title: Reassessing REDD+ project effectiveness using multiple synthetic control methods: Evidence on additionality and location bias in the Brazilian Amazon
Authors: Etienne Wijler, Marina Friedrich, Thales A.P. West
Abstract: This study re-evaluates the impacts of the twelve voluntary REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and forest Degradation, plus other forest-related activities) projects in the Brazilian Amazon from West et al. (2020) on avoided deforestation and carbon credit generation. Although these initiatives are widely regarded as important tools for climate change mitigation, their effectiveness has come under increasing scrutiny. To shed light on this issue, we employ three causal inference methods—the original synthetic control method (SCM), Augmented SCM (ASCM), and Bayesian SCM (BSCM)—to construct counterfactual scenarios for the REDD+ projects and estimate their impact on avoided deforestation. Next to placebo tests, we employ conformal inference to evaluate statistical significance. In addition, we investigate adverse selection by developing two measures of deforestation threat and comparing the distribution of these between projects and control areas. Our objectives are three-fold: to compare the performance of the three methods, evaluate the robustness of the results across them, and to analyze potential location bias using our deforestation threat measures. Our findings corroborate the mounting literature indicating that most REDD+ projects overstate their climate impacts, consequently claiming more carbon credits than warranted. Moreover, the analysis reveals that most projects did not significantly reduce deforestation, with several more closely associated with increases in post-intervention deforestation than with decreases. Our findings also indicate that REDD+ projects are disproportionately located in areas facing relatively low deforestation pressure. These results highlight the need for more rigorous and transparent impact assessments of REDD+ projects to strengthen the credibility of carbon offsetting and have important implications for the integration of voluntary projects into regulated carbon markets under the Paris Agreement.

Title: Driving impact? How imperfect displacement shapes heterogeneous rebound in carsharing
Authors: Tamar Meshulam, Jozef Cossey, David Font Vivanco, Tamar Makov
Abstract: Green technologies, products, and services, such as carsharing, are commonly promoted as pathways to lower environmental impacts by increasing efficiency. Yet rebound effects, behavioral and economic responses to improved efficiency, may erode these environmental impact reductions. Many rebound studies assume perfect displacement, where a new technology or mode of service provision fully replaces an existing service on a one-to-one basis. While analytically convenient, this assumption overlooks real-world complexity and consumer heterogeneity. Using survey data from nearly 4500 Belgian carsharing users, we compare rebound estimates under perfect displacement with those based on reported shifts in mobility. Under the perfect displacement assumption, we find a 53% rebound effect. When accounting for imperfect displacement, however, rebound effects vary widely across users. While median effects remain positive (20%–46%), at the individual level rebound effects range from substantial net benefits to strong rebound (5th–95th percentile: −331% to 147%). A cluster analysis further reveals distinct user groups with systematically different impacts, underscoring that displacement patterns vary not only in scale but also in direction. These findings suggest that carsharing's environmental impact is highly user-dependent, and that relying on a single aggregate estimate may mask critical behavioral variations. As this case study demonstrates, accounting for imperfect displacement in rebound analysis is critical for advancing theory and for tailoring more effective policy interventions.

Title: Can natural capital accounting bring accountability for nature?
Authors: Rowan Alden Hull, Maree Fudge, Claire A. Horner, Leon A. Barmuta, Menna E. Jones, Elizabeth Pinkard, Emma tebrakunna country and Lee, Peat Leith
Abstract: With increasing global ecosystem degradation, new ways of governing the relationship between people and nature are needed. As Western societies increasingly turn to the emerging practice of Natural Capital Accounting (NCA), this is a critical time to consider its institutional role. In this paper we consider the effectiveness of NCA in bringing accountability for nature. This study theorises the link between accountability and NCA practice and explores this link empirically through quantitative and qualitative analyses of four methods of practice - the Capitals Coalition, Integrated Reporting, the System of Environmental Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting, and Accounting for Nature®. The study found that NCA methods employ a range of technical mechanisms for delivering accountability, including data processes, external audit, and participation of, and transparency with, stakeholders; however, there were substantial limitations for their effectiveness. Our results highlight five challenges for NCA in delivering accountability for nature, underpinned by the broader governance environment in which this institution operates. We discuss governance options for bringing accountability for nature both with, and without, NCA. The findings of this study will help academics and policy makers to design institutional arrangements which are fit-for-purpose for bringing accountability for nature.

Title: Benefit-principle accounting of CO₂ emissions in the global textile and clothing value chain
Authors: Lila Ballav Bhusal
Abstract: Existing emission accounting frameworks assign CO₂ responsibility to producers or final consumers but do not identify factor-provider beneficiaries within bilateral trade flows. This study extends benefit-principle emissions (BPE) accounting by introducing a trade-pattern decomposition for the global textile and clothing (T&C) value chain. Using the multi-regional input-output table, the framework distinguishes producers, factor providers, final producers, and consumers, and separates final-goods, intermediate, and global value chain (GVC) trade. Consumer economies retain the largest single shares of their own T&C BPE. Developed-economy providers generally receive BPE above the consumption-based emissions (CBE) in their economies, while production-linked developing providers fall below. Bangladesh, the world's second-largest garment exporter, accounts for only 0.13% of EU-27 consumer T&C BPE despite its assembly role. Foreign factor-provider attribution rises in GVC-related trade, where assembly economies face higher CO₂ per dollar of factor-provider value added than in direct final-goods trade. Although final demand targets T&C products, emitted BPE concentrates in electricity, gas, and water, separating the consumer product from the emitting sector. Aggregate BPE-CBE ratios sit near parity for Bangladesh and selected developing-country pairs, while GVC-specific BPE exceeds CBE in most bilateral pairs. Bangladesh's economy-wide BPE exceeds its territorial emissions by 19%, showing that sectoral value capture and economy-wide balances can classify the same economy differently. Border carbon instruments based only on emission location or final-product origin can place compliance costs on actors capturing limited factor-provider benefit. Benefit-principle metrics give an additional diagnostic for border adjustment design, product-level disclosure, revenue recycling, and climate finance allocation.

Title: Livestock ownership and child nutrition: Empirical evidence from East Africa
Authors: Astewale Bimr Melaku, Bethelhem Legesse Debela
Abstract: Livestock keeping constitutes an integral component of smallholder livelihoods in developing countries, yet its linkages to child nutrition outcomes remain understudied. In this paper, we explore the relationship between ownership of different species of livestock and nutritional status of children using largescale cross-country household survey panel data from Ethiopia, Tanzania and Uganda, comprising over 19,000 child-year observations. We find that livestock ownership is positively associated with child height-for-age z-score (HAZ), with some variations across countries. Analyses of potential mechanisms reveal that the positive relationship between livestock ownership and child nutrition is channeled through increased household animal source food consumption, income, and food availability during food shortages. Further heterogeneity analyses show that the relationship varies widely across household income groups, agroecological and farming system classifications.

Title: Protected areas: questioning the development-conservation system. A socio-political-economic and ecological framework for a bottom-up approach
Authors: Mireille Razafindrakoto, François Roubaud, Florent Bédécarrats, Stéphanie M. Carrière, Emmanuel Pannier
Abstract: Despite repeated calls for urgent action to address biodiversity loss, the resounding verdict is that most conservation policies, in particular their main policy measure, Protected Areas (PAs), have failed to halt environmental degradation and achieve meaningful social outcomes. Yet, the international community has committed to extending PA coverage to 30% of the planet by 2030, and with one-third of the Global South’s population already living in or near a PA, this proportion is set to become a majority. In view of this, the current practice, which is supposed to promote sustainable development but is problematic, consists of juxtaposing socioeconomic policies and environmental policies, often regarded as mutually antagonistic, without considering a comprehensive view of governance issues. This article reviews the impact of PAs on biodiversity and the populations’ living conditions and identifies the knowledge gaps, before looking into why biodiversity conservation has been prioritised, inconclusively, to the detriment of local sociopolitical and economic dynamics and why the narrow principle of ‘inclusive governance’, more words than deeds, falls far short of the mark. The traditional approach, which is blind to the fact that conservation and development objectives are embedded within power relations and a broader sociopolitical dynamic, dominated by extractivist and capitalist logic, should be challenged. We propose a novel analytical framework with an operational methodological approach grounded in critical political ecology in order to take a bottom-up approach rooted in a territory and improve our understanding of the complex interactions between local socioecological, socioeconomic and sociopolitical concerns. This approach will help put in place more effective and inclusive policies consistent with local livelihoods, ways of life, equity and justice.

Title: The politics of environmental peacebuilding: global agendas, advocacy networks, and domestic policy arenas
Authors: Jacobo Grajales, Meryam El Bouhati, Benjamin Lévy, Toni-Giovanni Pegurri
Abstract: This article examines how environmental conflict narratives emerge and are used in peacebuilding policies. It advocates for a multi-level perspective that systematically connects global intervention agendas to political struggles in domestic policy arenas. Through a comparative analysis of four case studies—Liberia, Colombia, Côte d’Ivoire, and Lebanon—it investigates how environmental considerations are framed as security issues and incorporated into peacebuilding agendas. It explores how actors construct causal stories linking environmental issues to conflict, and how these narratives shape policy design, implementation, and resistance to change. It highlights how environmental conflict narratives are shaped by security concerns and donor-recipient relationships. While such narratives can support policy change by providing advocacy coalitions with a platform, their effects vary significantly depending on the domestic political context. This article contributes to environmental peacebuilding research by highlighting the strategic and contested nature of how environmental concerns enter peacebuilding discourse and practice.

Title: Income inequality as a barrier to the CO2-reducing potential of public investment: evidence from Latin America
Authors: Tainari Taioka, Marina da Silva Sanches, Gilberto Tadeu Lima
Abstract: This paper aims to empirically analyze the association between public investment and carbon emissions relative to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for a panel of Latin American countries from 1994 to 2019. Given that reduced income inequality can enhance the effectiveness of environmental policies, the estimations are carried out under two income inequality regimes: higher and lower. A nonlinear Local Projections model with a threshold is employed, dividing the sample into two groups based on the Gini index. The results show that, during periods of relatively low income inequality, the estimated response of carbon-intensity growth to changes in public investment is negative over time. In contrast, under conditions of relatively high income inequality, the estimated association is not statistically significant at the 10% level. Our estimates suggest that a 10% increase in public investments is associated with an approximately 4.40% reduction in the growth rate of carbon intensity in the low-inequality regime, as measured by the Gini index, until the fourth year following the increase in public investment. These empirical findings support existing literature highlighting the positive association between income inequality and carbon emissions.

Title: Gender, risk aversion, and panic withdrawal in bank runs: Experimental evidence
Authors: Shaen Corbet, David Staunton, Steven Tucker
Abstract: Despite extensive evidence that women are more risk-averse than men, experimental bank run studies do not find consistent gender differentials across withdrawal behavior. We examine this puzzle using data from an incentivized laboratory experiment based on a two-bank Diamond–Dybvig game, with elicited risk preferences and variation in the banks’ portfolio-transparency policies. Results indicate that women are not more likely than men to withdraw early despite exhibiting greater risk aversion. We provide suggestive evidence that risk tolerance is related to beliefs about counterpart behavior among women while the corresponding relationship among men is small. Our findings indicate that beliefs about counterpart behavior, rather than risk preferences alone, are the dominant driver of withdrawal, and that the absence of gender differentials in the prior literature is a predictable consequence of effect size rather than evidence against a risk channel.

Title: Neutralizing hidden green protectionism: The efficiency of national treatment with internal taxes
Authors: Yaqiong Lin

Title: Dynamic resource allocation with karma: An experimental study
Authors: Ezzat Elokda, Saverio Bolognani, Florian Dörfler, Heinrich H. Nax
Abstract: We perform a behavioral experiment of karma, a class of mechanisms for repeated resource allocation with attractive fairness and efficiency properties, in theory. Individuals in these mechanisms bid non-tradable credits that flow from resource consumers to yielders, like karma. Human subjects recruited on Amazon MTurk are repeatedly and randomly paired to bid karma according to time-varying and stochastic individual preferences or urgency to acquire resources. Treatments varied in the dynamic urgency process (frequent moderate urgency versus sporadic high urgency) and the richness of the bidding scheme (binary versus full range). Results are benchmarked against random allocation, and karma achieves a (almost) Pareto improvement over random, despite the MTurk subjects deviating significantly from the theoretically optimal Nash bidding policy. Maximum improvement is attained by subjects that deviate from Nash by up to one karma bid unit on average, and positive improvement is attained with average deviations of up to 3-4 bid units. These findings hold across all treatments, among which no significant differences are found, with the exception of the sporadic high urgency process with binary bidding treatment being (weakly) favorable over others. These results offer behaviorally robust lower bounds for the expected performance of karma in human populations. They also provide guidance for future testing and implementation of karma mechanisms in the real world.

Title: The latency location-or-routing problem
Authors: Alan Osorio-Mora, Eduardo Álvarez-Miranda, Francisco Saldanha-da-Gama
Abstract: This paper introduces the latency location-or-routing problem (LLoRP); a variant of the location-or-routing problem (LoRP) and an extension of the latency location-routing problem. The LLoRP consists of selecting (opening) a set of depots to serve a set of customers, which can be visited as part of routes also to be decided. The maximum number of depots to open is assumed to be exogenous. For the customers lying within a certain coverage range from an open depot, direct service is an alternative. A set of capacitated homogeneous vehicles is available to be assigned to the selected depots as needed. The goal is to minimize the sum of the waiting times of the customers for being served (latency). Several customer-centric applications of the LLoRP are discussed. Three mixed-integer-linear-programming formulations are developed and two lower bounds on the optimal latency value are devised. A tradeoff between LLoRP and LoRP is considered within a bi-objective modeling framework that is tackled using the ε − constrained method. An outcome of this analysis are compact formulations for the standard LoRP. This type of model is in itself a novelty for that problem. Finally, extensive computational results are discussed to assess the relevance of the LLoRP and the efficacy of the models and bounds proposed. The results highlight multiple distinguishing features of the LLoRP while identifying the most promising optimization models to use. They also provide strong evidence for the relevance of looking into tradeoff solutions when a cost-oriented objective becomes of interest in addition to latency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Impacts of subway line extension on economic vitality and social cohesion: Evidence from Boston’s Green Line Extension through a double machine learning DID approach
Authors: Xinyi Huang, Yunhan Zheng, Dingyi Zhuang, Yuebing Liang, Jinhua Zhao
Abstract: Public transit has long been viewed as a great equalizer in urban life, expected to break down barriers among social groups and stimulate economic growth. However, empirical evidence on both dimensions remains limited to aggregated proxies such as property values, which may not capture actual and timely behavioral changes, particularly in the post-pandemic context. The Green Line Extension (GLX) in Somerville, Boston Metropolitan Area, which opened in December 2022, provides a natural experiment to examine these relationships. We analyze over 300,000 daily observations of points of interest (POIs) across three cities over 438 consecutive days, measuring economic vitality through daily visit counts and social cohesion through the income segregation of venue visitors. These two outcomes have rarely been studied together using granular behavioral data in the transit literature. We employ a double/debiased machine learning difference-in-differences (DMLDID) approach, which uses data-adaptive estimation to handle the nonlinear covariate-outcome relationships, where traditional linear DID would be misspecified. Our findings reveal a decoupling between the two outcomes. GLX significantly enhanced economic vitality, increasing average daily visits by approximately 23% per POI (95% CI: 13.4%–32.7%). The effects were strongest in retail trade and food service sectors. By contrast, its impact on income segregation at nearby venues was statistically insignificant, challenging the assumption that improved physical connectivity automatically promotes social mixing. The economic effects vary across sectors, while social cohesion effects are statistically insignificant in every sector examined, indicating that this decoupling holds across the sectoral composition of our study area rather than being confined to particular venue types. These findings suggest that, in this short- to mid-term post-pandemic window, transit investment alone did not advance social mixing, pointing to a potential role for complementary interventions alongside infrastructure expansion.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Are there similarities between the spatial patterns of autonomous and human-driven vehicle crashes? Evidence from a data-driven case study in California
Authors: Tianyi Chen, Kaidi Yang
Abstract: Comparisons between autonomous vehicles (AVs) and human-driven vehicles (HDVs) have been widely adopted as a means of assessing AV safety. This study provides a new data-driven perspective for such comparison-based assessments by quantitatively measuring the similarity between the spatial patterns of AV and HDV crashes. Using crash records of both vehicle types as inputs, the proposed method comprises three main steps: (1) reconstruction of investigated road network for in the absence of publicly disclosed AV operational routes; (2) crash hotspot identification using Network Kernel Density Estimation (NKDE); and (3) quantitative spatial similarity analysis based on multiple similarity indicators. The method is applied to case studies in two urban areas in California, San Francisco and the Silicon Valley area, across three time periods: 2016–2018, 2019–2021, and 2022–2024. The results reveal three key findings. First, the spatial patterns of AV crashes gradually become more similar to those of HDV crashes over time. Second, AV crash spatial patterns exhibit substantially greater temporal variability than their HDV counterparts. Third, notable differences are observed between the two urban areas in terms of the spatiotemporal patterns of vehicle crashes. These findings are plausibly attributable to the expanding scale and spatial coverage of AV operations, as well as ongoing advances in human-like AV control and decision-making mechanisms over time. This study provides practical insights for urban traffic management and AV manufacturers by improving understanding of how AV crash risks evolve relative to conventional traffic systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A planning framework for enhancing power supply resilience from a climate risk perspective: evidence from the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region in China
Authors: Bowen Yi, Yulu Ji, Ying Fan
Abstract: Climate change is making extreme weather increasingly consequential for power systems, yet the economic implications of climate resilience under deep decarbonization pathways remain poorly quantified. This study develops an integrated climate stress-informed planning framework that links meteorological hazards, coupled supply-demand impacts, and long-term capacity investment, and applies it to China's Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. Using meteorological records from 1980 to 2023, we construct four extreme-weather scenarios, including extreme cold, extreme heat, stagnation, and overcast, and further develop a compound extreme-weather scenario to capture combined climate stresses. These scenarios are embedded into a multi-stage generation-transmission expansion model with hourly dispatch over 2035–2055. Three findings emerge. First, short-duration extreme-weather events can substantially reshape long-term capacity portfolios, as the reliability of high-renewable systems is increasingly determined by a small number of critical hours rather than average conditions. Second, the nature of climate resilience evolves along the decarbonization pathway: early-stage impacts are dominated by demand-side operational adjustments, while later-stage resilience increasingly depends on renewable and storage investment, operational flexibility, and the spatial reallocation of capacity across regions. Third, interprovincial transmission undergoes functional differentiation, shifting from primarily continuous energy delivery toward complementary roles in energy supply and capacity support under climate stress. These findings highlight the importance of coordinated deployment of renewable resources, storage, and transmission infrastructure to maintain power system resilience during deep decarbonization.

Title: Reducing carbon emission by optimizing container liner fleet deployment and sailing speed
Authors: Siqi Yuan, Jian Gang Jin, Xiangdong Xu
Abstract: Facing stringent environmental regulations and an aging fleet, container liner shipping companies face mounting pressure to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. This paper optimizes tactical fleet deployment and sailing speed by explicitly incorporating vessel heterogeneity. A mixed integer nonlinear programming model is formulated, and a Velocity-Discretization-Based Dynamic Algorithm is developed to improve computational efficiency. Practical fleet adjustment constraints are further considered to evaluate the achievable benefits under limited vessel redeployment. Numerical experiments based on real-world operational data demonstrate that considering vessel heterogeneity and jointly optimizing deployment and speed can significantly reduce fuel consumption and CO 2 emissions. The proposed algorithm achieves reliable solutions with substantially shorter computational time than the direct solution, providing a practical decision-support tool for sustainable liner shipping operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Dynamic decarbonization pathways for inland shipping under energy system and policy uncertainties
Authors: Jun Yuan, Yuwei Zhang, Jian Gang Jin, Victor Nian, Xunpeng Shi
Abstract: Inland shipping decarbonization requires coordinated changes in fleets, fuels, infrastructure, and policy that static life cycle assessments cannot capture. This study develops a framework coupling Power-to-X pathways, dynamic hybrid life cycle assessment, a fleet digital twin, and multi-objective optimization. Applied to 2,100 weighted representative vessel records in the Yangtze River Delta from 2025 to 2050 under four policy scenarios, the selected integrated policy knee solution reduces diesel from 99.0% to 15.5% of fleet shaft energy demand. Battery electricity becomes the largest low-carbon pathway (30.3%), followed by hydrogen (22.1%), e-methanol (16.4%), and ammonia (15.6%). Cumulative life cycle emissions are 298.8 Mt CO 2 -eq, 10.4% below business as usual, while net present resource cost is 166.3 billion 2025 USD. Deep inland shipping decarbonization is feasible but back-loaded and depends on coordinated fleet renewal, infrastructure deployment, and fuel diversification.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Environmental impacts of development of railways in a road dominated infrastructure
Authors: Vinicius Donisete Lima Rodrigues Goulart, William Leles de Souza Costa, Rodrigo Affonso de Albuquerque Nóbrega
Abstract: Railway infrastructure plays a pivotal role in economic development, with well-documented environmental implications. However, emerging global agreements, and environmental policies introduce new dimensions that must be considered. The expansion of Brazil’s railway network has the potential to transform landscapes. This study evaluates the environmental effects of railway expansion, focusing on landcover conversion risk driven by proximity to infrastructure, population density, and agricultural potential. Spatial analysis and Random Forest modelling identified population and proximity to railways as the strongest contributors to landcover conversion risk revealing relevant environmental impacts, with overlap between estimated conversion risk and ecologically sensitive regions, and threatened species. While scenario-specific analyses highlight variations in potential impacts, the primary finding is: railways function as major drivers of landscape transformation, amplifying anthropogenic pressures on natural habitats. These results underscore the urgent need for proactive conservation planning to mitigate ecological impacts and ensure that infrastructure development aligns with global biodiversity goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Does Goliath help David? Anchor firms and startup clusters
Authors: Rahul R. Gupta
Abstract: Does attracting a “Goliath” firm to a county anchor the growth of regional industry clusters? Matching a hand-collected dataset of major corporate site selection contests to restricted-use U.S. Census microdata, I show that winning a Million Dollar Plant (MDP) generates 2515 net supply chain jobs in the first four years after announcement, declining to 1622 in the subsequent four years. Over the last four years of the panel between four and seven years after the MDP is announced, startups remain the largest contributor to job gains at 1694 jobs, more than offsetting a decline among other incumbents (-61% of the net total), with local incumbents (41%), and affiliated firms (15%) also contributing positively. Post-announcement startups are more numerous but smaller and slower-growing than comparable cohorts in runner-up counties. The two main sources of job creation draw on distinct segments of the local labor market: relative to those in finalist counties, startups in winning counties rely disproportionately on immigrant workers whereas local incumbents employ more local workers, and neither shows evidence of worker flows from the MDP’s corporate network.

Title: Opportunistic Upskilling in European Labour Markets—Evidence From a Wide Replication
Authors: Anil Yadav, John McHale, Jefferson R. B. Galetti
Affiliations: Central Bank of Ireland Ireland; University of Galway Ireland
Abstract: ABSTRACT We build on Modestino et al., who analysed “opportunistic upskilling” during the 2007 recession in the US, by extending their approach to European labour markets following recent economic shocks. Using a comprehensive dataset of online job postings (2019–2023) and an instrumental variable approach leveraging Ukrainian refugee inflows, we find that increases in labour supply have a significant positive effect on both education and experience requirements. Our findings reinforce the idea that employers opportunistically upskill labour demand in different but challenging macroeconomic contexts. The identification of such patterns, however, depends on the presence of a plausibly exogenous shock to labour markets.

Title: Multivariate Trend Inflation in the United States and the Euro Area
Authors: Max‐Sebastian Dovì
Affiliations: International Monetary Fund Washington DC USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT I provide a precision‐sampler‐based replication of the multivariate unobserved component stochastic volatility outlier‐adjusted model of Stock and Watson (2016) applied to inflation in the United States and the Euro Area (EA). I find a substantial post‐2020 increase in trend inflation for both the United States and the EA, and estimate end‐2024 trend inflation at 2.3 and 2.0 percent, respectively.

Title: Identifying Peer Effects in Networks with Unobserved Effort and Isolated Students
Authors: Aristide Houndetoungan, Cristelle Kouame, Michael Vlassopoulos
Affiliations: Department of Economics Laval University Quebec Canada; Education and Skills World Bank Group Washington DC USA; University of Southampton Southampton UK; Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) London UK; IZA@LISER Network, Esch‐sur‐Alzette/Belval Luxembourg
Abstract: ABSTRACT Peer influence on effort devoted to some activity is often studied when effort is unobserved, and the researcher instead observes an outcome that combines effort with other shocks. For instance, in education, achievement measures such as GPA reflect both effort and idiosyncratic GPA shocks. We propose an alternative approach that circumvents this approximation. Our framework distinguishes unobserved shocks to GPA that do not affect effort from preference shocks that do affect effort levels. We show that peer effects estimates obtained using our approach can differ significantly from classical estimates (where effort is approximated) if the network includes isolated students. Applying our approach to data on high school students in the United States, we find that peer effect estimates relying on GPA as a proxy for effort are 40% lower than those obtained using our approach.

Title: Fast Likelihood‐Free Parameter Estimation for Lévy Processes
Authors: Nicolas Coloma, William Kleiber
Affiliations: Department of Applied Mathematics University of Colorado Boulder Colorado USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Lévy processes are widely used in financial modeling due to their ability to capture discontinuities and heavy tails, which are common in high‐frequency asset return data. However, parameter estimation remains a challenge when associated likelihoods are unavailable or costly to compute. We propose a fast and accurate method for Lévy parameter estimation using the neural Bayes estimation (NBE) framework—a simulation‐based, likelihood‐free approach that leverages permutation‐invariant neural networks to approximate Bayes estimators. We contribute new theoretical results, showing that NBE results in consistent estimators whose risk converges to that of the Bayes estimator under mild conditions. Moreover, through extensive simulations across several Lévy models, we show that NBE outperforms traditional methods in both accuracy and runtime, while also enabling two complementary approaches to uncertainty quantification. We illustrate our approach on a challenging high‐frequency cryptocurrency return dataset, where the method captures evolving parameter dynamics and delivers reliable and interpretable inference at a fraction of the computational cost of traditional methods. We investigate nearly a decade of high‐frequency Bitcoin returns, requiring less than one minute to estimate parameters under the proposed approach.

Title: Housing Supply Elasticities: A Structural Vector Autoregression Approach
Authors: Wesley A. Miller, Anthony W. Orlando, Christian L. Redfearn
Affiliations: University of Southern California Los Angeles California USA; California State Polytechnic University Pomona California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the first time‐varying, county‐level index of housing supply elasticities across the United States, using a structural vector autoregression model with sign restrictions to identify the effect of a positive demand shock. This index reveals four features of the supply curve in different local housing markets. First, supply elasticities are low, on average, generating faster price growth than housing unit growth for most of the country. Second, there is significant variation in elasticities across counties, both urban and rural. Third, elasticities have declined in more counties than they have risen over time, particularly in large urban markets. Fourth, these new estimates predict housing quantity growth better than previous models in the literature.

Title: A Smooth Specification Test for the Propensity Score
Authors: Shiyao Huang, Xiaojun Song
Affiliations: Department of Business Statistics and Econometrics Guanghua School of Management, Peking University Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes a simple smooth specification test for the propensity score in the spirit of Neyman (1937). We derive a particular restriction on the propensity score and construct the specification test based on it. Using the density‐weighting method, we transform the original specification testing problem into a test of the joint significance of the generalized Fourier coefficients. We propose a novel projection method to eliminate the parameter estimation effect arising from estimating unknown nuisance parameters. The proposed test is shown to follow a standard distribution under the null hypothesis and to possess nontrivial asymptotic power against local alternatives that converge to the null at the parametric rate , where is the sample size. To enhance the practical applicability of the procedure, we further introduce a data‐driven selection method for determining the testing order, enabling automatic selection based on the observed data. Compared to existing methods, our test does not suffer from the “curse of dimensionality” faced by Shaikh et al. (2009); at the same time, our test is both asymptotically pivotal and more computationally efficient than that of Sant'Anna and Song (2019). Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed test yields satisfactory empirical size and power. Compared with previous tests, our test exhibits comparable overall performance and delivers clear improvements in some cases, especially for high‐frequency alternatives. Two empirical applications further illustrate the practical applicability of our proposal, examining propensity score specifications in the Soviet 156 Program and the US Job Corps Program.

Title: Labor Market Institutions, Fiscal Multipliers, and Macroeconomic Volatility
Authors: Maximilian Boeck, Jesús Crespo Cuaresma, Christian Glocker
Affiliations: Vienna University of Economics and Business Vienna Austria; Friedrich‐Alexander University Erlangen‐Nuremberg Nuremberg Germany; Wittgenstein Centre for Demography and Global Human Capital (IIASA, ÖAW, UniVie) Vienna Austria; Austrian Institute of Economic Research (WIFO) Vienna Austria; CESifo Munich Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT How do labor market institutions shape the transmission of government spending shocks and macroeconomic volatility? We develop a theoretical model in which labor market institutions affect fiscal transmission through their effect on wage rigidity, job separation, and matching frictions. We estimate an interacted panel vector autoregressive model for 16 OECD economies and study how macroeconomic responses to government spending shocks vary with institutional labor market characteristics. In line with our theoretical predictions, we show that institutions that stabilize employment and wages tend to reduce output volatility and attenuate the response of output and employment to government spending shocks.

Title: Conditional Randomization Tests for the Specification of Interference Structure
Authors: Tadao Hoshino, Takahide Yanagi
Affiliations: School of Political Science and Economics Waseda University Shinjuku‐ku Japan; Graduate School of Economics Kyoto University Sakyo Japan
Abstract: ABSTRACT This study proposes specification tests for interference structure in causal inference with spillovers. We focus on experimental settings in which the treatment assignment mechanism is known. To test whether a given exposure mapping adequately summarizes the true interference structure, we develop conditional randomization tests by utilizing the hierarchical relationship between the null and alternative exposure mappings. When there are multiple candidate exposure mappings of interest, we propose a sequential specification testing procedure that controls the false discovery rate. Through extensive simulation exercises, we demonstrate that our tests have desirable size properties and satisfactory power. To illustrate the proposed methods, we revisit two existing social network experiments: One on farmers' insurance adoption and another on anti‐conflict education programs.

Title: Fiscal Policy Regimes in Resource‐Rich Economies
Authors: Hilde C. Bjørnland, Roberto Casarin, Marco Lorusso, Francesco Ravazzolo
Affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School Oslo Norway; Norges Bank Oslo Norway; CAMA Canberra Australia; Ca' Foscari University Venice Venice Italy; Department of Political Science University of Perugia Perugia Italy; Newcastle University Business School Newcastle upon Tyne UK; Free University of Bozen‐Bolzano Bolzano Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT We analyse fiscal policy in resource‐rich economies using a novel Bayesian regime‐switching panel model. The identified regimes capture pro‐ or countercyclical fiscal behaviour by allowing regime‐specific shifts in the average fiscal stance, while the switches between the regimes have the interpretation of changes in fiscal policy. Applying the model to a panel of sixteen oil‐producing economies, we show that fiscal policy has alternated between a procyclical and countercyclical regime multiple times over the sample. Furthermore, we find that fiscal policy is more volatile in the procyclical regime and that the probability of being in the procyclical regime is higher for OPEC countries than for non‐OPEC countries. We also show that following either an increase or decrease in oil revenues, the growth in government expenditures is mostly increasing, suggesting an upward bias in expenditures in oil‐producing countries. These are new findings in the literature.

Title: Regularization of Synthetic Controls for Policy Evaluation
Authors: Yi‐Ting Chen
Affiliations: Department of Finance National Taiwan University Taipei Taiwan
Abstract: ABSTRACT We propose a unified framework for interpreting and comparing a broad class of synthetic control (SC) methods. Our framework is built on an analysis of a mean‐squared prediction error (MSPE) bound for the counterfactual predicted by a generic SC method, without imposing a specific outcome model. Using this framework, we develop a generalized SC method that provides a more comprehensive regularization of the MSPE bound than several existing SC methods. Through simulation studies and placebo analyses, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in predicting the counterfactual.

Title: Triply Robust Panel Estimators
Authors: Susan Athey, Guido Imbens, Zhaonan Qu, Davide Viviano
Affiliations: Stanford University Stanford USA; Columbia University New York USA; Harvard University Cambridge USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies estimation of causal effects in a panel data setting. We introduce a new estimator, the Triply Robust Panel (TROP) estimator, that combines a flexible model for the potential outcomes based on a low‐rank factor structure on top of a two‐way‐fixed effect specification, with unit weights intended to upweight units similar to the treated units and time weights intended to upweight time periods close to the treated time periods. We study the performance of the estimator in a set of simulations designed to closely match several commonly studied real data sets. We find that there is substantial variation in the performance of the estimators across the settings considered. The proposed estimator outperforms Two‐Way‐Fixed‐Effect (TWFE) or Difference‐In‐Differences (DID), Synthetic Control (SC), Matrix Completion (MC) and Synthetic‐Difference‐In‐Differences (SDID) estimators. We investigate what features of the data generating process lead to this superior performance and assess the relative importance of the three components of the proposed estimator. We have two recommendations. Our preferred strategy is that researchers use simulations closely matched to the data they are interested in, along the lines discussed in this paper, to investigate which estimators work well in their particular setting. A simpler approach is to use more robust estimators such as SDID or the new TROP estimator, which we find to substantially outperform TWFE/DID estimators in many empirically relevant settings.

Title: Estimation of Heterogeneous Panel Data Models With Mixed Sampling Frequencies
Authors: Haoran Li, Haoyang Li, Naifu Xiao, Yimin Yang
Affiliations: School of Applied Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; College of Economics and Management Nanjing Agricultural University Nanjing China; School of Public Finance and Taxation, Zhongnan University of Economics and Law Wuhan China; School of Finance Renmin University of China Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies heterogeneous mixed‐frequency panel data models, focusing on linear specifications that allow heterogeneity in both aggregation weights and slope coefficients. To address potential correlations between the heterogeneity and the covariates, we first show that, under additional normalization conditions, the mean‐group estimator delivers consistent and asymptotically normal slope estimates but biased weights estimators. As an alternative, we propose a correlated random effects estimator using a generalized Mundlak specification. We further discuss the implementation of these two estimators when covariates are observed at substantially higher sampling frequencies. Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to assess their finite‐sample properties. As an empirical illustration, we revisit the impact of temperature fluctuations on economic growth using the proposed framework.

Exploring the application of statistical and symbolic AI in supply chain risk management: a systematic literature review

Title: Optimising robotic pick-and-place operations and the application of RMS principles
Authors: Konstantinos Giannakos, Dimitrios Tsakoumis, Gregory Koronakos, Stathis Plitsos, Pavlos Eirinakis, Giulio Vivo, Angelo Nicotera

Affiliations: Liaoning University; XLRI–Xavier School of Management; Huaiyin Normal University
