Title: Outpatient appointment scheduling with decision‐dependent unpunctual arrivals
Authors: Shenghai Zhou, Shuo Pang, Haiyue Yu, Yushu Zeng
Affiliations: School of Business Central South University Changsha China; MOE Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory of Intelligent Governance for Complex Social Systems, Changsha, China; School of Management and Engineering Nanjing University Nanjing China; Shanghai Municipal Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine Shanghai University of Traditional Chinese Medicine Shanghai China; Antai College of Economics and Management Shanghai Jiao Tong University Shanghai China; Shanghai Municipal Hospital Disease Quality and Safety Sub‐Research Center Shanghai China; IESEG School of Management Lille France
Abstract: Abstract This article investigates appointment scheduling with stochastic service times (exogenous uncertainty) and schedule‐dependent unpunctual arrivals (endogenous uncertainty). First, our empirical study confirms that patients exhibit unpunctual behavior that varies across different age categories, visit types, and departments. More importantly, the empirical results document a statistically significant association between appointment time and patient unpunctuality. Second, we develop a mathematical formulation of the problem within a stochastic‐optimization framework considering schedule‐dependent uncertainties. The empirically observed appointment‐time‐specific arrival pattern is incorporated as a planning input. We confirm the differentiability property of the objective function and that its derivative is uniformly bounded. Building upon this result, we obtain an unbiased estimator of the gradient for the objective function, enabling us to design a gradient‐based optimization approach. To further enhance optimization performance and avoid local optima, we integrate gradient‐based local refinement with a curvature‐informed Variable Neighborhood Search (VNS) procedure, resulting in a hybrid solution method. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the computational efficiency of the proposed method and show that appointment‐time‐dependent unpunctuality can materially affect optimal schedule structures. In particular, different unpunctuality profiles can lead to distinct scheduling arrangements.

Title: Strategic inventory holdbacks: Managing waste and backlog in humanitarian operations
Authors: Nesim K. Erkip, Vera Tilson
Abstract: Humanitarian organizations distributing relief supplies must allocate limited inventory across multiple locations under uncertain demand, donation-constrained replenishment, heterogeneous lead times, and operational losses such as theft, displacement, and handling damage. Existing policies are often myopic and can perform poorly under variability or shifting supply conditions. We propose a non-myopic holdback heuristic for a two-echelon humanitarian distribution system in which warehouse inventory is strategically retained and released using a two-period decision rule. The policy leverages warehouse-level risk pooling and balances current allocations against future inventory availability under uncertainty. Using discrete-event simulation, we compare the heuristic against a no-holdback policy, a reactive “chase” policy, a loss-adjusted order-up-to policy, and a clairvoyant benchmark across a wide range of supply and demand conditions. Performance is evaluated using waste, fill rate, backlog age, and retailer-level fairness measures. Results show that the holdback policy substantially reduces waste while maintaining competitive service and fairness performance. In many settings, it also improves the balance of service across retailers. The approach is simple, data-light, and practical for humanitarian operations, and highlights the value of strategic inventory retention under uncertainty and operational loss risk.

Title: Dynamic subsidy design for coordinated emission abatement: A differential game with reference and delayed effects in low-carbon supply chain
Authors: Zixuan Hu, Yongguang Zhong, Tao Chu, Lei Wang, Jiaxin Zhang
Abstract: Within the low-carbon development paradigm, we examine the dynamic impacts of consumers' low-carbon reference effect and delayed effects of the manufacturer's product low-carbon level and the retailer's low-carbon publicity level on low-carbon goodwill. Through differential game modeling, we investigate long-term dynamic joint emission reduction and government subsidy strategies in a two-tier manufacturer–retailer supply chain. Specifically, by applying the maximum principle, we systematically compare member equilibrium strategies, discounted supply chain profits, and government input–output performance under the following three decision-making models: decentralized without cost-sharing, decentralized under the two-way cost-sharing contract, and centralized. Key findings indicate the following: (a) As consumers' low-carbon reference effect grows stronger, the government's optimal subsidy rate for manufacturer's low-carbon R&D increases accordingly; (b) Longer delays weaken the marginal input–output effectiveness of low-carbon subsidies, thereby reducing the government's optimal subsidy rates; (c) Delayed effects interact with the low-carbon reference effect. Changes in delay duration affect the dynamic updating of consumers' reference low-carbon levels, while the low-carbon reference effect makes the adverse impact of delays on the discounted supply chain profit more pronounced; (d) Under the joint influence of delayed effects and the low-carbon reference effect, centralized decision-making generates higher low-carbon effort levels but yields the lowest discounted supply chain profit, whereas the relative profits of decentralized models vary across delay intervals. From the perspective of government input–output performance, decentralized decision-making under the two-way cost-sharing contract performs best.

Title: Full in-house operation, partial outsourcing, or full outsourcing? A game-theoretic analysis of collaborative strategies for retired electric vehicle battery recycling
Authors: Jiumei Chen, Fenfang Sun, Manman Wang
Abstract: The circular utilization of retired electric vehicle batteries (EVBs) is essential for the sustainable development of the new energy vehicle industry. Establishing an efficient recycling system has become a key issue facing the industry. In view of this, this paper employs game theory to model and analyze three representative industrial configurations: (1) full in-house operation, where the battery manufacturer (BM) establishes its own recycling channel and invest in process innovation for recycling (PIR); (2) partial outsourcing, where recycling is outsourced while PIR investment remains with the BM; and (3) full outsourcing, where both recycling and PIR investment are delegated to the battery recycler (BR). The findings reveal that the BM's optimal recycling mode is jointly determined by the PIR cost and the operational effort level of the recycling channel. Moreover, the PIR cost has distinct impacts on the PIR level across modes. In addition, the operational effort level of the recycling channel and the PIR cost coefficient have non-monotonic effects on the recycling rate and transfer price, respectively, due to the interaction between cost pressure and profit redistribution effects. The results provide a theoretical basis for BMs' strategic decisions regarding recycling channel structure and the allocation of responsibility for PIR investment.

Title: The long-term effects of teachers’ gender stereotypes on labor outcomes
Authors: Joan J. Martínez
Abstract: This paper links a teacher-level measure of gender-stereotyped grading — validated against their Implicit Association Test (IAT) scores — to the later schooling and labor-market outcomes of 1.6 million Peruvian students. Exposure to a more stereotyped teacher widens the gender gaps in high-school completion, formal-sector employment, and earnings, driven by boys’ lasting gains rather than by girls’ smaller, short-lived losses. A single year with a math teacher one standard deviation more stereotyped than average raises boys’ on-time graduation by 0.9 percentage points and lowers girls’ by 0.6. Over the five years after high school (ages 17–22), it raises boys’ formal employment by 4%–12% of the mean employment rate and widens the gender pay gap by about 11% in the first two years, while girls’ losses fade thereafter. These effects run through high-school completion, not test scores or college enrollment. The widening gap in male-dominated industries mainly reflects men's entry rather than women's exit, and students show little sign of adopting the stereotypes themselves. Where structural barriers already constrain access to higher education, teachers’ stereotypes shape who finishes school and their early labor-market outcomes, rather than who reaches college.

Title: Standards and technology innovation with search
Authors: Lluís M. Granero, Santiago J. Rubio
Abstract: This paper examines optimal environmental regulation based on emission or performance standards in the presence of consumer search and firm innovation. With an exogenous market structure, we find that the emission and performance standards lead to the same equilibrium level of innovation, which decreases in the degree of competition in a Schumpeterian way, and these two policy tools are equivalent in terms of total welfare but not in distributional terms because they give rise to different levels of consumer and producer surplus. Here, low search costs can lead to price-increasing competition for concentrated industries and spillovers determine the time consistency of the standards. With an endogenous market structure, the two regulatory instruments lead to different levels of total welfare, they both yield excessive firm entry, and the magnitude of the inefficiency from excessive entry is relatively greater under the emission standard.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: The impact of import competition on gendered labor market outcomes
Authors: Leandro Freylejer, Liam D. Kelly
Abstract: Using a longitudinal random sample of 20% of tax filers in Canada and a triple-differences identification strategy, we study the effect of the rapid increase in Chinese imports on a multiplicity of labor market outcomes across genders. We find that the shock caused a small reduction in the gender gap in annual employment earnings relative to its negative impact on the earnings of workers of each gender separately. Furthermore, we find that the shock caused a larger share of male workers than female workers to transition to non-employment. On the other hand, estimates of differential transitions across locations and to self-employment were small and not statistically significant. Estimates of the probability of exiting wage employment for workers in different segments of the within-local-labor-market earnings distribution suggest that the shock had significant implications for within-gender earnings inequality.

Title: Green product co-design within cheap-talk information disclosure in a supply chain
Authors: Mengfan Li, Zhaofu Hong, Yunrong Zhang
Abstract: Green product co-design in supply chains has become an important practice, with information disclosure serving as a key facilitator for collaboration. However, the effectiveness of information disclosure, which may involve cheap talk (unverified information), on the collaboration of the supply chain remains unclear. Therefore, this study develops a game-theoretic model to investigate the strategic role of cheap talk in green product co-design, where the supplier determines and discloses its green design strategy, which may involve cheap talk, and the manufacturer subsequently sets its green design strategy based on the received information. Our analysis derives the optimal information disclosure strategy for the supplier and the optimal green design strategies for both parties. We identify two behavioral patterns that cheap talk can induce in the manufacturer: Green Idleness , whereby the manufacturer free-rides on the supplier’s green efforts upon receiving high-greenness disclosures, and Green Anxiety , whereby the manufacturer over-invests in response to low-greenness disclosures. Both Green Idleness and Green Anxiety become more pronounced when consumers are more sensitive to product greenness or when uncertainty about the supplier’s greenness is greater, while higher green investment costs for the manufacturer weaken both effects Importantly, our findings reveal that false disclosure can benefit both parties under certain conditions, and that strategic cheap talk can simultaneously improve both profitability and environmental performance in green supply chains. Furthermore, to enhance the robustness of the findings, we conduct a sensitivity analysis and develop a model extension incorporating the green halo effect into consumer utility, which further supports the main qualitative findings.

Title: Diagnosing silent errors in replication packages: Evidence from an AI agent
Authors: Leslie Tianyuan Zhang, Zeju Zhu
Abstract: We test whether an autonomous AI agent (Claude Code) can diagnose errors beyond rerunning code. The agent audits 40 AEA packages and reproduces results in all 26 with public data. We then seed a defect in each of 13 packages and conduct 39 blind sessions. It detects the defect in 37 sessions and provides the correct fix and statistical consequence in 34. Performance remains strong for silent defects that would pass a check based solely on matching reported regression estimates. Our results suggest that AI agents can add diagnostic value beyond re-execution and therefore lower the cost of computational reproduction.

Title: Structural shocks and political participation in the US
Authors: Marina Chugunova, Klaus Keller, Sampsa Samila
Abstract: This paper examines the impact of the large structural shocks—automation and import competition—on voter turnout during US federal elections from 2000 to 2016. Although the negative income effect of both shocks is comparable, we find that political participation decreases significantly in counties more exposed to industrial robots. In contrast, exposure to rising import competition does not reduce voter turnout and may even boost it in House elections. A survey experiment reveals that divergent beliefs about the effectiveness of government intervention drive this contrast. Our study highlights the role of beliefs in shaping consequences of structural shocks.

Title: Constrained reinforcement learning for the dynamic inventory routing problem under stochastic supply and demand
Authors: Umur Hasturk, Kees Jan Roodbergen, Evrim Ursavas, Albert H. Schrotenboer
Abstract: Green hydrogen has multiple use cases and is produced from renewable energy, such as solar or wind energy. It can be stored in large quantities, decoupling renewable energy generation from its use, and is therefore considered essential for achieving a climate-neutral economy. The intermittency of renewable energy generation and the stochastic nature of demand are, however, challenging factors for the dynamic planning of hydrogen storage and transportation. This holds particularly in the early-adoption phase when hydrogen distribution occurs through vehicle-based networks. We therefore address the Dynamic Inventory Routing Problem (DIRP) under stochastic supply and demand with direct deliveries for the vehicle-based distribution of hydrogen. To solve this problem, we propose a Constrained Reinforcement Learning (CRL) framework that integrates constraints into the learning process and incorporates parameterized post-decision state value predictions. Additionally, we introduce Lookahead-based CRL (LCRL), which improves decision-making over a multi-period horizon to enhance short-term planning while maintaining the value predictions. Our computational experiments demonstrate the efficacy of CRL and LCRL across diverse instances. Our learning methods provide near-optimal solutions on small scale instances that are solved via value iteration. Furthermore, both methods outperform typical deep learning approaches such as Proximal Policy Optimization, as well as classical inventory heuristics, such as (s,S)-policy-based and Power-of-Two-based heuristics. Furthermore, LCRL achieves a 10% improvement over CRL on average, albeit with higher computational requirements. Analyses of optimal replenishment policies reveal that accounting for stochastic supply and demand influences these policies, showing the importance of our addition to the DIRP.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Control irreducibility in coupled ground-aerial logistics networks: A multi-configuration simulation study
Authors: Yue Chen
Abstract: The rapid deployment of drone-based logistics introduces a critical risk: cascading failures in coupled ground-aerial networks. This study investigates whether runtime adaptive control can prevent systemic collapse when vertiports become functionally isolated due to ground traffic congestion, and where the boundary of control effectiveness lies. An integrated co-simulation framework coupling SUMO with a custom aerial logistics model is developed. Three control strategies are evaluated across 11 network configurations, complemented by a healthy baseline search and gradual stress experiments. A no-disturbance benchmark confirms operation at > 99% completion, indicating that collapse is disturbance-triggered rather than inherently infeasible. Results reveal a “Control Irreducibility” regime under strong coupling and limited capacity: none of the runtime strategies produced statistically significant improvement over baseline (paired t -test, p > .05 across all comparisons), with completion rates remaining below 4% in the stressed regime. Gradual stress experiments identify a demand-dominated transition ( λ ≈ 2.0) from healthy to irreducible operation, with no intermediate controllable regime. This finding holds under alternative metrics, including effective throughput rate. Cascading collapse is consistently triggered by functional isolation, followed by overload propagation. In contrast, structural design interventions — capacity redundancy and topology-aware vertiport placement — achieve a sixfold improvement in completion rate and, when combined with adaptive control, extend network survival time by over 900 s, demonstrating design–control synergy. Validated across regular and real-world road networks, these findings establish that resilience must be embedded in network design, with runtime control serving as a complementary safety buffer.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Berth and yard space allocation optimization with mobile shore power under two carbon policies
Authors: Shumin Lin, Yinchen Zhu, Lu Zhen, Chunfeng Liu, Wencheng Wang
Abstract: Against the backdrop of increasingly stringent global decarbonization requirements, ports, as key nodes in global trade, have attracted growing academic and industrial attention regarding both operational efficiency and carbon emissions. To improve operational efficiency and reduce carbon emissions, this study proposes a comprehensive optimization model for berth allocation, quay crane (QC) allocation, yard space allocation, and mobile shore power scheduling under two carbon policies: a carbon tax policy, which imposes a predetermined tax on carbon emissions, and a carbon trading policy, under which emission allowances can be purchased or sold relative to an allocated emission quota. The model aims to balance port operational efficiency and carbon emissions, thereby minimizing the total cost of the port. A hybrid meta-heuristic algorithm, QL-ALNS, combining Q-learning with adaptive large neighborhood search is designed to solve large-scale optimization problems. By employing Q-learning as an intelligent decision-making mechanism to adaptively select removal and repair operators, the algorithm achieves a balance between efficient exploration and exploitation of complex solution spaces. In numerical experiments, the effectiveness and efficiency of the algorithm are validated by comparing it with Gurobi and the adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model and algorithm can effectively improve port operational efficiency and reduce carbon emissions. Several managerial insights are also derived from the sensitivity analyses. For example, carbon pricing promotes emission reduction, while excessively high carbon prices or scheduling costs may increase costs without proportional environmental benefits; carbon quotas mainly affect trading costs rather than operating decisions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Unified threshold strategies for online conversion problems with transaction costs
Authors: Wenming Zhang, Na Shu, Xiangyue Zhang, Chenlu Zhang
Abstract: Online conversion problems study how a trader should sell a given amount of asset over a finite horizon in order to maximize revenue under price uncertainty and fixed transaction costs. This paper develops a unified threshold optimization framework for both the continuous online conversion problem with transaction costs ((Formula presented) ) and the discrete online conversion problem with transaction costs ((Formula presented) ) under the competitive difference. For (Formula presented), we propose an optimal strategy (Formula presented) (Optimal Selling Continuous). For (Formula presented), we introduce an integer block selling structure and propose an optimal strategy (Formula presented) (Optimal Selling Discrete). When the transaction cost (Formula presented), (Formula presented) recovers the competitive difference performance achieved by (Formula presented) in Wang et al. (2022). For (Formula presented), the zero transaction cost case shows that (Formula presented) is less conservative than (Formula presented) in Zhang et al. (2011). Numerical experiments under simulated price sequences and real EUR/USD exchange rate data demonstrate that the proposed strategies achieve strong numerical revenue performance in the tested settings and provide implementable threshold rules for online trading environments with fixed transaction costs.

Title: What can we gain from pooling VAR and local projection impulse response functions?
Authors: Viet Hoang Dinh
Abstract: I show that pooling Vector Autoregression (VAR) and Local Projection (LP) impulse response functions (IRFs) may address the bias-variance trade-off in IRF estimation. I also propose a sequence-of-block bootstrap method, designed to construct confidence intervals for the pooled IRFs. I document three main findings: (i) Monte Carlo exercises suggest that the pooled estimator generally yields lower root mean squared error than both VAR and LP at short and medium horizons. (ii) Using the sequence-of-block bootstrap, inference based on the pooled estimator delivers coverage rates that are slightly lower than those under LP and more accurate than those based on VAR, while producing substantially shorter average interval lengths than LP. (iii) The pooling approach combined with the sequence-of-block bootstrap produces sensible results in an empirical application to monetary policy.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Forecasting the price of carbon with macroeconomic and financial variables
Authors: Andrea Bastianin, Elisabetta Mirto, Yan Qin, Luca Rossini
Abstract: We tackle the issue of producing point, sign, and density forecasts for the monthly real price of carbon in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). We show that Bayesian Vector Autoregressive (BVAR) models augmented with factors based on macroeconomic and financial variables yield improvements in point and density forecasting performance, with the largest point-forecast gains emerging at intermediate and longer horizons. In particular, the one-factor BVAR model provides lowest values at six and nine months ahead, while the baseline BVAR performs best at the one-year horizon. By contrast, a large BVAR including all predictors individually does not improve point forecast accuracy, supporting the use of parsimonious model specifications. Simple forecast pooling delivers modest gains from medium horizons onward, but does not mitigate the time variation in relative forecast performance. We also provide a qualitative comparison of model-based forecasts with survey expectations and forecasts released by data providers, which further highlights that relative forecast performance varies over time. Moreover, we consider verified emissions and show that stochastic volatility improves point forecasts, with reductions of about 6.5–7.1% at the one-year horizon. Lastly, we use model-based forecasts to construct market monitoring tools that track demand and price pressure in the EU ETS.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Do women comply more than men? Experimental evidence from a general population sample
Authors: Müge Süer, Nicola Cerutti, Jana Friedrichsen, Gyula Seres
Abstract: Women are typically perceived as more compliant than men; however, the literature provides inconclusive evidence. Using a novel experimental design comprising two complementary experiments, we test this claim in online samples representative of the German adult population. The first experiment (N = 1600) features a probabilistic social dilemma game (PDG) in which participants can increase their individual payoff at the expense of exposing themselves and their group to probabilistic losses. In two treatment conditions, they receive either a recommendation on socially optimal behavior or the same recommendation plus information on weakly non-compliant peer behavior. We find that the recommendation strongly affects behavior, but more so for women than for men. The welfare improvement is substantial. Information on the non-compliant behavior of others erodes compliance with recommendation but does not induce significantly different responses in men and women. In the second experiment (N = 522), we elicit empirical and normative expectations about behavior in the PDG with a behavioral recommendation, in order to study the role of norms in adhering to it. While men and women are expected to hold similar normative beliefs, men are expected to follow the recommendation less often, suggesting that compliance is a (strong) female social norm.

Title: Day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme via stochastic robust optimization
Authors: Álvaro García-Cerezo, Petra Miljan, Hrvoje Pandžić
Abstract: The high integration of renewable energy technologies in power systems represents a challenge due to the uncertainty in their production. In most European markets, producers should comply with their scheduled operation or face the penalties imposed through an imbalance mechanism. Renewable energy sources can be coordinated along with other technologies within a virtual power plant to mitigate the imbalance penalties. To mitigate this issue, in this paper a day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme is determined using a novel two-stage formulation. The first stage comprises the day-ahead market scheduling, while the second stage involves rescheduling of the assets once the deviations in the renewable production availability, modeled using scenarios, are known. Novelty of this work lies in the combination of scenario-based stochastic programming and robust optimization to model uncertainty in the imbalance price deviations. The risk of the decision maker is controlled using the conditional value-at-risk for a given confidence level. The presented case study is based on data from the Croatian power system. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed formulation outperforms the formulation of previous works in reducing the arbitrage between the day-ahead market and the imbalance settlement. Moreover, in-sample and out-of-sample simulations lead to similar profits. Furthermore, the benefits of changing the risk-aversion level of the decision maker at the different stages of the problem are evaluated.

Title: Measuring efficiency and abatement costs in waste-to-energy: A nonparametric shadow pricing approach
Authors: Zuyao Liu, Bin Zhang, Fawaz Baddar ALHussan, Zhaohua Wang, Zhiyang Shen
Abstract: Waste-to-energy (WTE) has become a crucial component of the circular economy and has attracted growing attention from environmental economists. In the waste-to-energy process, municipal solid waste plays a dual role: it is conceptually an output of human economic activities and an input for electricity generation. This dual nature makes the characterization of production technology particularly challenging. To address this issue, we develop a network by-production analytical framework and its corresponding multiplier model to evaluate the two operationally observable stages of WTE systems: energy conversion and pollution abatement. A distinctive feature of our approach is that the shadow prices of the equality-constrained linking input, municipal solid waste, are allowed to take either positive or negative values. The sign of the ratio between the shadow price of municipal solid waste and that of electricity provides an operational interpretation: for instance, when excessive waste input causes operational overload, the ratio becomes negative, indicating how much electricity output could increase if one unit of waste input were reduced. Furthermore, undesirable outputs such as carbon emissions and other pollutants are incorporated into production technology to assess the environmental performance of waste-to-energy generation. The proposed model is applied to a panel dataset of 167 Chinese cities over the period 2000–2022, yielding new insights into the efficiency of waste-to-energy plants and the marginal abatement costs of pollutants.

Title: Research on critical chain project buffer monitoring based on activity resilience
Authors: Junguang Zhang, Jiaqi Zhang, Jianfei Cui, Shanshan Guo
Abstract: As complex projects face frequent and diverse risk-induced disturbances, critical activities, which serve as key nodes for mitigating localized risks, have begun to play an increasingly important role in critical chain project buffer management. To address these dynamic risk disturbances effectively and enhance the resilience of critical activities, we propose a buffer allocation and control method for critical chain projects based on activity resilience theory. First, activity resilience is evaluated along two dimensions, namely resistance to disturbances and functional recovery capacity, and buffer allocation is determined accordingly. Second, to address different types of risk disturbances, buffer monitoring zones are streamlined, and differentiated monitoring strategies are implemented according to the resilience levels of the target activities. Finally, by integrating activity resilience indicators with the monitoring zone framework, buffer trigger points and corresponding response plans are established to facilitate the and precise real-time monitoring of critical chain project buffers. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively enhances the resilience of project activities, improves the efficiency of risk early warning, and increases project completion performance, thereby providing novel insights and strategies for critical chain project buffer management.

Title: A clustering-based framework for preference inference in inverse multiobjective optimization
Authors: Emilio Carrizosa, Nuria Gómez-Vargas, Veronica Piccialli
Abstract: Decision-making in real-world applications often involves multiple competing objectives, with decision-makers applying their own preferences to balance trade-offs. Inverse Multiobjective Optimization (IMO) aims to infer both the underlying objective functions and the implicit preferences that drive observed decisions. In this work, we propose an approach that integrates clustering into inverse optimization to group decision-makers based on their preference structures rather than their observed decisions. Our method is an optimization-based clustering IMO framework that minimizes regrets, which is the difference between the objective value of observed decisions and the optimal value under the inferred preference structure, resulting in Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programs (MIQPs). Additionally, we incorporate interpretability requirements to ensure that inferred preferences are meaningful and align with domain knowledge. To enhance computational efficiency, we derive a heuristic that provides a warm-start solution for the global optimization algorithms, improving convergence and solution quality. We validate our approach on synthetic datasets and a diet recommendation problem, demonstrating its ability to uncover interpretable and robust decision-making patterns.

Title: Convergence to collusion in algorithmic pricing
Authors: Kevin Michael Frick
Abstract: Artificial intelligence algorithms are increasingly used by firms to set prices. Previous research shows that they can learn to collude, but how quickly and reliably they can do so has remained an open question. I study average-reward soft actor-critic algorithms that set continuous prices in the workhorse environment of this literature: a repeated Bertrand duopoly with symmetric firms, deterministic logit demand, and constant marginal costs, where agents observe only market prices and their own profits. The algorithms can converge to a collusive outcome within 50,000 periods, and in 36% of simulations learned punishments make one-period deviations unprofitable, so that high prices are mutual best responses. Successful simulations show cooperative behaviour supported by reward-punishment schemes that discourage deviations. When high prices are not supported by punishments, profitable deviations are typically on the order of hundredths of a percent.

Title: Off the clock? Working time misperceptions and labour market outcomes
Authors: Thomas Breda, Vladimir Pecheu, Baptiste Roux
Abstract: This paper documents a gap between workers’ formal working time arrangements and their own reports of them, and examines what this gap reveals about informal working time flexibility. Combining administrative and survey data at the individual level, we construct a new and unique data set which shows that nearly 20% of the workforce mistakenly report that they work under day contracts, with no monitoring of hours, while they are actually paid through a standard hours contract. This reveals that many workers with various profiles may be misinformed about the legal environment governing something as fundamental as their working time. We show that these misreporting workers differ from classic workers in terms of working conditions: they perform more unpaid overtime hours but have a higher wage rate per contractual hour, so that their true compensation per hour worked is similar. Working time rules appear not to be fully applied to misreporters, but we find no evidence that employers use the discrepancy to extract rents. Non-compliance seems to operate as an informal working time arrangement facilitating a gradual transition between standard hours contracts and day contracts.

Title: Trends and structure of educational assortative mating
Authors: Edoardo Ciscato
Abstract: I study the structure and evolution of educational assortative mating in the U.S. using 1962–2025 Current Population Survey data. From observed marital patterns, I recover the full matrix of marital gains across educational groups within the equilibrium matching framework of Choo and Siow ( 2006 ) and provide a novel characterization of its complementarity structure using Singular Value Decomposition. This approach allows me to infer the number of relevant sorting dimensions, to describe how different educational attainments are valued along each dimension, and to develop aggregate measures of assortative mating based on local odds ratios. I show that the first dimension explains more than 90% of total sorting in all periods and ranks individuals monotonically by educational attainment, consistent with the presence of human capital complementarities à la Becker. However, higher-order dimensions capture homogamous preferences that help explain the prevalence of same-education couples in the data. I document evidence of a long-run increase in educational assortative mating, with a marked slowdown since the 1990s, although the magnitude of the long-run increase is sensitive to how educational categories are defined, partly due to a coding change in the CPS educational variable in 1992. I also show that high-school dropouts have become increasingly isolated, college and postgraduate groups have converged, and gender asymmetries in returns from sorting have declined.

Title: Machine learning and heterogeneity in food aid impacts: Foundations for improved targeting
Authors: Mai Mahmoud, Sikandra Kurdi

Title: Will new transportation technologies increase urban density?
Authors: Edward L. Glaeser
Abstract: Will 21st century transportation innovations work against urban density, as the car did in the 20th century, or promote urban centralization, as the railroad did in the 19th century? Reducing the cost of commuting always reduces urban centralization in the classic Alonso-Muth-Mills model but that result reverses if the number of trips is endogenous and the elasticity of trips with respect to their costs is greater than one. That elasticity may have increased over time, as an increasing share of daily trips seems to be discretionary and city centers increasingly provide entertainment. This paper asks discusses the urbanizing effects of four trends in transportation technology: shared mobility (such as Uber), autonomy (such as Waymo), vertical travel and green mobility, as provided by bike lane. As people spend more time traveling in denser, large areas, innovations that reduce the time cost of travel, such as autonomous cars, seem likely to complement urban living, as long as they don't excessively increase traffic. Sharing is also easier in big cities, so technologies that involve sharing are also centripetal. The other trends seem less likely to have major effects. Moreover, the forces of inertia, which include both regulation and legacy infrastructure, are likely to limit the impact of any new technologies in Europe and the U.S., so that the biggest changes in urban form are likely to appear in east Asia and the developing world.

Title: A simulation–optimisation framework for front-warehouse location planning in instant retail
Authors: Ruijing Wu, Cheng Zhang, Wei Xiao, Zhenyang Shi

Title: Bill of sustainability: integrating life cycle assessment into bill of materials and operations for sustainable manufacturing
Authors: Bening Mayanti, Petri Helo, Linda L. Zhang, Roger Jiao
Affiliations: University of Vaasa; Univ. Lille, CNRS, UMR 9221 – LEM – Lille Economie Management; Georgia Institute of Technology

Title: Going solo or joining forces? Carbon emission reduction strategies for manufacturers under carbon cap-and-trade regulation in a circular economy context
Authors: Jintao Lu, Shushu Xie, Zhencui Li, Georges Samara, Charbel Jose Chiappetta Jabbour, Mirco Peron
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Shanxi University of Electronic Science and Technology; School of Economics and Management, Taiyuan University of Science and Technology; School of Economics and Management, Shanxi University; Platform Economy Research Institute, Shanxi University of Finance and Economics; Olayan School of Business, American University of Beirut; Department of Information Systems, Supply Chain Management & Decision Support, NEOMA Business School

Title: Multi-objective energy-efficient flexible flow shop scheduling problem: integrating renewable energy and demand response programs
Authors: Joyce Mhanna, Hajar Nouinou, Simon Caillard, David Baudry
Affiliations: CESI LINEACT; ADEME, Agence de la transition écologique

Title: Revisiting Oil Supply News Shocks: Proxy vs. Non‐Gaussian Structural Vector Autoregressions
Authors: Helmut Lütkepohl, Till Strohsal
Affiliations: DIW Berlin and Freie Universität Berlin Berlin Germany; HWR Berlin and Freie Universität Berlin Berlin Germany
Abstract: ABSTRACT We replicate a study by Känzig ( American Economic Review , 111 (2021), 1092–1125), who employs structural vector autoregressive techniques to examine the impact of changes in oil supply expectations on the price of oil and other macroeconomic aggregates. Känzig identifies an oil supply news shock by constructing a proxy from OPEC announcements about their production plans. As an alternative approach, we use non‐Gaussianity and independence to identify structural shocks and find that one of them corresponds closely to Känzig's oil supply news shock, implying that the proxy is not necessarily needed to obtain a shock with the same characteristics.

Title: Dual‐Sourcing Logistics Network Design Considering Time‐Based Service Levels
Authors: Yuli Zhang, Ling Zhang, Ting Wang, Xiaotian Zhuang, Zhenyu Gao
Affiliations: School of Management Beijing Institute of Technology Beijing China; School of Management Science and Engineering Nanjing University of Finance and Economics Nanjing China; X‐Lab JD Logistics Beijing China; Department of Intelligent Supply Chain JD Logistics Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Effective logistics networks drive cost efficiency, reliable delivery, and customer satisfaction for e‐commerce companies. Motivated by JD Logistics' regional warehouse network operations problem under uncertain customer demand and delivery times, this paper proposes a dual‐sourcing location‐inventory model with time‐based service levels (DSLI‐T). We formulate the problem within a scenario‐wise distributionally robust optimization framework that incorporates continuous delay times via a conditional value‐at‐risk measure to address tail risks. By deriving tractable closed‐form expressions for the worst‐case risk‐adjusted costs and for distributionally robust cycle service‐level constraints, we reformulate the DSLI‐T model as an equivalent mixed‐integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) model with submodular objective costs. To solve this model efficiently, we propose improved extended polymatroid inequalities (I‐EPIs) that jointly exploit submodularity and generalized upper bound constraints. We prove that the I‐EPIs are facet‐defining for the corresponding polyhedron and, under mild conditions, strictly dominate classical extended polymatroid inequalities (EPIs). Based on these I‐EPIs, we develop an enhanced branch‐and‐cut (B&C) algorithm accelerated by a two‐phase implementation framework. Case studies on JD Logistics demonstrate that the dual‐sourcing strategy reduces the total cost by 12.01%. Numerical experiments show that the proposed enhanced B&C algorithm with I‐EPIs achieves reductions of 77.7% and 98.4% relative to EPIs and MINLP, respectively.

Title: The Markov switching regime global VAR model (MSR-GVAR)
Authors: Giorgos Kotsompolis, Konstantinos N. Konstantakis, Panos Xidonas, Panayotis G. Michaelides
Abstract: A Markov-Switching Regime (MSR) Global VAR (GVAR) framework is theoretically developed and empirically implemented for the analysis of regime-dependent financial spillovers in interconnected economies. The framework extends the regime-switching GVAR literature by allowing for variable-specific regime switching, rather than only entity-level regime switching. Our framework enhances strategic decision-making under uncertainty by capturing interactions across multiple regimes and units, such as economies, sectors, markets or firms. The model simultaneously addresses two (2) key challenges: (a) the quantification of systemic risk through regime-dependent dynamics, and (b) dimensionality reduction in networked environments via structured model aggregation. We demonstrate the utility of the novel MSR-GVAR through an empirical study of six (6) major Asian economies. The paper’s findings suggest that the MSR-GVAR model equips decision-makers with a useful tool for robust planning in volatile, interconnected environments.

Title: Solution methods for the dynamic and probabilistic profitable tour problem
Authors: Marvin Caspar, Daniel Schermer, Oliver Wendt
Abstract: Abstract Sequential decision-making under uncertainty plays a fundamental role in domains such as finance, healthcare, and supply chain management. Multistage stochastic programming and stochastic dynamic programming provide powerful mathematical frameworks for optimizing multistage decisions, but their practicality is often limited by the curse of dimensionality. To overcome this limitation, scalable approximate methods, such as reinforcement learning, have gained prominence. A central area of application is revenue management, historically used in the airline industry and now increasingly relevant in digital commerce, where demand management and logistics are closely intertwined. Motivated by these challenges, this paper studies the Dynamic and Probabilistic Profitable Tour Problem (DPPTP), a sequential decision-making problem involving two interdependent phases: an online phase, in which requests arrive dynamically and must be accepted or rejected in real-time, and an offline phase, in which accepted requests must be fulfilled by solving a Traveling Salesman Problem. We formulate the DPPTP as a Markov Decision Process and derive a stochastically optimal decision-making policy. Given the computational intractability of computing optimal policies for larger instances, we investigate heuristic and approximate solution methods, with a particular focus on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), a reinforcement learning algorithm. Our computational study provides a comprehensive evaluation of PPO’s performance relative to optimal and heuristic benchmarks, demonstrating that it achieves near-optimal performance while scaling effectively to problem instances with up to 96 distinct requests.

Title: Energy-aware planning of continuous casting and hot rolling considering steel grade upgrades
Authors: Nico Gärtner, Christopher Schulz, Thomas Volling
Abstract: Abstract Continuous casting (CC) and hot rolling (HR) are the key processes in steel production for turning liquid steel into solidified coils with order-specific properties and dimensions. Due to different process restrictions, planning and scheduling of both processes is traditionally completely separated. As a result, the intermediate products after CC, so-called slabs, are stored temporarily for further processing, where they cool down considerably. However, for HR slabs have to be reheated to a process temperature of approximately $$1,200^\circ $$ C, making the CC-HR interface one of the most energy-intensive stages in steel production. Integrated CC-HR planning could help minimize slab waiting times and maximize energy efficiency. To address this issue, we formulate a mixed-integer non-linear program (MINLP) that utilizes flexibility stemming from steel grade upgrades to improve coordination. We investigate the potential of integrated CC-HR planning and its dependence on upgrade flexibility and product variety through a numerical study. Problem instances with increasing planning horizons are considered to assess scalability. As larger instances cannot be solved by an exact solver within practical time limits, a GRASP-based heuristic enhanced by a local branching improvement phase is employed. The findings indicate considerable improvement potential at the CC-HR interface, with most benefits attainable under moderate flexibility. These effects remain stable across different planning horizons.

Title: Correction: Adaptive resource sharing strategies for grassroots epidemic response: framework, inference and evaluation
Authors: Yue Feng, Ming Cong, Yingyi Zhang, Lili Rong, Michele Nguyen

Title: Quality-driven long-haul routing optimization for perishable products with dynamic freshness decay
Authors: Xinyu Wang, Wei Shan
Abstract: Consumers exhibit a persistent preference for fresh geographical indication (GI) agricultural products from distant origins. However, the challenges of preservation and the risk of spoilage during long-distance transportation not only increase suppliers’ operational costs but also lead to considerable food waste, and the growing demand for high-quality organic products further intensifies the complexity of fresh GI agricultural product supply chains. This study investigates the transportation of long-distance organic fresh products. Considering product-specific quality degradation dynamics, and uncertainties in multi-stage transport durations, a quality-aware collaborative delivery model with multiple cross-docking centers is formulated as a mixed-integer programming problem. A time-expanded network is constructed to incorporate product quality states, enabling the integration of transportation time, customer delivery preferences, and perishability characteristics into vehicle routing and cargo allocation decisions. An enhanced logic-based Benders decomposition (LBBD) algorithm is developed to solve the model efficiently. The master problem determines vehicle assignment strategies by relaxing delivery time-related constraints, while the subproblem solves last-mile routing based on dynamic product quality. Additional valid inequalities based on product deterioration bounds are introduced to accelerate convergence. Numerical experiments using a real-world logistics network in Guangxi Province validate the proposed model and algorithm. Results indicate that the improved LBBD algorithm significantly outperforms the classical approach, achieving an average performance of 6.57%. Third-party logistics providers should differentiate delivery strategies based on the perishability and economic value of products. While high-value perishables require frequent and responsive deliveries to mitigate quality-related losses, even low-value perishables benefit from quality-driven transport planning, vehicle capacity and transport frequency should be flexibly allocated based on the characteristics of the product lifecycle to ensure overall cost efficiency and product quality.

Title: Strategic store brand quality and category assortment management under spillover effect
Authors: Shuang Dong, Yingchen Yan, Zhongfeng Qin
Abstract: The rapid growth in store brands (SBs) sales has attracted significant attention from category managers, prompting them to carefully evaluate whether to introduce SBs into the focal category and, if so, at what quality level. An evident benefit of introducing SBs observed in practice is the cross-category SB spillover effect, which complicates managers’ decisions in balancing focal category profit maximization with cross-category interactions. Taking SB spillover effects into account, this study analyzes the retailer’s decisions on SB introduction, quality level, and product assortment, and how these decisions impact the national brand manufacturer (NBM). First, we find that the threat strategy, where the retailer develops SB capability only as a strategic threat to pressure the NBM to decrease the wholesale price, may be effective even when SB quality is endogenous. Second, the retailer’s assortment and SB quality decisions exhibit multiple equilibrium outcomes with an increase in the level of the SB spillover effect. When the spillover level is low, the retailer carries only the NB product. When the spillover level is moderate, the retailer develops high-quality SB as a strategic threat. As the spillover becomes a high level, the retailer carries both NB and high-quality SB. Once the spillover level exceeds a high threshold, the retailer carries both NB and low-quality SB. Third, while the retailer’s assortment size adjustment intensifies competition and undermines the NBM, its endogenous SB quality decisions may enhance the NBM’s relative quality advantage, resulting in a win-win outcome.

Title: Consumption‐based analytics: Implications for sales and promotional strategies for digital content
Authors: Angela Aerry Choi, WanGyu Henry Heo, Wonseok Oh
Affiliations: Korea University Business School Korea University Seoul Republic of Korea; Kogod School of Business American University Washington USA; KAIST College of Business KAIST Seoul Republic of Korea
Abstract: Abstract The digital content market is expanding rapidly, yet how post‐purchase consumption trajectories relate to consumers’ responses to promotional incentives remains underexplored. Existing studies have offered valuable insights into digital content consumption by focusing on retention, churn, or recommendation outcomes but have paid limited attention to how these behavioral signals translate into economically consequential subsequent purchase decisions. We address this gap by investigating how completion rate and interruption frequency, two observable consumption signals, moderate the effectiveness of a price promotion in driving subsequent purchase, defined as the purchase of a different title on the same platform under renewed quality uncertainty rather than replenishment of the same product. To this end, we partnered with a major e‐book platform to develop a system for measuring real‐time consumption behavior. A field study involving over 20,000 participants examined how prior consumption patterns condition promotion‐induced subsequent purchase. Our findings reveal that consumers with lower completion rates and more fragmented consumption due to frequent interruptions exhibited significantly higher rates of promotion‐induced subsequent purchase. Importantly, these consumption signals were only weakly associated with subsequent purchase in the absence of promotion, whereas the causal effect of the randomized coupon was substantially stronger among consumers with lower completion and more fragmented reading. We interpret this heterogeneity as treatment‐effect variation across consumer types, pre‐treatment behavioral indicators that platforms can use for promotion targeting.

Title: Government policy incentives: Premium subsidy and risk compensation in credit guarantees
Authors: Bai Yang, Tengpan Wang, Nan Pan, Shuyi Sun
Abstract: In the manufacturing sector, micro and small enterprises (MSEs), which are generally associated with higher default risk, often rely on credit guarantee institutions (CGIs) to obtain bank financing. However, as CGIs have limited risk-bearing capacity, they are generally reluctant to provide guarantees for these MSEs. To encourage CGIs’ participation in MSE financing, governments typically implement two subsidy policies: premium subsidy, which subsidizes part of CGIs’ guarantee fee income, and risk compensation, which compensates CGIs for part of their compensation loss. We formulate a game-theoretic model to analyze how these two policies affect the decisions and profits of a firm and a CGI, and to examine how a government should choose between them. We find that, under the same subsidy rate, both policies improve the firm’s access to guarantee financing, but risk compensation is more effective than premium subsidy. Whether under the same subsidy rate or the same budget, risk compensation yields higher firm profit than premium subsidy. By contrast, the relative advantage of the two policies in terms of CGI profit and the total profit of the firm and the CGI depends on the firm’s default risk; premium subsidy performs better when default risk is low, whereas risk compensation performs better when default risk is high. Furthermore, under the objective of maximizing social welfare, risk compensation can usually achieve the optimal social welfare with a lower budget than premium subsidy. When the firm’s default risk is moderately high and the budget is sufficiently large, both policies can achieve optimal social welfare.

Title: A novel risk assessment model for assessing generative AI risks in sustainable manufacturing: Insights from SME machinery firms
Authors: Huai-Wei Lo
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly adopted in manufacturing to improve operational efficiency and production economic performance, but its deployment also introduces risks, particularly for small and medium sized machinery firms (SMEs) with limited resources, legacy assets, and reliance on external services. A key managerial issue is how to balance efficiency oriented AI adoption with effective risk control in sustainable manufacturing. This study develops an uncertainty aware risk assessment framework integrating an interval cloud model, improved ITARA weighting, and improved probabilistic grey relational analysis. The framework extends Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) by augmenting severity, occurrence, and detectability with cost of protection, impact on sustainability goals, and risk propagation. Linguistic expert ratings are mapped to expectation, entropy, and hyper entropy, while subgroup interval bounds are retained to avoid premature information loss. The approach is demonstrated in Taiwanese SME machinery enterprises using a panel of 24 senior practitioners, yielding 32 failure modes across technical, organizational and human, operational, supply chain, and legal, regulatory, and ethical dimensions. Detectability receives the highest weight, indicating the importance of early identification and containment. The highest risk modes are cybersecurity vulnerabilities from third party AI tools, institutionalized incorrect knowledge, and observability gaps on legacy equipment. Sensitivity analyses, including an epsilon sweep and leave five experts out replications, show stable criterion weights and an invariant top ten set. The results support a staged governance pathway that first reduces external exposure, then verifies knowledge and data, and finally strengthens shop floor observability and capability alignment for sustainability-oriented adoption.

Title: Accounting for the risk of restoration failure in ecosystem service valuation
Authors: Moritz Ptacek, Terese Venus, Fabian Frick, Johannes Sauer
Abstract: While ecosystem recovery is widely recognized to vary, valuations of ecosystem services often assume guaranteed outcomes. We examine whether omitting information on restoration failure risk causes bias in the utility estimates of ecosystem services. Further, we examine how two personal attitudes (connectedness to nature and place attachment) influence risk perception. In comparison to previous studies, we integrate both risk (known outcomes and their probabilities of ecosystem service provision following grassland restoration) and uncertainty (unknown outcomes and probabilities) within a single framework. We find that omitting information on risk leads to overestimation of the utility derived from ecosystem services. Controlling for subjective uncertainty and risk aversion using a hybrid choice model, we find no influence of connectedness to nature on risk perception, whereas the negative effect of high restoration failure risk on utility becomes weaker when place attachment is high. Both latent attitudes decrease the utility of uncertainty, i.e., of the opt-out alternative no restoration. Given the substantial utility implications of restoration failure risk, the EU should complement Member State-level monitoring under the Nature Restoration Regulation with project-level monitoring, open data sharing, and transparent reporting of restoration outcomes to the public.

Title: Single and multi-winner auctions with performance obligation
Authors: Marin Coerts, Florian Heine, Frank van Ommeren, Arjen van Witteloostuijn
Abstract: Auctioning access rights to private providers through competitive tendering has become a central instrument for governments to regulate markets and public services. While efficient in allocating licenses, such auctions may generate monopolistic market structures with adverse effects on consumer welfare. We experimentally evaluate two policy interventions to mitigate these outcomes: introducing post-tender competition and imposing minimum production obligations on winning firms. Our results show that performance obligations substantially improve welfare by raising output and consumer surplus, albeit at the cost of reduced auction revenue. Extending the design with additional treatments, we demonstrate that genuine competition yields even stronger welfare gains. These findings highlight a trade-off between government revenue and consumer welfare in auction design. We conclude that while obligations are an effective tool to counter monopoly distortions, sustaining competition remains essential to maximise total surplus at the market level.

Title: Agricultural input subsidy reform and water quality: Evidence from Zambia
Authors: Jiale Yan
Abstract: I study whether reforming the delivery of agricultural input subsidies can generate environmental benefits. I exploit Zambia’s staggered transition from a traditional physical fertilizer distribution program to a flexible electronic voucher system and combine this policy variation with a 5 km × 5 km panel of satellite-derived water quality measures from 2010 to 2023. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, I find that the e-voucher reform significantly improves downstream water quality, reducing chlorophyll- a concentration by 13.0%, phycocyanin concentration by 11.0%, and total suspended matter by 7.5%. The effects are larger in districts with denser private agro-dealer networks and in areas with highly leachable soils and intensive maize monocropping. Household-level evidence indicates that the reform reduces synthetic nitrogen use and increases crop diversification toward nitrogen-fixing legumes. These responses are consistent with reduced nutrient losses and improved soil retention. Overall, the findings suggest that increasing flexibility in agricultural subsidies can improve downstream water quality while encouraging more sustainable agricultural practices.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Flood shocks, income inequality, and local economic structure: Evidence from Italian NUTS-3 regions
Authors: Federica Cappelli, Mariagrazia D’Angeli, Alessandro Montanaro
Abstract: This paper estimates the dynamic effects of flood shocks on income inequality across Italian NUTS-3 regions over 2000–2020. Combining HANZE flood events with a newly constructed provincial Gini coefficients based on grouped municipal income tax records, we apply a local projections difference-in-differences (LP-DID) approach. Floods increase income inequality in the medium run, with effects peaking around three years after the event before declining. The impact is stronger in economically dense provinces and in areas with higher unemployment and agricultural employment, suggesting that local productive structure, labour market fragility, and sectoral exposure shape the distributional consequences of floods.

Title: Editorial Board
Price competition and inventory turnover along China’s new energy vehicle supply chain
Authors: Boqiang Lin, Zhangdong Guo
Abstract: Despite the rapid expansion of China’s new energy vehicle (NEV) market, inventory turnover among listed firms in the NEV supply chain has not improved consistently. This study examines how price-competition pressure is associated with days inventory outstanding (DIO), using lagged leave-one-out peer gross-margin compression as an accounting-based proxy. We develop a two-period model that connects product substitutability to equilibrium margin compression, derived demand, capacity-constrained inventory adjustment, and DIO. The predictions are tested using 2,426 firm-year observations for 390 Chinese A-share-listed firms from 2016 to 2024. A one-standard-deviation increase in peer gross-margin compression is associated with an approximately 3.0% increase in DIO, or 3.3 days at the sample mean. Cost of goods sold contracts substantially while average inventory changes little; their coefficient difference is 1.780 with a standard error of 0.276. The DIO response strengthens with customer concentration and is significantly larger for upstream and midstream firms than for downstream firms. Additional estimates reported in the Appendix link peer gross-margin compression to weaker profitability, higher inventory write-down provisioning, and longer accounts receivable days. The findings show that inventory turnover slows when operating activity adjusts faster than inventory, especially under greater customer dependence and derived-demand exposure.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Two-stage stochastic optimization for maritime search and rescue with service guarantees
Authors: Pengfei Zhang, Mingjun Ji, Jinpeng Liang, Wanwei Fang, Xinhao Hou
Abstract: Maritime incidents can lead to severe casualties, environmental damage, and substantial economic losses, making rapid and reliable emergency response a core task for maritime authorities. In practice, planning for maritime search and rescue (MSAR) is challenging because incident occurrence is uncertain in time and location, and rescue demand varies across scenarios. This paper studies a two-stage MSAR planning problem that jointly optimizes pre-incident facility location and resource prepositioning decisions as well as post-incident service assignment decisions under uncertainty. The objective is to minimize the total preparedness cost of facility construction and resource prepositioning while satisfying prescribed service guarantee requirements at all incident sites. We formulate the problem as a two-stage stochastic integer programming model with service guarantee constraints, where the service guarantee level of an incident site is defined as the probability that its demand is fully satisfied in demand-positive scenarios. To solve the model, we transform it into a feasibility verification problem by specifying service guarantee targets and, drawing on Blackwell’s approachability theorem, derive a necessary-and-sufficient feasibility condition for a given facility-location and resource-prepositioning plan. Based on this result, we develop a two-stage solution framework for solving the problem efficiently. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method outperforms deterministic benchmarks in total cost and remains comparable to the sample average approximation (SAA) method, with a maximum total-cost gap not exceeding 0.13%, while requiring substantially less computation time.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The rider-drone-locker routing problem in last-mile delivery
Authors: Hongyuan Luo, Yunting Chen, Yunuo He, Yuankang Xue, Yanhui Li
Abstract: This paper studies the Rider-Drone-Locker Routing Problem (RDLRP), a last-mile delivery problem in which riders collect orders from merchants under ready-time constraints, and each order is served either directly by a rider or, after depot handover, by a drone delivering it to a customer-accessible locker. The problem jointly determines rider routes, service modes, locker and drone assignments, and ground-air synchronization. Order-level depot copies are introduced to represent intermediate handovers and allow riders to revisit the depot within a route without using trip-indexed variables. We formulate a mixed-integer programming (MIP) model and a branch-and-cut (BC) exact framework with root-node separation of rounded capacity connectivity and mode-dependent rounded cover inequalities, and implement a problem-tailored adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) algorithm incorporating ready-time scheduling, delay-aware insertion, penalized infeasible search, and elite-pool restart. Computational results show that the ALNS reproduces all proven optima on the smallest instances and consistently obtains high-quality feasible solutions for instances with up to 100 orders. The sensitivity analysis further provides managerial insights into the effects of drone resources, locker deployment, self-pickup compensation, and drone operating costs on system performance and service-mode decisions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Understanding cycling route choice behaviour through street-level images and discrete choice models
Authors: Roosmarijn Terra, Francisco Garrido-Valenzuela, Oded Cats, Sander van Cranenburgh
Abstract: This study examines cyclists’ preferences regarding infrastructural and environmental attributes, including lane type, pavement, lane colour, and the presence of greenery, water, and buildings. To do so, we conduct an image-based stated route-choice experiment in which respondents evaluate alternatives that vary in cycling environment, travel time, and the number of traffic lights. For the survey design, we used over six thousand real-world street-level images of the cycling environment, providing a more realistic choice context for respondents than could be achieved with a traditional stated-choice experiment based on tabular data with text and numbers. We analyse these route-choice data using two complementary modelling approaches: traditional discrete choice models with interpretable environmental attributes derived from GIS data, and a recently proposed computer vision-enriched discrete choice model that integrates image-based information directly into the discrete choice modelling framework. Results show that cycling environments are important factors in explaining cyclist route choice behaviour, with cyclists preferring green areas and separated cycling lanes over urban areas and mixed-traffic roads. In addition, we use the developed models to map where the cycling network in Rotterdam, our case study, aligns —or conflicts— with cyclists’ preferences. Finally, we demonstrate how the developed model can provide planners with ex-ante evidence on the prospective effectiveness of proposed infrastructure upgrades.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Heterogeneity in electric light commercial vehicle preferences among small and medium enterprises
Authors: Nadiya Saba, Lisa Ryan, Aisling J. Reynolds-Feighan
Abstract: The transport sector remains one of Europe’s largest energy consumers, facing challenges like carbon emissions, fossil fuel dependency, and environmental impact. Electric vehicles offer a viable solution toward a low-carbon transportation system for freight. This study surveyed 446 Irish small and medium-sized enterprises, gathering 2,676 observations through a discrete choice experiment to assess vehicle preferences among internal combustion engine, battery electric, and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. Firms showed willingness to pay: €43 per additional kilometer of range, €42 per €100 reduction in fuel cost savings, and €60 for every hour of charging time reduced. These findings suggest that operational efficiency significantly impacts purchasing decisions, often outweighing the upfront costs. Latent class analysis found two distinct small and medium enterprise segments: an attribute-insensitive/status quo segment and an attribute-responsive/change segment. These insights point to the urgent need for targeted policy interventions and infrastructure enhancements to support commercial enterprises, accelerating electric light commercial vehicle adoption.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Special Issue: Innovative data collection methods to inform sustainable and innovative transport policies
Authors: Italo Meloni, Francesco Piras, Eleonora Sottile, Juan de Dios Ortúzar, Elisabetta Cherchi
Abstract: The collection of and access to high-quality data lie at the heart of transport and mobility research and policymaking. Reliable, valid, and representative data on the phenomenon under investigation are essential for designing effective transport and mobility policies and advancing our understanding of such a complex and multifaceted phenomenon, as they make it possible to identify and measure problems, understand their causes, model them, make forecasts, and ultimately help policymakers select the most effective and appropriate strategies to address them. The transport and mobility sector is evolving rapidly, as illustrated by emerging transport technologies (e.g., autonomous vehicles, urban air mobility, alternative-fuel vehicles) and related services (e.g., MaaS, ride-hailing, and micromobility). At the same time, travel behaviour is becoming increasingly complex, encompassing attitudes, perceptions, intuitions, human learning and adaptability, the effects of social norms, and lifestyle choices, particularly sustainable ones. These developments are accompanied by more traditional but still unresolved issues, such as voluntary changes in travel behaviour, habit, multi-level decision-making processes, and preference formation, all of which are pushing researchers to advance the state of the art in survey methods. At the same time, the richness of new information technologies currently available, which include GPS, smartcards, smartphones, social media, sensor data, and many others, is leading to unprecedented opportunities, particularly in terms of quantity (Big Data) rather than quality, to enrich the way in which transport and mobility are measured and analysed. This Special Issue aims to stimulate and advance the debate on the importance of improving the quality of data collection by promoting innovative and more effective methods for analysing mobility- and transport-related issues. In particular, it contains articles that propose and explore innovative methods for collecting, integrating and analysing both directly elicited and indirectly generated mobility data.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Who accepts parking pricing? trust and legitimacy in a contentious policy change
Authors: Matthew J. Beck
Abstract: This paper examines public responses to the introduction of paid visitor parking as a contentious local policy change in a tourism-dependent region. While parking pricing is widely recognised as an effective tool for managing demand and generating revenue, less is known about how such policies are interpreted and legitimised by affected communities. Using the Blue Mountains in New South Wales as a case study, the study treats the introduction of paid parking as a natural (albeit deliberate policy change) experiment in user-pays reform under conditions of infrastructure funding pressure and climate-related disruption. A mixed-methods approach is employed, combining survey data, factor analysis, clustering, and qualitative thematic analysis to identify patterns in attitudes and interpretation. The findings show that acceptance is not primarily driven by demographic characteristics or behavioural exposure, but by institutional trust, beliefs about collective responsibility, and perceptions of governance quality. Three distinct attitudinal segments are identified, reflecting differing configurations of support, trust, and normative beliefs. Despite the scheme’s demonstrated effectiveness as a revenue-generating instrument capable of supporting substantial infrastructure investment, public acceptance remains contested. The policy is frequently interpreted through a “revenue raising” frame, particularly where trust is limited. The paper argues that parking pricing operates not only as an economic instrument but as a governance signal, with legitimacy contingent on transparency, fairness, and the visible reinvestment of revenues.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: From fastest to safer and more experience-aware: an LLM-driven framework for personalized multimodal routing
Authors: Yiping Liu, Hyungchul Chung, Yuchen Song, Dongjie Liu, Tiantian Chen
Abstract: Smart transportation systems are increasingly influencing how travelers navigate multimodal networks. However, most routing services are still optimized for time efficiency and offer limited support for safety-aware, human-centric decisions. This gap is significant because travelers’ satisfaction and adoption of multimodal travel depend on how well route guidance reflects real-world trade-offs among efficiency, crash risk exposure, and experiential qualities of the street environment. At the same time, conventional personalization methods that infer preferences from historical behavioral data often face cold-start problems, high data requirements, and limited transferability across contexts. To address these challenges, this study proposes an end-to-end large language model (LLM)–enabled personalized multimodal route planning framework that integrates risk-aware multi-objective route search with human-centric recommendation. Specifically, we first generated Pareto-optimal feasible routes using a label-correcting multi-objective algorithm that jointly considers travel time, mode-specific traffic safety risk, subjective streetscape perception, and transfer burden. Safety risk was quantified through mode-specific multivariate crash models calibrated with historical crash records, and streetscape perception is predicted from street-view imagery using a deep learning model. To facilitate practical deployment, we employed a greedy hypervolume-based sampling strategy to reduce redundancy while maintaining the representativeness of the solution set. Building on the sampled candidate routes, we developed an LLM-based multi-agent recommendation workflow that interprets traveler profiles and trip contexts, generates transparent rationales, and iteratively improves via a self-evolving memory mechanism. Using real-world multimodal network, crash, and street-view data from Daejeon, South Korea, we demonstrate that the proposed framework improves profile–route alignment and identifies alternative routes with lower route-level safety risks across commuting, leisure, and shopping scenarios. The findings suggest that risk-aware, human-centric routing can support safer route-choice decisions in smart mobility services. Furthermore, the self-evolving mechanism mitigates performance disparities across different LLM scales, highlighting a feasible pathway for cost-effective deployment of safety-oriented personalized routing systems in real-world settings.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The causal relation between off-street parking and electric vehicle adoption in Scotland
Authors: Bernardino D’Amico, Achille Fonzone, Emma Hart
Abstract: The transition to electric mobility depends on widespread adoption and equitable access. We examine whether the “charging divide” between households with and without off-street parking reflects a true infrastructure constraint or underlying socio-economic disparities. We apply a probabilistic graphical model to nationally representative Scottish household data to identify the causal effects of parking access and income on electric vehicles (EV) adoption. Results reveal that access to private off-street parking increases EV ownership probability from 3.3% to 5.6%, an estimated causal effect of +2.3 percentage points (70% relative increase).
