The (1st; 99th) percentile bootstrap interval is + 0.26 ; + 4.77 percentage points, while the corresponding basic bootstrap interval is − 0.17 ; + 4.34 percentage points. The effect primarily operates by increasing conversion among households already intending to adopt, rather than expanding the pool of households considering adoption. In contrast, income is identified as the primary barrier to market entry, with higher-income households showing a 23.1 percentage point lower probability of no intention to purchase EVs compared to lower-income households. Models optimised for predicting observational outcomes overstate the effect of parking by conflating correlation with causation due to confounding bias, specifically by inflating its impact among households with no intention to adopt an EV.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Income inequality, household consumption and status competition in Germany
Authors: Jan Behringer, Lukas Endres, Till van Treeck
Abstract: We analyse the decline of household saving rates in the bottom half of the income distribution in Germany since the 2000s, which was accompanied by relatively limited increases in consumption inequality compared to income inequality. We combine survey data on household consumption with our own survey on consumption visibility and status relevance to test for upwards directed social status comparisons as an explanation of these trends. We find that non-rich households shift their income allocations towards more visible and status relevant areas of consumption when incomes at the top rise relative to their own. Renter households offset higher status consumption by reducing expenditures on other consumption components. In contrast, homeowners maintain higher status-oriented consumption expenditures, particularly on housing, by considerably reducing their saving rates.

Title: Unveiling the role of ESG ratings in corporate greenwashing: Impacts on corporate green development and regulatory dynamics
Authors: Fangxin Jiang, Ze Yu, Lei Zhang, Xiangxi Tang
Abstract: In recent years, ESG (Environmental, Social and Governance) ratings have become critical in guiding investment decisions and fostering corporate green development. However, the growing phenomenon of corporate greenwashing—where companies falsely enhance their environmental credentials—has raised concerns about the accuracy and reliability of ESG ratings. This paper addresses a key gap in the literature by investigating the reputational buffering role of high ESG ratings for greenwashing firms and their impact on corporate green development. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2021, we use machine learning to measure corporate green development and construct matched samples to improve comparability between treated and control firms. Our findings show that ESG rating disagreement increases after independently identified greenwashing events, suggesting that greenwashing adds firm-specific information ambiguity to the normal methodological divergence among ESG rating agencies. However, the results further show that high ESG ratings are associated with stronger corporate green development among greenwashing firms, consistent with a reputational buffering mechanism. Moreover, stricter environmental regulations and higher media ESG attention mitigate the rating disagreement, while lenient regulatory environments and lower media ESG attention exacerbates it. Heterogeneity analysis further shows that this reputational buffering effect is more pronounced among firms with a higher proportion of environmentally experienced executives. This study also finds that ESG rating discrepancy negatively moderates the reputational buffering effect of high ESG ratings in corporate greenwashing scenarios. The study makes a significant contribution by highlighting the limitations of the ESG rating system during the research period and calling for stricter regulatory oversight to ensure transparency and accuracy. It also offers a new approach for measuring corporate green development, providing valuable insights for investors, regulators, and corporate managers in addressing greenwashing and refining ESG evaluation systems.

Title: Risk-adjusted multi-objective optimization of industrial energy portfolios: The role of electrification in economic and environmental sustainability
Authors: Minhye Oh, Dong Hee Suh
Abstract: This study develops a risk-adjusted multi-objective optimization framework for the industrial energy portfolio, accounting for economic efficiency and environmental sustainability under energy price uncertainty. Using monthly energy data for Korea from 2010 to 2023, we identify time-varying price volatility among city gas, electricity, coal, and oil through a VAR-DCC-GARCH model. The resulting conditional covariance matrix is incorporated into a certainty-equivalent (CE) cost framework to reflect industrial decision-makers' risk aversion. Based on this risk-adjusted cost measure, we apply a multi-objective distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model that jointly minimizes CE-based energy costs and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The results reveal that the current industrial energy mix is inefficient and that ignoring price risk and risk aversion leads to substantial underestimation of energy costs. The results also indicate that electricity-intensive portfolios can provide lower emissions and greater cost stability, particularly under risk-averse preferences. Sensitivity analysis shows that higher risk aversion shifts optimal portfolios toward energy sources with lower price volatility, increasing costs with limited additional emission reductions. The findings highlight the importance of integrating price risk, risk preferences, and environmental objectives in industrial energy planning, while suggesting that electrification may serve as a potential pathway toward sustainable industrial energy transitions.

Title: Investment under government ownership: Evidence from oil and gas drilling on the Wyoming checkerboard
Authors: Eric C. Edwards, Trevor O’Grady
Abstract: We study how government ownership affects investment in oil and gas production using a natural experiment created by the Wyoming railroad checkerboard, where federally and privately owned parcels alternate at the square-mile level. Despite near-identical geology, federal land sees substantially less drilling over time. We estimate that the costs federal ownership imposes on operators are equivalent to 28 percent of drilling costs per well. Notably, operators bear less than half the total cost of federal ownership because the forgone rents from additional wells that would have been drilled under private ownership fall mainly on the public through reduced royalty and tax revenues. Because our analysis does not monetize the environmental benefits of federal ownership, these estimates measure economic costs rather than net welfare effects and should be interpreted as a benchmark against which those benefits can be evaluated. We find that increased permitting delays are the primary driver of our results, highlighting the economic importance of process costs in public bureaucracies.

Title: Environmental regulatory risk
Authors: H. Peter Boswijk, Cees Diks, Simon Trimborn, Matteo Valle
Abstract: The aim of this paper is to determine from market expectations how firms are affected by risks arising from environmental regulation. We use a text-based measure of environmental regulatory stringency derived from U.S. EPA legal documents and industry-level relevance scores to capture time-varying regulatory stringency exposure. We find that environmental regulatory stringency carries a positive and statistically significant return compensation, especially for firms with high cash holdings. For firms with low cash holdings, the effect is highly volatile, showing investors are uncertain about a firm’s future when faced with stricter regulation. Firms’ environmental profiles further matter, as high-emission firms’ returns are negatively affected when regulatory stringency increases. Because regulatory text is released infrequently, challenging real-time risk analysis, we utilise our studies insights to derive a high-frequency, market-expectation capturing Environmental Regulatory Risk Index (ERRI). We show that ERRI captures shifts in investors’ expectations of environmental regulatory stringency and how ERRI reacts during environmental policy and political developments.

Title: Measuring regional economic activity through electricity sales
Authors: Changhui Kang, Hwanoong Lee, Sangkon Park, Suyeon Cha
Abstract: Gross Regional Domestic Product (GRDP) is used as a proxy for regional economic activity, but its delayed publication limits its usefulness for real-time policy assessment. To address this, we propose electricity sales as a timelier, more reliable alternative in developed economies, where night lights—often used in data-scarce contexts—face limitations due to urban saturation. Using county-level electricity sales from Korea, we find that electricity sales consistently explain variations in GRDP across urban and rural areas and accurately predict GRDP one year ahead. This suggests that electricity sales can serve as a complementary indicator to GRDP in real-time policy evaluation.

Title: Carbon-price-equivalent signals in multilateral energy reforms: Evidence from developing and transition economies
Authors: Di Wang, Youwei Zhao
Abstract: Formal carbon pricing remains scarce in low- and lower-middle-income economies, yet multilateral programs often coincide with material changes in end-use energy prices. We assemble 45 documented IMF and World Bank program–price episodes during 2002–2023 and convert the observed price changes into carbon-price equivalents; 35 episodes support a same-object estimate, and five of these exceed the global social cost of carbon benchmark of US$184/tCO2. A 161-country panel with 2,368 country-year observations yields an annual price–emissions elasticity of −0.028, which conceals a pronounced income gradient: −0.111 for low- and lower-middle-income (LowMid) economies against a response close to zero in upper-middle- and high-income (Richer) economies. Applying these income-group elasticities to 26 road-fuel windows—18 price increases and 8 declines—as signed emission-equivalent scenarios, the main scenario maps to 4.34 MtCO2 and about US$0.80 billion in modeled global climate value, of which 98.2% is assigned to countries other than the reforming country; the outside share stays at or above 97% under every alternative accounting rule. Less than 2% of the value in the main scenario therefore accrues where the reform occurs, while in price-increase windows the political and distributional costs of higher fuel prices may fall on the reforming country itself.

Title: High-Speed rail expansion and avian Biodiversity Decline: Evidence from a Hub-Link Perspective
Authors: Quanfei Zhang, Wanjia Zhang, Mengrui Xie
Abstract: Although the economic effects of high-speed rail (HSR) are well documented, its implications for avian biodiversity remain unclear. Using a county-level panel for China from 2002 to 2020, we combine effort-adjusted indices from citizen science bird records with geospatial data on HSR lines and stations and estimate treatment effects using a Double Machine Learning (DML) framework. A hub-link decomposition indicates that the negative estimate for avian biodiversity is concentrated in counties with HSR stations, whereas pass-through corridors have no detectable average effect at the county scale. The mechanism analysis is consistent with increased human activity and land conversion around stations. A micro-spatial buffer analysis further shows that the avian estimates are most negative within 1 km of stations and diminish with distance. These findings suggest that ecological assessments of HSR projects should consider not only rail alignments but also station-area land development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Corrigendum to “Two-person bargaining when the disagreement point is private information” [Games and Economic Behavior, Volume 150 (2025), 387-400]
Authors: Eric van Damme, Xu Lang
Abstract: The authors regret that the following statement was omitted from the original article: “Both authors contributed equally to this work and are co-first authors.” The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.

Title: Dynamics and determinants of exporter survival: A machine learning approach
Authors: Abyaya Neopane
Abstract: Exporting is precarious. In Australia, one-third of exporters in a given year are entrants; however, around 60 percent of these entrants exit within their first year. These firms start small, but those that survive expand rapidly and drive the country’s total trade in the subsequent years. One explanation in the literature is that exporters are hit with an ex-post shock upon entry; hence, some survive, and others do not. The paper finds that the answer is more nuanced. Using Australian administrative data, the study: i) applies conventional econometric and machine learning techniques, along with Shapley values, to predict and understand exporter survival; ii) provides a systematic comparison of the predictive performance of ML and conventional approaches. The study documents two key findings. First, exporter survival is shaped by firms’ ex-ante heterogeneity, such as export portfolio, size, and prior export experience, as well as strategic complementarities through compatriot-firm networks. Second, ML models outperform conventional approaches in out-of-sample prediction and deliver more balanced reductions in misclassification errors and their associated costs. The results shed light on the determinants of exporter survival and highlight the value of ML for solving prediction problems such as targeting of export promotion activities, which tend to be distributed ad hoc.

Title: Shift design and assignment optimization to balance nurse workloads in the emergency department
Authors: Jan Schoenfelder, Sebastian Kraul, Steffen Netzband
Abstract: Abstract This paper addresses the issue of nursing workload imbalances in healthcare environments with highly stochastic patient demand. The core objective is to explore the effects of shift design and scheduling decisions on nursing workload in emergency departments, utilizing the German University Hospital Augsburg as a case study. By introducing a mixed-integer optimization model, we provide a method to balance hourly workload over a typical one-month scheduling horizon, measured as an acuity-adjusted patient-to-nurse ratio, where acuity is represented at the level of care activities rather than individual patients. Our model accounts for real-world parameters including staff details, qualifications, work preferences, and extensive patient data. We further explore the potential impact of various shift designs on the desired target level of workforce balance and care quality. The results provide actionable insights into strategic staffing decisions, their effects on nursing workload, and potential solutions to healthcare staffing challenges. The findings also form the basis for future research in workforce optimization in healthcare.

Title: Timeslot allocation for waiting list control
Authors: R. F. M. Vromans, J. T. van Essen, Y. M. van der Vlugt, M. Carlier
Abstract: Abstract As pressure on the healthcare system increases, patients who require surgery experience longer access times to pre- and post-operative appointments and surgery. Hospitals can control their waiting lists by allocating timeslots to the different types of appointments they discern. To inform patients about their appointments in a timely manner, they need to make this decision several weeks in advance. However, the precise consequences of the timeslot allocation on the future waiting list are uncertain, as not all patients follow the same treatment pathway. Furthermore, as these planning decisions are made weeks in advance, they are based on an uncertain prediction of future waiting lists. In this paper, methods are developed with the aim to support hospitals in optimizing their timeslot allocation to reduce patient access times and utilize all available capacity in the outpatient department and operating room. The problem is modelled as a Markov decision process (MDP). However, as the state, decision and outcome spaces grow exponentially in size, even for a single surgeon, an exact solution cannot be determined. We thus compare four alternative solution methods to the static allocation method that is common in hospitals. Least-squares policy iteration is used to find an approximate solution, an (integer) linear program is formulated to solve a deterministic variant of the MDP, several heuristic decision rules are investigated, and a hybrid method is proposed that statically allocates a percentage of timeslots and then dynamically allocates the remaining timeslots with the linear program when sufficient information is available to effectively deal with variability. The solution methods are tested on a case study at the orthopedic care chain of the Sint Maartenskliniek hospital in the Netherlands. Simulation results indicate that in balanced capacity scenarios, static allocation achieves the highest performance when planning more than 4 weeks ahead. In contrast, in unbalanced systems, steering capacity toward patient groups incurring the highest costs yields better outcomes. The hybrid method offers flexibility as it can be adapted to both balanced and unbalanced situations. For the case study, we find that statically allocating 60% of timeslots and dynamically allocating the remainder 4 weeks in advance provides the best results in terms of meeting access time targets and efficient resource utilization.

Title: Women’s economic rights and child education: evidence from historical reforms in the US
Authors: Yeonha Jung
Abstract: In the mid-nineteenth century, US states began implementing legal reforms that expanded the economic rights of married women. I hypothesize that these reforms improved child education by increasing the bargaining power of mothers, who tend to prioritize child welfare more than fathers do. Leveraging the variation in the timing of legislation across states, a border-county-pair analysis indicates that school enrollment rates increased following legislation. To further investigate the mechanism, I use linked census data to examine individual-level relationships. The results support both the impact on local populations and selective migration. Importantly, these relationships were more pronounced in households with literate mothers, who were likely more responsive to changes in the legal environment regarding women’s economic rights. In contrast, paternal literacy does not show similar patterns, supporting the distinct role of maternal influence in parental responses to the legal reforms.

Title: From commitment to routine practice: explaining uneven sustainability implementation in multi-tier value chains
Authors: Ramin Behbehani, Demir Kaya
Affiliations: Brunel University London Department of Business Analytics and Marketing, , Uxbridge; Strathclyde Business School Department of Management Science, , Glasgow
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine why sustainability initiatives in multi-tier value chains often fail to become embedded in routine practice, despite growing investment in traceability systems, reporting routines, digital tools, supplier development and process changes. It focuses on how such initiatives become consequential in practice and develop into uneven implementation trajectories that may stabilise, drift, become diluted, or be redirected across organisational positions. Design/methodology/approach Adopting paradox theory as a sensitising lens, the study uses an abductive, episode-based qualitative design in the petrochemical sector. It identifies 43 sustainability decision episodes and reconstructs 31 of them across linked organisational positions using interviews, follow-up interviews, focus groups or workshops, and documentary and workflow artefacts. Findings Sustainability initiatives became consequential as practical triggers that disrupted existing routines, accountabilities and coordination patterns. Their effects were shaped by how actors interpreted them through concerns about practical mastery, role and accountability, coordination and relational fit, and practical legitimacy. These concerns gave rise to defensive or integrative response patterns, depending partly on the relational conditions under which implementation unfolded. Over time, these responses accumulated into four recurring implementation trajectories: drift, toggling, stabilisation and recalibration. Originality/value The paper explains uneven sustainability implementation as a process through which sustainability initiatives are interpreted and enacted across multiple organisational positions and over time. In doing so, it extends sustainable value chain research beyond structural explanations and offers a process account of why similar initiatives stall, stabilise or are revised in practice.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: The dial-a-ride problem in primary care with flexible scheduling
Authors: Felix Rauh, Emma Ahrens, Christina Büsing, Martin Comis, Felix Engelhardt
Abstract: Abstract Patient transportation systems are instrumental in lowering access barriers in primary care by taking patients to their general practitioners (GPs). However, the economic sustainability of such transportation systems based on ride sharing strongly depends on how well transportation requests can be bundled. We consider a dial-a-ride setting where the transportation requests consist of a ride to the GP and back. Patients may be chronic or “walk-in” patients, with the latter requiring transportation on short notice. In the general setting, the GPs fix appointments without consideration of the transportation. In our flexible scheduling setting, for chronic patients only an appointment range is fixed a priori, and the exact time is determined when the vehicle routes are computed. To tackle this setting, we propose a novel extension of the dial-a-ride problem, the dial-a-ride problem with combined requests and flexible scheduling (DARPCF). We introduce a heuristic for the DARPCF, called MCLIH, that is designed to exploit this increased flexibility. Initially, MCLIH computes so-called mini-clusters of outbound requests. Then, the mini-clusters are linked by solving a traveling salesman problem and creating routes of outbound rides with a splitting procedure. Our computational study shows that in rural regions with MCLIH and the flexible scheduling of chronic appointments, the average number of served transportation requests can be increased by $$38\%$$ 38 % compared to a non-flexible setting.

Title: Integrated patient-to-room and nurse-to-patient assignment in hospital wards
Authors: Tabea Brandt, Tom Lorenz Klein, Melanie Reuter-Oppermann, Fabian Schäfer, Clemens Thielen, Maartje van de Vrugt, Joe Viana
Abstract: Abstract Assigning patients to rooms and nurses to patients are critical tasks within hospitals that directly affect patient and staff satisfaction, quality of care, and hospital efficiency. Both patient-to-room assignments and nurse-to-patient assignments are typically agreed upon at the ward level, and they interact in several ways, such as jointly determining the walking distances nurses cover between different patient rooms. This provides the motivation to consider both problems jointly in an integrated fashion. This paper presents the first optimization models and algorithms for the integrated patient-to-room and nurse-to-patient assignment problem. We provide a mixed integer programming formulation of the integrated problem that considers the typical objectives from the single problems and additional objectives that can only be properly evaluated when integrating both problems. Moreover, motivated by the inherent complexity that results from integrating these two NP-hard and already computationally challenging problems, we devise an efficient heuristic for the integrated patient-to-room and nurse-to-patient assignment problem. We conduct extensive computational experiments on both artificial and real-world instances to evaluate the runtime and quality of the solution obtained with the heuristic. The artificial instances are generated by a parameterized instance generator for the integrated problem that is made freely available.

Title: A case-individual data-driven optimization approach for surgery planning
Authors: Janine Rottmann, Kai Günder, Richard Pibernik
Abstract: Abstract Operating rooms generate more than 40% of a hospital’s total revenue, making effective surgery planning a highly relevant problem for many hospitals. Surgery planning is a challenging task that requires a decision maker to solve multiple interrelated (sub-)problems under uncertainty. An important source of uncertainty are surgery durations—their realizations can vary substantially, depending on a number of factors related to the type of surgery, as well as patients’ and surgeons’ characteristics. This paper proposes a data-driven approach to solve a complex and practically relevant surgery planning problem using case-individual information contained in electronic health records of past surgeries. Our approach combines machine learning models (Quantile Regression Forests) for estimating durations of individual surgeries and data-driven optimization techniques to assign a set of planned surgeries to operating rooms, and to simultaneously determine their sequence and starting times for a given workday. Numerical analyses based on a real-world dataset of a large university hospital demonstrate the value of our approach. Our approach leads to a cost improvement of 35% compared to a naive approach that reflects the current practice of our case hospital, and we can show that the largest part (approximately 23% points) of this improvement can be attributed to the sequencing and room assignment extensions in our model. We are able to quantify the value of case-individual information, identify the most relevant co-variates (“features”), and demonstrate how better uncertainty estimations affect the individual planning tasks, i.e., room assignment, sequencing, and appointment scheduling.

Title: Scarce, scarcer, scarcest: performance-flexible AI-based planning of elective surgeries for efficient and effective intensive care capacity management
Authors: Milena Grieger, Jens O. Brunner, Axel R. Heller, Christina C. Bartenschlager
Abstract: Abstract Operating room and intensive care unit (ICU) capacities belong to the scarcest resources in hospitals and strongly depend on each other. When planning elective surgeries, it is therefore important to consider both resources in an integrated way and to guarantee a certain flexibility in planning to avoid under- and overutilization, e.g., in the form of cancellations. In this work, we introduce a performance-flexible artificial intelligence (AI)-based planning approach for predicting whether an elective patient will be transferred to the ICU after elective surgery. This approach includes a performance-flexible loss function in a machine learning (ML) model and a subsequent simulation about ICU occupancy. The algorithm is evaluated by a large data set of the University Hospital of Augsburg, Germany, consisting of more than 26,600 elective surgeries between 2017 and 2021, and extensive simulation studies. This approach is generalizable as it uses data typically available during surgery planning in the outpatient clinic. Our findings demonstrate that, unlike state-of-the-art ML algorithms, our performance-flexible AI-based planning approach can prioritize a specific label in binary classification (i.e., ICU or non-ICU) subject to capacity considerations while maintaining high accuracy. This ensures a stable ratio of realized demand to planned ICU capacity that is close to 1 across different scenarios. Our performance-flexible AI-based planning algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art ML algorithms and supports hospital decision-makers with a flexible planning tool.

Title: The home health care routing with heterogeneous electric vehicles and synchronization
Authors: Eşref Cebeci, Eda Yücel, Çağrı Koç
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies the problem of heterogeneous electric vehicles, fast chargers, and synchronized jobs that have time windows in home healthcare routing and scheduling. We consider a problem that aims to establish daily routes and schedules for healthcare nurses to provide a variety of services to patients located in a scattered area. Each nurse should be assigned to an electric vehicle (EV) from a heterogeneous fleet of EVs to perform the assigned jobs within working hours. We consider three different types of EVs in terms of battery capacity and energy consumption. We aim to minimize the total cost of energy consumption, fixed nurse cost, and costs arising from the patients that cannot be served within the working day. We model the problem as a mixed integer programming formulation. We develop a hybrid metaheuristic based on a greedy random adaptive search procedure heuristic, to generate good quality initial solutions quickly, and an adaptive variable neighborhood search algorithm to generate high quality solutions in reasonable time. The hybrid metaheuristic employs a set of new advanced efficient procedures designed to handle the complex structure of the problem. Through extensive computational experiments, the performance of the mathematical model and the hybrid metaheuristic are evaluated. We conduct analyses on the robustness of the metaheuristic and the performance contribution of employing adaptive probabilities. We analyze the impact of problem parameters such as competency requirements, job duration, and synchronized jobs.

Title: Performance evaluation of supply chain resilience in epidemic crises: an extension of network non-parametric methodology
Authors: Majid Azadi, Reza Farzipoor Saen, Ali Ebrahimnejad
Abstract: In response to the imperative to fortify supply chain (SC) resilience amidst deep uncertainty, particularly in the context of a pandemic, this study endeavors to introduce a pioneering methodology termed fuzzy network data envelopment analysis. The developed model stands out for its adaptability, being capable of accommodating an array of membership functions tailored to varying network configurations. By synthesizing complex network dynamics into a unified framework, the proposed methodology offers a robust solution for evaluating SC resilience. Notably, its integration of a single objective function addresses disparate network complexities through efficient linear programming techniques, thereby providing precise resilience assessments essential for strategic decision-making. We present an empirical study that aims to conduct a thorough assessment and enhancement of the resilience within face mask supply chains, comprising suppliers, producers, and distributors, to demonstrate the capabilities of our novel model. The findings of this study provide insights into enhancing the performance of SCs in the face of unexpected events such as COVID-19, how uncertainty can affect the performance of SCs, and how inefficiencies can be identified and improved.

Title: Data-based optimisation of intra-hospital patient transport capacity planning
Authors: Tobias Kropp, Yuhao Gao, Kunibert Lennerts
Abstract: Abstract Efficient and timely organisational healthcare processes are urgent for patient satisfaction and medical success in hospitals. Despite process analysis and problem identification, there are especially challenges in evaluating and implementing planning alternatives. This is also valid for the planning of resource capacities. There are currently few use cases that offer data-driven, automated solutions and typically significant effort in modeling complex processes and systems is involved. Therefore, we explore the use of a combination of neural networks and metaheuristic algorithms to optimise organisational capacity planning in healthcare. These techniques allow for autonomous learning and optimisation of processes. A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is developed in a use case utilising data from approximately 3.5 years of accompanied intra-hospital patient transport in a German hospital in order to be able to make accurate predictions about delayed transports on a day of the week basis. A data preprocessing was performed, aggregating case-wise transportation information into hourly information to serve as input and labelling data for the MLP training. Using a genetic algorithm (GA), hourly input variables such as the number of active transporters, the number of planned transports, or the automation rate of transport dispatching are adapted in order to reduce the model predicted number of delayed transports throughout a day. Through this approach, a theoretical reduction in delayed transports on a day of the week ranging from 27% to 42% could be achieved merely through resource reallocating, without adding additional resources. The performance of both MLP and GA are validated using various measures.

Title: A column generation approach for the lexicographic optimization of intra-hospital transports
Authors: Andreas Bärmann, Alexander Martin, Alexander Müller, Dieter Weninger
Abstract: Abstract Over the last few years, the efficient design of processes in hospitals and medical facilities has received more and more attention, particularly when the improvement of the processes is aimed at relieving the workload of medical staff. To this end, we have developed a method to determine optimal allocations of intra-hospital transports to hospital transport employees. When optimizing transport plans in hospitals, there are various optimization goals to strive for. Therefore, we used a lexicographic approach to solve this multi-criteria optimization problem. To calculate optimal transport plans in a sufficiently short computation time, we have decomposed the problem at hand with the Dantzig–Wolfe reformulation and solved the resulting pricing subproblem with an enumerative column generation approach. To improve the efficiency of the column generation process, we have investigated and implemented different pruning methods, dominance rules and a column reuse mechanism for the online setting of the application at hand. In an extensive computational study, we first evaluated the efficiency of the different pruning methods before we compared our solution approach with the standard branch-and-bound column search approach, classical column generation methods and the solution of an integrated MIP model solved by a commercial solver. Finally, we present performance indicators of the transport optimization tool, which was developed from our method and is now productively used in a German hospital.

Title: Integrated planning in hospitals: a review
Authors: Sebastian Rachuba, Melanie Reuter-Oppermann, Clemens Thielen
Abstract: Abstract Efficient planning of scarce resources in hospitals is a challenging task for which a large variety of Operations Research and Management Science approaches have been developed since the 1950s. While efficient planning of single resources such as operating rooms, beds, or specific types of staff can already lead to enormous efficiency gains, integrated planning of several resources has been shown to hold even greater potential, and a large number of integrated planning approaches have been presented in the literature over the past decades. This paper provides the first literature review that focuses specifically on the Operations Research and Management Science literature related to integrated planning of different resources in hospitals. We collect the relevant literature and analyze it regarding different aspects such as uncertainty modeling and the use of real-life data. Several cross comparisons reveal interesting insights concerning, e.g., relations between the modeling and solution methods used and the practical implementation of the approaches developed. Moreover, we provide a high-level taxonomy for classifying different resource-focused integration approaches and point out gaps in the literature as well as promising directions for future research.

Title: Functional health prognosis approach for multistation manufacturing systems considering workpiece quality risk based on heterogeneous quality stochastic flow network
Authors: Qingxia Lin, Yihai He, Xiao Han, Haoyang Liang, Jing Lu
Affiliations: Beihang University; China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation Limited

Title: Selling mode strategy and streamer choice in a live-streaming supply chain considering product returns
Authors: Yi Tao, Meiping Wang, Xianjun Yan, Qiang Lin
Affiliations: Guangdong University of Technology
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Partial Identification of Population Average and Quantile Treatment Effects in Observational Data Under Sample Selection
Authors: Dimitris Christelis, Julián Messina
Affiliations: University of Glasgow, CSEF, and CFS Glasgow UK; Universidad de Alicante and IZA San Vicente del Raspeig Spain
Abstract: ABSTRACT This article partially identifies population treatment effects in observational data under both non‐random treatment assignment and sample selection. Bounds are provided for both average and quantile population treatment effects, combining assumptions for the selected and the non‐selected subsamples. We show how different assumptions help narrow identification regions, and we illustrate our methods by partially identifying the effect of maternal education on the 2015 PISA math test scores in Brazil. We find that while sample selection considerably increases the uncertainty around the effect of maternal education, it is still possible to calculate informative identification regions.

Title: Identifying good forecasters via adaptive cognitive tests
Authors: Edgar C. Merkle, Nikolay Petrov, Sophie Ma Zhu, Ezra Karger, Philip E. Tetlock, Mark Himmelstein
Abstract: Assessing forecasting performance is a time intensive activity, often requiring months or years before we know whether or not the reported forecasts were accurate. Cognitive tests can be quickly administered and are predictive of forecasting performance, but it is unclear which and how many tests are optimal. In this study, we develop adaptive cognitive tests that optimize the selection and efficiency of cognitive tests to assess forecasters of different skill levels. The tests are based on item response models and the adaptive testing procedures commonly used in educational testing. We show how the procedures can select highly informative cognitive tests from a larger battery of tests, thereby reducing the time taken to administer the tests. We use a second, independent dataset to show that the selected tests yield scores that are highly related to out-of-sample forecasting performance. The approach enables real-time, adaptive testing, providing immediate insights into forecasting talent in practical contexts.

Title: The competitive role of returnless refunds in an E-commerce duopoly
Authors: Yumin Fu, Wei Geng
Abstract: The returnless refund policy, which allows consumers to obtain a full refund without returning unsatisfactory products, has become increasingly prevalent in online retailing. Despite their operational appeal, little is known about how such policies shape competitive outcomes when retailers differ in the probability of a consumer finding a good fit and thus being satisfied with the product, which is formally defined as product–consumer fit. This study develops a game-theoretic model of an e-commerce duopoly in which two competing retailers strategically choose between a conventional return-with-refund policy and a returnless refund policy. The results reveal that the adoption of the returnless refund policy consistently leads retailers to increase equilibrium prices, but its profit implications critically depend on the product–consumer fit. Retailers with a relatively low product–consumer fit benefit from the adoption of returnless refunds, as this policy mitigates their competitive disadvantages and can exert downward pricing pressure on rivals. In contrast, retailers with a high product–consumer fit adhere to conventional return policies to preserve their competitive advantages. The resulting return policy game yields various equilibrium outcomes. Returnless refunds emerge only when the product–consumer fit of both retailers is relatively low, whereas differentiated return policies appear when product–consumer fit differs significantly. We further demonstrate numerically that returnless refunds do not necessarily increase consumer surplus and may reduce consumer welfare through higher prices despite the elimination of return frictions. However, a blanket prohibition on returnless refunds can also harm consumers when product–consumer fit is poor. This study provides novel insights into the strategic role played by returnless refund policies in competitive e-commerce markets and offers guidance for retailers and policy-makers seeking to evaluate the economic and welfare implications of such policies.

Title: Water expenditure, service quality and distributional outcomes in Latin America and the Caribbean
Authors: María Pérez-Urdiales, Carolina Tojal Ramos dos Santos
Abstract: Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) countries have made notable progress in reducing income inequality; however, the distributional incidence of water and sanitation expenditures across the income distribution remains poorly understood. In this sector, disparities emerge as lower-income households may encounter reduced access to clean water, utilize less water, or bear a disproportionately higher financial burden than higher-income households. In this paper, we document the distributional incidence of water expenditures in the water and sanitation sector in LAC. We compute and compare concentration indices for water expenditures and income for Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, and Uruguay using survey data from the AmericasBarometer of the Latin American Public Opinion Project (LAPOP). Our descriptive analysis shows that low-income households allocate a larger share of their income to water expenditures than high-income households. Comparing the concentration curve for water expenditures to the Lorenz curve for each country, we find that water expenditures are more evenly distributed across households than income, an inherently regressive pattern given that households spend similar absolute amounts regardless of income level. We further show that total water expenditures, encompassing piped water, bottled water, and water delivered by trucks, are distributed more similarly to income than piped water alone in Brazil, Costa Rica, and Uruguay, while the opposite holds for Colombia. We discuss how these cross-country differences are consistent with variation in water tariff subsidy designs and with the higher propensity of wealthier households to substitute toward bottled water.

Title: Can strong donor governance rescue projects in weak-governance recipient countries? Evidence from the World Bank
Authors: Mengqi Wang, Yongkui Li, Shenyang Jiang
Abstract: International aid is increasingly directed toward countries characterized by weak governance, institutional instability, and conflict, where achieving development outcomes is highly uncertain. As key governance actors in aid projects, donor agencies play an important role in driving project success. However, empirical evidence remains limited on how the relationship between donor project governance and project outcomes varies across recipient-country governance environments. To fill this gap, this study examines how recipient-country governance and donor project governance—both directly and jointly—relate to aid project outcomes. We compile a dataset of 6,773 World Bank projects completed in 167 countries between 1996 and 2025, linking Independent Evaluation Group (IEG) project performance ratings with the Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI). Our results indicate that donor project governance is positively associated with project success. This association is stronger in weaker-governance environments, indicating a compensatory pattern. However, when aiming for the highest levels of project performance, a complementary relationship emerges, in which donor project governance becomes more effective as recipient-country governance improves. A similar complementary pattern is observed in fragile and conflict-affected situations (FCS). Overall, donor project governance is important but context-dependent and bounded. It can partially alleviate institutional constraints in weak-governance settings, but cannot fully substitute for recipient-country governance capacity. These results highlight the need for donor agencies to adopt differentiated governance strategies tailored to local institutional conditions and project performance objectives.

Title: Economic abuse and food insecurity among women living with HIV in Ghana
Authors: Gervin Ane Apatinga, Eric Y. Tenkorang
Abstract: Economic abuse has recently gained recognition as a distinct form of intimate partner violence in sub-Saharan Africa, with women disproportionately affected. However, limited research has explored its consequences, particularly its impact on food insecurity among women living with HIV, who face compounded vulnerabilities due to stigma, poverty, and health challenges. This study addressed this gap by conducting 39 in-depth interviews with women living with HIV in Ghana who had experienced economic abuse, to understand how this abuse influenced their experiences of food insecurity. Using inductive thematic analysis, we identified critical connections between economic abuse and food insecurity. Participants shared narratives of financial withholding, income sabotage, and coercive control that prevented them from meeting their food needs and those of their children. Many described experiences of self-sacrifice, hunger, and dependence on kinship or religious networks as coping mechanisms. Addressing economic abuse requires stronger legal protections, increased public awareness, and tailored support for women living with HIV.

Title: Measuring global exploitation, 1990–2023: does globalization equalize exploitation rates?
Authors: Tomas N. Rotta
Abstract: This paper develops a novel empirical framework to estimate exploitation rates (the ratios of unpaid to paid labor time) and tests the hypothesis that globalization fosters their convergence. By integrating the Leontief input–output model with the New Interpretation of Marxian value theory, the analysis distinguishes between value production and value realization, exploring their distinct implications for global exploitation. Drawing on the GLORIA dataset, comprising 1.2 terabytes of input–output data covering 120 sectors across 164 regions from 1990 to 2023, this study offers the most comprehensive empirical investigation of exploitation rates to date. The analysis spans four levels of aggregation (global, national, sectoral, and country–sectoral) and incorporates alternative classifications of productive and unproductive activities. A key methodological innovation is the comparative estimation of exploitation rates before and after the cross-border and cross-sectoral reallocation of value-added. The findings reveal a global fall in exploitation rates accompanied by absolute convergence. Yet this coexists with relative divergence, sustaining a core–periphery structure within global value chains. While most value is produced in peripheral regions, value realization is concentrated in the core. Unequal exchange, manifested through value transfers from high- to low-exploitation activities, conceals the global hierarchy of labor. By focusing solely on realized value, the System of National Accounts obscures these transfers, attributing peripheral value creation to core economies. The data further highlight the growing relevance of the core–periphery divide across industries. The paper reflects on the implications of these dynamics for theories of uneven development.

Title: How cultural norms affect attitudes toward immigration
Authors: Yvonne Giesing, Björn Kauder, Lukas Mergele, Niklas Potrafke, Panu Poutvaara
Abstract: We examine how cultural norms shape attitudes toward immigration. Using representative survey data on German university students from the 1990s, we exploit the stark cultural differences between former East and West Germany to study whether moving to a different cultural environment impacts these attitudes. We address the endogeneity of the decision to move by comparing students who moved across the East-West border with those who moved within the former East Germany. We also exploit plausibly exogenous variation in exposure arising from the national allocation mechanism used to place students at universities. Students who moved from the former East to the former West Germany are around 7 percentage points less likely to strongly support limiting immigration than students who moved within the former East Germany.

Title: Retaking to succeed: Causal evidence on optional course retaking in college
Authors: Kelly Chen, Yingying Dong, Xuan Jiang
Abstract: Many colleges permit course retakes, yet their effects on academic success remain largely unknown. We study a four-year university that canceled a grade-replacement policy in 1995 and reinstated it in 2001. Exploiting these policy shifts and the disproportionate retaking response among D/F students relative to C students, we estimate the causal effects of retaking using an instrumental-variables design. Grade replacement substantially increased retaking among students who initially earned D/F grades. We find broadly robust evidence that retaking improves same-subject persistence and subsequent performance among students who continue in the subject. Estimates for university-level retention and four-year graduation are less robust, ranging from positive to no detectable effects. Overall, grade replacement encourages struggling students to retake courses without harming their short- or longer-run academic progress.

Title: Learning and probability matching in newsvendor decisions
Authors: Weiwei Han, Xun Wang
Abstract: Human decision making in the newsvendor paradigm systematically deviates from the predictions of expected profit maximization, yet the cognitive mechanisms underlying these deviations remain contested. We investigate whether these biases arise from distorted utility evaluation or from adaptive learning induced by repeated feedback. Across three laboratory experiments ( N = 214 ), we compare behavior under decision from description, decision from experience, and newsvendor environments while varying information availability. The first experiment combines behavioral and electroencephalographic (EEG) data, the second replicates the behavioral findings without EEG, and the third extends the analysis to a multi-alternative setting with continuous demand. We document two robust patterns in newsvendor environments: decision accuracy inferior to random guessing, and positive correlation between choice and realized demand. These patterns are absent in one-shot descriptive decisions and cannot be explained by standard utility-based models. Neural evidence shows that repeated environments engage parietal and frontal activity associated with choice deliberation and feedback-based learning, and that memory encoding differs systematically across demand outcomes. Motivated by these findings, we develop a model incorporating probability matching and asymmetric belief updating, which provides a substantially improved fit to observed choices. Our results demonstrate that repeated feedback fundamentally alters the mechanism of economic decision making, highlighting the central role of learning and belief dynamics in generating newsvendor biases.

Title: A large language model-empowered approach to trajectory prediction for edge deployment on ships
Authors: Yi Zuo, Licheng Zhao, Zhuo Sun
Abstract: Large language models (LLM) are driving the deep integration of artificial intelligence and intelligent shipping, ushering in a new technological paradigm. Although existing deep learning–based ship trajectory prediction methods have achieved significant progress, their capacity to integrate non-numerical semantic knowledge remains insufficient, yet such knowledge is crucial for accurately characterizing ship behavior patterns. To bridge this gap, we propose LLM-EdgeSTP, the first LLM-empowered and edge-deployable ship trajectory prediction framework that unifies continuous automatic identification system (AIS) trajectories with discrete maritime textual knowledge through cross-modal reasoning. The method comprises three core components. (1) The maritime semantic prompt unit (MSPU) transforms raw AIS trajectories into context-aware natural language prompts. (2) The navigational interaction representation unit (NIRU) models ship–ship interactions by fusing convolutional and attention mechanisms and maps them into the LLM embedding space through representation–language reconstruction to enable semantic understanding of encounter and avoidance intentions. Lightweight LLMs such as LLaMA and Gemma then fuse navigational states and interaction semantics to generate trajectory predictions in natural language form and decode them into precise coordinates. (3) Edge deployment supports real-time inference on low-power hardware. Experiments across three representative maritime regions demonstrate that LLM-EdgeSTP outperforms ten baseline models by an average of 40% in terms of average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) while satisfying real-time latency requirements. This work lays a key technical foundation for building interpretable, efficient, and practical autonomous navigation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Equitable and visually attractive arc routing for residential waste collection with heterogeneous fleets
Authors: Seungyeop Lee, Sangil Han, Byung-In Kim
Abstract: The residential waste collection problem (RWCP) is an arc routing problem in which multiple vehicles must service street segments while adhering to capacity and working-time constraints, with the possibility of multiple visits to landfills. In practice, route plans should be not only cost-efficient but also equitable across vehicles and visually attractive. This study addresses a multi-vehicle RWCP with heterogeneous fleets, where vehicles may differ in capacity and driver efficiency, and where route costs incorporate turn penalties. We formulate the problem as a mixed capacitated arc routing problem with intermediate facilities, in which service requirements are defined on both arcs (directed street segments) and edges (undirected street segments), and propose a hierarchical graph-partitioning-based matheuristic (H-GPM) to solve it. The proposed framework decomposes the problem into three stages: vehicle-level balanced clustering, trip-level capacitated clustering, and trip-level routing. At the vehicle level, it combines graph coarsening, Steiner tree-based route-cost estimation, initial solution construction, and local improvement to generate workload-balanced and spatially coherent task assignments. At the trip level, vehicle-specific subgraphs are partitioned into capacity-feasible trips, and routing decisions are determined by lexicographic MILP models that first minimize arc overlap and subsequently route cost. Computational experiments show that, compared with baseline methods for homogeneous fleets, H-GPM produces workload-balanced solutions while substantially improving visual attractiveness, particularly by reducing spatial overlap among vehicle routes. For heterogeneous fleets, H-GPM effectively accounts for turn penalties, vehicle capacities, driver efficiencies, and multi-trip operations, producing feasible and workload-balanced solutions. The evaluation of the embedded route-cost estimation procedure further supports the reliability of the proposed framework.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A Deep Reinforcement learning model for centralized route recommendation in multi-modal transit networks
Authors: Zijian Shen, Taijie Chen, Bin Zhou, Junheng Wang, Jintao Ke
Abstract: Rapid urbanization has outpaced public transit infrastructure expansion, leading to severe peak-hour congestion in various metropolitan areas. While route recommendation systems offer a solution, conventional passenger-centric approaches typically optimize trips in isolation, neglecting aggregate network effects and causing inefficiencies resulting from “selfish routing”. To address this, we propose Temporal Perception Multi-head Proximal Policy Optimization (TP-MPPO), a centralized Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework designed to optimize multi-modal public transit networks holistically. Acting as a virtual Traffic Management Center (TMC), the framework monitors vehicle loads and station queues to generate coordinated routing strategies for clusters of passengers. Rather than enforcing mandatory route assignments, TP-MPPO adjusts the displayed ranking of route alternatives in passenger-facing menus. Conditional on the ranking–choice association captured by a calibrated route-choice model, this reordering is used in simulation to redistribute demand toward less congested multi-modal alternatives while preserving passengers’ freedom to choose. The architecture combines a group-specific multi-head self-attention mechanism to process heterogeneous passenger data, a transformer-based module to model evolving traffic dynamics, and a multi-head PPO policy for targeted recommendations. Evaluated through three independent full-day simulation runs of Beijing’s multi-modal transit network, TP-MPPO achieves the best mean performance among the evaluated benchmark methods, reducing average waiting time by 11.8%, average trip time by 6.7%, the top-five hexagonal congestion index by 28.5%, and waiting passengers by 12.3% relative to the strongest baseline for each metric.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Hazardous materials multimodal transport routing Problem: A robust optimization approach based on Benders decomposition
Authors: Qianqian Zhang, Jun Wu, Weiwei Zhang, Ernesto DR Santibanez Gonzalez
Abstract: This paper develops a robust optimization framework for hazardous materials multimodal transportation under road congestion, carbon regulation, and uncertainty. Road impedance functions are used to characterize road congestion effects on travel time, carbon-emission cost, and transportation risk cost, and a budgeted box uncertainty set is introduced to capture operational uncertainty. Hazmat Scenario-Enhanced Adaptive Multi-Cut Benders Decomposition (HSA-MBD) algorithm is proposed to solve the resulting model efficiently. Experiments on the Shanghai network show that road congestion, carbon constraints, and uncertainty jointly affect route and mode choices. Road congestion shifts the optimal solution from road-intensive routes toward rail-waterway-based intermodal configurations and sharply reduces feasibility under severe conditions. Tighter carbon caps further encourage cleaner paths with lower road dependence, whereas across the tested deviation-ratio sensitivity ranges, uncertainty mainly amplifies total cost without changing the optimal path, although transportation-risk uncertainty can alter the route structure when it is introduced as the sole uncertainty source. For the Shanghai multimodal network, the hazardous-material shipment considered, and the tested uncertainty-budget and deviation-ratio ranges, transportation-risk uncertainty has a substantially stronger effect on total cost than freight-rate uncertainty. In addition, HSA-MBD obtains the same best-known objective values as the benchmark methods for all tested instances, while requiring fewer Benders iterations and less computational time.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Assortment planning with product customization capabilities in omni-channel retailing
Authors: Nadia Sadrmomtaz, Mohsen S. Sajadieh
Abstract: Customers are increasingly seeking personalized products, making customization a critical consideration for retailers. At the same time, many retailers are shifting from single- or multi-channel strategies to an Omni-channel approach. So, this study aims to develop a model that assists Omni-channel retailers in incorporating customization into their assortment planning decisions, which has been neglected in previous research. To address the issue of customization in an Omni-channel retailer’s assortment planning, identifying the Point of Differentiation (POD) is emphasized as a key component in implementing a delayed differentiation strategy that facilitates product customization. To simulate customer decision-making behavior and demand within the Omni-channel environment, an exogenous demand model is employed, and a quadratic function is introduced to model retailer profit. The proposed model is reformulated as a Binary Integer Programming model, and a heuristic method is introduced to solve it. Using this heuristic, two policies of demand acceptance are introduced and compared, several analyses are conducted, and managerial recommendations are provided. The study concludes that offering customization can enhance retailers’ profits and reduce lost sales; however, high customization setup costs and demand uncertainty may offset these benefits.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Review of flow capturing, flow covering, and flow interception models
Authors: H.A. Eiselt, Vladimir Marianov, Zvi Drezner
Abstract: This paper was written to honor John Hodgson and his contributions to location science. Starting with the usual location-allocation models, we follow flow interception, (including flow covering and flow capturing) models from their inception to today’s versions. We then demonstrate how their formulations relate to the corresponding standard models. These modifications in conjunction with the known degree of difficulty of the standard models provide a glimpse into the hardness of the flow covering, capturing, and interception models. We propose a variety of modifications to the models investigated in the literature that can result in future research papers. Such future papers will extend the applicability of flow capturing, covering, and interception models.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Investigation of the reservation-based travel scheme for the morning commuting problem with heterogeneous commuters
Authors: Dong Ding, Yue Bao, Zaihan Gao
Abstract: Morning commuting has long been a critical challenge for urban transportation systems, characterized by a large volume of travel demand concentrated within a short time window. Motivated by recent reservation-based travel experiments in Beijing, this study aims to theoretically explore the reservation-based travel scheme and the corresponding commuter behaviours, accounting for heterogeneity in commuters’ willingness to make reservations. Under this scheme, commuters with permits are granted access to the designated reservation lanes, while those without permits must use the conventional lanes. The conditions for an effective reservation scheme that avoids capacity waste are given. It has been shown that, under an effective reservation scheme, the travel cost for commuters using the reservation lane decreases, while that of commuters in the non-reservation lane remains unchanged. The optimal number of reservation permits to minimize the total travel cost is derived. Compared to that without a reservation scheme, the total travel cost for all commuters is reduced by a factor proportional to the relative capacity of the reservation lane, scaled by one-fourth, under the optimal number of reservation permits. The reservation scheme is extended to a multi-period scheme, in which the peak period is divided into several subperiods, requiring commuters to select a specific subperiod when making reservations. It is demonstrated that the multi-period scheme is significantly more effective in reducing travel costs for commuters.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Who travels for travel’s sake? Profiling undirected travelers and their built environments
Authors: Hannah Hook, Tanhua Jin, Frank Witlox, Feixiong Liao
Abstract: Undirected travel (UT, travel undertaken for its own sake) remains understudied despite its contributions to physical activity, mental well-being, and quality of life. Using the 2023 Dutch national travel survey (ODiN; 53,049 respondents), this study examines how built environment (BE) attributes, socio-economic demographics (SEDs), temporal variations (weekday vs weekend), and directed travel (DT) shape UT participation, frequency, and modal choice. Multigroup path analysis across four social participation groups (full-time workers, part-time workers, students, and retired individuals) reveals substantial heterogeneity in the pathways influencing UT. Findings suggest that DT rhythms strongly structure opportunities for UT. Higher DT frequency reduces UT participation, consistent with a travel time budget effect, while the use of sustainable modes for DT consistently predicts sustainable mode use for UT. BE effects were modest and mixed, with dense and cycling-oriented neighborhoods not consistently generating more UT, while access to green space was positively associated with UT frequency for some groups. SEDs, including gender, migration background, household composition, and car ownership, shape UT both directly and indirectly through their effects on DT, highlighting the role of structural constraints in determining who engages in UT and how. Results highlight UT as a meaningful, distinct form of mobility shaped by time availability, daily structure, and environmental context. Integrating UT into transport planning can support well-being-oriented, low-carbon, and equitable mobility strategies. The study underscores the importance of planning frameworks that value both the functional and experiential dimensions of travel in creating more inclusive and human-centered mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Does the Low-Carbon City Pilot policy promote green innovation collaboration? Evidence from knowledge embeddedness and complexity
Authors: Qijun Xie, Dengjie Yuan, Xiangyang Li
Abstract: Urban climate policies are increasingly expected not only to reduce carbon emissions but also to reorganize the collaborative networks through which green innovation is generated. While existing studies show that China’s Low-Carbon City Pilot (LCCP) policy increases green innovation output, little is known about whether and how it reshapes the structure of innovation collaboration across and within cities. Drawing on the extended Porter Hypothesis, this study examines the impact of the LCCP on green innovation collaboration by focusing on inter-city embeddedness and intra-city complexity. Using a balanced panel of 250 Chinese prefecture-level cities from 2006 to 2022, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach and construct patent-based indicators to capture cross-city collaborative integration and within-city technological diversity. The results show that the LCCP significantly increases both inter-city embeddedness and intra-city complexity. Digitalization and environmental regulation intensity positively moderate these effects, and the joint implementation of the Innovation City Pilot (ICP) and the LCCP generates strong complementary impacts. The effects are more pronounced in eastern and large cities, key environmental protection cities, and directly designated pilot cities, but are weaker in resource-based regions. These findings suggest that policymakers should integrate low-carbon city policies with innovation-oriented pilot programs, strengthen digital infrastructure that supports cross-city knowledge collaboration, and provide targeted institutional support for resource-based and less-developed cities to avoid uneven policy effects. This study contributes to the literature by moving beyond innovation quantity to examine how environmental regulation reshapes innovation collaboration networks, providing new evidence on the collaborative mechanisms through which low-carbon policies foster green technological upgrading.

Title: Green credit under carbon price risk: financing frictions, banking market power, and firm emissions
Authors: Lin Zigan, Lei Yihu
Abstract: Green credit can finance both abatement and output expansion, so its emissions effect is ambiguous for financially constrained firms. We develop an energy-finance model in which banks post project-contingent terms before a firm selects a verifiable production–abatement plan and carbon prices are realized. The main model separates verified abatement from positive carbon collateral. Green credit lowers emissions only when the technique effect dominates the scale effect. Competitive break-even pricing transmits carbon-price risk to loan rates without distorting risk-neutral operations, whereas lender market power can convert the same risk into lower abatement and higher emissions intensity. Paid allowance allocation acts as a policy-induced financing friction: competitive credit absorbs the upfront cost, while concentrated lending can amplify the debt burden and generate adverse emission responses. A transition-finance extension shows that carbon-deficit borrowers face a reversed default tail and may be harmed by carbon-price support. Additional contract extensions indicate that performance-linked pricing and use-of-proceeds restrictions improve environmental outcomes only when incentives are genuine and funds are not highly fungible. Carbon policy, banking structure, and loan design therefore jointly determine whether green finance produces real decarbonization.

Title: Estimating the impact of a star scientist move on their own research productivity
Authors: Akhil Sasidharan, John McHale, Jason Harold
Abstract: Star scientists can have significant impacts on their institutions both through their own productivity and through spillover effects on their co-located colleagues. For newly recruited stars, previous research has shown evidence of positive productivity effects on incumbent scientists in the institutions they join. This paper complements this research by using the same data source to examine the effects of a star’s move on their own research performance in three small open economies (SOEs) - Ireland, Denmark, and New Zealand. We estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) using an event-study difference-in-differences design that compares star movers with non-mover stars who exhibit parallel pre-move productivity trends. Analysing the quality-adjusted productivity of 161-star scientists, we find that moving to a new institution substantially reduces their productivity in the year of the move by 58%, and this effect persists in subsequent years, with an estimated reduction of 42% after four years. One explanation consistent with this combination of negative own-productivity effects and positive peer-spillover effects is that the arriving stars prioritise institution-building activities at their new institution rather than their own research output.

Title: Leveraging blockchain and contracts in fresh agricultural supply chains with information asymmetry
Authors: Longfei He, Yaxin Cao, Fangtong Liu, Xiaohang Yue
Affiliations: College of Management and Economics & The Laboratory of Computation and Analytics of Complex Management Systems (CACMS), Tianjin University; Lubar School of Business, University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee
Abstract: This study investigates a two-echelon fresh agricultural supply chain plagued by information asymmetry, where a supplier possesses private information regarding product freshness. The strategic distortion of this freshness information leads to escalated supply chain losses and diminished operational efficiency. Employing a game-theoretic model, we analyze how the integration of blockchain technology and contractual mechanisms can mitigate the adverse effects of such information asymmetry. Our analysis identifies the critical parameters that govern the thresholds for blockchain adoption and its requisite investment. Furthermore, a comparative evaluation reveals distinct optimal decision-making patterns for supply chain members under varying operational conditions. The principal findings are threefold: first, the supplier’s misrepresentation of freshness information generates private benefits at the expense of both the retailer’s profit and total supply chain welfare; second, the effectiveness of blockchain is parameter-dependent, indicating its non-universal applicability; and third, in low transaction-cost scenarios, contractual solutions can achieve informational accuracy comparable to blockchain, thereby challenging the presumed superiority of technological interventions. This research provides dual theoretical and managerial insights for mitigating informational opacity, offering evidence-based guidelines for optimizing blockchain deployment and designing contractual coordination frameworks. The findings establish pragmatic decision criteria for selecting appropriate countermeasures tailored to specific operational parameters.

Title: Innovative approaches in reshaping the supply chain for societal challenges
Authors: Rosanna Fornasiero, Andrea Zangiacomi
Affiliations: CNR-IEIIT, National Research Council; CNR-STIIMA, National Research Council
Abstract: 1. Supply chains are no longer merely the operational backbones of the global economy. They have increasingly become pivotal socio-technical and institutional infrastructures through which industry...

Title: Birds of a feather flock together: increasing social sustainability through supply chain visibility
Authors: Ricardo Zimmermann, César Toscano, Ana Carolina Chaves
Affiliations: INESC TEC
Abstract: This study reflects the assumption that all links in a supply chain (SC) must share responsibility for socio-environmental issues. One of the main barriers to ensuring the sustainability of an SC is the difficulty in accessing partners’ information, especially beyond the first tier. Due to the great geographical dispersion, large number of small companies, and, mainly, the growth of the fast fashion industry, the textile sector is recognised as a priority when it comes to social sustainability issues. Moreover, consumers are increasingly demanding information about the social footprint of products. Thus, this paper aims to contribute to a better understanding of how SC visibility can contribute to increasing the social sustainability of textile SCs. Using a longitudinal perspective and adopting mixed methods integrated into a design science strategy, we evaluate SC visibility in the context of two Portuguese textile supply chains, before and after the development of a technology-based solution.

Title: Value cocreation-oriented digital platform design: a method for requirements elicitation and platform assessment
Authors: Baris Ozkan, Noor Jungerius, Onat Ege Adali, Oktay Turetken
Affiliations: School of Industrial Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology
Abstract: In the evolving landscape of digital platforms, there is increasing emphasis on their role as facilitators of value co-creation, where diverse actors exchange and recombine resources within platform ecosystems for mutual benefit. The alignment between digital platform design and the diverse requirements of all value-cocreating actors is crucial for fostering value co-creation and mitigating value co-destruction as the platform and its ecosystem co-evolve. To address this need for alignment, this article proposes a method developed through design science research. The method guides requirement elicitation based on the desired value cocreation of actors within their platform ecosystems and supports platform assessment against these requirements. Applied to a digital healthcare platform business case and evaluated through a focus group study, the results provide positive evidence of the method’s usefulness, ease of use, and users’ intention to use the method.

Title: Managing public sector innovation for a better society: the case of public procurement of innovation
Authors: Andrea S. Patrucco, Ana-Maria Dimand, Tommaso Agasisti, Michele Benedetti, Marco Gaeta, Luca Tangi
Affiliations: Department of Marketing and Logistics, Florida International University College of Business; Askew School of Public Administration and Policy, Florida State University; Department of Management, Economics and Industrial Engineering, School of Management, Politecnico di Milano; EasyGov Solutions S.R.L; European Commission – Joint Research Centre
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between strategic management (SM) practices and performance in public sector innovation, focusing on Public Procurement of Innovation (PPI) as a policy mechanism to address societal challenges. Analyzing data from 185 PPI projects in Italy using Structural Equation Modelling, the findings show that strategic goal setting enhances performance outcomes, including local economic growth, community benefits, innovation promotion, and intellectual capital creation. Intra-agency collaboration facilitates the use of innovation policy instruments but does not directly improve performance. In contrast, instrument utilization positively affects strategic outcomes and mediates the link between goal setting and performance. This study contributes to procurement, innovation policy, and SM literature by demonstrating how procurement can drive innovation and societal impact. It provides actionable insights for managers and policymakers to strengthen PPI effectiveness through clear goal setting, internal collaboration, and targeted policy instruments.

Title: Public reaction to firms’ sustainable supply chain management: Evidence from social media analytics
Authors: Fan Zeng, Chris K. Y. Lo, Stacy H. N. Lee, Yi Zhou
Affiliations: School of Business, Macau University of Science and Technology; School of Fashion and Textiles, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, PolyU Business School, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Network of Empirical Operations Management, PolyU Business School, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Department of Hospitality and Retail Management, Texas Tech University; Department of Management, Monash Business School, Monash University
Abstract: Firms implement sustainable product design, sustainable manufacturing, and recycling as core sustainable supply chain management (SSCM) practices to address public demands.
