In Society 5.0, public engagement with these practices in cyberspace reshapes business designs and reflects them in physical spaces, driving societal transformation. Understanding public reactions is essential to align firms’ SSCM practices with public requirements, prioritising human well-being and advancing human-centric, citizen co-creation, and urban symbiosis logics. Analysing 26,620 social media posts from 19 fashion brands, we find sustainable product design and recycling initiatives have a significantly positive effect on public reactions. Sustainable manufacturing overall has insignificantly positive effects, but disaggregating it reveals sustainable sourcing has significantly positive effects on public reaction, while sustainable production does not have significant effects. Firms should prioritise investments in sustainable product design, sourcing, and recycling to enhance public reactions, gain legitimacy, and promote sustainable development for social benefit.

Title: Supply chain network design based on Big Data Analytics: heuristic-simulation method in a pharmaceutical case study
Authors: Fariba Goodarzian, Peiman Ghasemi, Andrea Appolloni, Irfan Ali, Leopoldo Eduardo Cárdenas-Barrón
Affiliations: Edinburgh Business School (EBS), Heriot-Watt University; Department of Business Decisions and Analytics, University of Vienna; Management and Law, University of Rome Tor Vergata; Department of Statistics and Operations Research, Aligarh Muslim University; School of Engineering and Sciences, Tecnológico de Monterrey
Abstract: Digital technology is a pivotal aspect of the ongoing digital transformation upon which supply chain networks (SCNs) heavily rely. Through the utilization of Big Data Analytics (BDA), organizations can gain insights into sales, production and formulate decision support systems. The pharmaceutical supply chain emerges as a crucial player in producing and distributing medications vital for treating COVID-19 patients. In this study, we have innovatively designed a multi-echelon Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Network (PSCN) using BDA during the COVID-19 pandemic. We have developed a novel Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming model addressing allocation, production planning, and inventory control decisions, known as the LAPI problem. A transformation method is employed to convert the non-linear model into a linear one to enhance computational efficiency. The primary objective of our mathematical model is to minimize the total cost and CO2 emissions of the transportation system and established centres while maximizing the shelf life of medicines. Our experiments reveal that medium- and large-scale problems, characterized by the three main attributes of BDA – variety, velocity and volume (3 V‟s), pose challenges for optimal solutions. We present a case study of Iran to validate the mathematical model for large-scale problems. Employing a simulation approach, we estimate the demand for required pharmaceuticals, underscoring our proposed model’s real-world applicability and effectiveness. This research contributes to the growing necessity of eco-friendly and efficient supply chain strategies, especially in the critical domain of pharmaceuticals during pandemic situations.

Title: A balance of economic advancement and social needs via improving supply chain traceability for future food sustainability: an empirical study from China
Authors: Xiongyong Zhou, Haiyan Lu, Zhiduan Xu
Affiliations: School of Economics and Management, Fuzhou University; Business School, Newcastle University; School of Management, Xiamen University
Abstract: Sustainability issues in the food industry have been witnessed to impact on public stability, human health and living standards in the past decades. Practitioners and academia have raised attention to develop supply chain traceability (SCT) in the context of Industry 4.0 technologies in order to improve operational efficiency and reduce environmental impact. Drawing on the extended knowledge-based view, this study has collected 303 questionnaire surveys to test the impact of SCT practices on improving food manufacturers’ sustainability performance, addressing on the economic, environmental and social sustainability, with consideration of knowledge integration and environmental dynamism. Our results show that: (1) SCT has a significant positive impact on the three pillars of sustainability performances among food manufacturers. (2) Knowledge integration mediates the relationship between SCT and sustainability performance; (3) Environmental dynamism plays a moderating role in the direct path between SCT and social performance. This study contributes new theoretical insights to highlight knowledge integration in support of traceback investigation for improving sustainability performance a dynamic environment. The results make substantial contributions on better implementation of sustainable food supply chain, to enhance operations and supply chain practices in the food chain, and to support government policymaking in an environmental dynamic context.

Title: Operational decisions of live-streaming platform supply chain based on control power: considering the dual preferences of consumers
Authors: Xiao Zhang, Guitao Zhang, Hao Sun, Cong Shi, Guoqing Zhang
Affiliations: School of Business, Qingdao University; Supply Chain and Logistics Optimization Research Center, Department of Mechanical, Automotive & Materials Engineering, University of Windsor
Abstract: As the problem of live streaming with goods ‘overturned’ has also emerged, it is crucial for supply chain members to make optimal decisions to maintain long-term cooperation relationship. Based on this background, we construct a new supply chain structure composed of a fresh food supplier, an online celebrity live-streaming base (OCLB) and a platform channel, and establish three game-theoretic models: the centralised decision model (CDM), two decentralised decision models (DDMs) led by fresh food supplier (P-S-L model) and OCLB (P-L-S model) to further explore the optimal decisions. The results show that, when consumers have higher dual preferences of freshness and live-streaming recommendation level, in the P-S-L model, it is in the best interest of the supply chain as a whole to pursue ‘neutral’ control power and choose a ‘moderate pricing and decent quality’ strategy, but in the P-L-S model, the OCLB as the dominant party can pursue higher control power, increase the selling price, or relax its preservation technology upgrading program, which may compensate for the loss of high preservation costs. This study follows the popular topic of live-streaming with goods, opens up new ideas to improve the high profitability of supply chain enterprises.

Title: Multi-win Analysis and Preference Elicitation with Immersive Technology that Updates Consumers’ New Product Knowledge
Authors: Baozhuang Niu, Shu Tao, Haotao Xu, Fanzhuo Zeng

Title: Consolidating circular economy, resilience and sustainability indicators for healthcare supply chain modelling
Authors: Fatemeh Alidoost, Navonil Mustafee, Thomas Monks, Alison Harper
Affiliations: University of Exeter

Title: Free medical consultations: a blessing or a curse? The trade-offs between patients and doctors in a two-sided healthcare platform
Authors: Hengjia Bao, Shaofu Du, Tengfei Nie
Affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China; Shandong University

Title: Scheduling algorithms for time-dependent V-shaped processing times with agreeable slopes around a common ideal time
Authors: Nir Halman, Helmut A. Sedding
Abstract: Abstract We study a single-machine problem with time-dependent processing times following a V-shape around a common ideal time. The slopes are under an agreeableness condition and can be asymmetric and job-specific. Its application lies in production with a moving assembly line, to minimize a worker’s walking time retrieving parts from a supply point, in which part weight affects walking velocity. In this problem, the global start time (or ideal time) can be fixed or variable. For both variants, we devise the first function-based monotonic dynamic programs, which let us derive fully polynomial time approximation schemes employing a recent framework for K -approximation sets and functions. For the variable variant with asymmetric, job-uniform slopes, we introduce a polynomial time algorithm.

Title: Multi-agent collaboration in infrastructure digital transformation: a dual-layer network evolutionary game analysis
Authors: Guolong Wei, Xin Ning, Bingsheng Liu
Abstract: As digital technologies and intelligence become deeply integrated, infrastructure is undergoing an unprecedented digital transformation. In this context, effective collaboration among multi-agents, such as digital technology firms (DTFs) and traditional infrastructure operating organizations (TIOs), is regarded as a crucial driver of digital infrastructure transformation (DTI). However, the divergence between the self-interested motivations of DTFs and the prosocial objectives of TIOs, coupled with the digital operational risks involved, poses significant challenges to multi-agent coordination. Adopting a dual perspective of both intra- and inter-agent levels, this study constructs a dual-layer network game model to investigate the formation mechanism of multi-agent strategic collaborative behaviors in environments characterized by conflict and uncertainty. The results indicate that the emergence of agent collaboration arises from the nonlinear interactions among multiple factors. Specifically, increases in benefits and policy guidance serve as positive drivers of collaboration, whereas costs and free-riding gains exert inhibitory effects. Interestingly, the dual-layer network topology moderates these effects. We find that collaborative stability is optimized when DTFs and TIOs are embedded in WS-WS and BA-WS structures, respectively. Furthermore, the intensity of these factors determines the sequence in which collaborative behaviors emerge. Under resource-constrained conditions, it becomes particularly critical to harness reputational benefits, manage free-riding gains, implement penalties for non-cooperation, and control collaboration costs. These insights help operations managers promote effective multi-agent coordination in DTI, ultimately enabling the realization of exceptional DTI value in the operational environment.

Title: Blessing or curse? User trading and its impact in three‐part tariffs
Authors: Weixiang Huang, Junjie Li, Shujun Li, Xuhui Wang, Han Zhu
Affiliations: South China University of Technology Guangzhou China; Dongbei University of Finance and Economics Dalian China
Abstract: Abstract Service providers across various industries frequently employ three‐part tariffs, characterized by an access fee, an allowance, and an overage price. Under demand uncertainty, subscribers with low realized demand may sell their unused allowances to those with high realized demand through a trading platform, a practice we refer to as user trading. This paper analyzes the impact of user trading within the framework of three‐part tariffs. We characterize the firm's optimal tariffs both without and with user trading. We show that user trading does not necessarily benefit the firm; its profit impact depends critically on marginal production cost. When marginal production cost is low, the production‐cost saving from trading is insufficient to offset the lower access fee. When marginal production cost is sufficiently high, trading becomes profitable because either the production‐cost saving exceeds the access‐fee loss or the access‐fee gain exceeds the displaced overage revenue. We further show that the firm optimally charges no transaction fee because such a fee weakens the benefits of user trading without increasing the firm's profit.

Title: The streaming games: A model of asymmetric competition in subscription video on demand platforms
Authors: Anurag Garg, Soohyun Cho, Subhajyoti Bandyopadhyay
Affiliations: Analytics, Information and Operations The University of Kansas Lawrence Kansas USA; Accounting and Information Systems Rutgers—State University of New Jersey Newark New Jersey USA; Information Systems and Operations Management University of Florida Gainesville Florida USA
Abstract: Abstract Subscription video on demand has matured quickly, and platform configurations have changed with it. The first wave of entrants competed on AI‐driven personalization; the field today is realigning around hybrid menus in which an advertising‐funded tier sits beside the premium one. We develop a game‐theoretic model of asymmetric competition between two platform archetypes: CP A , which invests in mass customization reach, and CP B , which versions its service into premium and ad‐supported tiers. We introduce a threshold‐based model of service quality degradation, in which consumers experience disutility only when ad intensity exceeds an individual‐specific tolerance. Integrating mass customization, service versioning, and two‐sided platform advertising in a single framework, we uncover an interaction none of these literatures reveals alone. Modeling customization reach as a costly capability the platform chooses, we find optimal reach is strictly higher when the platform also operates an ad‐supported tier: Personalization and versioning are complements, not competing strategies, and the case for pairing them strengthens as advertising revenue per user grows. Grounding the pivot decision in an explicit fixed cost of entering the advertising business, we characterize the ad‐revenue threshold at which a personalization‐led platform should launch its own tier and show platforms that acquire reach more cheaply cross that threshold sooner. This research contributes to the discourse on disruptive technologies by characterizing algorithmic personalization and ad‐tech infrastructure as jointly provisioned capabilities whose returns reinforce one another.

Title: Opening Hours and Consumer Behavior: Evidence From GPS Data and Deregulation
Authors: Javier D. Donna, Marit Hinnosaar, Toomas Hinnosaar, André Trindade
Affiliations: Herbert Business School and Rimini Center for Economic Analysis University of Miami Coral Gables Florida USA; School of Economics University of Nottingham and CEPR Nottingham UK; Nova School of Business and Economics Nova University of Lisbon and FGV EPGE Lisbon Portugal
Abstract: ABSTRACT In 2019, North Dakota repealed its Sunday closing law, which had required most non‐grocery stores to close between midnight and noon. Using this policy change and consumer GPS data, we study the impact of opening hours on shopping behavior and welfare. We compare visits before and after the repeal in North Dakota and neighboring states using difference‐in‐differences and event‐study designs. The repeal caused a large increase in Sunday morning visits, originating partly from intertemporal, store‐type, and cross‐border substitution. The closing law's welfare loss is equivalent to increasing the travel distance to affected stores by about 1.4 miles per consumer.

Title: FOMC Announcements and Household Expectations
Authors: Fiorella De Fiore, Marco Lombardi, Johannes Schuffels
Affiliations: Monetary and Economic Department Bank for International Settlements and CEPR Basel Switzerland; European Commission Brussels Belgium
Abstract: ABSTRACT We study the impact of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcements on household expectations by comparing responses to the Survey of Consumer Expectations before and after Federal Open Market Committee meetings, over the period 2013–2019. We find that Fed decisions strongly affect expectations of interest rates on savings accounts, but the impact on the expectations of other variables, notably inflation, is muted. We explore three possible factors that can rationalise our results: (i) Lack of information, that is, the signals sent by the Federal Reserve on its actions via the media are not sufficiently strong to reach a sufficiently large share of the households; (ii) lack of understanding, that is, not enough households grasp the transmission of monetary policy to real activity and/or inflation; and (iii) lack of attention, that is, most households neglect monetary policy news as they focus on issues that are perceived as affecting them more closely. We provide evidence that these explanations partly contribute to the results, but none of them fully accounts for the insensitivity of household inflation expectations.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Reconfiguring supplier networks for net-zero supply chains: Mechanisms and trade-offs of resource orchestration
Authors: Umair Tanveer, Shamaila Ishaq, Thinh Gia Hoang, Fosso Wamba Samuel
Abstract: This study investigates how firms in orchestrate and reconfigure their supplier networks to achieve low-carbon outcomes and examines the trade-offs they face throughout this process. Guided by Resource Orchestration Theory, a qualitative multiple-case research design was employed, drawing on 56 semi-structured interviews, archival documents and field observations from eight anonymised firms across diverse sectors. The analysis reveals a four-stage orchestration process, resource identification and selection, configuration and integration, activation and mobilisation, and adaptation and renewal, each stage associated with distinctive trade-offs between agility and quality, investment and efficiency, margin and supplier uptake, and flexibility and scale. The study advances Resource Orchestration Theory (ROT) by conceptualising low-carbon supply-chain transformation as a multi-tier, trade-off-laden capability rather than a one-off resource alignment. Practically, it offers managers a roadmap for building low-carbon supplier networks through collaborative engagement, embedded carbon criteria in procurement and adaptive planning to deliver emissions reductions without undermining operational performance.

Title: The fantasy of digital immateriality: AI, ecologically unequal exchange, and appropriation of lived human time
Authors: Maximilian Mai Pieper, Alf Hornborg
Abstract: The purported immateriality of AI technologies is as illusory as the general understanding of conventional technologies as simply the application of politically neutral knowledge to nature. The materiality of technologies and their foundation in global inequalities has been illuminated by studies of ecologically unequal exchange (EUE). The aim of this article is to extend the applicability of EUE theory to digital technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) by highlighting how even the data that they process have an inevitably biophysical history. AI technologies represent a novelty mainly in the sense that, in addition to exploiting extractive areas through EUE, they are based on the appropriation of data from the public. We argue for understanding the materiality of data as derived from lived human time. AI's dependence on data can thus be regarded as representing and embodying biophysical processes and asymmetric transfers implicating issues of justice.

Title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions
Authors: Christopher Martin, Hiroe Ishihara
Abstract: The dialectic relationship between the production of post-growth knowledge and ongoing construction of social reality is a complex one, but one that warrants attention. In this scoping review, we respond to the emergent interest in post-growth politics and theories of change. We aim to complement existing reviews of post-growth policy proposals and recommendations with an analysis of peer-reviewed studies on interventions – deliberate attempts by one state, market or civil society actor to influence another. Drawing on a socio-ecological systems leverage points perspective embedded within a political economy inspired mapping of social forces, we develop a conceptual framework for explaining strategic trade-offs made by actors to achieve various forms of depth.Our findings point to asymmetrical relationships between actors-executor pairs and a pattern of neoliberal subjectification in both intervention design and analytical focus. We also find that whilst post-growth interventions can readily achieve discursive depth, it is often accompanied by institutional shallowness and temporal fragility. We conclude with reflections on strategic implications for post-growth researchers and movements.

Title: Incomplete markets, crop portfolios, and agricultural productivity
Authors: Albert Rodríguez-Sala
Abstract: Using the Uganda National Panel Survey, I document that farmers face a trade-off between crop yields and risk, that most grow both high- and low-yield crops, and that poorer farmers concentrate on the low-yield, low-risk ones. I then develop an incomplete-markets model with a crop-portfolio choice, in which households trade off income returns against consumption smoothing. Wealth-poor households optimally under-invest in intermediates and shift toward safer crops. Crop portfolios, intermediate input use, and the wealth distribution are jointly determined in equilibrium. The model also reproduces the low pass-through of both income inequality and income volatility into consumption. Calibrated to rural Uganda, it implies that completing markets raises agricultural productivity by 12.8%, with 15.8% of the gain coming from eliminating the misallocation of inputs across farmers and crops. Consumption rises by 17.6% and welfare by 17.4%, with income inequality rising slightly and consumption inequality unchanged.

Title: Together or apart? Migration, education access, and intergenerational mobility in China
Authors: Jingxuan Du
Abstract: This paper studies how hukou-based education wedges and child-arrangement costs jointly shape welfare and intergenerational educational mobility in China. I develop a quantitative spatial model with overlapping generations in which households sequentially choose education, migration, and child arrangement, and estimate it using census and household-survey data. Under a common financing rule, two child-targeted policies raise the co-migration rate to a similar extent but differ sharply in welfare and mobility. Subsidizing co-migrating families in high-cost destinations generates 1.4 times as much welfare per unit of government revenue as removing migrant children's education-access wedges. These gains concentrate on recipients. Removing the education-access wedges delivers over four times the mobility gain per unit of revenue, and the resulting human capital generates growing welfare gains across generations. A broader reform that equalizes public-service access for all migrants is the most welfare-efficient but does not raise mobility.

Title: Skill certifications and migrant labor market integration: Experimental evidence from Colombia
Authors: Matias Busso, Carolina Gonzalez-Velosa, Juan Muñoz-Morales, Juanita Ruiz, Juan D. Valencia, Cynthia van der Werf
Abstract: This paper studies whether government-issued skill certification improves labor market integration when workers’ skills are hard to verify. We evaluate a randomized offer of access to an occupation-specific certification program in Colombia among locals and migrants, two groups with different ex ante signaling capacity. The program certifies existing skills rather than providing training. Among locals, the offer increases employment by reducing inactivity and raises hours worked. The effects persist unevenly over time and are robust to attrition bounds and alternative outcome measures. Among migrants, estimates are less precise and provide no evidence of effects in employment, hours, or wages. The results show that a common skill certification generates different patterns of labor-market adjustment among locals and migrants.

Title: Green credit financing versus buyer direct financing: Strategic choice of financing scheme under capital constraint and cap-and-trade regulation
Authors: Qi Lin, Qiuhong Zhao, Peter Shi, Yao Li
Abstract: Carbon emissions reductions have been recognized as global priorities. Cap-and-trade regulations are commonly used by policymakers to reduce carbon emissions. However, many enterprises are troubled by limited capital. We consider a supply chain consisting of an upstream manufacturer under capital constraint and a downstream buyer under cap-and-trade regulation, highlighting the link between upstream product greenness and downstream carbon emissions from a carbon footprint perspective. Three financing schemes are considered: no financing (NF), green credit financing (GCF), and buyer direct financing (BDF). We model the supply chain under GCF and BDF by imposing a hard constraint on carbon emissions and introducing cost sharing for carbon emissions, respectively. We compare equilibrium financing decisions and expected profits across the three financing schemes. Our results show that BDF performs best in promoting product greenness in most cases because it relaxes the capital constraint and avoids the carbon emissions constraint imposed under GCF. BDF can achieve a win-win outcome for supply chain members and is often preferred by the buyer, whereas the manufacturer's financing choice depends on specific operational parameters. When the buyer's carbon cap is large, the buyer has an incentive to offer BDF, and even a manufacturer with sufficient initial capital may still seek BDF because it reshapes the manufacturer's cost structure. We also find that a larger carbon cap and higher product greenness efficiency do not necessarily lead to carbon emissions reductions. These findings provide insights into how financing schemes can coordinate green investments and carbon emissions reductions.

Title: How does information about inequalities affect fairness views and policy preferences?
Authors: Julia Baarck, Mathias Dolls, Lisa Windsteiger
Abstract: This study investigates how information about intragenerational and intergenerational inequalities shapes fairness perceptions and policy preferences. Using a large-scale randomized survey experiment with 4900 respondents in Germany, we examine how exposure to information about wealth and age disparities affects (i) perceptions of distributive and intergenerational fairness, and (ii) support for redistributive and future-oriented policies. We find that roughly two thirds of respondents underestimate the extent of existing inequalities. Moreover, providing accurate information about wealth and age disparities has little effect on left-leaning and centrist respondents, but it produces a peculiar response among right-leaning individuals: the information increases their perceptions of the fairness of the status quo and reduces their support for redistributive and future-oriented policies. Overall, the findings suggest that informational interventions in politicized domains such as inequality may have limited effects when they are perceived as politically biased.

Title: A sequential fix-and-optimize framework and pricing-guided search for efficient truck scheduling at a cross-docking terminal
Authors: Bokang Li, Ren Moses, Eren E. Ozguven, Seckin Ozkul, Amir M. Fathollahi-Fard, Maxim A. Dulebenets
Abstract: Cross-docking facilities play a critical role in modern freight distribution systems by enabling rapid consolidation and redistribution of shipments with little or no intermediate storage. As cargo handling volumes continue to increase, inefficient coordination between inbound unloading, internal transshipment, and outbound loading operations often leads to severe congestion, prolonged truck waiting, and departure delays, significantly increasing operational costs. This paper addresses a cross-docking truck scheduling problem aimed at determining coordinated service plans that minimize total operational cost, including truck waiting, freight handling, temporary storage, and delay penalties under tightly coupled inbound-outbound interactions. An efficient mixed-integer linear programming model is developed together with two innovative solution frameworks designed to overcome the computational complexity of the decision problem. The first framework adopts a sequential fix-and-optimize strategy that progressively constructs a feasible service plan through precedence-consistent batching, thereby substantially reducing problem dimensionality while preserving global scheduling feasibility. The second framework introduces a pricing-guided search mechanism in which single-truck insertion pricing is exploited to systematically identify cost-reducing schedule modifications, allowing promising structural adjustments to be explored without repeatedly resolving the full optimization model. A comprehensive computational study demonstrates that the proposed formulation and solution frameworks consistently produce high-quality schedules with significantly improved computational efficiency across a wide range of problem instances, thereby providing an effective and scalable decision support tool for managing large-scale and congestion-sensitive cross-docking operations in modern freight distribution systems. Moreover, a series of sensitivity analyses is performed to gain strategic insights regarding the key tradeoffs during cross-docking operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Out-of-sample performance of robust inventory policy: Evaluation and sensitivity analysis
Authors: Hancheng Lu, Jia Zhao, Jianping Li
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the out-of-sample performance of a data-driven newsvendor model built from historical demand data. We develop a closed-form representation of the out-of-sample expected profit under robust inventory order policy, providing a tractable tool for performance evaluation and for the selection of ambiguity-aversion level. We then conduct a sensitivity analysis of the out-of-sample profit with respect to cost and price parameters. We show that, under demand ambiguity, a reduction in cost or an increase in price at finitely many points could hurt the out-of-sample expected profits. Higher ambiguity-aversion level reduces the likelihood of these monotonicity reversals. Our results offer a clearer understanding of how robust inventory decisions behave out of sample.

Title: Pareto ranking identification for multi-objective stochastic simulation models
Authors: Byeong Soo Kim, Seon Han Choi
Abstract: Multi-objective stochastic simulation is widely used to evaluate candidate designs with conflicting performance measures, but simulation noise makes it costly to reliably determine Pareto dominance relationships. Ranking and selection (R&S) methods reduce this cost by selectively allocating simulation replications; however, existing multi-objective R&S methods have mainly focused on selecting the first Pareto set. In practice, decision makers may also need lower Pareto-ranked alternatives because final decisions can depend on qualitative, operational, or political factors not captured by the simulation model. This study proposes an R&S method for identifying Pareto-ranked sets, defined as successive layers of nondominated alternatives, up to a user-specified rank h[jls-end-space/]. The proposed method evaluates the statistical evidence for the observed Pareto-ranking structure and sequentially allocates additional replications to designs whose ranks remain uncertain. Experiments show that the proposed method requires substantially fewer replications than equal allocation and a sequential Pareto set selection baseline. Additional results show that the method remains effective under objective correlations and in a practical simulation case study. Furthermore, its integration with the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) improves multi-objective evolutionary optimization in noisy environments.

Title: Cost-effectiveness assessment for China's emission reduction in steel, cement, and electrolytic aluminum industries
Authors: Zhaohua Wang, Yukun Wang, Hongzhi Zhang, Hao Li, Zhijie Jia, Yuli Shan
Abstract: Industrial carbon emissions contribute substantially to global warming, and China has the highest industrial output globally. Among the industrial sectors, iron and steel, cement, and electrolytic aluminum account for over one-third of China's total carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions and are critical for climate change mitigation. This study assesses the CO 2 mitigation potential, multiple mitigation costs, and cost-effective mitigation strategy portfolios of three typical industrial sectors using the global change analysis model coupled with bottom-up technology-specific models under three mitigation scenarios based on the shared socioeconomic pathways with representative concentration pathways framework. Under the carbon neutrality scenario, these three sectors contribute a cumulative emission reduction of 60.4Gt during 2020–2060, accounting for 21.1% of the national CO 2 emission reduction targets by 2060. Achieving such emission reduction could result in total cumulative mitigation costs of 1019.7 billion constant 2020 US dollars (USD) during 2020–2060 for these three sectors. Specifically, a higher CO 2 reduction scenario in line with the 1.5 °C target requires more ambitious mitigation strategies, which cost 833.7 billion USD of additional costs more than the carbon neutrality scenario (CNS). Despite a short-term cost increase after 2050 in the iron and steel and cement sectors, mitigation costs are concentrated before 2040, driven by the large mitigation potential of relatively low-cost technologies such as fuel substitution and energy efficiency improvements in the two sectors. CO 2 reduction strategies in the three industrial sectors will be more cost-effective than other industries, with the unit mitigation cost being 1.2%–12.3% lower than the national average. Our findings quantify the multiple mitigation costs of these three sectors and inform policy support that prioritizes earlier financing for low-cost options before 2040, continued support after 2050 for capital-intensive technologies (e.g., CCS), and sector-specific, staged transition pathways.

Title: Assessing determinants of CO2 emissions trajectory under technology uncertainty: A probabilistic approach to index decomposition analysis
Authors: Hui Wang, Yupeng Wang, Yong Yang, Peng Zhou
Abstract: Assessing determinants of emissions paths is critical to climate policymaking. Since energy technology uncertainty has profound and prevalent impacts on future emissions paths, examining the emissions determinants under technology uncertainty is essential to identify robust mitigation measures. However, a formal characterization of the uncertain patterns of emissions determinants is lacking in the literature, which further makes the uncertainty in emissions determinants implicitly quantified. To address this gap, we introduce a probabilistic approach to index decomposition analysis. The uncertain patterns of determinants are first characterized using the nonparametric kernel method, based on which probabilistic methods are adapted to measure the degrees of uncertainties in the determinants and examine their uncertain roles. The proposed approach is thus able to quantify the uncertain determinants of future emissions paths under technology uncertainty. Applying the proposed model to China's electricity sector reveals the evidently uncertain determinants and their overall pattern under technology uncertainty throughout 2060. While phasing out fossil electricity and deploying CCS are two robust mitigation measures, the emissions effects of energy intensity improvement and greening fossil electricity structure are fairly unstable. Policy implications of the results are further discussed.

Title: On the optimization of warehousing handling unit partitioning
Authors: Jay Amer, Xueping Li
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Systems Engineering, University of Tennessee—Knoxville
Abstract: This study examines handling-unit partitioning (HUP) for parts-to-picker systems under stochastic demand—an NP-hard design problem—and propose a practical framework for industrial deployment. We develop two complementary solvers: an exact two-stage stochastic mixed-integer program (SMIP) for moderate sizes and a two-stage genetic algorithm (GA) for larger instances, both using sample-average approximation to represent demand uncertainty. We introduce a simple HUP pattern-distance metric and show that maximizing the minimum distance among selected patterns reliably shortens SMIP convergence time without degrading objective value. Using data from a U.S. distribution center, we find that allowing two patterns (vs. one) reduces required pod faces by about 10.6–12.6% (statistically significant), with diminishing returns beyond two—yielding meaningful footprint and capital savings. The stochastic design consistently outperforms a deterministic average-demand baseline, while the incremental benefit available even with perfect foresight is modest, indicating that most of the achievable improvement is already captured. Across instances, GA attains about 95% of SMIP’s objective on average while generally running faster and scaling to e-commerce–sized assortments.

Title: Platform’s information sharing strategy in a supplier encroachment context with economies of scale
Authors: Pengwen Hou, Zihan Liu, Hubert Pun, Jun Wang
Affiliations: Business School, Nankai University; Ivey Business School, Western University; School of Management Science and Engineering, Tianjin University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: This paper investigates a new business phenomenon where platforms nurture contract manufacturers (CMs) by sharing market demand information. We consider a game-theoretical model that an original brand manufacturer (OBM) outsources the production to a CM, who encroaches the end-customer market with a competing product. The CM’s production cost can benefit from economies of scale. Both the OBM and the CM sell their product through a common online platform. The platform has accurate market demand information and determines whether to share with the CM. When it does, a signaling game between the OBM and the CM arises. Unlike a typical signaling game, we show that each type of CM may have an incentive to mimic the other type. This is driven by the CM’s two opposite drivers: wants the OBM to order more to achieve economies of scale, versus wants the OBM to order less to reduce competition at the end-customer market. We also find that information sharing may lead to lower demands and higher prices, and customers and social welfare may suffer as a result. Lastly, due to this information sharing option, we demonstrate how economies of scale can hurt the platform and the OBM.

Title: Time-varying capacity planning for designing large-scale homeless care systems
Authors: Graham C. M. Burgess, Dashi I. Singham, Luke A. Rhodes-Leader
Affiliations: STOR-i Centre for Doctoral Training, Lancaster University; Operations Research Department, Naval Postgraduate School; Department of Management Science, Lancaster University
Abstract: Many people in communities around the world are facing homelessness due to housing shortages. The San Francisco Bay Area has struggled to provide housing for thousands of people who are unsheltered. Permanent housing is the ideal solution for most people entering the system, but temporary shelter is also critical. Investment in housing and shelter is paramount to providing a long-term solution to serve the current and future homeless population. We construct a queueing model for tracking the flow of single adults through shelter and housing based on Alameda County’s coordinated entry system. In contrast to routing or allocation policies, we optimize the system through increasing shelter and housing server capacities. We formulate optimization problems to reduce the size of the unsheltered population given cost constraints by varying investment in housing and shelter over time. Additionally, we impose policy-based shape constraints to reflect the time-dependence and feasibility constraints associated with planning decisions. We thus show how resources can be allocated between housing and shelter over time. While this joint optimization approach can be used to analyze homeless populations outside of Alameda County, it also can be broadly applied to capacity investment decisions for tandem queueing systems, for example, in healthcare settings.

Title: Self-sustained community emergency preparedness and initial response planning considering volunteer dispatching
Authors: Qingyi Wang, Yonghuan He, Xiaozhou He
Affiliations: Business School, Sichuan University; Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Management Science and Operations Research Institute, Sichuan University
Abstract: Self-sustained emergency preparedness and response planning, considering the dispatch of registered volunteers, is crucial for protecting human life safety in some isolated communities that cannot quickly obtain external support and lack official emergency human resources in the initial response phase after disasters. However, this problem is rarely addressed in the literature. To fill the research gap, this study proposes a two-stage stochastic programming model that facilitates the integrated management of pre-disaster emergency supply pre-stocking and post-disaster response, including supply delivery and service provision via volunteer dispatching, under goals of cost effectiveness and response fairness. We examine five comparison plans to show the benefits of our proposed model. With a real-world case study, we highlight its effectiveness and obtain managerial insights for better field practice. This study emphasizes the importance of improving self-sustained community emergency response ability through emergency supply pre-positioning and coordinated volunteer dispatching.

Title: Dynamic and static item allocation for the in-store front warehouses
Authors: Chu Chu, Shiming Deng, Wen Luo
Affiliations: School of Management, Huazhong University of Science and Technology
Abstract: In response to furious competition from emerging online retailers, traditional supermarkets begin leveraging their brick-and-mortar store chains by setting up small in-store front warehouses to facilitate order picking processes for online orders. In this paper, we investigate how to select products and allocate space for the in-store front warehouse under dynamic and static strategies to minimize the total order-picking workload. For the dynamic allocation problem, we formulate it as a mixed-integer programming (MIP) model, which can be decomposed into a master multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) and an order picking problem (OPP) as sub-problems. An exact algorithm and a heuristic that is 1/2-bounded under certain routing policies are proposed. For the static allocation problem, we construct a stochastic gradient estimator of the expected travel distance by infinitesimal perturbation analysis (IPA) and introduce a discrete Frank-Wolfe algorithm to solve it. Numerical results reveal that the logic of dynamic allocation for the in-store front warehouse is different from that for regular warehouses, and the storage location assignment for the shelf area in supermarkets greatly impact the performance of these allocation strategies. The experimental results using data from a real retailer validate the effectiveness of proposed algorithms.

Title: Wavelet Gaussian process for multi-scale monitoring of imaging data
Authors: Runsang Liu, Hui Yang
Affiliations: Complex System Monitoring, Modeling, and Control Laboratory, The Pennsylvania State University
Abstract: Advanced sensing brings a plethora of imaging data to handle process variations in additive manufacturing (AM). Realizing the full potential of sensor-based statistical process control (SPC) methods greatly depends on the delineation of defect characteristics and anomalous patterns. However, traditional methods primarily focus on analyzing and monitoring AM images in a single scale. It is common that these images contain hidden patterns pertinent to process deviations that are not accessible in a single-scale view. This paper presents a new wavelet Gaussian process (WGP) framework for multi-scale analysis of variance (ANOVA) and image-guided SPC of AM. First, AM imaging data are examined through multi-scale wavelet lenses to reveal hidden defects in different spatial-frequency resolutions. Second, WGP models are developed to analyze different sources of variation in wavelet coefficients. Specifically, we separate the contribution of standard profile, layerwise variation, and process shifts. We further design generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) formulation and multi-scale hypothesis testing approaches to fuse test statistics from different wavelet sub-bands for AM quality monitoring. The proposed WGP approach is evaluated and validated through simulation and real-world case studies. Experimental results demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed WGP method for multi-scale analysis and monitoring of imaging data.

Title: Combating wage theft in subcontracted day labor markets
Authors: James P. Bailey, Bahar Çavdar, Yanling Chang
Affiliations: Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; Department of Operations Research and Engineering Management, Southern Methodist University
Abstract: In subcontracted day labor markets, workers are especially vulnerable to wage theft, particularly in sectors like construction where subcontracting industry structures complicate accountability. This article introduces a principal-agent model to examine the conditions necessary to mitigate wage theft in subcontracted labor arrangements, focusing on the relationship between subcontractors and day laborers. We find that the fines necessary to eliminate theft are significantly larger than those imposed by current practices, making wage theft likely to persist under penalty-based methods alone. Through numerical analysis, we show how wage theft disproportionately affects workers with lower reservation utilities, and observe that workers with similar reservation utilities experience comparable impacts, regardless of their skill levels. To address the limitations of penalty-based approaches, we extend the model to a repeated game that formally characterizes the impact of worker awareness. We prove that wage theft becomes a dominated strategy—and is thus fully eliminated—when workers are fully aware of a subcontractor’s history, even when formal penalties are weak. More broadly, our analysis reveals the complementary relationship between wage theft prevention policies and information sharing: modest penalties become highly effective when paired with transparency initiatives, while heightened awareness can successfully deter theft even in environments with limited enforcement. This highlights that fostering worker awareness is a powerful and viable policy lever for preventing wage theft.

Title: A hybrid exact algorithm for order batching and assignment in warehouses
Authors: Jiajing Gao, Lu Zhen, Zheyi Tan, Shuaian Wang
Affiliations: School of Management, Shanghai University; Faculty of Business, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University
Abstract: This paper studies an order batching and assignment problem for an warehousing system considering uncertain future orders. Orders that continuously enter a pool are handled in batches, and the core decision of the problem is to categorize the orders in the pool into batches and assign the orders in the current batch to picking stations in the system. When making the decision for the current batch of orders, we consider future orders with uncertain Stock Keeping Units (SKU) requirements and their quantities. Using mixed-integer linear programming, this paper proposes a two-stage stochastic programming model with integer recourses, which is difficult to solve using traditional algorithms. Thus, a hybrid exact algorithm that combines the branch-and-price algorithm, column generation, and the logic-based Benders decomposition is designed and implemented to solve the model. To accelerate the algorithmic solving process, we propose some new cuts and apply parallel computing techniques to solve some of the subproblems embedded in the algorithm. We also conduct experiments to validate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm and derive some potentially useful managerial insights. For example, a counter-intuitive result is that the more picking stations there are, the worse the objective is (i.e., the total travel time of used pods). In addition, the more SKUs are required per order, the worse the objective is, while the more SKUs are stored per pod, the better the objective is. Furthermore, the deployment of picking stations along one short side of the warehouse is the best layout for the system.

Title: Corporate strategy for the green transition: Are executive incentives effective?
Authors: Cécile Cezanne, Francesco Quatraro, Sandra Rigot, Eleonora Rubichi
Abstract: This paper examines whether green incentives embedded in executive compensation schemes are associated with a reorientation of firms' innovative activities toward environmentally sustainable technologies. Drawing on agency theory and the attention-based view of the firm, we conceptualize green incentives as governance and management-control devices that can mitigate managerial short-termism and channel executive attention toward long-horizon environmental objectives, thereby redirecting firms' technological search. Using a panel of publicly listed U.S. and European firms that participate in the Carbon Disclosure Project over the period 2010–2020, we analyse green innovation as a multi-stage process comprising the reorientation of technological search (the distance of firms' patent portfolios from green domains), knowledge recombination (the citation of green prior art in non-green patents), and realized green innovation output (green patent counts and shares). Firms adopting green incentives exhibit higher green innovation output, a significant repositioning of their knowledge portfolios toward green technological domains, and a greater integration of green knowledge into non-green technologies. These associations are weaker among firms experiencing a recent deterioration in carbon performance, and are strongest among continental European firms. Overall, the findings suggest that executive green incentives are associated with the direction, and not merely the volume, of firms' innovative activities, highlighting the role of internal governance mechanisms in sustainability transitions while recognising the limits of causal inference in observational data.

Title: Gendered environmental leadership and the rise of biodiversity finance
Authors: Sinda Hadhri
Abstract: This paper examines whether gender diversity in environmental governance is associated with biodiversity-finance outcomes across the 27 European Union countries between 2012 and 2023. We distinguish between administrative, ministerial, and legislative dimensions of women's representation and evaluate their relationship with biodiversity-finance volume and intensity using fixed-effects Poisson and fractional-response models. The results provide limited evidence that gender representation alone systematically predicts biodiversity-finance outcomes. Female representation in environmental administrations is negatively associated with biodiversity-finance intensity, while female environment ministers are positively associated with intensity. No robust unconditional relationship is observed for biodiversity-finance volume. However, several conditional patterns emerge. In the later years of the sample, higher female representation in environmental administrations, ministerial positions, and parliamentary environmental committees becomes more strongly associated with biodiversity expenditure. Similarly, the positive association between female ministers and biodiversity-finance outcomes is stronger in countries characterized by higher levels of women's political empowerment. By contrast, threshold analyses provide little evidence of critical-mass effects. Overall, the findings suggest that the relationship between gender diversity and biodiversity finance is conditional on institutional and policy context rather than representation alone. These results contribute to the emerging literature on biodiversity finance by highlighting how governance structures may shape biodiversity-related public spending.

Title: Secure and efficient networks
Authors: Oleh Stupak
Abstract: More connected networks are often regarded as more efficient, yet increased connectivity can elevate security risks, suggesting that sparser networks may be preferable from a security perspective. In this article, we study the trade-off between efficiency and security in networks. We develop a model in which a Defender and an Attacker engage in a two-stage game. First, the Defender builds a network by establishing costly links, where each node’s value is determined by its degree. Then, the Defender protects a limited number of nodes while the Attacker selects a node to target. Our analysis yields three main insights. First, by choosing the network’s degree sequence in the first stage, the Defender shapes the second-stage equilibrium and limits the expected loss from an attack. Second, the optimal network becomes sparser as link costs rise: a complete network is optimal when costs are low, while the centrally protected star, often regarded as the most secure configuration, arises only when costs are high. Third, when defensive resources are limited, a novel “maxi-core” structure arises in equilibrium, with a fully connected core surrounded by a sparse periphery.

Title: Land registration and conflict reduction: Evidence from the Brazilian Amazon
Authors: Nilesh Shinde, Stella Z. Schons, Alexandre G. Maia, Gregory S. Amacher
Abstract: Environmental land registries are increasingly used to support forest governance, yet their potential contribution to reducing rural land conflict remains poorly understood. Brazil’s Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR) requires landholders to self-declare property boundaries and land use for environmental compliance but neither confers legal title nor resolves competing land claims. Before becoming mandatory under Brazil’s 2012 Forest Code, the CAR was mandated in the Amazonian state of Pará beginning in 2008. We exploit this early implementation to examine whether an environmental land registry can reduce rural violence in frontier regions characterized by weak property rights and limited state capacity. Using municipality-level panel data (2001–2012) and a synthetic difference-in-differences design, we estimate that early CAR implementation reduced land conflict events by 11.5%, families affected by conflict by 33.4%, and land-related death threats by 10.0%. Murders and attempted murders are too rare for the design to detect effects of plausible magnitude. The estimated reductions are not uniform across outcomes or institutional environments. Death threats decline consistently across all estimation samples, whereas reductions in conflict events and families affected are concentrated in municipalities with complementary governance programs and stronger pre-treatment enforcement capacity. These findings are consistent with environmental registration operating through complementary informational and institutional channels. Documenting land occupation appears sufficient to discourage lower-intensity forms of conflict, while larger reductions in realized conflict require institutions capable of acting on the information the registry provides. More broadly, the results suggest that information-based land administration can improve land governance before formal property rights are resolved.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Threshold HAR model for interval-valued time series
Authors: Changryong Baek, Chihoon Lee, Seungwon Lee
Abstract: We propose a threshold heterogeneous autoregressive model for interval-valued time series (THARI). Building on the heterogeneous autoregressive (HAR) framework, THARI combines threshold interval autoregression with daily, weekly, and monthly aggregation, allowing multi-horizon interval dynamics to vary across regimes. Estimation uses minimum-DK distance with a feasible positive-definite kernel update. For fixed and feasible kernels, the threshold estimator is T[jls-end-space/]-consistent and the regression estimator is T[jls-end-space/]-consistent. For Ethereum intervals constructed from the 50th and 95th quantiles of 5-minute intraday squared returns, THARI improves DK2 forecasts over TARI(3), while comparison with a non-threshold interval HAR benchmark identifies horizon-dependent threshold gains.

Title: Coordination and leadership: The impact of artificial intelligence
Authors: Maria Bigoni, Damiano Paoli
Abstract: Coordination failure is an obstacle to collective efficiency in many economic and social settings. Leadership can attenuate this problem by providing a focal point through public communication. Yet, the effectiveness of such communication relies on shared trust that the leader’s recommendations will be followed by others. As generative artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly accessible, leaders may use AI-generated texts in their public communications. Whether transparent AI assistance weakens the coordinating role of leadership remains an open question. We investigate this issue through an online experiment based on the minimum effort game with leadership. Leaders could send either a human-written or a ChatGPT-generated message, and followers were informed of the message’s source. Results reveal that coordination outcomes do not differ across treatments: AI-generated and human-written messages are equally effective in promoting coordination on the Pareto-dominant equilibrium. In addition, both leaders’ and followers’ beliefs about other players’ behavior are unaffected by the source of the message. These findings suggest a leader’s transparent choice to communicate through AI-generated messages does not undermine strategic communication or followers’ trust in successful coordination.

Title: Toward efficient urban regional mobility: a region-oriented optimization framework for high-capacity autonomous ride-sharing
Authors: Qiming Su, Xia Luo, Hongjie Wang, Toshiyuki Yamamoto
Abstract: High-capacity autonomous ride-sharing services have significant potential to improve urban mobility efficiency and enhance transportation accessibility, particularly in areas characterized by concentrated travel demand and homogeneous trip patterns. To advance the performance of high-capacity ride-sharing systems in such environments, this study proposes a region-oriented optimization framework that integrates mobility-driven regional partitioning, intra-regional high-capacity ride-sharing, and cross-regional vehicle coordination within a unified operational architecture. Real-world ride-hailing data are utilized to identify tightly connected mobility communities and translate them into operational regions for subsequent ride-sharing operations. Within each region, a path-set-based vehicle-passenger matching model is developed by integrating offline shareable-path-set generation with online vehicle-passenger matching. To address spatiotemporal demand fluctuations, cross-regional vehicle dispatching is further incorporated as a system-coordination mechanism for balancing vehicle resources across operational regions. Case studies based on New York City ride-hailing data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework under heterogeneous urban demand conditions. The identified operational regions effectively capture areas dominated by short-distance travel demand. Across regions with different demand densities, the proposed matching optimization model improves vehicle utilization and service accessibility while substantially reducing total vehicle mileage, with limited impacts on passenger waiting times and detour distances. In addition, the cross-regional dispatching strategy alleviates supply–demand imbalances and further enhances passenger service performance. This framework provides actionable insights for the design of high-capacity autonomous ride-sharing services and supports the transition toward more efficient and sustainable urban transportation systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Long- and short-run determinants of metro ridership in Seoul: A vector error correction model approach
Authors: Saehim Kim, Inseong Lee, Seunghwa Jang, Joonho Ko
Abstract: The metro system is essential infrastructure underpinning urban sustainability and citizen mobility. The Seoul metro system has experienced continuous infrastructure expansion, multiple policy changes, and major external shocks over the past 25 years. This study examined the short- and long-run dynamics of Seoul Metro ridership using 300 monthly time-series observations from January 2000 to December 2024. The analysis considered monthly total metro ridership together with population, bus ridership, precipitation days, gasoline prices, and seasonality and incorporated major policy changes, such as the integrated fare system, metro line extensions, and fare increases, as well as the external shock of the COVID-19 pandemic. Methodologically, a Vector Error Correction Model, in conjunction with Impulse Response Functions and Forecast Error Variance Decomposition, was employed to analyze the short-run dynamics and long-run equilibrium relationships. The Johansen cointegration test identified two cointegrating relationships among Seoul Metro, Seoul bus, and Gyeonggi bus ridership. The empirical results indicate that Seoul Metro demand exhibited a negative short-run association with Seoul bus ridership, suggesting a substitution relationship, and a positive association with Gyeonggi bus ridership, suggesting a complementary relationship at the metropolitan scale. Gyeonggi population showed a significant negative association with metro ridership, while gasoline prices showed a positive association. Seasonal effects were also significant, whereas precipitation days were not statistically significant. By contrast, the short-run effects of the integrated fare system, fare increases, metro line extensions, and COVID-19 were not statistically significant. This study demonstrates how multiple socioeconomic, transport, and policy-related factors are associated with metro demand at the aggregate metropolitan-system level and fills a critical gap in the literature, which has focused on short-term impacts. The findings provide empirical evidence to support sustainable public transport policies in large metropolitan areas.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The traveling salesman problem with release dates and drone resupply: A new formulation and a matheuristic approach
Authors: Claudia Archetti, Maurizio Boccia, Adriano Masone, Claudio Sterle
Abstract: Drones are increasingly used in last-mile logistics to streamline the final, and often complex, delivery stage. While synchronized truck-and-drone systems have been widely studied, direct drone deliveries face regulatory and safety challenges. An emerging alternative is to use drones to resupply delivery trucks in transit, mitigating some regulatory and safety barriers and enhancing efficiency without direct-to-customer deployment. This new system reduces reliance on centralized depots, improves delivery speed, supports real-time order fulfillment, and enhances flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and sustainability. By delivering new packages to trucks on the road, drones can cut detours and fuel use, especially in rural areas, while better matching fluctuating demand. In this context, we tackle the Traveling Salesman Problem with Release Dates and Drone Resupply ( TSP-RD-DR ), which consists of determining the truck route and the drone resupply schedule to serve all customers in accordance with their release dates while minimizing the delivery completion time. We propose a novel formulation for the TSP-RD-DR and a matheuristic approach that exploits this formulation. The proposed methods are tested on benchmark instances and compared with the state of the art for the TSP-RD-DR . The proposed formulation can solve benchmark instances with up to 20 customers within a one-hour time limit. The matheuristic provides high-quality solutions in limited computational times and scales effectively to instances with up to 100 customers.

Title: Best-worst dual-population dual-stage differential evolution for 2D irregular multi-plate layout optimization
Authors: Qifang Luo, Huijie Xu, Yongquan Zhou
Abstract: The two-dimensional irregular layout problem, a classic NP-hard challenge in operational research, is critical for resource-intensive manufacturing industries aiming to minimize material waste. This paper introduces a novel hybrid metaheuristic, the best-worst dual-population dual-stage differential evolution (BWD2S-DE) algorithm, designed to efficiently solve both single-plate and multi-plate variants of this complex nesting problem. BWD2S-DE integrates three key synergistic components: (1) an enhanced mutation operator guided by the best and worst individuals in the population, coupled with a success-history-based adaptive parameter mechanism to refine local exploitation; (2) a dual-population dual-stage evolutionary architecture, where one sub-population employs the full algorithm while another uses a simplified variant, periodically exchanging information to maintain diversity and implementing a staged placement strategy (large items first, then small items) to structure the search process; and (3) a robust geometric foundation using a vector-based No-Fit Polygon (V-NFP) method for fast and accurate overlap detection during layout decoding. While each component draws from prior literature, their coordinated integration for multi-plate irregular layout optimization is novel. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on extended benchmark sets from ESICUP and datasets used in recent literature. Ablation studies confirm the significant contribution of each proposed component. Comparative results against state-of-the-art methods, including the improved dotted board model (IDBM), decimal artificial bee colony (DABC), and various hybrid algorithms (e.g., MAHA), demonstrate that BWD2S-DE achieves competitive material utilization rates (e.g., up to 85.34% for single-plate and 87.32% for multi-plate) with comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, tests on large-scale and real-world garment-cutting scenarios validate the algorithm’s practical effectiveness and robustness, highlighting its potential for industrial adoption.

Title: The spoils of algorithmic collusion: Profit allocation among asymmetric firms
Authors: Simon Martin, Hans-Theo Normann, Paul Püplichhuisen, Tobias Werner
Abstract: We study the propensity of independent algorithms to collude in repeated asymmetric Cournot duopolies, specifically the predictive power of various oligopoly and bargaining solutions with respect to the effect of asymmetry among firms. We find that total quantities are below the static Nash level in all specifications, and they increase with asymmetry. Thus, both consumers and firms can benefit from asymmetry. For low (high) levels of asymmetry, the simulated quantities are above (below) the joint profit-maximizing output. While the static Nash equilibrium provides accurate predictions regarding total welfare, bargaining solutions, such as equal relative gains, better capture our finding of convergence to Pareto-efficient outcomes.

Title: The structure of discrimination against Turkish migrants in Germany
Authors: Silvia Angerer, Hanna Brosch, Daniela Glätzle-Rützler, Philipp Lergetporer, Thomas Rittmannsberger
Abstract: We study the structure and heterogeneity of discriminatory behavior using an incentivized choice experiment with a representative sample of over 2000 adults in Germany. Decision-makers allocate a fixed endowment between two receivers whose migration background, education, gender, and age are randomly varied. This design allows us to compare discrimination across attributes within an integrative framework, analyze how these dimensions interact, and classify individuals into behavioral types. We show pronounced discrimination against Turkish migrants in allocation choices, comparable in magnitude to gender-based preferential treatment in favor of women. Discrimination against Turkish migrants varies systematically with other receiver attributes and across decision makers, and is particularly strong among non-migrants and individuals with right-wing political preferences.

Title: Energy market bubbles under the green transition
Authors: José Manuel Cueto, Isabel Figuerola-Ferretti
Abstract: The 2021–2022 energy crisis generated pronounced episodes of explosive price behavior followed by sharp corrections in gas and electricity markets and raised concerns about whether observed price surges reflected fundamental scarcity or speculative dynamics. This paper examines the presence and synchronization of explosive price behavior across a comprehensive set of European and U.S. gas and electricity benchmarks, as well as carbon-neutral hydrogen and renewable Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) price series. We apply the multiple-bubble testing framework of Phillips, Shi and Yu (2015) and its panel extension to detect and date-stamp common episodes of explosivity across fossil-fuel and transition-related markets. Our results reveal synchronized explosive dynamics during the crisis period, with evidence that exuberance was not confined to traditional energy markets but also extended to hydrogen and renewable PPA benchmarks. For gas and electricity markets, where futures data are available, spot-forward diagnostics provide additional evidence on the interpretation of explosive episodes. Overall, the findings offer new insights into the propagation of instability across fossil and green energy price benchmarks and contribute to the debate on energy market dynamics during periods of systemic stress.

Title: Carbon pricing instruments and the sustainable energy transition: evidence on energy concentration and the energy industry
Authors: Xuguang Zuo, Boyu Wu, Chuanwang Sun
Abstract: The effective use of carbon pricing instruments to promote a sustainable energy transition has become a central issue in international climate negotiations. Using energy concentration as a proxy indicator, this paper evaluates the effects of the carbon emissions trading system (ETS) and carbon tax (CTax) on the sustainable energy transition drawing on global data on energy consumption and the energy industry. The results indicate that the ETS directly and significantly reduces energy concentration, whereas the CTax shows no direct effect. Specifically, the ETS has led to a significant increase in the consumption share and number of generating units based on clean fossil and renewable energy sources. In contrast, in countries implementing a CTax, although the renewable energy industry has expanded, there has been no significant increase in renewable energy consumption, nor a notable reduction in the scale of coal mining or the coal-based steel industry. A portfolio of carbon pricing instruments currently fails to generate effective linkage effects. Given the expansion of energy consumption and increasing uncertainty, the ETS is better suited to a sustainable energy transition. Therefore, developing countries should actively participate in the design of ETS mechanisms to ensure a sustainable energy transition.

Title: Do low emission zones generate car fleet renewal? A quasi-natural experiment
Authors: Craig Morton
Abstract: This study evaluates whether the introduction of Low Emission Zones accelerates car fleet renewal. To achieve this aim, this study uses the 2017 introduction of the Ultra Low Emission Zone in London, United Kingdom. This policy required drivers of older cars (EURO 4 or older) to pay a £10 charge per day to enter a specific area of central London. A spatial difference-in-differences empirical design is implemented to estimate the causal impact of the policy. The finding of the analysis is that the introduction of this policy increased vehicle fleet renewal by 2.2%. A practical use of this finding is that such ancillary benefits can now be included in the business case development for these policies, quantifying the broader spectrum of positive outcomes that can be realised.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Commuting matters: Association between work travel and perceived health and well-being in Canada
Authors: Andie Heck, Hisham Negm, Bogdan Kapatsila, Jonas De Vos, Ahmed El-Geneidy
Abstract: Beyond its functional role, commuting can have far-reaching consequences on the health and well-being of workers. This study examines the relationship between commute mode choice and physical health (PH), mental health (MH), and life in general (LiG) using data from the Canadian Mobility Survey (N = 6,671). We estimate weighted logistic regression models, accounting for commute duration, reasons for mode choice, sociodemographic characteristics, and concurrent life and health satisfaction. Results show that cycling and walking to work were associated with better PH, MH, and LiG than driving. Rapid transit users reported better PH, while bus commuters had lower odds for LiG than drivers. Overall, the findings highlight that commuting experiences are linked to multiple dimensions of well-being. Policies that prioritize active commuting and improve the quality and accessibility of public transit may contribute to better physical, mental, and overall well-being of commuters.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Simulation optimization approach for managing appointments of a multi-stage multi-server system
Authors: Can Zhao, Miao Bai, Zheng Zhang, Xuan Liao
Abstract: Appointment scheduling is essential for healthcare services to streamline patient flow and improve operational efficiency. This study focuses on patient appointment management in healthcare services involving multiple service stages and multiple service providers at each stage. Real-world multi-stage, multi-server systems often adopt a queue-like service flow, which is characterized by the First-Come, First-Served rule for fairness and the work-conserving rule that starts services immediately when patients and resources are available. To incorporate these operational practices into the appointment decision-making process, we adopt a simulation optimization approach. However, these practices introduce discontinuities in the sample path cost function, resulting in biased gradient estimators. To address this challenge, we apply the conditional Monte Carlo technique to smooth the cost function and develop a tailored stochastic gradient descent algorithm based on an unbiased gradient estimator for optimizing appointment decisions. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms benchmark stochastic gradient descent algorithms across various settings. Based on these results, we further derive managerial insights into shift design and patient sequencing in healthcare operations.

Title: Adjustable robust disassembly planning and dynamic capacity expansion for reverse supply chain network
Authors: Yao Gao, Wenjie Huang, Xinbao Liu
Abstract: The accelerating obsolescence of household appliances has led to a surge in end-of-life (EOL) products, creating significant challenges for sustainable resource recovery and environmental protection. This study develops a multi-stage adjustable robust optimization (MS-ARO) model to design an efficient and resilient reverse supply chain network for EOL appliances under uncertainty. The model jointly optimizes strategic decisions, including disassembly center location and initial capacity, and operational decisions, including dynamic capacity expansion and product allocation. It incorporates key real-world factors such as uncertain EOL product quantities, government-imposed recycling subsidies and penalties, and discrete predetermined capacity levels. To enhance adaptability, affine decision rules are employed for adjustable variables, enabling decisions to respond dynamically to unfolding uncertainty. Under these decision rules, the original MS-ARO model is reformulated as a two-stage robust optimization model with a nested max–min–max structure. Given the tri-level max–min–max structure and binary recourse decision variables, an improved column-and-constraint generation framework is developed to solve the resulting problem. The proposed solution approach is further enhanced by a warm-start strategy and a scenario management mechanism, which strengthen the initial master problem and improve computational efficiency. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed model significantly improves profitability, reduces conservatism, and ensures compliance with regulatory requirements. Sensitivity analyses highlight the critical roles of financial incentives and penalty mechanisms in shaping recycling performance. The findings offer valuable insights for policymakers and manufacturers aiming to enhance the sustainability, flexibility, and regulatory alignment of reverse logistics systems in the context of a circular economy.
