Title: Optimal maintenance scheduling and vessel routing in offshore wind farms: A tailored column generation approach
Authors: Xiangda Li, Lingxiao Wu, Hao Lang, Jian Gang Jin, Ping He
Affiliations: Department of Logistics and Maritime Studies, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; Department of Aeronautical and Aviation Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; School of Ocean and Civil Engineering, and MOE Key Laboratory of Marine Intelligent Equipment and System, Shanghai Jiao Tong University
Abstract: The globally installed capacity of offshore wind farms has witnessed significant growth to support carbon neutrality targets, which brings increased requirements on maintenance activities to ensure their safe and reliable operations. To conduct maintenance activities, there is a need to deploy a service vessel fleet to transport technicians and spare parts to multiple wind turbines in offshore wind farms, which has an important consequence on maintenance costs and power generation losses due to delayed maintenance. For developing cost-effective maintenance schedules, this paper investigates a novel maintenance routing and scheduling problem that integrates multiple key factors: available maintenance time windows due to weather conditions, multiple maintenance types, heterogeneous vessel fleets, and cross-vessel technician sharing. Each shared technician is dispatched to a wind turbine by a vessel and picked up by another. To handle this intricate problem, a mixed-integer linear programming model is formulated for the problem, which is then reformulated as a route-based set-partitioning model based on a time-space network. Then, a tailored column generation approach is proposed to address the problem. Numerical experiments on real-world cases are conducted to validate solution quality and computational efficiency of the proposed approach. Besides, the importance of technician sharing and vessel fleet composition on reducing maintenance costs is confirmed by cost-effectiveness analysis.

Title: Transition from a fund-based to a lifecycle-oriented EPR system: the evolution of extended producer responsibility for electrical and electronic equipment in China
Authors: Tao Chu, Kannan Govindan, Yongguang Zhong, Weiqiang Jia
Abstract: Abstract The Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) system for electrical and electronic equipment in China has evolved from a “fund-based” to a “special fund” model. To transcend conventional end-of-pipe governance, we propose an “EPR 3.0” framework that extends environmental responsibility to the consumption stage. The model centers on consumer responsibility and is operationalized through an advance disposal fee (ADF) with transfer payments, complemented by carbon taxation and subsidy mechanisms. Using a tri‑party evolutionary game model and system dynamics simulation, we identify two evolutionary stable states: a government‑led collaborative governance phase and a market‑driven circular endogenous phase. Results show that consumer preferences drive producers’ adoption of eco-design, and the policy mix of the ADF and transfer payments significantly enhances producer compliance, while consumer responsiveness to public education campaign exhibits an optimal sensitivity range. Based on the analysis of system feedback mechanisms, we further propose a four-stage evolutionary framework of EPR development (EPR 1.0–4.0), revealing the transition of the EPR system from exogenous policy-driven development to endogenous market-driven evolution. The proposed evolutionary pathway and integrated policy framework provide valuable insights for developing countries seeking to establish effective e-waste management systems.

Title: Representation Theorems for Convex Expectations and Semigroups on Path Space
Authors: David Criens, Michael Kupper
Affiliations: Department of Mathematical Stochastics, University of Freiburg, Freiburg 79104, Germany; Department of Mathematical Stochastics, University of Konstanz, Konstanz 78357, Germany
Abstract: The objective of this paper is to investigate the connection between penalty functions from stochastic optimal control, convex semigroups from analysis, and convex expectations from probability theory. Our main result provides a one-to-one relation between these objects. As an application, we use the representation via penalty functions and duality arguments to show that convex expectations are determined by their finite-dimensional distributions. To illustrate this structural result, we show that the axiomatic description of G-Lévy processes in terms of finite-dimensional distributions by Hu and Peng extends uniquely to the control approach introduced by Neufeld and Nutz. Finally, we show that convex expectations with a Markovian structure are fully determined by their one-dimensional distributions, which give rise to a classical semigroup on the state space. As an application of this result, we establish a Laplace principle for entropic risk measures associated with controlled diffusions. Funding: D. Criens gratefully acknowledges travel support from the Freiburg Center for Data Analysis, Modeling and AI.

Title: Mobile internet connectivity and household wealth in the Philippines
Authors: Zhiwu Wei, Neil Lee, Yohan Iddawela
Abstract: Mobile internet has become a fundamental modern infrastructure. We consider how access influences household wealth in the Philippines using a granular measure of local connectivity based on geocoded cell towers and identify causal impact through an instrument based on proximity to submarine cable landing points. Our results show that mobile internet connectivity increases household wealth, with effects across education levels and most pronounced in urban areas. We investigate potential mechanisms and find that improved connectivity stimulates activity in key economic sectors, improves educational outcomes, and increases female labor force participation, primarily in occasional work. Given the context of the Philippines as a major migrant-sending country, we conduct a complementary event study which suggests that tower rollout may facilitate international labor migration and increase remittance flows to origin households.

Title: Who should press “start”? Blockchain initiator identity and strategic performance in a green food supply chain
Authors: Miaomiao Wang, Mengying Li, Cuiwei Lin
Abstract: Blockchain can enhance the credibility of traceability and support consumer trust in green food supply chains. However, who initiates the implementation shapes its practical welfare and performance owing to the distinctive structure of such supply chains. This study investigates manufacturer-initiated, retailer-initiated, and joint-initiated blockchain modes in a green food supply chain with endogenous product greenness and traceability level. The results show that the retailer-initiated mode strengthens the manufacturer's green R&D incentive and generally leads to higher product greenness, traceability information level, demand, consumer surplus, environmental benefit, and social welfare than the manufacturer-initiated mode. However, superior operational and welfare outcomes do not necessarily coincide with each member's private preference. The manufacturer and technology service provider earn higher profits under the retailer-initiated mode, whereas the retailer's profit advantage depends on the green R&D cost. Although the technology service provider charges the same optimal unit service fee under the two modes, stronger market demand allows it to earn more under the retailer-initiated mode. The extended analysis further shows that the joint-initiated mode does not uniformly outperform single-party initiation, and its relative performance depends on the joint initiation cost. Overall, the appropriate initiation mode depends on the initiator's ability to convert credible traceability into market demand and capture sufficient value to cover its initiation burden.

Title: A note on fixed-k spot volatility inference under roughness
Authors: Wenhao Cui, Wenjing Liu, Haibin Zhu
Abstract: This note studies fixed- 𝑘 spot volatility inference in the framework of Bollerslev et al. (2021) when volatility has rough local regularity. We show that pointwise inference is robust to roughness. The fixed- 𝑘 statistic retains the same scaled chi-square limit as in the semimartingale benchmark, although the approximation rate deteriorates with the roughness exponent. We also show that roughness affects uniform inference by increasing the required block size. A sufficient condition for valid uniform confidence bands is 𝑘 > 2 + 2 / 𝐻 , where 𝐻 is a local moment-regularity exponent. In the fBM-driven volatility specification discussed below, 𝐻 may be taken equal to the conventional Hurst parameter 𝐻 0 .

Title: When incentive transparency undermines persuasion
Authors: Renzo Pardo-Figueroa
Abstract: Can revealing how strongly a sender wants to persuade make persuasion less effective? I study a binary-action game in which the sender privately chooses between two noisy information technologies after observing an incentive intensity and an implementation cost. Stronger incentives make the more permissive technology more attractive. Under transparency, the receiver conditions skepticism on motive intensity; under opacity, low-incentive types lend credibility to high-incentive types through pooling. For an open set of parameters, opacity raises approval. At a fixed mean, dispersion magnifies this penalty when types straddle the credibility threshold. Transparency nevertheless raises receiver welfare.

Title: Perceptions of inequality and group-specific public goods
Authors: Maurizio Bussolo, Akshay Govind Dixit
Abstract: We use data from a survey of 116,061 households in India to study beliefs about inequality. We uncover large differences between where individuals believe their household stands on the income distribution and their actual position. However, informing individuals that their household is poorer than they thought has no discernible effect on support for reducing inequality. We posit that support for reducing inequality may be unresponsive to information because such information disregards the sharing of resources within religious or ethnic groups, in the form of religious and social goods. Households, especially those in the lower rungs of the distribution, benefit from these goods, which may shape their beliefs about inequality and their demand for redistribution. In districts with a greater supply of religious or social goods, we find that the average individual perceives their household as richer. Our findings suggest that group-specific public goods, found in many countries beyond India, deserve greater consideration in studies of inequality.

Title: Editorial Board
Achieving net-zero emissions in logistics and operations: The net zero plus framework
Authors: Peiyi Liang, Tsan-Ming Choi, Eric Ka Ho Leung, Zhen Xu
Abstract: Today, achieving net zero in logistics and operations is a top agenda for almost all organizations. In this context, there is no doubt that enabling technologies are critical for facilitating decarbonization (e.g., emissions reduction, offset, and removal). Moreover, fulfilling the net-zero goal naturally requires the participation of all stakeholders, within and beyond the traditional supply chains. This paper aims to critically examine the relevant studies on net-zero emissions in the operations and logistics literature, with the focal points on different major stakeholders (e.g., non-governmental organizations, governments, investors, service providers, supply chains, and consumers) as well as the role of enabling technologies. We also examine several real-world practices implemented by prominent firms (such as Apple, Amazon, and Nike). Based on the findings of literature review and observed practices, we establish a novel “Net Zero Plus” framework, where we highlight the underexplored potential of enabling technologies as a key “plus” to help achieve net-zero emissions. We further develop several propositions. Finally, we identify several research-practice gaps and then establish a real-practice driven future research agenda.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Mesoscopic pedestrian dynamics enhancement robust optimization for signage collaboration in metro stations under uncertainties
Authors: Xiaoxia Yang, Chunyue Cui, Wenbo Zhang, Jinli Wei, Botao Zhang, Yongxing Li, Zhilu Yuan, Chuan-Zhi Thomas Xie
Abstract: Dynamic guidance signage in metro stations demonstrates significant potential for enhancing evacuation efficiency, primarily by proactively adapting to passenger flow distributions and the evolution of risk, thereby optimizing the overall evacuation route network. To address the uncertainty of fire risk, this paper proposes a dynamic guidance signage coordinated control method incorporating robust optimization. First, a cell transmission model is constructed to dynamically model the passenger evacuation process in metro stations, capturing the temporal evolution of passenger flows under fire conditions. Second, a budget uncertainty set is introduced to characterize fluctuations in fire risk, and the dynamic guidance signage optimization problem is formulated as a robust decision-making problem that seeks an optimal and stable coordinated guidance strategy under the worst-case realizations of uncertain parameters. Subsequently, a solution algorithm is developed by integrating a local search mechanism with a global optimization framework. Compared with conventional metaheuristic algorithms, the proposed approach exhibits significant advantages in both solution quality and convergence efficiency. Finally, extensive numerical experiments are conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results indicate that, compared with static guidance strategies, the coordinated dynamic guidance signage strategy could significantly improve evacuation performance. In addition, the impacts of key factors, including robust parameters, weight configurations, solution algorithms, crowd density, fire scenarios, and signage adjustment frequency, on the dynamic guidance system performance are systematically analyzed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Acquiring and managing additional railcars attached to passenger trains for freight on rail transit under demand uncertainty
Authors: Ze Wang, Yuguang Wei
Abstract: When faced with freight surges, fossil-powered trucks often incur negative externalities such as traffic congestion and environmental pollution, along with prohibitive costs and land limitations linked to road infrastructure expansion. To address these concerns, under-exploited rail transit has emerged as a freight alternative over recent decades. This paper investigates an innovative logistics approach that attaches additional railcars to intercity passenger trains within an unsaturated rail network for flexible freight transshipment and long-distance transport. To launch this, decision-makers need to, at strategic level, acquire and assign additional railcars to rail stations, followed by tactical decisions on selecting trains for railcar attachment and generating space-time cycles repeated within planning horizon. These interwoven decisions are complicated by demand uncertainty due to a lack of adequate historical data or accurate forecasting methods appropriate for this emerging freight alternative. Based on a space-time network representation of associated operations and decisions, we construct a mixed integer model that can render the strategic and tactical decisions robust and hedge against demand uncertainty. Given computational difficulties, we decompose the monolithic formulation into manageable problems and devise a constraint-and-column-generation (CCG) algorithm. Numerical experiments conducted on real-world problem instances with diverse network dimensions and characteristics demonstrate the computational superiority of CCG; elucidate the value of robust solutions; validate the benefits of jointly optimized decisions; and offer managerial insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Instant retail strategies for online order fulfillment under consumer time sensitivity
Authors: Zonghuo Li, Lu Wu, Xiangfeng Chen, Shanliang Li
Abstract: This study develops a game-theoretic framework to examine an instant retail strategy in which an online platform collaborates with a physical retailer to provide a buy-online-ship-from-store (BOSS) service. We analyze two scenarios—without instant sale and with instant sale—based on the platform’s self-sale format and the retailer’s normal sale format. For each introduction scenario, we discuss two sub-scenarios depending on whether the delivery timeliness of the platform sale dominates that of the normal sale. These two sub-scenarios are defined as platform-led delivery advantage and retailer-led delivery advantage. Consumers exhibit time-sensitivity in receiving their online orders. Our findings reveal that when consumers exhibit strong time sensitivity, the adoption of the instant sale enables both the platform and retailer to elevate retail prices. Meanwhile, in the platform-led delivery advantage case, implementing an instant sale reduces the prices of the platform’s and retailer’s respective self-operated sale formats when the instant sale’s shipping cost is low. Conversely, a high shipping cost for the introduced instant sale allows for those price increases. In this high-shipping-cost circumstance, competition among the three sales formats can be softened. The results also demonstrate that the instant sale benefits the platform and retailer when the instant sale’s delivery time and shipping cost are either sufficiently low or high enough. Notably, in the retailer-led delivery advantage case, the platform and retailer always benefit from the instant sale. For the retail system, introducing an instant sale format enhances consumer surplus and social welfare regardless of the delivery advantage. These findings remain robust under various extensions, including uniform price strategies, differential commission fee structures, and the incorporation of store sales.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Capitalization of environmental change: Road noise trajectories and housing prices
Authors: Radoslaw Trojanek, Jeffrey P. Cohen
Abstract: Transportation noise is a disamenity that is often capitalized into home prices, but standard hedonic models typically condition on noise levels at a single point in time. Housing markets may also respond to the trajectory of noise exposure that leads to those levels. We propose a two-dimensional classification framework that distinguishes both net outcomes (improvement vs. deterioration) and temporal patterns, while accounting for spatial dependence and using a generalized difference-in-differences estimation approach for generating causal effects. Using three versions of noise maps (2012, 2017, 2022) from Warsaw, Poland that we link to more than 168,000 apartment sales, we find that noise improvements are capitalized into significant price premia that vary by trajectory type. Improvements sustained over the entire decade (locations whose noise level falls on each successive map) command the largest house price premia of 2.6–3.9%, while locations that experience interruptions or partial reversals along the way realize smaller premia of 1.5–1.8%. Moreover, the implied per-decibel capitalization rate is roughly 50% larger for persistent improvements than for improvements arriving only late in the decade (0.50% vs. 0.33%), suggesting that housing markets value demonstrated persistence over and above the most recent noise conditions. Noise deterioration effects are statistically insignificant in the spatial error model, consistent with both spatial confounding and limited statistical power, and suggesting that standard hedonic estimates may overstate deterioration effects when spatial dependence is ignored.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Optimizing integrated passenger-freight transport in demand-responsive services: System efficiency and policy insights
Authors: Mohammad Sadrani, Silvio Nocera, Constantinos Antoniou
Abstract: This paper examines an Integrated Passenger-Freight Transport (IPFT) approach for Demand-Responsive Transport (DRT) services that serve parcel deliveries alongside passenger trip requests in low-demand or rural mobility contexts while preserving passenger service reliability. The problem distinguishes passenger and freight services through their flow structures, capacity dimensions, service-time components, time-window treatments, and cost representations. It is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model that minimizes total system costs, including vehicle and driver operating costs, passenger travel time costs, freight time-window penalties, and emission costs. To solve realistic-size instances, we develop a new hybrid solution algorithm, PSA-GA, combining Population-based Simulated Annealing (PSA) with parent selection and crossover mechanisms from a Genetic Algorithm (GA). Planning and policy implications are assessed through a real-world case study in Kirchheim bei München, Germany, supported by extensive sensitivity analyses on cost structures, demand levels and heterogeneity, temporal demand alignment, travel time uncertainty, and vehicle utilization. Results show that IPFT can reduce total costs by 24 % compared with conventional segregated passenger-freight transport (SPFT) systems. Cost savings increase when freight demand is shifted toward lower-passenger-demand periods, whereas overlapping passenger and freight peaks reduce the benefits of integration. IPFT performance is more strongly linked to overall vehicle utilization than to passenger occupancy alone; although passenger occupancy is slightly lower in the IPFT fleet than in the SPFT passenger-only fleet, the integrated system achieves higher combined utilization through joint passenger-freight routing. Fleet size results further indicate that passenger time value and vehicle operating costs are the most influential planning parameters.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Green jobs require green skills: Why production subsidies are not enough
Authors: Shisham Adhikari
Abstract: Large structural transitions require both firms and workers to act: firms must create jobs in expanding sectors, and workers must acquire the skills to move into them. The green transition is a leading example, yet most climate policy focuses on the firm side. This paper asks whether production support alone is sufficient for the constrained-efficient allocation, or whether worker-side support is also needed. I develop a two-sector Diamond–Mortensen–Pissarides model with sectoral choice and pre-match human-capital investment. Green workers acquire sector-specific skills before matching with firms; because training is sunk at the time of wage bargaining, workers do not internalize the full social return to their investment, even under the Hosios condition. A Pigouvian production subsidy corrects the environmental wedge and aligns vacancy creation for a given level of human capital, but it does not implement the planner’s training choice; so exact decentralization also requires a worker-side training subsidy. In a calibration to the United States, the central quantitative comparison holds fixed the green-employment target: a production-only policy is chosen to reach the same 14% benchmark as the coordinated policy, but it does so with lower green human capital and lower output. The break-even environmental value of green output for the coordinated policy is 1.13% of the numeraire output unit. It thus shows that, even conditional on the same green employment expansion, policy design determines the skill intensity and productivity of the green expansion.

Title: The empirical impact of energy transition on developing economies: Sectoral analysis and predictive insights
Authors: Alain Soliman, Ilyes Abid, Khaled Guesmi, Christian Urom
Abstract: Energy transition has become a central topic in economic and financial studies. This article examines the empirical impact of the energy transition on the returns and risk of the energy, transportation, and agriculture sectors in 16 developing countries over the period 2014–2023. Using the Bayesian FAVAR process, we account for dynamic common factors in returns and study the evolving relationship between the Energy Transition Index (ETI) and sectoral returns and risk. Overall, we find that strong energy transition performance of a country has a negative significant impact on returns in the short run. However, it increases sectoral returns in the long run. In contrast, we observe the opposite pattern when examining risk. While improvements in energy transition reduce sectoral risk in the short run, they induce a rise in risk over the long run. Our findings also demonstrate the importance of country-specific differences, as the sign and the significance of this impact vary across countries. Additionally, through a bootstrap Granger causality test, we find a unidirectional predictive relationship between the energy transition index and sector’s return and risk. Finally, the estimated impulse response functions confirm the significant impact of the energy transition on the returns and risk of the three sectors studied.

Title: Conflict or synergy: exploring the interaction between carbon pricing policy and capacity mechanism
Authors: Yilun Luo, Esmaeil Ahmadi, Benjamin Craig McLellan, Tetsuo Tezuka
Abstract: The increasing complexity of electricity market reforms highlights the importance of understanding how multiple policy instruments interact. Designing coherent policies is crucial for balancing emission reduction objectives with economic stability. Focusing on Japan's ongoing electricity-market liberalization and reform agenda, this study examines how carbon pricing and capacity mechanisms interact in a liberalized electricity market, and whether they generate conflict or synergy under alternative policy settings. A hybrid System Dynamics model is adopted to investigate conflicts and synergies between the two policies in terms of technological, environmental, and economic aspects. The findings suggest that policy interactions are shaped by both design details and implementation timing. When emissions reduction is the primary objective, a higher early-stage carbon floor price combined with a technology-differentiated capacity mechanism produces synergies by accelerating renewable integration and reducing compliance costs. In contrast, a low carbon price with indiscriminate capacity payments reinforces fossil lock-in and creates policy conflict. Sensitivity tests further show that lowering investment hurdles fosters VRE adoption and reduces costs, while delaying carbon pricing may temporarily ease fiscal burdens but increases cumulative emissions and risks price volatility. These findings highlight the need for early and credible carbon pricing, targeted support for flexible resources, and careful attention to financing conditions. The study provides practical insights for designing coordinated policy packages that align environmental goals with economic stability in liberalized electricity markets.

Title: Exploring future sustainable urban transport through scenarios: a critical review of contemporary practice
Authors: Paul Haggar, Omer Rana, Jonathan Radcliffe, Ashish Sharma, Dimitris Potoglou
Abstract: Under deep uncertainty, long-range transport forecasts are prone to inaccuracy. Scenario planning – a foresight approach from futures studies – offers a means to explore different long-range transport possibilities while also engaging transport stakeholders. Transport scenario narratives constitute a rich dataset of qualitative insights to draw upon concerning contemporary transport foresight. In this paper, thematic analysis and synthesis were utilised both to identify key ideas being explored through transport scenario planning and to evaluate sampled published transport scenario narratives critically. Through standardized keyword queries of Google Scholar, published documentation from 40 scenario planning projects were identified that met the study criteria. Sampled published transport scenario narratives (n = 173) from 40 scenario planning projects, across 25 countries, were analysed; 95% of projects were published in peer-reviewed academic journals. This study’s results provide a thematic map exploring the principal concerns captured by sampled published transport scenario narratives and opportunities for improvement are discussed as a set of recommendations for enhancing transport scenario narrative quality.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Effects of station-area built environment on urban rail transit passenger flow
Authors: Xiaolan Wang, Wenbin Tang, Hongyan Yan, Qifeng Xu, Mingxia Shu
Abstract: The spatiotemporal mismatch between urban rail transit (URT) stations and surrounding urban functions challenges operational efficiency worldwide. Existing research predominantly focuses on average daily ridership, offering limited insights into how built environment influences vary across station types, time periods, and spatial scales. This study develops an integrated framework combining station classification with multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR) to investigate the mechanisms linking built environment to passenger flows. Using Changsha, China as a case study, stations are classified into residential, employment, and mixed-use types via K-Means clustering. The MGWR model is compared with OLS model and GWR model. Results reveal three key findings: built environment effects exhibit spatiotemporal heterogeneity, functional-type dependence, and spatial scale variability; factors such as office density have divergent effects across station types and between morning and evening rush hours. The framework effectively identifies local and global operational scales, supporting a paradigm shift towards station-specific, refined governance strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Balancing sustainability and employer attractiveness: strategy–structure alignment in corporate mobility management
Authors: Luisa Stöhr, Philipp Scharfenberger
Abstract: Commuting and business travel significantly contribute to transport emissions, requiring companies to reduce their environmental impact. Simultaneously, mobility benefits have become an important factor in employer attractiveness. Corporate mobility management is therefore gaining relevance for organizations, aiming for sustainable and attractive concepts. This study examines strategic drivers, organizational structures, and their relationship in corporate mobility management. The analysis draws on an exploratory case study of seven employers, using multiple data sources. First, the results show that organizations often perceive tensions between sustainability and employer attractiveness, as key drivers of new mobility initiatives. Second, the structure of corporate mobility management ranges from dedicated to distributed roles. Lastly, the primary driver of an initiative is typically reflected in the department leading it. This study thereby conceptualizes corporate mobility management as a peripheral, cross-functional organizational domain in which strategy–structure alignment emerges through parallel and overlapping arrangements shaped by multiple strategic drivers.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: The effect of online sales bans on e-cigarette use
Authors: Ege Aksu, Charles J. Courtemanche, Dhaval Dave, Daniel Dench, Michael Grossman, Jooyoung Kim, Selen Ozdogan, Shubhsri Rajendra, Joseph J. Sabia, Henry Saffer

Title: The effects of improving working conditions on teacher turnover: Heterogeneous responses by work stress levels
Authors: Tom Rongen, Luc Cobben, Frank Cörvers, Raymond Montizaan
Abstract: ABSTRACT Teacher shortages remain a persistent challenge in Dutch primary education. Improving working conditions may help retain current teachers and attract former ones, but the relative effectiveness and cost-efficiency of specific measures are not well understood. This study uses a vignette experiment to estimate how changes in six key working conditions influence the turnover intentions of current and former primary school teachers in the Netherlands. We find that wage increases and the provision of teaching assistants have the largest effects on both retaining current teachers and attracting former teachers, though they are not the most cost-efficient. Increased control over working time emerges as the most cost-efficient intervention. Our results also show that teachers who report higher levels of work stress, measured through their need for recovery, are more likely to consider leaving the profession. At the same time, these teachers respond more strongly to enhanced working conditions than their less-stressed peers. This suggests that the impact of workplace improvements depends in part on teachers’ existing stress levels. Finally, heterogeneity analyses by baseline turnover intentions, sex, age, and experience are informative about potential compositional effects and sorting mechanisms of specific interventions. The findings underscore the value of targeted policies that address both structural working conditions and teacher well-being.

Title: How does entrepreneurial experience affect future employment? Evidence from two correspondence studies
Authors: Lulu An, Haoran He
Abstract: Many entrepreneurs eventually transition back into the labor market. While existing research documents discrimination against former entrepreneurs in developed economies, the sources of this discrimination and the extent to which this evidence generalizes to developing-country contexts remain poorly understood. By sending fictitious resumes to employers in which we vary the presence of entrepreneurial experience and whether it occurred before or after paid employment experience in two resume correspondence studies, we investigate whether and why former entrepreneurs face hiring discrimination in the Chinese labor market. We find substantial discrimination against former entrepreneurs. Guided by an employer decision model, we show that statistical discrimination is the primary source of this penalty, while finding no clear evidence regarding the presence of taste-based discrimination. A complementary survey-based choice experiment further indicates that employers’ concerns about former entrepreneurs’ commitment and fit can largely explain this discrimination. These results underscore that mitigating hiring discrimination for former entrepreneurs in emerging economies may require a combination of employee-side strategies, such as strategically acquiring paid employment experience, and employer-side interventions that reduce information asymmetries.

Authors: Bart Lameijer, Indji Tan, Amrik Sohal

Title: Navigating the digital shift: Stakeholders’ power and social sustainability in Agri-food supply chains
Authors: Xiongyong Zhou, Haiyan Lu, Ying Yang
Affiliations: Department of Management Science and Engineering, School of Economics and Management, Fuzhou University; Newcastle University Business School

Title: Using Distribution Regression Difference‐in‐Differences to Evaluate the Effects of a Minimum Wage Introduction on the Distributions of Wages, Earnings, and Working Hours
Authors: Martin Biewen, Bernd Fitzenberger, Marian Rümmele
Affiliations: University of Tübingen Tübingen Germany; IZA@LISER Luxembourg Luxembourg; RFBerlin Berlin Germany; Institute for Employment Research (IAB) Nürnberg Germany; FAU Erlangen‐Nürnberg Nürnberg Germany; IFS London UK
Abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the causal effects of the introduction of the minimum wage in Germany on the distributions of hourly wages, monthly earnings, and hours worked, combining rich large‐scale data sources. We compare linear and non‐linear versions of distribution regression difference‐in‐differences (DR‐DiD) and also estimate bivariate DR‐DiD. We show that the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015 led to shifts in low hourly wages around the minimum wage threshold including spillover effects up to 50%–70% above. We present evidence for working hours effects in different parts of the hours distribution, though the magnitudes are small. The minimum wage explains a sizeable share of the recent fall in wage and earnings inequality. We show that groups that were later more strongly affected by the minimum wage already experienced higher wage growth before the introduction, leading to an overestimation of minimum wage effects if not accounted for.

Title: Visibility of Technology and Cumulative Innovation: Evidence From Trade Secrets Laws
Authors: Bernhard Ganglmair, Imke Reimers
Affiliations: University of Mannheim Mannheim Germany; ZEW Mannheim Mannheim Germany; Cornell University Ithaca New York USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Innovation depends on the incentives to create new ideas as well as access to existing ones. Access, in turn, depends on the inherent visibility of an initial invention and on the inventor's decision to disclose it, for example, by patenting. Compared to product innovations, process innovations tend to be less visible, making secrecy as an intellectual property strategy relatively more attractive; and stronger trade secrets protection laws could hamper their disclosure even further. Using exogenous variation in the level of trade secrets protection from the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, we show that stronger protection has a disproportionately negative effect on patenting of processes. We further show in simulations that these changes in disclosure can have large implications for follow‐on innovation and welfare.

Title: What drives happiness in 15 European Union countries? The role of income inequality, democracy, and environmental quality
Authors: Umut Uzar, Elif Duygu Kömürcüoğlu, Ömer Faruk Kömürcüoğlu
Abstract: This study examines happiness as a key dimension of sustainable development by focusing on its socio-economic, political, and environmental correlates. In recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that happiness cannot be explained solely by economic prosperity but is strongly influenced by structural factors such as income distribution, democratic institutions, and environmental conditions. Despite growing interest, empirical studies examining the simultaneous effects of these three fundamental factors on happiness are scarce. This creates a noteworthy gap in the literature. This study aims to fill this gap by empirically examining the effects of income inequality, democracy, and environmental degradation on happiness in 15 European Union countries, including the United Kingdom for comparability, between 2011 and 2022. Per capita income and health expenditure are included as control variables. Methodologically, the study employs MMQR and assesses the robustness of the findings using FGLS, PCSE, and HPJ approaches. The findings suggest that income inequality and environmental degradation are negatively associated with happiness, whereas democracy is positively associated with individuals' happiness. Furthermore, it is found that per capita income and health expenditure are found to be positively related to happiness. The results point to the need for sustainable development goals to be addressed within a holistic framework rather than independently, offering important implications for policymakers.

Title: The welfare effects of input price discrimination under endogenous horizontal differentiation
Authors: Duarte Brito, Markos Tselekounis
Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between input prices set by an upstream monopolist and the location choices of two downstream firms engaged in spatial competition. It focuses on the welfare effects of input price discrimination (IPD) when compared to the benchmark case of uniform input pricing (UIP). In addition to cost asymmetry, IPD is justified by the existence of a multimarket downstream firm. This allows us to avoid potentially infinite equilibrium input prices arising from the ubiquitous full market coverage assumption: an elastic demand for the input is introduced by considering that one downstream firm monopolizes one market, while competing à la Hotelling in another market. The two retailers play either the input-price-then-location game or the location-then-input-price setting, depending on whether the upstream supplier can credibly commit to input prices before location choices take place. A global result is that, regardless of which firm is more efficient, the upstream monopolist sets a lower input price to the multimarket firm under IPD. Our main finding is that IPD always harms welfare in the location-then-input-price setting; by contrast, when firms play the input-price-then-location game, IPD can increase welfare while not affecting total output, even when the positively discriminated firm is less efficient than its single-market rival. This striking result arises because, under this timing, the reduction in transportation costs induced by endogenous location choices can more than offset the increase in production costs caused by the reallocation of output toward the less efficient firm.

Title: Customization with additive manufacturing: Blessing or curse for society?
Authors: Julian Schwierzy, Tobias Wenzel
Abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) enables large-scale product customization and is increasingly adopted in traditionally standardized product markets. We examine how industrial AM for customization affects competition and welfare in such markets. To this end, we develop a spatial competition model in which firms using traditional manufacturing (TM) technologies offer standardized products, while an AM firm supplies customized products. TM firms enter endogenously, so that AM adoption can shape market structure. We show that AM entry lowers the prices of standardized products but allows the customized product to ask for a price premium relative to a pure-TM benchmark. At the same time, AM adoption reduces the equilibrium number of TM firms. In welfare terms, AM adoption always increases total surplus, but consumer surplus increases only when AM is sufficiently disadvantaged relative to TM. In particular, when AM has a positive advantage, AM adoption lowers consumer surplus: the gains from customization and efficiency are more than offset by stronger AM market power and reduced TM variety. Building on these findings, we discuss policy instruments for promoting AM, highlighting that subsidies to AM fixed costs can enhance both efficiency and consumer welfare, provided that AM does not gain excessive market power.

Title: Discrete lot-sizing and scheduling problem with remanufacturing: Formulations and analysis under flexible production speeds
Authors: Juan I. Álvarez, Daniel A. Rossit, Pedro Piñeyro
Abstract: The Extended Producer Responsibility paradigm makes producers responsible for end of life management, incentivizing design for recovery and shifting waste costs from governments to manufacturers. To comply, firms must integrate forward and reverse flows efficiently; remanufacturing is a proactive strategy that recovers value from returned products. However, hybrid manufacturing–remanufacturing systems pose significant challenges to production planning. This paper extends the discrete lot sizing and scheduling problem (DLSP) to hybrid manufacturing–remanufacturing systems that permit discrete choices among multiple production speeds. We present mixed integer linear programming formulations for three variants: a baseline DLSP with return costs, the DLSP with remanufacturing (DLSR) and fixed manufacturing/remanufacturing speeds, and the DLSR with variable production speeds. Models address single product and multi product settings with shared resources, capturing setup costs, mode dependent processing costs, and inventory dynamics for finished goods and returns. Computational experiments assess total cost, return utilization, inventory, and solver performance across scenarios varying return volumes and cost parameters. Results indicate that production speed flexibility increases remanufacturing uptake, reduces new production and inventory holding, and delivers significant cost savings (especially for dedicated single product lines) while supporting lean objectives. However, variable speeds markedly increase computational complexity in multi product, shared resource instances, motivating tailored heuristics or decomposition for larger horizons.

Title: Unlocking legal efficiency gains in school switch programs
Authors: Tommy Andersson, Nils Lager, Dany Kessel
Abstract: We study school switches in which students who have already been assigned seats request reassignment. Unlike in regular school choice, stability need not be legally binding in such programs, since students’ priority-based claims have already been satisfied upstream. Efficiency then naturally becomes the primary design objective. To quantify the potential legal efficiency gains, we compare Deferred Acceptance (DA) with Top Trading Cycles (TTC) and an efficiency-adjusted DA (EADAM) using Swedish data. TTC and EADAM triple switching rates compared to DA. This difference is driven by the absence of slack in effective capacity and shrinks rapidly when introducing additional seats.

Title: A note on spurious regressions in fixed effects models
Authors: Dierk Herzer
Abstract: This study examines spurious fixed-effects (FE) regressions in large- N , small- T panels. We derive the fixed- T , large- N behavior of one-way and two-way FE estimators and their conventional and cluster-robust t -statistics under different random-walk processes and provide supporting Monte Carlo evidence. Two-way FE models with cluster-robust standard errors (SEs) do not exhibit a substantially higher risk of spurious regressions under pure random walks or random walks with homogeneous drift. In the correlated heterogeneous drift case, however, the risk of spurious inference can be substantial even with cluster-robust SEs. This risk increases with both T and N , but remains non-negligible even when T =5.

Title: Supply chain resilience to geopolitical risks: integrative insights and future research directions
Authors: Imran Ali, William Ho, Sara Saberi, Andy C.L. Yeung
Abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly exposed to persistent geopolitical risks arising from trade restrictions, sanctions, armed conflicts, export controls, and strategic competition among nations. These risks challenge traditional assumptions underpinning globally integrated and efficiency-oriented supply chains and call for a broader understanding of supply chain resilience. This editorial paper synthesises findings of nine articles examining how organisations and supply chain networks respond and adapt to geopolitical risks. Three interrelated themes emerge: geopolitical risks and strategic responses; network, collaboration, and alliance-based resilience; and strategic capabilities and technology-enabled adaptation. Synthesising these insights, we conceptualise supply chain resilience to geopolitical risks as the capacity of firms and their supply chain networks to anticipate and absorb geopolitical disruptions, adapt to changing exposure, and strategically reconfigure relationships, resources, and network structures while maintaining viable business operations. Such resilience is multidimensional and contingent, arising from the interplay among strategic choices, collaborative relationships, technological and operational capabilities, resources, and network structures. Six future research frontiers are identified concerning dynamic and multilevel geopolitical risks, resilient network design, capability configurations, inter-organisational governance, strategic reconfiguration, and methodological advancement. Together, the findings advance a more integrated, dynamic, and configurational understanding of how firms and supply chain networks remain resilient under persistent geopolitical uncertainty.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Contradictory capitalization: the uneven effects of subway expansion on second-hand housing prices in Beijing
Authors: Tiantian Dai, Yu Fang, Shenyi Jiang, Yilin Jiang
Abstract: Urban rail expansion is widely viewed as a catalyst for accessibility gains and housing price appreciation. Yet little is known about how the capitalization effects of new rail investments depend on baseline transit conditions. This study evaluates the housing market impacts of the second phase of Beijing Subway Line 10 using a hedonic Difference-in-Differences design extended with a spatial autoregressive specification. Exploiting variation in pre-existing subway access, we show that treatment effects are sharply heterogeneous. In the baseline DID estimates, neighborhoods without prior subway access experience post-opening increases of approximately 10% in both total transaction prices and price per square meter, along with anticipation effects of 14–15% during the announcement period. By contrast, neighborhoods already served by subway stations experience post-opening declines of 3–4% in the same price measures. Spatial autoregressive estimates indicate significant spillover effects, suggesting that housing market responses extend beyond directly treated areas. Further analysis reveals that negative post-opening adjustments in transit-rich neighborhoods are less pronounced around commercially integrated stations. These findings highlight the importance of baseline accessibility, spatial interactions, and station-area land-use context in shaping the distributional residential market effects of urban rail investments. Our results suggest that transit expansions in mature networks may generate uneven and spatially dependent residential capitalization effects, with important implications for transportation planning and policy evaluation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Non-linear drivers of urban-to-rural mobility in China’s Greater Bay Area: insights from mobile phone big data
Authors: Dongting Bao, Pengjun Zhao, Xuejie Zhang, Zhengying Liu
Abstract: Persistent urban–rural disparities hinder global sustainable development goals, while rural revitalization plays a pivotal role in advancing these objectives. High-frequency urban-to-rural mobility strengthens functional linkages between cities and rural areas by facilitating recurrent movements of people and their associated activities. However, existing research predominantly focuses on rural-to-urban migration, with less attention to high-frequency, recurrent and non-permanent urban-to-rural mobility. Moreover, current studies on reverse mobility mainly describe flow patterns rather than examining driving mechanisms. These knowledge gaps result in inefficient population attraction, resource misallocation, and policy misalignment. Here, using mobile signaling big data and the XGBoost model integrated with SHAP interpretability analysis, we identify the factors associated with urban-to-rural mobility in China’s Greater Bay Area, revealing their nonlinear responses and threshold effects. Results demonstrate that, beyond the common effects of logistics and accessibility, driving mechanisms vary significantly across rural area types: ecological-agricultural areas remain significantly influenced by traditional factors such as destination population size and road; the number of enterprises and GDP exert the strongest positive effect in industrial-productive areas; while the betweenness centrality of township nodes within the regional road network contributes significantly to population inflows in suburban-touristic areas. These insights advance theoretical understanding of urban-to-rural mobility drivers, calling for differentiated strategies to be adopted for distinct rural area types, effectively promoting urban-to-rural mobility and achieving rural revitalization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Decomposition method for a capacitated single-vehicle covering tour problem with intermediate facilities
Authors: Vera Fischer, Antoine Legrain, Patrick Munroe, David Schindl
Abstract: We consider a waste collection problem with intermediate disposal facilities to accommodate the usage of smaller, but more sustainable vehicles, with less capacity than the traditional waste collection trucks. The optimization problem consists in determining the locations to place the collection points and the routes of a capacitated collection vehicle that visits these locations. We first present a mixed-integer linear programming formulation that exploits the sparsity of the road network. To efficiently solve practical instances, we propose a solution method that decomposes the problem into a set covering problem to select the locations and a capacitated vehicle routing problem with intermediate facilities to determine the routes and price the set covering solution. We apply column generation to solve this routing problem and present a novel approach for the set covering problem that exploits the properties of the problem to efficiently find a set cover by using a graph theoretical approach. We compare our method with the set construction method presented in a previous work and the direct resolution of the MILP formulation by a state-of-the-art commercial solver. Computational experiments on instances derived from real-life data confirm the difficulty of our problem and show the superior performance of the developed decomposition method with respect to the number of best solutions and the average gaps to the best solution.

Title: A robust unified model for scalable TSP tour length estimation with size-adaptive target transformation
Authors: Sangil Han, Byung-In Kim
Abstract: In various routing and logistics problems, rapid and accurate estimation of the traveling salesman problem (TSP) tour length can provide useful surrogate route length estimates when repeated route evaluations are required. Existing estimation models often exhibit limited predictive accuracy or show performance degradation when applied to different node distributions, indicating insufficient robustness. Moreover, methods designed to handle multiple distributions typically rely on size-dependent correction terms or require retraining for different instance sizes, which restricts their scalability and practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a robust unified TSP tour length estimator that integrates a graph neural network (GNN) with global geometric features and a size-adaptive target transformation. The estimator achieves consistently high accuracy across varying node distributions and instance sizes with short prediction times, while offering the practical advantage of using a single model for multiple instance sizes. Although the GNN-based estimator with global geometric features improves predictive performance, it does not generalize satisfactorily beyond the training size range when trained on raw tour lengths. The proposed size-adaptive transformation, motivated by the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley asymptotic law for the Euclidean TSP, removes the dominant size-dependent scaling of tour length and enables the model to generalize to unseen large-scale instances with up to 1000 nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that the estimator achieves both higher accuracy and faster inference than existing baselines across diverse distributions and instance sizes. Notably, on large-scale instances, the size-adaptive transformation reduces the average prediction error from 49.68% with the raw target to 2.54%.

Title: A note on a heuristic for the maximal covering location disruption problem
Authors: Markus Sinnl, Kübra Tanınmış
Abstract: A recent paper published in the journal Computers & Operations Research introduced the so-called maximal covering location disruption problem and presented two heuristics based on mathematical programming techniques for it. The paper additionally gives a proposition which is claimed to make it possible to prove optimality for a solution obtained by solving a mathematical program, which is part of one of the presented heuristics. This proposition is then used to claim that one of the heuristics has superlative performance, as according to the proposition, it finds the optimal solution in many cases (Lunday, 2024, Section 5.2). In this note, we show that the proposition does not hold as stated, and consequently the claimed optimality certificates and reported optimality gaps are not supported. We complement this theoretical result with a computational study using an exact branch-and-cut algorithm from the literature.

Title: I think you think I think: Hierarchical belief learning and endogenous volatility dynamics
Authors: Tao Wang
Abstract: This paper develops a hierarchical belief learning model that endogenizes recursive expectation formation in financial markets. Agents form multi-level beliefs about future prices and about how other market participants forecast them, creating a finite, alternating cognitive hierarchy that links the depth and composition of recursive cross-type inference to aggregate price dynamics. The deterministic analysis shows that faster price adjustment or stronger recursive cross-type feedback can induce transitions from local stability to persistent oscillations and bounded irregular fluctuations. The stochastic extension demonstrates that small random shocks interacting with hierarchical feedback can generate volatility clustering, heavy tails, and persistent dependence in volatility proxies. Analytical characterization through local stability conditions, the Jacobian spectrum, and Lyapunov-based numerical evidence confirms that instability emerges endogenously from belief feedback rather than from exogenous disturbances. Empirical estimation using daily S&P 500 returns verifies that the model reproduces the principal stylized facts of financial markets and achieves the strongest overall joint fit in the benchmark set while remaining highly competitive in out-of-sample forecasting relative to econometric, behavioral, and machine-learning alternatives.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: High frequency measurement of consumer price inflation using scanner data
Authors: Daniel Melser, Robert J. Hill, Alicia Rambaldi
Abstract: Consumer price inflation is conventionally measured at a monthly or quarterly frequency. However, the increased availability of electronic point-of-sale data (scanner data) raises the possibility of constructing indexes at higher frequencies, such as weekly. This is likely to benefit many users, such as central banks, who closely follow consumer price trends. A key challenge in building high frequency weekly price indexes is intertemporal substitution. The dependence of current expenditures on past prices can introduce bias into the index. The paper proposes a novel solution to address this problem. We construct low frequency cost-of-living comparisons between two spans of weeks. Then show how to identify high-frequency weekly price changes from these low frequency multi-week price comparisons. Our approach to constructing weekly indexes is illustrated using a large US scanner data set from 2006 to 2020. We find modest increases in the variability of weekly compared with monthly indexes. Our results highlight that high frequency weekly indexes can be readily constructed in practice and that they are likely to provide new insights to policymakers.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Deconstructing energy inefficiency in China's manufacturing enterprises: Evidence from a machine learning evaluation method
Authors: Jiasen Sun, Yuchen Jiang, Jie Wu
Abstract: As China's manufacturing industry enters a pivotal phase of high-quality development, accurately assessing its energy efficiency (EE) has become essential for advancing green transformation. However, traditional approaches to measuring EE are prone to distortion from extreme observations, thereby limiting their effectiveness in capturing firm-level EE. Therefore, machine learning (ML) techniques are employed in this study to optimize EE assessment. The primary innovations of this paper are summarized as follows. First, ML-based decision-making units are constructed and introduced into the traditional efficiency evaluation model. Second, EE at the firm level is precisely measured using the proposed model, which improves the reliability of efficiency evaluation. Third, inefficiency is decomposed into internal and external components to identify targeted improvement directions. The empirical analysis based on the panel data of listed manufacturing firms in China yields several key insights. First, the proposed method provides a more rigorous efficiency benchmark and improves the discrimination among efficient firms. Second, firm-level EE exhibits a hierarchical distribution pattern with a small number of highly efficient firms and a large number of relatively low-efficiency firms. Third, EE varies significantly across industries and regions. Fourth, inefficiency mainly originates from either internal or external constraints, indicating heterogeneous improvement directions among firms. Accordingly, a set of differentiated policy recommendations tailored to these firms is proposed to improve their EE.

Title: Environmental impacts of bidirectional charging for electric school buses: a cross-regional assessment
Authors: Pranab Kar, Sabyasachee Mishra
Abstract: Electric school buses can interact bidirectionally with the grid during overnight idle periods, but their environmental consequences are poorly understood. This study develops a multi-objective overnight scheduling framework for electric school bus fleets that jointly optimizes charging costs, grid export, and age-dependent battery degradation under discrete charger-assignment constraints. A cross-regional assessment across six US grid subregions shows the net CO 2 effect is region-dependent, yielding reductions where the peak-to-off-peak marginal emission factor ratio is high and increases where it is low; coal-dominated grids produce net increases under current generation mixes. Benchmarking against smart unidirectional charging isolates what export itself contributes: deeper CO 2 and NO x reductions, but higher SO 2 and a reversal of the PM 2.5 benefit that unidirectional charging delivers. These outcomes are robust across five fleet scales, six utility tariffs, and five climate zones, though their magnitude depends on regional grid composition, arguing against blanket environmental credits and in favor of region-specific policy design.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Balanced fare inspection districts for large-scale urban bus transportation systems: A workload-sharing approach
Authors: Pablo Escalona, Luce Brotcorne, Daniel Cerda, Nathalia Wolf, Pablo Torrealba-González
Abstract: To inhibit fare evasion in proof-of-payment bus transportation systems, the transit authority schedules unpredictable passenger inspections conducted by inspection teams. The heterogeneous operating conditions and workloads faced by fare inspectors can be addressed by partitioning the transportation network into districts that ensure the efficient allocation of inspection teams to/from their assignments, as well as the fair distribution of workload among inspection teams. In this paper, we address the design of compact and balanced districts under an on-board fare inspection system, where the workload is defined in terms of the number of buses. Since buses travel throughout the transportation network, the workload is shared among bus stops, defining a novel districting problem. The problem of districting a bus transportation network under shared workload is formulated as a mixed-integer programming model for which a cutting-plane based branch-and-cut solution approach is proposed. The computational results highlight the effectiveness of the solution approach for large-scale networks when a tessellation technique and a well-designed restricted set of candidate district centers are used. Furthermore, we observe that a more balanced network design in terms of the number of buses leads to unbalanced designs in terms of geographic size.

Title: A hybrid machine learning framework for supplier risk prediction and segmentation: an automotive supply chain case study
Authors: Zahra GolchinZar, Bakhtiar Ostadi, Ehsan Nikbakhsh, Mahdi Esmaeili
Affiliations: Tarbiat Modares University Faculty of Industrial and Systems Engineering, , Tehran; Iran Khodro Company Department of Logistics Affairs, , Tehran, , and Department of Management and Accounting, Allameh Tabataba’I University, Tehran, Iran
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a hybrid data-driven framework for supplier risk assessment in automotive supply chains. It seeks to integrate predictive modeling with clustering techniques to proactively identify and categorize supplier risks, enabling enhanced operational stability and resilience. The research focuses on creating a decision-support tool that combines expert-validated risk indicators with advanced machine learning (ML) methods to address gaps in traditional risk management approaches. Design/methodology/approach A systematic methodology was used, combining Delphi-based expert validation (28 indicators from 36 initial factors) with ML. Data from 500 suppliers were preprocessed (K‑nearest neighbor (KNN) outlier removal, MinMax scaling), and feature selection was performed using PCA/LASSO/Ridge. Six regression models were optimized (Grid Search and Optuna), with support vector regression (SVR) showing best performance. Agglomerative clustering segmented suppliers based on risk profiles. Findings Support vector regression achieved superior predictive accuracy among tested models. Clustering revealed a significant future shift toward higher-risk supplier segments, with low-risk suppliers decreasing notably. The study confirms that increasing budget allocation does not automatically reduce risk or enhance resilience. Expert-validated indicators proved crucial for accurate risk assessment, while the hybrid framework effectively segments suppliers for targeted risk mitigation strategies. Originality/value This research contributes a novel hybrid framework integrating prediction and clustering for supplier risk management. It introduces expert-validated indicators through Delphi methodology and demonstrates their critical role in risk modeling. The study provides automotive manufacturers with a practical decision-support tool for proactive risk mitigation and resource allocation, bridging the gap between theoretical risk models and practical supply chain challenges.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Reputational risk and artificial intelligence: Critical research recommendations
Authors: Remko van Hoek, Robert Glenn Richey, Matthew D. Reid
Abstract: Recent global and technological disruptions have made reputational risks in purchasing and sourcing more consequential. These risks remain more difficult to conceptualize and measure than other risks. As digitization expands, they are becoming more visible. Generative and agentic AI applications enhance firms’ ability to monitor supplier and buyer behavior and performance across a broader range of variables. These applications can also help managers treat reputational risk as an intangible liability when issues become both visible and traceable.We advance the conceptualization of reputational risk as an intangible liability in supply chains. We identify key supply chain dimensions of reputational risk and incorporate the influence of digitization and artificial intelligence as a new dimension. We explore key considerations for managerial decision-making, noting that reputational risk spreads through the supply network structure. Digitization and generative AI influence how visible, fast-moving, traceable, and manageable reputational risk becomes. Purchasing and supply management decisions determine how that intangible reputational liability is absorbed, shifted, priced, or reduced.Reputational risk is multifaceted, consequential, and potentially substantial. It may propagate across the extended supply chain through spillover effects and reputational borrowing. Industry effects and partner profiles are among the primary considerations when quantifying the duration and intensity of reputational damage. We conclude with research questions intended to advance the purchasing and supply management body of knowledge.
Journal: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

Title: Automated vision-based dimensional inspection in car body assembly line with image sequence processing
Authors: Yifei Zhang, Theodore T. Allen, Ramiro Rodriguez Buno, James A. Paskett
Affiliations: The Ohio State University; University of Massachusetts Amherst

Title: On the use of a discrepancy decomposition model for calibration experiments
Authors: Yang Li, C. F. Jeff Wu, Shifeng Xiong
Affiliations: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences; SKLMS, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences; School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

Title: R&D Consortia in Competitive Supply Chains
Authors: Pascale Crama, Gaoyan Lyu, Yi Xu
Affiliations: Lee Kong Chian School of Business Singapore Management University Singapore Singapore; School of Management Beijing Institute of Technology Beijing China; Jiaxing Key Laboratory of Digital Economy and Data Operations Yangtze Delta Region Academy of Beijing Institute of Technology Jiaxing China; Robert H. Smith School of Business University of Maryland Maryland USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT R&D consortia, which coordinate R&D activities of their member firms, have been successful in many industries. We study a model with two competing supply chains each consisting of a manufacturer and a supplier. The manufacturers compete in the final product market, and can conduct R&D to reduce unit product costs of their final products. The R&D can be done in three different ways: by the two manufacturers independently, by them jointly in a horizontal R&D consortium, or by the supplier and the manufacturer jointly in each supply chain in two vertical R&D consortia. We find that as compared to independent R&D, both the horizontal consortium and the vertical consortia lead to higher R&D effort, wholesale prices, and output quantities in the supply chains. However, different supply chain parties' preferences over the two types of consortia are not necessarily consistent. We then consider a game where the firms endogenously determine to form which type of R&D consortium in the industry. We show that vertical consortia emerge in industries with high R&D uncertainty and effort cost, and the horizontal consortium is likely to emerge otherwise. Our results provide plausible explanations on why different types of R&D consortium emerge and flourish in different industries and shed light on their potential benefits for consumers and social welfare.

Title: Variational Bayesian inference for accelerated degradation tests with heterogeneity
Authors: Min Zhou, Xiujie Zhao, Zhen He, Min Xie
Abstract: This study proposes a comprehensive framework to analyze accelerated degradation tests (ADT) data for highly reliable systems. Motivated by complex degradation behaviors observed in practice, we study the inherent unit-to-unit heterogeneity. A generalized Wiener process is formulated to assign independent random effects to both the drift and diffusion coefficients while accommodating nonlinear degradation dynamics. Considering the computational intractability induced by high-dimensional random effects, we employ a variational Bayesian expectation–maximization (VB-EM) algorithm to efficiently estimate the unknown parameters. Moreover, to accurately capture the stress-degradation relationship, a confidence density approach is utilized to hierarchically estimate the parameters of the acceleration link function. Further, precise confidence intervals for reliability metrics are derived via a parametric bootstrap procedure. Extensive simulation studies and a real-world LED case study demonstrate the practical applicability of the proposed framework. The results confirm that the proposed VB-EM paradigm delivers overwhelmingly superior computational efficiency without compromising estimation accuracy, in comparison to the traditional Monte Carlo EM approach.

Title: Are Consumers Myopic? Evidence from Handset and Mobile Services Choices
Authors: Ambre Elsas‐Nicolle
Affiliations: Mines Paris, PSL University, Centre for Economics and Public Decision (CEDP), i3 UMR9217 CNRS Paris France
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, I estimate discrete choice models for the joint selection of handsets and mobile tariffs, using data on 10,738 subscribers of a European mobile telecommunications operator observed between April 2011 and December 2014. The estimates are used to compute an attention weight on future recurring tariff payments, measured relative to the upfront handset cost. I interpret this weight as a ‘revealed‐choice’ measure of consumer myopia. The results show that consumers substantially underweight future costs on average, with heterogeneity across consumer groups and, more importantly, over time. The average attention weight increases sharply during the period studied, coinciding with the diffusion of SIM‐only tariffs and the entry of a new competitor. These market changes affected prices and variety, but also increased the salience and transparency of total contract costs. Counterfactual simulations show that consumer welfare gains come from both the decline in tariff prices and the availability of SIM‐only offers. The price decline accounts for a large share of the gains, while SIM‐only tariffs provide additional welfare gains by expanding the choice set. Comparing the estimated attention weights with a full‐attention benchmark further shows that consumer underattention shapes predicted choices.

Title: Identification of Relationship Lending in Bank–Borrower Networks
Authors: Yoshitaka Ogisu, Shoka Hayaki, Masahiko Shibamoto
Affiliations: Faculty of Economics Konan University Kobe Japan; Research Institute for Economics and Business Administration (RIEB) Kobe University Kobe Japan; Graduate School of Business Administration Kobe University Kobe Japan; Center for Computational Social Science (CCSS), Kobe University Kobe Japan
Abstract: ABSTRACT Relationship lending refers to lending based on close bank–borrower relationships, expected to increase credit availability and support real economic activity. This paper proposes the ST‐B filter, a novel framework identifying significant ties in temporal bipartite networks. Applying our method to Japanese financial data (1977–2021), relationship lending comprises about 10%–35% of total lending and is associated with 33% larger loan volume than transaction lending. Our method uniquely enables the analysis of relationship lending using only transaction data, without requiring detailed information on bank–borrower relationships.
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Managing geopolitical risk in global supply chains: A qualitative study of European multinational enterprises
Authors: Arnd Huchzermeier, Mark Kuppek
Abstract: Geopolitical risk has emerged as a major disruptive risk to global supply chains and the operations of multinational enterprises (MNEs) today. Drawing on a qualitative content analysis of the annual reports of 20 European MNEs across five industries, supported by a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline, this study examines how companies strategically manage geopolitical risk in their supply chains. We extend an established supply chain risk framework by conceptualizing geopolitical risk management (GRM) as a distinct strategic risk management dimension centered on reducing geopolitical exposure, in contrast to supply chain risk management (SCRM), which enhances operational resilience within existing supply chain structures. Applying this distinction, we identify seven key GRM strategies, including localization, decentralized procurement and R&D, direct sourcing, supplier diversification, geographical production diversification, circular economy initiatives, and political engagement. Furthermore, applying the Triple-P framework in a disclosure-based setting suggests that companies facing different forms of supply chain complexity across the partnership, product, and process dimensions disclose distinct portfolios of GRM strategies. The findings of this study provide cross-industry insights into the strategic orientation of large European MNEs and support managerial decision making to strengthen resilience in the face of supply chain and geopolitical risk.

Title: Modelling the macroeconomic impact of Brazil's ecological transformation plan: a stock-flow consistent approach
Authors: Matías Torchinsky Landau, Sebastián Valdecantos, Etienne Espagne
Abstract: In 2023, the Brazilian government launched the Ecological Transformation Plan (ETP), a new development strategy aimed at promoting environmentally sustainable economic growth while enhancing productivity and social equity. This paper evaluates the macroeconomic impacts of the ETP's financial policy mix, by developing a stock-flow consistent model. The analysis focuses on representing the policy mix embedded in the ETP—particularly its financial instruments—and evaluating its implications for investment, growth, and macroeconomic stability. A key contribution of the paper is the explicit modelling of financing mechanisms designed to mitigate currency risk, a structural constraint that affects many EMDEs and limits the scalability of low-carbon investments. By incorporating these features into an SFC framework, the paper provides new insights into how financial structures and policy interventions interact with real economic dynamics. Simulations through 2030 indicate that the ETP is expansionary, with projected GDP growth rising up to 1.6% and the creation of 360,000 to 900,000 new jobs. While the plan improves the primary fiscal balance by increasing tax revenues, it introduces specific trade-offs: the reduction in unemployment may prompt the Central Bank to raise the Selic rate to curb inflation, and increased demand for capital goods is expected to widen the current account deficit by 0.2–0.4 p.p. of GDP.

Title: Reducing transport externalities through nudging: Results from a GPS-tracked experiment
Authors: Laura Schwab, Beat Hintermann, Alexander Goetz, Joseph Molloy
Abstract: This study presents results from a randomized controlled trial in Switzerland that investigates the effects of a non-monetary intervention on transport choices.
