A GPS-based tracking app records the movements of 814 participants for several months, and automatically detects their travel modes. The treatment consists of sending personalized transport reports to a randomly selected subgroup. These reports contain personalized descriptive and prescriptive information on participants’ transport-related external costs. The treatment reduces the external costs of transport by 12.4%, but only on weekends, and only during the first half of the study. In the second half, the effect dissipates to zero. Based on participants’ travel response and their willingness-to-pay for future reports, we estimate average gross welfare gains of 1.6–3.6 Swiss francs per participant per week in the short run. Of this, 0.8–2.8 Swiss francs reflect the private value of the reports rather than the temporary behavioral change.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Debt management and strategic interactions in top-down bureaucracy: Evidence from China
Authors: Xi Qu, Zhiwei Xu, Jinxiang Yu, Xinyu Zhan
Abstract: Strategic interactions between political agents shape the allocation of public resources. This paper empirically investigates how newly increased debt ceilings are allocated to prefectural cities in China following its debt management reform. We document both demand-side and supply-side forces in debt quota allocation. In addition to observable factors specified in the official formula, political connections with provincial leaders and local applications induced by regional competition significantly raise newly increased debt ceilings. The two channels operate through distinct mechanisms: political connections primarily affect supply-side allocation and facilitate borrowing driven by rollover pressure, whereas regional competition is more closely linked to ceilings on special debt, active investment demand, and the intensive utilization of approved debt ceilings. Further, we estimate the real consequences of debt ceiling allocation. An increase in the debt ceiling promotes short-run GDP growth but depresses total factor productivity (TFP). Additionally, cities with tighter ceilings tend to accumulate more implicit debt through local government financing vehicles.

Title: Value co-creation through C2M and live-streaming in platform-based supply chains
Authors: Shuwen Ding, Zhaofu Hong, Peng Wang, Zihao Mu
Abstract: Customers increasingly demand customized products, prompting manufacturers to shift from mass production toward Customer-to-Manufacturer (C2M) strategies within platform-based supply chains characterized by closer manufacturer-customer connections. To support this shift, many platforms integrate live-streaming functionalities that directly link manufacturers and customers through real-time product demonstration and interaction. However, it remains unclear how live-streaming reshapes manufacturers’ C2M decisions and whether it improves outcomes for different participants in the platform-based supply chain. This study develops a game-theoretic model to analyze the strategic interactions between a manufacturer and a platform under traditional e-commerce and live-streaming channels. Our findings reveal that live-streaming affects the manufacturer’s customization and pricing decisions in a non-monotonic manner. Interestingly, the manufacturer prefers live-streaming only when the streamer has a low or high display ability, while a moderately capable streamer creates a “moderate capability trap” in which live-streaming generates only limited market benefit. From the platform’s perspective, live-streaming expands market demand but requires balancing revenue sharing, such that a mutually beneficial outcome between the platform and the manufacturer arises only when the commission rate lies within a feasible interval. Moreover, a “win–win–win” outcome in which the manufacturer, platform, and customers all benefit can emerge only under sufficiently strong display ability and appropriately aligned revenue allocation. These findings provide insights into how live-streaming can be effectively leveraged to support C2M strategies in platform-based supply chains.

Title: ECB monetary policy transmission to unilaterally euroised economies
Authors: Georgi Krustev
Abstract: Leveraging the unique setting of unilateral euroisation, this paper examines the spillover effects of euro area monetary policy on Montenegro and Kosovo. Through the lens of a structural VAR model with block exogeneity, it shows that euro area monetary policy shocks can significantly influence output and inflation in these economies, albeit with a delayed response, while contributing only modestly to their overall business cycle fluctuations.

Title: Exact inference after data-driven control-unit selection in difference-in-differences
Authors: Ryoya Nakano, Takahiro Hoshino
Abstract: In comparative case studies that select a single control using a centered pre-treatment fit criterion, researchers report a difference-in-differences interval treating the selection as fixed. Under a Gaussian panel model with known covariance, a centered criterion yields exact naive intervals when the covariance is separable with a spherical time factor, for any cross-sectional covariance. Otherwise, given the selection and an independent residual, the estimator is truncated normal; the pivot yields exact selective coverage. In our simulations, naive coverage was often conservative and never materially below nominal; working-model plug-in inference exhibited modest undercoverage under strong serial correlation.

Title: Coordinating the port-carrier supply chain: Optimal design of volume-commitment discount contracts
Authors: Chengyu Du, Yineng Wang, Fang He, Zuo-Jun (Max) Shen
Abstract: Ports operate as capacity-constrained service platforms that face substantial demand volatility and congestion risk from multiple heterogeneous carriers. In this context, effective contracts between ports and carriers can help mitigate the inefficiency. This study develops a contract-based coordination framework that enables risk sharing and efficiency improvement in port-carrier cargo transfer. Specifically, we focus on volume-commitment discount contracts, under which the port offers a price incentive in exchange for the carriers’ binding commitment to a specific cargo volume, enhancing resource planning and operational efficiency. We first demonstrate that simple volume-commitment discount contracts, while Pareto-improving compared to no contract, fail to achieve full coordination due to double marginalization. In a multi-carrier context, shared and congestible port resources further make the contract design problem nonseparable across carriers. To achieve coordination, we develop a coupled volume-commitment discount and shortage-subsidy contract that induces system-optimal commitments, mitigates congestion externalities, and flexibly allocates surplus among participants. Comparative statics show that carrier heterogeneity shapes differentiated contract design. In particular, a substitution effect is revealed: the port tends to offer deeper discounts to carriers with lower shortfall-settlement costs when commitments from other carriers are harder to secure. The port also offers stronger incentives to carriers with higher demand uncertainty to manage congestion-related risks. Moreover, our findings further suggest that differentiated incentive contracts are more valuable for congestion-vulnerable ports with high planning benefits.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Transforming on-street parking in the city center: Evidence on public acceptability before and after implementation
Authors: Kostas Mouratidis, Hans Skov-Petersen, Trine Agervig Carstensen
Abstract: Despite the key role of parking policy in sustainable transport, there is surprisingly limited research on how people view and experience parking policies. This study investigates changes in public acceptability of a real-world parking transformation. Approximately 50% of existing parking spaces were removed from the streets of the city center of Copenhagen with the purpose of being reused as space for street life, bicycle infrastructure, and greenery. Longitudinal survey data (N = 1378) were collected immediately before and one year after policy implementation, as part of a before-after panel study. Results show that acceptability of on-street parking transformation was generally high, with the majority of respondents supporting the policy both before and after implementation. However, acceptability declined after implementation, indicating a possible gap between expected and experienced outcomes. Furthermore, panel data analysis shows that travel satisfaction, intentions to reduce car use, younger age, higher education, and cohabitation status are linked to higher acceptability across the study period. Conversely, residence in the intervention area, preference for car-based mobility, car dependence, and car availability are associated with lower acceptability. Analysis of residents’ evaluations reveals differing attitudes towards the policy. Positive attitudes include support for car-free zones and for expected improvements in walkability, bikeability, livability, and sustainability, while negative attitudes revolve around perceived inconvenience for residents of the city center, anticipated negative impacts to local businesses, and exclusion of car drivers from the city center.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: HDO-RRT*: An enhanced RRT* path planning algorithm with hybrid directional exploration and adaptive obstacle-aware optimization
Authors: Zimin Xu, Lin Lin, Yanying Chen, Guangcheng Pang, Jinyan Huang, Jianlei Zhang
Abstract: Path planning is a fundamental challenge in autonomous robotics, where sampling-based algorithms such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree Star (RRT*) have demonstrated asymptotic optimality but suffer from slow convergence and suboptimal path quality in complex environments. This paper presents HDO-RRT*, an enhanced sampling-based algorithm that systematically improves RRT* through three synergistic strategies. First, Hybrid Directional Exploration (HDE) adaptively integrates goal-directed guidance with stochastic exploration using an exponentially decaying weight, accelerating convergence while preserving exploration capability. Second, Density-Aware Adaptive Step Regulation (DASR) dynamically adjusts expansion step sizes based on local obstacle density via a moving average reference, improving safety in cluttered regions and efficiency in open spaces. Third, Obstacle-Aware Local Refinement (OALR) performs backtracking-based path optimization using obstacle proximity information to generate refined intermediate nodes, significantly reducing path length while maintaining collision-free feasibility. Comprehensive experiments across four representative environments demonstrate that HDO-RRT* consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art algorithms (RRT*, Informed-RRT*, PQ-RRT*, F-RRT*, C-RRT*), achieving path length reductions up to 9.2% and planning time improvements up to 40.2% compared to baseline RRT*. Ablation studies validate the individual and combined contributions of each strategy, while validation in realistic scenarios confirms practical applicability. The results establish HDO-RRT* as an effective solution for autonomous navigation in complex, obstacle-rich environments.

Title: Metaheuristic-assisted constraint programming for resource-constrained flexible job shop scheduling with separable setup times and parallel-sequential transfers
Authors: Ankun Chen, Jianjun Liu, Ting Liu
Abstract: Addressing the research gap in integrating advanced production organization approaches for the Flexible Job Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP), this paper proposes a novel Resource-Constrained FJSP (RCFJSP-SP), which incorporates Separable Setup Time (SST) and Parallel-Sequence Transfer (PST). The proposed model enables the parallel processing of setup and process stages through the SST mechanism, while ensuring synchronization between operation transfer and machine processing via the PST strategy, thereby enhancing production flexibility. However, the synergistic effect of these two mechanisms introduces dual challenges of dynamic resource competition and strict temporal constraints, significantly increasing the problem complexity compared to conventional FJSP. The resulting scheduling problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Quadratically Constrained Programming (MIQCP) model with bilinear setup-triggering constraint. To solve this NP-hard problem, we developed an Improved Genetic Algorithm Assisted Constraint Programming (IGAACP) method. The main contribution lies in establishing a collaborative optimization framework that effectively combines the global search capabilities of population intelligence with the exact resolution advantages of constraint satisfaction techniques. Key implementation challenges include the design of collaborative mechanisms, complex constraint handling, and balancing computational efficiency. Experimental results based on 27 test cases generated from household appliance component manufacturing characteristics demonstrate that the IGAACP framework significantly outperforms individual algorithms, achieving 14.39% and 6.15% improvement in average makespan compared to the improved genetic algorithm (IGA) and constraint programming (CP) approaches, respectively.

Title: Persistent and transitory inflation in the euro area: Insights from global and domestic shocks
Authors: Clemente Pinilla-Torremocha
Abstract: This paper investigates the post-COVID inflation surge in the euro area, combining three features: decomposition of long-term trends and business-cycle dynamics—such as potential GDP, trend inflation, output-gap, and inflation-gap; time-varying volatility and fat-tailed distributions to accommodate extreme observations; and structural shock identification, distinguishing shocks by their persistence (permanent-vs.-transitory) and domain (global-vs.-domestic, demand-vs.-supply, or energy-specific). Unlike the existing literature, findings show that domestic supply shocks feed into the persistent component of euro area inflation, raising trend inflation to 3% by 2022. Demand shocks—domestic and global—manifest in the transitory component (inflation gap), explaining 85% of the post-COVID inflation surge.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Reference-point effects in bargaining
Authors: Olivier L’Haridon, Noemí Navarro
Abstract: This paper investigates whether an earned endowment can serve as a salient reference point in unstructured bargaining and thereby reshape focal agreements. In a laboratory experiment with 166 participants, subjects earn endowments in a real-effort task, and subsequent bargaining menus are framed as changes relative to these earned endowments, while disagreement yields zero payoffs. The design distinguishes agreements that equalize total earnings (equal splits in final payoffs) from agreements that equalize the incremental surplus relative to the reference point (equal changes). Under symmetric endowments these notions coincide; under asymmetric endowments they diverge, so equalizing total earnings requires an unequal division of the incremental surplus. Results show that equal splits are not universal even under symmetry, and when endowments are asymmetric they lose focality in favor of equal-change and intermediate compromise agreements. The findings are robust across environments in which the reference point is available, dominated by some feasible agreements, or an infeasible claim. The results highlight how the salience and asymmetry of a reference point affects which notion of equality is focal in bargaining.

Title: Local shocks and internal migration: The disparate effects of robots and Chinese imports in the US
Authors: Marius Faber, Andrés Sarto, Marco Tabellini
Abstract: Migration is a key mechanism through which local labor markets adjust to economic shocks. In this paper, we analyze the migration response of American workers to two of the most important shocks that hit US manufacturing since the 1990s: Chinese import competition and the introduction of industrial robots. Exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in exposure across US local labor markets over time, we establish a new fact. Even though both shocks drastically reduced employment in the manufacturing sector, only robots led to a sizable decline in population size. We provide evidence that negative employment spillovers outside manufacturing, caused by robots but not by Chinese imports, can explain the different migration responses. We interpret our findings through the lens of a model that highlights two mechanisms: the cost savings that each shock provides and the degree of complementarity between directly and indirectly exposed industries.

Title: Editorial Board
Housing type mix as a lever for sustainable urban mobility
Authors: Peter Berrill
Abstract: Land use-transport interactions are well documented in literature using urban form metrics including density, land–use mix, and destination accessibility, but rarely housing type shares. This study demonstrates the overlooked explanatory and causal relevance of housing typology, specifically the single–family housing share, for four mobility outcomes: car travel, transit travel, car ownership, and CO 2 emissions. Using postcode–level data for 13 cities in Germany and France, we compare the role of urban form metrics across linear regression, gradient–boosted decision trees, artificial neural networks, causal discovery, and double machine learning methods. Single–family share consistently outperforms conventional urban form indicators in explaining each outcome. Given its strong predictive power, causal relevance, and ease of measurement, housing typology offers substantial potential for modelling land use-transport interactions and provides a promising cross–sectoral focus for climate and mobility policy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Social influences on the adoption of electric vehicles: A meta-analysis
Authors: Wen Wen, Yue Lv, Peng Zhou
Abstract: This study conducts a meta‑analysis of 152 primary estimates to examine how social influences affect electric vehicle (EV) adoption. We distinguish between informational influences (social interaction and neighborhood effect) and normative influences (social norm and social symbolism). The results confirm a significant overall effect of social influences on EV adoption, with normative influences outweighing informational ones. Over time, the dominant normative driver shifts from social symbolism to social norm. Cross‑sectionally, social norm is more influential in collectivistic cultures and for conservative innovations, whereas informational social interaction is more influential in individualistic cultures and for radical innovations. Based on these findings, we recommend celebrity endorsements to amplify social symbolism in early market stages, and green labelling to reinforce social norm in mature markets. Community-based campaigns that foster social interaction are suggested for individualistic regions and radical innovations, while broad publicity emphasizing social norm is suggested for collectivistic regions and conservative innovations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: JUE insight: Soft infrastructure and the location choice of multinational firms: Evidence from Japanese investment in the United States in the 1980s
Authors: Shuichiro Nishioka, Eric Olson, Haoyu Wang
Abstract: We examine whether culture-specific educational infrastructure influenced the location decisions of multinational enterprises by analyzing Japanese foreign direct investment (FDI) in the United States over the 1980s. Using the expansion of Japanese FDI following Reagan-era trade tensions, we test whether preexisting Japanese Studies programs at U.S. universities predict subsequent Japanese investment across 722 commuting zones. We find that zones with Japanese Studies programs in 1975 were approximately 25 percentage points more likely to receive Japanese investment in 1992, controlling for traditional determinants like Japanese population, manufacturing infrastructure, agglomeration, and market access. The results are robust to alternative empirical methods, including the instrumental variable approach. Our results suggest that “soft infrastructure”—culture-specific human capital pipelines—represents an overlooked location advantage in attracting FDI.

Title: The adverse effects of weight reports in schools
Authors: Yuliya Kazakova, Birgitta Rabe
Abstract: Using rich survey data for England, we investigate whether providing parents with information about the weight status of their children reduces children's weight and improves health behaviors, or whether it has adverse effects. We exploit the timing of survey interview compared to the timing of sending out weight reports to parents in a difference-in-differences framework. Our analysis does not reveal the intended effects on body weight or health behaviors. Instead, we find adverse effects for children with overweight that are concentrated in disadvantaged families and driven by increases in breakfast skipping and feeling tired and unhappy at school.

Title: An experimental study on the effect of knowledge on idea generation and idea selection
Authors: Bernd Irlenbusch, Katharina Laske, Marina Schröder, Rika Stoczek
Abstract: How firms generate and select ideas influences their strategic path and the development of entire industries. To better understand this process, we experimentally analyze the impact of knowledge on idea generation and selection in an incentivized ideation task. Between treatments, we vary whether or not ideators are provided with examples of previous successful ideas before working on the task. We provide causal evidence that knowledge about such example ideas leads to path dependencies, i.e., knowledge increases the similarity of new ideas to those provided. Consistent with the hypothesis that knowledge affects the search for new ideas, we find evidence of path dependencies during idea generation, but do not find statistically significant evidence of additional path dependencies during idea selection. Overall, when knowledge is provided, we observe an increase in selected innovative ideas that are similar to previous ideas and a decrease in selected innovative ideas that are different from previous ideas.

Title: Multi-objective design of the material handling system in zone-based job shop manufacturing environments using supervised machine learning
Authors: Hani Pourvaziri, Uday Venkatadri, Sadan Kulturel-Konak, Hamid Afshari, Hassan Sarhadi, Majid Taghavi
Affiliations: Dalhousie University; Penn State Berks; Acadia University; Saint Mary's University
Abstract: Zone-based and flexible bay layout concepts are essential tools for facility designers, particularly in job shop manufacturing environments characterised by medium-to-high product variety and flexible routing. While traditional approaches focus primarily on optimising zone dimensions and allocating departments within zones, this paper advances the design process by investigating the subsequent steps required to finalise layout configurations in zone-based job shop systems. Specifically, these steps include identifying material-handling input/output points along cell boundaries, determining appropriate aisle dimensions, and selecting suitable material-handling transporters. To address these interrelated decisions, the study proposes a cascading methodology that integrates design of experiments (DOE), discrete-event simulation, supervised deep learning, and multi-objective optimisation. The optimisation process employs the Non-Dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II) in conjunction with an adaptive direct-search strategy implemented through NOMAD, a black-box optimisation solver. A numerical case study of a zone-based job shop system is presented. Computational results show that the optimised layouts achieve substantial reductions in material-handling time and work-in-process (WIP); for instance, one solution reduces average transport time by approximately 25% and WIP by approximately 35%, with only a modest increase in handling cost. These findings highlight the practical value of the proposed multi-objective approach.

Title: Two-dimensional extended warranty menu design and pricing with usage rate heterogeneity and transferability
Authors: Meng Zhou, Ken Chen, Shuguang He, Zhen He
Affiliations: Tianjin University
Abstract: Extended warranty (EW) is an option to customers to pay for extending the basic warranty of purchased products. Recently, EW is critical for improving after-sales profitability as well as customer loyalty. Nevertheless, conventional EWs are constrained on first owner of the product, which means the EW expires when the product ownership transferred. Furthermore, the EWs are often offered to customers with uniform issues and same price. However, the utility of an EW offer differs to customers of products with different usage rates and usage patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a menu-based design framework that integrates both transferable EW (T-EW) and non-transferable EW (NT-EW) options, incorporating usage-based pricing and differentiated service levels. The expected costs for both T-EW and NT-EW are first derived on the basis of actual usage rates. Customer choice behaviour is then modelled using a multinomial logit (MNL) model, capturing how customers trade off between price, service coverage, and transferability when making purchase decisions. The prices and service levels of each EW option are jointly optimised to maximise the expected profit. Numerical experiments are provided to illustrate the consideration of transferability and usage rate heterogeneity.

Title: Constructed by multiple on-machine inspection: intelligent machining system driven by digital twin
Authors: Yumeng Zhang, Neng Wan, Zhaolong Zeng, Xujie Li, Zujie Zheng, Hui Sun, Xiaolong Zhou
Affiliations: School of Mechanical Engineering, Northwestern Polytechnical University; Shanghai Spaceflight Precision Machinery Institute; Shaanxi Wangao Aeronautical & Astronautical Intelligent Manufacturing Technology Co., Ltd.
Abstract: There are many precise parts in aerospace products whose dimensions are difficult to ensure one-time due to multi-source errors, even though fabricated by the precision machine tool. The reason is that the cutting instruction cannot be adjusted in terms of the practical status of the error sources during the machining. Thus, the intelligent machining system (IMS), composed of an intelligent machine tool, intelligent fabrication instruction and twin model factory, is required for precise part fabrication, which can improve machining accuracy without manual intervention. In this paper, the digital twins from different perspectives are investigated with the help of multiple on-machine inspection techniques. The digital twins are integrated into traditional machine tools and cutting instructions to obtain abilities such as on-machine inspection, edge computing in machine tools, compensation fabrication, and process optimisation. Furthermore, analyzing the digital twin model interactions and evolution can enable the self-adjusting fabricaiton of difficult-to-cut parts. At last, a typical difficult-to-cut part is used to verify the capacity of the intelligent machining system. It is proven that the digital twin models can help build intelligent machine tools and processes to improve the accuracy and efficiency of machining.

Title: Identical parallel machine scheduling with tool changes under the peak power consumption constraint
Authors: XiYing Li, ChenGuang Liu, Mengxing Gao
Affiliations: Northwestern Polytechnical University
Abstract: In practical CNC machining for aerospace and automotive components, machine availability is constrained by tool changes due to tool wear, while each machine's continuous processing time is limited by tool life. Furthermore, total real-time power consumption must not exceed the predetermined peak power threshold at any time within the planning horizon. This study investigates an identical parallel machine scheduling problem with tool changes under the peak power consumption constraint, aiming to minimise the makespan. We propose two Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) models: one based on the traditional scheduling procedure and the other inspired by the two-dimensional Strip Packing (SP) problem, and develop a Greedy heuristic to efficiently solve large-scale instances. Experimental results show that both models yield optimal solutions only for small-scale instances. The proposed Greedy heuristic is capable of obtaining near-optimal solutions for small-scale instances and outperforms three adapted benchmark algorithms (LJM-LMM, MSA and HGA) in both efficiency and solution quality for large-scale problems. Finally, we derive managerial insights to support industrial decision-making, offering a systematic approach to simultaneously meet peak power requirements, optimise tool utilisation, and enhance production effectiveness in real-world manufacturing settings.

Title: Energy-aware production scheduling considering energy consumption in storage under time-of-use tariffs
Authors: Hongguang Bo, Xiao Alison Chen, Shiqi He, Qian Luo
Affiliations: Dalian University of Technology; University of New Hampshire; Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
Abstract: In this paper, we investigate energy-aware production scheduling under Time-of-Use (TOU) tariffs, specifically for industries where inventory storage incurs significant energy costs. We develop a mixed-integer programming model that minimises total costs, including production energy costs, storage energy costs, and late-penalty costs. Given the model's complexity, we propose two algorithms: Multicost-Based Adaptive Genetic Algorithm (MBAGA) and Multicost-Based Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (MBALNS). These algorithms integrate cost-based weighting mechanisms to efficiently balance trade-offs between different cost components. Numerical experiments demonstrate that, given a computational time constraint, our algorithms significantly outperform the exact method in efficiency and solution quality. Compared with three benchmark algorithms for scheduling under TOU tariffs, both MBAGA and MBALNS consistently achieve lower total costs and faster convergence. Sensitivity analyses with respect to key model and algorithmic parameters confirm the robustness of the proposed approaches. Our results highlight the importance of considering energy consumption during storage in scheduling models and offer a scalable and adaptable framework for optimising late-penalty cost and energy cost during production and storage.

Title: A scenario-based robust optimisation approach for social cost vehicle routing problem in disaster response
Authors: Azadeh Sadeghi, Hadi Mosadegh, Roohollah Younessinaki, Felipe Aros-Vera
Affiliations: University of Michigan-Flint; Amirkabir University of Technology; Northern Illinois University; Ohio University
Abstract: Efficient, effective, and equitable disaster response is critical yet challenging due to uncertainties, particularly those in vehicle travel times caused by infrastructure damage. To address this, current study proposes a scenario-based robust optimisation social cost vehicle routing problem (SRO-SCVRP) that minimises three objectives: (1) social cost, balancing logistics and deprivation costs, with the latter quantifying survivors’ suffering from delayed access to critical supplies; (2) the variation in expected deprivation cost across travel time scenarios, reflecting solution robustness; and (3) penalties for exceeding service coverage windows (SCW), which are thresholds set by decision-makers to ensure timely deliveries, thereby enhancing model robustness. Logistics and deprivation costs operationalise efficiency and effectiveness, respectively, while the second and third objectives promote equity by reducing disparities in access and ensuring the timely fulfilment of demand. Numerical results from the SRO-SCVRP highlight a trade-off wherein gains in robustness and equity are achieved with only a modest impact on logistics cost. To assess robustness and equity, a Time and Inventory Service-Level Metric (TISM) is developed and applied to alternative water distribution strategies. Among them, the hybrid strategy yields the highest overall TISM, making it the most robust and equitable option across varied SCW thresholds and resource availability.

Title: Robust sustainable sourcing and inventory planning under stochastic carbon emissions
Authors: Md Tanweer Ahmad, Mohammad Firouz
Affiliations: Department of Quantitative Techniques, Indian Institute of Foreign Trade, Gift City Campus, New Delhi, India; University of Alabama at Birmingham
Abstract: In this paper, we study a generalised two-tier supply chain wherein a firm with multiple facilities seeks to select a subset of suppliers with different prices, qualities, capacities, and carbon emissions. Exogenous demand in the second tier then is satisfied by the selected suppliers in a multi-sourcing framework. The firm in our setting seeks to minimise the integrated cost of sourcing, inventory planning, and emission penalties while adhering to operational limitations as well as regulatory constraints. In our setting, we assume that each supplier produces a stochastic amount of greenhouse gas emissions per unit supplied, leading to environmental cost for the sourcing facilities proportionate to the amount sourced. We develop an iterative heuristic coupled with an accelerated Bender's decomposition to solve the underlying NP-hard MINLP robust formulation. First, we demonstrate the superior performance of our methodology against a benchmark commercial solver in terms of both solution quality and run time. Next, utilising data motivated by a real case study, we derive extensive managerial insights with regards to robustness analysis, price of sustainability, and supplier selection. We conclude our analysis by explaining the implications of various parameter settings in practical decision-making.

Title: TRIZ-AI approach for next-gen solutions
Authors: Giampiero Donnici, Marco Freddi, Leonardo Frizziero
Affiliations: Alma Mater Studiorum – University of Bologna
Abstract: This study proposes an innovative approach that integrates the classical TRIZ methodology with Artificial Intelligence (AI), broadening the scope for developing alternative and innovative technical solutions. TRIZ is used to resolve the main technical contradictions in a project. Instead, AI is exploited to translate the generic outputs of the TRIZ into specific technical solutions for the product under development. In particular, various Large Language Models (LLM) pre-trained chatbots, such as GPT-4, Gemini, You, and others, are used for this part of the method, acknowledging their advanced capabilities. This work demonstrates the practical applicability of this integration in a real-world context, suggesting its potential application across diversified technological domains (Yu et al. 2023). Based on the responses and results obtained, the discussed approach has potential, although limited to the product concept phase and preliminary project stages. However, the fusion of TRIZ and AI still emerges as a significant contribution within the discussed studies (a wheel support for skate, innovative earphones, a mini collaborative robot for educational applications, glasses for visually impaired users) and from a broader, multi-context perspective of mechanical design.

Title: Disaster assessment of oil and gas supply chain based on data-driven dynamic Bayesian networks
Authors: Wei Xie, Zhenzhong Guan
Affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University
Abstract: The oil and gas supply chain (OGSC) constitutes a fundamental pillar of the global economy, providing vital energy resources, bolstering industrial activities, enabling international trade, and safeguarding national security. However, existing risk assessment approaches exhibit significant limitations: traditional methods predominantly rely on expert judgment or static probabilistic frameworks, often neglecting the temporal evolution of disruption factors and lacking robust data-driven methodologies. These critical gaps necessitate an interpretable, data-driven, and temporally-aware framework capable of accurately identifying, quantifying, and predicting OGSC disruption risks. This study introduces a novel, data-driven methodology that incorporates a word embedding model and develops a Data-driven Dynamic Bayesian Network (DDBN) to assess the impact of seven significant factors, including technology and economy, on disruptions within the OGSC. Our exhaustive analysis reveals a consistent 71% probability of disruptions in the OGSC. Among the seven factors, environmental influences are the most significant, while technical factors have the least impact. Sensitivity analysis and belief propagation are employed to derive valuable managerial insights into the efficacy of the proposed model. The code and associated data supporting this study are accessible at https://github.com/raichll/Research-on-oil-and-gas-supply-chain-disruption.git.

Title: Experimental study on human–robot collaborative assembly: cognitive load and effects on quality
Authors: Sotirios Panagou, Monica Sileo, Fabio Fruggiero, W. Patrick Neumann
Affiliations: University of Basilicata; NTNU; Toronto Metropolitan University
Abstract: Human–robot interaction is becoming a prevalent design choice for workplaces. Robots can provide support in tasks and processes, while humans can provide flexibility in certain aspects. However, as seen in the literature reviews, the implementation of human–robot systems does not consider the effects on operators, which can increase mental demands and raise safety concerns. This work presents the results of an experimental study on human–robot collaboration, targeting the connection between cognitive load and quality of processes, products, and human work. The results show that the temporal demand of collaboration is one of the associated reasons behind cognitive load and stress. The authors use the demand-control model to understand the empirical results and provide design guidelines for engineers and practitioners to improve task and process design for collaborative robot systems. Future research directions are also provided.

Title: An interpretable product demand forecasting framework incorporating domain knowledge: a case study of substitution effects in community group-buying
Authors: Tao Zhu, Xiangpei Hu, Shaoze Cui, Yu Song
Affiliations: College of Systems Engineering, National University of Defence Technology; Dalian University of Technology; Beijing Institute of Technology; Social Science Domain, Beijing Institute of Technology; Shenzhen Dibo Enterprise Risk Management Technology Co., Ltd; Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)
Abstract: With the rapid rise of social e-commerce, an increasing number of consumers now purchase goods through social community networks. However, substitution effects arising from limited inventories and stockouts can seriously impair demand forecasting accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose XAI-Sub, an interpretable demand forecasting framework that systematically incorporates domain knowledge via text mining and biclustering to improve both transparency and predictive performance. By aggregating sparse sales records into substitution-aware clusters and estimating scenario-specific substitution matrices using a novel alternating minimisation algorithm, XAI-Sub explicitly quantifies substitutive relationships while preserving interpretability. Validated on data from a large community group-buying (CGB) platform, our framework achieves a relative improvement of 38% in forecasting accuracy compared with conventional methods. The approach introduces three key advancements in explainable artificial intelligence (XAI): (1) domain-knowledge anchoring: text-derived semantic features anchor substitution patterns within business logic, facilitating human-AI alignment; (2) scenario-driven interpretability: biclustering decomposes demand dynamics into actionable substitution typologies; and (3) causal pathway visualisation: the substitution matrix serves as an interpretable interface, delineating demand redistribution pathways across clusters. This work demonstrates how formalising domain knowledge can bridge the ‘explanation gap’ in complex demand systems and provides CGB enterprises with practical tools to audit and exploit substitution mechanisms.

Title: Contextual distributionally robust optimisation for inventory replenishment optimisation under uncertain demand
Authors: Qingyang Wang, Yang Chen, Yijia Mi, Chengxi She, Piaoyang Zhao, Caihua Chen
Affiliations: Nanjing University; Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
Abstract: Demand uncertainty poses a significant challenge in inventory management, where conventional strategies often fail to adapt to complex and fluctuating demand patterns. To address this critical issue, we propose a novel contextual distributionally robust optimisation (CDRO) framework that integrates advanced machine learning with robust decision theory. Our solution features the HOA-CITransformer predictor, which combines a Transformer neural network optimised via the Hiking Optimisation Algorithm (HOA) with Conformal Inference (CI) to generate accurate demand forecasts (95.6% accuracy) with reliable uncertainty quantification (88.9% coverage probability). Building on these probabilistic predictions, we develop a Wasserstein distance-based CDRO model that constructs ambiguity sets to ensure robust inventory decisions under demand variability. Experimental validation using power grid material management data (2020-2023) demonstrates the framework's effectiveness: it achieves efficiency improvement by 56.15%−69.29% with high guarantee of satisfaction rate compared to traditional methods. This research provides practitioners with a principled approach to overcome demand uncertainty challenges in supply chain operations.

Title: Optimal cybersecurity investment with collaborative defense in scale-free supply chain networks: a stochastic game-based dynamic programming approach
Authors: Ying Wang, Fuwei Xu
Affiliations: Shandong University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: We investigate cybersecurity investment strategies in scale-free supply chain networks where risk propagates directly and indirectly through data connections. A stochastic game framework is developed, incorporating a Gordon–Loeb direct attack function and multi-path cumulative indirect risk propagation. A collaborative defense coalition with joint investment pooling and shared liability is introduced to internalise externalities. An iterative best-response algorithm combined with dynamic programming is proposed to compute approximate Nash equilibria. Theoretical propositions characterise investment monotonicity, spillover effects, and the non-trivial impact of collaboration. Numerical experiments on a representative network reveal that collaborative defense does not always reduce total cost, especially when investment caps bind. The findings offer actionable insights for designing resilient cybersecurity strategies in interconnected supply chains.

Title: Optimising two-echelon spare parts inventory: a case study from Amazon's operations
Authors: Marco Caserta, Luca D'Angelo
Affiliations: Department of Operations, IE University; Amazon RME – Decision Science and Technology
Abstract: This paper is motivated by a real-world challenge faced by Amazon in managing spare parts inventory across its extensive logistics network. Traditional single-echelon inventory systems often lead to high capital immobilisation and inconsistent service levels, creating inefficiencies in large-scale operations. To address this, we develop and implement a two-echelon inventory optimisation approach, structuring clusters of sites around central hubs to pool demand risk, reduce lead times, and enhance service reliability. The resulting mixed integer formulation is solved using a column generation algorithm that overcomes the computational limitations of standard MILP solvers. Through an extensive case study involving 24 Amazon sites across five clusters, we demonstrate significant operational and financial benefits, including a 14–27% reduction in immobilised working capital and a 0.4–3.2% improvement in service levels. These improvements correspond to projected capital savings on the order of tens of millions of dollars when extrapolated to Amazon's global network, along with reduced downtime costs. Beyond its methodological contributions, this study delivers actionable managerial insights by providing a scalable decision-support tool for firms seeking to optimise distributed inventory systems. The column generation algorithm enables real-world implementation for large-scale high-volume supply chains. By bridging optimisation theory with industry implementation, this research offers a concrete roadmap for improving supply chain resilience and cost efficiency in multi-echelon inventory management.

Title: An optimal sampling-inspection policy for a partially observable production process
Authors: Rui Zheng, Yutong Ma, Yifan Zhou
Affiliations: Hefei University of Technology; Southeast University
Abstract: In production processes, sampling and inspection serve as complementary techniques for assessing conditions of facilities and quality. While sampling offers partial insights at a lower cost, inspection provides more accurate condition monitoring at a higher expense. Effective production control requires the strategic integration of both approaches. This paper proposes a sampling-inspection policy for an economic production quantity (EPQ) model with a partially observable production process. The real operational state of the process can be partially inferred through online sampling and fully revealed through offline inspection. Samples of a certain size are taken periodically during each production run. At each sampling epoch, decisions are made on whether to perform inspections. The objective is the joint determination of the sampling interval, the sample size, and the sampling-inspection policy, minimising the long-term expected average cost per unit time. The optimisation problem is addressed in the partially observable semi-Markov decision process (POSMDP) framework. First, Bayes' theorem is used to update the belief of the process state based on sample information. Second, a semi-Markov decision process is constructed, and a policy-iteration algorithm is developed to find the optimal solution. A numerical example illustrates the effectiveness of the proposed optimal policy.

Title: Research framework and evolutionary trends of smart supply chain in industry 4.0: a hybrid methodology integrating BERTopic and Holt-ARIMA
Authors: Jingrong Zhang, Yanning Hou, We Song, Jingwen Shen, Yumin Li
Affiliations: Zhengzhou University; Henan University of Economics and Law
Abstract: Driven by Industry 4.0, traditional supply chains are undergoing a profound intelligent transformation enabled by digital technologies. However, existing research lacks a systematic analysis of the research framework and evolutionary trends in smart supply chains. Therefore, this study adopts the BERTopic and Holt-ARIMA models to analyze 7,238 relevant publications from the Web of Science core database (2014–2023), revealing the research topics, directions, frameworks, and evolutionary trends in smart supply chain research. The findings show that the research field covers 36 topics and nine directions, and has experienced three stages. It is evolving toward a new supply chain ecosystem featuring intelligence, collaboration, resilience, traceability, and sustainability. Its underlying logic is evolving from a ‘problem-solving’ paradigm to one centered on ‘defining the future supply chain’. Based on these findings, this study innovatively constructs a research framework including the underlying technical support layer, the core application scenario layer, and the management optimization and decision-making layer, and proposes future research directions. The study fills the research gap in the research framework and trends of smart supply chains and provides valuable references for enterprises to optimize decision-making and for governments to formulate relevant policies.

Title: Cooperative quality investment in contract manufacturing: balancing incentives and encroachment threat
Authors: Le Wang, Zhen He, Shuguang He, Ken Chen
Affiliations: Tianjin University of Technology; Tianjin University
Abstract: In addition to providing contract manufacturing services for original brand manufacturer (OBM)'s national brand (NB) product, contract manufacturer (CM) has the motivation to build private brand (PB) with higher- or lower-quality to encroach the retail market. Faced with CM encroachment, a crucial question OBM needs to address is how to incentivize contract manufacturing quality effort and improve the quality of NB. This work constructs a cooperative quality investment (CQI) model considering CM encroachment. Interesting findings include: (i) CQI strategy will always promote the CM to achieve quality improvement. Moreover, when the encroachment cost is relatively large, the OBM can achieve higher profit by adopting CQI. (ii) Both higher- and lower-quality encroachment improve NB quality without CQI. Under CQI, the impact of encroachment on NB quality depends on the type and cost of encroachment, and the quality decision rights. (iii) If the CM has NB quality decision right, the CM always has motivation to encroach with lower-quality PB which may achieve a win-win situation for the two parties. Otherwise, (iv) whether CM encroaches depends on the encroachment cost and CQI strategy. The impact of encroachment on the OBM is determined by both the encroachment cost and the type of encroachment.

Title: A project-specific bill of materials framework for material management and cost control in engineer to order environments
Authors: Benedetta Franco, Valentina De Simone, Valentina Di Pasquale, Mario Caterino, Raffaele Iannone
Affiliations: University of Salerno; University of Campania “Luigi Vanvitelli”
Abstract: Traditional MRP systems struggle with the high customisation and variability of Engineer to Order (ETO) environments, where predefined Bills of Materials (BoMs) are often impractical. They are generally time-consuming to develop and rarely reusable across future projects. A review of the existing literature identifies several unmet needs in ETO contexts, including poor traceability of materials, inefficient information exchange, limited process integration, and limited project-specific cost reporting. To address these challenges, the study introduces a comprehensive framework based on the Integrated Definition (IDEF) graphical modelling method. This approach captures the unique characteristics of each business process involved in materials management, proposing an alternative framework that ensures material traceability and cost monitoring without relying on fixed, pre-defined BoMs. The proposed framework allows companies to define and track material requests, purchases, and consumption throughout the production of highly customised products. It supports complete traceability, enables accurate product revisions and maintenance, and improves control over project costs. To validate the framework, a software tool based on a relational database was developed, and a pilot case study was subsequently conducted within an ETO company specialising in the production of electric components, demonstrating the practical applicability and benefits of the framework.

Title: Jidoka just-in-time cycle – from genba kaizen to the introduction of artificial intelligence
Authors: Taho Yang, Takahiro Fujimoto
Affiliations: National Cheng Kung University; Waseda University
Abstract: Rooted in the TPS pillars of Jidoka and JIT, the Jidoka-JIT Cycle (JJC) described here is presented as a decision support system (DSS) aimed at supporting genba kaizen through the integration of machine and human intelligence. The establishment of an effective DSS requires the integration of information technologies and operational technologies, which is challenging because they have very different requirements. This problem is alleviated by adopting the proposed digital genba, simplified intelligence, and limited information principles. JJC aligns with the Lean 4.0 concepts, emphasising zero waste, achieved by addressing stagnation and inventory, and promoting genba kaizen cycles. JJC comprises three models, JJC 1.0, 2.0, and 3.0, which are developed by moving from basic knowledge to specific details along the IT development path. JJC 1.0 focuses on establishing a kaizen culture. JJC 2.0 targets the integration of digitalisation and lean practices. Finally, JJC 3.0 introduces artificial intelligence applications based on the screened data from JJC 1.0 and JJC 2.0. Although they are discussed separately, each model version should be regarded as a necessary precondition for the next version. Three cases with promising results are adopted here for illustration purposes, representing a snapshot of JJC’s applications.

Title: Disruption in horizontal collaborations: a cost-trust analysis for coalition-based supply chain network design
Authors: Reza Alikhani, Mahnaz Hosseinzadeh, Hannan Sadjady Naeeni
Affiliations: MBS School of Business; University of Sheffield; Longwood University
Abstract: Horizontal collaboration in distribution networks can reduce transportation costs and environmental impacts, yet many initiatives fail due to rising coordination expenses and fragile trust among partners. This paper proposes a bi-objective, two-stage robust optimisation model for designing coalition-based supply chain networks under uncertainty, explicitly accounting for collaboration costs and measurable trust between carriers. The model captures how first-stage coalition decisions may be affected by potential disruptions in the second stage, where trust levels determine coalition feasibility and influence worst-case recourse flows. To handle realistic coalition sizes, we develop a decomposition-based solution approach using a column-and-constraint generation algorithm that incrementally adds the most informative coalition and disruption constraints. Computational experiments across multiple spatial network structures show that partial coalitions with strong inter-firm trust often outperform grand coalitions, yielding lower total costs and reduced disruption exposure. Results further reveal that transportation savings increase with coalition size only up to a threshold; beyond that point, collaboration costs dominate, producing an optimal coalition range rather than a single best partner set. The model also identifies strategic distribution centers and carrier relationships whose trust characteristics disproportionately influence coalition stability. Overall, incorporating trust as a formal decision factor leads to more resilient and cost-efficient coalition structures.

Title: It is all connected: a large-scale study on the reach of modern slavery in complex global supply networks
Authors: Jack Foster, Alexandra Brintrup
Affiliations: University of Cambridge; Alan Turing Institute, British Library
Abstract: Forced labour remains a pervasive problem throughout global supply chains. Overcoming it is predicated upon understanding how firms are connected to modern slavery via their supply chains. In this work, we present the first large-scale, global data study on how firms are connected to forced labour via their supply networks. We analyse forced labour across the Automotive, Chocolate and Fashion and Textiles industries. We find that although the number of firms that directly engage in forced labour is relatively low at 0.42%, the topology of supply networks implicates over 70% of all consumer-facing firms in these sectors in propagating goods handled by forced labour firms. This is mainly due to the ultra-small-world and scale-free structures found in these networks. As forced labour overwhelmingly occurs in the third or fourth tiers in the network, current regulations that ask Western firms to perform due diligence in their first tier are not effective. At the same time, we highlight that the small-world property in these networks could be used to communicate information on non-compliance rather effectively. Finally, to address the limited visibility found in the supply chains of multi-national corporations, we show that simple machine learning methods are effective tools at predicting the existence of, and reliance upon, forced labour within the three industries studied.

Title: Reliability-oriented and cost-saving stochastic selective maintenance optimisation using a learning-driven multi-objective artificial bee colony algorithm
Authors: Pei Liang, Haobo Qiu, Keqing Chang, Jie Shang, Chen Jiang, Liang Gao
Affiliations: Huazhong University of Science and Technology; Beihang University
Abstract: Selective maintenance problems are intensively investigated by both scholars and practitioners. Nonetheless, existing research on such problems usually overlooks the comprehensive consideration of diverse decision criteria and uncertain maintenance environments in terms of stochastic mission and break durations. This work proposes a stochastic multi-objective selective maintenance problem that considers stochastic mission and break durations and puts forward the corresponding optimisation method. First, a stochastic multi-objective mixed-integer nonlinear chance-constrained programming model is constructed to maximise mission reliability and minimise maintenance cost under maintenance time constraints. Second, a learning-driven multi-objective artificial bee colony algorithm is tailored to tackle the proposed model. In the designed approach, a Q-learning method in the employed bee phase and an iterative local search method in the onlooker phase are deployed to enhance the exploration and exploitation abilities. Finally, through conducting comparison experiments between the customised method and five popular methods on several real-world cases, the experimental results confirm its feasibility and superiority in addressing the problem of interest.

Title: Economic Inquiry 2025 Editor's Report
Authors: Timothy C. Salmon
Affiliations: Southern Methodist University Dallas Texas USA

Title: In This Issue
Early career effects of entering the labor market during higher education expansion
Authors: Johannes Goehausen, Stephan L. Thomsen
Abstract: Abstract We evaluate the labor market effects of an increasing supply of high-skilled labor, resulting from a higher education expansion at established German universities. Exploiting variation in exposure across regions and cohorts, we estimate early career effects for labor market entrants. We find that high-skilled wages decline initially, particularly in non-graduate jobs, but recover over the first 5 years of experience. For graduate job takers, we even report positive wage effects after 5 years. We explain the dynamics of the effects by the interplay of several mechanisms: immediate supply effects, recovery through regional mobility, and increased productivity of graduate jobs.

Title: Driving in the wrong direction? Modelling policy mixes for EV adoption
Authors: Miquel Bassart i Loré, Daniel Torren-Peraire
Abstract: Car-centric societies face challenges in transitioning to sustainable mobility, with electric vehicle adoption depending on the interaction of consumer behaviour, firm innovation, and policy incentives. To examine these dynamics, we develop an agent-based model calibrated on California data from 2001-2023. Heterogeneous consumers influence each other in their acceptance of EVs, while manufacturers incorporate these changes into their innovation and product-mix strategies. We evaluate individual and combined policy instruments, including carbon pricing, new and used purchase rebates, production subsidies, and electricity price subsidies. Results show that only carbon pricing and new vehicle purchase rebates achieve 95% electric vehicle adoption by 2035. Each policy has trade-offs: carbon pricing reduces consumer welfare, while new purchase rebates create heavy fiscal burdens. Policy combinations reduce the intensity of interventions and transitional costs, while mitigating trade-offs. By 2050, combinations of carbon price and subsidies yield 30% reductions in cumulative emissions against the business-as-usual scenario.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Route-aware detection of ship collision avoidance manoeuvres via change point analysis with intention inference
Authors: Boyuan Zhang, Hao Rong, Huanhuan Li, Zaili Yang
Abstract: Reliable and human-consistent collision avoidance is essential for Maritime Autonomous Surface Ships (MASS) operating in mixed traffic environments. A key challenge is the extraction of representative critical encounter scenarios from real-world data without relying on predefined risk thresholds or expert-driven rules. This study proposes a data-driven, route-aware framework for detecting ship collision avoidance behaviours and extracting the critical encounter scenarios in which such behaviours occur. The framework comprises three components. First, ship motion patterns are analysed to characterise normal route-following behaviour, enabling collision avoidance behaviour to be distinguished from routine navigation. Second, a unified cost function is formulated to jointly evaluate multiple kinematic features while explicitly incorporating planned route information, enabling separation of route-following course changes from potential avoidance actions. Change Point Detection (CPD) method is then applied to identify behavioural transitions and segment ship trajectories into candidate collision avoidance manoeuvres. Third, an intention-informed encounter identification approach is introduced, where avoidance intent is inferred by comparing observed trajectories with virtual route-following trajectories. This enables confirmation of true collision avoidance behaviour and extraction of the associated critical encounter scenarios. The proposed method is validated using Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from the high-traffic Øresund region, including the Helsingør-Helsingborg ferry corridor. Results on a labelled dataset show strong performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.8203 and 0.7443 in behaviour identification and encounter extraction, respectively. The findings demonstrate that the framework can robustly identify avoidance manoeuvres and capture critical encounters. Moreover, the proposed behaviour identification method is further applied in various navigational environments to verify its generalisation. The proposed critical encounter extraction framework provides empirically grounded insights into MASS development and testing, maritime situational awareness enhancement, and traffic management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Single-machine just-in-time scheduling problem with learning/deterioration effects and past-sequence-dependent delivery times
Authors: Dan-Yang Lv, Yu-Bin Wu
Affiliations: School of Mechatronics Engineering, Shenyang Aerospace University; School of Science, Shenyang Aerospace University
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Mitigating human review bottlenecks in AI evaluation pipelines: A queueing theory approach
Authors: Munil Yang
Affiliations: Institute for Industrial Policy Studies (IPS)
Abstract: Human review stages in AI-assisted evaluation pipelines can become throughput bottlenecks when automated upstream processes generate cases faster than reviewers can assess them—a problem acute when information availability varies across client types, a form of structural information asymmetry whose operational consequences remain underexplored. We quantify this bottleneck and identify the efficiency gain that explainable-AI (XAI) support must provide to restore stability. We develop an M/G/1 queueing model of a technology-valuation pipeline, motivated by an anonymised case in which the human pricing-decision stage requires up to 72 h for information-scarce small firms versus about 5 h for information-rich mid-size firms. With small firms at 70% of the portfolio, the two-point mixture yields a mean service time of 51.9 h (standard deviation 30.7); being a discrete mixture rather than exponential, it requires M/G/1 rather than M/M/1. Using the Pollaczek-Khinchine formula, we derive a critical-α curve giving the minimum XAI gain needed for stability. Three scenarios are evaluated analytically and cross-checked against simulation (agreement within 3%). An interview-grounded, conservative estimate approximately doubles stable capacity; a full-deployment scenario suggests up to 8.6-fold, but this rests on assumed reductions and is an upper-range illustration. Future work should calibrate the framework empirically, for instance through controlled measurement of Stage-5 review times under varying levels of XAI assistance.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Navigating the exploitation–exploration paradox: the impact of industry 4.0 technologies on supply chain performance from the Organisational ambidexterity lens
Authors: Nur Ayvaz-Ҫavdaroğlu, Sercan Demir, Jiju Antony, Arshia Kaul, Michael Sony
Affiliations: Department of Operations Management, Newcastle Business School, Northumbria University; School of Business and Law, Central Queensland University; Oxford Brookes Business School, Oxford Brookes University
Abstract: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) technologies have significant potential to improve supply chain performance, yet organisations often struggle to realise these benefits in practice. Drawing on Structural Ambidexterity Theory, this study examines how specific I4.0 technologies affect core supply chain functions, identifies the principal barriers to implementation, and explores how organisational and sectoral characteristics influence implementation success. The study conducted 19 semi-structured interviews with supply chain directors, digital transformation leaders, and I4.0 consultants across the automotive, pharmaceutical, food and beverage, construction, and high-technology manufacturing sectors. Data were analysed using a three-stage thematic coding process (open, axial, and selective coding) anchored in Simsek et al. (Citation2009) partitional ambidexterity framework. The findings reveal that different I4.0 technologies generate distinct impacts across supply chain functions. Base technologies, including IoT, sensors, machine learning-driven forecasting, robotics, and big data analytics, deliver measurable improvements in demand planning, inventory management, manufacturing operations, and logistics through enhanced visibility, automation, and operational efficiency. In contrast, advanced technologies such as AI-driven decision intelligence, digital twins, simulation, and augmented reality offer greater transformative potential but require substantially higher levels of organisational learning, experimentation, and integration capability. The study further identifies five interconnected implementation barriers: process immaturity, legacy system integration challenges, human resistance to change, workforce capability gaps, and investment uncertainty. Organisational culture, leadership commitment, firm size, and sector-specific regulatory and competitive conditions are found to shape the success and pace of I4.0 adoption. Building on these findings, the study argues that I4.0 adoption creates a fundamental socio-technical tension between exploitation and exploration. Structural separation of exploitative and explorative technology initiatives, enabled through cloud computing and big data analytics, emerges as a viable mechanism for managing this tension. The study extends the partitional ambidexterity framework through the concept of Connected Partitioning and introduces Virtual Integration as a digital mechanism linking differentiated capability streams. It further proposes Structural Buffering as a mechanism for protecting explorative technology initiatives from the socio-technical resistance concentrated in that domain, and identifies a sequential ambidexterity pathway in which exploitative stabilisation is a precondition for explorative capability. The research provides a theoretically grounded and empirically rich understanding of I4.0-enabled supply chain transformation and offers actionable guidance for managers navigating digital transformation initiatives.

Title: Dynamic inverse optimization under drift and shocks: Theory, regret bounds, and applications
Authors: Jinho Cha
Affiliations: Department of Computer Science, Gwinnett Technical College
Abstract: Operational decisions often reflect priorities that evolve gradually and may shift abruptly after disruptions. We develop a dynamic inverse optimization framework for recovering time-varying preference parameters from observed allocation trajectories. The framework separates an offline temporally regularized trajectory formulation from an online mirror-descent estimator for streaming recovery, thereby linking inverse optimization with online convex optimization under nonstationarity. We establish sufficient conditions for local identifiability and existence, static regret of O(T), dynamic regret of O(T(1+VT)) for the online estimator, and a residual-to-parameter stability bound governed by the conditioning of the projected inverse map. The analysis distinguishes uniqueness of the inverse explanation, conditioning of the recovery map, existence of a batch trajectory solution, and sequential performance under a moving comparator. Controlled experiments on two stylized allocation benchmarks examine noiseless recoverability, finite-horizon regret, gradual drift, observational noise, abrupt shocks, and temporal coupling. These experiments are interpreted as finite-sample diagnostics rather than proofs of asymptotic bounds. Across the tested settings, temporal coupling moderates the trade-off between static under-adaptation and excessive variation from independent period-by-period inversion. The resulting framework provides an interpretable foundation for online inverse optimization and nonstationary decision analytics under evolving priorities. It also clarifies when structural recovery and sequential adaptation require distinct guarantees.

Title: Batch Scheduling on Parallel Machines With Submodular Costs
Authors: Tao Sun, Alessandro Agnetis, Paolo Detti, Jun‐Qiang Wang
Affiliations: Institute of Operations Research Qufu Normal University Rizhao People's Republic of China; Department of Information Engineering and Mathematics University of Siena Italy; Performance Analysis Center of Production and Operations Systems (PacPos) Northwestern Polytechnical University Xi'an People's Republic of China; Department of Industrial Engineering, School of Mechanical Engineering Northwestern Polytechnical University Xi'an People's Republic of China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper is motivated by the characteristics in the quenching and tempering process of steel workpieces, where the batch processing time is increasing and exhibits diminishing marginal returns. We model the batch processing time using submodular functions and study batch scheduling problems on identical parallel machines with bounded machine capacity. When the batch processing time is characterized by a submodular function, we provide a counterexample for the single‐machine problem, showing that the full batch strategy is not always optimal. We then focus on the parallel‐machine problem, where we establish the worst‐case performance ratio of the full‐batch longest processing time (FBLPT) algorithm and present a corresponding tight instance. When the batch processing time is characterized by a value‐monotone submodular function, we establish the worst‐case performance ratio of Algorithm FBLPT and provide a tight instance, and further design a modified version of this algorithm and analyze its performance. Finally, when the batch processing time is characterized by a nondecreasing concave function of the total processing time of the jobs in a batch, we design the longest processing time first‐full batch‐batch moving algorithm. We then analyze its worst‐case performance ratios for both unbounded and bounded machine capacity cases, where the result for the unbounded case serves as a theoretical foundation for the analysis of the bounded case. The effectiveness of the proposed algorithms is verified through computational experiments.

Title: Channel expansion or cannibalization? The role of food-waste consciousness and consumer dilution in online promotion design
Authors: Wei Liu, Heli Chen, Yijiang Liu
Abstract: Firms increasingly adopt Online-to-Offline (O2O) dual-channel strategies, maintaining physical stores while simultaneously leveraging online platforms for product promotion. While channel expansion typically stimulates demand, it may risk cannibalizing higher-margin offline sales. This trade-off is further complicated by two critical demand-side factors: consumer food-waste consciousness and consumer dilution. We develop an analytical model to examine the optimal channel and promotional strategies for a firm offering a core product alongside an add-on. The firm chooses between a single-channel or a dual-channel structure and evaluates two promotional strategies: bundling and coupon. Our analysis yields several key insights. First, the profitability of introducing an online channel is conditional. While channel expansion increases demand, it may reduce margins through dilution. In the absence of dilution, higher food-waste consciousness enhances the attractiveness of a dual-channel strategy. Second, food-waste consciousness fundamentally reshapes strategy effectiveness. It mitigates optimal profits at its low-to-moderate levels. Moreover, bundling is the optimal strategy when food-waste consciousness is moderate but loses its advantage when consumers strongly avoid add-on purchases to minimize waste. Third, while consumer dilution consistently expands total demand, it only enhances profits under specific thresholds of food-waste consciousness. Furthermore, dilution weakens the relative advantage of bundling in high food-waste consciousness markets. This study contributes to the literature on sustainable marketing and multi-channel management by identifying a behavioral mechanism, through which food-waste consciousness interacts with consumer dilution to shape optimal channels and promotional strategies. Our findings also provide managerial insights into firms navigating the O2O landscapes.

Title: Robust optimality and solution existence for multiobjective optimization problems under data uncertainty
Authors: Liguo Jiao, Nguyen Canh Hung, Thai Doan Chuong
Abstract: Abstract In this paper, we examine robust optimality and solution existence for a multiobjective nonsmooth optimization problem involving data uncertainty. To this end, we first introduce the concept of an extended tangency variety associated with the feasible set and a tangency value set for the corresponding robust multiobjective optimization problem. We then show that the proposed tangency variety is unbounded whenever the feasible set of the considered problem is unbounded. We further establish that the robust multiobjective optimization problem can be equivalently reformulated as a relaxed optimization problem defined over the corresponding tangency variety. With the help of the problem reformulations and the tangency value set, we provide necessary/sufficient optimality conditions for weak Pareto solutions and investigate the existence of solutions to the underlying problem.

Title: Importance of diversity in the permutation flowshop scheduling problem
Authors: J. A. Alejandro-Soto, Carlos Segura, Joel Antonio Trejo-Sanchez
Abstract: Most recent advances in the design of population-based optimizers for the Permutation Flowshop Scheduling Problem (PFSP) are based on further improving their intensification capabilities. Differently, in some related scheduling problems, important advances have been achieved with components that are almost problem-independent and which are based on relating the management of diversity to the stopping criterion set in the optimization process. This paper integrates PFSP state-of-the-art components into a Memetic Algorithm with Explicit Diversity Management ( $$\text {MA-EDM}$$ MA-EDM ) to minimize the makespan. The contribution lies in the careful engineering of this integration and in the time-aware diversity schedule, which together improve the performance of existing approaches. The experimental validation shows the benefits of explicitly managing the diversity in PFSP. Both premature convergence and divergence could be avoided. Moreover, new best-known solutions were generated in 295 out of the 480 instances of the VRF benchmark, which is the most complex set designed so far. The Average Relative Percentage Deviation (ARPD) with respect to previous best-known solution was $$-0.3486$$ - 0.3486 .

Title: Forecasting declining demand in the end-of-life phase
Authors: Robyn Goldsmith, Anna-Lena Sachs, John Boylan

Title: Syrian refugees and the resilience of European economic freedom: Evidence from Austria, Germany, and Sweden
Authors: Benjamin Powell, Leonel Regalado
Abstract: The Syrian Civil War led to a mass outflow of refugees. More than one million of them fled to Europe. Did refugees fleeing an origin country with poor economic institutions erode the high-quality economic institutions in destination countries as posited by the “new economic case for immigration restrictions?” We take advantage of the fact that most Syrian refugees settled in only a few European destination countries and use the synthetic control method to create counterfactuals to evaluate the evolution of economic freedom in refugee destination countries against. We do not find robust evidence of a large negative impact on European destination countries’ overall economic freedom; however, we do find some suggestive evidence of a negative effect on Germany and Sweden’s Legal System and Property Rights.

Title: A Heavy Traffic Theory of Matching Queues
Authors: Sushil Mahavir Varma, Siva Theja Maguluri
Affiliations: Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109; Industrial and Systems Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, Georgia 30332
Abstract: Motivated by emerging applications in online matching platforms and marketplaces, we study a matching queue. Customers and servers that arrive in a matching queue depart as soon as they are matched. It is known that a matching queue without an external control is unstable, and so we study its behavior for a general state-dependent control.
