Whereas state-dependent control is an effective lever to regulate the throughput and delay, it often comes at a cost for matching platforms in practice. Optimizing this fundamental trade-off motivates the use of small amounts of control, so we study a matching queue in an asymptotic regime in which the state-dependent control decreases to zero. Unlike the heavy traffic regime in classical queues, there are two different ways the control can be sent to zero: via a magnitude scaling parameter [Formula: see text] that goes to zero and a time scaling parameter [Formula: see text] that goes to infinity. Depending on the cost of control, we show that the rates of [Formula: see text] and [Formula: see text] that optimize the trade-off between delay and cost of control could correspond to three different regimes. As we traverse these regimes, we observe a phase transition in the limiting distribution of the matching queue. We show that a low cost of control corresponds to the regime [Formula: see text], and we call it the delay-driven regime. The limiting behavior in this regime is an asymmetrical Laplace distribution. On the other hand, [Formula: see text] is the cost-driven regime corresponding to a high cost of control in which the limiting behavior is either a uniform or a truncated exponential distribution. We christen the in-between regime of [Formula: see text] the hybrid regime in which the limiting behavior is a Gibbs distribution. These results are obtained by novel generalizations of the transform method, in which each regime requires new ideas. The hybrid regime employs inverse Fourier transforms, whereas the other two regimes engineer multiple complex exponential test functions. Title: Roads and carbon: Suburbanisation versus induced demand in U.S. states
Authors: Richard Jaimes, Carlos Fernando Varela Pérez
Abstract: Highway infrastructure spending has large but opposing effects on sectoral CO 2 emission intensity in the United States. Using a panel of 50 states over 1993–2019, we show that a one-standard-deviation increase in the highway expenditure share of GDP (i) reduces residential emission intensity by 4.5%, consistent with suburbanisation-driven spatial reorganisation, and (ii) increases transport emission intensity by 2.3%, consistent with induced vehicle travel demand. A formula-based instrument built on predetermined federal highway apportionments confirms both channels, and direct evidence on intermediate outcomes – a shift towards service-sector activity on the residential side, and expanded road capacity and vehicle travel on the transport side – ties each effect to its proposed mechanism. Both effects are robust to controlling for manufacturing structure, electricity prices, climate variables, population density, state-specific trends, and time-varying state policies, and a distributed-lag specification indicates that they accumulate over a three-year horizon. These findings demonstrate that aggregate analyses of fiscal decentralisation and emissions conceal economically important but offsetting sectoral mechanisms.

Title: A farm-level framework for integrating ecosystem service supply, scarcity, and feasibility: The case of crop pollination
Authors: Adrian Lüdtke, Stefan Burkart, Christian Lippert
Abstract: Biodiversity decline in agricultural landscapes is well documented, yet decision-support approaches rarely connect ecologically plausible ecosystem service (ES) diagnostics with farm-level constraints and implementable management decisions. This article introduces a codebook-based, farm-level framework integrating ES supply, multidimensional scarcity, and implementation feasibility into a transparent decision-support logic. It addresses three persistent limitations: the disconnect between spatial or biophysical ES supply assessments and farm-level decision-making; the reduction of relevance to monetary valuation, which obscures a farm's dependence on the ES and its exposure to risk; and the insufficient integration of feasibility constraints such as labor, costs, and coordination. Derived from a thorough literature review, the framework combines qualitative, rule-based scorecards for ES supply potential, a multidimensional scarcity concept capturing ecological, functional, spatial, and institutional constraints, and a structured cost module reflecting farm-operational feasibility, all governed by a transparent codebook that ensures traceability and auditability under realistic data conditions. The framework is operationalized for crop pollination and tested, as a proof of concept, on four southwestern German farms through single-farm interviews, without additional biophysical data or specialist expertise, the conditions most farms and advisory services in agri-environmental schemes actually face. Results show that supply, scarcity, and feasibility do not necessarily align, and that implementation barriers can outweigh ecological scarcity. By linking ecological diagnostics to farm-level decision logic, the framework offers a transferable approach to biodiversity-related decision-making, with the scarcity dimension requiring re-specification for services with strong public-good characteristics. It presents a conceptual framework and a first tentative application, not a statistically validated tool.

Title: Valuing the ecosystem service gap in private forestland management: evidence from Texas and Louisiana
Authors: Wei Li, Richard T. Woodward, Eric L. Taylor, Michelle Moore, Eric Wannlund
Abstract: Private forestlands generate substantial ecosystem services that function as positive externalities, often requiring private operations to bear costs. This market failure creates a gap between private incentives and socially optimal forest stewardship, which leads to chronic underinvestment in sustainable forestry management practices. Using the contingent valuation method, we measure the divergence in forest stewardship by evaluating five practices across NIPF operations in Texas and Louisiana. Results show that thinning requires the highest average cost-share at around 53%, while prescribed burning presents the lowest barrier at around 30%. When translated to monetary terms, establishment commands the highest private valuation at around $308 per acre, whereas prescribed burning shows the lowest Implied WTP at around $42 per acre. We find that the willingness to pool management with neighboring operations is associated with lower required cost-share percentages across all practices. Land size is associated with lower required cost-share percentages for establishment, but shows limited evidence of association for the other practices. These findings illuminate the economic mechanisms underlying the market failure in ecosystem service provision and demonstrate how practice-specific incentive design and landscape-scale collaboration can more efficiently align private operation behavior with social objectives for forest-based natural capital stewardship.

Title: Turning climate concern into climate courage: Female parliamentarians, environmental taxation and SDG13
Authors: Asif Saeed, Samreen Hamid, Ghulame Rubbaniy, Thanarerk Thanakijsombat
Abstract: Environmental issues, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and air pollution, have received heightened international attention following the adoption of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), which aim to promote global sustainable development. The presence of women in parliament has proven to be highly effective in advancing environmental tax policies that help reduce vulnerability to climate change. Using panel data from G20 and N11 economies between 2002 and 2022, this study provides evidence that women's presence in parliament is a critical determinant of achieving environmental sustainability. The models' results show that female parliamentarians with significant representation are more effective, and they reach the ‘Climate Action’ goal by reducing CO2 and GHG emissions, among other environmental targets. Notably, the country's ecological achievements can be intensified by implementing more efficient environmental taxation policies. We mitigate endogeneity by using Lewbel-IV and GMM estimation. Moreover, this study also highlights the significance of this relationship when the government invests more in renewable energy, emits less CO2, has a significant forest reserve, and offers better employment opportunities.

Title: Compulsory education, life trajectories, and intergenerational mobility: evidence from Mexico’s 1993 schooling reform
Authors: Diego De la Fuente Stevens
Abstract: Mexico's 1993 reform extended compulsory schooling from six to nine years, creating a birth-cohort discontinuity in educational exposure. This paper exploits that discontinuity to identify the causal effects of schooling expansion across the life course. Using a regression discontinuity and instrumental variable strategy applied to the 2020 Mexican Census, it traces the reform's consequences from educational attainment through fertility, child mortality, labour market participation, and geographic mobility, and into the schooling outcomes of the next generation. The reform raised educational attainment across all groups, but its effects were concentrated among Indigenous communities and rural populations, where baseline attainment was lowest and barriers to secondary schooling were greatest. For Indigenous individuals, literacy rates increased by 4.5 percentage points and lower-secondary completion by 3.8 percentage points, from baselines of 78 and 29 per cent respectively. These gains translated into lower fertility, reduced child mortality, higher employment, and a reallocation of workers out of low-productivity agriculture into higher-productivity sectors. Using census household identifiers to link parents to children, the analysis further finds that an additional year of parental schooling raised the probability of children's secondary school enrolment by 3 to 4 percentage points and upper-secondary enrolment by 5 to 8 percentage points. Together, the results show that a single compulsory schooling reform generated a sustained, multi-domain shift in life trajectories that extended across generations.

Title: Banks and informality: Two perspectives of microenterprises’ balance sheets
Authors: Prabhat Barnwal, Ritam Chaurey, Reajul Chowdhury, S.K. Ritadhi
Abstract: Our paper studies how the nationwide expansion of bank branches affects the performance of informal microenterprises. We exploit the Branch Authorization Policy (BAP) in India, which directed banks to open branches in “underbanked” districts. Using a regression discontinuity design, we find that microenterprises in underbanked districts report higher value-addition, revenues, and productive assets, but no increase in local registration. However, borrowings on the enterprise balance sheet do not increase. The household balance sheet offers a second perspective that reconciles these findings: households in underbanked districts increased their bank borrowings for non-farm business by an amount comparable to the increase in microenterprise productive assets. Micro-entrepreneurs thus accessed bank credit as households rather than as enterprises, weakening a key incentive to formalize and helping explain how expanded access to finance can coexist with persistent informality.

Title: Uncertainty in data and decision analytics – IUKM 2023
Authors: Van-Nam Huynh, Katsuhiro Honda, Bac H. Le, Masahiro Inuiguchi

Title: Approximate omitted variable bias-adjusted confidence intervals
Authors: Deepankar Basu
Abstract: In this paper, I propose a formal covariate benchmarking-based method to compute approximate omitted variable bias-adjusted confidence intervals in linear regression models estimated with OLS.

Title: Automation and the demand trap: A model of robot taxation
Authors: Yifeng He, Zhiyi He, Yong Ma
Abstract: This paper develops a task-based model linking automation, income distribution, effective demand, and employment. The installed robot stock determines the rental rate and constrains task assignment. With a downward-rigid real wage, automation can reduce expenditure by shifting income toward lower-spending capital owners and by raising unemployment, which further depresses worker spending. A unit tax on installed robots finances a uniform dividend. The tax raises short-run output when the redistribution gain exceeds the associated decline in robot investment. Although the stock is predetermined on impact, persistent taxation changes investment and the long-run tax base. The model provides sufficient conditions for equilibrium uniqueness and an expansionary tax effect. An illustrative calibration quantifies these mechanisms without interpreting the results as an optimal-tax prescription.

Title: The winner’s bliss in common-value auctions under horizontal differentiation
Authors: Jiawei Chen, Anh Nguyen, Matthew Shum
Abstract: We study common-value auctions in which bidders have horizontally differentiated preferences. In a specific two-bidder parameterization, winning conveys good news about the object's value to the winner, a phenomenon we call the winner's bliss in contrast to the conventional winner's curse. Additional implications also differ from the conventional analysis. When bidders'preferences are horizontally differentiated, seller revenue is reduced with information disclosure, and advantageous selection sustains bilateral trade under asymmetric information.

Title: Sustainable public procurement and firm dynamics: Evidence from Spanish contracts
Authors: Enrique Carreras, Marco Sanfilippo, Davide Vannoni
Abstract: Securing a government contract is commonly seen as a driver of firms’ growth. In recent years, the practice of considering sustainable award criteria (SAC) to select the winning firm in public auctions has gained popularity. However, the role it plays in shaping the selection process, influencing the decisions of winning firms, and ultimately affecting their growth remains unclear. This paper combines data from public procurement contracts with firm data from Spain to examine how firms winning SAC contracts evolve compared to those awarded standard contracts. We find that the use of SAC is associated with 7% lower employment and 11.4% lower sales relative to non-SAC contracts. This gap is concentrated among larger contracts and is particularly pronounced in the two most relevant sectors: health and social work and construction. We provide evidence consistent with a potential mechanism behind this pattern, driven by contracting authorities implementing SAC for the first time. As they gain experience with SAC, the undesired disruption for firms winning their contracts disappears. Less experienced authorities tend to assign higher weights to sustainability criteria and devote a larger share of the award-criteria description to them.

Title: The heterogeneous impacts of the residential component of a training program: A semiparametric analysis
Authors: Jun Cai, Alfonso Flores-Lagunes, Xintong Wang
Abstract: Several training programs worldwide are residential, bringing enrollees to live in facilities and thus increasing program costs. In the U.S., the Job Corps (JC) program for disadvantaged youth includes a residential component. Despite extensive literature evaluating JC, the impact of the residential component has received limited attention. We develop and employ a semiparametric model to estimate the average causal effects of this residential component, accounting for selection into both the program and the residential feature. Our findings indicate that, among JC enrollees, the residential component boosts earnings and educational-degree attainment among adolescents. For other subgroups, the residential component has minimal impact on labor market outcomes, with the notable exception of reduced earnings among young adults; it also increases substance use among some subgroups. For example, the average treatment effect of the residential component raises hard drug use by 183 percent among young adults and by 122 percent among females without children. Negative peer effects may explain the increase in detrimental health behaviors.

Title: Social control and the dispersion of beliefs: Evidence from cross-country data and German reunification
Authors: Mark Gradstein, Luigi Ventura
Abstract: We study how political regimes affect the dispersion of attitudes within societies. We develop a framework in which authoritarian regimes, through stronger social control and norm enforcement, compress heterogeneity in beliefs, whereas democratic regimes allow greater diversity. Using cross-country survey data, we find positive associations between democracy and attitudinal dispersion across several domains. To provide more diagnostic evidence, we examine differences between former East and West German residents immediately after reunification. Former East German residents exhibit lower attitudinal dispersion in domains plausibly subject to social control, with no comparable difference for private preferences. These findings highlight the role of political regimes in shaping the distribution of beliefs through behavioral channels such as conformity pressures and socialization.

Title: Multi-modal transportation network design integrating UAM mode: an activity capacity-based approach
Authors: Tong Zhang, Dawei Li, Chongqi He
Abstract: With the rapid development of electric Vertical Take-off and Landing (eVTOL) technology, Urban Air Mobility (UAM) has emerged as a promising travel mode. However, its early development faces critical challenges, including the design of the low-altitude transportation network, which serves as essential infrastructure, and the need for seamless air-ground coordination due to a limited number of eVTOL airports and their restricted coverage, necessitating strategies like transportation capacity matching and timetable synchronization. Simultaneously, substantial growth in urban residents’ activity demands places immense pressure on transportation networks, potentially hindering urban vitality if not adequately addressed (e.g., residents forgoing additional activities due to congestion). Therefore, developing a multi-modal network design method that integrates UAM and tackles these pressing issues is increasingly urgent. While Traffic Network Capacity (TNC) is a commonly used optimization objective in network design, existing methods often fall short in areas such as analyzing activity-oriented travel demand, incorporating land-use information, and supporting design requirements from the activity perspective, such as maximizing the capacity to accommodate activity flow. To address these critical gaps, this paper introduces the concept of Activity Capacity (AC). This concept addresses two major challenges: integrating early-stage UAM and alleviating the negative impacts of traffic congestion on urban vitality. Building on this concept, we propose a novel Multi-modal Network Design Problem (AC-MNDP) model. Our model optimizes urban infrastructure to maximize its capability for accommodating activity flows and balancing activity-travel demand and flow distribution. This framework offers practical, quantitative insights for urban planners. The model is structured into a three-layer programming approach: the upper-level model considers network design under investment constraints, the middle-level model focuses on maximizing AC within land-use and activity structure constraints, and the lower-level model is a multi-modal activity-travel assignment model. A sensitivity analysis-based algorithm is developed to solve the AC-MNDP model. Numerical case studies validate the model’s ability to generate multi-modal network design schemes under varying investment constraints, comparing AC-based with TNC-based design methods, and offering insights from a sensitivity analysis of UAM travel costs and capacity thresholds, which are valuable for urban air-ground network planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The incentive schemes of ride-hailing platforms for passengers with heterogeneous behaviors: Coupons or priority matching?
Authors: Fapeng Nie, Xiang Li, Chang Zhou, Bo Feng
Abstract: In the ride-hailing market, heterogeneous passenger behaviors during a ride lead to differences in whether they are willing to exert effort to maintain civilized behavior and obtain a high behavioral score, while passengers who do not exert effort may impose a loss on drivers. The platform operates a scoring system and decides whether and how to incentivize passengers to maintain high scores. To analyze this problem, we develop a game-theoretic framework involving three parties (the platform, passengers, and drivers) and compare three platform policies: no-incentive scheme, coupon incentive scheme, and priority matching scheme. The results show that without incentives, collective effort would improve outcomes for all participants. However, passengers have no individual incentive to exert effort, even when the platform sets a relaxed scoring standard, thus trapping the market in the civilization dilemma. This dilemma can be perfectly resolved by the coupon incentive scheme, consequently creating a civilized market with a “triple-win”. While the priority matching scheme only partially addresses the civilization dilemma, it outperforms the coupon incentive scheme in platform profitability when the platform sets a relaxed scoring standard. We further examine the dual-incentive schemes and observe that it yields lower platform profits than a single-incentive scheme. These results can guide platforms to optimize the ride-hailing operation environment and improve their profitability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Simulation-based Bayesian optimization for large-scale dynamic lane allocation
Authors: Zhixiong Jin, Nikolas Geroliminis, Ludovic Leclercq
Abstract: The current traffic research highly relies on Simulation-Based Optimization (SBO) to evaluate complex operational strategies. However, large-scale network problems often involve hundreds of control decisions that make the search space extremely high-dimensional and computationally prohibitive. This study develops an advanced Bayesian Optimization (BO) method for the large-scale SBO and applies it to solve the Dynamic Lane Allocation (DLA) problem, which grants ride-sharing vehicles conditional access to Dedicated Bus Lanes (DBLs) with allocation decisions varying across both location and time. As a result, the problem requires binary decisions across hundreds of space–time units, creating an extremely high-dimensional, combinatorial search space that existing optimization methods cannot handle efficiently. To address this challenge, we introduce a Grouped Automatic Relevance Determination (GARD) Hamming kernel that separates temporal and spatial relevance in the Gaussian Process (GP) surrogate, a dynamic group-aware dimension-reduction mechanism that identifies influential regions of the solution space, and a trust-region adaptation tailored to binary decisions to improve sampling efficiency. These components are combined with hybrid candidate generation and mixed batch sampling to enhance robustness under limited simulation budgets. The method is evaluated using a trip-based Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram (MFD) multimodal simulator on both a controlled virtual grid and the large-scale Barcelona network. Results show that the proposed BO approach consistently converges faster, achieves higher solution quality, and maintains feasibility under strict bus-service constraints compared with metaheuristic methods. The framework also demonstrates stable performance across varied OD patterns and scalability to real-world city networks.On the large-scale Barcelona network, the proposed method achieves, on average, a 14.2% lower final objective and 2.16 × faster convergence than Large Neighborhood Search (LNS), as well as a 1.1% lower final objective and 1.52 × faster convergence than Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS). These findings highlight the potential of the proposed method to support efficient decision-making in large-scale, binary, network-level traffic optimization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Multi-level optimization for the deployment of battery swapping in inland waterways
Authors: V.M.J. Ramos, Bilge Atasoy
Abstract: Containerized battery swapping offers a promising pathway to zero-emission inland waterway transport. However, its deployment requires coordinated decisions among actors with conflicting objectives. We introduce a multi-level optimization model with three actors: a policymaker who allocates subsidies to maximize adoption, an infrastructure developer who selects station locations to maximize profit, and fleet operators who minimize operating costs. We formulate this as a multi-level optimization problem, reduce it to a bilevel program via Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions, and solve it using an iterative bilevel decomposition and a problem-specific large neighborhood search. Experiments on the Dutch–Belgian inland waterway corridor show that a market equilibrium cannot exist without public intervention, the optimal subsidy mix depends on the available budget, and that within an intermediate price range the minimum budget for full adoption remains stable. Sensitivity analyses on costs, battery range, and network size are reported together with an alternative emissions-reduction objective.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Examining impacts of tradable credit schemes on delivery services using an agent- and activity-based simulation framework
Authors: Anke Ye, Roman Engelhardt, Klaus Bogenberger
Abstract: This paper presents a generalized Tradable Credit Scheme (TCS) framework for urban logistics. We rigorously compare an integrated market (MoLoCo), where urban mobility and last-mile delivery activities share a unified currency (Coins), against a sector-specific market (LoCo) with an independent emission cap for logistics. This study explores the regulatory effectiveness of these frameworks and evaluates the efficacy of adaptive operational strategies employed by a monopoly logistics provider. Using an agent- and activity-based simulation for Munich, Germany, we evaluate regulatory effectiveness and adaptive logistics strategies. Results indicate that MoLoCo framework benefits from a “Coupling Effect,” where the mode shift to low-emission travel modes stabilizes the Coin market prices, yet this triggers a “Green Logistics Paradox” by stimulating online shopping. Conversely, LoCo framework generates high Coin market prices that force decarbonization but risk a “Reverse Modal Shift,” driving cost-sensitive users back to physical stores and worsening congestion. Regarding logistics strategies, fleet electrification is cost-effective but fails to mitigate congestion. True spatial efficiency is achieved only through cargo bikes in the dense city center. We therefore propose a sequential TCS implementation roadmap: initiate sector-specific regulation to enforce technological adoption, then transition to an integrated market to maximize societal welfare.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Global maritime logistics resilience amid trade conflicts: forecasting port risk and identifying critical roles via spatiotemporal graph neural networks
Authors: Jia Shi, Jinyu Xu, Haiwei Fu, Jihong Chen, Weipan Zhang, Jun Ye, Xizhi Chen
Abstract: The escalation of trade conflicts since 2018, compounded by geopolitical disruptions including the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia–Ukraine conflict, and the Red Sea crisis, has placed unprecedented strain on global maritime logistics. Using a spatiotemporal graph neural network framework and AIS data from January 2019 to December 2024, this study aims to forecast port operational risk and identify critical port roles in risk propagation. We construct monthly shipping networks for four vessel types, namely container ships, bulk carriers, general cargo ships, and oil tankers, and synthesize a composite risk index from standardized in-port time and waiting time. The selected ST-GNN models outperform both the LSTM and ARIMA baselines, while the neighborhood dependency analysis provides further evidence that network information contributes additional predictive value. Model-extrinsic counterfactual analysis quantifies three port role dimensions, namely Source, Sink, and Mediator, representing risk emission, risk absorption, and network bridging, respectively, and identifies differentiated role profiles and high-intensity transmission links. Results reveal that the most active ports in risk propagation are predominantly small and medium-sized specialized ports, and that the strongest transmission follows direct Source-to-Sink connections. Risk propagation patterns differ across vessel categories and are consistent with differences in their network structures and underlying shipping and trade patterns during a period characterized by sustained disruptions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Drivers of public engagement in social media discourse on self-driving vehicles: psychological and emotional determinants
Authors: Zsofia Baruwa, Swagato Chatterjee, Preetam Basu, Prasenjit Mandal, Devika Kannan
Abstract: Research on self-driving vehicles (SDVs) has largely overlooked the influence of framing strategies on public interests and public engagement on social media discourse regarding SDVs. We address this gap by analysing 102,174 Twitter posts to examine how emotional sentiment and psychological distance shape engagement across private, public, and commercial SDV contexts. Grounded in Construal Level Theory and Appraisal Theory of Emotion, we identify thematic and emotional drivers of interaction. By leveraging large-scale social media analysis, this study advances understanding of the cognitive and emotional mechanisms underlying SDV discourse, offering insights for more effective public communication and consumer engagement strategies. Our analyses show that psychologically proximal topics (e.g., safety or pricing) elicit stronger engagement in private vehicle discourse due to personal relevance. Further, high-arousal negative emotions (fear, anger) spark immediate, intense responses, while low-arousal positive emotions (happiness) encourage sustained, reflective engagement.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Stochastic two-echelon vehicle routing with mobile satellites: Adaptive large neighborhood search with stochastic approximation scheduling
Authors: Aria Dahimi, Mehrdad Mohammadi, Virginie Lurkin, Tom Van Woensel
Abstract: This paper studies the stochastic multi-commodity multi-depot two-echelon vehicle routing problem with mobile satellites (3M-2E-SVRP), where first-echelon vehicles serve as mobile transfer points for second-echelon deliveries under synchronization and time-window constraints. Travel and service times are modeled as independent truncated log-normal random variables in controlled stochastic benchmark instances. To solve the problem, we develop SAS-ALNS, an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm that integrates deterministic approximation scheduling with stochastic approximation scheduling to evaluate feasibility, reliability, and expected failure costs during the search. Two stochastic planning perspectives are considered: a penalty-based model (PBM), which minimizes deterministic routing cost plus expected failed-delivery penalties, and a chance-constrained model (CCM), which imposes minimum customer-level on-time service probabilities under the modeled uncertainty. Computational experiments show that deterministic planning substantially underestimates late-arrival risk: under stochastic evaluation, deterministic solutions incur high expected failure costs and leave 27.1% of customers below a 95% success-probability threshold. PBM and CCM reduce expected failure costs by approximately 96% while achieving average customer success probabilities above 99%. SAS closely matches Monte Carlo simulation for both central and upper-tail arrival-time statistics while requiring substantially less evaluation time. Representative in-search comparisons with simulation-based candidate evaluation further show that SAS provides a favorable balance between solution quality, reliability stability, and computational effort. The results show that distribution-based stochastic schedule evaluation can be embedded efficiently into ALNS and improve the reliability of synchronized mobile-satellite routing decisions within the controlled benchmark and independence assumptions considered.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Subsidizing buyers or stage-stations? Platform subsidy strategies in community group buying
Authors: Zihao Zhang, Qian Gao, Feng Yang, Liyuan Lin
Abstract: As an innovative e-commerce model, community group buying (CGB) has grown rapidly since the pandemic period, especially in developing countries. In CGB, a platform (serving as an e-tailer) selects nanostores as community stage-stations to provide consumers with services such as order notification, storage, and after-sales support. After orders are placed, goods are delivered to stage-stations, where consumers pick them up. Platform subsidies are widely used in e-commerce to encourage participation and expand markets. What distinguishes CGB is that, because buyers and stage-stations are interdependent, the platform can subsidize not only buyers (i.e., consumers) but also stage-stations to coordinate the market. We investigate the implications of subsidy strategies in both incremental (noncompetitive) and competitive markets using a stylized model. Our analysis shows that subsidies are not always profitable for the platform: The platform subsidizes buyers or stage-stations only when consumers’ basic valuation is sufficiently low. Conditional on subsidizing, stage-station subsidization becomes more attractive when the unit unfitness cost is low. Interestingly, buyers or stage-stations may benefit more from indirect rather than direct subsidies. By comparing incremental and competitive markets, we further show that the platform is more likely to prefer buyer-side subsidization in the competitive market. In particular, as competition intensifies, the platform can earn higher profit by adopting more flexible subsidy strategies, although social welfare may decrease. Our study provides important implications for how CGB platforms can use subsidy strategies to expand their markets and consolidate their positions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: How does metro expansion shape the determinants of commuting mode choice? The rising transportation characteristics
Authors: Xiang Wang, Mengyao Hua, Xiangxi Liu, Tianqi Gu, Jason Cao
Abstract: Few studies have explored how the primary determinants of commuting mode choice change following metro network expansion. This research uses Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT) and travel survey data from Suzhou in 2018 and 2023 to investigate the nonlinear relationships of metro travel with demographic, transportation, and location characteristics, emphasizing stage-dependent changes in their impacts. The results show that as the network expands, the importance of transportation characteristics, namely commute distance and proximity to metro stations, increases substantially, while the relative contribution of location characteristics declines. In 2023, commute distance emerges as the most important predictor of metro travel, indicating the enhanced capability of the metro system to accommodate long-distance commuting. Furthermore, workplace-side accessibility to metro stations became more important, highlighting a growing demand for last-mile connectivity at destinations. To promote sustainable mobility, planners should expand mid-line park-and-ride facilities for long-distance commuters, improve metro–bus integration for seamless transfers, and strengthen last-mile connections in major employment areas through shuttles and shared mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Capabilities Imprint: A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Transport Infrastructure-Based Capabilities Evaluation
Authors: Sangeeta, Rui Teixeira, Hrishikesh Dev Sarma, Helen McHenry, Beatriz Martinez-Pastor
Abstract: This paper introduces the Capabilities Imprint , a novel conceptual and quantitative Capability Approach (CA) to assess how spatially embedded infrastructure enables individual human capabilities. The framework models dependencies on essential infrastructure and amenities using transport networks and allows for graph-theoretic metrics to quantify individual capabilities through their imprints. The premise of this approach is that, from a CA perspective, each person is at the centre of a network of infrastructure and amenities that has a role in the potential of that person to achieve the life they value, and this is their Capabilities Imprint . This imprint can then be quantified using network theory through metrics such as Connectivity Scores (CS) and Betweenness Centrality (BC), enabling an understanding of the transport infrastructure context for individuals. CS quantify access to key amenities, while BC identifies critical nodes within the imprint, whose disruption would disproportionately affect multiple capabilities. In this work, capabilities are conceptualized as locational, focusing on domain-specific infrastructural and spatial conditions that shape opportunities through transport network connectivity and integrity. A case study in Swords, Ireland, demonstrates the methodological implementation of the Capabilities Imprint framework and its ability to generate actionable insights for planning and policy. Clustering analysis of connectivity profiles reveals distinct community archetypes, highlighting areas facing systemic infrastructure exclusion. Simultaneously, high-betweenness nodes pinpoint network bottlenecks, informing prioritization for planning or further action. The approach also captures overlapping dependencies across capabilities, showing how failures at a few critical junctures can cascade through multiple facets of urban life. The framework relies on open-source data and a two-metric approach combining accessibility and network vulnerability, enabling a spatially disaggregated and network-aware assessment of infrastructure-enabled capabilities. In doing so, the Capabilities Imprint supports equity-oriented spatial analysis and accessibility-informed urban planning, offering policymakers a practical tool for human well-being–centred decision-making and more just prioritization in urban transport planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Exploring the dynamic effects of emission recall policies: A hybrid framework combining system dynamics and large language models
Authors: Wen Shi, Yuhao Qi, Xiang Xie
Abstract: Global warming represents a critical environmental challenge, with vehicle emissions being a major contributor to carbon output. Although there is extensive research on product safety recalls, the impacts of emission recall policies on carbon emissions are not well understood. This study employs a hybrid methodology that combines system dynamics (SD) and large language models (LLMs) to investigate the dynamic effects of these policies. Our SD model captures the intricate interactions among consumers, government agencies, and manufacturers involved in the emission recall system. Additionally, we introduce a novel three-stage scenario generation process using LLMs to explore potential policy strategies that extend beyond current implementations. We utilize the GPT-5.5 model (OpenAI) to support policy generation and analysis. Analyzing data from China, our findings indicate that while current vehicle emission recall policies enhance the identification of defective vehicles, they may not significantly accelerate the achievement of peak carbon emissions. Simulations show that strengthening legislation, leveraging social media for consumer awareness, enhancing information sharing, and implementing stricter penalties are vital for improving recall effectiveness and reducing emissions. Furthermore, a policy generated by LLMs to subsidize consumers significantly increases recall completion rates. This study offers valuable insights for policymakers aiming to refine emission recall strategies and achieve carbon reduction objectives.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A high-performance hybrid metaheuristic for the survivable one-fault-tolerant ring star problem
Authors: Herminia I. Calvete, Carmen Galé, Aitor Hernández, José A. Iranzo
Abstract: The Ring Star Problem (RSP) arises in the design of communication and distribution networks that combine a ring connecting a subset of nodes, called hubs, that includes the depot, with star-shaped assignments of the remaining nodes, called terminals, to the hubs. To address survivability issues in such networks, the 1-Survivable Ring Star Problem (1-S-RSP) extends the classical RSP by enforcing survivability against the failure of at most one node, which means preserving the ring–star structure via the inclusion of additional edges and arcs. The resulting problem is computationally challenging due to the strong interdependence among ring construction, node assignments, and survivability requirements. In this paper, a hybrid metaheuristic based on evolutionary algorithms is proposed to efficiently solve the 1-S-RSP. The algorithm relies on a compact chromosome representation that encodes only hub-related information, while complete feasible solutions are constructed through dedicated procedures that determine the ring structure, backup edges, and terminal-to-hub assignments. The method is further enhanced by problem-specific local search mechanisms, including 2-opt and 3-opt backup procedures that explicitly account for survivability considerations. An extensive computational study is conducted on benchmark instances. After tuning the main design parameters of the algorithm, the proposed approach is evaluated against the best feasible solutions reported in the literature. The results show that the hybrid metaheuristic consistently produces solutions of comparable or superior quality, while requiring significantly shorter computing times. These outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for addressing large-scale instances of the 1-S-RSP and highlight its potential for practical applications in survivable network design.

Title: On the role of uncertainty in timing environmental policies
Authors: Christian Oliver Ewald, Tiancheng Pei, Yihan Zou
Abstract: We develop a real options framework for the optimal timing of climate policy when both economic cost and stocks of environmental pollutants evolve stochastically and are correlated. By modelling environmental damage as a mean-reverting pollution stock jointly driven with uncertain economic losses, we extend the single-uncertainty specifications of Pindyck (2000) and the uncorrelated two-dimensional specification of Pindyck (2002). The resulting policy-adoption problem is formulated as a two-dimensional variational inequality (VI). We derive the post-policy value function in closed form and obtain an analytical necessary-condition curve that provides a sub-optimal stopping rule. Consistent with the correction of the proposed closed-form pre-policy stopping solutions by Balikcioglu et al. (2011), we compute the pre-policy value function and the globally optimal boundary numerically from the contact set of the VI. Across the configurations considered, the optimal stopping boundary is decreasing and predominantly convex in the pollution stock. The effect of uncertainty on policy timing is not uniform. In the main sensitivity exercise, positive correlation causes greater pollution-stock volatility to lower the boundary and accelerate adoption, whereas greater economic-cost volatility raises the boundary, with a smaller additional increase at higher volatility levels. Under negative correlation, greater volatility in either state variable raises the boundary and delays adoption. Under the nested single-uncertainty and uncorrelated zero-decay benchmark specifications (Pindyck, 2000, Pindyck, 2002), our numerical solutions produce the conventional uncertainty-delay ordering, qualitatively consistent with the corrected numerical boundaries reported by Balikcioglu et al. (2011). In a positively correlated extension of the uncorrelated two-dimensional benchmark, however, greater economic-cost volatility lowers the boundary. Policy timing therefore depends on the full joint-risk specification and the broader parameter configuration, rather than on volatility or correlation considered alone.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Ratcheting up Paris
Authors: Humberto Llavador, John E. Roemer, Thomas Stoerk
Abstract: The Paris Agreement is designed to increase climate ambition gradually through a process of ratcheting up. What is the plausible endpoint of this process? We develop a tractable integrated assessment model in which countries interact through a decentralized general equilibrium and negotiate unanimously over a global carbon budget, with all mitigation implemented via a global carbon price. We prove existence and uniqueness of a unanimous international agreement on global emissions, in which carbon pricing revenues are redistributed across countries in proportion to marginal climate damages. In a quantitative application for 154 countries, the resulting equilibrium limits global mean surface temperature change to 1.51C, at a carbon price of 320 USD/tCO2. The associated international transfers of carbon pricing revenue are progressive toward lower-income countries and amount to about 0.8% of global GDP annually - an order of magnitude larger than the Paris Agreement's climate finance target.

Title: Dynamic collaborative optimization of wind-assisted ship energy efficiency under variable navigational conditions
Authors: Diankang Zhang, Kai Wang, Zhongwei Li, Hongzhi Liang, Xinyue Zhang, Ranqi Ma, Lianzhong Huang, Jianyi Wu, Xiaowu Li, Jianlin Cao
Abstract: Ship energy efficiency (SEE) optimization is an effective method to promote energy conservation and emission reduction for the shipping industry. Existing optimization techniques are limited to single-dimensional optimization of sailing route or speed, lacking a comprehensive approach that can achieve dynamic and synergistic optimization of ship energy efficiency, especially for wind-assisted ships. Therefore, a dynamic collaborative optimization method for the wind-assisted ship energy efficiency is proposed in this paper. The coupling effects among sailing speed, sail’s angle of attack (AOA), and various environmental variables are integrated into a unified framework to achieve the dynamic SEE optimization. The case study demonstrates that the proposed dynamic collaborative optimization method can reduce fuel consumption by 4.03 %. Compared with static optimization method, the optimization effects can be further improved by 1.19 %. The proposed method is of great significance for further improving the wind-assisted ship energy efficiency, thus promoting the shipping decarbonization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multi-source data fusion for ship carbon emission prediction with language-model decision support
Authors: Xingyun Yan, Jie Hu, Lingyu Wang, Jin Qi, Bin Chen, Mingzhu Fang, Meixing Guo, Hairui Wang
Abstract: International maritime transport contributes 2.89% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, and International Maritime Organisation (IMO) and European Union (EU) rules increasingly require voyage-level prediction with auditable guidance. This study proposes Maritime-FTNet, a multi-source fusion model encoding Automatic Identification System (AIS) kinematics, meteorological reanalysis and vessel static parameters through vessel-conditioned feature selection, gated temporal-channel attention and Mixup regularisation. On 18 months of US-coastal container-shipping data, it attains a coefficient of determination of (Formula presented) for next-day prediction over ten seeds and outperforms ten 10-seed baselines spanning tree-based, recurrent and Transformer families (all p < 0.01 with bootstrap intervals); at multi-day horizons a gradient-boosting baseline becomes competitive. An optional tool-augmented language-model layer grounded in six engineering tools and self-verification delivers emission attribution, Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) compliance assessment and speed recommendations. Built on public input sources, the framework supports IMO and EU compliance monitoring.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Environmental operating points in the AV era: beyond capacity maximization
Authors: Sion Kim, Yongryeong Lee, Sungjin Park, Seungjae Lee
Abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) can increase network capacity, but capacity-oriented control may keep urban traffic near instability-prone states and intensify environmental burdens. This paper develops a macroscopic framework for identifying an operating point that minimizes environmentally augmented social cost (EASC) in AV-era networks. The framework represents urban traffic network operating conditions using an MFD-based formulation, combines jam-state travel-time reliability risk with a link-speed-volatility proxy for stop-and-go emissions, and validates the baseline volatility proxy against CAPSS-based emission estimates. AV penetration, effective response delay, and routing coordination are modeled as macroscopic levers reshaping capacity, jam prevalence, and dynamic burdens. Under AV scenarios in Seoul calibrated using human-driven traffic, the EASC-minimizing operating point can lie below the conventional MFD capacity density, suggesting that maximum throughput is not necessarily environmentally desirable. Sustainable AV control may therefore need to prioritize reductions in jam-state risk, travel-time unreliability, and speed-volatility-induced emissions rather than capacity maximization alone.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Perceived neighbourhood environments, social trust, and intentions to purchase alternative fuel vehicles
Authors: Juhee Park, Jinhyun Hong
Abstract: Despite advances in transport technology, ownership of alternative fuel vehicles (AFVs) remains markedly lower than that of conventional vehicles. While prior work has highlighted the influence of the built environment on AFV ownership, the social mechanisms underlying this relationship are less well understood, particularly the mediating role of social trust. This study investigates the direct and indirect associations between the perceived neighbourhood environment and intention to purchase AFVs, with trust in public institutions and neighbours as mediators. Our findings show that neighbourhoods characterised by good physical activity infrastructure, greater accessibility, and perceived safety are associated with higher levels of trust in public institutions, which in turn increases individuals’ intention to purchase AFVs. The results emphasise the relevance of land-use policies for promoting environmentally sustainable cities and underscore the modest but significant role of social mechanisms in linking land-use policy to AFV ownership.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Road contexts shape spatial patterns of bat assemblages in tropical dry forests
Authors: Danny Zurc, Juan Carlos Jaramillo-Fayad, Jordi Viñas, Antonio Guillén-Servent, Jorge Antonio Mejía, Mauricio Corredor
Abstract: Road infrastructure can shape biodiversity patterns, yet evidence from tropical systems remains limited. We assessed variation in bat assemblages across four road contexts (Old, Operational, Under Construction, Mitigation area) and three distances from the road edge (0, 300, 2000 m) in a Colombian tropical dry forest. Assemblages were sampled using mist nets and passive acoustic monitoring and integrated as operational taxonomic units (OTUs). Taxonomic diversity and composition varied among road contexts and sampled distances. After standardization to a common sample coverage, Hill diversity was higher at the sampled 2000 m distance than at 0 m in the Under Construction and Operational contexts, whereas the Mitigation area and Old context showed different spatial patterns. Beta-diversity analyses showed that compositional differentiation among sampled distances involved both taxonomic-unit turnover and nestedness, with the relative contribution of these components varying among road contexts. Guild representation also varied among contexts and distances, with aerial insectivores predominating in most context × distance combinations. Because environmental drivers were not directly measured and each context corresponds to a single site, these results are descriptive rather than tests of causal road effects. These findings reveal context-dependent spatial variation in bat assemblages across the sampled distances and provide a descriptive baseline for designing future studies that explicitly evaluate the mechanisms and spatial extent of road-associated effects.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: An option-insurance hedging framework for EU ETS maritime compliance costs
Authors: Fangping Yu, Heting Cao, Xing Gao, Rui Zhang, Shengshuai Guo
Abstract: The inclusion of the maritime sector in the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) exposes shipowners to dual compliance risks: carbon price volatility and unexpected excess emissions from emission-reduction equipment failures. We propose a novel risk management framework integrating an EUA Price Call Option (EPCO) and a Carbon Emission Equipment Loss Insurance (CEELI). We develop a rigorous pricing model that incorporates the joint stochastic dynamics of carbon prices and EUR/USD exchange rates, alongside the “bathtub” reliability curve of abatement technologies. A case study demonstrates that the framework successfully translates operational risks into transparent, budgetable upfront premiums, providing a “cost of certainty” for operators. Furthermore, scenario analyses reveal a dynamic operational-financial interaction mechanism: EPCO adoption is driven by EEA voyage exposure and cost pass-through capacity, whereas CEELI acts as a strategic financial enabler for fleet retrofitting. We provide a highly adaptable financial toolkit for shipping operators navigating the EU ETS transition.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Spatial variations of non-exhaust emissions across seasons using fixed-site and mobile measurements
Authors: Cheol-Heon Jeong, Yee Ka Wong, Nicole Trieu, Christi Jose, Xing Wang, Junshi Xu, Milad Saeedi, Yushan Su, Chris Charron, Arthur Chan, Marianne Hatzopoulou, Greg Evans
Abstract: Urban exposure to particulate matter (PM) from road dust and brake and tire wear (BTW) is an emerging health concern. Mobile and fixed-site PM sampling was conducted seasonally in Toronto. Mobile sampling employed paired window and wheel-well inlets to estimate resuspended PM, alongside ultrafine particles and black carbon as indicators of exhaust emissions. Analysis of 900+ weekly filters from 40 sites showed the strongest roadway contrasts for barium. Source apportionment resolved distinct contributions from road dust and BTW. Road dust dominated the trace element mass in PM, peaking in construction areas, while BTW contributed 10–15 % and peaked near expressways. Mobile measurements revealed steep near-road ultrafine particle gradients and increased resuspended PM on local roads, particularly in winter. However, non-exhaust emission rates remained greatest on expressways. This study presents the first integration of fixed-site and mobile measurements with spatial source apportionment and land use regression with kriging to characterize non-exhaust emissions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Can you give me a hand? A case study of the effect of collaborative robot implementation from an operator perspective
Authors: Mario Henrique Callefi, Elias Ribeiro da Silva, Kristina Diekjobst, Elaine Mosconi, Moacir Godinho Filho, Matthias Thürer
Affiliations: Production Engineering Department, School of Engineering of São Carlos, University of São Paulo; Department of Technology and Innovation, University of Southern Denmark; École de Gestion, Uiversité de Sherbrooke, boulevard de l’Université; Department of Supply Chain Management and Decision Sciences, EM Normandie Business School, Metis Lab; Department of Production Engineering, Federal University of São Carlos; Chair of Factory Planning and Intralogistics, Chemnitz University of Technology

Title: Using parabolic partial differential equation systems for effective counter-terrorism strategies
Authors: Jun Wang, Fanxing Meng, Yiran Wang, Yuxue Gao
Affiliations: School of Mathematics & Statistics, Changchun University of Technology
Abstract: Counter-terrorism is a critical national security issue in modern society. Considerable research on counter - terrorism has been conducted in fields such as military science, management, and economics. However, these studies primarily focus on temporal changes, which are insufficient to address the increasingly complex international situation. This study uses a system of partial differential equations to construct a game model for an in-depth analysis of the equilibrium strategies of the government against terrorism. In particular, the model considers the significant impact of time and economic growth rate on counter-terrorism issues. The economic growth rate, which represents key static economic indicators across regions, enables the model to reflect regional responses and strategies to terrorist attacks. Furthermore, the dynamic relationship between government counter-terrorism inputs and the intensity of terrorist attacks is analyzed. Finally, the validity of the model is demonstrated using two examples, France and Israel. The study has the potential to significantly improve both theoretical understanding and practical application of counterterrorism strategies globally.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: The value-added service investment strategy for the incumbent platform in response to a competitor entry
Authors: Xumei Zhang, Ronghua Sui, Bin Dan, Xiaoyu Zha, Molin Liu
Affiliations: School of Economics and Business Administration, Chongqing University; School of Economics and Business Administration, Chongqing Technology and Business University
Abstract: For increasing users’ stickiness and enhancing competitive advantage, numerous third-party platforms are now concentrating on developing value-added services (VASs). This article concentrates on an incumbent platform that provides parts trading services for both side users (i.e., manufacturer-side and supplier-side). Considering that a potential entrant platform may enter the market to snatch users with the incumbent platform, we analyse how the incumbent platform deploys VAS and the relevant prices to cope with the competitor’s entry, taking into consideration cross-network effect (CNE). We find that when the entrant invests in more VAS to attract the users, it may be more beneficial for the incumbent not to provide VAS. When the CNE strength of manufacturer-side is strong, compared to the entrant, the incumbent should deploy more VAS and charge more for supplier-side but give manufacturer-side higher subsidies to deter the entrant entry. However, when the CNE strength of manufacturer-side is weak, the incumbent charging manufacturer-side an entrance fee can also discourage the entrant. Finally, when the incumbent cannot deter the competitor from entering, the incumbent may adopt “high service and high fee” strategy to supplier-side while “high service and high subsidy” strategy to manufacturer-side.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Optimizing disaster preparedness: considerations for multiple-cycle triggers, fleet capacity, shipment intervals, and transportation modes
Authors: Minlian Wu
Affiliations: School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China
Abstract: This paper proposes a three-tier reserve system for disaster preparedness at various administrative levels, including provinces, counties, and districts. It develops three transportation modes: hierarchical, cross-level, and flexible. The design considers factors such as shipment intervals, affected intervals between disaster areas, and fleet capacity to meet the demands of disaster-stricken regions with varying population densities. The study examines losses or gains that exceed predicted losses across various routing scenarios, including direct economic losses, social costs, and ecological costs, which are categorized into slight, moderate, and severe levels based on the magnitude of the disaster. The direct economic loss function is derived from statistical data from 2019 to 2023. The social cost includes logistics and deprivation costs based on the simulation of transportation modes. Key findings: (1) The hierarchical model suits small-scale, rapid-response disasters but not sudden high-demand scenarios. (2) Cross-level scheduling offers greater flexibility and performs better under pressure. (3) As shipment intervals increase, the hierarchical approach improves, while cross-level trends become complex. (4) Fully flexible scheduling works best for low social cost weights and short intervals.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Behavior-based pricing: an analysis of the impact of social interactions
Authors: Mengzhuo Wang, Wenjie Bi
Affiliations: School of Business, Central South University
Abstract: New information technologies enable firms to identify customers and offer personalized pricing, while also facilitating extensive social interactions among consumers. Existing research mainly explores firms’ use of behaviour-based pricing (BBP) through information technology and ignores consumer behaviour. This paper expands on this by examining how consumers’ social interactions affect BBP. In a two-period game model, consumers derive additional utility in each period through social interactions with other consumers who purchase the same product. Customers who have socially interacted will experience diminishing marginal utility when they socially interact again. We find that social interaction lowers the price that firms charge to new and old customers, while diminishing marginal utility raises the price that firms charge to new and old customers, and overall promotes consumer switching. Firms will gain higher second-period profits by adopting BBP than by adopting uniform pricing when consumers exhibit social interaction. Prior research shows that BBP reduces firms’ total profits. In contrast, we find that when consumers exhibit social interaction, firms implementing BBP can achieve higher total profits, and this advantage increases with the levels of social interaction and diminishing marginal utility. However, implementing BBP reduces consumer surplus and ultimately leads to lower social welfare.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Contract manufacturer’s platform channel strategy for private brand product in outsourcing
Authors: Jie Wei, Yunchao Jiang
Affiliations: Hebei University of Technology
Abstract: Shrinking demand and intensifying competition brought about by anti-globalization cause numerous contract manufacturers (CMs) to suffer from the decline in original equipment manufacturers’ (OEMs’) outsourcing orders. Introducing private brand (PB) products to compensate for the loss and adopting platform channel to sell PB products for the CMs are very widespread. Motivated by the observation, this article investigates the performance of CM’s different platform channel strategies for PB products. Our results reveal that when consumers’ willingness-to-pay for PB products is high, if agency fee is low, the CM’s optimal platform channel strategy is to directly sell PB products through the common platform retailer (p-retailer), who also sells OEM’s national brand products; as agency fee increases, the CM should shift to directly sell PB products through the exclusive p-retailer, who does not sell OEM’s national brand products; if agency fee exceeds a certain level, the CM should wholesale PB products to the exclusive p-retailer. Moreover, wholesaling PB products to the common p-retailer creates a “win-win-win” outcome for the CM, the OEM and the common p-retailer if consumers’ willingness-to-pay for PB products is low.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Green supply chain coordination with profit-sharing and government intervention: a game-theoretic approach applied to the pharmaceutical industry
Authors: Milad Darzi Ramandi, Armin Jabbarzadeh, Amin Chaabane, Lionel Amodeo
Affiliations: Department of Systems Engineering, École de technologie supérieure (ÉTS), University of Quebec; Computer Science and Digital Society Laboratory, University of Technology of Troyes
Abstract: Amidst the global focus on sustainable development and environmental well-being, the adoption of green Supply Chain (SC) management has emerged as a pragmatic solution for mitigating Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions across various operational facets. This study employs a comprehensive approach, concurrently examining GHG emissions in production, transportation, and warehousing within a two-echelon SC framework involving a single vendor and buyer. Their joint objective is to optimize profitability while adhering to governmental regulations targeting GHG emissions reduction. The vendor’s visits to downstream sites are pivotal in fulfilling ordered products dispatched following fixed lead times. The buyer faces stochastic demand and employs a periodic inventory review policy, making service-level decisions contingent on market demand volatility and vendor visit intervals. The vendor’s production processes, requiring energy consumption, prompt investments in green technology to curtail emission rates. Governmental involvement extends to environmental safeguarding through tax policies. Introducing a game-theoretic approach, this study illuminates decision-making processes among SC stakeholders regarding replenishment strategies and emission reduction measures. Mathematical models and solutions for decentralized and centralized setups scrutinize how the SC leader orchestrates a profit-sharing contract to incentivize follower engagement in a comprehensive optimization strategy. The application of the proposed approach is investigated using real-world data from the pharmaceutical SC. In particular, a case study of the inventory control policy at the University of Michigan’s Central Pharmacy is presented to validate the model empirically. The results highlight the significant potential of green investments in reducing GHG emissions and emphasize the critical role of government incentives in driving these investments. The proposed coordination mechanism is shown to markedly enhance supply chain performance. Analytical findings indicate that government incentives lower both the minimum and maximum profit-sharing thresholds necessary for effective coordination, whereas high emission taxes without complementary incentives may discourage collaboration. Sensitivity analyses further reveal how holding costs, emission intensities, and energy prices differently affect service levels and green investments across decentralized and centralized structures. Notably, the study quantifies a 3% decline in service level when GHG emission taxes increase from 0.05 to 0.2, illustrating the need for balanced policy design in pharmaceutical supply chains. Computational experiments, calibrated with real-world pharmaceutical data, validate the model and demonstrate up to a 52% increase in total supply chain profit, over 20% improvement in service level, and reductions of up to 70% in transportation-related and 11.5% in production-related GHG emissions. These findings offer actionable insights for aligning environmental sustainability with profitability through contract-based coordination mechanisms.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Dynamic control of pure content quality and recommendation intensity on UGC platform considering reference effect
Authors: Yashu Yao, Zhihan Zhang, Qi Chen, Jiazhen Huo
Affiliations: Tongji University; University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Shanghai Open University
Abstract: Many User-Generated Content (UGC) platforms are transitioning towards a new business model where content creators engage users with pure content, while platforms’ revenue increasingly relies on shoppable content. This paper investigates the strategic balance between pure content and shoppable content on UGC platforms, and how this balance, along with dynamic pure content quality and consumer reference quality uncertainty, affects profit optimization for both UGC platforms and content creators. Employing a game-theoretic framework, we model three scenarios: (1) static pure content quality and recommendation intensity (i.e., the frequency of pure content recommendations or space allocation of pure content recommendations); (2) dynamic quality and recommendation intensity without uncertainty in reference quality; and (3) dynamic scenarios with uncertainty in reference quality. Our findings indicate that adopting dynamic strategies can enhance platform profits compared to the static scenario, but it may reduce content creators’ earnings relative to a static environment. Interestingly, while dynamic uncertainty leads to a decline in profits for the UGC platform, it also offers content creators opportunities to increase their profits. When facing higher uncertainty in reference quality, the UGC platform should increase recommendation intensity, while content creators will reduce the quality of their output.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Enhancing intangible CSR compliance in supply chains: an analysis of contractual incentives
Authors: Junlin Chen, Xiaohan Li, Yu Zhang, Jinting Wang
Affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics
Abstract: We examine a supply chain consisting of one supplier and one retailer. In this scenario, the supplier may engage in low-cost production practices that do not align with corporate social responsibility (CSR) standards but are difficult to detect. The disclosure of such non-compliant production could potentially harm the reputation of the downstream retailer, leading consumers who prioritize social consciousness to exit the market. To address this issue, we propose implementing contracts to evaluate their effectiveness in fostering supplier adherence to CSR standards during the production process, influencing the order quantity set by the retailer, and assessing the overall impact on supply chain profitability. The findings indicate that: (1) In a single-period scenario, both lump-sum penalty and bonus contracts, as well as option contracts, have been found to be effective in increasing CSR-compliant production to full compliance, aligning with the level of the centralized supply chain; (2) Compared to lump-sum penalty and bonus contracts, an option contract can efficiently boost the order quantity set by the retailer to align with the centralized scenario, leading to a win-win equilibrium; (3) The preferred deposit ratio may differ between retailers and suppliers; however, generally, a moderate ratio is preferable for both parties. Extreme ratios, whether too low or too high, can diminish the optimal order quantity and CSR-compliant proportion, affecting profitability across the supply chain; (4) In the long-term scenario, contingent renewal contracts possessing endogenous renewal probability can effectively improve the supplier’s CSR-compliant production to attain full compliance. However, their performance in increasing the retailer’s order quantity to the centralized level is limited. (5) In the extensions, we validate the performance of proposed contracts using the IPE enterprise regulatory record data and provide relevant management suggestions.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Redefining competitive industrial performance indicator: a multiplicative data envelopment analysis approach
Authors: Abdel Latef Anouze, Chixiao Lu, Ali Emrouznejad
Affiliations: College of Business and Economics, Qatar University; Surrey Business School, University of Surrey
Abstract: The competitive industrial performance (CIP) index is introduced to assess countries’ capacity to produce and export manufactured goods, technological upgrading and deepening, and impact on world production and trade. In this research, these dimensions are reflected by eight sub-indicators which are integrated into a comprehensive composite indicator (CI). However, the value of the weight corresponding to each sub-indicator may significantly affect the value of the CI. In the meantime, the ignorance of the benchmark construction and consideration of decision makers’ preference and attitude may restrict the application of CIP. Therefore, a comprehensive CI evaluation and benchmark-generating system with an objective weighting incorporating process is needed. This research aims to propose a geometric CI evaluation based on a multiplicative data envelopment analysis (DEA) model without explicit input (Multiplicative-WEI) where the benchmark can be represented by a projection point. We propose the generalized Multiplicative-WEI model whose linear representation is under the unified non-radial measure framework. The proposed model is further extended to the closest target model to reflect an optimistic evaluation strategy and super-efficiency model to increase the discriminant power. Within the introduction of parametric regarding decision makers’ preferences and attitudes, we apply our comprehensive CI framework to 153 countries to evaluate their CIP in year 2016 and year 2021. The results provide countries with more valuable insights regarding their performance change based on the weight of the sub-indicator, benchmark, and CI score.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: On the inventory performance of hierarchical forecasting approaches: case of a vaccine supply chain
Authors: Oussema Omri, Nadine Kafa, M. Zied Babai, Zied Jemai, Bahman Rostami-Tabar
Affiliations: Laboratoire Genie Industriel (LGI), CentraleSupélec, Université Paris-Saclay; Centre of Excellence in Supply Chain (CESIT), Kedge Business School; OASIS, Ecole Nationale d’Ingénieurs de Tunis, University of Tunis El Manar; Data Lab for Social Good Research Group, Cardiff Business School, Cardiff University
Abstract: Accurate demand forecasts are crucial for effective planning and decision-making in vaccine supply chains (VSCs). VSCs exhibit a hierarchical structure, a feature often overlooked in both research and practice. Moreover, while some studies assess the accuracy of hierarchical forecasting approaches, they do not investigate their impact on inventory performance. This paper empirically analyzes both the forecast accuracy and inventory performance of multiple hierarchical forecasting approaches, including Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Minimum Trace Reconciliation, using two forecasting methods: Error-Trend-Seasonality (ETS) and Auto-Regressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA). A periodic reorder-point order-up-to-level policy is applied for inventory control at different hierarchy levels, with performance measured by combined inventory holding volumes and achieved service-level efficiency. The empirical investigation uses data from the childhood VSC in an African developing country, which follows a four-level geographical hierarchy: national, regional, district, and subdistrict. The results show that while the Bottom-Up approach consistently delivers high forecast accuracy and strong inventory performance, the Top-Down approach occasionally yields better inventory efficiency despite its lower forecast accuracy.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Markov Walk and Walmart sales prediction
Authors: Giacomo Sbrana
Affiliations: NEOMA Business School – Campus de Reims
Abstract: Sales prediction is an essential and challenging task for business. A typical visible feature of retail sales is their intermittent behaviour, switching between zero and positive values, whose dynamic properties are worth exploring. Indeed, this behaviour remains an uncharted issue for standard time series models since they can hardly control for it. This paper provides a simple approach that embeds a Markov chain within a traditional random walk, we define as “Markov Walk”. This combination allows introducing dependency between switching observations as well as measuring the degree of persistence of sales over time. In addition, we provide closed-form results for estimating the parameters, forecasting future observations and constructing prediction intervals. It turns out that this combination greatly improves the predictive performance. Indeed, an empirical analysis, carried out over more than 30000 products sold by Walmart, shows that the proposed approach is definitely more accurate than several benchmarks, providing a useful tool for practitioners.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: An evacuation planning model considering stochastic non-compliance behaviour and shelter-in-place strategy
Authors: Aocheng Xu, Stein W. Wallace, Qingyi Wang
Affiliations: Business School, Sichuan University; Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong; Department of Business and Management Science, Norwegian School of Economics
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: A regulated many-to-one two-sided matching model for emergency teams: a university case study
Authors: Ahmet Bahadır Şimşek, Zekiye Göktekin, Tuğçe Şimşek, Dilara Tunçer
Affiliations: Health Care Management, Gumushane University; Health Management Master’s Program, Graduate Education Institute, Gumushane University, Gumushane
Abstract: In workplaces, emergency teams comprised of employees play a critical role in minimising damage during emergencies through rapid response. This study introduces a multi-objective employee-team matching model that optimally assigns employees to emergency teams, balancing stakeholder preferences and physical requirements. Using a regulated many-to-one matching framework, this model accounts for employee preferences, decision-maker evaluations, and team-specific physical standards, addressing limitations in current manual matching practices. Tested through a real case study in a university setting, the model demonstrates its efficacy by achieving stable, satisfactory matches that outperform traditional methods.
