Abstract: Conventional first-order stochastic dominance tests have two important limitations: non-rejection does not provide strong evidence of dominance, and the simple “reject” or “not reject” decision loses much information. Instead, we learn inductively about the set of values on which one CDF lies below another (restricted stochastic dominance). With high asymptotic probability, this set is contained within our outer confidence set and contains our inner confidence set. These confidence sets provide a richer picture than a global test’s single binary decision, and a large inner confidence set provides strong evidence of restricted stochastic dominance. Our theory allows generic non-iid sampling.

Title: Liquidity withdrawal before scheduled macroeconomic announcements
Authors: Guanchen Lv, Weidong Li, Yaqiong Zhou
Abstract: This note tests whether displayed liquidity deteriorates before scheduled macroeconomic announcements. Using millisecond-level E-mini S&P 500 futures order-book data at 78 announcement times in 2024, we find that spreads widen by 5.3% and best-quote depth falls by 8.7% in the final ten seconds before release, relative to minutes 1–10 before release. These changes persist locally and are not mirrored in 58 matched pseudo-windows without material scheduled releases. During the first ten seconds after release, message-sequence classification assigns 31.2% of absolute midquote adjustment to execution-driven depletion and 64.0% to cancellation-driven depletion and explicit non-trade quote updates. The findings are consistent with anticipatory liquidity withdrawal.

Title: Shared parental leave, male board directors, and firm performance: A corporate governance perspective
Authors: Ylva Baeckström, Onur Kemal Tosun
Abstract: To explore a broader dimension of board gender diversification, we investigate whether increased gender-equal government policy in relation to shared parental leave (SPL) affects the governance behavior of male board directors. We analyze the influence of the 2015 UK SPL policy using data on 1930 UK firms and semi-structured interviews with board directors. Consistent with social influence theory, we observe changes in male directors’ governance decisions after SPL. Attributable to better corporate governance, financial performance improves in firms with predominantly male boards. Director interviews reveal increased board level focus on gender equality and SPL, often facilitated by considerate, yet powerful, male directors. Broadening research on corporate governance and gender, our study suggests the positive influence of increased commitment to gender equality on the corporate governance behavior of the predominant cohort of male directors. For board gender diversity to contribute to meaningful performance improvements diversity must be embedded at deep organizational levels, and women directors must be granted sufficient power to effect strategic change. Governments need to ensure gender egalitarian policies foster structural equality and encourage fathers to take parental leave. In addition to focusing on gender representation targets, firms must address boardroom gender power imbalance.

Title: Competing for commoditization or platforming for de-commoditization: The role of salient thinking
Authors: Qingyuan Zhu, Jiong Sun, Guowei Liu
Abstract: Consumer preferences are often context-dependent, with attention naturally drawn to a product’s most prominent attribute. Applying the behavioral framework of “salient thinking,” this paper examines how firms strategically design channel architecture to manipulate consumer focus. We reveal a fundamental asymmetry in the incentives for firms to transition from direct competitors to cooperative complementors. Under direct competition, markets often devolve into a “commoditized,” price-salient equilibrium. However, we demonstrate that relative product quality allows firms to escape this trap. When a lower-quality firm resells a premium competitor’s product, the resulting contrast shifts consumer focus from price to quality; this “de-commoditization” fosters a market environment that can overcome double marginalization, particularly when quality-production costs remain moderate. Crucially, this mechanism is structurally asymmetric: it fails if the high-quality firm acts as the reseller, as low-quality firms prefer price-salient competition. These insights provide a novel, cognition-driven rationale for why premium and budget brands selectively co-locate in modern retail ecosystems.

Title: A robust optimization approach for the urban last-mile network of high-speed rail logistics integrating drone delivery
Authors: Shengdong Li, Li Shi, Chuijiang Guo, Jingshuai Yang, Changan Xu, Wenqing Li
Abstract: As a sustainable and efficient freight transport method, high-speed rail (HSR) logistics is developing rapidly. However, its potential is limited by the inefficiency and uncertainty of urban last-mile delivery. This paper proposes a two-stage robust optimization model for designing an urban last-mile delivery network of HSR logistics that integrates drone delivery. This paper focuses on the practical scenarios the model jointly optimizes the activation modes of logistics functions at HSR stations, the location selection of urban distribution centers, and their hierarchical affiliation relationships, while considering factors such as differentiated facility construction modes, drone flight range, and no-fly zones. To solve the model efficiently, an improved column-and-constraint generation (C&CG) algorithm is developed, and acceleration strategies such as scenario reduction are introduced. Numerical experiments based on real-world data from Shenzhen City, China show that the improved C&CG algorithm outperforms the Benders decomposition algorithm and the basic C&CG algorithm in terms of the number of iterations and computation time. Additionally, the two-stage model demonstrates better cost efficiency and demand satisfaction rate than the single-stage robust model in an uncertain environment. Sensitivity analysis further reveals the trade-off relationships among drone delivery costs, network robustness, and facility investment. This study can provide an efficient decision-making method for the layout optimization of urban delivery networks in HSR logistics.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Robustness-led and stability-responsive rescheduling: A Stackelberg game-theoretic formulation
Authors: Man Li, Shuqi Li, Junpeng Wang, Xuanfei Wang, Junwei Wei, Qinmin Yang, Xiangmin Zhang
Abstract: Scheduling under disruptions poses a fundamental challenge in operations research, as decision makers must hierarchically prioritize system robustness while responding with schedule stability in real time. Existing rescheduling approaches typically rely on symmetric or weighted formulations, which obscure the leader-follower decision asymmetry inherent in disruption management and fail to provide a principled coordination mechanism between robustness and stability. This study formulates disrupted rescheduling as a hierarchical decision-making problem and proposes a Stackelberg game-theoretic formulation grounded in bilevel optimization. The structure explicitly models robustness as the Leader’s strategic objective and stability as the Follower’s responsive objective, thereby capturing the endogenous priority structure observed in practical rescheduling decisions. A baseline schedule is first constructed via multi-objective optimization to define the feasible and performance-relevant region for subsequent adjustments. Under disruptions, rescheduling decisions are then derived through backward induction by characterizing the subgame-perfect Nash equilibrium (SPNE) of the Stackelberg game, yielding sequential and priority-aware responses that coordinate stability within robustness-led constraints. Computational experiments on standard benchmark instances demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a robustness-stability coordination unattainable by conventional strategies. In particular, the Stackelberg-based model attains robustness levels statistically indistinguishable from robustness-dominant complete rescheduling, while simultaneously improving schedule stability by an average of 39.52% relative to stability-oriented right-shift rescheduling. These results indicate that explicitly modeling rescheduling as a hierarchical bilevel game enables superior performance continuity under disruptions. The study contributes to the literature by introducing a decision-theoretic perspective on rescheduling under disruptions, establishing Stackelberg games as a unifying framework for robustness-stability coordination, and offering a transferable modeling paradigm for complex scheduling problems with hierarchical priorities.

Title: Heuristics for balancing cost and diversity in wire harness routing layouts
Authors: T. Karlsson, E. Åblad
Abstract: This paper addresses the harness dissimilarity problem—a generalization of the path dissimilarity problem—in which the goal is to select ℎ dissimilar yet low-cost wire harness routing layouts, providing alternatives for engineering decision-making. Our approach involves two stages: first, generating a diverse pool of candidate routings; second, constructing subsets of size ℎ that are well-distributed along an approximated Pareto front. We analyze three methods for generating the candidate pool: the iterative penalty method, the pathway reward method, and NSGA-II. To approximate a Pareto front for the bi-objective problem of maximizing diversity while minimizing the total cost of selected candidates, we propose a weighted-sum constructive heuristic combined with local search, which outperforms a GRASP metaheuristic from related work. The method is also evaluated against an exact solver for small instances.

Title: Introduction to the special issue honoring Michel Juillard’s contribution to macroeconomics
Authors: Thomas Lubik, Isabelle Salle, Gauthier Vermandel
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Diagnostic expectations and cryptocurrency returns
Authors: Weijia Xue, Chunyang Zhou
Abstract: This paper studies whether standard tokenomics can account for the strong hourly return reversals observed in cryptocurrency markets. Using 319 Binance USDT pairs, we document pervasive short-horizon negative return predictability: past one-hour returns forecast subsequent one- to four-hour returns with negative coefficients for most coins, including BTC and ETH. We then show that a benchmark tokenomic model with rational expectations cannot generate this pattern because equilibrium token prices follow a geometric Brownian motion and therefore exhibit no non-overlapping return predictability. To explain the data, we introduce diagnostic expectations (DE) as the only wedge relative to the rational benchmark. Recent news shifts perceived platform productivity through a representativeness term and induces price overshooting, which is subsequently corrected as sentiment mean-reverts. The model matches the observed reversal pattern, implies that sentiment is priced in equilibrium, and generates endogenous boom-bust dynamics. We also show that the framework extends tractably to settings with heterogeneous coins and demand.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: History-dependent monetary policy – less is more
Authors: Olena Kostyshyna, Luba Petersen, Jing Yang
Abstract: History-dependent monetary policies (HDMP) can potentially address the challenges that standard monetary policy frameworks face, especially at the ELB. Using controlled laboratory experiments, we identify several vulnerabilities in HDMP. Our analysis of experimental data shows that a weakened expectations channel can undermine HDMP. Experimental participants’ expectations feed off past data; they are not forward-looking and do not internalize the stabilization properties or future make-up strategies of HDMP. Conditional on these expectations, we highlight two risks associated with HDMP: inflation overshoots under average inflation targeting and deflationary spirals under price level targeting and nominal GDP level targeting. However, effective central bank communication through medium-term macroeconomic projections can improve the performance of price level targeting.

Title: Economy-wide and international spillovers of the economic impacts of climate change
Authors: Maksym Chepeliev, Dominique van der Mensbrugghe, Toon Vandyck
Abstract: Estimates of the economic consequences of climate change diverge widely and are influenced by methodological choices. Here, we explore different approaches to quantifying economic damages by leveraging a structural model of the global economy. We decompose macroeconomic outcomes by region, factor, and sector to reveal differences between top-down aggregate productivity shocks and a bottom-up representation of impact channels. While aggregate economic outcomes are comparable, region-specific results differ substantially between approaches at the tails of the distribution, driven by divergent international trade responses. Allowing for economic adaptation in production and trade flows, our findings indicate that international spillovers raise global welfare losses from climate change by 1%–7% relative to the sum of domestic impacts. Overall, our results suggest that a disaggregated representation of climate change impact channels is important for improving the understanding of aggregate economic outcomes and for informing effective adaptation policies that account for international trade spillovers.

Title: Carbon emissions intensity and idiosyncratic volatility: Evidence from Indian firms
Authors: Ushmeet Kaur, Wasim Ahmad
Abstract: Climate change has become an increasingly important source of financial risk, attracting growing interest in how carbon emissions are priced in equity markets. Although the literature is expanding, firm-level evidence from emerging markets remains limited. In this paper, we examine whether corporate carbon emissions intensity predicts future idiosyncratic stock return volatility among Indian listed firms over the period 2009–2023. We find that firms with higher CO 2 emissions intensity, measured as Scope 1 and Scope 2 carbon-dioxide-equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions scaled by revenue, exhibit significantly higher one-period-ahead idiosyncratic stock return volatility. Specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in emissions intensity increases annualised idiosyncratic volatility by 1.32 percentage points, representing 4.6% of the sample mean. The relationship is driven primarily by direct (Scope 1) rather than purchased energy (Scope 2) emissions and is stronger for firms covered by India’s Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme and during periods of elevated economic policy uncertainty, but weaker for firms that use renewable energy. We also find evidence that stock illiquidity is a potential channel through which carbon emissions influence future firm-specific stock return risk. The results remain robust to alternative measures of emissions intensity and risk, sample-selection corrections, a lead test, an instrumental-variables analysis, and additional robustness checks. Overall, our findings suggest that firm-level carbon emissions are an important determinant of firm-specific stock return risk in an emerging equity market.

Title: The impact of Daylight Saving Time (DST) on electricity consumption in Iran
Authors: Amirhossein Rafati Sahneh Saraei, Ali Jadidzadeh
Abstract: Daylight Saving Time (DST) shifts clock time relative to daylight and routine activities, with ambiguous effects on electricity consumption: later evening daylight may reduce lighting demand but may also affect cooling, heating, and activity-related load. This paper evaluates the effect of DST on electricity consumption in Iran using nationwide hourly load data from 2015 to 2021, weather and calendar controls, and a Regression Discontinuity in Time (RDiT) design around legally fixed spring-forward and fall-back transition dates. We distinguish local boundary effects from the season-average daily effect over the full DST-active period. The national season-average daily ATE is positive, corresponding to a 2.24% increase in national daily electricity consumption during DST, but is not statistically significant at the 5% level under Newey–West inference. In contrast, the boundary RDiT estimates reveal significant local discontinuities: the spring-forward transition is associated with a 3.87% increase in residualized electricity consumption, while the DST-normalized fall-back estimate indicates an 11.14% decrease under DST relative to standard time. These transition-specific effects should not be netted out to infer the full-season effect. Heterogeneity analyses show that effects vary across tariff periods and consumer categories, with stronger spring-forward responses during on-peak hours and different fall-back responses for RECs and EDCs. Overall, the results do not support a simple electricity-saving interpretation of DST in Iran; the estimated effect depends on the estimand, timing of demand, and consumer composition.

Title: Route-informed planning for medium- and heavy-duty truck charging infrastructure in California
Authors: Runhua (Ivan) Xiao, Miguel Jaller, Anmol Pahwa, Claudio B. da Cunha
Abstract: California freight electrification depends as much on charging access and corridor planning as on vehicle adoption. Public agencies and fleets need evidence on whether depot and public charging networks can support truckload operations without increasing empty repositioning, modeled charging-stop requirements, and route infeasibility. This study develops an operations-based freight charging assessment for mixed diesel and battery-electric truck operations and applies it to controlled California truckload scenarios. Rather than optimizing final station sites, the framework evaluates predefined depot-adjacent and public fast-charging sites through route feasibility, total and deadhead VMT, modeled charging stop rows, active charging locations, and cost-accounting indicators. The results are scenario-level route-record comparisons and do not reflect observed daily truck operations or session-level charging dwell measurements.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Data-driven modelling of passenger-car stock electrification: validation and cross-country scenarios
Authors: Dominik Fink, Harald Lerch, Vladislav Kemka, Pavel Žlábek, Jan Kovanda
Abstract: Electrification policy targets new registrations, but the transition of the national passenger-car stock depends jointly on BEV adoption and vehicle retirement. This study models both, using the Czech Republic as an ageing-market case. A power-law registration function is calibrated on Czech data for 2016–2024 and benchmarked against five reference countries; a fixed-lifetime stock-turnover model, with an age-structured extension, then gives post-2035 trajectories. The adoption parameter α is a reduced-form capacity measure reflecting affordability, policy continuity and charging access. Adjusted MAPE is 6.1–17.2 % with R 2 above 0.92; the Czech in-sample fit gives MAPE 5.8 %, R 2 0.974, α cal 0.034 and n cal 2.81. Vehicle lifetime alone sets the nominal replacement horizon r d = r 0 + L: 2047 for L = 12 years, 2055 for L = 20, while α scn = 0.10–0.40 governs the stock trajectory, not the terminal year. Results are scenario comparisons, not forecasts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Supervised dimension reduction for autoregressive time series based on sliced inverse regression
Authors: Ying Liao, Yifan Huang, Zhigen Zhao, Yisha Xiang
Abstract: Supervised dimension reduction is crucial for time series analysis, yet standard methods often ignore temporal dependencies, leading to information loss and suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we extend the conventional sliced inverse regression (SIR) method to propose an effective dimension reduction (EDR) framework for autoregressive (AR) time series. Within this framework, we introduce two ways (denoted by SIR-T-1 and SIR-T-2) to more efficiently utilize the available data by leveraging AR structures. SIR-T-1 incorporates lagged information by establishing an equivalence between the conditional covariance matrices of current and lagged observations. SIR-T-2 employs a weighted aggregation scheme to combine EDR directions estimated from multiple lags. Extensive simulation experiments show that SIR-T-1 significantly outperforms the basic SIR in prediction accuracy and robustness, particularly in challenging scenarios with small sample size, high noise, and nonlinearity. SIR-T-2 proves to be an effective approximation for time series with low noise levels. A case study on superconductor data demonstrates that the proposed framework achieves 28.6%–63.9% lower prediction error than SIR for data-limited manufacturing stages, confirming its practical utility. The results underscore that leveraging AR structures is essential for EDR in time series and the resulting EDR directions provide practical insights for real-world applications.

Title: When Should Service Firms Engage in Co‐Opetition? Reliability, Pricing, and Market Dynamics
Authors: Zichen Liu, Qi Fu, Zhaotong Lian
Affiliations: Faculty of Business Administration University of Macau Macao SAR China
Abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates strategic repair co‐opetition between two rival service providers with unreliable servers. We develop a two‐stage queueing game, where in Stage 1, the competing firms select their repair mode: either operating independent repair teams (competition) or sharing resources (co‐opetition). In Stage 2, they set service prices for delay‐sensitive customers. We analyze how these repair modes influence steady‐state service availability, pricing equilibria, and profitability. Our findings reveal that sharing resources does not universally improve service capacity; the outcome depends on the firms' relative repair efficiency. Additionally, although higher availability increases maximum throughput, it simultaneously intensifies price competition. Consequently, firms' preferences are contingent on market demand. When demand is high, the capacity benefits dominate, driving firms to choose the repair mode that yields higher availability. Conversely, in low‐demand scenarios, firms favor the mode with lower availability to restrict capacity and soften price competition. In markets with intermediate demand, asymmetric pricing equilibria tend to drive firms toward divergent repair modes, preventing the formation of co‐opetition. Finally, we show that while a social planner prefers higher capacity to maximize welfare, independent firms may strategically restrict capacity, leading to a divergence from the social optimum.

Title: Reinforcement learning for train marshalling in flat yards: a decision transformer approach
Authors: Amit Kumar, T. M. Rofin, Milind Akarte
Abstract: Railway freight transportation plays a vital role in sustainable logistics, offering a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to road transport. Within this domain, shunting yard operations are critical for forming outbound trains by rearranging wagons. This paper addresses the train building by a single shunting engine problem, a challenging operational problem observed in flat shunting yards, where a single engine must reassemble wagons into a predefined sequence using a minimal number of moves. We develop a simulation-based framework using the Gymnasium library to model the physical and operational constraints of a realistic rail yard environment. This simulation serves as the foundation for a Hybrid Model that combines the simulation model with three solution approaches which are then explored and evaluated. First, an online deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agent using the proximal policy optimization (PPO) algorithm, which learns by interacting with the environment Second, a recursive search heuristic (RSH) method that mimics rule-based operational strategies. Third, a decision transformer (DT) model that utilizes offline trajectory data to learn a sequence-to-action mapping, leveraging recent advances in attention-based architectures. A dataset of RSH generated trajectories is used to train the DT model, allowing it to perform effectively without online environment interaction. Comprehensive experiments are conducted on multiple problem instances of varying complexity, comparing the quality of the generated shunting plans, training times, and policy generalization capabilities. The results show that while the PPO performs competitively on small instances, it struggles with scalability. DT performs similar to RSH in small instance and outperforms PPO in all problem instances, offering a promising approach for deploying such trained Artificial Intelligence agents in operational setting. This study demonstrates the potential of Hybrid Model paradigm by combining simulation, heuristic search, and both online DRL and offline DT sequence modelling techniques for addressing complex combinatorial optimization problems.

Title: Privatization Under Political Ties
Authors: Matteo Broso
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Management University of Brescia Brescia Italy
Abstract: ABSTRACT I study a product differentiation model with endogenous entry where a politically connected public firm competes with a private one. Consumers are heterogeneous in their willingness to pay. I argue that—because of political ties—the public firm may mimic the preferences of the consumer with the median willingness to pay. I show that as privatization (i.e., the weight on profits in the public firm's objective function) increases, the equilibrium market structure shifts from a welfare‐inefficient public monopoly to a duopoly. Under duopoly, the public firm can set a relatively low price to attract and please the median consumer. In this way, the public firm gains market shares and, consequently, market power. In equilibrium, the public firm can then end up being more profitable than its private, profit‐seeking competitor. Finally, I show that full privatization is not socially optimal.

Title: ESG performance and supply chain risk: A partner management perspective
Authors: Shuaiwen Chang
Abstract: A focal firm depends on trading partners it does not control, whose disruptions interrupt its own operations. Based on resource dependence theory, we argue that a firm's ESG performance reflects the routines, assessment capability, and incentives with which it selects and develops partners on their ESG performance, so that it holds a stronger partner portfolio and can spread its dependence across more partners and regions. Using Chinese A-share listed firms over 2014–2024 and a text-based supply chain risk measure, we find that stronger ESG performance lowers supply chain risk, more for routine than for shock-driven risk and more where the firm depends most on partner management. The partner portfolio's ESG performance rises with the firm's own. At firms with stronger ESG performance, suppliers are already stronger before admission, weaker suppliers are more likely to be terminated, and continuing customers improve. Reductions in partner composition and geographic concentration each carry part of the effect, and the composition channel is broader where more qualified candidates are available. Across the network, connected firms' supply chain risk falls with the focal firm's ESG performance; associations consistent with ESG requirement diffusion extend across tiers in both directions, whereas those consistent with shock contagion do so only downstream. ESG performance lowers supply chain risk by shaping whom the firm depends on and how far that dependence is spread, extending its risk-mitigating role beyond the firm's own operations. Managers can assess partners' ESG performance at admission and during relationships and set selection standards alongside diversification targets.

Title: Fuzzy demand-driven multi-objective procurement planning in computer manufacturing
Authors: Huai-Wei Lo, Ching-Yun Chi, Chun-Jui Pai, Yi-Xuan Liu
Abstract: This study develops a data-driven two-stage framework that integrates fuzzy demand forecasting with multi-objective supplier selection and procurement planning (SSPP) for computer manufacturing. In Stage 1, historical quarterly demand data are adjusted using centered moving-average seasonal indices, and fuzzy regression is applied to generate triangular fuzzy demand forecasts expressed as lower, central, and upper values. The expansion bands are calibrated according to historical coverage so that component-specific demand uncertainty can be represented. In Stage 2, the fuzzy demand information is incorporated into a multi-period SSPP model that considers five objectives: procurement cost, delivery delay rate, defect rate, sustainability performance, and disruption risk. The model is solved using an augmented max–min fuzzy multi-objective linear programming approach to obtain a single implementable compromise plan. A real case analysis of a multinational computer assembly company involving two core components and four candidate suppliers is presented. The results show that the forecasting stage captures seasonal variation and long-term growth while generating component-specific uncertainty bands. Additional analyses, including fuzzy regression band calibration, rolling-window validation, forecast accuracy and benchmark comparison, and method comparison, further support the applicability of the proposed framework. The procurement results indicate that the proposed approach can generate balanced quarterly sourcing plans and help decision makers coordinate multiple objectives. The study contributes an integrated forecasting-to-procurement framework that translates demand uncertainty into actionable supplier selection and procurement decisions.

Title: Can a wealth tax reduce CO2 emissions in Europe?
Authors: Alexander Guschanski, Rafael Wildauer
Abstract: We analyse the potential of wealth taxes to reduce CO2 emissions through two transmission channels: the inequality channel, which links reductions in wealth inequality to lower emissions, and the consumption channel, which operates through the effect of wealth taxes on consumption by top wealth holders. We simulate the effects of various wealth tax designs over one- and ten-year horizons using harmonised microdata from 22 European countries. Our analysis accounts for survey non-response bias, heterogeneous rates of returns across households, and behavioural responses to taxation. We find that, through the inequality channel, a recurrent annual progressive wealth tax could reduce annual CO2 emissions by 7.5%–14.7% after 10 years relative to a no-tax scenario, depending on tax progressivity. Through the consumption channel, the average reduction is 1.5%–3.6% after 10 years. In addition, we show that the revenues generated cover the entire investment gap identified by the European Commission’s ‘Fit for 55’ emissions reduction programme. These findings highlight the potential of wealth taxes to serve a dual purpose: curbing wealth concentration and contributing meaningfully to climate mitigation and justice, by focusing on high-net-worth households that account for a disproportionate share of emissions.

Title: Fostering institutional trust and organ donation: Evidence from a randomized informational intervention in Tunisia
Authors: Christina Sarah Hauser, Maleke Fourati
Abstract: Organ transplantation saves lives and improves the quality of life of patients who would otherwise depend on costly and invasive treatments. The technology is becoming available in low- and middle-income countries, but the gap between the demand for and the supply of organ transplants remains large. In a randomized controlled trial at a Tunisian university, we evaluate an expert-led intervention designed to inform about organ donation and strengthen trust in medical institutions. The intervention consists of a short video testimonial from a heart transplant survivor, a presentation led by a medical doctor and a short Q&A session. We find that the intervention significantly increases deceased donor registration, with suggestive evidence of positive spillover effects on the control group. The survey data provides little support for changes in attitudes and social expectations as potential mechanisms. Instead, it reveals large and statistically significant increases in medical and legal knowledge, religious beliefs supportive of donation, and institutional trust among treated students. Finally, we show that treatment effects on organ donor registration are driven by male students and those whose families likely support organ donation. Targeting older segments of the population may further increase the impact and cost-effectiveness of this intervention.

Title: Recent stock prices as reference points and the disposition effect
Authors: Julia Brettschneider, Giovanni Burro, Vicky Henderson
Abstract: We quantify how the magnitude of the disposition effect changes when gains and losses are defined relative to recent stock prices rather than the original purchase price. Our study uses the LDB dataset containing trading records of individual investors. Using recent prices as the reference point lowers the disposition effect. This reduction is more pronounced for active traders. Our central finding is a monotonic increase in the disposition effect with price lag length. We observe a tendency to sell stocks that recently appreciated (depreciated) with respect to stocks that recently depreciated (appreciated) in the gain (loss) domain.

Title: The entrepreneurship U-shape: Pattern or path?
Authors: Dragos Radu
Abstract: A familiar U-shape links early-stage entrepreneurship to income per capita and is often read as a development path. I test that reading by asking whether the curve turns inside observed support, where it is located, and whether it survives within countries. The pooled quadratic opens upward but does not turn inside observed support. The in-support U-shape appears only among high-income economies. Within that group, country fixed effects detect no significant curvature, and the Mundlak point estimates show positive between-country but near-zero within-country curvature. The evidence is stronger for a cross-sectional pattern among rich economies than for a common within-country path.

Title: Does equal treatment help consumers? Evidence from Amazon’s Buy Box remedy
Authors: Muxin Li
Abstract: Using data on electronic products across Amazon marketplaces, I study the effects of an antitrust case requiring Amazon to provide equal treatment to sellers in Buy Box, Amazon’s featured offer displayed to consumers. The remedy addresses concerns that Amazon engaged in biased Buy Box allocation and potentially distorted competition. Buy Box prices increased sharply when the decision became legally binding, with no additional increase observed at the remedy implementation deadline. Prices rose across all sellers, while Buy Box allocation shifted from Amazon toward Fulfilled by Merchant (FBM) sellers, third-party sellers responsible for their own fulfillment, whose prices increased the most.

Title: Beyond GDP tournaments: Cadre evaluation reform and sectoral credit allocation
Authors: Zeyuan Huang, Shirong Zhao
Abstract: Against China’s growth slowdown, we study how China’s staggered “de-emphasizing GDP” cadre evaluation reforms that reduce emphasis on relative GDP growth performance reweight local policy responses across multiple evaluation objectives. Using prefecture-level adoption (2013–2023) and city commercial bank loan-level data, we find reforms shift local credit toward high-tech firms and away from real estate and elevated housing downside risk, with larger effects where promotion incentives are stronger. The response is concentrated in local CCB lending to local firms, and a scale–composition decomposition attributes the sectoral effects almost entirely to within-portfolio reallocation. A Holmström–Milgrom multitask framework rationalizes this reallocation.

Title: A Fisher-consistent measure of real interest rates from inflation fixing swaps
Authors: Marco Bernardini, Lara D’Arrigo, Alessandro Lin, Andrea Tiseno
Abstract: Conventional market-based measures of real interest rates violate the Fisher equation. Because of lagged inflation indexation, nominal and inflation components cover different horizons, creating a timing distortion that can bias real-time assessments of the monetary policy stance. We propose a Fisher-consistent measure of the short-term real rate using inflation fixing swaps, whose monthly maturities allow precise alignment across horizons. In euro-area data, our measure diverges substantially from the conventional one around sharp inflation repricing, by up to 3 percentage points. Ahead of several ECB meetings, it even points to opposite dynamics: real-rate tightening instead of easing, and vice versa.

Title: Endogenous location and pricing policy: Mixed strategies make uniform pricing commitment successful
Authors: Iñaki Aguirre
Abstract: We study the strategic choice of spatial price policy (uniform pricing versus spatial price discrimination) in a linear city with quadratic transport costs and endogenous locations, under two alternative three-stage game orderings (following Eber, 1997). The asymmetric subgame (in which one firm discriminates while the other prices uniformly) is solved via the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium under simultaneous price competition, replacing the Stackelberg standard of Thisse and Vives (1988). In Game I (location/pricing policy/prices), the policy game is a coordination game : both are Nash equilibria but mutual uniform pricing Pareto dominates mutual discrimination. This overturns the Prisoner’s Dilemma that arises under the Stackelberg standard, in which price discrimination is a dominant strategy. In Game II (pricing policy/location/prices), mutual uniform pricing is the unique equilibrium.

Title: Frontier technology adopters and the aggregate decline of routine jobs
Authors: Melanie Arntz, Sabrina Genz, Terry Gregory, Florian Lehmer, Ulrich Zierahn-Weilage
Abstract: We provide micro-founded evidence on how establishment-level adoption of frontier technologies shapes the economy-wide occupational employment structure. Linking survey data on technology adoption between 2011 and 2016 by 1660 German incumbent establishments to administrative worker records, we find that establishments adopting frontier technologies such as AI or smart factories contributed disproportionately to the overall decline in routine jobs. Crucially, these overall effects do not stem from average within-establishment adjustments but from a subset of large and less routine-intensive adopters. Our findings highlight that frontier technology adoption is not routine-replacing per se: establishment size and an initially non-routine-intensive workforce are key conditions for de-routinization to occur.

Title: Willing to pay for security: A discrete choice experiment to analyse labour supply preferences
Authors: Nikhil Datta
Abstract: This paper investigates workers’ valuations of the job attributes that distinguish atypical work arrangements from traditional employee relationships. Using a vignette-based discrete-choice module fielded to samples of UK and US workers, I estimate willingness-to-pay distributions for contract security, work-related benefits, flexibility, autonomy, and tax treatment. Across both countries, workers place substantially higher value on job security and employment protections than on flexibility-related attributes. Interestingly, this pattern holds even among the self-employed: almost two-thirds of UK self-employed workers and just under half of US self-employed workers are estimated to prefer the traditional-employment bundle. Despite institutional differences between the UK and US, average valuations are closely aligned. The heterogeneity analysis shows that most observable characteristics account for only limited variation in preferences, but risk aversion and parenthood are notable exceptions, with both substantially increasing the value workers attach to contract security.

Title: A unified deep reinforcement learning framework for solving the heterogeneous fleet vehicle routing problem
Authors: Shihong Huang, Shengjie Wang, Lei Gao, Hong Ma, Zhanluo Zhang, Feng Zhang, Weihua Zhou
Abstract: The Heterogeneous Fleet Vehicle Routing Problem (HFVRP) incorporates diverse vehicle capacities, fixed costs, and variable travel costs, making routing decisions highly sensitive to vehicle selection. Most existing Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods assume homogeneous fleets, leading to suboptimal performance when applied to HFVRP. To address this, we investigate HFVRP under complex constraints and develop a unified DRL framework capable of solving the problem across diverse settings. We formulate a Mode-Switching Markov Decision Process, modeling the generation of HFVRP solutions as a single-stage autoregressive decision process. Accordingly, we propose a Mode-Switching Cross-Semantic Multi-View framework (MS-CSMV), a unified architecture featuring a cross-semantic encoder and a multi-view decoder that effectively addresses diverse problem constraints and captures the complex mapping relationships between vehicle heterogeneity and customer node attributes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MS-CSMV significantly outperforms state-of-the-art neural solvers and achieves a favorable balance between solution quality and computational efficiency, producing solutions within seconds. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robust zero-shot generalization capabilities across large-scale instances and previously unseen problem variants.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Data-driven robust optimization for emergency facility deployment under ambiguous demand position
Authors: Yuchen Li, Daniel Zhuoyu Long, Jianghua Zhang
Abstract: Under the uncertainty of disaster locations, the deployment of emergency facilities is a core challenge, which directly determines the efficiency of emergency response and thereby reduces the time required to deliver emergency services. To address the spatial uncertainty of future demand points, we propose a cluster-wise Wasserstein distance-based spatial ambiguity set via historical demand clustering to characterize future demand distribution. We first formulate a distributionally robust optimization model for locating emergency facilities from the perspective of minimizing the transport distance. Then from the target-oriented decision-making perspective, we propose a cluster-wise robust satisficing model to maximize the robustness to the uncertainty of achieving a specified satisfactory target transport distance. A solution technique based on row-and-column generation is proposed to tackle the large-scale discrete models efficiently. We conduct numerical experiments to verify the validity of the discretization method in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy under the proposed algorithm. The results show that the robust satisficing model has better average performance than the benchmark models. Finally, the robust satisficing framework is applied to deal with a real case of locating emergency facilities in Sichuan, an earthquake-prone region of China.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Real-time yard slot allocation for outbound containers in an automated container terminal based on deep reinforcement learning
Authors: Weixuan Niu, Yanwei Zhang, Mengyu Tang, Yuhan Song, Heng Huang, Suikai Li, Yu Tian
Abstract: Efficient yard slot allocation for outbound containers is paramount to enhancing ship loading efficiency in automated container terminals (ACTs), where the perpendicular yard layout and the twin yard crane (YC) configuration are widely deployed. In such ACTs, the storage of an arrived outbound container relies on a twin-YC relay process where the container is initially stacked in a temporary handshake slot by the landside YC and subsequently remarshalled to a seaside slot by the seaside YC, presenting a complex relay-type yard slot allocation problem (RYSAP). This problem essentially comprises two decision-making processes: Decision 1 allocates a handshake slot for an arrived outbound container, while Decision 2 selects an outbound container from the handshake area and allocates a seaside slot for it. Structurally, each decision-making process is decomposed into two hierarchical stages: Stage 1 constructs a stack-set to bound the decision space for Stage 2, and Stage 2 determines the specific slot within the stack-set. To cope with the uncertainties in container arrivals and decision triggering, this problem is addressed in real time via a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based method. For Stage 1, the stack-set selection strategy is designed to construct the stack-set at each decision-making point. For Stage 2, a DRL method is proposed for specific slot allocation, aiming to reduce the number of blocking containers and enhance space utilization. By integrating the two interconnected decision-making processes, a comprehensive Markov Decision Process (MDP) is formulated. Crucially, the mathematical expectation of the number of future blocking containers at the current state is incorporated into the reward function, thereby guiding the DRL agent to learn a forward-looking policy. To accelerate training convergence and enhance policy performance, a Double Dueling Deep Q-Network with effective random exploration (D3QN-ERE) is developed. Numerical experiments verify the effectiveness, stability, and favorable generalization capability of the proposed method. Further analysis of the experimental results provides some suggestions for improving the yard operation and management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: A data-driven framework for characterising road freight transport using GPS data
Authors: Emma Ceulemans, Ivan Cardenas, Ivan Sanchez-Diaz, Edwin van Hassel
Abstract: Granular insights into road freight transport are essential for evidence-based policy-making, yet a persistent gap remains between regulatory frameworks and policy objectives due to a lack of disaggregated data. While GPS data offers a low-resource pathway to detailed truck movement analysis, existing literature focuses heavily on stop identification, leaving systematic, national-scale characterisations of road freight transportation systems relatively scarce. This study addresses this gap by developing a data-driven framework that utilises GPS data to comprehensively characterise the road freight transport system across four dimensions: truck flows, network, trips, and activities. Because raw GPS data lacks event descriptors, we develop a multi-step processing approach using machine learning to identify truck stops, which then serve as the foundation for the characterisation. We utilise a decision tree model with thresholds calibrated via sequential unsupervised clustering, bridging natural data patterns with domain expertise. The model's internal consistency is assessed through a cross-model agreement audit with a Random Forest classifier. We demonstrate the framework's utility through a nationwide case study in Belgium using tolling data from heavy goods vehicles. To assess the results’ external plausibility, the GPS-inferred metrics are compared against national aggregated data. This systematic characterisation of a country's road freight transport system provides a scalable foundation for targeted policy-making, enabling a deeper understanding of its challenges and the evaluation of measures to improve transport sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Bridging scenario generation and regulatory standards: A physically plausible generative AI framework for automated vehicle safety certification
Authors: Jintao Huang, Yanyong Guo, Pan Liu, Yuguang Chen, Hongliang Ding
Abstract: The transition from mileage-based to scenario-based validation is emerging as a critical requirement for the regulatory certification of automated driving systems. However, establishing a standardized testing framework is hindered by the scarcity of safety-critical scenarios in naturalistic data and the tendency of existing methods to sacrifice physical plausibility for high collision rates. To address this gap, this study proposes TraSafeDiff, a conditional diffusion-based framework designed to generate safety-critical traffic scenarios that are both adversarially challenging and physically consistent. The framework integrates multimodal scene information through a deep encoder, while differentiable kinematic, boundary, and angular-motion energy penalties guide generated trajectories toward greater physical plausibility. In an open-loop evaluation on nuScenes, TraSafeDiff achieves a higher collision rate and a lower off-road rate than the evaluated scenario-generation baselines, while its acceleration and jerk distributions show closer alignment with naturalistic data. By balancing adversarial severity with kinematic plausibility, this study provides a candidate-scenario generation approach that may complement broader evidence-based safety evaluation and regulatory-assurance workflows.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Benchmarking informal mobility in Africa: Evidence from Kigali for inclusive transportation planning
Authors: Agnes Nakalembe, Vital Ahishakiye, Neza David Tuyishimire, Emily Aiken, Patrick McSharry, João Barros
Abstract: Urban mobility in sub-Saharan African cities is shaped by the widespread presence of informal transport services, yet their operational performance and spatial role remain insufficiently quantified. This study analyzes approximately 5 million motorbike taxi trips and 80,000 ride-hailing car trips in Kigali, Rwanda, to benchmark major transport modes across operational, spatial, and socio-economic dimensions. Motorbike taxis travel 16.5% faster than ride-hailing cars during peak hours and involve substantially shorter waiting times, making them the most effective option among commonly used public transport modes once waiting time is incorporated into travel performance. Ride-hailing cars are significantly more expensive and spatially concentrated, while buses lose efficiency due to long waiting times. Spatial connectivity metrics show that motorbike taxi trips connect a larger number of locations across the city, whereas ride-hailing flows distribute demand more evenly across a smaller set of connections. Regression analysis further reveals distinct spatial correlates for the two services. Nighttime light radiance strongly predicts ride-hailing activity ( R 2 = 0.77 for origins and 0.82 for destinations), while population density better explains motorbike taxi origin activity. Infrastructure variables substantially improve model performance for ride-hailing services, with improvements in origin models roughly nine times larger than for motorbike taxis, suggesting that ride-hailing activity is more closely associated with highly electrified, economically intensive urban areas with dense road infrastructure. Our results provide empirical evidence on how formal and informal services jointly shape urban accessibility, offering guidance for inclusive transportation planning and intelligent transportation systems in rapidly growing African cities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Direct purchase subsidies and their impact on electric vehicle adoption in European countries
Authors: Josef Gotvald, Markéta Arltová
Abstract: This study examines the causal effect of direct purchase subsidies on electric vehicle market share in 30 European countries from 2014 to 2024. Employing a quasi-experimental difference-in-differences approach, the research reveals a significant heterogeneity in the effectiveness of these public finance instruments. On a Europe-wide average, subsidies act as a positive stimulus, increasing new registrations by 112.5%, with the impact progressively strengthening over a three-year horizon. Aggregately, this support expands both battery electric vehicle and plug-in hybrid electric vehicle sales. Crucially, distinct regional differences exist. Subsidies exhibit no statistically distinguishable average effect in original member states (EU-15), a pattern consistent with the possibility of lower additionality in more mature markets. Conversely, they serve as a primary driving factor in the new member states (EU-13), triggering an average registration increase of 244.1%. Furthermore, analysis by recipient type shows that subsidies expand total registrations by 235.3% for private and 129.4% for corporate buyers. Specifically, the impact on battery electric vehicles peaks in the second year, reaching a 339.3% increase for private and a 235.8% increase for corporate buyers, while private incentives drive a 250.6% surge in plug-in hybrids by the third year. Sub-analyses based on policy design frameworks reveal that the split into capped and uncapped subsidy regimes yields statistically inconclusive results within regional sub-samples. These findings suggest that future policy designs should consider geographical differentiation and the role of recipient eligibility and price ceilings; however, the evidence on cap-related heterogeneity remains statistically inconclusive within regional sub-samples.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Macroeconomic stability of price level targeting in a model of heterogeneous expectations
Authors: Tomasz Makarewicz
Abstract: This paper studies the efficacy of Price Level Targeting (PLT) under the Heuristic Switching Model (HSM). PLT has been considered as an alternative to the traditional inflation targeting in the aftermath of the 2008 Great Recession. However, this policy was not thoroughly tested in real life, whereas the experimental evidence remains contradictory. This study contributes to the discussion by extending the HSM by Hommes and Lustenhouwer (2019) with the PLT Taylor rule. The properties of the PLT rule under the behavioral expectations are mixed. On the one hand, the fundamental steady state becomes the unique fixed point of the system in this setup. However, the stability of this fixed point is highly sensitive to the calibration of the underlying New Keynesian economy, and the exact specification of the HSM. As a result, policy makers can use this policy only if they understand well the way in which the economic agents form their expectations.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Generalized canonical correlation estimation of the multilevel factor model
Authors: Rui Lin, Yongcheol Shin
Abstract: This paper proposes a Generalized Canonical Correlation (GCC) approach for identification, estimation, and inference in multilevel factor models with a finite number of blocks. GCC extends canonical correlation analysis to a multiblock setting and identifies the global factor space as the intersection of all block-specific factor spaces. Unlike existing pairwise approaches, GCC remains valid when local factors are shared by arbitrary proper subsets of blocks, a setting that can lead to identification failures under pairwise methods. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimated factors and loadings for any finite number of blocks and develop robust covariance estimators for inference. We further propose an eigenvalue-ratio criterion for determining the number of global factors that remains valid in the presence of partially shared local factors. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that GCC outperforms existing methods, particularly when local factors overlap across blocks. An application to house-price dynamics in England and Wales uncovers a hierarchical dependence structure consisting of national, areal, and regional factors.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Oil prices and inequality
Authors: Xiaowen Lei, Julian F. Ludwig, Xiaohan Ma
Abstract: This paper provides a unified framework to understand the effect of oil price changes on the dynamics of consumption, income and wealth inequality. Using data on macroeconomic aggregates, oil prices, and inequality metrics, we first employ a structural vector autoregressive model to show that an increase in oil prices leads to a persistent rise in income and wealth inequality. To understand these dynamics, we then solve an incomplete market model with aggregate oil price shocks, and calibrate the model to the US data. We find that when oil serves as both a consumption good and a production input, positive oil price shocks increase inequality. While the initial rise in inequality is driven by oil-induced stagflation, which forces poorer households to deplete more of their wealth to cover basic consumption, the quicker rebound in interest rates compared to the slower recovery in wages explains why inequality remains persistently elevated.

Title: Bubble detection with application to green bubbles: A noncausal approach
Authors: Francesco Giancaterini, Alain Hecq, Joann Jasiak, Aryan Manafi Neyazi
Abstract: This paper introduces a new approach for bubble detection based on mixed causal and noncausal autoregressive processes and their tail process representation during an explosive episode. Departing from traditional definitions of bubbles as nonstationary and temporarily explosive processes, we adopt a perspective in which prices are assumed to follow a strictly stationary process, with the bubble considered an intrinsic component of its nonlinear dynamics. The proposed approach provides a bubble indicator for detecting bubbles and measuring their duration. We implement our strategy to investigate the phenomenon called the “green bubble” in the field of renewable energy investment.

Title: The collaborative road clearing problem for Post-Disaster emergency response
Authors: Luana Souza Almeida, Alireza Ghasemi, Floris Goerlandt
Abstract: After a disaster, the immediate response operations focus on reducing human suffering by restoring access to essential relief services, while long-term recovery emphasizes infrastructure reconstruction. This study addresses road clearing decisions in the immediate response phase, when restoring critical connectivity is crucial and conventional repair models may be inadequate. Approaches based solely on cost or speed may fail to reconnect the most critical routes for isolated communities. To address this gap, we propose the Collaborative Road Clearing Problem for Post-Disaster Emergency Response, which prioritizes reconnecting affected areas to critical infrastructure such as ports and airports. The model explicitly accounts for collaboration among multiple clearing teams, allowing joint operations on severely obstructed roads. A mixed-integer linear programming formulation and a heuristic are introduced. The numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of collaboration, particularly in large networks and scenarios with long clearance times.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Multi-agent contract design with a budget
Authors: Sumit Goel, Wade Hann-Caruthers
Abstract: We study a multi-agent contract design problem with moral hazard. In our model, each agent exerts costly effort towards an individual task at which it may either succeed or fail, and the principal, who wishes to encourage effort, has an exclusive-use budget that it can use to reward the agents. A motivating application is crowdsourcing for innovation, where a fixed budget is provided to a crowdsourcing platform to use for rewarding participants based on their submissions. Our main contribution is to introduce a novel class of contracts, which we call Luce contracts, and show that there is always a Luce contract that is optimal. A Luce contract assigns weights and a priority order to the agents, and distributes the entire budget among the highest-priority successful agents in proportion to their weights. Furthermore, we characterize effort profiles that can be implemented by Luce contracts and show that Luce contracts offer a way to mitigate the uncertainty in total payments compared to alternative contracts—such as piece-rate or bonus-pool contracts—suggesting their desirability even in environments without budget constraints.

Title: Competing for power in multilateral negotiations under majority and unanimity rules
Authors: Andrzej Baranski, Ernesto Reuben
Abstract: Competition for power is a costly practice present in organizations and groups where collective decisions are made. In a multilateral bargaining experiment, we study how different agreement rules affect competition for power through a contest for the right to propose a distribution of benefits. Although unanimity leads to less wasteful competition investments, it also generates a greater delay in negotiations and a higher likelihood of disagreement. These opposing inefficiencies offset each other across a wide range of bargaining horizons, contest technologies, voting procedures, and subject pools. We find no statistically significant evidence of efficiency dominance by either rule over the parameters studied once competition for power is taken into account. Under equal proposal rights absent a contest, agreements are reached more quickly, demonstrating the causal effect of competition for power on bargaining gridlock and its compounding effect on efficiency losses. In addition, we find that bargaining behavior is conditioned on prior power-seeking efforts: subjects reward higher effort with higher shares, indicating that efforts enter fairness considerations despite their unproductive and competitive nature.

Title: Eliciting moral preferences under image concerns: Theory and experiment
Authors: Roland Bénabou, Armin Falk, Luca Henkel, Jean Tirole
Abstract: We analyze how the impact of image motives on behavior varies with two key features of the choice mechanism: single versus multiple decisions, and certainty versus uncertainty of consequences. Using direct elicitation (DE) versus multiple-price-list (MPL) or equivalently Becker-DeGroot-Marschak (BDM) schemes as exemplars, we develop a game-theoretic model to characterize how image-seeking inflates prosocial giving. The signaling bias (relative to true preferences) is shown to depend on the interaction between elicitation method and visibility level: it is greater under DE for low image concerns, and greater under MPL/BDM for high ones. We experimentally test the model’s predictions and find the predicted crossing effect. Keywords Moral behavior; Social image; Self-image; Preference elicitation; Multiple price list; Experiments

Title: Enhancing the value of residential energy storage using a two-threshold control policy: A household-level analysis
Authors: Na Rea Cho, Youngsoo Kim, Karthik Murali, Mesut Yavuz
Abstract: The intermittent and unpredictable nature of renewable energy sources has spurred growing interest in energy storage. However, effective management of energy storage is far from trivial for residential consumers owing to various compensation and pricing structures, as well as uncertainties in electricity demand and generation. This paper studies the battery control problem for a grid-connected residential prosumer with renewable generation and battery storage under two-tiered time-of-use tariffs with sellback compensation. We find that the structure of the optimal policy critically depends on the price configuration: under high sellback compensation, a policy requiring no calibration is optimal, whereas in the complementary case of reduced sellback compensation, careful household-specific calibration is warranted. We therefore propose an effective battery operating policy utilizing two thresholds — a “purchase-up-to” threshold in the off-peak period and a “sell-down-to” threshold in the peak period — together with an efficient heuristic to calibrate them. Through a case study using real data from 56 households in a U.S. city, we show that this simple and interpretable control policy can significantly increase the value of home energy storage and achieve performance close to that of theoretical battery optimization under certainty, thus highlighting its appeal relative to more complex control approaches in this setting. Our findings provide valuable insights into the effective operation of residential energy storage systems from an individual household's perspective.

Title: When bin packing meets facility location: A case study of unmanned aerial vehicle charging-station location and task assignment for insulator cleaning
Authors: Ling Gai, Meng Li
Abstract: We study a facility-dependent bin-packing problem in which item sizes are not fixed in advance: the capacity consumed by an item is determined by its distance to the facility that serves it. Facility placement, item assignment, and packing decisions are therefore coupled. Three one-dimensional variants are analyzed. For one undetermined facility, we prove strong NP-completeness and show that a median-based FFD algorithm has a tight asymptotic approximation ratio of 2. For two fixed facilities, nearest-facility assignment followed by FFD has an absolute ratio of at least 2 and an asymptotic ratio between 3/2 and 2; a structured stress test attains the 3/2 lower bound. We also develop a pattern-based column-generation formulation that gives LP lower bounds and certifies integer optimality when the restricted integer solution reaches the rounded LP bound. For k undetermined facilities, a one-dimensional k-median dynamic program followed by independent FFD packing uses at most 2OPT+k bins, yielding a 2-asymptotic approximation for fixed k. The model is motivated by UAV cleaning of high-voltage insulators, where a bin is one battery-use period between recharge interruptions and station locations determine flight-time consumption. In the UAV case study, the k-facility algorithm reduces aggregate bin counts by 21.4%–23.9% relative to a reproducible random-placement baseline, and the conclusions remain stable under ±20% perturbations of key operating parameters.

Title: Projection uniqueness in data envelopment analysis with no free disposability
Authors: Yongbin Pan, Haoxiang Liu, Ya Chen, Liang Liang

Title: Risk, time, and diet quality: Evidence from a general population survey
Authors: Antoine Nebout, Noémi Berlin, Emmanuel Kemel, Emmanuel Paroissien
Abstract: This paper explores the relationships between overall diet quality and attitudes toward risk and time using a general population survey. We combine a food frequency questionnaire and a choice-based preference module to elicit individual risk and time preferences. The online questionnaire was administered to a socioeconomic panel representative of the French population. We show that risk and time preferences are associated with individual heterogeneity in key aspects of diet quality, a result that holds across a wide range of robustness checks. Using a hierarchical Bayes framework, we jointly estimate individual risk aversion and impatience parameters and show that associations hold for both model-free and structural estimates of risk and time preferences. We further show that these associations account for a substantial share of the heterogeneity in dietary outcomes beyond sociodemographic controls. Risk and time preferences contribute to both the income–diet-quality and education–diet-quality gradients, but in opposite directions, resulting in a limited net contribution to explaining socioeconomic inequalities in diet quality.

Title: Circular procurement as a multi-phase innovation process: managing paradoxical tensions through sequenced coping strategies
Authors: Francesco Cafforio, Roberta Cappiello, Giovanni Francesco Massari, Ilaria Giannoccaro
Affiliations: Department of Mechanics, Mathematics and Management (DMMM)

Title: Machine learning-based performance prediction in quantum queueing: comparative evaluation of tree and neural models for fidelity, heat and latency
Authors: N. Micheal Mathavavisakan, M. Lakshmi, Shey-Huei Sheu
Abstract: Abstrct In this paper, we address the critical challenge of performance evaluation in complex quantum queueing systems, where traditional analytical methods are often mathematically intractable and direct simulation is computationally prohibitive. Initially, we formulate a comprehensive quantum queueing model incorporating entropy-dependent service degradation, thermodynamic feedback and multi-mode server dynamics and derive the steady-state probability equations using the supplementary variable technique. Subsequently, we propose a novel data-driven methodology that leverages Machine Learning (ML) techniques to provide fast and accurate predictions of key quantum-specific performance metrics. To achieve this, a comprehensive dataset is generated through offline simulations guided by a Deep Q-Network (DQN) policy, capturing the system dynamics under an optimized control strategy. Further, several ML models, including Decision Trees, Random Forests, Gradient Boosting and Artificial Neural Networks, are trained and comparatively evaluated to predict important performance measures such as average queue length, fidelity of quantum states and heat generation rate from the system parameters. Moreover, the proposed framework demonstrates outstanding predictive performance, with all models achieving exceptionally high accuracy and $$R^2$$ R 2 values consistently exceeding 0.9995 across all target metrics. The predictive capability of the models is further validated through scatter plots comparing predicted and actual values, dependency plots illustrating the relationships between performance metrics and key input parameters (e.g., arrival rates and service rates) and detailed analyses of prediction errors. Finally, this work bridges the gap between quantum queueing theory and data-driven performance evaluation by integrating rigorous stochastic modeling with modern ML techniques, thereby providing an efficient, scalable and practical framework for the analysis, prediction and optimization of quantum technologies while explicitly accounting for quantum-specific constraints and thermodynamic costs. Graphical Abstract

Title: System reliability evaluation of a labor-intensive flow shop network considering learning effect and human error rate
Authors: Yi-Kuei Lin, Ding-Hsiang Huang, Yu-Hsuan Chang, Louis Cheng-Lu Yeng
Abstract: Abstract Labor-intensive flow shops are common in many manufacturing systems. In these environments, the efficiency of human workers can vary due to factors such as fatigue, injury, or psychological state, leading to multistate production capacities. Furthermore, the repetitive nature of tasks in a flow shop induces a learning effect, where workers' efficiency improves with experience, reducing the processing time per unit. In this paper, we model such a system as a multistate labor-intensive flow shop network (MLFSN) and use system reliability as the primary performance metric. System reliability is defined as the probability of meeting a specified demand within a given time constraint. The proposed approach first establishes a probability distribution for processing times and then dynamically transforms it into a capacity distribution using a learning curve model that accounts for the number of repetitions. The model is further extended to incorporate the Human Error Rate (HER), which also decreases as a function of the learning effect. Considering HER necessitates producing additional units to meet demand, which in turn impacts system reliability. The proposed algorithm reevaluates system reliability by integrating both the learning effect and HER, providing managers in the MLFSNs with a more accurate and realistic tool for decision-making and production planning.

Title: Parameterized Local Search for Max c-Cut
Authors: Jaroslav Garvardt, Niels Grüttemeier, Christian Komusiewicz, Nils Morawietz
Abstract: Abstract In the NP-hard Max c -Cut problem, one is given an undirected edge-weighted graph G and aims to color the vertices of G with c colors such that the total weight of edges with distinctly colored endpoints is maximal. The case with $$c=2$$ c = 2 is the famous Max Cut problem. To deal with the NP-hardness of this problem, we study parameterized local search algorithms. More precisely, we study LS Max c -Cut where we are also given a vertex coloring and an integer k and the task is to find a better coloring that changes the color of at most k vertices, if such a coloring exists; otherwise, the given coloring is k -optimal. We show that, for all $$c\ge 2$$ c ≥ 2 , LS Max c -Cut presumably cannot be solved in $$f(k)\cdot n^{\mathcal {O}(1)}$$ f ( k ) · n O ( 1 ) time even on bipartite graphs. We then present an algorithm for LS Max c -Cut with running time $$\mathcal {O}((3e\Delta )^k\cdot c\cdot k^3\cdot \Delta \cdot n)$$ O ( ( 3 e Δ ) k · c · k 3 · Δ · n ) , where $$\Delta $$ Δ is the maximum degree of the input graph. Finally, we evaluate the practical performance of this algorithm in a hill-climbing approach as a post-processing for a state-of-the-art heuristic for Max c -Cut . We show that using parameterized local search, the results of this state-of-the-art heuristic can be further improved on a set of standard benchmark instances.

Title: Bayesian School Choice: Welfare Comparison of Immediate Acceptance and Deferred Acceptance Mechanisms
Authors: Ethem Akyol, Isa E. Hafalir, Antonio Miralles
Affiliations: Department of Economics, TOBB University of Economics and Technology, Ankara 06560, Turkey; Business School, University of Technology Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales 2007, Australia; Department of Economics, The University of Messina, Messina ME 98122, Italy
Abstract: We compare the welfare implications of two widely used school choice mechanisms, Deferred Acceptance (DA) and Immediate Acceptance (IA), under incomplete information. Our baseline model features two schools and three students, where each student’s valuations are drawn from a joint distribution, schools have no priorities, and ties are broken by a single lottery. We show that, except in the extreme cases of perfectly correlated or uncorrelated preferences, neither mechanism generally interim dominates the other in any nonextreme case. This result reveals the fragility of existing findings in the literature that establish the interim welfare superiority of IA. This non-dominance result extends to more general environments, including markets with an arbitrary number of students and schools, and large markets with a continuum of students. Moreover, we construct environments arbitrarily close to those previously studied in the literature in which DA does interim dominate IA. Finally, we characterize necessary conditions for interim dominance and explain why such relationships rarely arise. History: This paper has been accepted for the Mathematics of Operations Research Special Issue on Market Design. Funding: No funding was received for this research.

Title: Infrequent Resolving Algorithm for Online Linear Programming
Authors: Guokai Li, Zizhuo Wang, Jingwei Zhang
Affiliations: Desautels Faculty of Management, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec H3A 1G5, Canada; School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong - Shenzhen, Shenzhen, Guangdong 518172, People’s Republic of China
Abstract: Online linear programming (OLP) has gained significant attention from both researchers and practitioners because of its extensive applications such as online auctions, network revenue management, order fulfillment, and advertising. Existing OLP algorithms fall into two categories: LP-based algorithms and LP-free algorithms. The former typically guarantees better performance but requires solving a large number of LPs, which could be computationally expensive. In contrast, LP-free algorithms only require first-order computations but induce a worse performance. In this work, we bridge the gap between these two extremes by proposing a well-performing algorithm that solves LPs at a few selected time points and conducts first-order computations at other time points. Specifically, for the case where the inputs are drawn from an unknown finite-support distribution, the proposed algorithm achieves a constant regret (even for the hard “degenerate” case) while solving LPs only [Formula: see text] times over the time horizon T. Moreover, when we are allowed to solve LPs only M times, we design the corresponding schedule such that the proposed algorithm can guarantee a nearly [Formula: see text] regret. Our work highlights the value of resolving both at the beginning and the end of the selling horizon, and provides a novel framework to prove the performance guarantee of the proposed policy under different infrequent resolving schedules. Numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithms. Funding: G. Zhang is partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72394361] and the Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Mathematical Foundations for Artificial Intelligence [Grant 2023B1212010001]. Title: All Finite Lattices Are Stable Matching Lattices
Authors: Christopher En, Yuri Faenza
Affiliations: IEOR, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027
Abstract: We show that all finite lattices, including nondistributive lattices, arise as stable matching lattices when all agents have path-independent choice functions. This result answers an open question of Blair. In the process, we introduce new tools to reason on general lattices for optimization purposes: the partial representation of a lattice, which partially extends Birkhoff’s representation theorem to nondistributive lattices; the distributive closure of a lattice, which gives such a partial representation; and join constraints, which can be added to the distributive closure to obtain a representation for the original lattice. Then, we use these techniques to show that the minimum cost stable matching problem under the same standard assumptions on choice functions is NP-hard, by establishing a connection with antimatroid theory. Funding: This work was supported by the Division of Computing and Communication Foundations, NSF [Grant 2046146]; by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research [Grant FA9550-23-1-0697]; and by a Cheung-Kong Innovation Doctoral Fellowship.

Title: Navigating uncertainty: Supply chain risk exposure and corporate investment efficiency
Authors: Shiqiang Chen, Hua Xiao, Yun Liu, Xiaomeng Li
Abstract: Supply chain risk not only disrupts operations but can also distort firms’ investment decisions, affecting long-term value creation. Using natural language processing on quarterly earnings call transcripts, we construct firm-level measures of supply chain risk exposure and examine its effect on investment efficiency. We find that higher supply chain risk primarily induces underinvestment, rather than overinvestment.
