Affiliations: Naveen Jindal School of Management University of Texas at Dallas Richardson Texas USA; Durham University Business School Durham University Durham UK; School of Economics and Management University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Beijing China
Abstract: ABSTRACT We consider a joint production and delivery problem in multi‐factory multi‐DC (distribution center) multiproduct systems with limited production and delivery capacities over a finite horizon. The objective is to minimize the system's expected total cost. Since the structure of the optimal policy is hard to find, we propose a Lagrangian relaxation heuristic to solve the problem. The proposed heuristic is based on solving a Lagrangian relaxation of the original problem. Although the Lagrangian relaxation problem remains challenging due to the joint production and delivery decisions, we identify a zero‐inventory policy that enables further decomposition into independent single‐product, single‐DC subproblems, each of which can be solved independently. We evaluate the heuristic's performance by deriving a theoretical upper bound on its expected loss. In numerical experiments, we compare the Lagrangian relaxation heuristic with a benchmark myopic heuristic. The results consistently show that the Lagrangian relaxation heuristic achieves a significantly smaller expected relative loss and exhibits greater stability than the myopic heuristic.

Title: Improving Affordability and Accessibility for Socially‐Beneficial Services via Government Incentives
Authors: Xiaoyan Zhao, Venus Lo, Stephen Shum
Affiliations: Department of Decision Analytics and Operations City University of Hong Kong Hong Kong SAR People's Republic of China
Abstract: ABSTRACT Many socially‐beneficial services, like dental care, suffer from a dual challenge: Low affordability for citizens and long waiting times due to insufficient provider capacity. We model a government's problem of designing subsidy policies to address this issue. We analyze three financial interventions: Consumer vouchers, which are on the citizen side; and two provider‐side subsidies aimed at increasing capacity: Fee‐for‐service subsidies and downtime rebates. Using a continuous‐time Markov chain model, we capture the dynamic interactions between citizens and the service provider in response to these policies. Our findings yield several structural insights into subsidy design. We prove that subsidizing idle service capacity (a form of risk mitigation) always outperforms fee‐for‐service subsidies (a form of reward enhancement) in terms of cost‐effectiveness. However, the choice between citizen‐side and provider‐side policies depends critically on the primary system bottleneck. To further improve the government's cost efficiency, we propose a mixed‐subsidy policy. Although optimizing this policy is intractable, we develop an algorithm to find near‐optimal solutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that a mixed policy combining consumer vouchers with idle‐time rebates can offer substantial cost savings compared to the best single‐subsidy approach, highlighting the potential efficiency gains of a more integrated subsidy structure.

Title: Information Design for Early‐Stage Dose‐Finding Trials
Authors: Amin Khademi, Ningyuan Chen
Affiliations: Department of Industrial Engineering Clemson University Clemson South Carolina USA; Rotman School of Management University of Toronto Toronto Canada
Abstract: ABSTRACT To enhance enrollment rates in early‐stage dose‐finding clinical trials, we propose an information design approach, where the clinical investigator (CI) commits to an information releasing mechanism (IRM) based on the treatment's uncertain efficacy and toxicity to encourage patients to participate in the trial. The optimal IRM has a threshold structure, involving completely revealing/pooling the state (utility) when the realization is in the respective region. We analyze the comparative statics under the optimal IRM. Because general IRMs may be difficult to implement in practice, motivated by response‐adaptive clinical trials where information from past patients will help drive decisions for future patients, we consider a practical IRM, where the CI decides on the number of patients to recruit, whose efficacy/toxicity outcomes will be used as information for future patients. For example, the proposed IRM may be the number of patients in the first batch in dose‐escalation methods in Phase I, the expansion cohort at the end of Phase I, or the number of patients assigned to the maximum tolerated dose in Phase II. We show that this practical IRM can achieve at most 50% of the value of the optimal abstract IRM. Since patients' risk attitude toward toxicity may be private, we study the impact of belief about it on the optimal IRM and show that the structure of the optimal IRM can be in sharp contrast with that in the public information setting, depending on the distribution of risk attitude toward toxicity. To better understand the impact of the association between efficacy and toxicity on the optimal IRM, we study a bivariate Bernoulli model and show that the optimal IRM has a threshold structure, and the region in which it is a randomized recommendation, when the treatment is ineffective and toxic, shrinks when the association becomes larger.

Title: Integrated Production and Delivery Scheduling With Multi‐Machine Open Shop Processing and Capacitated Vehicle Batch Deliveries
Authors: Jianming Dong, Weitian Tong, Yao Xu
Affiliations: School of Management and E‐Business, Contemporary Business and Trade Research Center Zhejiang Gongshang University Hangzhou Zhejiang China; Department of Computer Science Georgia Southern University Statesboro GA USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT We consider an integrated production and delivery scheduling (IPDS) problem where each job must be processed on multiple machines in an open shop environment and then delivered in batches to a single customer using a capacitated vehicle. The objective is to minimize the makespan, which captures both production and delivery stages. This model arises in several practical settings, including additive manufacturing and diagnostic laboratories, where tight coordination between production and outbound logistics is critical. Although IPDS has been extensively studied under single‐machine, parallel‐machine, and flow shop models, the open shop variant has received limited theoretical attention. This paper presents the first constant‐factor approximation algorithms with provable worst‐case guarantees for the multi‐machine open shop IPDS problem. We first introduce a simple two‐phase algorithm that achieves a approximation ratio for any fixed number of machines. We then develop a refined approximation algorithm based on a novel framework that combines instance scaling, schedule discretization, configuration enumeration, and LP‐based assignment. In the special case of two open shop machines, our result significantly improves upon the best known 2‐approximation by tightening the bound to . Importantly, we observe that no algorithm can achieve an approximation ratio below unless , establishing that our algorithm is nearly optimal.

Title: Dynamic Lot Sizing With Multiple Age‐Differentiated Demands of a Perishable Product
Authors: Jie Fan, Jinwen Ou, Vernon N. Hsu
Affiliations: School of Management Guangdong University of Technology Guangzhou People's Republic of China; Department of Business Administration, School of Management Jinan University Guangzhou People's Republic of China; CUHK Business School The Chinese University of Hong Kong Hong Kong People's Republic of China
Abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, we study a dynamic lot sizing problem in which a manufacturer produces a perishable product and supplies it to several customers, each having a different requirement on the product freshness and only accepting inventory stock whose age is not older than a customer‐dependent threshold. Both production and inventory holding cost functions are assumed to be concave. The manufacturer makes joint production and inventory allocation decisions to minimize the total cost. We explore structural properties and develop an optimal algorithm for solving the problem in polynomial time. More efficient optimal algorithms are also developed for two important special cases. We conduct computational experiments to demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms the commercial solver CPLEX. Through computational experiments, we also obtain managerial insights into the bottleneck customer, who has the highest freshness requirement.

Title: Issue Information
Optimal emission reduction strategy for carbon neutral target: cap-and-trade policy and supply chain contracts with uncertain demand under SDG 13-climate action
Authors: Jing Li, Ling Liang, Jiaping Xie, Guangsi Zhang
Abstract: Motivating manufacturers to reduce carbon emissions is an effective way to achieve sustainable development goals (SDGs). However, the carbon-constrained manufacturers are under pressure to consider market uncertainty, consumer’s green behavior, and supply chain cooperation when optimizing strategies under government regulations. Therefore, we deserve a detailed theoretical examination of cap-and-trade policy with supply chain cooperative contracts, depict uncertain demand by the newsvendor model, and optimize the emission reduction, order quantity, and pricing strategies in three cooperative cases: wholesale price, cost-sharing, and collaborative contract. Moreover, we analyze the effects of carbon regulations on the optimal decisions and profits, then conduct a comparative study on these results under three cooperative contracts. Our findings show that the manufacturer will purchase more emission rights rather than invest in reduction when the government-given carbon quotas decrease. Besides, the cost-sharing contract promotes greener production and higher reduction level compared to the wholesale price contract, but damages the manufacturer’s profit as the cost-sharing ratio and green preference rise. In this case, the government should increase the emission quotas and meanwhile enhance consumer’s green awareness based on a substantial growth of potential market. Furthermore, to improve the positive effect of cost-sharing contract on emission reduction levels, the government should increase carbon quotas when the carbon trading price fluctuates in a relatively higher range.

Title: Mastering supply chain’s decision-making establishing SDG’s goal: a social media analytics study of the electronic devices in developing and developed countries
Authors: Sajjad Shokouhyar, Mohammad Hossein Shahidzadeh
Abstract: This research proposed a multi-industry framework that aims to clarify reverse logistics decision-making through a social media analytics approach analyzing the electronics industry in developing compared to developed countries in separated case studies. By leveraging deep learning on social media data, this study intends to elucidate ideal product return policies and strategies aligned with sustainability, circular economic principles, and sustainable development goals. Furthermore, this work outlines the potential of social media analytics to align consumer expectations with supply chain decisions across geographic contexts and identify the missing potential stream of material in supply chains. Overall, this study utilizes social media data mining and sentiment analysis to shed light on optimal reverse logistics decision-making for electronics firms in diverse national settings pertinent to circular economy ideals. The juxtaposition of developing and developed nations provides an enhanced understanding of how optimal return policies may differ given geographic and economic contexts. In summary, this research elucidates data-driven reverse logistics insights via social media analytics to inform electronics sector circular economy strategies tailored to national development levels.

Title: Achieving sustainable development of green tourism supply chain: the trade-off between environmental and economic performances
Authors: Shigui Ma, Yong He, Ran Gu
Abstract: The sustainable consumption and production of tourism products are the foundation for the sustainable development of the tourism industry. How to reduce the consumption of tourism resources and avoid the destruction of the tourism environment while improving the consumer experience of tourists and enhancing corporate profits is an urgent problem to be solved in the tourism industry. However, tourism enterprises frequently face the trade-off between green performance and economic performance, that is, tourism enterprises improve their green performance through green technology investment, and the green performance positively stimulates the tourist demand, resulting in the increase of tourist numbers in the tourism environment, which not only improves the economic performance, but also worsens the green performance. Based on the above trade-off and considering a green tourism supply chain (GTSC) composed of one green scenic spot and one travel agency, we model and derive the optimal green technology investment, pricing, advertising, and subsidy decisions of the green scenic spot and travel agency in the decentralized, centralized and bilateral cost sharing scenarios. Meanwhile, we explore the impacts of green preference, brand awareness, and tourism environment carrying capacity on the optimal decision makings and performances of the GTSC. Results show that although higher brand awareness can bring higher economic performances to enterprises, it seriously hurts the green performance of the tourism environment; Lower tourism environmental carrying capacity is not conducive to improving the green performance of the tourism environment, and can not create a higher economic performance for tourism enterprises. There is a relative unity between the economic and green performances of tourism enterprises when tourists’ preference for green tourism is high.

Title: Understanding throughput degradation in automated material handling system-integrated flexible manufacturing systems: structural drivers and operational implications
Authors: Minsoo Kim, Young Jae Jang, Shin Woong Sung
Affiliations: Samsung Electronics; Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST); Tech University of Korea (TU Korea)

Title: A Beta-Bernoulli composite index
Authors: Mariateresa Ciommi, Paolo Giudici, Francesca Mariani, Gloria Polinesi, Maria Cristina Recchioni
Affiliations: Marche Polytechnic University; University of Pavia; University of Macerata
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: War of attrition and random walks
Authors: Vladimir Mazalov, Anna Ivashko
Abstract: The article presents a game-theoretic model of a multistage game with imperfect information War of Attrition , first investigated by John Maynard Smith, 1974. In this model, players (animals) fight for a resource (territory, sphere of influence, etc.), but are not aware of the adversary’s real capacity and can evaluate it after each stage of the fight. The fight consists of repeated iterations of one type of interaction. We suggest a model of the adaptive behavior of players based on dynamic programming and an evaluation method based on Bayesian updating. Thereby, we study the properties of non-homogeneous random walks in the space of parameters that represent the current number of the player’s wins and losses. The optimal rule for stopping the fight is determined for each player. The results of numerical experiments are reported.

Title: Wage Theft, Market Power, and Outsourcing: The Case of H‐1B Workers
Authors: Jed DeVaro, Peter Norlander
Affiliations: Department of Economics and Department of Management, College of Business and Economics California State University Hayward California USA; Department of Economics University of California Merced California USA; Department of Management, Quinlan School of Business Loyola University Chicago Chicago Illinois USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Wage violations against H‐1B visa holders (i.e., cutting their wages below a legally required prevailing wage) are analysed using detailed firm‐level data. The incidence of violations is 25%–35% lower in a monopsony versus a competitive labour market, and 60% of firms with at least one violation are subcontractors. A new theoretical model provides an interpretation for these findings, predicting that violations are more likely when firms have less labour market power and generally wherever firm profit margins are more vulnerable to a negative shock (e.g., in subcontractors that have been outsourced work and firms seeking to hire lower‐skilled workers).
Journal: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

Title: Spatiotemporal collision risk mapping for port traffic management
Authors: Dong Yang, Kaisen Yang, Yuxu Lu, Zhaoya Gong
Abstract: Vessel collision risk analysis is built on the foresight of maritime traffic. In complex port encounters, current indicator-based risk analyses provide limited support for global navigation guidance because they report isolated vessel-pair risks without describing their correlations. Surface risk mapping methods have therefore been introduced to represent these correlations on the water surface and provide a more human-intuitive geospatial visualisation for navigation guidance. However, the “risk-first, aggregate-second” framework in existing surface risk mapping diffuses risk over broad areas, increasing false-alarm frequency in high-traffic waters. To reduce false alarms, this paper proposes a more refined surface risk mapping method. The proposed method adopts an “aggregate-first, risk-second” analysis framework, dispersing predicted vessel positions into a probability distribution over the surface. Collision risk is considered the probability of surface units being co-occupied. It thereby reduces redundant risk diffusion and provides a more precise description of future spatiotemporal risk to support global navigation decision-making. In the experiments, we trained prediction models and used them to iteratively predict along the resampled 21,612 real trajectories. Based on the trajectory collection, we simulated 9600 collision and near-miss scenarios to observe the responses across different risk analysis methods. The results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively reduces false alarms while generating precise spatiotemporal risk characterization, which contributes to joint navigation guidance for port traffic management. The implementation code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Risk_Mapping-F8D0 .
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Joint optimization of pricing and routing for flexible bus services under stochastic demand
Authors: Yuhang Guo, David Z․ W․ Wang, Kun An, Wanjing Ma
Abstract: Flexible Bus (FB) systems have emerged as a promising solution for connecting transport hubs with urban areas. However, existing studies often decouple tactical pricing from operational routing decisions, which can lead to suboptimal system performance. To address this issue, we propose an integrated optimization framework that jointly optimizes pricing, maximum detour limits, and vehicle routing to maximize platform profit under demand uncertainty. At the tactical level, we design a detour-based pricing rule in which the fare is dynamically adjusted based on the realized detour. Consequently, we utilize a logit framework to capture the passenger service choice behavior based on both monetary incentives and detour-based service guarantees. At the operational level, routing decisions are formulated over a hyper-dimensional space–time–state network, and interact with the pricing mechanism to maximize profit. To solve this model, we propose the Iterative Pricing-Routing Algorithm (IPRA), which integrates three main components: (i) grid search for tactical parameters, (ii) Sample Average Approximation (SAA) for stochastic demand, and (iii) an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM)-based algorithm to optimize routing. Numerical studies on the Solomon dataset demonstrate that the detour-based pricing approach increases average platform profit by 45% compared to uniform pricing. Moreover, the results confirm that the algorithm can achieve near-optimal solutions within a reasonable timeframe. Finally, a large-scale case study using Shanghai Hongqiao hub data is conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed solution algorithm in practical applications.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Where machines improve: Automation direction, task boundaries, and the skill premium
Authors: Wei Xiong
Abstract: Automation technologies can affect wage inequality differently even when they automate the same measure of tasks. This paper studies a task-assignment model in which capital performs an endogenous interior interval of tasks. A uniform rise in machine productivity expands that interval from both sides. A rightward shift in the location of peak machine productivity moves both boundaries to the right and lowers the skill premium, while automated width may expand, contract, or remain locally unchanged. A closed-form boundary formula explains why the location of machine improvements matters separately from automated extent.

Title: A partitioning-based heuristic for large-scale fleet assignment problems
Authors: Reinout Annaert, Pieter Smet, Greet Vanden Berghe
Abstract: The fleet assignment problem concerns assigning rental jobs to a jointly managed fleet of heterogeneous resources. Each job is characterized by a rental period, pickup and drop-off locations and resource requirements. It further involves decisions on whether it is worthwhile to offer resource substitutions when resources with the requested properties are unavailable. It also involves decisions on whether it is worthwhile to transfer resources between depots, which represent the locations where resources are based when not assigned to rentals, given the resulting transfer costs and the temporary unavailability of resources. The objective is to maximize total profit arising from assignments, minus transfer costs and substitution costs. In practice, fleet assignment requires acceptable solutions within short computation times for daily operations, as well as high-quality solutions for longer overnight algorithm runs. This paper investigates how such computational requirements can be met for large-scale fleet assignment problems. We propose a flow-based mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulation. To reduce the number of variables and constraints, we aggregate resources into resource groups. In addition, this paper proposes a partitioning-based guided ruin and recreate approach for solving large-scale fleet assignment problems. Experiments conducted on real-world data from three vehicle and equipment rental companies demonstrate the approach’s general applicability across different problem scales, fleet compositions, transfer policies and decision horizons. Both the MIP formulation and the heuristic improve all best-known solutions for a publicly available benchmark instance set. To stimulate further research on fleet assignment, the datasets used and solutions generated are made publicly available.

Title: How do monetary incentives affect the measurement of social preferences?
Authors: Ernst Fehr, Julien Senn, Thomas Epper, Aljosha Henkel
Affiliations: University of Zurich; University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne; CNRS, IESEG School of Management; KOF Swiss Economic Institute
Abstract: Abstract In this registered report, we investigate (i) whether incentives affect subjects’ willingness to pay to increase and to decrease the payoff of others, (ii) whether they affect the distribution of social preference types, and (iii) whether they affect the strength and the precision of individuals’ structurally estimated social preference parameters. Using an online experiment with a general population sample, we show that the use of monetary incentives, as well as the size of the stakes, have little impact on subjects’ modal choices (descriptive analysis), as well as for the distribution of qualitatively distinct preference types in the population (clustering analysis). However, monetary incentives affect quantitative measures of the strength and the precision of social preferences. Indeed, a structural analysis reveals that the preference elicitation with merely hypothetical stakes leads to an overestimation and a less precise measurement of social preferences. Together, these results highlight that incentivizing the elicitation of social preferences is most useful when interested in quantitative estimates. For researchers interested in identifying merely qualitative preference types, however, hypothetical stakes might suffice.

Title: History-dependent monetary policy: a lab experiment and a HENK model
Authors: Jasmina Arifovic, Isabelle Salle, Hung Truong
Affiliations: Simon Fraser University; University of Amsterdam and Tinbergen Institute; University of Ottawa; VNU University of Economics and Business, Vietnam National University
Abstract: Abstract Price-level targeting (PLT) is theoretically optimal under the full information rational expectations (FIRE) benchmark but has not been implemented in practice. We use a laboratory experiment to collect data on expectations, inflation and output dynamics under a traditional inflation targeting (IT) framework and a PLT regime with both deflationary and cost-push shocks. A heterogeneous expectation New Keynesian (HENK) model with forward-looking communication can replicate the dynamics observed in the lab. We do not observe the benefits of PLT over IT because both human subjects and HENK agents are unable to learn the history-dependent inflation path, which results in excess macroeconomic volatility. However, once augmented with an inflation guidance consistent with closing the price gap, the advantage of PLT materializes, both in the lab and in the model, and the inflation gap is minimized no matter the type of shocks. The model offers a behavioral narrative for the cross-regime differences observed in the experiment. Combining laboratory data with the HENK framework is a promising addition to the central banks’ toolkit since it offers a first test of their policies.

Title: A matheuristic approach to multi-objective batch scheduling of parallel diffusion furnaces with slot-eligibility and non-product wafers
Authors: Ahyoung Kim, Min-Geol Kim, Hyunjoon Kim
Affiliations: Hanyang University; Hanyang University ERICA
Abstract: Diffusion processes in semiconductor manufacturing are frequently identified as primary bottlenecks due to their extensive processing times and complex batching requirements. This study investigates a multi-objective batch scheduling problem for identical parallel diffusion furnaces, explicitly incorporating two practically important constraints: slot-eligibility and the strategic usage of non-product wafer (NPW) lots. Slot-eligibility constraints are imposed to ensure thermal uniformity and process stability within the furnace, while NPW lots are employed to satisfy minimum loading requirements, resulting in capacity loss. We formulate a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model to minimise a weighted sum of the makespan, the number of tardy lots, and NPW usage. To address large-scale industrial instances that are computationally intractable for exact methods, we propose Product-based Reconstruction and Iterative Sequencing Matheuristic (PRISM), which integrates product-based decomposition, MILP-based batch reconstruction, and iterative sequencing refinement to navigate the complex solution space efficiently. Numerical experiments on benchmark instances generated to reflect practical fab operating characteristics demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the direct solution of the MILP formulation and conventional metaheuristics, providing high-quality schedules within practical computational time limits.

Title: Digital platform selection and decision optimization for service-oriented manufacturing
Authors: Na He, Zhong-Zhong Jiang, Yilong Liang, Xinying Yang
Abstract: Digital platforms present great opportunities for companies to transform their operations. However, platform selection is both critical and complex, especially in service-oriented manufacturing (SOM), where after-sales service is as important as production. In practice, manufacturers often face resource constraints that prevent them from adopting multiple digital platforms simultaneously, making it important to determine which type of platform should be prioritized. This study develops an analytical framework of an SOM supply chain with one manufacturer and multiple heterogeneous operators, and compares three platform-adoption scenarios: no digitalization platform (NDP), a production digitalization platform (PDP), and a service digitalization platform (SDP). The results provide clear guidance for manufacturers: platform choice depends on the relative benefit–cost ratio of PDP versus SDP and the equipment's per-use price, and it shapes key decisions by both manufacturers and operators. Manufacturer and operator preferences may diverge in certain cases, underscoring the need for coordination within the supply chain. As an extension, we further examine a full-process digitalization platform (FDP), in which the manufacturer adopts both PDP and SDP, and show how full-process digitalization changes the benchmark comparison. This study contributes an integrated framework for analyzing digitalization platform selection in SOM supply chains and offers actionable insights for manufacturers considering digital platform adoption.

Title: Effects of out-migration on local deforestation: Evidence from rural Myanmar
Authors: Wentian Jiang, Mateusz Filipski, Susana Ferreira
Abstract: This study examines the relationship between rural out-migration and local deforestation in Mon State, Myanmar, using a novel panel dataset that combines household-level migration surveys with high-resolution remote sensing observations from 2000 to 2015. Employing dynamic panel estimation methods with a 1000-meter buffer to capture local forest changes, we find robust evidence that out-migration significantly mitigates deforestation at this hyper-local scale, with each additional migrant associated with more than 5 square meters of forest loss reduction per year. Extensive robustness checks, including falsification tests and reverse causality assessments, further reinforce the credibility of our findings. Exploring potential mechanisms, we provide suggestive evidence that remittance income facilitates household energy transitions away from biomass fuels toward electricity, thereby potentially reducing reliance on firewood and charcoal and alleviating local deforestation pressures. By identifying a novel energy-transition channel through which migration may promote environmental sustainability, this study contributes new empirical evidence to the migration–environment literature and shows that out-migration’s environmental effects extend beyond household-size changes to reshape household energy use and land-sustainability pathways in rural frontier regions.

Title: Barriers and innovation pathways for Europe's circular bioeconomy: grassroots stakeholder insights from 43 multi-actor workshops
Authors: Bas Paris, Athanasios T. Balafoutis, Clio Christopoulou, João Santos, Natasha Ristovska, Luka Juvančič, Maja Berden Zrimec, Boglárka Vajda, Dimitris Michas, George Papadakis
Abstract: The bioeconomy is a key pillar of the European Green Deal, yet its implementation remains constrained by entrenched linear value chains, fragmented logistics systems, and regulatory uncertainty. This paper examines how practitioners across Europe envision circular bioeconomy transitions, drawing on 43 harmonised multi-actor workshops conducted in 14 countries with 1078 participants from primary production, processing industries, technology provision, public authorities, and civil society. Using a structured participatory canvas and comparative thematic analysis, we analyse how stakeholders redesign existing value chains, which innovation pathways they prioritise, and which barriers they encounter in practice. Across agriculture, forestry, aquatic systems and bio-based industries, stakeholders consistently shift the focus from expanding biomass production toward better use of residues and side-streams. Dominant innovation pathways include residue valorisation, nutrient and water recycling, integrated bioenergy systems, and emerging biomaterials. Four interlinked barrier domains recur across countries and sectors: economic barriers, technological limitations, feedstock logistics and infrastructure constraints, and policy and regulatory challenges. The findings suggest that circular bioeconomy transitions are constrained less by a lack of innovation opportunities than by recurring economic, technological, infrastructural, regulatory, and knowledge-related barriers across countries and sectors. Providing one of the most extensive cross-country, practitioner-led analyses of circular bioeconomy transitions to date, the study offers insight into the conditions shaping circular bioeconomy development across Europe. The findings point to a policy agenda focused on regulatory clarification, coordinated investment in residue aggregation and pre-treatment infrastructure, while highlighting the need for complementary sustainability assessments to evaluate ecological effectiveness and broader socio-ecological implications.

Title: Healthy food transitions: Product-line design under consumer self-control heterogeneity
Authors: Yanping Liu, Xiaoxiao Liang, Lingxiao Wu, Haifang Yang, Thuy-Tien Nguyen, Na Luo
Abstract: This study investigates a food manufacturer’s optimal product-line design in a health-oriented supply chain characterized by consumer self-control heterogeneity and stochastic demand. Utilizing a newsvendor analytical framework, we examine the manufacturer’s choice among Pure-Healthy, Pure-Unhealthy, and Dual-Product strategies, where low self-control consumers prioritize hedonic attributes and high self-control consumers balance health and indulgence. Our results characterize the optimal product-line strategy regions and identify the Dual-Product strategy as a critical mechanism for retaining demand that internalizes heterogeneous consumer switching behavior. We further analyze demand shaping forces such as firm-led marketing and government interventions including sugar taxes and subsidies, finding that while marketing lowers the threshold for adopting healthy products, its profitability is contingent on consumer composition and reputation effects. We demonstrate that policy instruments exert asymmetric operational pressures, with sugar taxes compressing margins and subsidies expanding market reach; however, excessive subsidies may diminish social welfare if fiscal costs exceed demand expansion benefits. Ultimately, this research highlights that fostering a healthier food supply chain requires the coordinated management of consumer behavior and demand, production decisions, product line interactions, and policy intensity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Interaction-enhanced lane-change early warning in congested traffic: a spatial risk propagation-aware approach
Authors: Yue Zhang, Xinzhi Zhong, Soyoung Ahn, Zhengbing He, Yajie Zou
Abstract: This paper presents an interaction-enhanced Lane-Changing Early Warning (LCEW) system designed to issue reliable early warning signals through a spatial risk-propagation-aware approach. The system is built upon interpretable multi-vehicle trajectory predictions and collision risk identification within an extended LC zone, including multiple downstream and upstream vehicles. We first investigate the stochasticity and hazardousness of LCs, characterized by (i) variable-size multi-vehicle interactions within the LC zone and (ii) the resulting risk propagation from downstream to upstream traffic. To model these stochastic interactions, a Social Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Neural Network framework informed by mutual information (social STGCNN-MI) is introduced to predict multi-vehicle trajectories. By leveraging a mutual information-based kernel function, the framework enhances trajectory prediction accuracy while providing interpretable representations of vehicle interactions. Then, oriented bounding box detection is employed on the predicted trajectories to identify direct collision risks between the LC vehicle and adjacent vehicles and indirect risks among non-adjacent vehicles. These components jointly quantify and characterize how risks originating from downstream interactions influence LC behavior and subsequently propagate to upstream traffic. Finally, awareness of this spatial risk propagation enables the generation of an early warning signal that informs the LC decision-making with potential collision locations within the predicted time window. Traffic simulation experiments conducted in SUMO demonstrate that the proposed LCEW effectively improves vehicle-level safety and comfort, while maintaining system-level traffic safety and efficiency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The grass is not always greener: The effects of local labor market information on search and employment
Authors: A. Nilesh Fernando, Niharika Singh
Abstract: We examine how information about local labor market conditions shapes search and employment outcomes for Indian job seekers. Participants were randomly shown information about either job postings, job applicants, or both from a popular job portal for their preferred city and occupation. Treated respondents are more likely to be employed seven months later. This overall effect varies considerably by baseline employment status. Among the initially employed , treatments reduce search off the portal and increase employment, with suggestive evidence of higher persistence in baseline jobs. In contrast, among the initially unemployed , treatments increase search activity but do not raise employment. Employment gains are concentrated among job seekers with less optimistic beliefs about labor market conditions. These findings suggest that limited information about labor market fundamentals may contribute to job churn in lower-income countries.

Title: Work-from-home and wage convergence across cities: An exploration
Authors: David R. Agrawal, Jan K. Brueckner
Abstract: This paper provides evidence on a WFH-related hypothesis that has not previously been tested empirically. The hypothesis is that the presence of fully remote workers, for whom residence and work locations are decoupled, should create a tendency toward wage convergence across cities within teleworkable occupations. The reason is that, since fully remote workers can work anywhere, local wages must match those available in other cities for employers to attract any of these workers. By combining occupational wage data with data on which occupations are teleworkable, the paper attempts to test the wage-convergence hypothesis. The results are mixed, but some evidence does emerge in favor of the hypothesis.

Title: Strategic deployment and adoption for AI streamer on live commerce platforms
Authors: Yu Ning, Xudong Lin, Su Xiu Xu
Abstract: The integration of AI streamers into live commerce platforms represents a transformative shift in product promotion and consumer engagement strategies. This paper develops a sequential game-theoretic model to examine the strategic interactions between platforms and sellers. With the platform acting as the Stackelberg leader determining AI deployment and technological investment, and the seller following with streamer adoption and pricing decisions, we analyze how outcomes are shaped by commission rates, consumer schedule flexibility, and baseline trust in AI. Our results show that the seller's profit under AI streaming follows an inverted U pattern with respect to the commission rate. Furthermore, consumer flexibility and a non-monotonic trust effect jointly govern the strategic alignment between both parties. Human streaming is optimal when the flexible segment is large, whereas a mutually beneficial agreement on AI adoption emerges only when time-constrained consumers prevail and baseline trust is either sufficiently low or sufficiently high. Under moderate trust, the equilibrium defaults to traditional human streaming. This research provides a structured analytical framework to guide platforms and sellers in aligning their operational strategies within the evolving live commerce ecosystem.

Title: The persistent legacy: Colonial railroads and agricultural productivity in Africa
Authors: Andu Berha, Sandeep Mohapatra
Abstract: This paper examines the long-term impacts of colonial-period railroads on agricultural productivity in sub-Saharan Africa. Using granular data from 22 countries, we show that historically rail-connected regions remain more productive today. We also find that these regions are more integrated into modern road-based urban markets. We interpret this pattern as evidence of path-dependent spatial equilibrium, where early investment in the transportation network helped coordinate the location of economic activities in the post-colonial period. However, the evidence does not rule out the possibility that colonial railways and the modern road network both followed persistent favorable geographic fundamentals. More broadly, the findings show how early transport investment can leave durable effects on rural development by shaping the geography of market access.

Title: Rethinking pilot fatigue evidence for risk management: An LLM-assisted knowledge-graph synthesis for policy appraisal
Authors: Yang Cao, Y.J. Zhou, Zixiang Guan, Hyungchul Chung, Xiaowen Fu, Hongliang Ding
Abstract: Fatigue Risk Management Systems (FRMS) are now central to commercial aviation safety policy, but their provisions depend on a research base that is large, heterogeneous, and increasingly shaped by AI/ML-based fatigue-detection studies. Existing reviews usually summarise pilot-fatigue evidence by study type or measurement modality, which makes it difficult to judge whether the specific exposure-outcome relationships used in FRMS are stable, conditional, or provisional. This study develops an LLM-assisted, knowledge-graph synthesis of 262 peer-reviewed studies published between 2010 and 2026. A large language model (LLM) was used as a structured extraction aid to convert full-text articles into 3,224 traceable atomic claims, each anchored to canonical exposure and outcome variables. The resulting graph linked 115 canonical variables through 368 exposure-outcome relationships. Mechanism claims dominated the corpus (57.8%), whereas direct Intervention/FRMS evidence was comparatively scarce (9.7%). Evidence clustered in a few large thematic communities, and among relationships examined by two or more studies most (78.3%) carried a conflict, predominantly disagreement over the direction of the effect. Detection evidence was extensive but less policy-portable: many classifier-performance claims lacked explicit exposure or outcome anchors needed for cross-study appraisal. Because fatigue, sleepiness, workload, vigilance, and situation awareness are related but not interchangeable operational states, FRMS evidence should be graded at the relationship level while preserving construct specificity. The findings support a graded evidence-to-action approach to FRMS: stable and well-anchored relationships may inform stronger provisions; context-dependent relationships require conditional implementation and monitoring; and direction-conflicted or weakly anchored relationships should remain subject to evaluation or precaution rather than automatic operational intervention. More broadly, the study positions LLM-assisted synthesis as a traceable evidentiary infrastructure for transport-safety policy, not as a substitute for expert or regulatory judgement.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A multi-period vehicle routing problem with driver consistency and arrival-time diversification
Authors: Jahir Llagas, Foteini Stavropoulou, Sanne Wøhlk
Abstract: We study a Multi-Period Vehicle Routing Problem that integrates driver consistency and arrival-time diversification. Driver consistency requires each customer to be served by the same vehicle across all service periods, while arrival-time diversification enforces temporal separation between visits in different periods. We first propose a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming formulation and an exact Logic-Based Benders Decomposition implemented through a Branch-and-Check scheme, where a multi-period VRP with driver consistency is handled in the master problem and arrival-time diversification is addressed in the subproblem. Building on this structure, we develop a matheuristic that exploits the subproblem in an efficient and targeted manner. As arrival-time diversification checks are computationally expensive, we propose a feasibility check procedure over a restricted search space. Computational results show that the branch-and-check approach solves medium-scale instances to optimality, while the matheuristic achieves near-optimal solutions in significantly shorter computation times. Lastly, the impact of arrival-time diversification is examined and managerial insights are derived.

Title: A reinforcement learning-guided breakout local search algorithm for the heaviest subgraph problem
Authors: He Zheng, Jin-Kao Hao, Rafael Martí, Yang Wang
Abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning-guided breakout local search algorithm for the Heaviest k[jls-end-space/]-Subgraph Problem, a general optimization graph model with many applications. This algorithm combines a powerful local search procedure with a learning-guided perturbation strategy to achieve an effective balance between intensification and diversification in the search for high-quality solutions. The local search procedure explores two neighborhoods reinforced by a neighborhood reduction strategy. The learning-guided perturbation strategy uses Q-learning to select the most promising perturbation during the search. Computational results on benchmark instances show that the algorithm competes very favorably with the state-of-the-art approaches. It provides improved best results (new lower bounds) for 128 out of 177 instances and matches the best-known solutions for most remaining instances. The algorithm’s competitive performance on three related problems (Densest k-Subgraph, Maximum Clique, and Hidden Clique) demonstrates its potential for broader applicability.

Title: Dual-resource flexible job shop scheduling problem considering no-tardiness constraints
Authors: Shuangyuan Shi, Hegen Xiong, Chang Liu
Abstract: With increasingly strict customer requirements for order delivery deadlines, on-time delivery has become a critical challenge in production scheduling. This study addresses a dual-resource constrained flexible job shop scheduling problem with no-tardiness constraints (NT-DRCFJSP), aiming to enhance the production capacity through the efficient utilization of both machine and multi-skilled worker resources. A mathematical model is first established to formulate the problem, with the objective of minimizing both the workload imbalance among workers and among machines. To effectively solve the problem, a hybrid optimization method (HNSGA-II) combining non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) with adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) is proposed. The algorithm incorporates a three-layer encoding strategy, a two-stage decoding method, and a rule-based population initialization approach to enhance its search efficiency. Moreover, seven destroy operators and four repair operators are designed to maintain population diversity and strengthen local search capabilities. The experiments are conducted in five phases: validation of the developed mathematical model using CPLEX, Taguchi-method-driven parameter calibration for the algorithm, feasibility testing of the hybrid algorithm, performance assessment of the proposed improvement strategies, and comparative evaluation against state-of-the-art algorithms. Results demonstrate that HNSGA-II is effective in solving the multi-objective NT-DRCFJSP, and outperforms other comparative algorithms.

Title: Neural networks vs. traditional methods: A hybrid nonlinear approach for solving large OLG models
Authors: Michael Reiter
Abstract: This paper develops a hybrid nonlinear solution method for large-scale dynamic macroeconomic models, combining insights from the deep learning literature with the strengths of traditional perturbation and projection techniques. The method embeds economically motivated functional forms and perturbation-based derivatives within an approximation that uses deep function composition. Applied to a large OLG model with borrowing constraints and multiple aggregate shocks, the solution method achieves high accuracy over a wide range of the relevant state space.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Machine learning Calvo’s optimal plan
Authors: Thomas J. Sargent, Ziyue Yang
Abstract: A computer program calculates a pair of infinite sequences of price level inflation and money creation rates (θ→,μ→) that maximizes a benevolent time 0 government's objective function. The limit of a monotonically declining sequence of continuation values is a worst continuation value associated with a “timeless perspective”. The time-invariant inflation rate associated with the worst continuation Ramsey plan is not the inflation rate associated with a restricted Ramsey plan in which a time 0 government is constrained to choose a time-invariant money creation rate. We Bellmanize the continuation Ramsey problem.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: Goal setting and feedback: the power of joint use
Authors: Basak Altan, Begum Guney, Neslihan Uler
Abstract: This study examines the effects of goal setting and feedback, both in isolation and in combination, and how these effects vary depending on who sets the goal. We study these effects in a non-pecuniary environment common to workplace settings such as the public sector. We compare outcomes across treatments with no goal setting, worker-set goals, and employer-set goals, each implemented with and without employer feedback, and document several key findings. Employers set substantially higher goals than workers, and this gap widens with feedback because employer-set goals increase significantly while worker-set goals remain unchanged. Effort is significantly higher only under the joint use of employer-set goals and feedback; otherwise, effort levels are similar. Specifically, neither feedback nor goal setting has a significant effect on effort when used in isolation. The effect of feedback on effort is positive and statistically significant only when goals are employer-set. Likewise, when feedback is present, only employer-set goals raise effort significantly relative to no goal setting. Finally, employer feedback is sensitive to goal attainment only when goals are set by employers. One possible explanation is that employer-set goals, when paired with feedback, create a sense of social pressure or accountability that leads workers to increase effort.

Title: Explaining COVID-19 Tokyo metro station-level ridership disruption and recovery: pre-pandemic demand, built environment and centrality
Authors: Xi Lin, Giuseppe Vizzari, Claudio Feliciani, Daichi Yanagisawa, Katsuhiro Nishinari
Abstract: COVID-19 caused severe and uneven metro ridership declines. This study examines station-level annual ridership change in Tokyo from 2020 to 2023 relative to 2019, integrating pre-pandemic demand, built environment, and network centrality. Its main contribution is to identify how these factors shaped ridership resilience from acute disruption to recovery using ordinary least squares (OLS) and geographically weighted regression (GWR). Results show that high pre-pandemic demand and Production and Service intensity are associated with larger proportional losses, especially in 2020–2021. Road density is consistently linked to smaller declines and stronger recovery, indicating the importance of local access networks. Land-use mix becomes increasingly positive during recovery, suggesting that functionally diverse station areas better supported localized daily activities. Destination accessibility and centrality show more spatially uneven and temporally unstable effects. These findings suggest that resilience-oriented planning should combine targeted operations for vulnerable high-demand stations with local access improvements and mixed-use station-area development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Dynamic pricing and adoption of electric vehicles under critical mineral resource constraints
Authors: Hongtao Ren, Zanfeng Wang, Xiao-Bing Zhang, Wenji Zhou
Abstract: The global transition to electric vehicles (EVs) is a critical strategy for decarbonizing transportation, yet the role of critical mineral scarcity has not been fully incorporated into dynamic policy design. This study develops a dynamic optimization model that integrates endogenous lithium extraction costs under resource depletion with learning-by-doing to examine their joint effects on EV market evolution and social welfare. We show that neglecting lithium supply constraints may lead to overly optimistic projections. Rising extraction costs partially offset learning-induced cost reductions, generating an inverted U-shaped adoption path rather than sustained growth under the calibrated baseline. This suggests that resource scarcity may slow the EV transition and elevate long-term costs. We further evaluate and compare prevalent policy instruments, including subsidies, carbon taxes, and fuel economy standards, under varying market conditions across 435 scenarios. The relative effectiveness and welfare performance of these policies depend critically on learning rates, extraction cost dynamics, lithium recycling efficiency, and demand elasticity. Subsidies are more effective when cost pressures are alleviated, whereas tax- and regulation-based instruments perform better under binding resource constraints and stronger demand responsiveness. Our findings highlight the necessity of incorporating resource constraints into environmental policy planning. Policies that promote recycling and alleviate supply-side pressures are important for both the effectiveness and fiscal sustainability of the EV transition.

Title: Recent minimum wage policy and its impacts on birth outcomes
Authors: Yuji Mizushima, David Powell, Margaret Weden, Kate Strully, Allison Appleton
Abstract: After a pause in statutory minimum wage increases during the Great Recession, several states increased their minimum wages, including increases as large as 60% over just a few years. Using a triple difference-in-differences framework and data on the universe of births from 2010 to 2019, this study investigates how recent minimum wage hikes affected birth outcomes. We first document sizeable negative impacts of minimum wage policy on the labor supply and economic well-being of females aged 16-44. We then document small adverse effects on birth outcomes, estimating that minimum wage increases led to lower birthweight, fewer normal birthweight births, and more small for gestational age births. These findings generally contrast with an earlier literature relying primarily on much smaller minimum wage increases which showed more evidence of positive impacts on birth outcomes.

Title: Impact of a TB epidemic on worker and firm productivity: the regional perspective from Ukraine
Authors: Olena Nizalova, Oleksandr Shepotylo
Abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the indirect economic effects of tuberculosis (TB) in a high TB burden country, focusing on worker and firm productivity. Using unique administrative data from Ukraine, in 2003–2009, we find that TB prevalence leads to significantly lower wages and total factor productivity (TFP), while higher TB incidence, reflecting risk of exposure, is linked to higher wages and productivity. Additional analysis reveals strong spatial spillovers, underlining the contagious nature of the disease and the need for coordinated policy responses. Our estimates suggest that a 10% reduction in TB prevalence could yield a 1.05% GDP gain (0.15% from higher wages and 0.89% from higher TFP), compared to TB-related spending of only 0.04% of GDP that same year. These findings highlight the underinvestment in TB control and the broader economic stakes of epidemic containment.

Title: Universal child benefit and child poverty: the role of fertility adjustments
Authors: Jan Gromadzki
Abstract: Abstract I study fertility adjustments after the introduction of a large universal child benefit in Poland. Nine months after the program’s announcement, births increased discontinuously by 6%. Patterns of selection into parenthood changed significantly and persistently, with a weakening of positive selection based on education and a strengthening of negative selection based on income. The share of births in the bottom half of the income distribution increased from 51% to 58%. Using a microsimulation approach, I combine changes in the births structure with existing estimates of the transfer’s effect on labor supply to study the impact of these adjustments on poverty reduction. These impacts are very small due to the exceptional generosity of the transfer, but they become more pronounced in the middle of the income distribution.

Title: The health burden of job strain: evidence from Europe
Authors: Petru Crudu, Giacomo Pasini
Abstract: Abstract This paper studies how occupational stressors and job tasks over the life course are associated with health later in life. Using SHARE data and retrospective job histories for individuals across Europe, we construct career-long exposure to occupational stressors by linking 4-digit ISCO occupations to external measures of job demands. We find that physical job intensity, measured by the metabolic equivalent of task, is associated with worse later-life health, and this result remains stable across sensitivity analyses. Higher exposure is also associated with a greater incidence of some cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and with an earlier onset of several cardiovascular, metabolic, and respiratory conditions. We use detailed task information and a LASSO-based approach to identify the job tasks most strongly associated with poor health and to build a Job Strain Intensity index. This task-based framework offers a granular and scalable way to detect harmful dimensions of work and inform policy discussions.

Title: A Model of Consumer Choice for National vs Private Label Brands
Authors: G. Baltas, P. Doyle, P. Dyson
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Dynamic lead time coordination in supply chains under bilateral operational information asymmetry
Authors: Emma Salatiello, Francesca Papa, Silvestro Vespoli, Andrea Grassi
Abstract: Coordinating modern supply chains (SCs) is hindered by market volatility and, critically, by bilateral operational information asymmetry, where partners hold private, unverifiable information about their real-time capabilities. This study addresses this challenge by developing and testing a novel coordination framework for a dyadic SC, centered on a dynamic lead time negotiation coupled with an adaptive revenue-sharing mechanism. A comparative simulation analysis reveaals that while lead time negotiation alone enhances responsiveness by significantly reducing delivery times, it can paradoxically destroy total SC profit in decentralized settings due to uncompensated operational costs. However, the proposed integrated framework—combining negotiation with adaptive revenue sharing—proves highly effective. It not only fosters cooperation but also recovers nearly all profit losses from decentralization, while ensuring an equitable profit distribution. Furthermore, the study uncovers a critical insight into pricing power: a leader’s ability to charge for faster service is fundamentally limited by the partner’s economic viability, with a clear threshold beyond which an aggressive pricing strategy becomes value-destructive for the entire SC. This research contributes a novel operational contract that effectively mitigates the impacts of information asymmetry and enhances system-wide efficiency by explicitly linking dynamic operational decisions (lead time) to their shared financial consequences, offering a practical path toward resilient and profitable SC collaboration.

Title: The relevance of traditional postal services in a diversifying last-mile delivery landscape: The role of human to human (H2H) interactions
Authors: R. Merkert, S. Hess, F. Khan, M.C.J. Bliemer
Abstract: Last-mile delivery research increasingly focuses on business-to-consumer (B2C) automation to satisfy consumers with an ‘I want it now’ mentality, reduce firms’ carbon footprints, and improve cost efficiency. Much less attention has been given to the possibility that there might be differences across consumer segments in their preferences for technology‑enabled or more traditional, human-mediated delivery modes. Building on random utility theory, we developed a hybrid choice model with a latent class kernel and applied it to stated choice data on delivery service preferences collected from 1,007 customers across metropolitan and regional areas of Australia. Our results reveal two latent classes of consumers with distinctly different preferences. The largest group, which we label techies , value speed and low cost last-mile delivery and prefer traditional postal services, followed by aerial drones and parcel lockers, with the effect moderated by parcel value and the availability of a safe place for unattended delivery. The second group, relational, trusting people , place a stronger emphasis on trust and interpersonal aspects of service and substantially prefer traditional postal services (assuming a safe place for delivery is available) and lockers while showing a strong dislike of aerial drones. To interpret these patterns, we draw on social exchange theory and the human-to-human (H2H) relationship model to explain how relational considerations may influence delivery mode preferences. H2H interactions matter for a subset of consumers. Importantly, our broader findings highlight the continued relevance of traditional postal services in a diversifying delivery landscape. Although no direct spatial effect emerges in the class allocation model, our results suggest that residential location (metropolitan versus regional) has a structural effect by influencing consumers’ underlying latent attitudes.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Drone fleet resupply in same-day delivery with fair customer service
Authors: Liang Chen, Shuyi Wang, Qi Wang, Liujiang Kang, Jianhua Xiao, George Q. Huang
Abstract: Fairness in same-day delivery (SDD) becomes increasingly important as customers demand equitable service pledge, yet cost-driven merchants’ preferences for nearby customers create service disparities across regions. Drone fleet resupply presents a fast and traffic-free solution capable of navigating complex terrains, while truck-based delivery complements it by overcoming the drone’s limitations in endurance and operational range. Previous studies mainly address single-drone, single-truck problems, with limited attention to the potential of drone fleet resupply with multi-truck systems to solve fairness issues. This research fills this gap by originally proposing a drone fleet resupply system for stochastic requests, where drones perform multiple trips to replenish any truck as needed, with consideration of drone endurance limitations. This problem is formulated as a sequential decision process (SDP) and solved through a deep Q-learning (DQL) approach to maximize service rates while ensuring fairness. A piecewise linear reward function is designed to improve convergence. Comparative results against benchmark policies demonstrate DQL’s potential to manage highly stochastic logistics operations. Key findings include: (1) Drone fleet resupply enhances regional fairness and overall service rates, demonstrating strong robustness in serving long-distance and time-sensitive deliveries; (2) An appropriate reward function significantly facilitates fairness, while penalties further improve it but are ineffective alone; (3) An optimal drone-truck fleet mix exists to balance service rates and associated costs, while adding more trucks alone substantially improves service rates but incurs larger costs; (4) The proposed approach remains effective across drone capacities, while extended drone endurance yields limited gains in service rate but significantly lowers delivery costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrated berth allocation and quay crane scheduling optimization under shore power connection policy with JIT-driven vessel departures
Authors: Li-Jun Yue, Hou-Ming Fan, Shao-Fang Wen
Abstract: The energy consumption from vessel waiting and handling at ports needs to be addressed, giving rise to policies such as Shore Power Connection (SPC) and Just In Time (JIT). However, converting these policies into operational decision metrics is challenging. This study fills that gap by embedding key indicators, such as Berth Occupancy Rate (BOR), Shore Power Utilization Ratio (SPUR), Quay Crane Utilization Ratio (QCUR), and Average Vessel Completion Rate (AVCR), into a novel optimization model for the integrated Berth Allocation and Quay Crane Scheduling Problem (BAQCSP). The model incorporates a dynamic prediction mechanism to estimate quay crane handling times, accounting for real-world variables such as tidal conditions and container stowage positions. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model demonstrates superior performance in resource utilization compared to sequential scheduling, single-objective optimization, and fixed quay crane handling time strategies. Additional ablation studies quantify the individual impact of each sustainability indicator on scheduling outcomes. The findings provide port authorities with actionable evidence to operationalize sustainability goals into enforceable strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Integrating parking delay uncertainty in urban delivery tour planning
Authors: Giacomo Dalla Chiara, Claudia Fasano, Klaas Fiete Krutein, Paul Buijs, Todor Dimitrov, Sarah Dennis-Bauer, Anne Goodchild
Abstract: Securing curb space near a delivery location is a major source of uncertainty for urban commercial vehicle drivers. While tour planning tools increasingly account for time-dependent traffic conditions, they typically ignore parking delays, even though evidence shows they vary systematically across locations and times of day. This paper empirically examines how expected parking delays affect urban delivery tour planning. Using GPS data from real-world delivery operations, we estimate time- and location-specific parking delays and incorporate them into a Time-Dependent Traveling Salesman Problem with Time Windows. We compare conventional parking-blind planning, which considers only travel times, with parking-aware planning, which additionally accounts for expected parking delays. The results show that parking-blind planning substantially underestimates tour duration and overestimates schedule feasibility. When realistic parking conditions are considered, parking delays accounted for about 33% of total delivery tour duration and generate substantial increases in lateness and time-window violations. Parking-aware planning reduces tour duration by 3.4% on average (17.4 min), with some instances obtaining total tour duration reductions of more than 10%, by trading slightly longer driving times for lower parking delays, while reducing time spent in parking delays by 11% on average. More importantly, it substantially improves service reliability, reducing average lateness and greatly decreasing the frequency of time-window violations. These improvements are achieved primarily through small adjustments in stop sequencing and service timing that shift deliveries toward periods with lower expected parking delays.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The health effects of genetically modified crops
Authors: Zhiqiang Wang, Xianling Long
Abstract: Public debates on genetically modified (GM) crops center on environmental and health risks, yet evidence remains limited and focuses largely on herbicide-tolerant varieties or on local exposure, leaving the broad consequences of insect-resistant crops unclear. Insect-resistant crops can reduce pesticide use and generate health effects beyond directly exposed farmers. Yet their net effects are ambiguous, as any environmental gains may be offset by crop substitution, pest resistance, industrial expansion, and land-use change. We exploit the staggered approval of Bt cotton across China, combined with river networks that link cotton-growing areas to downstream residents. Bt cotton approval leads to significant downstream reductions in under-five mortality by 4.2%, driven by reduced pesticide use and improved water quality. In aggregate, Bt cotton approval reduces national pesticide use by 3.2%. The findings show that the social value of insect-resistant GM crops can be significantly underestimated, as they generate positive health externalities through environmental spillovers.

Title: Perceived need and measured well-being: How well do subjective rankings capture relative poverty?
Authors: Immacolata Ranucci, Kibrom A. Abay, Luca Tiberti
Abstract: Subjective well-being rankings are increasingly used to target social protection programs, yet their ability to capture relative welfare and wealth remains debated. This study benchmarks self-, peer-, and elite-based poverty rankings against consumption- and wealth-based measures using Ethiopian household survey data, where about 20 households per village were ranked from neediest to least needy by themselves, peers, and community leaders. We assess concordance between subjective and conventional welfare rankings and explore sources of divergence. Subjective rankings align more with relative wealth than consumption and with total rather than per capita welfare, suggesting they overlook household composition. Elite-based rankings best capture conventional measures, followed by peers’ and self-rankings. Subjective rankings also better reflect relative deprivation among households exposed to covariate shocks. A composite index combining all three improves agreement with standard metrics. Information asymmetries, favoritism, and welfare dynamics partly explain discrepancies, offering insights for enhancing targeting in data-scarce settings.

Title: Does product quality matter in sales mode selection on platforms? Strategic vertical co-opetition in e-channels
Authors: Tian Li, Zixiang Zhou, Yucheng Xin, Tijun Fan, Meiqi Feng
Abstract: As horizontal competition among online platforms becomes increasingly intense, a platform and her upstream manufacturer forge subtler vertical co-opetition relation than ever to strive together for a greater market share. Consider two competing e-commerce channels, each composed of a downstream platform and an upstream manufacturer, which offer quality-differentiated and substitutable products. The ordinary product and the fine product are endowed with basic functions and premium functions, respectively. Each manufacturer can choose his sales mode, resale or agency, on his platform. We analyze the equilibrium pricing and sales mode choices and show how they depend on product quality. The main findings are as follows. First, if the commission rate is low (resp. high), both manufacturers adopt the agency (resp. resale) mode. Second, at an intermediate commission rate, the fine manufacturer adopts resale while the ordinary manufacturer adopts agency, highlighting product quality as a pivotal driver of sales mode selection. Third, as the ordinary product’s quality improves, the fine manufacturer may switch from resale to agency and back to resale, reflecting a strategic balance between vertical pricing and horizontal competition. Moreover, the fine manufacturer’s quality advantage can lead to a lower sales price under resale than under agency, while the ordinary manufacturer can be negatively affected by an improvement in the quality of its own product.

Title: The price of hope: Reference-group mobility and the subjective value of income
Authors: Alpaslan Akay, Nur Banu Kartal
Abstract: We examine whether upward mobility within a person’s reference group changes the subjective value of own and reference income. Standard relative-income models interpret higher peer income mainly as status loss. We argue that this view is incomplete. In mobile reference groups, higher peer income may also signal attainable opportunities, consistent with a “tunnel effect”; at the same time, mobility can raise aspirations and reduce satisfaction with one’s own income, creating what we call the “price of hope”. Using the Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP) for 2000–2020, we combine individual fixed effects with leave-one-out reference income and leave-one-out reference-group-year measures of realised upward income dynamics. Among individuals below their reference income, the negative association between reference income and life satisfaction is strong in low-mobility environments but largely attenuated when mobility is high. The own-income gradient is also smaller in high-mobility environments. These patterns are weaker among individuals at or above their reference income and robust across alternative mobility measures, reference-group definitions, median reference income, and controls for within-group inequality. Mobility, therefore, changes the meaning of income: it makes richer peers less costly as a status benchmark, but lowers the subjective return to current own income by shifting aspirations upward.

Title: Who is concerned about climate change when forests are burning? Evidence from Swedish forest fires
Authors: Xiao Hu
Abstract: I examine how individuals update their environmental attitudes in response to climate events using the extensive Swedish forest fires in 2018. Political scientists have suggested that motivated reasoning contributes to divergence in environmental attitudes over time. It remains empirically unclear whether the growing prominence of climate events could potentially widen or bridge these political divides. I document rising environmental concerns following the fires. The extent of these increases did not appear to be associated with the intensity of local fires but varied significantly by individuals’ prior beliefs. Green-left-leaning individuals exhibited stronger prior concerns and showed larger increases in concern after the fires than conservative-right-leaning individuals. The growing concern suggests that climate events exacerbate political polarization in environmental attitudes rather than mitigating it. I also find no evidence that exposure to climate change news explains the observed political polarization in concerns. These patterns are consistent with motivated reasoning along partisan lines shaping differential reactions to climate disasters. In contrast, I do not find similar patterns for support for a higher carbon tax, indicating that increased concern does not necessarily translate into support for climate policy.

Title: Activity-driven dual exposure to congestion and crowding: Exploring multiple constraints for peak-hour bus travel burdens using smart card data
Authors: Jiaomin Wei, Zihan Kan, Mei-Po Kwan
Abstract: Traffic congestion and in-vehicle crowding represent critical barriers to urban efficiency and public health. Bus passengers uniquely face a dual exposure to external congestion delays and internal physical discomfort. This compounded burden may be due to the spatiotemporal fixity of daily activities, compelling individuals into unavoidable peak-hour bottlenecks. However, few studies have examined these concurrent exposures from a daily activity perspective, overlooking how multiple constraints shape when, where, and how individuals encounter these travel adversities, especially for vulnerable populations like older groups. By reframing congestion and crowding as activity‑induced and cumulative experiences, the study moves beyond trip‑level analysis to reveal the mechanisms through which daily schedules translate into unequal mobility burdens. Adverse travel refers to a journey during which passengers simultaneously experience congestion and crowding. By using one-month smart card data and Point of Interest (POI) data in Beijing, China, this study reveals that nearly 50% of senior cardholders’ peak-hour adverse bus trips involve maintenance and discretionary activities (e.g., medical and recreation), while regular cardholders tend to encounter adverse travel during their mandatory commuting. Per-km cumulative exposure is primarily driven by travel distance, whereas adverse trip transitions are shaped by the spatiotemporal flexibility of activities, both of which are amplified by metro feeder routes and morning-peak travel pressure. These findings reveal where people travel from, how far they travel for conducting activities, and the constraints that shape these experiences. This study provides a methodological framework and empirical foundation for identifying where and how interventions are needed to improve urban mobility equity.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Scheduling electricity production units to mitigate severe weather impact: An efficient computational implementation
Authors: Yongzheng Dai, Antonio J. Conejo, Feng Qiu
Abstract: Extreme weather events in electric power systems can cause line trips or physical damage to transmission infrastructure, potentially leading to large-scale load shedding. To mitigate this risk, we propose a framework that strategically pre-positions the commitment of generation units--particularly slow-start units--to adapt to transmission topologies that may arise following such events. The objective is to minimize load shedding under worst-case conditions. This paper makes two main contributions. First, we provide a more accurate representation of the underlying physical laws than those used in prior studies. Second, we develop a highly efficient solution algorithm that outperforms state-of-the-art, off-the-shelf solvers. The proposed framework is formulated as a two-stage robust optimization model. In the first stage, generation units are scheduled in anticipation of disruptions. In the second stage, power dispatch decisions are optimized to minimize load shedding under the worst-case transmission topology. To ensure system reliability and security, we incorporate convexified AC power flow constraints. The resulting model is a tri-level mixed-integer nonlinear optimization problem.
