To address its computational complexity, we design a problem-specific outer approximation algorithm embedded within a column-and-constraint generation framework. Computational results show that the proposed model and solution approach can achieve solutions within a standard optimality gap in a reasonable time for moderately large instances.

Title: Higher-moments-robust monetary policy shocks
Authors: Francesco Fusari
Abstract: This paper develops a novel measure of monetary shocks that accounts for the endogenous response of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) to higher moments of expected economic outcomes. First, I use quantile regression to estimate the conditional distribution of Federal Reserve forecasts and construct indicators of uncertainty and skewness. Second, I show that, unlike other measures proposed in the literature, these indicators have strong predictive power for the changes in the Federal funds rate deliberated by the FOMC. This suggests that point forecasts alone do not fully capture the FOMC’s systematic response to the economic outlook, with implications for the identification of monetary policy shocks. In particular, once higher moments are controlled for, the response of macroeconomic and financial variables is more closely aligned with theoretical predictions.
Journal: Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control

Title: For the future of our grandchildren: Grandparenthood and climate change concerns
Authors: Lieke Voorintholt, Gerard J. van den Berg, Adriaan R. Soetevent
Abstract: Concerns about offspring’s life quality are often cited as a motivation for caring about climate change. This paper investigates the hypothesized causal effect of grandparenthood on climate change worries, using panel data surveys among British families. Specifically, we study whether becoming a grandparent increases these worries. We employ two different study designs to deal with endogeneity of grandparenthood. Across designs, the assumptions required to identify causal effects differ and are non-nested but give a remarkably congruent result: We find no empirical support for a relationship between grandparental status and concerns about climate change.

Title: Battery storage cannibalization of price spreads in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas
Authors: Karl Li
Abstract: Does battery deployment compress the price spreads that pay for it? This paper measures it in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), where battery storage grew from 124 megawatts in January 2020 past 14 gigawatts by July 2025 beside a solar buildout. The two capacities correlate at 0.95 in levels and minus 0.06 in monthly increments. Day-ahead prices at five hubs run from January 2020 through February 2026. The daily top-four bottom-four spread, a day’s four highest hourly prices minus its four lowest, is 53.69 USD/MWh (standard error 16.27) lower per gigawatt along the joint battery and solar path, 16 percent of the 334 USD/MWh mean. The largest ten percent of days carry 62 percent of total spread, so the level estimate is fitted by the days that pay for storage. The proportional estimate of 4.8 percent per gigawatt takes 6.3 USD/MWh off the 132 USD/MWh median day. A mechanism decomposition finds the evening peak margin narrowing with battery capacity and the midday dip flattening as storage charges at midday and discharges into the evening peak. In the midday equation the battery and solar coefficients are statistically distinguishable. Gross perfect-foresight energy-arbitrage revenue fell from 213 USD per kilowatt-year in 2023 to 61 in 2025 while average capacity rose from 2.7 to 13.0 gigawatts and gas prices rose 40 percent. New storage interconnection requests fell from 246 in the first half of 2025 to 97 in the second. ERCOT storage is now large enough to discipline its own entry.

Title: Estimating drivers’ time cost function for California’s freeway system
Authors: Jinwon Kim, Jucheol Moon, Dongyun Yang
Abstract: This paper estimates drivers’ time cost function, a causal relationship between traffic volume and travel time, representing the California freeway system as a whole. For identification, we instrument for traffic density using California's March 2020 COVID-19 lockdown — a large shock to travel demand — interacted with county-level work-from-home potential, which captures each area's exposure to the shock. For estimation, we use freeway–county-level aggregates of traffic variables, constructed from the extensive network of traffic sensors on California freeways. We find that OLS estimates are substantially larger than IV estimates. After ruling out alternative explanations, we attribute this gap primarily to a reverse-causality bias that follows mechanically from the capacity constraint of freeways: observed traffic volume is censored at capacity, steepening the OLS slope. Based on our preferred IV estimate, optimal congestion tolls average about 10 cents per vehicle-mile under typical conditions, rising to about 36 cents under extreme congestion. Such tolling would yield annual welfare gains of up to $0.74 billion.

Title: How return policies impact the brand owner’s AI adoption strategy
Authors: Jing Lyu, Yanju Zhou, Ming Chen
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in online retail to reduce product fit uncertainty. This paper develops a game-theoretic model with consumer learning to investigate how platform return policies shape AI adoption and market outcomes. The model assumes that a brand owner sells through an e-commerce platform. The analysis examines the brand owner's pricing and AI adoption decisions under no-return and lenient return policies. It allows for three types of AI adoption strategies: no AI, platform-provided AI, and jointly developed AI. The results show that return policies alter the economic value of AI-generated information, thereby shaping the brand owner's pricing and AI adoption decisions. Under a no-return policy, the belief enhancement effect of AI can strengthen the brand owner's pricing power, while the profitability of AI adoption depends on the market fit rate. Under a lenient return policy, the screening effect of AI can reduce purchases by poorly matched consumers and the resulting return-processing losses. When the market fit rate is low, such screening can also reduce the attractiveness of a high-price strategy and lead to a lower equilibrium price. These differences reshape the brand owner's AI adoption incentives across return policy environments and alter the relative attractiveness of AI options with different effectiveness and implementation costs. Consequently, the distribution of benefits among market participants also varies across return-policy regimes. Under a no-return policy, AI adoption may be more favorable to the brand owner and the platform, whereas under a lenient return policy, it is more likely to generate a triple-win outcome for the brand owner, the platform, and consumers.

Title: Employment effects and fiscal spillovers of a public sector employment program
Authors: Eva Mörk, Lillit Ottosson, Ulrika Vikman
Abstract: We evaluate a temporary public sector employment program targeted at individuals with a weak labor market attachment. To account for dynamic selection into the program, we apply the dynamic inverse probability weighting approach. We show that the program is successful in terms of increasing employment and reducing social assistance. The positive employment effects are driven by individuals placed at regular workplaces. For participants with temporary employments at a non-regular workplace, we instead find negative employment effects. The decrease in social assistance is partially countered by an increase in the share receiving unemployment insurance benefits, indicating that municipalities are able to shift costs from the local to the central budget. We further find that cost-effectiveness, as measured by the marginal value of public funds, varies depending on which level of government is considered.

Title: Operationalising cognitive digital twins through a cognitive-function framework and GenAI tools
Authors: Yangyang Liu, Tang Ji, Xiangyu Guo, Yinwang Ren, Xun Xu, Jan Polzer
Affiliations: University of Auckland; China Academy of Engineering Physics
Abstract: Cognitive Digital Twin (CDT) is emerging as an evolution of Digital Twin (DT) for smart manufacturing, but most CDT studies remain at the conceptual level and lack implementable cognitive-module architectures. This paper proposes an implementation-oriented CDT reference architecture that formalises four cognitive functions, Perception, Attention, Reasoning & Problem Solving, and Memory & Learning, through defined computational roles and interaction mechanisms. To examine how these architectural roles can be operationalised, we instantiate a bounded subset of their interactions as an L3 geometric-modelling workflow in a robotic cell. In this prototype, YOLOv11 provides coarse asset-detection and position-change cues, precise device poses are obtained from a pre-calibrated registry with human confirmation, and a GPT-5.1-driven agentic workflow performs spatial-instruction parsing, geometric constraint formulation, verification, bounded replanning, and FreeCAD-script synthesis. Controlled experiments with 2–32 devices characterise the pre-execution workflow time, token consumption, internal constraint acceptance, and replanning outcomes. The results provide initial evidence that selected architectural interactions can be translated into an executable CDT function, while also revealing limitations for large, structurally over-dense layouts.

Title: Scheduling of AGVs in AGV-supported assembly lines consisting of zero-buffer workstations
Authors: Tao He, Hu Yu, Yugang Yu
Affiliations: School of Management, University of Science and Technology of China
Abstract: Discrete assembly lines (DALs), in which each product is assembled workstation-by-workstation while AGVs take care of transporting products from one workstation to the next workstation, become increasingly popular due to their high flexibility. Scheduling AGVs is the most critical decision, as it significantly affects DALs’ production rate. This decision will be much more complicated when the buffer size at each workstation becomes smaller, because in this case AGVs’ schedules are more tightly coupled. This paper studies the scheduling of AGVs in a DAL consisting of zero-buffer workstations, aiming to minimize the total time required to complete the assembly of any given set of products. We first build a mixed integer programming model and prove that it is harder than a longstanding open problem. Note that zero-buffer means the highest coupling degree of each AGV’s schedule. We show that this makes the success rate of finding a feasible neighborhood solution from an initial feasible solution low, i.e., heuristics based on neighborhood moves often fail in our problem. Therefore, we develop a new constructive algorithm called “discrete-event-driven rule-based heuristic with tie-branching (DERHwTB)" as well as its accelerated variant called ADERHwTB. Numerical results show that for small-size instances, ADERHwTB is near-optimal because the average percentage gap between the objective value of solutions obtained using ADERHwTB and the optimal objective value obtained using Gurobi is no more than 2.99% in all tested instances (and most of those gaps are less than 2%); while for large-size instances, ADERHwTB can respectively bring at least 38.69%, 21.22%, 22.66%, 28.38%, and 29.06% performance improvement compared with five existing solution methods. We also derive three interesting managerial insights. First, 60%-80% of the total benefit from adding significantly more AGVs to a DAL with 10 workstations can be captured by a DAL with only 2 to 3 AGVs. Second, the role that each AGV plays is larger in a longer DAL, because the ratio between the minimum number of AGVs required to achieve 90% of the maximum possible benefit of a DAL and the number of workstations w decreases with increasing w. Third, the widely believed idea that “balanced allocation of a product’s assembly time among workstations improves the production rate of a continuous assembly line" does not always hold in a DAL, especially when the number of AGVs is small and the distance between two adjacent workstations is large.

Title: Black‐Box Optimization With Simultaneous Statistical Inference for Optimal Performance
Authors: Teng Lian, Jian‐Qiang Hu, Yuhang Wu, Zeyu Zheng
Affiliations: School of Management Fudan University Shanghai China; Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research University of California Berkeley Berkeley California USA
Abstract: ABSTRACT Black‐box optimization is often encountered for decision‐making in complex systems management, where knowledge of the system is limited. Under these circumstances, it is essential to balance the utilization of new information with computational efficiency. In practice, decision‐makers often face the dual tasks of optimization and statistical inference for the optimal performance, in order to achieve it with high reliability. Our goal is to address the dual tasks in an online fashion. Wu et al. (2025) point out that the sample average of performance estimates generated by the optimization algorithm does not necessarily admit a central limit theorem (CLT). We propose an algorithm that not only tackles this issue, but also provides a consistent online estimator for the variance of the performance. Furthermore, we characterize the convergence rate of the coverage probabilities of the asymptotic confidence intervals.

Title: Designing cost-effective climate policies through preference prediction: Evidence from Chinese households’ low-carbon alternatives
Authors: Yuanyuan Tang, Bowei Guo
Abstract: Designing cost-effective climate policies requires understanding not only who accepts low-carbon alternatives but also heterogeneous household preferences. Using a unique household survey from China, this study examines household willingness to accept (WTA) low-carbon alternatives and evaluates the potential efficiency gains from predicting these preferences. The results suggest that demographic characteristics such as location, gender, education, and income are associated with systematic differences in WTA. Knowledge of carbon neutrality and related policies is correlated with WTA in a non-linear manner. Households with basic awareness tend to report lower compensation requirements, while those with greater familiarity report higher stated WTA, possibly reflecting skepticism about the costs and perceived fairness of low-carbon transitions. To translate these insights into policy design, we compare econometric and machine-learning approaches to predicting household preferences. Compared with random assignments, predictive models substantially increase acceptance rates while reducing average compensation. However, the simulation results indicate that targeted investments in public education may generate long-term efficiency gains comparable to or even exceeding those from predictive precision alone

Title: On the optimal size of a joint savings association: Part 2 - efficiency
Authors: Oded Stark, Grzegorz Kosiorowski
Abstract: A joint savings group, JSG, is a form of micro-financing by which people who have limited or no access to formal financial markets can expedite the acquisition of a desired (often indivisible) good. Because typically multiple arrangements of joint saving are feasible, a rule is needed for admitting group formations that bring the expected waiting time to a minimum and rejecting group formations that do not: when people form a JSG, they will want to know the efficient group size. Somewhat surprisingly, the existing literature does not address this need. This lacuna prompted us to develop an analytical framework that yielded the following rule: for a given number of co-savers, N , and a given cost of the desired good, C , the efficient sets of JSGs are sets in each of which every group except for at most one group is of a size that is a multiple of C . Analyzing the robustness of our rule to a change in N and C , we find that the number of efficient sets of JSGs does not change monotonically with respect to N and C . In particular, an increase in N and a decrease in C may actually decrease the number of efficient sets of JSGs.

Title: The Incentive Virtues of Performance‐Based Trade Allowances and Loss Leading
Authors: David Martimort, Jérôme Pouyet
Affiliations: Toulouse School of Economics Toulouse France; ESSEC Business School, CNRS, THEMA Cergy France
Abstract: ABSTRACT A retailer can boost demand for a manufacturer's product through non‐verifiable activities. Performance‐based trade allowances—rebates conditional on the retailer's successful sales efforts—help mitigate this moral hazard problem. In equilibrium, the wholesale contract includes a retail price set below cost, complemented by a rebate for incremental units purchased when efforts successfully increase sales. Loss leading thus emerges as an incentive mechanism, rather than a practice driven by anti‐competitive or exploitative intent. A ban on below‐cost pricing leads to higher retail prices and reduced promotional efforts.

Title: A Markov-based analysis to assess economic feasibility of integration of passenger and freight transport
Authors: Federico Cavallaro, Silvio Nocera, Francesco Rossi
Abstract: This contribution proposes a new method to evaluate economic feasibility of the integration of passenger and freight transport services within a shared operational framework (IPFT). Although the integration of public transport (PT) and freight transport has recently received a great deal of attention in the pursuit of sustainable and efficient mobility, analysis has been mostly limited to a single stakeholder within the system (e.g. PT operator, freight operator, PT user or community member). Few systematic analyses have examined the feasibility of such integration from the perspective of an overall economic gain. However, without shared advantages, the incentive for integration diminishes, and operators are likely to continue working independently. To address this issue, we propose a structured framework based on the Markov’s inequality to assess the circumstances in which integration could be economically viable for operators, while also being environmentally beneficial from a global perspective, considering the implications for each of the aforementioned actors. We present a mathematical model to determine the economic feasibility of such a result and identify the conditions under which it can be achieved. We then apply the model to an urban bus line in the Italian city of Forlì. We find that positive results from an integrated system are guaranteed only if there are specific reductions in the number of kilometres travelled by light commercial vehicles and in the commercial speed of public transport. The implications in terms of absolute operational costs are also presented for a specific configuration, i.e. if the reduction of kilometres driven by LCV is 30% and the reduction of commercial speed of IPFT buses is 15%. In all configurations, PT users and clients face increased costs, which must be offset by measures such as reduced fares and increased service frequency. These findings are supported by a case-based sensitivity analysis and provide valuable insights for transport planners and policymakers aiming to promote more integrated and sustainable transport systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Can the optimal modal split be achieved in multi-modal transportation networks? A dynamic modeling perspective
Authors: Chentao Li, Peng Liu, Pengfei Wang, Xiangyu Wang, Hai-Jun Huang
Abstract: The optimal modal split (OMS) has long been a central topic in transportation research. While previous studies often presuppose the attainability of the OMS in multi-modal transportation networks, this foundational assumption warrants further scrutiny. In reality, travel demand evolves over time, and a fraction of users may deviate from prescribed modal choices. To reflect these practical considerations, this study incorporates demand evolution and user incompliance, and investigates the dynamic adjustment process (DAP). The study aims to identify the conditions under which the OMS can be continuously sustained. Based on this framework, both static and dynamic modal shift strategies are proposed. A simplified Beijing-inspired numerical example is used to illustrate the proposed models and theoretical findings. Theoretical analysis and numerical simulations yield the following key conclusions: (i) A convex stable zone always exists. When the optimal modal split lies within this zone, there exists a feasible modal shift strategy that can continuously maintain it. (ii) The size of the stable zone expands with diagonal dominance in the mode transition matrix and travel demand growth rates, but contracts as the proportion of incompliant users increases. (iii) The proposed static modal shift strategy ensures convergence of the DAP, whereas the dynamic strategy more rapidly approaches the OMS. (iv) Under the static strategy, the convergence zone is a subset of the stable zone. When the OMS lies within the stable zone but outside the convergence zone, its continuous attainment requires the dynamic modal shift strategy.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: To charge or to transfer? Coupled scheduling in smart operating rooms with reinforcement learning-based neighborhood search
Authors: Ziqin Wei, Zongli Dai
Abstract: Powered patient-transfer beds and smart transport systems are increasingly being introduced in hospitals to reduce the manual-handling burden and support patient movement. When such equipment is used for time-critical transfers, finite battery capacity and state-of-charge-dependent availability can couple transport decisions with operating-room schedules. This paper formulates a heterogeneous three-stage surgical scheduling problem that jointly optimizes patient selection, clinical-stage sequencing, PHU/OR/PACU resource assignments, ITB transport-task assignment and order, and SOC-triggered charging. Unlike conventional surgery-scheduling models that treat inter-stage transport as exogenous or resource-free, and unlike AGV logistics models that take clinical service processes as given, the proposed formulation makes clinical and transport-energy decisions mutually endogenous: the clinical schedule releases transport tasks, whereas ITB availability and charging feed back into patient arrival times and medical-resource utilization. The resulting problem has a large decision space with tightly coupled scheduling and energy constraints. We propose QH-MLNS, a reinforcement-learning-enhanced, multi-destruction-strength large neighborhood search algorithm that combines a destroy–repair strategy with multiple destruction strengths, Q-learning-based adaptive operator selection, and dynamic dual-pool retention. The study examines a deployment regime in which battery-powered transfer devices are shared and charging can restrict their availability; it does not assume that such devices are already standard in all hospitals. On the tested resource-constrained and resource-abundant scenarios, QH-MLNS yields 30.3% and 52.5% higher mean hypervolume and 45.6% and 96.2% lower mean inverted generational distance than H-MLNS and MLNS, respectively.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Harness the power law: Robust estimation of tail index and threshold
Authors: Kailin Ding, Zhenyu Cui, Qian Pan, Lingjiong Zhu
Abstract: Accurate tail index estimation is critical for measuring extreme risk in economic and financial systems. We propose a closed-form estimator, the Method of Truncated Moments (MTM), based on matching empirical and theoretical truncated moments. Unlike classical approaches, our method jointly determines the tail index and optimal tail region threshold, which reduces sensitivity to tuning parameters. MTM is asymptotically valid for regularly varying tails and offers an accuracy superior to modern benchmarks. It performs robustly in small samples and remains stable even when convergence to the Pareto limit is slow.

Title: When trust attracts fraud: AI and trust arbitrage
Authors: Xieyu Yin, Fenghua Wen
Abstract: Trust can attract fraud when it delays verification. We develop a two-market signaling model in which generative AI lowers fabrication, verification, and targeting costs. When fabrication becomes profitable before verification, claim credibility first falls and later recovers. Across markets, higher prior quality can delay verification, creating an interval in which only the lower-quality market checks. If targeting becomes profitable in this interval, deceptive sellers enter the higher-quality but less vigilant market, and their entry can initially reverse its reliability advantage. The inflow also triggers verification and deters further entry. We call this self-limiting mechanism trust arbitrage. In the age of generative AI, trust can thus create an endogenous but temporary protection gap that redirects deception across markets.

Title: Does LaTeX enhance perceptions of research quality in economics?
Authors: Alexander James, Tyler Kjorstad
Abstract: We conducted two online survey experiments examining how writing style influences economists’ perceptions of research quality. Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate manuscript cover pages that varied by document editor (Microsoft Word versus LaTeX) and the presence of a spelling or grammar error. In the original experiment, conducted among U.S. economists, spelling and grammar errors significantly reduced perceived research quality, whereas document editor had little effect. In a follow-up experiment, conducted among an international sample of economists, LaTeX use was substantially more common, and manuscripts prepared in LaTeX were generally evaluated more favorably than those prepared in Microsoft Word. Taken together, our findings suggest that careful proofreading and preparing manuscripts in LaTeX are prudent best practices. Depending on the reader, both may improve perceptions of research quality while carrying little or no downside risk.

Title: Ancestral origins of democratic preferences: The role of state experience
Authors: Jaeyoung Hur, Yeonha Jung
Abstract: This study proposes an inverted U-shaped relationship between ancestral state experience and democratic preferences. Compared to stateless societies, primitive states are likely to foster proto-democratic values through a nascent balance between central authority and local autonomy. In contrast, more consolidated pre-modern states typically entrench authoritarian regimes, thereby undermining norms of participatory individual engagement. Evidence aligns with this hypothesis. Using data from the Ethnographic Atlas, we show that moderate exposure to ancestral statehood is positively associated with democratic preferences, while excessive exposure has the reverse pattern. Survey-based evidence corroborates this pattern, suggesting the intergenerational transmission of the ancestral legacy on democratic orientations.

Title: Corporate contributions and political selection: Evidence from Brazil
Authors: Julieta Peveri
Abstract: This paper studies the influence of corporate contributions on political selection and electoral outcomes. To identify the effects, I analyze a Brazilian reform that banned firms’ contributions using a weighted difference-in-differences strategy, exploiting variation in candidates’ reliance on corporate funding prior to the reform. I find that the ban fosters political competition by encouraging challengers and new candidates to run for office. Instead, the reform penalizes incumbents funded by firms by decreasing their likelihood of re-election. These adverse effects are particularly pronounced among underperforming incumbents. I also show that firms tend to donate more to mayors associated with higher corruption, a pattern that does not emerge for other donor types.

Title: Modelling of public transport route choice adaptations to unplanned metro disruptions using smart card data
Authors: Lawrence Christopher Duncan, Benjamin Cottreau, Ouassim Manout
Abstract: It is vital that public transport disruption mitigation strategies are supported by a clear understanding of travel behaviour and preferences, including of disrupted route choices. This paper, for the first time, uses smart card data to analyse multimodal public transport route choices immediately after being disrupted by an unplanned metro service closure while en route. We develop methodologies for identifying commuters and their usual commute route, approximating home/work locations, and identifying disrupted trips and onward post-disruption routes. These methodologies are operationalised in a case study of Lyon, France, where 5031 post-metro-disruption routes are identified, including routes taking bridging buses (bus replacement services). These route observations are used to estimate a multimodal route choice model with a detailed utility function that provides good fit to the data. Route choice preferences and behaviours are analysed and compared with those from usual commute route choices. Some of the key findings are that, post-disruption: there is a stronger dispreference for transferring and a lower dispreference for in-vehicle time, metro is less innately attractive than bus/tram, contrasting with usual commuting preferences, bridging bus is the least innately attractive mode, users have a stronger dispreference for egress time than access time (from the disrupted metro), and there is a positive preference for route robustness. Results are also compared with those from existing studies, impacts of disruptions on travel times are evaluated, and policy implications of the work are discussed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Network motifs reveal mobility disruption during Hurricane Ian
Authors: Zeyu He, Yujie Hu
Abstract: Understanding how natural disasters reshape daily mobility is essential for improving preparedness and strengthening community resilience. This study develops a motif-based analytical framework to quantify mobility disruption during Hurricane Ian in Lee County, Florida, using high-resolution smartphone location data. Daily mobility motifs are constructed at the individual trajectory level and classified by their relationship with inferred home locations, distinguishing home-anchored, home-passing, and non-home mobility structures. Motif changes are then aggregated to the census block-group scale to examine spatial disparities through canonical correlation analysis, clustering, and ordinal logistic regression. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across both motif types and neighborhoods. Within Lee County, Hurricane Ian weakened home-anchored routines, increased home-only and non-home mobility, and produced sharper contractions in simple motifs relative to more complex ones. At the community scale, home-anchored disruption was primarily associated with household composition, education, age structure, and commuting patterns, while non-home motif increases were more strongly linked to geographic exposure, population density, local service proximity, and income conditions. By capturing both routine contraction and disruptions to home anchoring across scales, this study demonstrates a motif-based approach for examining mobility disruption in a severe hurricane context and provides a common analytical basis for comparative applications across geographies and disaster types.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Measuring perceived long-distance accessibility
Authors: Milan L. Moleman, Bert van Wee
Abstract: Over recent years, perceived accessibility has gained interest, yet is primarily studied in the context of daily travel. Relatively little is known about perceived long-distance accessibility, that is, the perceived ability to reach distant destinations of at least 100 km away. This paper develops and tests a measurement scale for perceived long-distance accessibility using data collected in 2025 among long-distance travellers in the Netherlands. First, we conduct an exploratory factor analysis to identify the underlying factors of perceived long-distance accessibility. Next, we apply a confirmatory factor analysis to validate the factor solution. Lastly, we explore relations between perceived long-distance accessibility levels and background information (among others, gender, age, educational attainment, employment status, household income, and level of urbanity) using a linear regression model and latent class analysis. Our analysis reveals four key dimensions of perceived long-distance accessibility among Dutch long-distance travellers: travel options, digital skills, needs and desires, and time availability. Overall, the measurement scale developed in this paper allows to quantitatively identify differences in levels of perceived long-distance accessibility among individuals, which in turn equips policymakers and practitioners with insights necessary to promote a more inclusive long-distance passenger transport system.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Designing transport systems for people with non-visible disabilities
Authors: Chu Shi Qi Chloe, Mikela Chatzimichailidou
Abstract: The accessibility and inclusivity of transport systems are critical to promoting health, equity, and participation, and require an understanding of the experiences and diverse needs of all users. Persons with disabilities, who are recognised as vulnerable road users, face elevated transport risks and increased challenges in navigating transport environments, often resulting in reduced accessibility and participation. Among them, individuals with non-visible disabilities experience compounded challenges, arising not only from the functional limitations of their impairments, but also from social and systemic obstacles due to the unseen nature of their conditions. Despite this, mobility studies specifically focusing on non-visible disabilities – conditions in which impairments are not outwardly apparent – remain limited and fragmented, often confined to condition-centric studies. This scoping review aims to identify the barriers and impacts experienced by individuals with non-visible disabilities when using transport systems, and to highlight key considerations for future interventions. Three non-visible disabilities – autism, dementia, and anxiety disorders – were selected to guide the literature search and analysis. Findings reveal the heterogeneity across the three selected conditions, along with common mobility barriers such as confusion and complexity in transport systems, and the overwhelming nature of the travel environment. Consequently, individuals across the three selected conditions often modify their travel behaviour and reduce social participation. The review identifies key principles for inclusive design, including people-centric planning, systemic integration of support and training, and an emphasis on actionable design changes to create accessible environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: QUBO formulations for parallel machine scheduling
Authors: Frank Phillipson, Yoseph Y. Hutten
Abstract: This paper investigates several Quadratic Unconstrained Binary optimisation (QUBO) formulations for the parallel machine scheduling problem (Formula presented) with the goal of assessing their suitability for quantum annealing and related heuristic optimisation methods. Three QUBO models are constructed, ranging from formulations derived from classical integer and one-hot encodings to a more compact load-balancing based representation. Extensive computational experiments using Simulated Annealing (SA) and Quantum Annealing (QA) reveal substantial differences in scalability and solution quality among the formulations. The alternative load-balanced model consistently yields near-optimal makespans, typically within 1%–3% of the theoretical lower bound, highlighting its stability and effectiveness compared to the more penalty sensitive formulations, whose performance deteriorates for larger instances. Sensitivity analyses further reveal that the appropriate selection of penalty weights and problem-specific parameter tuning significantly influences both solution accuracy and computational effort in QUBO formulations. While current quantum hardware limitations restrict experimentation to small problem sizes, the findings illustrate how compact QUBO designs can better exploit quantum optimisation frameworks. The insights gained in this study provide practical modelling guidelines for future quantum scheduling research and lay the groundwork for extending QUBO-based approaches to more complex scheduling environments.

Title: A time-varying approach to assessing fiscal cyclicality: The role of the European fiscal framework
Authors: Giovanni Carnazza, Francesco Tomasone
Abstract: This paper offers new empirical insights into the relationship between the European fiscal framework and the cyclical stance of fiscal policy in EMU countries. By employing a Time-Varying Coefficient (TVC) model, we generate country- and year-specific measures of fiscal cyclicality from 1995 to 2019. We then quantify the evolving intensity of fiscal rules through a country- and year-specific composite index and examine its relationship with fiscal cyclicality via panel regressions with multiple estimators, including a robust IV-GMM specification that addresses endogeneity concerns. This dual-framework strategy enables us to capture the distortion introduced by real-time revisions and identify a significant procyclical bias in peripheral countries, which is largely masked when ex post data are used. In other words, our findings reveal a marked asymmetry: while the estimated relationship between fiscal rules and cyclicality is neutral or mildly countercyclical in core countries, it is significantly procyclical in peripheral ones when real-time data are considered. These results have important implications for the revised European fiscal framework, as the new indicator (i.e., net expenditure) continues to rely on cycle-sensitive variables and may therefore perpetuate the same structural basis. Our analysis calls for a deeper reconsideration of the methodology used to estimate potential output in the EU. By demonstrating how the interaction between fiscal rules and real-time macroeconomic estimates can generate unintended policy outcomes, this study contributes to a more informed debate on the future of fiscal governance in the euro area.

Title: The macroeconomic effects of a greener technology mix
Authors: Fabrizio Ferriani, Andrea Gazzani, Filippo Natoli
Abstract: What are the macroeconomic implications of a technology-driven green transition? Leveraging granular data on the universe of patents granted in the U.S., we construct a monthly green-innovation indicator defined as the share of U.S. patents filed since 1980 that are classified under climate change mitigation categories. After purging this measure from the effects of oil shocks, credit conditions, and other predictable macroeconomic components, we use it in a structural VAR model as a proxy for reallocation from brown to green innovation and we document that a positive green-innovation shock generates a temporary negative supply effect: industrial production falls, unemployment rises and consumer prices increase, reflecting lower aggregate productivity. These short-run costs, however, are not permanent and the negative implications for economic activity and prices dissipate in the medium run. Technology adjustment leads to a persistent decline in the emissions intensity of output and a shift in energy mix towards renewables, resulting in an overall Pareto improvement for the economy. Our findings are independent of variations in national and international climate policy commitments and point to a dynamic trade-off: greening the technology mix is costly in the short run, but it delivers lasting environmental gains without permanent macroeconomic losses.

Title: Bidding strategies for energy storage operators in a 100% renewable electricity market: A game-theoretic approach
Authors: Arega Getaneh Abate, Dogan Keles, Xiufeng Liu, Salim Hassi, Xiao-Bing Zhang
Abstract: Large-scale energy storage is expected to be a pivotal source of flexibility in electricity systems supplied entirely by renewable energy sources (RES). However, its strategic role in market-based dispatch remains insufficiently understood. In a 100% RES market setting, storage can improve adequacy and renewable utilization by shifting energy across time. It can also acquire market power as the main flexible, price-making technology. In this paper, we develop a Cournot competition model in which storage operators choose quantity bids to maximize profit in a stylized day-ahead electricity market supplied only by RES. Market clearing is represented through residual-demand blocks so that renewable intermittency appears as an intertemporal arbitrage opportunity for storage operators. We formulate the storage operators’ problem in two tractable ways: (ii) a continuous reformulation based on demand blocks, and (ii) an equivalent mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model with big- M linearization. Nash equilibria are computed with an iterative best-response procedure and benchmarked against a centralized social planner problem to quantify efficiency losses from strategic behavior. The model is calibrated to Denmark’s DK1 bidding zone using 2024 day-ahead data and 2030 renewable-capacity and demand projections. The results show that storage reduces imbalances and improves welfare relative to a no-storage case. Concentrated ownership also creates incentives to withhold flexibility, raise prices, and slow the reduction of unmet demand and curtailment. These findings position storage as both a stabilizing resource and a potential source of market power, highlighting the importance of market designs that jointly consider competition, concentration, and capacity deployment in high-RES systems.

Title: From terroir to quality: Handling the run for efficiency across time and space for Italian agri-food firms
Authors: Anna Rita Dipierro, Pierluigi Toma
Abstract: In the actual increasingly competitive market for agricultural firms, the ability to turn inputs into outputs named efficiency has to be pursued by exploiting quality. We conceive quality as a game changer within the per se complex agriculture-environment link. We aim at exploring the critical junctures between efficiency, quality and territorial riskiness, considering space-sensitive products, whose quality is certified as linked to the terroir. We employ an integrated methodological approach of efficiency analysis, causal inference and machine learning. A conditional nonparametric efficiency estimator is assisted by the causal evaluation of the certification effects on efficiency over time, through difference-in-differences technique and genetic matching. Also, a machine learning technique called feature selection is used to make out-of-sample prediction of the efficiency score. The approach is applied to 1133 Italian agri-food firms, measured over 24 internal and external characteristics from 2015 to 2020. Italy stands for a best-practice in the quality products market, despite increasing territorial vulnerability. We question and later find that the collaboration – which is needed to sell certified products of origin – is a vital expedient to run for efficiency over time and by less-caring of spatial threats. Results are relevant for researchers, and promote some win-win strategies for governors and producers in a long-term oriented vision of the sector.

Title: Navigating blockchain assimilation in supply chain organisations: an integrated institutional and innovation assimilation perspective
Authors: Colin Callinan, Trevor Clohessy, Amaya Vega, Graham Heaslip
Affiliations: Atlantic Technological University Department of Business and Marketing, , Sligo; Atlantic Technological University Department of Electronic, Software and Advanced Manufacturing Engineering, , Galway; Atlantic Technological University Department of Enterprise and Technology, , Galway; Atlantic Technological University Faculty of Engineering and Computing, , Galway
Abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how institutional pressures shape the adoption, assimilation and integration of blockchain technologies in supply chain organisations. By combining Gallivan’s innovation assimilation model with institutional theory, the paper explains why blockchain projects frequently stall or regress. Design/methodology/approach Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with blockchain vendors, adopters and ecosystem actors are triangulated with a systematic literature review to map institutional influences across assimilation stages. Findings The analysis identifies four institutional mechanisms; network legitimacy, coordinated uncertainty reduction, institutional paradoxes and cross-organisational cognitive reframing which collectively explain non-linear and uneven assimilation trajectories. Regulative, normative and cognitive pressures function as both enablers and constraints at different stages, particularly during routinisation and infusion. Practical implications The findings provide managers and policymakers with guidance on reducing institutional friction, aligning incentives across supply chain tiers and supporting stable governance and assurance structures required for sustained blockchain integration. Originality/value The study advances supply chain management research by showing how multi-tier governance, power asymmetries and certification regimes shape blockchain assimilation. It offers a multi-level explanation for why blockchain rarely progresses beyond early pilots into embedded, long term practice.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: Integration of planning and scheduling in silicon industry: A bi-level perspective
Authors: Zuocheng Li, Aodong Ma, Rongjuan Luo
Affiliations: Kunming University of Science and Technology, Kunming; School of Logistics and Management Engineering, Yunnan University of Finance and Economics, Kunming
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Editorial: Reproducibility at the International Journal of Forecasting
Authors: Pierre Pinson, Christophe Pérignon, Olivier Akmansoy, Nesrine Dali, Bahman Rostami-Tabar

Title: Beyond circularity: Topological and temporal limits of the circular economy
Authors: Nicolas Merveille
Abstract: The circular economy has established itself as a dominant sustainability paradigm, yet the formal properties of its foundational metaphor, the circle, remain unexamined. This paper identifies two analytically distinct constraints embedded in the dominant circular imaginary. The first is topological: when the operative metaphor functions as a single closed loop, it reproduces the cycle graph, a one-dimensional structure with zero redundancy and minimal resilience. The second is temporal: the assessment apparatus associated with circularity operates within quantitative, sequential time (chronos) and renders qualitative, heterogeneous temporalities (kairos) structurally invisible. The claim defended here is specific. Sustainability paradigms generally pose time as a problem left open; the circular economy's founding metaphor figures time as resolved (return, cycle, regeneration) while its apparatus operationalizes only chronos. This blindness is not general ignorance but performative contradiction. Empirical evidence from three continents (African solar projects, Mexican circular assessment, Peruvian extraction) substantiates the diagnosis. We propose a polyrhythmic completion structured as a wheel, with Doughnut Economics as the rim, regeneration as the hub, and ArtefactKairos (institutional devices for temporal composition) as the spokes, operationalized through the Temporal Composition Diagnostic (TCD), a four-step governance protocol. The TCD is applied to a published sugar beet pulp biorefinery assessment that models feedstock as a fixed daily input without addressing the seasonal harvest sustaining it, then calibrated ex ante against the Antamina mining region in Peru. In both settings it reveals what standard assessment cannot detect and specifies the institutional clauses it would generate.

Title: Beyond generation: Clean energy accommodation and health-related defensive expenditure among Chinese households
Authors: Jing-Yue Liu, Xiang-Jie Liu, Yue-Jun Zhang
Abstract: The social value of clean electricity depends not only on how much is generated but also on whether power systems can absorb and deliver it for use rather than curtail it. This study examines whether improved clean energy accommodation reduces households' health-related defensive expenditure. Using China's Plan on Clean Energy Accommodation as a quasi-natural experiment and micro-panel data from the China Family Panel Studies for 2012–2022, we find that the policy reduced residents' out-of-pocket medical expenditure in policy-targeted regions by about 18% on average, with larger reductions among rural residents and in regions facing larger pre-policy accommodation gaps. Consistent with this reduction, supporting evidence indicates that the policy reduced renewable curtailment, increased realized clean electricity output, and improved ambient air quality; it was also associated with cleaner household energy use and more frequent exercise, especially in rural areas. These gains, however, were unevenly distributed, with larger effects in net electricity-exporting and resource-rich regions, areas with limited healthcare service capacity, and among lower-income, male, and middle-aged residents. An illustrative calculation suggests potential annual savings of RMB 261.2 billion (US$38.3 billion) in out-of-pocket medical expenditure across the policy-targeted regions. These findings underscore the importance of clean energy accommodation and provide evidence to inform policies aimed at translating renewable electricity into more equitable household welfare gains.

Title: A bi-level optimization model for urban bicycle lane planning with a globally optimal branch-and-price-and-cut algorithm
Authors: Lexing Zhang, Michael W. Levin, Mobina Nankali
Abstract: Cycling safety remains a major challenge because riders are frequently exposed to mixed traffic, which suppresses cycling adoption and limits the growth of sustainable mobility. To address this issue, we model the problem as a Stackelberg game in which the planner seeks to minimize cyclists’ exposure to mixed traffic while users respond by choosing routes that minimize their perceived travel times, and we develop a bilevel network design model that selects protected bicycle lanes under a construction-length budget to reduce cyclists’ unprotected exposure. The model is solved using a branch-and-price-and-cut framework with finite-convergence and global-optimality guarantees. Experiments on several benchmark city-scale networks demonstrate that the approach effectively lowers exposure and can solve practical urban networks to small certified optimality gaps within reasonable computation times. The results further show that key algorithmic parameters shape both the resulting network designs and the computational performance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: The (hidden) Samaritan contest
Authors: Rabah Arezki, Youssouf Camara, Frederick Van Der Ploeg, Grégoire Rota-Graziosi
Abstract: This paper explores whether foreign aid is driven by a (hidden) contest amongst donors to access natural resources, exploiting the timing and size of major mineral discoveries using a gravity model for a large panel of countries. Results show that recipient countries that experience major discoveries receive more, not less, bilateral aid, all else equal. Our main result is driven indirectly by China's entry into the World Trade Organization in 2001, which intensified global competition for access to natural resources. We conclude that the energy transition and its requirement in minerals will further exacerbate the (hidden) contest amongst aid donors.

Title: The macroeconomic effects of purely forward-looking uncertainty shocks: Evidence from the euro area
Authors: Svetlana Rujin
Abstract: If the underlying data-generating process operates at a higher frequency than observed data, timing and dynamic restrictions in structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) may be misspecified. Building on Berger et al. (2020), I propose an alternative identification scheme that jointly relaxes the zero-impact restriction on realized volatility and the zero-lag restrictions on macroeconomic variables in the volatility block, estimated with a richer twelve-lag specification. Applied to euro area data, the identified shocks depress real activity gradually and with a delay, unlike the macro-neutral U.S. evidence, though they account for only a modest share of real fluctuations.

Title: Weaponized reputation: Experimental evidence on the misuse of coordinated punishments
Authors: Haihan Yu
Abstract: This paper experimentally studies how coordinated punishment can be misused. In a repeated trust game with public reputation, we compare a silent commitment treatment, where Agents privately choose a review threshold (the minimum payment required for a positive review), with a public commitment treatment, where the review threshold is observable before Principals choose payments. Public commitment significantly reduces cooperation: effort and payments fall relative to silent commitment. Public commitment also turns posted review thresholds into more enforceable demands: Principals are substantially more likely to meet visible thresholds. Successful zero-effort extraction, in which an Agent exerts no effort but sets a positive review threshold met by the Principal’s payment, is significantly more frequent under public commitment. Coordinated punishments can therefore discipline misconduct, but may also create tools for extortion.

Title: A rational bubble model with momentum
Authors: Feng Liu, Joseph S. White
Abstract: Standard rational greater-fool models (e.g., Allen et al., 1993; Liu and Conlon, 2018) generate bubbles but do not generate momentum. Behavioral models with bounded rationality (e.g., Hong and Stein, 1999) generate momentum but do not generate rational bubbles. We expand an existing rational greater-fool model to show how momentum emerges during asset bubbles.

Title: Geopolitical risk and fiscal financing capacity in E7 economies: does institutional quality matter?
Authors: Umar Farooq, Mosab I. Tabash, Abdulrahman Alomair, Abdulateif A. Almulhim
Abstract: This study examines whether geopolitical risk (GPR) affects tax revenue mobilization (TXR) in E7 economies and whether institutional quality (INQ) helps mitigate this effect. Using annual data for China, India, Brazil, Russia, Mexico, Indonesia, and Türkiye over 1985–2024, the study employs the Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) estimator, with Fully Modified Ordinary Least Squares (FMOLS) used for robustness. The results indicate that geopolitical risk significantly reduces tax revenue mobilization, while stronger institutional quality improves revenue performance. Moreover, the interaction between GPR and INQ is positive and significant, confirming that institutional quality weakens the adverse effect of geopolitical risk on tax revenue. The findings highlight the importance of institutional capacity in strengthening fiscal resilience and sustaining government financing capacity during periods of geopolitical uncertainty.

Title: The exchange rate puzzle and the systematic component of monetary policy: Evidence from Mexico
Authors: Jesús Eduardo López-Mares, Rogelio Varela-Llamas, Juan Manuel Ocegueda-Hernández
Abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate puzzle following contractionary monetary policy shocks in a small open economy. Using a Bayesian SVAR for Mexico, we compare three cumulative identification schemes: pure sign restrictions on impulse response functions (IRFs), a closed-economy Taylor-type rule with contemporaneous sign and zero restrictions, and an exchange-rate-augmented rule. Neither pure sign restrictions nor the closed-economy rule yields a precisely estimated overshooting pattern—only the augmented rule does. Robust to alternative specifications, these results suggest that omitting the exchange rate from the systematic component of monetary policy may hinder shock identification in small open economies.

Title: Endogenous depopulation and economic growth
Authors: Alberto Bucci, Klaus Prettner
Abstract: Fertility rates have declined dramatically across almost all high-income countries over the past decades. In some countries, population growth is already negative and many more are projected to exhibit negative population growth in the future. This raises concerns about potential economic prospects. Indeed, endogenous and semi–endogenous growth models imply that a shrinking workforce would lead to declining income growth and, perhaps, even to stagnation. We include an endogenous quantity/quality trade–off between fertility and human capital accumulation in these models to assess the extent to which a declining number of people (i.e., workers) may be compensated by increasing education. We demonstrate that economic growth does not necessarily decline with population shrinkage: in many scenarios, human capital investment can offset demographic headwinds and sustain technological progress.

Title: Approximately efficient resource allocation: A theoretical and experimental evaluation
Authors: Nicole Immorlica, Robizon Khubulashvili, Sera Linardi, Brendan Lucier, Joshua Mollner, Glen Weyl
Abstract: Matching mechanisms that elicit strength of preference can exhibit efficiency gains over those that do not. To quantify these gains, we propose a measure of approximate ex-ante Pareto efficiency. We use this notion to quantify the efficiency improvement of the raffles mechanism (which we define) over the deferred acceptance mechanism (DA). We complement our theoretical analyses with experimental results. Using human subjects, we find that the raffles mechanism yields higher average payoffs as predicted by the theory, despite the fact that subjects play only approximately optimal strategies.

Title: Fare evasion strategies, perceived safety, and travel choices in public transport: evidence from a vignette experiment
Authors: Benedetto Barabino, Martina Carra, Jérémy Celse, Roberto Ventura
Abstract: Fare evasion poses persistent challenges for public transport systems, with implications for financial sustainability, social norms, corporate image, and perceived safety and security. While deterrence strategies such as increasing inspection frequency or fine severity are widely used, their effects on passengers’ perceptions and behavioural spillovers remain weakly evidenced. This study examines how anti–fare evasion cues influence travel preferences, perceived safety and security, and fare‐evasion intentions, accounting for time of day and competition from a ride‑sharing service (RSS). Four research questions were examined through a vignette‑based randomised experiment. Participants chose among a non‑manipulated bus route, a manipulated route (enforcement or service cue), and an RSS alternative across seven conditions crossing enforcement cues (inspection, fines, neutral) and period (day/night). The results showed that the effects of anti–fare evasion cues were small and statistically uncertain. Neither inspections nor fines produced clear improvements in perceived safety or security (RQ1), and the enforcement type showed no consistent direct effect on the choice of the manipulated route (RQ2). Night-time conditions did not meaningfully change safety or risk perceptions, nor did they reliably moderate the association between perceived route safety and route choice (RQ3). Fare evasion was more frequent at night and less frequent on the manipulated route yet contrasts between Fine and Inspection treatments remained small and imprecisely estimated (RQ4). The RSS garnered only 3.73% choices amid price differentials. Thus, deterrence failed to bolster reassurance or ridership proxies, with choices driven by safety and security perceptions independently of cues. Night primarily led to increased evasion without corresponding gains in safety and security. Policies should pair targeted enforcement with service enhancements, particularly nocturnal, in multimodal contexts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Underestimation of the costs of owning and running a car
Authors: Adam Joachim Shier, Shane Timmons, Peter D. Lunn
Abstract: Car ownership and use appears less responsive to cost increases and income declines than might be expected, a pattern often attributed to habit formation and lifestyle adjustment. An additional explanation is that motorists may underestimate how much they spend on owning and running a car, but there is little empirical evidence testing this possibility. Using a representative sample of 801 motorists, we compare intuitive estimates of the annual motoring costs with detailed itemised expenditure across all major fixed (e.g., tax, insurance) and variable (e.g., fuel/charging, parking) costs over the same period. Total reported costs are almost 50% higher than motorists intuit. Median intuitive costs were €2,000, while median itemised costs were €2,923, excluding purchase price and depreciation. Most motorists (over 70%) exhibit this underestimation bias, with similar rates across engine types and socio-demographic groups. These findings are consistent with recall failures and salience bias when motorists consider the costs of owning and running a car, with potential implications for the persistence of car ownership. Improving the visibility and aggregation of motoring costs may complement fiscal and infrastructural measures aimed at supporting sustainable modal shift.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Container shipping disruptions and the economics of decarbonization
Authors: Hugo Morão
Abstract: This paper examines how containerized shipping disruptions affect macroeconomic and financial conditions for decarbonization. The analysis identifies supply chain shocks using exogenous price surcharges from major container carriers in a structural vector autoregression. Supply chain disruptions weaken the economic case for clean energy investment through three channels. Policy uncertainty raises the Transition Risk Index while depressing carbon prices on impact. Clean technology costs rise and suppress expected decarbonization investment returns. Damage to climate policy credibility advantages fossil fuel interests. Carbon prices fall on impact before recovering as substitution toward more carbon-intensive production raises allowance demand. Expected decarbonization investment returns remain depressed while fossil fuel stocks appreciate, as markets price in weaker future climate policy. Supply chain vulnerabilities generate persistent headwinds for the energy transition that operate through financial market channels.

Title: Trading electrons: Predicting DART spread spikes in ISO electricity markets
Authors: Emma Hubert, Dimitrios Lolas, Ronnie Sircar
Abstract: We study the problem of forecasting and optimally trading day-ahead versus real-time (DART) price spreads in U.S. wholesale electricity markets. Building on the framework of Galarneau-Vincent et al., we extend spike prediction from a single zone to a multi-zone setting and treat both positive and negative DART spikes within a unified statistical model. To translate directional signals into economically meaningful positions, we develop a structural and market-consistent price impact model based on day-ahead bid stacks. This yields closed-form expressions for the optimal vector of zonal INC/DEC quantities, capturing asymmetric buy/sell impacts and cross-zone congestion effects. When applied to NYISO, the resulting impact-aware strategy significantly improves the risk-return profile relative to unit-size trading and highlights substantial heterogeneity across markets and seasons.

Title: Deployment-oriented validation of vessel energy efficiency inference for maritime decarbonisation policy
Authors: Xun Yang, Ran Yan
Abstract: AI-based vessel fuel-consumption models are used for emission accounting, compliance screening, and decarbonisation planning, but their reported accuracy depends on how validation is designed. Using high-frequency data from 27 ocean-going vessels, this study tests whether random mixed validation overstates model performance. We compare it with maritime use-case tests for later-period prediction, unseen trips, unseen vessels, cross-type transfer, and data-scarce transfer. Across 64 model-task combinations, use-case-aligned held-out errors are 9.18 percentage points higher on average than random mixed-validation estimates. Prediction error also reverses direction across settings, indicating that accuracy metrics alone can hide policy-relevant over- or under-estimation. In a container-ship CII case study, rating accuracy ranges from 34.4% to 71.7%, while 11.7% to 100.0% of action-required D/E vessel-years are missed. These results indicate that regulatory and planning applications require validation aligned with the intended maritime use case, with reporting of both error magnitude and bias direction.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Do aviation hazard rankings overlook conservation-concern birds in U.S. wildlife strikes?
Authors: Amir Rafe, Subasish Das
Abstract: Airports concentrate aircraft and birds in shared space, making wildlife strikes a flight-safety problem and a documented source of avian mortality. We analyze 343,997 U.S. wildlife-strike records from 1990 to 2025 with a framework that corrects for reporting growth, models per-strike severity, and ranks species by aviation hazard and conservation status. A detection-aware count model bounds the true rise in the strike rate between 3.4 and 8 fold, below the widely cited fourteen-fold rise in the reported rate. A random-parameters ordered probit shows that engine ingestion and body mass dominate severity, with the mass effect growing more variable at higher impact speeds. Conservation weighting shifts 112 of 310 ranked species by more than 30 places, elevating aerial insectivores, migratory warblers, and grassland passerines, including the Vulnerable Chimney Swift. The results support region- and season-specific mitigation that protects aircraft and declining birds together.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Challenges in comparing measured and modelled annual average noise levels around airports
Authors: Rebekka C. van der Grift, Alireza Amiri Simkooei, Mirjam Snellen
Abstract: Aircraft noise has a significant impact on communities near airports. To regulate noise, annual average levels such as L den are modelled across large areas. This study examines the consistency between L den predicted by the European Civil Aviation Conference Doc 29 model and measurements from noise monitoring terminals around Amsterdam Airport Schiphol from 2017 to 2024. While strong correlations confirm Doc29′s suitability for system-level assessments, systematic biases persist, with nighttime levels L night generally overestimated and L den underestimated. Three potential sources were identified: difference between modelled and flown tracks, background noise influencing measured levels, and undetected flights, particularly for quieter aircraft and in low noise regions. Accounting for these factors improves correlation and reduces deviation between measurements and predictions. These results demonstrate promising methods for enabling noise model validation near airports. Further improvements in detection methods and operational modelling will increase the robustness of noise assessments and better support evidence-based policy development around major airports.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Pragmatism, not ideology: drivers of e-bike sharing usage intensity
Authors: Michael Stiebe, Frank Christian Krysiak, Widar von Arx, Benjamin Weggelaar
Abstract: What drives usage intensity among registered e-bike sharing system (EBSS) users – distinguishing power users from dormant registrants – remains underexplored despite its importance for system viability. We link survey responses from 1,844 registered users to their individual trip histories within an operational dataset of 1.4 million trips from free-floating S-Pedelec and dock-based e-bike sharing systems operating concurrently in Basel, Switzerland. Using Gaussian Mixture Model clustering and an ordered logit model, we find that usage is highly concentrated (Gini = 0.77) and primarily substitutes public transport. Pro-environmental self-identity negatively associates with high-intensity user (“power-user”) status. Instead, intensive use is associated with multimodal integration and perceived functional superiority over public transport. System design distinguishes two distinct pragmatic archetypes: dock-based “routine optimizers” and free-floating “flexibility maximizers”. These findings suggest EBSS policy should emphasize multimodal integration and service reliability calibrated to EBSS’s genuine but bounded role in sustainable urban mobility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Trade and uneven development: evidence from China’s tea exports
Authors: Xinsheng Cui, Ruixia Cui, Guangbin Cheng
Abstract: Why could the expansion of international trade contribute to industrial development in one part of the world while reinforcing Malthusian forces in another? We examine this question through the dramatic expansion of Chinese tea exports to Western markets between 1776 and 1910. Exploiting variation in local exposure to changes in national tea exports based on agro-climatic suitability and trade costs, we show that greater export exposure increased population growth. The demographic response operated through a relaxation of preventive checks, reflected in earlier marriage and higher fertility. In contrast, tea exports generated no persistent gains in per-capita income or human capital. The findings suggest that the gains from international trade can be absorbed primarily through demographic expansion in economies subject to Malthusian forces, shedding light on the uneven developmental consequences of global economic integration.

Title: Recovery strategies for disrupted seaside planning in container terminals: a systematic review
Authors: Fabricio Niebles-Atencio, Eduardo Lalla-Ruiz, Stefan Voß
Affiliations: University of Hamburg; University of Twente; Escuela de Ingeniería Industrial, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso
Abstract: Disruptions in container terminal operations, such as vessel delays, equipment failures, and weather-related uncertainties, significantly affect the efficiency and reliability of seaside planning activities. This paper presents a systematic and synthesis-driven review of recovery strategies for disrupted seaside planning problems, focussing on the Berth Allocation Problem (BAP), Quay Crane Assignment Problem (QCAP), and Quay Crane Scheduling Problem (QCSP). Based on a systematic analysis of 46 studies – predominantly peer-reviewed journal and conference papers, complemented by a small number of closely related scholarly works – published between 2007 and 2025, this review provides a unified framework that links disruption characteristics, recovery strategies, solution methods, and operational outcomes. The literature is examined from a decision-support perspective, identifying dominant recovery paradigms, including disruption management, rescheduling, and hybrid proactive–reactive approaches, and analysing their associated trade-offs in terms of solution quality, computational effort, and schedule stability. The results reveal several key limitations in existing research, including the limited consideration of disruption sources and propagation effects, the scarcity of integrated recovery models, and the reliance on narrow performance metrics focused primarily on cost and delay. In addition, the review highlights the emerging potential of adaptive and learning-based approaches for real-time recovery under dynamic conditions. The paper contributes to the operations research and maritime logistics literature by providing a structured synthesis of recovery strategies and by identifying critical research gaps related to integration, evaluation frameworks, and data-driven decision support. These insights support the development of more resilient and adaptive planning systems for container terminal operations.

Title: Synchronous production and intralogistics of smart assembly cell line under graduation intelligent manufacturing system
Authors: Shiquan Ling, Binyang Liu, Mingxing Li, Daqiang Guo, Ting Qu, Zhen He, George Q. Huang, Ming Li
Affiliations: School of Intelligent Manufacturing, Shenzhen Polytechnic University, Shenzhen, People’s Republic of China; Jinan University (Zhuhai Campus); The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou); Tianjin University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University; The Hong Kong Polytechnic-Daya Bay Technology and Innovation Research Institute, Huizhou, Guangdong, People's Republic of China
Abstract: Assembly cell lines (ACLs), originating from the Toyota Production System and widely adopted in electronics manufacturing, divide a conveyor line into multiple assembly cells (ACs). Each AC stores the required parts, enabling multi-skilled workers to complete the entire product assembly at their own pace. With the advancement of Industry 4.0 technologies, smart ACLs increasingly integrate human and machine capabilities and support flexible reconfiguration to meet personalised production demands. However, variability in manual operations and manufacturing uncertainties poses significant challenges. These factors not only affect the performance of ACLs but also hinder the synchronisation between production activities and material supply (intralogistics), leading to waiting times, downtime, and reduced productivity. This challenge is referred to as the production-intralogistics synchronisation (PiLS) problem. To address this issue, this paper proposes a real-time, data-driven PiLS mechanism based on the Graduated Intelligent Manufacturing System (GiMS) framework. A human-cyber-physical architecture and a multi-objective optimisation model are developed, and an improved multi-objective simulated annealing (IMOSA) algorithm is introduced. Case studies demonstrate superior PiLS performance compared with traditional scheduling approaches, offering an effective solution for dynamic manufacturing environments with human involvement.

Title: Managing a continuous-time make-to-stock system with finite resources
Authors: Qian Luo, Qingguo Bai, Jianxin Fang, Nicholas Yeo
Affiliations: Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University; Qufu Normal University

Title: A new school bus location routing problem with mixed loads and bus stop selection
Authors: Willem Gerhard Meiring, Jan H. van Vuuren
Affiliations: Stellenbosch University

Title: Intrafirm integration versus separation in product and digital service competition
Authors: Li Li, Mengqing Zhang
Affiliations: Sun Yat-Sen University
Abstract: Digital servitization increasingly requires manufacturing firms to coordinate product and digital service decisions. We develop a duopoly model in which each firm chooses between integration, where product and digital service decisions are jointly coordinated, and separation, where the manufacturing and digital service units make these decisions independently. We characterise equilibrium digital service levels, prices, demand, profits, and organisational choices under symmetric and asymmetric structures. Integration yields higher digital service levels and greater demand than separation when both firms adopt the same structure, while the price ranking reverses as digital research and development (R&D) cost increases. Separation can generate higher profits when competition is sufficiently intense and also under relatively weak competition when digital R&D cost is low; integration becomes more profitable under relatively weak competition when digital R&D cost is high. Profitability also depends on the rival's organisational structure, making firms' choices strategically interdependent. Integration by both firms can constitute a Nash equilibrium even when both would earn higher profits under separation, giving rise to a prisoner's dilemma. Extensions with heterogeneous digital R&D cost coefficients and strategic transfer pricing show that this equilibrium tension can persist.

Title: Profile Bayesian optimization for expensive computer experiments
Authors: Courtney Kyger, James Fernandez, John A Grunenwald, James Braun, Annie S Booth
Affiliations: Department of Statistics, Vriginia Tech; Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, NC State University
Abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian optimization (BO) procedure aimed at identifying the “profile optima” of a deterministic black-box computer simulation that has a single control parameter and multiple nuisance parameters. The profile optima capture the optimal response values as a function of the control parameter. Our objective is to identify them across the entire plausible range of the control parameter. Classic BO, which targets a single optimum over all parameters, does not explore the entire control parameter range. Instead, we develop a novel two-stage acquisition scheme to balance exploration across the control parameter and exploitation of the profile optima, leveraging deep and shallow Gaussian process surrogates to facilitate uncertainty quantification. We are motivated by a computer simulation of a diffuser in a rotating detonation combustion engine, which returns the energy lost through diffusion as a function of various design parameters. We aim to identify the lowest possible energy loss as a function of the diffuser’s length; understanding this relationship will enable well-informed design choices. Our “profile Bayesian optimization” procedure outperforms traditional BO and profile optimization methods on a variety of benchmarks and proves effective in our motivating application.

Title: Are international diversification benefits still achievable? turn on machine learning
Authors: Ana Sofia Monteiro, Silva Nuno, Helder Sebastião
Abstract: This study uses multivariate Machine Learning—Dynamic Conditional Correlation (DCC) models to dynamically forecast returns and covariances. The resulting forecasts are then used to select international diversified portfolios.
