To mitigate that problem, in this paper, we propose a ShiftedDEA approach that applies the MEP to a modified, bias-corrected sample. Specifically, a non-oriented proportional Directional Distance Function (pDDF) model and homogeneous bootstrap are used to estimate the bias-corrected efficiency of the observations so that the DEA frontier is shifted accordingly. The projection onto the ShiftedDEA frontier can be done in a second phase and using any metric or orientation. The proposed approach can be used with convex or non-convex technologies as well as with multiple heterogeneous technologies. Computational experiments to test the proposed approach under different circumstances, gauging its predictive accuracy as well as its computational expense are presented. The proposed approach has been applied also to a real-world case study involving 31 energy savings projects.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Dual-sourcing or backup supplier? Building a viable supply chain under supply disruption risk with quality heterogeneity
Authors: Jiasen Sun, Wenbo Shao
Abstract: Firms can establish redundancy mechanisms through the dual-source procurement (DP) or backup supplier (BS) strategy to build viable supply chains that can combat supply disruption risks. However, structural redundancy can lead to product quality heterogeneity. This study examines three procurement strategies under supply disruption risk: single-source procurement, DP, and BS. This study constructs differential game models for the three procurement strategies to explore how firms make strategic choices to enhance supply chain viability (SCV) in the presence of quality heterogeneity. Findings indicate that under the DP and BS strategies, the wholesale price and procurement volume vary in a U-shaped manner as the impact of quality heterogeneity on product goodwill (IQHPG) increases. Intuitively, an increase in the disruption incidence rate will induce the suppliers to reduce their quality investments before the disruption. Counterintuitively, under the DP strategy, the high-quality supplier’s pre-disruption quality investment increases with the disruption incidence rate. Under the DP and BS strategies, the manufacturer’s pre-disruption advertising investment decreases as the IQHPG increases to mitigate the free-riding effect. From the perspective of firm profitability, the manufacturer will tend to prefer the DP strategy when the supply disruption incidence rate is high and the IQHPG is low. However, the manufacturer and suppliers will not be able to reach a consensus on their strategic choices. From the perspective of SCV, when the disruption incidence rate is low and the IQHPG is high, the DP strategy will be the optimal choice for SCV; conversely, the BS strategy will be the optimal choice.

Title: Cassandra: An automated AI-based surveillance system to forecast bank distress from financial news
Authors: Anastasios Petropoulos, Luca Parafioriti, Alexandros Kouris, Javier Arranz Barquero, Christoffer Kok
Abstract: This article introduces Cassandra , an AI-driven automated surveillance system designed to predict bank distress using only financial news, enabling more timely and proactive supervision by drawing on a broader real-time data source, never exploited before for this purpose. Unlike traditional approaches to forecasting bank distress, Cassandra overcomes the endogeneity and time-lags inherent in balance-sheet-based indicators by accounting for the financial sector’s overall perception of the entity derived exclusively from financial news. To process such qualitative unstructured data, Cassandra’s infrastructure incorporates advanced NLP techniques, such as named entity recognition and sentiment analysis, in a novel application. The system leverages a mix-of-agents approach built on a heterogeneous array of general and financial sentiments obtained via large language models. Building on this foundation and marking an innovation in this field, we build a set of regulatory-focused sentiment analysis models. This comprehensive architecture forms an automated pipeline for banking supervision applications, serving as a proof-of-concept early-warning system for potential distress events with an out-of-time tested hit rate above 80%.

Title: Work “as if people mattered”: Reassessing the contribution of E. F. Schumacher
Authors: Franck Bailly, Benjamin Dubrion
Abstract: While academic literature has widely acclaimed E. F. Schumacher's work for its critique of the industrial production system and its contribution to the depletion of natural resources, it has downplayed the author's reflections on work. This article aims to reassess Schumacher as a genuine theorist of work. By conceptualising ecological and work issues as two sides of the same productive reality, we demonstrate that Schumacher emerges as a proponent of the thesis of the centrality of work in human life, outlining concrete pathways to strive towards what he terms “Good Work”. Schumacher's reflections on work thus serve not only to critique the manner in which mainstream economics apprehends the nature and purposes of work, but also to more broadly question the conceptual and normative assumptions underlying that paradigm.

Title: Strategic analysis meets the black box in public transport network design
Authors: Valentina Gómez, Sergio Jara-Díaz, Andrés Fielbaum
Abstract: Public transport network design lies at the intersection of strategic theory and algorithmic complexity. While strategic models offer general insights using simplified representations, and algorithmic approaches solve large-scale problems via heuristics, these two perspectives have largely evolved in isolation. This paper bridges the gap by enhancing a state-of-the-art genetic algorithm with a theoretically grounded decision rule: the Divisibility Index introduced by Gómez et al. (2026) , a strategic quantity that determines whether a public transport line should be split into two. This index is integrated into a genetic algorithm, potentially splitting the candidate lines in every iteration when convenient. This enhanced method is tested on a stylised city under four distinct demand scenarios, each favouring a different network topology: hub-and-spoke, feeder-trunk, direct-based, and exclusive-based. In all cases, this seemingly minor (yet strategic) tweak leads to significant performance gains: the modified algorithm consistently finds better solutions in a single iteration than the original version does in fourteen. Notably, the resulting networks match expected topologies for each demand pattern. Similar results arise in adapted real-city representations. Those results highlight the potential of combining strategic public transport analysis and complex algorithms − not only to improve solution quality and speed, but also to reveal new strategic insights.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Learning-based model predictive control for train timetabling and rolling stock circulation planning with flexible train composition on Y-type metro lines
Authors: Kun Ji, Yihui Wang, Andrea D’Ariano, Zhengwen Liao, Jiateng Yin
Abstract: To better satisfy the uneven spatiotemporal distribution of passenger demand on the Y-type metro line, the concept of flexible train composition is explored, where the train compositions can be changed flexibly at a joint station and terminal stations connected to depots. A mixed-integer nonlinear programming model is developed to jointly optimize train timetables, rolling stock circulation plans, and flexible train compositions on a Y-type metro line. Using standard linearization techniques, the model is reformulated as a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model with an objective that balances operating cost and passenger service quality. To incorporate short-term demand variations and support real-time operations, the integrated MILP is embedded into a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework, which updates timetabling decisions dynamically based on demand forecasts. However, solving the resulting MPC-based MILP in real time is computationally challenging due to the large number of binary decision variables. To overcome this limitation, we propose a learning-based optimization framework that integrates offline learning with online mixed-integer optimization. The learning module is trained offline on historical MPC solutions and is designed to selectively predict a subset of high-impact binary decisions, including train composition and routing choices, thereby reducing the combinatorial complexity of the online optimization problem. The predicted decisions are then fixed in an online MILP to optimize the remaining variables while preserving feasibility and consistency across rolling horizons. In addition, a feasibility-efficiency balancing strategy is introduced through selective decision prediction and feasibility-aware penalized training, which reduces infeasible learning outputs. Numerical experiments based on real-world operational data from Guangzhou Metro Line 14 show that the proposed learning-based MPC framework achieves real-time timetabling, while maintaining solution quality comparable to a full MPC-based optimization benchmark, with only a marginal loss in feasibility. Computational results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating learning and MPC for real-time timetable optimization.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Ex-ante distributionally robust fleet deployment and slot allocation on liner shipping networks
Authors: Kang Chen, Zhongyang Wei, Xu Xin, Qiangqiang Jiang, Zhongzhen Yang, Jihong Chen
Abstract: We study ex-ante fleet deployment and slot allocation on fixed weekly liner networks. Before O–D demand, freight-rate coefficients, and deliverable capacity are realized, the carrier chooses vessel deployment, cadence, and baseline slot allocation; the fixed plan is evaluated for profit and reliability, with no scenario-dependent re-optimization. The central idea is to let one deployment-allocation plan carry three linked roles: it protects accepted O–D demand, prices accepted flows through offline conservative revenue coefficients, and enforces correlated deliverable-capacity safeguards over shared disruption regions. We formulate a mixed-integer conic model that links these three uncertainty blocks through common decisions, not one estimated joint ambiguity set. Demand and deliverable capacity receive moment-based distributionally robust safeguards: Cantelli lower-confidence caps and a Boole-based second-order cone approximation for protected capacity reliability. Freight rates enter only as fixed offline conservative revenue coefficients, not dynamic prices, recourse decisions, or an in-model pricing-optimization block. In this formulation, the fleet, cadence, and voyage decisions directly set how much correlated capacity loss each shared disruption region is exposed to. To keep the conic model tractable at network scale, a PCA-based outer-approximation layer reduces the covariance dimension in the capacity certificates, retaining the leading directions and bounding the residual tail. On LINER-LIB-derived instances, out-of-sample diagnostics, component ablations, a 21-point PCA threshold sweep, and a public-data calibration and holdout plausibility check show how the safeguards change deployment decisions and when PCA-OA improves tractability. The evidence supports internal consistency and plausibility, not operational validation on proprietary carrier data.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Strategic service network design for integrated road-rail express freight based on existing passenger train services and road service networks
Authors: Qi Li, Yuguang Wei, Bo Fang, Yang Xia, Ziqiang Hu
Abstract: Railway-based express transportation has become an important component of modern logistics systems, offering an alternative to express deliveries. To enhance coordination between road and rail transportation, this study investigates a strategic service network design and freight flow allocation problem for integrated road-rail express freight, in which shipments can be transported either entirely by road or through a combination of road transport and existing passenger trains equipped with attached parcel carriages. An integrated road-rail express service network is constructed to support flexible mode choice, road-rail transfers, and cross-line transshipment within the railway service network. Based on this network, an integer linear programming model is established to jointly optimize the design of the railway express service network and freight flow allocation, to minimize total system operating cost. To address the computational challenges in large-scale instances, a hybrid solution framework combining adaptive large neighborhood search (ALNS) with a commercial solver is developed. The effectiveness of the methodology is evaluated through numerical experiments of different scales and a case study based on a realistic service-network setting. The results indicate that the integrated road-rail express service network achieves a lower total system cost than a road-only transportation alternative and better accommodates degraded road operating conditions. In addition, the optimization model tends to select long-distance train services for express freight operations.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Passenger-level response based resilience assessment of urban rail transit systems under daily disturbances
Authors: Xiaowei Liu, Bo Du, Jinqu Chen, Tao Liu, Qiyuan Peng, Xu Yan
Abstract: The emergency response capability and resilience of urban rail transit (URT) systems are critical to smart cities. Beyond widely studied severe disturbances, low-intensity but high-frequency daily disturbances likewise continuously challenge operational stability and can accumulate into systemic risks. However, the mechanisms and effects of such “quasi-emergency” disturbances have not been systematically studied yet. To extend research on URT resilience from severe and low-frequency disruptions to daily disturbances, this study proposes a micro–macro resilience assessment framework grounded in the passenger-level disturbance response chains. The framework integrates a fine-grained passenger itinerary inference approach incorporating daily disturbance effects, with a multi-source feature driven daily disturbance identification model. This integration overcomes the critical challenge of lacking daily disturbance data, enabling multi-dimensional resilience quantification from passenger-level micro-behaviors to system-wide macro-performance. Empirical analysis of the Chengdu Metro shows a generally favorable baseline resilience performance, with 18/31 of study days classified as good or very good. Resilience patterns are closely linked to passenger flow regularities and distributions of daily disturbances, revealing spatio-temporal heterogeneity and functional dependency. Spatially, it exhibits structural and functional weaknesses. Temporally, holidays with surging passenger demand represent the resilience troughs, with the lowest value of 0.8540. In the disturbance process dimension, delayed responses following disturbance onset and inadequate recovery during the terminal phase are identified as the primary deficiencies. Based on the numerical results, relevant management strategies and optimization measures are proposed, offering actionable insights for enhancing the disturbance-handling capacity and resilience of URT systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Climate-induced migration or immobility? Evidence from Nigeria
Authors: Marco Letta, Pierluigi Montalbano, Adriana Paolantonio
Abstract: The complex relationship between climate shocks, adaptation, and migration hinders a rigorous understanding of the heterogeneous mobility outcomes of farm households exposed to climate stress. To unpack this heterogeneity, we couple causal machine learning methods, tailored to a conceptual framework bridging economic migration theory and the poverty traps literature, with longitudinal multi-topic household data from Nigeria. This approach allows us to produce fine-grained, non-parametric evidence that identifies the factors driving divergent mobility outcomes across different household groups affected by the same shocks. The estimated conditional average treatment effects suggest that key variables—pre-shock asset levels, in situ adaptive capacity, and weather exposure during the previous survey period—shape not only the magnitude but also the sign of the impact of agriculture-relevant weather anomalies on the mobility outcomes of farming households. While in situ adaptation serves as an alternative to migration, the role played by wealth constraints and multiple shock exposure is consistent with the existence of climate-induced immobility traps.

Title: Political patronage, rent-extraction, and social costs: Evidence from China's environmental cleanup
Authors: Cong Zhang, Ming Li, Fubing Su, Ran Tao
Abstract: This paper investigates how informal political patronage subverts environmental regulation and local economic performance in China. We demonstrate that patronage provides local officials with political insurance, enabling them to safely shield polluting firms from top-down enforcement. Contrary to the promotion tournament hypothesis, this forbearance does not drive GDP growth. Instead, it is sustained through localized rent extraction. Utilizing firm-level data and shocks induced by provincial party secretary turnover, we find that connected officials extract a political tax, measured via perk expenditures, from both polluting and non-polluting enterprises. This systemic extortion generates broad negative spillovers: while shielding incumbent polluters, patronage crowds out productive investment and deters clean market entrants, ultimately degrading both environmental outcomes and the regional business environment.
Journal: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

Title: Who scores from hosting sports events? Local spending evidence from the EURO 2024
Authors: Florian Dorn, Marie-Theres Gasser, Kevin Kloiber, Simon Krause, Carla Krolage
Abstract: Hosting mega-sports events generates optimistic projections of economic benefits, yet empirical evidence on actual local returns remains mixed. Focusing on the UEFA EURO 2024 in Germany, we provide causal evidence on short-term local consumption effects using anonymized daily card-spending data. Using a difference-in-differences and local-projection framework, we document a 3% increase in consumer spending in host cities during the tournament, driven almost entirely by international visitors. Effects are concentrated in the group stage, on match days, in city centers, and in tourist-facing sectors. Domestic spending exhibits spatial displacement but no aggregate crowding out.

Title: Robotic assembly line balancing with on-site renewable energy supply
Authors: Yuchen Li, Francisco Saldanha-da-Gama, Ibrahim Kucukkoc, Dan Liu
Abstract: In this paper, a multi-criteria robotic assembly line balancing problem is integrated with long-term aggregate energy supply decisions. Three objectives are considered: production efficiency, carbon footprint, and cost. On-site renewable energy generation is assumed as an alternative to energy supply from the main grid. Two technologies are available: photovoltaic and wind power. To capture the uncertainty intrinsic to such energy output, a constraint is considered that imposes an energy supply feasibility margin. A deep Q-learning algorithm enhanced with fixed Q-target mechanisms and experience replay is proposed to find approximate Pareto-optimal solutions to the problem. Using a set of synthetic instances, this procedure is compared with a well-established metaheuristic. Additionally, an empirical case study, based on data from a manufacturing enterprise planning the long-term production of a specific engine type, is conducted to validate the proposed modeling framework and solution procedure. The results provide evidence that the methodological developments proposed can effectively inform the decision-making process, contributing to improved sustainability and operational performance in a production system.

Title: Authenticity in ESG disclosure: A systematic review, current challenges, and future perspectives
Authors: Nanning Guo, Ming Li, Arjun Rachana Harish, Jingzheng Ren, George Q. Huang
Abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) is a framework for measuring corporate sustainability and ethical business practices. By enhancing transparency and authenticity in ESG disclosure, corporations can better identify and mitigate supply-chain risks, thereby building greater operational and reputational resilience. Based on bibliographic databases from 2007 to 2025, this study presents a systematic literature review of efforts to improve the authenticity of ESG disclosures. A review of 65 articles was conducted using an inclusion and exclusion framework. The paper lists current ESG authenticity evaluation methods, including measures of disclosure volume, consistency with the disclosure framework, and the evaluation of disputed information. The advantages and disadvantages of such methods in practical applications are comprehensively discussed. Following a critical examination of current methods for assessing the authenticity of ESG disclosures, this paper proposes applying emerging technologies to enhance the collection, generation, and verification of information on the authenticity of such disclosures. In addition to addressing gaps in the existing literature, this study offers a fresh perspective on future ESG evaluation technologies, aiming to enhance the supply chain resilience and corporate sustainability performance.

Title: The impact of responsible technological transformation on firm performance: A cost-benefit perspective
Authors: Jianhu Cai, Jiaqi Tian, Lishuang Jia, Xiaoqing Hu
Abstract: With the technological revolution and industrial transformation, responsible technological transformation (RTT) has emerged as a critical agenda for rebuilding the corporate image. Based on panel data of Chinese listed firmss from 2010 to 2023, this study constructs an RTT measurement index by applying natural language processing technique. Using the cost-benefit analysis, this study digs out the inverted U-shaped relationship between RTT and firm performance. In the early stages, the increase of RTT leads to a relatively high benefit accompanied by a relatively low cost. However, the further increase of RTT may cause the cost outweighing the benefit. This study further examines the moderating effects of ownership balance and financial slack, finding that both factors significantly attenuate the inverted U-shaped relationship.

Title: How many sign restrictions are needed? A sharp lower bound for identifying multiple shocks in SVARs
Authors: Xuewen Yu
Abstract: This paper derives the exact minimum number of impact sign restrictions required to identify m shocks in a structural vector autoregression under a natural pairwise separation condition. The answer is (Formula presented). The proof follows from deriving a sharp lower bound using a Kraft-type inequality and then constructing an admissible restriction matrix that attains the bound. Our result reveals a significant sparsity gain: while traditional recursive orderings require (Formula presented) restrictions, sign-based separation requires only (Formula presented), providing a transparent benchmark for designing sparse identifying schemes in large SVARs.

Title: Fiscal decentralization and the FDI–growth nexus
Authors: Damien Cubizol
Abstract: This paper contributes to the recent literature on the FDI–growth nexus by investigating whether fiscal decentralization moderates the growth effects of foreign direct investment (FDI). Using a panel of 69 countries over 1996–2020 with fixed-effects and system-GMM estimations, we show that while FDI generally promotes economic growth, its positive effect is significantly attenuated in countries with higher levels of fiscal decentralization, on both the revenue and expenditure sides. We further identify infrastructure quality as a transmission channel through which expenditure decentralization dampens the FDI–growth nexus, suggesting a reduced capacity to finance national public goods in highly decentralized settings. These findings highlight the importance of intergovernmental coordination in preserving the growth effectiveness of foreign investment, and open new avenues for research on the institutional determinants of the FDI–growth nexus.

Title: Examining well-being orientations in sustainable mobility choices: a Japan–Germany comparison
Authors: Chun-Chen Chou, Christine Eisenmann, Masanobu Kii, Kento Yoh, Kenji Doi
Abstract: The adoption of sustainable mobility reflects interactions between service attributes and personal values, yet the role of deeper, self-determined well-being orientations remains underexplored. This study examines choices among privately owned gasoline vehicles, electric vehicles, car-sharing, and ride-sharing in Japan and Germany, two highly developed countries with different mobility cultures. It focuses on how individual values and service attributes dynamically interact to shape service preferences. Using a comparative survey design across cities of different sizes and drawing on Cognitive Appraisal Theory, structural equation modeling results show that well-being orientations mediate the influence of travel attitudes on mobility lifestyle preferences. Specifically, eudaimonic and cooperative well-being shape tendencies toward authentic decision-making and conformity to social expectations and sustainability policies. Latent class choice modeling and subsequent policy scenario analyses further reveal behavioral heterogeneity and cross-national differences. In both countries, three distinct latent classes are identified. Japanese consumers are highly time-sensitive, whereas German consumers are more cost-driven yet more responsive to awareness campaigns. Across both countries, approximately 20% of respondents are cost-insensitive but norm-responsive, highlighting the importance of integrating value-based strategies alongside financial incentives. Overall, the findings offer policy-relevant insights to support inclusive and value-driven mobility strategies.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Should I stay or should I travel? An analysis of increasing petrol prices on travel behaviour
Authors: Andrea Pellegrini, Matthew J. Beck, John M. Rose
Abstract: This paper examines how rising petrol prices affect weekly travel behaviour, with particular attention to modal substitution and trip suppression. The analysis draws on stated responses from 808 Queensland residents, each of whom first reported their travel behaviour for the week prior to the survey and then indicated how that behaviour would change under three hypothetical petrol price scenarios set at AUD 2.50, AUD 3.00, and AUD 3.50 per litre (noting fuel prices at the pump varied between an average of AUD 2.20 and AUD 2.53 during the survey period). Weekly trip frequencies are jointly modelled for eight travel outcomes, including car travel as driver, car travel as passenger, public transport, taxi, rideshare, cycling, walking, and avoided trips. The latter category is included within the hypothetical setting to capture the extent to which increase in petrol prices may lead travellers to cancel or forgo trips altogether, rather than simply reallocate travel across modes. The empirical analysis is performed implementing a multivariate Generalised Poisson framework with dependence across travel alternatives introduced through a Gaussian copula. The results indicate that higher petrol prices substantially reduce car travel both as driver car passenger, while increasing public transport use, particularly at the higher price scenarios. However, the substitution towards public transport is only partial. A sizeable share of the adjustment instead occurs through avoided trips, suggesting that fuel price increases are more likely to suppress travel rather than simply induce a reallocation across modes. The findings further show that behavioural responses vary with socio-economic circumstances and perceived transport disadvantage, implying that the burden of higher fuel prices is unevenly distributed. Overall, the paper shows that rising petrol prices affect not only mode choice, but also the ability of individuals to maintain everyday mobility and activity participation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Group compromise rankings with indirect preference information: Maximizing pairwise- and rank-based support
Authors: Zhuolin Li, Zhen Zhang, Miłosz Kadziński
Abstract: In recent years, deriving compromise rankings that reconcile the diverse opinions of Decision Makers (DMs) has become a central theme in group decision making. Yet, most existing methods assume that DMs can directly specify the parameters required by the underlying model (e.g., criteria weights or marginal value functions), which may impose a considerable cognitive burden. To address this, we develop novel methods for constructing compromise rankings from a preference disaggregation perspective, relying solely on indirect preference information provided by DMs. Two complementary variants are considered: one based on pairwise preference relations and the other on rank assignments. In both cases, individual support degrees are first defined – either for preference/indifference relations among alternatives or for assigning alternatives to specific rank positions. Optimization models are then formulated to aggregate these individual measures into group support degrees. Finally, subsequent models maximize group support across all pairs or all rank assignments, thereby producing the group compromise ranking. The proposed methodology is illustrated with a project proposal ranking problem from the literature, followed by robustness analyses. Computational experiments under varying parameter settings further benchmark the methods against existing approaches, confirming their effectiveness. A comparative discussion further clarifies the methodological and practical advantages of the proposed approaches.

Title: Publicly funded R&D networks, knowledge spillovers and innovation performance: Evidence from Norway
Authors: Fulvio Castellacci, Arvid Raknerud, Massimo Riccaboni, Marina Rybalka
Abstract: Many countries provide public policy support for R&D networks. In publicly funded R&D consortia, firms collaborate with each other and with public scientific institutions to carry out joint innovation projects. The idea behind these policy schemes is that collaborative innovation enables firms to benefit from knowledge spillovers within R&D networks. Surprisingly, however, there is no empirical research showing that spillover effects actually exist in publicly funded R&D consortia. This paper seeks to investigate the extent and sources of knowledge spillovers in R&D networks and to distinguish them from other drivers of additionality generated by collaborative innovation policy programs. Our empirical analysis focuses on Norway and encompasses the entire population of firms supported by R&D policy programs over the period 2002–2022, comprising approximately 15500 collaborative projects. Based on the information on each project, we construct networks of innovators and new R&D spillover pool variables. We use a spatial autoregressive econometric approach and estimate a network regression estimator that endogenizes peer effects related to knowledge spillovers. The econometric results show that the knowledge spillovers arising from publicly funded R&D networks are positive. We also find that the spillover effects resulting from Research Council programs are much stronger than those of tax incentives, and that the spillover effects are much stronger for collaborations between firms operating in different industries than for within-industry collaborations.

Title: Determinants of gender discrimination by teachers: Evidence from an online experiment
Authors: Marion Monnet, Etienne Dagorn, Philippe Colo
Abstract: This paper examines whether teachers' gender biases stem from discrimination, and focuses on two of its potential drivers: gender preferences and beliefs. In an online experiment, 1,840 teachers evaluated fictitious transcripts with randomized gender information. Preferences were measured via dictator games, and beliefs through an Implicit Association Test. While teachers showed no gender preferences, they did hold gender beliefs. Analyzing 19,000 transcript evaluations, we find no evidence of gender-based discrimination. Our findings suggest that simply disclosing a student's gender does not trigger discrimination, implying that such behaviours are more likely to emerge during direct student-teacher interactions.

Title: Financing the low-carbon transition: Do energy transition investments improve ESG performance?
Authors: Kwamie Dunbar, Mohammed Alrashdani
Abstract: Energy transition investment ( eti ) has emerged as a central component of global climate finance, yet its firm-level consequences remain insufficiently understood. Using BloombergNEF energy-transition investment data and Refinitiv ESG measures, we examine whether aggregate transition-finance deployment influences corporate sustainability performance. We find that higher eti exposure is associated with significant improvements in environmental, social, and governance ( esg ) performance, with the strongest gains observed in the environmental pillar. The positive association is stronger among firms with greater climate-related innovative capacity and among low-carbon firms, whereas esg gains are comparatively smaller in high-carbon sectors despite the economic importance of eti for managing transition risk. Robustness analyses based on dynamic System Generalized Method of Moments (SGMM) estimation, external instrumental-variable techniques, and Granger-causality tests indicate that eti precedes and predicts subsequent esg improvements. Overall, the findings identify a macro-to-micro transmission mechanism through which large-scale transition-finance deployment shapes firm behavior and sustainability outcomes, establishing eti as an important driver of multidimensional corporate sustainability performance.

Title: Tournaments with managerial discretion
Authors: Peiran Xiao, Hashim Zaman
Abstract: We study tournaments with managerial discretion in hiring. A manager selects a coworker from a pool of candidates and then competes against him in a Lazear--Rosen--style tournament with a prize equal to a share of total output. A profit-maximizing principal sets the prize share together with a head start (or handicap)---an advantage (or disadvantage) in the output comparison---granted to the manager. The head start affects output through three channels: (i) encouraging the manager, (ii) discouraging the new hire, and (iii) inducing the manager to hire a stronger candidate. The hiring effect dominates the discouragement effect until the strongest candidate is hired; beyond that point, any further head start discourages the new hire more than it encourages the manager. The optimal contract therefore grants a head start just large enough to induce the manager to hire the strongest candidate.

Title: The power of purpose – lessons in agility from the Ventilator Challenge
Authors: Andrew Fearne, Beverly Wagner, Natalie McDougall, David Loseby
Affiliations: University of East Anglia Norwich Business School, , Norwich; University of Strathclyde Department of Marketing, , Glasgow
Abstract: Purpose COVID-19 has shaken views of what is normal and what is possible, raising questions about conventional norms, ways of working and our understanding of agility. This paper aims to respond to calls for empirical research of supply chain capacities in times of crisis and offer a unique perspective on agile procurement and supply chain management from a case study of the Ventilator Challenge. Design/methodology/approach A descriptive case study was undertaken, adopting an inductive approach. Interviews were conducted with the major stakeholders tasked with the design, sourcing and assembly of ventilators. Findings Findings are delivered across four key areas: context; procurement and supply chain management; technology and culture; and environment. Key challenges and enablers are discussed, highlighting the critical roles of trust, empowerment and enabling technologies in the construction of an entirely new ventilator supply chain, from scratch, in five weeks. Originality/value This paper delivers contributions for both academic research and practice. The case study offers rich new insights relating to procurement in times of crisis, contributing to efforts to advance beyond outdated approaches for resilience in literature. Practical contributions arise in highlighting the significance of adapted sourcing and recruitment, technology, collaboration, people and power of purpose in enabling agility and achieving the impossible.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: The role of digital technologies in supply chain resilience for emerging markets’ automotive sector
Authors: Balakrishnan A.S., Usha Ramanathan
Affiliations: Department of Material Planning and Logistics, Ford Motor Private Limited, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India; Nottingham Trent University Nottingham Business School, , Nottingham
Abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to examine the role of digital supply chain (DSC) technologies in automotive supply chain resilience (SCR) practices to improve the supply chain performance (SC-Perf.) objectives of companies operating in the automotive industry. This study also compares the results of the associated SC-Perf objectives before and after the COVID-19 pandemic outbreak lockdown situation. Design/methodology/approach The authors undertook in-depth empirical research using a questionnaire survey to explore the performance of automotive supply chains. The sample for this study consisted of practitioners from supply chain entities such as automotive original equipment manufacturers, Tier-1 component manufacturers and lead logistics providers in Asia-Pacific (AP) emerging markets. Research questions, framework and hypotheses were developed using the literature review. Findings The research outcome from analysis of the data the authors collected from an emerging market context, specifically the automotive sector, emphasizes the role of DSC technologies and encourages the firm’s SCR practices which, in turn, supports the SC-Perf objectives. The DSC technologies competency moderates the SCR and SC-Perf objectives relation, and the moderation effect is higher for post-COVID-19 pandemic outbreak lockdown situation than at prior state. Research limitations/implications The scope of the study is restricted to the automotive firms in the AP region. The data were collected from a representative sample of the population through a questionnaire survey. The small size of the sample incurs a certain level of subjectivity. Practical implications This research provides practical insights for practitioners and academicians on DSC technologies’ influence in SCR practices to improve the firm’s SC-Perf. This research shares the literature insights on use of DSC technologies across the sector to allow the automotive firm to reassess the existing operational practices. Originality/value The paper adds insights on introducing or implementing DSC technologies across AP automotive firms to increase the operations’ performance by improving SCR practices and sustainability.
Journal: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

Title: A bio-inspired reorder optimisation framework for lumber supply chain management using a problem-adapted European beaver optimiser
Authors: Robertas Damaševičius, Rytis Maskeliūnas
Affiliations: Vytautas Magnus University; Asia University; Kaunas University of Technology
Abstract: The paper proposes a problem-adapted bio-inspired optimisation framework, termed the European Beaver Optimiser (EBO), to improve reorder process optimisation in lumber supply chain management. A lumber supply chain decision problem is formulated with ordering, holding, shortage and transportation costs, incorporating lead times and inventory balance constraints. The supply chain is modelled via an agent-based approach, where an inventory-management agent uses EBO to optimise reorder point and order quantity under stochastic demand and operational uncertainty. Across all scenarios, EBO produces lower median total supply chain cost than the non-optimised baseline policy. Cost distributions under EBO exhibit reduced variance (narrower interquartile ranges), indicating more predictable performance, particularly under high demand variability and supply disruptions. The work contributes (i) a problem-adapted bio-inspired optimisation scheme tailored to reorder-point, order-quantity and safety-stock search in lumber supply chains, (ii) an integration framework linking the search process with operational supply chain decisions under uncertainty and sustainability-related cost components and (iii) comparative evidence against a non-optimised baseline and established benchmark optimisers, supported by sensitivity and runtime analyses.

Title: Large neighbourhood search for coil stowage planning with pallet sequencing considerations
Authors: Yeeun Kim, Sangwoon Lim, Byung-In Kim
Affiliations: Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH); Graduate School of Artificial Intelligence, Pohang University of Science and Technology (POSTECH)
Abstract: The coil stowage problem in ship loading is a critical factor affecting logistics efficiency in the steel industry. Despite its operational significance, research on optimising coil stowage sequences remains limited. This study proposes a mathematical model and a large neighbourhood search algorithm to jointly optimise the positioning and sequencing of coils. As coils are typically transported on pallets from warehouses to a loading dock, and the dock can accommodate only a limited number of pallets, optimising the loading sequence can significantly reduce the frequency of costly and time-consuming pallet recalls. The proposed approach improves overall stowage efficiency. The algorithm was validated using real-world industrial data, demonstrating its practicality and effectiveness. Performance evaluations showed that the proposed method outperformed the comparative methods in most tested instances, particularly in sequence optimisation. This study provides valuable insights and a practical solution for enhancing logistics efficiency in coil stowage operations within the steel industry.

Title: An LLM-based framework for event-driven operating room scheduling
Authors: Yifan Bao, Lei Liu, Zhen Tan, Chandra Ade Irawan
Affiliations: University of Nottingham Ningbo China

Title: Designing efficient line feeding systems for low-volume, high-variety manufacturing
Authors: Hannah Verplancke, Emmanouil Thanos, Gohar Porbar, El-Houssaine Aghezzaf, Veronique Limère
Affiliations: Ghent University; Flanders Make@UGent – core lab CVAMO & ISyE
Abstract: Designing an efficient and effective line feeding system is crucial for manufacturing facilities operating in low-volume, high-variety mass customisation environments. Shorter takt times, which drive operational performance, combined with limited space at the border of line, have led to the development of advanced line feeding policies to ensure timely and accurate part delivery. Low-volume, high-variety systems typically require large numbers of different components and complex sets of constraints to be accurately modelled. This paper proposes a comprehensive, integrated mixed integer programming model for the strategic assembly line feeding problem. The goal of this problem is to optimise line feeding system design by jointly determining the placement and sizing of preparation cells, along with selecting and sizing vehicle fleets for various line feeding policies. The proposed model explicitly captures the interdependencies among these key components, offering a more realistic and comprehensive decision-support framework. Its effectiveness is evaluated using a diverse set of real-world inspired instances, showcasing both the feasibility and the benefits of integrated decision-making.

Title: Reverse scheduling on a single machine with adjustable release and processing times: optimal algorithms and applications
Authors: Kuo-Ching Ying, Xin-Yu Chen
Affiliations: National Taipei University of Technology; Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) Limited
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: Capacity trilemma: robust capacity planning for demand, productive scale size and sustainability
Authors: Wei Kang, Chia-Yen Lee, Yu-Hsueh Fang
Affiliations: Department of Information Management, National Taiwan University
Abstract: Capacity planning is a critical issue for business, particularly when addressing demand volatility, production scale, and pollutant emissions in a highly uncertain and environmentally sustainable context. Considering the harmful effects of byproducts while meeting market demands and maintaining optimal productivity is crucial yet challenging for manufacturing plants. This study proposes a mathematical model that incorporates data envelopment analysis constraints to formulate an efficient target that represents the trade-off between productivity, sustainability, and demand fulfilment. This study also applies a robust optimisation approach to address demand uncertainty. The results demonstrate how the decision-making units should allocate resources based on a given set of inputs, outputs, and undesirable outputs. The computational study and empirical study are conducted to validate the proposed framework, and the results show that it can significantly reduce the expected value of perfect information compared to a baseline benchmark. Sensitivity analysis also shows that the proposed framework is suitable for high demand fluctuation scenarios.
Journal: Journal of the Operational Research Society

Title: BERT-based twitter sentiment analysis for stock return prediction and portfolio optimization
Authors: Mobin Golabzaei, Seyed Jafar Sadjadi, Rassoul Noorossana, Babak Amiri
Abstract: This research introduces a hybrid framework combining sentiment analysis from social media and technical indicators within machine learning models to predict stock returns and optimize portfolios. Sentiment scores were obtained from Twitter utilizing a fine-tuned BERT model and integrated with five technical indicators RSI, MACD, MA, EMA, and Williams %R to create a thorough feature set. Four machine learning models LSTM, CNN, SVR, and Random Forest were developed to predict daily stock returns. The anticipated returns were subsequently applied in three portfolio optimization techniques: Mean–Variance (MV), Omega Ratio (OR), and Sparsity-Constrained Optimization (SC), all adhering to practical constraints like cardinality and floor-ceiling restrictions. Findings suggest that including sentiment data greatly enhances predictive accuracy and portfolio outcomes. The MVO model provides the most favorable risk-return trade‑off across most prediction scenarios, generally achieving higher Sharpe ratios than the other approaches. Notably, the combination of CNN predictions with MVO yields the strongest portfolio performance among the examined cases. This study highlights the importance of merging behavioral insights with machine learning for effective and sensible investment decision-making. This study contributes to the literature by integrating BERT-based sentiment analysis with traditional technical indicators for stock returns prediction and evaluating the resulting forecasts within a portfolio optimization framework.

Title: Individual adaptation to extreme heat and the interpretation of risk perceptions: Evidence from counterfactual beliefs
Authors: Masahide Watanabe
Abstract: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, heat-health policies increasingly use alerts, forecasts, and behavioral guidance to encourage individual self-protection. Evaluations of such policies often track survey-based intermediate outcomes, including warning awareness, perceived heat risk or vulnerability, and protective behavior, in addition to health outcomes. Yet routine self-protection can make reported risk perceptions difficult to interpret: perceived risk may motivate prevention, while reported risk may already reflect the protection that respondents have adopted. In a web-based survey of residents of Tokyo's 23 wards, we elicit subjective probabilities of heatstroke under realized and counterfactual prevention scenarios. Respondents are randomly assigned to evaluate either a no-prevention scenario or a full-prevention scenario. Reported risk changes systematically with the assumed level of prevention, suggesting that reported risk perceptions may reflect both perceived susceptibility and behavior-conditioned reappraisal and may be misleading as stand-alone indicators in adaptation monitoring and evaluation. We also find that perceived risk under the no-prevention scenario is positively associated with realized preventive effort, suggesting that this counterfactual belief provides a more interpretable basis than realized-prevention risk for examining how perceived susceptibility relates to preventive effort.

Title: Voyage-induced contrastive adaptation for Cross-voyage vessel emission estimation
Authors: Xun Yang, Ran Yan
Abstract: Data-driven vessel emission models can appear reliable under segment-level validation while showing larger errors under voyage-level distribution shift. This paper investigates transductive target-unlabelled adaptation, with labelled source voyages and target-voyage trajectory records available during model development. Target-voyage emission labels are reserved exclusively for evaluation. It proposes voyage-induced contrastive adaptation (VCA), a representation-learning framework for this setting. VCA combines a voyage-induced hierarchical state, debiased contrastive learning, supervised emission regression, and conditional alignment. Representation-based uncertainty analysis (RepUA) calibrates representation discrepancy against target-voyage error to estimate deployment risk. In the reported single-vessel, voyage-level evaluations, VCA achieves lower estimation errors than the compared methods, and RepUA relates representation discrepancy to target-voyage error.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Port-side solar-to-hydrogen bunkering system design for green shipping corridors: A data-driven robust optimization approach
Authors: Jing Wang, Yibai Zhang, Shuai Jia, Ran Yan, Dong Yang
Abstract: Green shipping corridors (GSCs) are emerging as a key strategy to accelerate maritime decarbonization by linking ports committed to using zero- and low-carbon fuels, such as renewable fuels. A key challenge for the ports along the GSCs is to develop reliable energy infrastructure capable of meeting the growing fuel demand of ocean-going visiting vessels. This study develops an integrated solar-to-hydrogen bunkering system to support port-side renewable hydrogen supply. Using Automatic Identification System (AIS)-derived vessel activity data and satellite-derived meteorological records, the proposed data-driven framework characterizes realistic hydrogen demand and renewable electricity generation under uncertain operating conditions. A two-stage robust optimization (TSRO) framework is developed to jointly determine the robust optimal plan on the capacities of solar photovoltaic (PV) panels, battery energy storage, and hydrogen production. The model is solved using a tailored column-and-constraint generation algorithm that considers uncertainties in both solar irradiance and vessel hydrogen demand. For solving the mixed-integer max-min subproblem, we first establish a branch-and-KKT method as a general exact method, and then develop an efficient fix-and-dualize scheme that uses an auxiliary optimization problem with dominance cuts to generate representative binary solutions and then evaluates each fixed-binary subproblem through dual reformulation. The results show that hydrogen storage serves as the primary long-duration flexibility resource, substantially reducing the need for battery energy storage. For the Rotterdam–Singapore GSC, the optimal system consists of approximately 4000 t of hydrogen storage capacity and 18,800 MWp of solar PV capacity, achieving a reliable port-side hydrogen supply with the minimum investment cost. The economic analysis further indicates that the system becomes financially attractive when hydrogen profit margins exceed 1 USD/kg. The proposed data-driven framework provides a practical decision-support tool for planning hydrogen-ready port infrastructure and can be applied broadly to ports developing zero-carbon GSCs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Cryptocurrency denomination and NFT pricing
Authors: Jaehyeong Park, Euro Bae, Daegon Cho, Donghoon Kim
Abstract: Using transaction data from OpenSea, we examine how cryptocurrency price fluctuations affect NFT returns and whether these dynamics depend on denomination of cryptocurrency, across sequential stages: price setting (purchase-to-list) and price taking (list-to-sale). Panel regressions on 46,671 repeated NFT sales reveal that sellers anchor listing prices to acquisition prices, generating asymmetric mark-ups during ETH appreciation and mark-downs during ETH depreciation. Buyers exhibit similar anchor sale prices to listing prices. Stablecoin-denominated acquisition prices partially mitigate these distortions. These findings extend the denomination and anchoring literature to highly volatile, multi-currency marketplaces.

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part E: Logistics and Transportation Review

Title: Fare enough: A quantitative spatial transport model for transit pricing
Authors: Isaac Mann, David M. Levinson
Abstract: Standard transport appraisal treats fare regulation in isolation, ignoring how price signals reshape urban geography. We bridge regulatory practice and quantitative spatial economics by constructing a Quantitative Spatial Transport Model (QSTM) for Greater Sydney, endogenising household and firm locations in response to transport shocks. Our framework extends the canonical quantitative spatial model by endogenising commuter mode choice and internalising network externalities through road congestion and the Mohring effect. Evaluating three public transport pricing interventions, including zero-fare, flat-fare, and fare-cap policies, we find that free transit is welfare-suboptimal, driven largely by operator revenue losses. In our setting, distance-based fares provide a spatial price signal that helps internalise resource costs and discourage sprawl, a signal that uniform flat fares mute. The model demonstrates that allocative efficiency requires a higher user contribution, revealing that weekly fare caps function as implicit subsidies for long-distance commuters. Higher fares trigger a spatial reorganisation where residents centralise to minimise commuting costs and firms decentralise to access labour. Ultimately, efficient distance-based pricing promotes a compact residential form, encourages polycentric employment, and reduces operator resource costs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Regional collaborative emission reduction under carbon transfer: A differential game analysis of China's three major urban agglomerations
Authors: Ze Yang, Haoning Li, Yuchen Zhang, Yongling Li
Abstract: Urban agglomerations are the core engines of economic growth and energy consumption, yet they face complex challenges in coordinating regional emission reductions—particularly due to industrial relocation and the resulting inter-regional transfer of carbon emissions. Traditional jurisdiction-based governance often fails to address these cross-border carbon spillover effects due to spatial mismatches between production and consumption. This study constructs a tripartite differential game model that endogenizes carbon emission transfers and benefit distribution parameters. This study systematically characterizes the dynamic impacts of carbon transfer behaviors on regional emission trajectories, welfare distribution, and institutional performance. Using numerical simulations calibrated for the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, Yangtze River Delta, and Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area agglomerations, we identify optimal benefit distribution ratios for each region. The results demonstrate that cooperative mechanisms significantly outperform non-cooperative scenarios in optimizing resource allocation and enhancing overall regional welfare. Furthermore, when facing the problem of carbon transfer, the introduction of the compensation mechanism of “moderate benefit-sharing” can significantly reduce the overall carbon emissions and enhance the overall economic benefits. This study proposes a “compensation-driven reduction and concession-driven cooperation” governance pattern, offering theoretical support for differentiated, multi-level coordinated emission reduction policies.

Title: Understanding e-cargo bike substitution of car, cycling, and walking through domestic trials in three UK cities
Authors: Labib Azzouz, Noel Cass, Zhaoqi Zhou
Abstract: This study examines ECB mode substitution using a mixed-methods approach combining travel diaries from 42 households participating in real-world ECB trials across Leeds, Oxford, and Brighton with 111 interviews. ECB trips mostly replaced car travel (60%), followed by conventional cycling (23%) and walking (17%). Regression analysis showed that car substitution was more likely among men, older adults, retirees, multi-car households and for passenger-carrying, shopping, child-escorting, and leisure trips. Qualitative findings further described a gradual process of building confidence, adapting routines, and integrating the ECB into everyday mobility, enabling progressively greater car substitution. For some, the ECB was viewed as a realistic alternative to a second car. The findings show that ECBs offer a versatile family mobility solution with substantial sustainability potential by reducing vehicle mileage and emissions, while supporting transitions towards car ownership renunciation. The study details targeted policy interventions that can maximise ECBs uptake and their contribution to sustainability.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Managing autonomous vehicle accessibility to mitigate environmental rebound effects
Authors: Sunghee Lee, Jooyoung Kim
Abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) services can improve urban mobility, but excessive door-to-door convenience may shift users from public transport and increase zero-occupant vehicle (ZOV) circulation. This study treats AV access time as a policy-controllable variable and evaluates its environmental and operational effects under fixed peak-hour demand. An integrated framework combines synthetic demand preprocessing, multi-modal user equilibrium assignment, explicit ZOV loading, and reinforcement-learning policy search. Results show that reducing access time below about five minutes sharply increases empty vehicle movements, total system travel time, and CO 2 emissions. Within a restricted generic road-charging framework, a six-minute access time with a moderate per-trip charge forms a constrained Pareto-knee. Extending the policy space to ZOV-targeted instruments, including empty-VKT charges, reduces reliance on generic road charges and improves network performance, reducing CO 2 emissions by up to 15.0% relative to the fixed reference condition (Base=100) while preserving public transport shares.
Journal: Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment

Title: Routing optimization for mixed fleet of single and multi-compartment vehicles considering oriented semi-hard arrival time consistency
Authors: Mahnaz Shoeib, Jafar Bagherinejad, Mahdi Bashiri
Abstract: Each perishable food must be stored at a specific temperature to ensure freshness and safety. Single compartment vehicles carry these incompatible products separately, while multi-compartment vehicles enable the joint delivery of these items. To meet customers’ demands over a multi-period planning horizon, a cost-effective combination of these vehicles should be used in a mixed fleet. Customers prefer consistent arrival times for deliveries during each period, which can improve service quality but may increase distribution costs. Therefore, the level of consistency should be carefully determined. This paper examines the oriented semi-hard consistency of arrival time in a multiperiod vehicle routing problem with split deliveries that arises in the distribution of incompatible products. The focus of this paper is on evaluating the effect of fleet type (single-compartment, multi-compartment, and mixed) on arrival time consistency. A mathematical model is presented to describe the problem of determining the consistency level along with the fleet type. Considering the NP-hardness of the problem, a matheuristic algorithm that includes fix-and-optimize and local search modules has been developed and compared against an adaptive large neighborhood search algorithm (ALNS). The developed mathematical model and solution algorithms have been tested and evaluated using numerical instances adopted from the literature. The experimental results indicate that the mixed fleet performs better than other fleets in terms of cost reduction and service consistency. Furthermore, the matheuristic algorithm outperforms the ALNS in terms of computational time and solution quality. The overall findings provide managerial insights for decision-makers involved in distributing various incompatible products.

Title: Editorial Board
Pollution, reproductive health capital, and fertility
Authors: Akira Yakita
Abstract: Recent research indicates that human infertility rate is increasing. This study explores the hypothesis that this change has occurred because of increasing pollution, which damages the reproductive health of individuals. Individuals can choose the number of their children without worrying about pollution effects when pollution is small relative to reproductive health capital. Nevertheless, when pollution becomes large in a relative sense, it constrains the number of children that individuals can bear and rear. Reduced childrearing time enables young workers to work longer and to earn more, accelerating physical capital accumulation and consequently boosting economic growth. The accelerated physical capital accumulation in turn increases pollution, thereby lowering the fertility rate further. On a balanced growth path, the fertility rate remains constant over periods, but the fertility rate might be lower than the population replacement rate. Pollution abatement measures raise the fertility rate by reducing pollution damage to reproductive health. Although the long-term growth effect of pollution tax changes is ambiguous, the growth rate after the tax changes is lower than the balanced growth rate without a binding fertility constraint.

Title: Guns for butter: Trade effects of arms transfers
Authors: Penglong Zhang, Tianhan Liu, Yushan Hu
Affiliations: School of Public Policy and Management Tsinghua University Beijing China; School of Economics Renmin University of China Beijing China; Institute of China's Economic Reform & Development Renmin University of China Beijing China
Abstract: Abstract Using a global dyadic panel from 1950 to 2021, we find a positive association between arms transfers from an exporter to an importer and general goods exports to that partner. The effects are short‐run: export responses peak around the transfer and fade within a few years. The arms‐trade linkage is smaller among highly institutionalized, high‐income partnerships and larger where security and commerce are more tightly bundled, especially in dyads linked by overseas military presence. Consistent with a political‐alignment channel, arms transfers are followed by lower United Nations voting disagreement. The associated trade increase does not reflect a symmetric improvement in relations.

Title: Development economics and the colonial encounter: Informality, caste, and postcolonial capitalist development in India
Authors: Snehashish Bhattacharya, Surbhi Kesar
Abstract: This article posits the contradictory relation between capitalist and non-capitalist segments of an economy as a key dimension of the colonial encounter and as a critical and constitutive element in the contemporary process of postcolonial capitalist development. It points to the obfuscation of this contradiction in the prevalent theoretical approaches in development economics, particularly focusing on the discourse on informal economy and the role of identity. It then foregrounds an emerging theoretical framework on postcolonial economic dynamics — and its key methodological tenets — that frames the development process as being marked by this on-going and ever-occurring contradiction. The article, however, highlights a key gap in this framework to grapple with the role of identities in these development dynamics, and points to some critical methodological approaches to identity that may be productively integrated to further develop it. Finally, the article provides empirical illustrations from the Indian context that underscores the constitutive role of caste in shaping both the reproduction of non-capitalist informal enterprises that sustain the working populations excluded from the capitalist segments, as well as the selective inclusion of parts of this population into capitalist segments as informal wage labor — processes that can be generatively interpreted through the above theoretical framework. Through this intervention, the article aims to clear grounds towards formulating a pathway to build a decolonized approach to contemporary processes of economic development.

Title: Breaking bonds, building mistrust: how coups reshape social capital in Africa
Authors: Linfeng Wang, Michael Appiah-Kubi, Joseph Amoah, Philip Akrofi Atitianti, Jeneshia Jarrett
Abstract: Military coups have become an increasingly common yet understudied form of institutional shock across Africa, with consequences for social capital that remain poorly understood relative to their economic and political costs. This paper provides the first comprehensive causal analysis of how successful coups affect both horizontal (interpersonal) and vertical (institutional) trust. Using Afrobarometer data (2005–2015) from 24 African countries, we show that successful coups reduce interpersonal trust by 3.3 percentage points and institutional trust by 6.7 percentage points, after controlling for regional coup dynamics. These effects are specific to successful seizures of power: failed coup attempts have no significant effect on interpersonal trust and produce only a short-lived boost in institutional trust that quickly reverses. Temporal dynamics reveal a critical asymmetry: interpersonal trust recovers gradually over 15–20 years, whereas institutional trust follows a boom-bust cycle before entering a monotonic decline, driven primarily by deteriorating government performance evaluations rather than by economic disruption. Young adults and members of ethnic majority groups bear disproportionately severe institutional trust deficits, and the interethnic trust response is itself heterogeneous, with majority group members showing a temporary upward adjustment while minority group members show a much smaller gain. These findings challenge narratives that portray coups as corrective mechanisms, calling instead for sustained, targeted reconstruction that addresses both dimensions of social capital simultaneously.

Title: Editorial Board
Do individualists and collectivists cooperate differently?
Authors: Aidin Hajikhameneh, Erik O. Kimbrough, Brock Stoddard
Abstract: Do cultural mindsets shape cooperation? Individualists, who view people as independent, and collectivists, who see them as interconnected, make different decisions that impact governance and economic outcomes. This study tests individualism and collectivism (I/C) in indefinitely repeated prisoner’s dilemmas (IRPD) among in- and out-group members. We hypothesized that collectivists would cooperate more with in-group members, while individualists would treat all groups similarly. To explore causality, participants completed a group-identity task before the I/C measure in Strong-Identity treatment, but not in Weak-Identity treatment. Results show largely null I/C effects; only higher defection payoffs consistently reduced cooperation. Some evidence supports the Strong-Identity treatment leading to lower defection in groups exhibiting greater cohesion in the group-identity task.
